## Chapter 24

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Azula captures the Avatar. Zhao doesn’t take it very well.

#### Chapter Notes

Trigger warnings contain spoilers - see end of chapter notes for them

### Text

Zuko had always figured if his sister caught the Avatar, she would announce it in the most dramatic way possible, parading through the city to the palace, the airbender displayed prominently for all to see. Of course, this fantasy failed to take into account that Azula was cautious; she had a flair for the theatrical, but not at the expense of quality. She was always two steps ahead of everyone because she meticulously planned those steps.

So when the day finally arrived two months after her initial departure, the royal palace did not discover through a grand entrance. Instead, Azula sent word ahead of her arrival by messenger hawk. She wanted reinforcements to receive her at the docks to prevent the possibility of escape between her ship’s brig and the dungeons of Caldera. The parade through the city would still come, of course. But only after they’d ensured the float had a hundred chains and a hundred men to hold them.

In a stroke of luck that could only bless Azula, the messenger who sprinted into the throne room to relay the news of the Avatar’s capture did so mere minutes after Zhao had convinced everyone of the need to expand the northern campaign’s manpower twofold. This development prompted Qin (shaved bald except for his topknot, and now the de facto punching bag of all other members of the council for his Agni Kai disgrace) to wonder aloud if such a massive invading force was necessary for a campaign that had lost all its urgency. By the time the uproar died down and the war council exited the chamber, the northern campaign was cut to a quarter of its previous size.

Needless to say, Zhao was not thrilled.

---

That morning, three separate serving girls, two guards, and a maid had each come running up to Zuko to breathlessly tell him the news. By the time he finally stood in the Great Hall, he felt as though he’d relived the moment of discovery a hundred times. He had dreaded seeing Zhao’s reaction to Azula’s triumph, but given how public this venue was, Zhao kept his rage buttoned up; Zuko could only detect the faintest note of displeasure in the curl of his husband’s lip, a stiffness that made his smiles unconvincing and even a bit hostile. Zuko took up his dutiful place by Zhao’s side, trying to soothe him with a gentle touch on his arm. But his heart wasn’t in it, or else it wasn’t enough; Zhao flashed him one sharp, testy smile before shaking him off.

Once the guards pushed open the massive double doors of the Great Hall, Azula practically *flounced* into the foyer. The sheer glee radiating off her person doused Zuko and his husband in an arctic chill. They bowed in greeting even as she didn’t.

“Congratulations on your triumphant mission, Princess Azula,” said Zhao, voice curling like the leaf of a rotting fruit.

“How sweet of you to congratulate me when I’m sure you’d rather be ringing my neck,” she replied. “I’ll be stepping up security in the Great Hall tonight, so don’t even try it. Kidding!” She said, before he could protest. “Well - partly kidding. I *will* be stepping up my security. Where’s Father?”

Iroh shuffled into the room amidst a phalanx of guards, greeting everyone with a warm smile. Zuko realized this was the first time he had seen his uncle since they had parted on such bad terms. His gaze leapt from Iroh to the floor, unsure how to proceed, when he found himself wrapped in a warm embrace. He returned it, smiling softly.

“Welcome home, Uncle,” said Zuko.

“I missed you, my boy,” said Iroh. “I have been on so many adventures - you wouldn’t believe the food in the Earth Kingdom! So much better than when I last went. There was this little restaurant in…”

He suddenly hushed up, pulling out of the embrace. Ozai had finally deigned to join them. Although he was trying to maintain his usual stony exterior, there was a glint in his eye as his gaze settled on his daughter. They all bowed in deference to their Fire Lord, Azula adding a sweeping flourish to hers as she declared:

“My lord, I present to you the Avatar himself!”

A whole new crowd of guards filed into the room, but even amongst the dozens of bodies, it was easy to make out the person who didn’t belong, the orange monk’s clothes standing out against the black and red armor. Although still lean, the Avatar’s shoulders were much broader than expected; Zuko had been picturing a boy for so long, he was surprised to see a young man who stood taller than most of the guards who now held him in place. Even when restrained this way, there was an airiness to his posture; he rocked on his heels like a child trying to see over crowds at a festival.

Not that he *could* see very much at all. There was a hood drawn over the Avatar’s head, so Zuko didn’t get a chance to compare the infamous wanted poster smile to the real thing.

Ozai scowled at the sight of it. “Why have you covered his face?”

“So he can’t memorize the means of escape,” Azula answered. “And while we haven’t seen him do it yet, plenty of strong benders can make use of their mouths. I didn’t want him blowing up a dust storm and escaping.”

It was spectacular foresight, but her father only harrumphed. “How can you even tell it’s him?”

There was a twitch at the corner of her mouth. “Seeing as I *caught* him-”

“When he is properly immobilized, you will show me his face,” Ozai declared. Azula acquiesced with a tight smile. Next to her, Zhao’s previously strained smile took on some levity.

“Incredible work, Azula,” Zhao praised. “Where are the others in the Avatar’s party? Already sent ahead to the dungeons?”

Azula scoffed. “My goal was to procure the Avatar. The rest were incapacitated.”

“Ah,” said Zhao. “Incapacitated how?”

“You’ll have to ask Uncle,” Azula said breezily, checking her nails. “I was busy facing down the Avatar one-on-one. And *winning* .”

The air between her and her brother-in-law was electric. Zuko glanced up to catch Iroh’s eye, and saw his uncle looked as nervous as he felt.

“Even though you weren't able to capture the whole set, we’ll have to make a point of celebrating this feat,” said Zhao. “Maybe a banquet is in order? Something to show our people the strength and prosperity of the Fire Nation.”

“That sounds like a good time, but highly unnecessary,” said Azula. “The security risk-”

“You would rob the Fire Lord of his chance to celebrate one of the greatest victories of his reign?” Zhao’s expression was faux-mortified.

Ozai gave a stern nod. “I like the idea. See to it that it happens smoothly.”

Azula looked irritated with the decree, but did not protest further. Iroh returned to her side to lay a soothing hand on her shoulder. “I’m sure if you keep him as secure as you have been, it shouldn’t be an issue,” he tried.

“Transfer the Avatar to the dungeons,” the Fire Lord declared. “I will be back later to see him.

It was jarring how they discussed one of the most powerful human beings alive like he was an object to be freely moved wherever they desired. Zuko raked his eyes over the hooded face, noticing for the first time the thick iron collar latched around his throat. The hood, too, looked difficult to breathe in. This was the sort of humiliation reserved for honorless criminals. As they took him away, Zuko wondered if it was treasonous of him to expect better treatment of the Avatar, or if the rest of the royal family had simply lost all sense of shame.

---

All who stayed behind to work in the Lesser Hall knew the moment Zhao returned. The slam of the front door echoed like cannon fire, followed by imperious footsteps down the hall. Zuko trailed behind at a distance, careful to remain out of his husband’s reach. When they finally got to their bedroom, Zhao threw the screen door open with such force, it would be a miracle if it was ever able to shut properly again.

“So much for an heir,” he snarled. “There’s no way your father’s replacing Azula *now*.”

Zuko shut the door behind them as best as he could. Azula’s triumph had certainly thrown his plans into chaos. It felt like he’d only just gotten all his tiles in a row, before she had come and swept them all off the table.

Apprehensive, Zuko asked, “How does this affect the invasion of the north…?”

“How do you *think*, Zuko?” Zhao rounded on him, causing the slighter man to flinch away, his back hitting the door. “All the urgency is gone! Everyone on the war council is already carving it up for resources! There’s nothing left but a bloody stump, and if I’m going to salvage it, I am going to need nothing short of a miracle. I am going to need every waterbender on the fucking *earth* incapacitated.”

Zuko bit his lip to hold in the *no* that wanted to tear its way out of his throat. Zhao watched him with a steely eye, waiting for him to protest. When it didn’t come, he scoffed as if disappointed by the lack of a fight, and stomped over to the window to glare out of it.

Zuko’s knees felt like they were about to give out. Zhao was going to leave him. Zhao was going to go north, and he was going to destroy a people that had managed to remain isolated for the entire war as revenge. While the Avatar was rotting in the dungeons under Caldera, the moon was going to be forever darkened in the sky. Agni knew that Ozai’s reign would become the dividing line for a new era - it was the stuff of legends and of nightmares. Zuko felt like there was a noose around his neck, and struggled to catch his breath.

In need of some comfort, he crept to his desk and opened the top drawer, reaching blindly for the prayer beads. He needed to roll the ancient wood in his fingers, to count them. But when he reached inside, his hands were shaking, and he knocked loose a small knapsack that had been hidden in the drawer.

Fear shot through Zuko like lightning when he saw the familiar heart-shaped plant pods scattering from the mouth of the bag. Frantic, he dropped to his knees on the floor and started to try to clean up the suppressants before Zhao realized what he was doing. Above him on the desk, the prayer beads, placed haphazardly on the ledge, rolled and hit the ground with a wooden clatter.

It was the sheer noise that drew Zhao’s attention. He turned to see what on earth had his spouse in such a scrambling panic. He may have even crouched down beside him with the intention of helping when he held that small plant in his fingers. But the shape was unmistakable; everyone across the four nations knew what silphium looked like, because it was the primary source of birth control they trusted. Zuko watched as the little green pod was crushed under the weight of thumb and forefinger until the leaves split, showing the delicate pink skin of a seed hidden inside.

“I’m not using them anymore,” Zuko whispered. He could barely hear his own words, for the blood rushing in his ears. “I haven’t used them in a *while* - I’m sorry I didn’t tell you, I just - I wasn’t ready - I’m *sorry-* ”

Zhao punched him hard enough to knock him to the ground. All of Zuko’s combat training left him in an instant; he was ten years old again, or maybe seven, or five, cowering under his father’s boot and waiting for the worst to be over. His nails scrambled for purchase on the floor, his breath beating a loud and steady rhythm against the unyielding wood. His left eye squeezed shut, but he could still see stars exploding in the dark behind his swelling eyelid.

One step. Another step. Too close to his head. He curled his arms around his face in anticipation of an oncoming kick, or the weight of a boot on his splayed hair.

“I’m sorry,” Zuko said again, his apology echoing back into his face as it was borne against the floorboards. “I’m sorry I betrayed your trust. Please-” Here, he choked on the words, tears burning his injured eye. “Please forgive me.”

“You can apologize all you want, Zuko, but I don’t know if I can believe a single word coming out of your mouth!” Zhao’s shout was inches from his ear; the unexpected proximity only made Zuko cower further into the floor. “Do you *want* an heir? Do you *want* a family? Or do you just want to manipulate me?” Even without seeing it, he could imagine the way Zhao’s eyes swiveled as they searched him for an answer, for some justification for this act. When Zuko didn’t respond, he bellowed, “ANSWER ME WHEN I’M TALKING TO YOU!”

Zuko couldn’t help the sob of fear that escaped his mouth ahead of his explanation. “I w-want a family with you, I do, but I thought you would leave the moment I got pregnant a-and I - I want you to stay, Zhao. I care about you-”

“If you cared about me, you wouldn’t try to sabotage me at every turn!”

Zhao swore and Zuko tensed, body curling in on itself. When no violence came, Zuko knew better than to unfurl himself and look; he stayed in the dark shelter of his arms, what little cracks of light that filtered through blurred by the tears in his eyes.

“Would you stop *whimpering*, Zuko?” Zhao snapped. “You’re making me feel like a monster. If you don’t want me to treat you this way, you shouldn’t have fucking LIED to me in the first place!”

“I’m n-not trying to make you feel bad,” Zuko insisted, embarrassed by how audibly his voice trembled. He gave a cry of pain as his husband grabbed a fistful of his hair and yanked his head back.

Zhao inspected his face, scowl deepening the longer he looked. “Great. That’s bound to leave a mark. I can only *imagine* the fucking scene your uncle is going to make over this. Am I supposed to tell the entire court what you’ve done to justify myself? Am I supposed to *humiliate* myself by admitting how you’ve lied to me?”

“N-no-”

“Then you’d better think of something to shut your uncle up, because I am not having this court turn on me because of what *you* did!”

“I-I’ll make sure no one sees it, I’ll cover it up,” Zuko babbled, afraid that the grip on his hair could tighten any time, now.

“I can already tell that’s not going to work.” Zhao reached out to press against the injured eye, not viciously, but not gently, either; Zuko shuddered as pain exploded under his thumb. “You’re going to have to think of something else, Zuko.”

“I will,” Zuko promised. He had never meant any two words as deeply as he meant those. After a tense pause, Zhao released his hair.

---

It hurt for Zuko to open his left eye the next morning. Staring up at the ceiling, waiting for his vision to adjust, he found himself wondering if it had swollen any larger. He felt like he could see pretty much everything he could out of the right. It just - throbbed, when he looked around too quickly, and he had a small headache.

There was a heavy weight on his chest. His eyes swiveled, straining to get a look at his partner without disturbing his sleep, but it simply wasn’t enough. He had to turn his neck to get a good look. He did so slowly, with the dread of a man anticipating the hollow eyes of some name-stealing spirit.

Zhao’s face was relaxed with sleep. At some point during the night he had thrown one arm across Zuko’s chest, the weight of which now held him in place. Zuko studied the slackened eyebrows. The slope of his nose. The bow of his lips. All of it intimately familiar, and yet unrecognizable.

Slowly, carefully, Zuko shimmied his way out of the covers, stopping every time Zhao stirred. All he wanted was to go to the bathroom and come back before Zhao woke up. It wasn’t much to ask, but it felt like an impossible tightrope walk even to get out of bed. Once, when Zuko had a leg out of the covers and was ready to swing his whole body free, Zhao’s brows knitted, making Zuko go as still as a corpse, terrified he’d be caught.

Then Zhao muttered something incoherent and rolled to the other side of the bed in his sleep. Zuko could finally slip away.

Only when he got to the bathroom and stood in front of the mirror did he finally understand why every blink hurt; his upper and lower lid were a reddish-purple, the crease under his eye chased by a streak of dark blue. There was the smallest spot of red in the white of his left eye, the blood vessel burst from the force of the hit. He reached up to trace the edges of the injury, the flushed tips of his fingers contrasting to the exotic litany of colors on his face. One typically only ever saw those shades in the palace gardens.

Zuko was so lost in the details of his face that when he opened the door to the bathroom, he was startled by the sight of his uncle. Iroh had one hand raised to knock, and upon seeing Zuko, his lips curved upwards as if to laugh at the coincidence or say hello.

But the longer his eyes roamed over Zuko’s face, the longer his mouth hung open without saying a single word. Zuko knew exactly how bad it looked. And with the intent of returning straight to bed, he had done little to make it look better.

Then Iroh’s expression went hard, and he turned on his heel to storm silently away. Zuko was so stunned by the development that it took him a moment to run and catch up.

“Uncle, where are you-?”

“I’m going to talk to Zhao,” Iroh said with finality. He was heading towards Zuko’s bedroom. He had cut to the heart of the matter in a moment. Instead of feeling vindicated, Zuko’s gut seized with a vivid fear -

(*Zuko ran behind Lu Ten’s legs, babbling faster than his mind could follow, and Lu Ten, bless him,* *went straight to Ozai to give him a piece of his mind. Ozai had received his nephew’s anger with a* *steely calm, seizing upon the doubt created by Zuko’s infant vocabulary, his voice like a knife as it* *cut into the truth and carved away. He waited out his chastisement like a hunter following prey* *through the wilderness for days, until he had Ursa alone again. Then he made sure she would* ***never*** *let that god damned brat out of her sight again - that she would never again allow a* ***child*** *to* *tattle on her* ***husband,*** *as if he has to answer to anyone but himself, you stupid useless bitch stop* ***whimpering-***)

“He doesn’t have anything to do with it!” Zuko cried out, skidding into the hall in front of his uncle, hands outstretched to block his path. They were only a few feet from his door.

Iroh’s gaze remained determined. “Forgive me, nephew, but I don’t believe you.”

“He *doesn’t*,” Zuko insisted. “I-I’m horrified you would ever jump to that conclusion! It was an accident. He would *never-* ”

“How did it happen?”

Zuko swallowed. He’d had plenty of time to think of this. He’d lost nearly the entire night’s sleep over this. (*Zhao blocking the door, refusing to let him leave. “I’ll have someone bring a plate.* *You’re not getting out of this room until you have a good enough cover story for* ***that****.”* ) His mind was blank.

“I. I dropped a book on my face, when I was lying on my back, reading.” Zuko cursed himself for how raw his voice sounded; he wouldn’t have believed him, either.

Iroh gave a deep sigh. “Zuko. Get out of my way.”

“Uncle, *no*.” They were far too riled up to resolve this calmly. His uncle made as if to go around him, and Zuko held out his hands, grabbed his shoulders, voice dropping to a frantic whisper to avoid waking his husband. “You can’t - you can’t confront Zhao, please, he - he doesn’t know how I got this black eye, either, and if you kick up a fuss he’ll only get upset!”

Iroh had reached out to gingerly peel Zuko’s hands off him, but he stopped short now, expression puzzled. “What do you mean he doesn’t-?”

“Shh,” Zuko hushed, glancing over his shoulder. The door to his room remained shut. After a pause, he started to usher Iroh back down the hall. After some gentle pushing, the old man went where lead. It gave Zuko time to think of a second lie. A better lie.

“You can’t tell a soul what really happened,” said Zuko, when they had gotten a distance away. “Zhao will be furious if he finds out.”

Iroh nodded to show he understood, clearing the way for Zuko to tell his story. The young prince paused again under the guise of looking for listeners. His door was down the hall, well within earshot, but it was still shut.

“...You know how we continued my firebending training against my father’s wishes,” Zuko whispered. Iroh nodded. “Last night, I couldn’t resist the urge to practice my kata. I was too restless to get any sleep-”

“Because of the Avatar,” Iroh cut in. His voice was much graver than Zuko would expect it to be, given it was a triumph he had played a part in.

Zuko faltered only for a moment before grasping onto the connection. “Perhaps. I won’t pretend his appearance didn’t play a part. In any case, on my way to find a room where I could practice discreetly, I ran into one of the night guards. I ended up asking him to spar with me.”

“Why didn’t you ask me?” Iroh asked.

Zuko blinked. “What?”

“Why didn’t you ask me to spar?”

Zuko shook his head. “It was a spur of the moment decision, and the guard was right there. Besides, Uncle, that was the first chance you’d gotten to sleep in your own bed in ages; I’m sure even if I’d thought of you, I wouldn’t have wanted to wake you.

“To his credit, the guard was reluctant. I really should’ve let him go, but I was desperate for a distraction, and he clearly saw that, so he indulged me.” Zuko’s heart ached at the memory of how the guard’s eyes had softened. It made him feel even worse for the lie he was about to tell.

“We got up a good rhythm, and I was trying to dodge a punch when my foot slipped and I fell. The guard was already aiming for me, and it happened too fast - he punched me right in the face, full force! Oh, he was *so* sorry. You should have seen the way he was babbling apologies.”

Despite himself, Iroh let out an alarmed laugh, hand coming up to cover his mouth. “Zuko - for a guard to injure a member of the royal family…”

“I know,” Zuko said, voice grave. “That’s why I want to keep this quiet. Never mind that I shouldn’t be sparring in the first place, but that guard doesn’t deserve to be punished when it was only an accident.”

“What a comedy of errors…” Iroh shook his head. “The poor man. You’re certainly right to assume Zhao would react poorly to this.”

“He’s terribly protective,” Zuko agreed, stomach lurching.

The relief Iroh exuded was palpable; he even seemed to breathe easier now that he’d been given permission not to worry. He took his nephew’s hands in his. “I’m sorry for jumping to conclusions, Zuko. I’ve caused so much tension in your marriage already - you won’t mention this slip to Zhao, will you?”

Zuko’s heart softened. “Of course not. You were only looking out for me.”

Iroh nodded, gaze tender. “I’m glad all is well on that front. Although I must admit, I have different concerns, now.”

Zuko wavered. “What do you mean?”

“It’s not good for a marriage to contain too many secrets, Zuko. It may be time to let Zhao know your desire to keep firebending.”

It was disorienting, to see Iroh go from hating Zhao to advising Zuko to confide in him so quickly. “No,” Zuko said definitively. “I’m not ready to tell him that.”

“He could be more understanding than your father was…” Iroh coaxed.

Zuko swallowed the bile rising in his throat. “He - like you said, Zhao is protective. I don’t think telling him that right after I injured myself training is a good idea.”

“Very true,” Iroh relented. “Perhaps later. I suppose I’ll be living here in the Lesser Hall, again, now that your sister has accomplished her goal. You can train with me any time.”

“Thank you, Uncle.” He gave his uncle’s hands one last squeeze, and then dropped them.

Eventually they parted ways, Zuko watching his uncle retreat down the hall. He stayed standing there a moment even after he rounded the corner, as if to catch his breath after such an exhausting lie. Then he softly padded back to his bedroom.

“That was good,” Zhao said when he opened the door. “You used just enough truth that it felt believable.”

He was sitting up in bed, his arms crossed, appraising Zuko with a soft smile. After the shock of seeing him awake wore off, Zuko hurriedly closed the door behind himself.

“So you heard…?”

“Yes. Good thing you weren’t actually trying to hide anything from me.” Zhao grinned as if this was all a terribly funny turn of events. When it was clear Zuko was going to keep standing by the door, he threw open the covers and patted the space next to himself. Zuko obeyed, returning to the bed and crawling in beside him. Zhao pulled the blankets and sheets around Zuko’s shoulders until they were padded twice their size, slinging his arms around them as the final layer. The contact was oddly comforting, a warm contrast to his behavior the night before.

“Iroh was right, by the way,” Zhao said. “The book thing wasn’t believable. Maybe if you read histories, but none of your flimsy little plays could give you a bruise like that. Thankfully you thought of the guard story. That was a nice touch, saying I don’t know - it doesn’t only shift the blame, but it makes him feel like he’s got a secret to keep for you. Maybe next I can ‘find out’ and banish that guard in a fury.”

“You don’t have to,” Zuko murmured. It was bad enough, lying to Iroh. He didn’t want anyone else getting hurt as a result.

Zhao shrugged. “It’s fine. I wanted to get rid of him, anyway.”

“Why? All he did was spar with me.”

Zhao rolled his eyes. “Don’t be naive, Zuko. A well-intentioned alpha never would have agreed to be alone with you.”

“But he never once...”

“Keep your voice down,” Zhao chided. Zuko hadn’t thought he’d been raising his voice at all, but still found himself going quiet. “That guard didn’t do anything because I was there. Same with the others. Really, Zuko, I forget the age difference between us until moments like this one. You’re too trusting.”

“Others?” Zuko echoed. He was impressed he could force out a sound at all.

“It’s not like I’ve gotten rid of that many,” Zhao said. “Just a guard here or there who got too familiar. The odd servant. You can’t be too trusting of anyone; people will do whatever they can to gain access to the royal palace. You should read up on the bloodier side of your family history, sometime - when royal blood is shed, it’s rarely on a battlefield. It’s usually right at home, surrounded by familiar faces.”

Zuko didn’t know what to say to that. At least Zhao was happy with him again. Wrapped in his embrace, things almost felt normal. He could push away all the rest if he focused on this small triumph. He didn’t have to think about how this was the first one-on-one conversation he’d had with his uncle since they’d last seen each other; he didn’t have to think about how, despite the bad terms they had parted on, his uncle had been so concerned for his well being; he didn’t have to think about how the first thing he’d said to his uncle after months apart was a lie.

---

Zuko stared out the window of their carriage, awaiting their arrival at the Great Hall with dread. It’d been bad enough to be observed in his own living space, seeing the way servants’ eyes flickered towards his face and then away, afraid to be caught staring. The Great Hall was always in a furor of preparation, staffed with ten times the personnel of the Lesser Hall and hosting high-ranking members of the military or nobility. It would be all the more audience to gawk at his black eye.

The sky outside the carriage window was dull and overcast. Zhao hoped aloud that Azula’s banquet would be drenched in rain. Zuko still didn’t entirely understand his husband’s motives for getting involved in the banquet preparations; only that whenever Azula was in earshot, Zhao would loudly proclaim how the Avatar’s capture was such a victory for the Fire Lord.

“I have to admit that was a smart move, when you tried to convince me Ozai would steal credit for the moon spirit,” Zhao said. “It’s not entirely unfounded, although I have no choice, now. But if I have to hand over that victory to him in order to rescue my invasion, I might as well use this underhanded tactic on someone else. See how Azula likes losing credit for her accomplishments.” Zuko shuddered at the memory of that night in the reception room with Zhao. He’d wanted so badly to make him stay that he’d been willing to say anything. It’d been cruel of him to manipulate his husband’s feelings like that, just as it had been cruel to lie to him about the suppressants. As he agonized over the memory, the carriage came rolling to a stop. He saw his sister standing at the entrance of the palace, waving with both hands, and stiffened at the sight of her. One foot out of the carriage, Zuko wished more than anything he could vault back inside and ride to the Lesser Hall, or even to the stables - anywhere but here. Zhao’s hand on his lower back forced him to step out onto the wide stone steps, struggling to keep his expression cool as he tensed himself for an onslaught of cruel comments from Azula.

“Hello, Zuz - oh, for *spirits’* sake,” Azula exclaimed, her greeting aborted the moment she got a good look at his face. She turned to Zhao open-mouthed. “And *you’re* here. I’m surprised you’re alive. Has Uncle not seen either of you yet?”

Zhao sucked his teeth. “I don’t know what you’re *implying*, Azula-”

“That this is your handiwork,” she said immediately, gesturing to her brother’s face. Despite himself, Zuko could feel a flush rise to his cheeks.

Zhao raised his hands, not to fend her off, but as if reasoning with someone who was being altogether too aggressive. Voice even-keeled, he said, “Look, I sympathize with how you’d come to that conclusion, but this is all a misunderstanding. A guard-”

“A book,” Zuko corrected. The guard hadn’t been fired, yet. That would make for a serious continuity error.

Azula cocked an eyebrow. “You didn’t even get the story straight before coming out in public?”

Zhao shot a brief, poisonous look at his spouse before melting back into his reasonable persona. “Ignore him. It was a guard. They were sparring and he hit Zuko with a little too much force.”

“A *little*,” Azula repeated.

“Zuko’s description of events, not mine.” Zhao’s smile was tight. “My exceedingly soft-hearted husband was trying to hide it from me for the guard’s sake, but it’s too late for all that, now. I’ve dealt with the matter. We’re moving on.”

“So succinct.” Azula looked at her brother. “Do you have any comments, considering you’re the one with the black eye?”

Zuko willed his voice not to break as he confirmed, “No. That’s… the gist of it.” He looked at his sister’s face, made older than her years by a skillful application of makeup. If they had a normal sibling relationship, maybe he could ask her how to hide his bruise. When he’d tried himself earlier, the white powder had failed to cover it entirely, instead making him look like an injured corpse. His reflection seemed such an ominous vision of the future that he’d washed it all off immediately.

Azula narrowed her eyes, inspecting them both before she gave an irritated scoff. “Fine. Whatever. This whole spectacle is distracting from the real star of the show, anyway: *me*.” She grabbed Zuko by the arm as she might have when they were younger, possessive and affectionate. “Zuzu, you happen to be in the presence of someone who has *captured the Avatar* . Take advantage of this great privilege and ask me some questions.”

She tugged him towards a side hallway. Zuko glanced nervously at Zhao, as if asking permission. He didn’t seem terribly eager to grant it, and Azula picked up on this. She pouted. “Am I allowed to talk to my brother alone, or are you not letting him out of your sight?” Then, when Zhao took too long to answer, “If you’re innocent, then there’s no need for all this clingy watchfulness.”

Thank the spirits who took pity, then; the palace event planner rushed outside to greet them, intercepting Zhao in a panic. “The banners,” she was saying. “The new ones won’t be done in time.”

Zhao pulled a face. “Can’t we reuse whatever they had at our wedding?”

“Oh, no, sir.” The event planner’s expression went ashen. “The Fire Lord would be *furious*.”

Azula took the opportunity while Zhao was distracted to pull Zuko into the hall and around a corner. When they were out of earshot, she sighed. “At least Mother and Father had the sense to agree on a story beforehand. And *really,* Zuzu, why did he bring you here where everyone can see?”

Zuko blushed angrily. “I’m here because we don’t have anything to hide. He’s telling the truth.”

“Ugh, *whatever*,” she groaned, rolling her eyes. “Ask me about the Avatar, already!”

As he followed his sister’s lead down the darkened corridors of the Great Hall, he thought back to how inert the Avatar had seemed the day they’d brought him to the palace. His long limbs bound in chains. The many hands gripping him and holding him still. The hood.

“How did he move when he was airbending?” Zuko found himself asking. “Was it as different from the other elements as they say?” *Does he really move like the wind?* he wanted to ask.

“Sort of,” Azula breezed. “Truthfully it was hard to tell. By the time I got to him, he’d been awake for two days straight with little to no sleep, so he was more… floppy than anything.” She glanced over her shoulder at her brother, noting his disbelief, and smirked. “I think we forget, given his mythic status, but he is *only* a man. Same as anyone else, he has limits. Fire Lord Sozin understood that - it’s why he took advantage of the volcanic eruption to let Roku suffocate. We just had to run our man down until he was too exhausted to fight back.”

Such an undignified end. Zuko swallowed, throat burning. “You said the rest of his party... wasn’t an issue anymore?”

She nodded. “Thanks to Uncle. You know, I had my doubts about him, especially with how soft he’s become in his old age, but he delivered. I suppose I should’ve expected more from a man who razed half the Earth Kingdom to the ground.”

Despite having heard Iroh’s old war stories a hundred times, the thought of his gentle uncle doing anything like that made Zuko sick to his stomach. He changed the subject. “What about the bison?”

Azula heaved a sigh of frustration. “No use lugging all that dead meat halfway across the world. A shame; it really would’ve been such a delight to have an exotic pet like that.” She smirked at Zuko none too kindly. “You know, Zhao used to brag to the war council about what a pretty pet the sky bison would make for you. It would’ve been *so* fun to shove that in your face. Such a missed opportunity.”

They’d been walking for a while, now, and Zuko couldn’t help but notice that they were in the deeper recesses of the palace, the sort of depths ventured only by explicit invitation by the royal family. It had been some time since he’d seen another person around, even a servant.

“There’s something I’ve always wondered about the Avatar,” Zuko said, casting a careful look around the room. Empty, with not even a past Fire Lord glaring down at them from the walls. “What’s his second sex?”

“Couldn’t you tell when you saw him yesterday?” Azula asked.

Zuko shook his head. “Too many guards.” It had been a wall of scent. Too many people to pick a single person out.

“He’s a beta,” Azula said. Then, “...Why is that making you pout? Did I ruin your fantasy of cuckolding Zhao with the Avatar?”

“Don’t be disgusting,” Zuko huffed. For a moment, he considered hiding his theory from her. But it would be useless to; the Avatar was in the Fire Nation’s grasp, where he would stay until the end of his life. He might as well confide in her. “I always thought the Avatar was an omega. There were so many gaps to his travel patterns that suggested heats. Given how slowly they’ve made their path north…”

Azula didn’t mock his idea. She pursed her lips, contemplating. “I guess that’s not impossible - anyone can change their scent nowadays. We’ll certainly see the longer we keep him captive.” Her gaze darkened. “If he *does* go into heat, I don’t want some idiot guard staking a claim. We’ll have to switch to betas, only. No use letting anymore airbenders pop up in captivity. As fascinating as they would be to study, we can’t risk that getting out of…”

“Azula,” Zuko interrupted, “why aren’t you making fun of my face?”

She stopped walking so she could show him how dramatically she was rolling her eyes. Hands on her hips, she said, “Typical - I’ve accomplished what’s only ever been done by a sitting Fire Lord, and you have to make it all about *you.* ”

“You’ve never let a chance to bully me slip past you before,” Zuko pointed out. “In fact, the last time you were home-”

“Zuzu, please!” she huffed. “Teasing you over this would be so - boring!”

He stared at her, at first unsure he’d heard her right. There was being cruel, and then there were the innovative ways Azula kept finding to hurt his feelings. “*Boring?”* he repeated.

“Yes,” she said. “I mean - I *knew* this would happen, eventually.”

He remembered to act confused. “You knew I’d get a black eye sparring with a guard?”

She narrowed her eyes at him. “Stop it.”

“But Zhao didn’t-”

“Zhao didn’t do it, whatever.” Azula waved a dismissive hand. “This is exactly what I was talking about. ‘Prince Zuko had to marry a man exactly like his father!’ What a fucking twist, except it’s not. It’s rote. It’s boring.”

For the second time in only a few minutes, she’d said something that had left him thoroughly addled. “Zhao’s nothing like Father,” he said, disbelief seeping into his voice.

Azula groaned, rubbing her temples like he was giving her a migraine. “Zuko, did you get hit in the head while I was gone? Your husband is a cheap knockoff of the Fire Lord, down to the temper. That Agni Kai with War Minister Qin? Such a Father move.”

“Maybe, but Zhao isn’t temperamental *exactly* like Father is. He’s-” Images rushed through his mind of apologies, embraces, laughter, only to end hours before, with Zhao wrapping the blanket around him, praising him for a job well done. “He’s too *soft* .”

Azula actually guffawed. “What, because he hasn’t broken one of your bones? Give him time. He’ll get there.”

Zuko opened his mouth. Then closed it again.

“What’s the matter?” Azula asked. “It’s like you told me the last time I was in Caldera. You’ve lived with this your whole life, so there’s no use getting upset about it. Right, Zuzu?”

They locked eyes, glaring steadily at one another even as they heard footsteps approaching from down the hall.

“There you are,” came Zhao’s voice. “I didn’t think you’d get this far away.”

There was a warning in his tone. Zuko broke eye contact with Azula to look at him, to whisper, “I’m sorry.”

“It’s fine. Come along, now.” Zhao didn’t wait for Zuko to follow; he grabbed him by the elbow and pulled him away. Zuko hazarded a look back at Azula; there was an ugly twist to her mouth that smoothed over as she called out, “He refused to budge on your cover story, Commander. I haven’t gotten anything disloyal out of him.”

Zhao’s response was more muted than either of them expected. He simply muttered, “Shut up, Azula,” without turning around, and continued on his way, dragging Zuko with him. After a certain distance, it almost looked as if they were holding hands like a normal couple would. Azula refrained from shouting this after them, her mouth still tasting like bile after Zhao’s curt dismissal.

---

Word of the Fire Lord’s triumph over the Avatar spread throughout the capital, followed closely by news of the banquet that would be held in celebration. Although invitations were only extended to the highest echelons of Fire Nation nobility, the prospect filled the air with excited chatter nonetheless. By the end of the day, anyone who ventured into the city would have overheard the news.

There was one young woman who pondered the banquet with great interest. Although she hadn’t been formally invited, she thought it might be nice to drop by the royal palace tomorrow, weather permitting. After all, it was her first time in the city, and she’d never seen it before. She’d have to convince her friends it was worth it, but they hadn’t come all the way here just to sit around and mope. This banquet could be just the thing to lift their spirits.

Tipping her face towards the grey skies above, the young woman couldn’t help but think a little rain would do the capital some good.

## Chapter 25

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

The time has come for the Fire Nation to celebrate its victory over the Avatar.

### Text

As the hour of the banquet drew near, the royal family convened in the Great Hall to await the Fire Lord’s arrival. Although they lived together, it was miraculous they should all find themselves in the same room twice in the same week; Zuko couldn’t even think of an instance during his wedding where they had all stood in such close proximity.

When Ozai entered, they made their usual bows, and he addressed their tilted heads: “I expect all of us to behave in a manner befitting royalty today. We will not be fighting amongst ourselves like savages. Is that clear?”

“Yes, my lord,” they answered, not entirely in unison. The comment was clearly addressed to Zhao and Azula, who had spent the better part of the morning arguing over whether to postpone. Outside, the sky was still heavy with the threat of rain. Eventually it was Ozai who had ended things, declaring that whether it had to be moved indoors or not, this celebration *would* move forward. Nobility had been streaming through the capital all day, crowding up against the gates of the palace; there were even a few senators from the colonies who had managed to make it here on short notice. He would not turn them away before they’d had a chance to bask in his - in *their* victory.

As they unbent themselves and stood at attention, Zuko saw his father’s eyes flicker over his face. Then a transformation took place; there was the usual disinterest he held whenever he looked at his son. Then puzzlement, chased close by realization, chased ever faster by a white hot *fury*. Zuko took a step back as his father stormed over to him, only barely restraining himself from running away. He should be more afraid of the consequences of disobedience than of the hand that shot out to grab him by the chin.

“What is *this?* ” Ozai snarled. At once, Zhao and Iroh stepped forward, hands outstretched - but they stopped short, frozen to the spot the same as Zuko had been, weighing the risk of approaching the Fire Lord so directly.

Then they both started talking at once.

“It’s nothing, my lord,” said Zhao.

“It was an accident,” Iroh said.

“I didn’t do anything, you see, a guard-”

“Zhao is innocent. A book-”

“I don’t *care* how it happened!” Ozai thundered. He released Zuko so roughly that he scratched his face; Zuko winced, cupping his cheek.

“Today we stand before our nation as a symbol of its indomitable strength - I will *not* have my victory minimized by this lowborn display!” Ozai glared down at his son. “Return to the Lesser Hall, now, and do *not* show your face again for the duration of the banquet. Do you understand me?”

Zuko nodded. A pained look crossed Iroh’s face. Azula shook her head at him, reaching out to lower the hand that had stretched out in sympathy for his nephew. Determined, Zhao took another step forward. “My lord-”

In his defense, he was the only one to speak out after the decision was made. But the moment those eyes like fiery coals swiveled onto him, his mouth snapped shut.

Zuko wanted to tell everyone that it would be fine; he was relieved not to have to show his face to anyone else. But to speak without the Fire Lord’s permission would only invite more anger, and he had already done enough to ruin the mood of this momentous occasion. He gave one last bow to his father, then walked out of the Great Hall.

---

The dour skies seemed to perfectly match the weight in Zuko’s chest. The air was wet, prickling with the promise of rain as he walked in silence across the lawn. He passed by the pavilion, where several palace staff were finishing the last touches for the banquet, draping banners in shades of blood red over the roof. Even these failed to pierce the gloom, desaturated by the grey light coming through the clouds overhead. Underneath the pavilion, rows of tables and chairs had been set up for the visiting nobility. And to its left, on a raised platform for all to see… an empty cage made of iron. The bars were thick enough that a grown alpha would struggle to wrap his hands around them. Zuko turned away from it.

It was one of the first times in days that he found himself without a chaperone. Zhao had kept him affixed to his side for most of the banquet preparations, dragging him around by the elbow when his pace wasn’t fast enough to meet his husband’s liking. Now, though, there were no eyes on Zuko. Servants rushed across the lawn, ignorant of him as they carried out their duties. On either side of the pavilion stood two lines of guards, looking bored out of their minds. Zuko saw one nudge another and point to the sky, followed by an unmistakable pout. Thunderstorms were one thing; that electrical impulse in the air had an invigorating, almost heady effect on firebenders. Something about the promise of that intense crack of heat pulled like invisible hands on your chi. It was as much a power-up as it was a forfeit of control, your aim never quite as precise when lightning was in the mix. But rain? Rain only handicapped you in obvious ways.

Zuko sighed, pulling his robe closed tighter over his neck to brace against the wind. In the distance, he could see another group of guards approaching from the direction of the volcano itself, where the mouth of the dungeons lay. His stomach sank as he took in the sight of the Avatar, once again hooded and shackled. His wrists were manacled close together in a mock-prayer, while a short chain separated the cuffs on his ankles - allowing him to walk, but with considerable difficulty. Zuko stood at a distance and watched as the guards worked on transporting their prisoner to his cage.

“Did you hear the Fire Lord wants the hood off when the guests arrive?” asked one of the guards, a tall woman with willowy limbs.

The guard to her left, a man at least a head shorter than her, rolled his eyes at her. “That sounds like he’s asking for disaster.”

“How are people supposed to know it’s him if you can’t see his face, though? The arrows are crucial,” she told him. In fact, in his current state, one could only just make out the tattoos on his hands.

The shorter guard brushed his companion off with a harrumph. “Unless Princess Azula asks me directly, I’m not doing it.”

“Fine,” the willowy guard scoffed. “If *you* want to face his wrath…”

The shorter guard shot a scowl at her, which died away when he caught sight of Zuko standing nearby. “Prince Zuko.” He stopped walking, forcing the rest of the regiment to stop with him as he saluted the prince. “We didn’t mean to talk out of turn...”

Zuko saw how each guard’s eyes flickered over his face, no doubt assessing the damage. He wondered if they had heard rumors, if the whole *palace* was talking about him. He set his jaw. “I won’t bother my father with such insolence today, but I *will* take note of your comments.”

Zuko drew closer to the guards. There were five in total. Really only the two, the willowy guard and the shorter guard, physically held onto the Avatar; the rest were simply there for support in the event a struggle broke out.

It didn’t. The Avatar stood quietly between them; the only sign he was alive was a quick, almost silly wiggle of his fingers. He probably needed to keep the blood flowing, with how tightly his wrists were bound together. Zuko frowned more deeply at the sight.

“Well? Carry on with your work,” he ordered.

The shorter guard gave a salute of affirmation. He and his partner proceeded to open the cage and push the Avatar inside, the rest of the troop readying their stances if he tried anything. It was certainly a two man job to get the Avatar secure; they threaded a chain that was bound to his manacles over a bar on the roof of the cage. This allowed them to suspend his arms up over his head, rendering him more effectively immobilized. Once this was done, the shorter guard stepped out of the cage, and the willowy one was about to follow when Zuko stopped her.

“The hood,” Zuko said.

She glanced at her partner nervously. When he nodded, she turned back around towards the Avatar.

In that same instant, the sky opened up and let loose a torrent of rain. One of the guards cursed. Another pulled off his jacket and moved towards Zuko, to cover him.

“You don’t have to…” He trailed off as, chin tipped upwards, he noticed something in the distant sky. A large, rapidly moving shape. Zuko pointed to it and asked, “Do you see that?”

The guards turned to look. The flying object didn’t move like a bird, and it was too thick and dark to be a cloud. Instead, the shape seemed to undulate as it moved, using its wide tail to direct the current of air around it.

It was hard to make out any finer details in the rain, yet as it drew closer, Zuko’s heart swelled in his chest. It couldn’t be. Azula had implied it was *dead*.

“Hey,” said one of the guards. “Is that a *bison?* ”

Nearby, Zuko heard the metallic clattering of weapons. The guards lined by the pavilion must have seen the Avatar’s bison, too, as they were all running in its general direction, to meet it if it eventually landed.

The willowy guard gasped and exited the cage without pulling off the Avatar’s hood, throwing the door closed behind her. She was still fumbling with the lock on the cage when the bison let out a cry and swept low to the ground. If it was possible for an animal to feel anger, then this creature was furious with all of them; it glowered, mouth opening to reveal rows of flat, dull teeth. On its back, a feminine figure in blue stood up, arms extended. The very rain seemed to go still in the air around them, trembling in anticipation of her orders.

With a clap of her hands, the rain came together like two massive waves, knocking a horde of guards that had been running towards the bison to the ground. Once the bison was low enough, a figure in green leapt from its back, landing gracefully on its feet; in an instant, a wall of stone shot up out of the earth and knocked another group of men backwards.

“They’re - they’re crazy,” breathed the willowy guard.

Another guard in the group shook her head. “They can’t possibly think they can simply walk in here and take him?”

Zuko was fascinated to observe the Avatar’s companions in action, having for so long only known about them through second and third-hand accounts. The earthbender was a newer addition, but the waterbender, he knew, had travelled with the Avatar from the beginning; he watched her create a raceway of ice in an attempt to glide past a tangle of guards, only for a battalion of them to beat her back. She wasn’t down for long, both hands arcing through the air as she conjured a whip of water that knocked a gaggle of men twice her size away from her. Zuko felt something unnamable swell in his chest at the realization of how much she’d grown as a bender in the time since he’d started following their journey.

Although the guards had the advantage of numbers, they were barely holding the two women off, the rain hindering their firebending while keeping the waterbender well-supported. Even the bison seemed eager to shift the tide in their favor, circling low at the behest of its pilot, sending great gusts of air at the men who dared to point their spears at its face.

Zuko rounded on the guards who had brought the Avatar to his cage. “You need to go back to the Great Hall and tell my father what’s going on!”

They stared at him, eyes frantically switching from his face, to the fight a few yards away, to their prisoner.

“But the Avatar-” started the shorter guard.

“He’s *chained up* *in a cage!”* Zuko shouted, allowing a spurt of fire out of his heel as he stomped it imperiously into the ground. “He’s not going anywhere - *you* need to get to the palace to protect your Fire Lord! *Now!”*

The shorter guard had only a moment to hesitate. The air was lashed by screams as a fissure the size of the sky bison opened in the earth, sending guards tumbling down into the dark. It couldn’t possibly be that deep with only one earthbender in the fray. Yet they watched as six men were swallowed up, never to resurface. Although she had moved, Zuko pinpointed the figure in green, locked in a typical earthbending stance with her legs wide and elbows bent. Perhaps it was the distance and the rain playing tricks on his eyes, but she seemed quite small from where he was standing.

The guards nearest to him no longer needed convincing. Led by the shorter guard, they turned and began to hurry towards the palace. The willowy guard was the last of the group, slowed down by her nervous fumbling with the padlock. She started to run after her companions, but was stopped short as Zuko snatched her by the sleeve.

“Wait,” he commanded, allowing his anxiety to shake his voice.

“Prince Zuko,” she said, startled. “It’s not safe here. We should really join the others.”

“I know what I said. But I need you to triple check the padlock,” he said. “I’m the one who told you all to get to safety, so my father will blame *me* if the Avatar gets out.”

The other guards were fairly far ahead, by now. Looking past the willowy guard’s stricken expression, he could see they were wholly focussed on getting to the palace in one piece. They probably hadn’t noticed the two people missing from the group.

“Please,” Zuko said to guard, hands folded in front of his face. “Quickly.”

The guard nodded once, then returned to the door of the cage. She crouched down, teeth chattering from the frigid rain as she handled the padlock. It was enormous even in her wide hands. She shook it with all her might.

“Seems secure to-”

Grabbing a fistful of her hair for leverage, Zuko smashed her forehead against one of the iron bars of the cage. Thankfully he’d put enough strength into it that he didn’t have to do it twice; she was knocked out cold in an instant, her body slumping forward like a sack of potatoes. Panicked by her limpness, he let go of her hair and pressed an ear up against her chest to listen, only to find she was still breathing.

“Sorry,” he whispered.

Zuko peaked around the corner of the raised platform where the cage was mounted, ensuring there were no witnesses; the guards he had sent to the Great Hall had disappeared inside, and as far as he could tell, anyone entangled in the fray across the lawn was too occupied trying to subdue the waterbender and the earthbender to pay attention to him. He ducked down to root around in the guard’s pockets for a key.

His fingers were chilled to the bone, making his wet grip on the key all the more unsteady as he fumbled at the padlock. “Damn it,” he muttered to himself as it slipped from his grasp.

“Are you okay back there?” said a voice.

Startled, Zuko looked around. But there was no one close enough to have spoken. The willowy guard was still unconscious. The servants had scattered, running back towards the palace once the fight had started, and those guards still on the lawn were occupied with the struggle happening a few yards away. That left only the hooded figure caged before him.

“Can you do me a favor?” asked the Avatar, his voice muffled by fabric. “I can’t really see what’s going on, so can you confirm - this is a jailbreak, right?”

“Y-yes.” The padlock clicked in Zuko’s hands and fell open. “You can talk?”

He felt stupid as soon as the question stumbled out of his mouth. But given how quiet the Avatar had been up until now, he’d assumed he’d been gagged. Or worse.

The Avatar chuckled in a way that made Zuko feel as though they were talking over a casual lunch, not drenched in rain in an iron cage. “Of course. You should’ve seen me yesterday, when the Fire Lord visited me. I had plenty to say then.”

This was so surreal. Zuko opened the door to the cage and stepped inside. “Yeah? Like what?”

The Avatar cocked his head, chains rattling as he moved. “Well… I told him what I thought of his war. The destruction he’s caused, the lives that have been lost during his selfish quest for power.”

Zuko’s stomach lurched. “It’s not *his* war. It’s the legacy of our - of *his* forefathers.” He crouched down to check the manacles around the Avatar’s ankles for a keyhole or a weak point. “The Fire Nation is the most prosperous country in the world, and we want to share our civilization with everyone else. I promise you the intentions of our leaders have always been good.” He reached into his hair for a pin and began to fiddle with the lock.

“How is forcing your way into countries that don’t want you there a way of spreading civilization?” the Avatar asked.

“They just don’t know any better. It’s like with children - sometimes you have to drag them kicking and screaming to the doctor even when they don’t want to go.” No matter how long Zuko picked, the manacles wouldn’t budge. In fact, his hairpin was getting horribly twisted in the thick iron of the lock, too flimsy to force it to bend to its might. He shot the lock a glare before standing back up.

“Doesn’t that analogy fall apart quite easily, though? We’re not talking about pure acts of goodwill. The Fire Nation razes villages to the ground. It culls other benders for mass execution. What good could all that death and destruction possibly do?”

Zuko faltered, hands stuttering over the Avatar’s chains. “I - I don’t pretend to have all the answers. But war is a necessary evil, and more complex than you’re making it seem. Sometimes we have to trust that the people in charge have chosen to do things that seem terrible because they have the foresight to understand how it’ll all improve things in the long run.”

The Avatar chuckled. “I think some tiny part of you knows that’s wrong.”

Zuko’s breath hitched. “How do you figure?”

“Well - I think most people know by now that the Avatar wants to stop the war. And here you are, setting him free.”

“That’s different. I’m setting you free because…”

“Because?” Said in an almost teasing tone. Anyone else would be worried about scaring their rescuer off by giving them second thoughts, but the Avatar seemed confident that Zuko was on his side.

And he was correct. Zuko couldn’t explain how he knew, but setting the Avatar free was simply the right thing to do. “We can’t waste time talking,” he huffed, grateful the other man couldn’t see the flush rising to his skin. “It won’t be long before reinforcements come.”

Zuko grabbed the manacles around the Avatar’s wrists, hoping against all logic that his sister had been lazy enough with security that they had the same key as the cage’s padlock. No such luck; it couldn’t even fit in the keyhole. So how could he remove these? Perhaps the guard he’d knocked out had some sort of weapon he could use. He stepped out of the cage and crouched down to rummage through her possessions again, looking for a knife holster, some pockets, but evidently she had been a firebender. There was nothing here he could use. He cursed to himself; any second now, someone could come out here and see what he was doing. His eyes fell upon the rows of tables and chairs set up for the banquet, and suddenly, he had an idea.

The Avatar was *humming* to himself by the time Zuko returned, swinging open the cage door with a clatter. “Watch your head,” he warned.

“I can’t see to - *ow*.”

Zuko bumped him with a side of the chair as he jammed one of the legs into the least sturdy-looking chain link he could find. “If I use all my weight, I think I can break this off and free you.” The chair leg got wider the further up it went; hopefully with enough force applied to it, it could bend the chain link open.

“You’ve already done enough for me,” said the Avatar. “I have a friend who can bend-”

Zuko shoved down on the chair. The Avatar, thinking fast, got a grip on his manacles and held firm to avoid his arms being yanked even higher over his head. The chain remained intact. Zuko scowled and said, “Hold tight,” before trying again, bringing the chair down with a swifter, more forceful motion.

There was a metallic *ping* of the link breaking, followed by a rattle as the chain looped through the roof of the cage and fell to their feet. The Avatar’s hands were still manacled, but once the chain was pulled through the fastenings on the wrists, he could separate them, at least, allowing for more freedom of movement.

“Nice work,” the Avatar complimented. “Think you may’ve bruised my wrists, though.”

Before Zuko could offer an apology, their attention was torn away by a primal scream that erupted from the direction of the Great Hall. He looked up in time to see a figure appear in its wide entrance, crackling with an aura of blue electricity.

*Azula* . As she raced down the great stone steps of the Great Hall, a wall of earth rose up and blocked her path. Even so, Zuko knew he had little time. Zuko leapt out of view behind the much taller man, hoping the earthbender could hold his sister off long enough before he was discovered.

Zuko grabbed the Avatar by the shoulder, pulling him down to speak directly into his ear - wherever it might be, under all that burlap. “Don’t go to the North Pole. The Fire Nation has been planning its invasion for months; they’ll be looking for you.”

“...Sounds like all the more reason to go,” mused the Avatar. He was digging into the iron collar around his neck, pulling the edges of the hood free.

Zuko glared at his back. “Are you crazy? You could be captured again - or worse!”

“I’m always going to be in danger,” the Avatar said, voice muffled. “I might as well go where people need me most.”

Before Zuko could retort, the Avatar pulled off his hood.

It was just as Azula said: he was only a man. A *boy,* really. Although his jaw had a little definition, much of it was illusory, brought on by the thin beard he wore. And for all of his height, there was an obvious youthfulness to him, shiny about the eyes, like life hadn’t had a chance to snatch the spark from him, yet.

He seemed to catch Zuko’s disbelief and chuckled. “What? Is it the arrow? The shaved head? I swear, back in my day, this look was all the rage.”

“I’m sorry for staring,” Zuko said, catching himself. “It’s just - weird, that you’re only a teenager.”

The Avatar fixed Zuko with a friendly, lopsided sort of smile. The young prince couldn’t help but think that while he understood the urge to immortalize it, none of the wanted posters had done it a stitch of justice.

“Yeah,” he said. “So are you.”

Zuko blinked, taken aback. *He* wasn’t anyone special. “Um - I guess. Can you walk with your legs bound?” He felt like there was infinitely more he needed to do for this man, to make up for all the anguish his family had caused him.

“I’ll be fine,” the Avatar promised. His gray eyes went soft. “Thank you for everything you’ve done for me. Now please - get to safety.”

Zuko wanted to say more. He wanted to say he’d dreamed of this meeting for what had only been months, but felt like an entire lifetime. He wanted to ask if the Avatar was learning the elements in the wrong order now that the earthbender had joined their group, skirting his firebending lessons in favor of earth.

A tiny part of him even wanted to ask if they needed a firebending teacher to come along with them.

It was a silly thought. There would be better teachers for the Avatar than an omega teenager who’d never been in a real fight. Besides, his time was up. The moment the Avatar told him to go, Zuko heard his sister give another furious scream. It sounded not so far away, now. It was the wakeup call he needed.

Zuko ran from the open door of the cage, a great wind chasing his heels. Squinting into the rain, he ran from the pavilion, not allowing himself to watch how the Avatar might be rising into the air, wreathed by spiralling elements, not allowing himself to see the fight that may ensue between him and Azula, not allowing himself to give into that same wretched weakness that had moved him to free the airbender in the first place.

---

When Zuko finally stumbled into the Lesser Hall, it was eerily empty. It cut a stark contrast against both the chaos he knew waited outside and that which raged inside his own body. His lungs were burning from his escape, heart racing from the fact he’d taken every step in terror, unsure if he would be spotted or if the danger would spread to where it could reach him. Yet the longer he stood in this still silence of the hall, the calmer he became. Everything that had happened with the Avatar seemed to belong to an afternoon spent lost in a daydream or a story scroll. Now all that color had been sapped away to reveal the dull tones of the real world.

He knew he should be more worried about what would happen to him. Whether the Avatar successfully escaped or not, there was a high chance someone had witnessed Zuko setting him free. But all sense of urgency slipped away beneath the suffocating weight of exhaustion. Standing in his bedroom, Zuko stripped the wet layers of his robes off his body and let them fall into a matted heap on the floor. Then, naked, his hair still damp, he crawled into his bed and slept.

Zuko wasn’t sure how long he slept. One moment he was dreamless, drifting, and the next, he was jerking awake to the clatter of his bedroom door. He lifted his head from the nest of blankets to see Zhao marching into the room, dripping with rain, his expression haggard. Seeing him, Zuko registered that something was wrong, but not what. He swung his legs out of bed and was thrown off by the sight of his own bare skin. He remembered he’d gotten into bed without getting dressed. Then remembering everything else.

“You let the Avatar go,” Zhao said.

There was a terrifying moment where he reached out, hands clamping onto Zuko’s naked flesh. The young prince went rigid instantly, anticipating pain, arms flying up to block whatever Zhao was about to do.

And then he was pulled close to Zhao’s body as the other man spun them around in elation.

“I can’t *believe* I ever doubted you,” Zhao laughed, and it took Zuko a second to accept the warmth in his voice, to understand that the grip on his body was joyful, their shared momentum triumphant. Zhao set the younger man back down and grinned at him. “You really did this for me?”

Zuko had already told so many lies that day. One more seemed inconsequential. So he said, “Yes.”

“I knew it,” said Zhao. “I *knew* the suppressants were a blip, I *knew* you were loyal, after all.” He was grinning as he shook his head. “This is the most amazing thing anyone’s ever done for me. So perfect, yet so simple: set the Avatar free, fuck Azula’s little plan, and afford *me* a second chance to catch him. I’m furious I didn’t think of it myself.”

“I didn’t think of it myself until I saw him there, and I just…” Zuko trailed off, unsure how to explain the urge that had seized him in that moment. “But how did you know I did it?”

“In the aftermath, when the Avatar’s party got away. Some guards were talking. Don’t worry about it, though; I’ve made sure they won’t blab another word. We lost so many guards today. What’s a few more?”

Zhao gave Zuko another one of those helpless grins, like he was confessing to love, not treason. Maybe it was all the same to him. He pulled Zuko close again, causing the younger man to flinch as the freezing cold metal of his belt buckle hit his naked stomach.

“Thank you,” Zhao whispered, breath hot against his ear. “Thank you for - for saving my campaign, and giving me the chance to prove myself to your father, and - thank you for giving me the chance to prove myself to *you* .” He pulled back so he could take Zuko’s face in his hands and tilt it up towards his, his expression one of adoration until his eyes started to roam over the details of his sins. Then his smile slipped away.

“I’m sorry, Zuko,” Zhao said, still cradling his face. “I shouldn’t have lost control of myself.”

Zuko didn’t know what to do with the stark silence that followed his apology but fill it. “Don’t be. I betrayed you.”

“Still - I shouldn’t have punished you so severely.” A thumb smoothed over his left cheek. Zhao’s eyes searched his face as if looking for the means to remove the bruise entirely. “I’ll make it up to you. Every day from here on out, I’m going to show you what you mean to me.”

Zuko wrapped his fingers around Zhao’s wrists with an uncertain grip. “Every day...”

“The invasion of the North Pole is back on, but I’ll be sending someone else there in my place,” Zhao said. “And with the kind of forces your father has agreed to give me, I’m not going to need anything else to win, so I. I can be persuaded to hold off on the moon spirit, too. At least for the time being.”

Zuko was speechless. This morning, he’d had nothing. No future with Zhao. An impending world without an Avatar, thrown out of spiritual balance. And suddenly it had all shifted. He had gotten what he wanted. He had gotten *everything* he wanted.

The realization was so overwhelming he had to bite his lower lip to bleeding, then press the heel of his hand over his mouth to stifle the storm of emotion that tore through his chest. Throughout it all, Zhao held him close; he pressed their foreheads together, cradling the back of Zuko’s head as the younger man shook with relief.

It was the second time in their marriage that he stifled a sob pulling Zhao into a kiss. His lips were still cold from the rain; Zuko took it upon himself to warm them. Immediately there were hands on his hips, possessive and reverent, wet nails biting into his skin. Maybe this was the natural progression of his relief, the realization he wouldn’t have to be alone, or maybe there was something headier brewing in the black clouds outside their window. In any case, when broad hands squeezed over Zuko’s ass, started to stroke between his legs, he shuddered like he was the one frozen to the bone.

He yanked away the wet layers of Zhao’s clothing, both their hands rushing to untie his shoulder guards, to pull away the armour so Zuko could bring himself flush against him and will his skin to warm up with a torrent of body heat. Zhao fell back on the bed into the tangled mess of their blankets, and Zuko climbed on top to straddle his hips, to rock his erect length against Zhao’s until he was hard enough Zuko could take him inside in one swift motion.

They didn’t have a habit of doing it this way, and Zuko supposed he understood why; it was too close to switching roles, the way Zhao was laid out underneath him, prone, with Zuko setting the rhythm of things. He found he liked this, liked Zhao’s panting breaths, the way he for once was forced to adapt to the pace Zuko set.

As he rode Zhao’s cock, Zuko traced his hands over the planes of his husband’s muscles, mapping out the defined shoulders, the oversized pectorals, the toned abdomen. He hadn’t ever allowed himself to look at anyone else, too much the model omega to admit such fault, but he found his fingers tracing over a bulging vein that ran down Zhao’s forearm, parallel to those invisible lines of chi, like rivers running wild over uncharted land, like arrows of blue tattooed against his skin.

Zuko’s orgasm hit him by surprise. While he tensed around Zhao, shuddering, his husband took it upon himself to thrust upwards once, twice, three more times, fingers digging into the flesh of Zuko’s thighs as he came inside him.

---

Thousands of feet in the air, the thick rainclouds provided the perfect cover for their escape. Although they were drenched to their bones, the four of them rejoiced as if it was a gorgeous and sun-drenched day, throwing their arms around one another in triumph as the bison flew them out of the Fire Nation capital to safety.

“HA!” Grinning from ear to ear, the Water Tribe girl pointed an accusing finger at her brother. “You said a full-frontal assault would never work, but it totally did!” She brought a hand to her chin, framing her face with a smug little sister smile. “Maybe *I* should be the plan guy from now on.”

Her older brother’s face twitched, and it wasn’t just because of the wind whipping her hair into his face. Although that was certainly part of it. “*First* of all, Katara, barging into the royal palace and attacking everyone in sight *doesn’t count as a plan!*”

“But we timed it with that rain storm,” said the earthbender to Katara’s right.

Sokka scowled even though the earthbender couldn’t see it. “Still doesn’t count! We’re lucky Appa didn’t get skewered by those flaming arrows they shot at us on the way in!”

“Well, luckily the *rain* put those out,” Katara said, giving another cheeky grin.

“*Secondly*,” Sokka went on, voice rising to drown out all further interruptions, “the only reason that non-plan DID work is because Aang broke free *by himself*, which allowed us to get the hell out of there.”

The airbender chuckled. “Well, I think it helped a *little* that Katara and Toph fended off a whole squadron of Fire Nation soldiers.”

“Hell yeah!” Toph cried, raising her fists into the air. “Remember when I punted that psycho princess clear across the lawn?”

Katara cocked her head in thought; she hadn’t seen the absolute extent of her companion’s imprisonment, but she had seen the thick iron bars of the cage and the team of guards surrounding it. “Hey, Aang - how *did* you get out?”

“Did you take a page out of Toph’s book and do some metal bending?” Sokka asked, jerking a thumb at the tiny earthbender.

“I didn’t do anything,” Aang said with a shrug. “A prince rescued me.”

*That* revelation filled Appa’s saddle with near-incoherent crosstalk, as too many of them tried to ask the same questions at once.

“The psycho’s *brother* helped you?”

“A *prince?* ”

“Are you sure?”

“I wasn’t sure at first, but when I watched him leave, I saw the hairpiece,” Aang said, pointing to a place on his bald head said hairpiece would struggle to find a grip. “It was exactly like the one the princess wore.”

The group went strangely quiet at this revelation. Aang took the opportunity to reflect on the moment he’d lifted his hood and seen the face of his rescuer. For all its severity, the bruise hadn’t registered much to him (other than to make Aang feel remorse; it looked painful, and was no doubt sustained during the rescue attempt). Instead, Aang had been drawn in by the young man’s other delicate features, most of all his earnest golden eyes. Even with the urgency of the situation, Aang had been unable to resist the urge to pause before his ascent into the fray and glance back at his rescuer one last time.

Aang had been rewarded for his sentimentality: his rescuer’s hair shone down his back like a river in starlight, robes clinging to his lithe body, the richness of the material obvious even when heavy with rain. And of course, perched in the retreating figure’s hair, glinting from the distant flashes of lightning, was that golden flame. Aang didn’t know what to make of the fact that a member of the royal family had set him free; there could be a network of conspiracy at play he didn’t understand, in-fighting amongst royalty in which he was merely another tile on the board. Yet he hoped it was a sign that there were those in the Fire Nation as opposed to this senseless war as the rest of them.

He was pulled from his reveries by Toph chuckling quietly to herself. “Kidnapped by a princess, rescued by a prince… You sure live one wonky, storybook life, Twinkletoes.”
