## Chapter 26

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Following the Avatar’s escape, the couple is closer than ever. At Zhao’s urging, they attend a party.

#### Chapter Notes

see end of chapter notes for triggers warnings, as they contain spoilers

this chapter is a behemoth. if you're on a late night fic binge and looking for a place to stop, this is the place.

### Text

Hours after the Avatar’s escape, the royal palace was thrown into an absolute chaos of preparations. While uninjured forces were preoccupied tracking the bison’s flight path, Zhao found himself back in the same councilroom where he’d earlier been humiliated, preening as his campaign was once again bolstered with reinforcements. The turnaround had him in such a good mood, he figured he ought to show his gratitude.

“My lord, I will *not* let you down,” Zhao promised. “This invasion is exactly what we need to restore our glory.”

“It had better be,” Ozai muttered. “It is our last possible option.”

The throne room was barren, no roiling fire on the dais nor palace aids nor war council to speak of. It was Ozai alone revising the war plans, making decrees while his son-in-law took notes. It felt like they were doing something wrong, although Zhao supposed that was because he had forgotten the true nature of the war council: it was not the final authority on how the Fire Nation conducted its war, but an entity meant to aid to the Fire Lord in such decisions. In the end, Ozai needn’t ask anyone’s permission to change it all on a whim.

“Quite.” Zhao smiled despite the sting of the Fire Lord’s tone, and carried on verbally prostrating himself. “For what it’s worth, I do want to apologize for earlier, my lord. While I’m not admitting fault for *putting* it there, I should’ve known it would be unseemly for Zuko to show his face in such a state and encouraged him to conceal it before the festivities.”

Ozai returned Zhao’s earnestness with a blank stare. “What is this about?”

A lot had happened that day. The Fire Lord could be forgiven for forgetting this small detail, even if he did make a scene over it in the first place. “I mean Zuko’s bruise, sir.”

Ozai scowled. “I don’t care about that. He is yours to do with as you please; I merely ask that in the future, you aim where it’s more easily concealed.”

Zhao let out a nervous laugh. “Thank you, my lord, but honestly, that’s not what-”

“Please, Zhao, I’m not Iroh. You don’t have to scramble for a lie with me.” The Fire Lord punctuated this with a put-upon sigh. “Really, though - only peasants aim for the face. I’d have thought your father would teach you that.”

The mention of his father made any further denial Zhao had prepared die on his tongue. His father’s tempers had been nothing if not perfectly timed. He could remain straight-faced despite all manner of mischief and misbehavior, enduring every humiliation his children put him through. But by the time the guests’ carriage had pulled away, you’d have better found a *damn* good hiding place.

Zhao’s father would have never lost control of himself in front of any of his son’s friends, let alone a prince. If Ozai knew about the man’s temper, it could only be because Wei had commiserated with him about it... although the thought of Ozai having a heart-to-heart with anyone was impossible to imagine.

Zhao smiled tightly. “Yes, well. Thank you again for this show of faith. I’ll do you proud up north.”

Ozai cocked his head like a vulture-falcon spotting prey across a field. “Come again?”

Zhao pushed past the sinking feeling in his stomach. “Well, sir, when I’m leading the invasion of the Northern Water Tribe-”

And he was unable to finish, drowned out by Ozai’s laughter. It was the first time he’d ever gotten such a reaction out of the Fire Lord. It should have been an honor, but the sound ripped through Zhao like the claws of a wild animal, pinning him there to bleed while the Fire Lord had his fun.

“Of *course* you’re not going to the North Pole,” Ozai cackled. “Whatever gave you *that* ridiculous idea?”

If Zhao were a remotely spiritual man, he would thank Wan Shi Tong, Tui, La, and all the rest that it was just the two of them in the throne room. The only thing that made this humiliation bearable was the fact it was private. “My lord,” he started, before pausing to gather his bearings. “I don’t think it’s so ridiculous an assumption. It was my idea to invade-”

The Fire Lord interrupted him with the flick of a wrist. “As eager as you are to die in the arctic, that has never been your role. You promised to manage Kirachu, which is an effort even from the capital. I shudder to think how you would shirk your duties from *that* far away.”

Ozai had never expressed discontent with how Zhao was handling Kirachu before, so this vitriol came as something of a surprise. Zhao cleared his throat to shake the fury loose from his voice before defending himself. “I’d like to think Kirachu has flourished since I took my position here.”

“Because your brother has been courteous enough to run things in your absence.” Ozai lanced him with a steely glare. “Wei’s told me you hardly write home.”

Why on earth would Wei be running things? Had something happened with Darah he wasn’t aware of? Zhao was going to throttle his older brother the next time he saw him, and in picturing this moment, he was able to inject some warmth into his response to the Fire Lord. “Wei’s never mentioned that you two got back in contact. How nice for old friends to reconnect.”

---

“Azula, wait. Please let me explain!”

Eyes forward, Azula marched through the palace, pace impossible to match without breaking out into a run. Iroh would rather she stop to scream at him in fury; at least that would afford him a chance to catch his breath. He was unaccustomed to having to give chase in his old age, and quickly found himself winded trying to follow her.

“It was all just a misunderstanding,” Iroh panted. “I know I failed you, but next time we see him-”

Her compliance with his wish to stop was so sudden and unexpected, he nearly stumbled into her. Her back to him, she said in a calm voice, “You promised we’d be honest with each other.”

Iroh hung his head. “I know. Azula, I should have never let you believe that the Avatar’s friends were taken care of. I was caught up in the moment, and you seemed so assured of your victory that I didn’t have the heart to tell you I had merely lost sight of them. I truly meant no harm done.”

Azula scoffed. “Bullshit.”

Iroh raised his hands almost reflexively in defense. “Azula-”

“Bullshit!” she said again, turning to face him. Although anger arched her brows, she still didn’t lash out at him; instead she addressed him in cold tones. “You don’t make mistakes, Uncle. Not like that. If you let them get away, it’s because you were having doubts in the mission altogether, and *that* is what makes me furious. If you didn’t want to help me capture the Avatar, you should have told me!”

Iroh paused, about to push yet another excuse, then stopped himself for her sake. His arms fell to his sides, his eyes stormy. “Azula. If I had told you not to pursue the Avatar, would you have listened?”

She scoffed. “Of course not. But I would’ve at least been given the chance to disagree. If you would treat me as your intellectual equal instead of a child to be lied to-”

Iroh shook his head. “Azula, this isn’t a matter of intellect and opinion, it is a matter of right and wrong.”

“That’s what *you* believe, but I see differently. My *father* sees differently. If we’re going to win this war-”

“I’ve told you this before,” Iroh cut in. “You could capture the Avatar, conquer Ba Sing Se, and pull the very moon from the sky - none of it will impress your father.”

*That* finally tipped her over the edge. “I am not doing this for *him!”* Azula snapped, face reddening in a flash. “I was doing this for myself!”

“Azula, you and I both know that your father gave you this assignment to-”

“My father *nothing*,” she said, stamping her foot petulantly. “That was *my* humiliation! *My* disgrace! And you let me walk right into it! Why? Uncle, you’re supposed to be there for me! You’re supposed to be the only person who’s looking out for me!”

Her expression twisted with a vulnerability he had never seen from her outside their most private conversations; although they were already alone in the corridor, he wanted to banish every living being from the Great Hall to protect her from anyone who would witness her this way.

He reached out for her, but she struck his hand away, the impact of skin to skin deafening in the quiet corridor.

Iroh resisted the urge to cradle his hand. It surely didn’t hurt as badly as she did now. “In all truthfulness, Azula, I would have never let things get so far. But you are far too talented for your own good. You cornered the Avatar as few else could. And that is why I urge you to think carefully before you proceed.”

She let out a hollow laugh. “I can’t believe you’re trying to convince me of this *moments* after admitting you lied. You’ve lost your chance to speak with me candidly about this or anything else. In a matter of days I’ll be leaving the capital to regain my honor, and you’re not coming with me.”

Iroh took a deep breath. “...Very well. If that is what you wish. Only know that if you later decide you want me, I’ll be there. You need only ask.”

Azula was not touched by this promise; hands on her hips, she huffed, “I’ll be just fine without you. Worry about your other child.” Her eyes narrowed. “Which reminds me - I’m angry at you for that, too. How dare you defend Zhao to my father?”

The change in subject jarred Iroh. Perhaps this was about the budding rivalry between herself and Zhao, that she couldn’t stand to see her uncle take his side. “Azula, I happen to know he’s telling the truth about his innocence.”

“So you *witnessed* the guard hitting Zuko?” she asked dryly.

Iroh frowned. “No, but the story is sound. Zuko told me himself, and there are details that only he and I-”

Azula cut him off with a sigh that could wither a whole field of crops. “Despite the ‘innocent old geezer’ act you so like to indulge, Uncle, I know you aren’t *blind*. You should be able to see what’s in front of you.” She paused. “Or maybe not - family has always been your blind spot.”

She gave him little chance to react. They had come upon her bedroom door, and so she punctuated this last derisive note by spiriting herself away, the door snapping shut behind her.

---

When Zuko was small, acting out stories under blanket forts with his mother, he used to be in awe of how masterfully she would perform her lines. Maybe that near-worshipful love of a child for his mother had muddled his memory, but he seemed to remember her practically transforming into a different person whenever she played a part. It was as if she believed what she was saying with her entire heart.

“How do you *do* that?” Zuko would ask.

Smiling, his mother would run her fingers through his hair and say, “It’s all part of acting, Turtle-duck.” At such a young age, it was near-impossible to understand she had a life before he existed. Even though he knew she used to be in plays, he didn’t know how long she’d done that, or why she’d stopped.

“Teach *me*,” Zuko insisted. He tugged the scroll in her hands towards him as if it held all the secrets of acting in its depths; even if it had, it would’ve been little help to him. He was young enough at the time he couldn’t read, the words like smudgy blurs of ink beneath the vivid illustrations.

Ursa laughed and kissed his head. “It’s all in the repetition. You have to practice the words over and over until you believe them. Then everything you say becomes as good as true.”

So Zuko took this to heart. And now, at eighteen, finds himself with a mantra he repeats as dutifully as a daily prayer:

*I am happy. I am happy. I am happy.*

And why shouldn’t he be? The Avatar is alive. His husband is home, safe, and will stay that way. Better yet, Zhao has been treating him something like he had in the early days of their marriage, but with a smidge less lust and a bucketful more of audacity. Every day, he’s taken to soliloquizing *-* yes, *soliloquizing* - his return from the Great Hall with grandiose exaltations of Zuko, his beauty, his wit, and the adoration he inspires.

Zuko tells himself he isn’t mortified when Zhao launches into one of these dramatic speeches, especially in front of Iroh or the staff. It is, after all, an improvement on how he behaved only days ago. And even if Zuko *were* mortified, it would be welcome, the soft embarrassment of being loved rather than the abjection of shame or humiliation. And he’s certainly had enough of that to last a lifetime.

So when Zhao appears in one of these loving moods, Zuko plays along. A little repetition always helps the strength of a performance. Perhaps Zhao knows that as well as he does.

“*Hours* I’ve suffered, listening to those old corpses on the war council muddle over the fate of our countrymen; the only thing that got me through was the knowledge that at the end, I’d be reunited with absolute, shining perfection.”

Zhao’s voice booms close to Zuko’s ear, and Zuko’s laugh comes more naturally than it did the day before as he holds onto Zhao for dear life - on top of delivering this speech, Zhao has elected to twirl him around and around, his robes fanning out like the sails of a Water Tribe ship as they fly through the air. Zuko bites the inside of his mouth to stifle a particularly idiotic smile he can feel building in his cheeks. (How bizarrely triumphant he is, with how easily the reaction comes. He can’t stifle the hope that one day he’ll wake up and won’t have to remind himself to be happy, because it’ll already be true.)

“Surely you don’t mean me?” Zuko says innocently, once placed back onto the ground.

“I do mean you,” Zhao affirms, hands resting on Zuko’s hips. “You are perfection incarnate, such that I’m in awe of you every time we’re reunited.”

Zuko’s lips twist. “Hm. Pretty words.” He digs his fingers into one thick sideburn and shoves Zhao’s face away. His husband fakes offense to the gesture.

“Excuse you, Prince Zuko, but those words are from the depths of my soul. I adore you.” He speaks louder, then, to spite the hand that is now trying to press itself - *playfully* - over his mouth. “You will not drown me out. I *adore* -”

Hands proving an ineffective gag, Zuko stands on his toes and uses the added leverage of a hand at the nape of his husband’s neck to drag him into a kiss. Zhao gladly surrenders. Then tries to incorporate a little too much tongue than acceptable for a kiss shared in the middle of the hallway. He allows Zuko to break the seal between their mouths, but the rest of them stay melded together, his arms wrapped possessively about his husband’s waist.

“How *was* your day?” Zuko breathes against his lips, eager to divert the subject from his many charms.

“Awful,” Zhao reaffirms. “Even with your sister disgraced and the royal court throwing itself at my feet, your father treats me like-” He stumbles over the comparison. “He treats me poorly.” Here is a dent in the armour. Azula’s downfall is not synonymous with their victory; they have yet to do anything worthy of the Fire Lord’s approval, and as such, he continues to be frosty and distant, with Zuko, especially. Often he wonders if a grandchild will be enough for his father to talk to him again, or if he’ll have to wait all the day until his child presents as alpha.

“Well - he doubled your forces, didn’t he?” Zuko asks, trying to be optimistic.

“He did,” Zhao confirms.

“And gave your fleet permission to set out two months early?”

“He *did*.” Zhao leans forward to sigh into Zuko’s neck. “But outside the northern campaign, he’s displeased with me. Apparently there’s been renewed fervor in Kirachu. Yet another dissident group. They haven’t *killed* anyone, but they held up some stupid trade ship, made a few scary demands for hand-outs and the usual anti-national garbage. Although the hostages are *alive* , your father has been on my case about it. I think he’s just taking out his anger over the Avatar on everyone around him.”

They stand quietly a moment, Zhao’s grip tightening. Zuko is afraid his anger is bleeding outwards with intent to hurt, and tenses in anticipation. It takes him a while to accept that this is a normal hug.

“I imagine my father’s not pleased,” Zuko eventually muses, which is an understatement. Were anyone but the Avatar’s companions under suspicion for allowing his escape, those guilty parties would surely meet an agonizing fate. Zuko can’t see Zhao’s eyes with the way they’ve embraced, and can only imagine what he’d find there. The complicated storm that indicates Zhao, too, is thinking about their shared secret.

Swiftly, as if also yearning to see his face again, Zhao pulls his head out of Zuko’s neck to look him in the eye. “No regrets,” he says, curtly.

Zuko shakes his head and affirms: “None.” And he means it. Even if he still doesn’t understand why he let the Avatar go, even as he still wrestles with the guilt of it, Zuko knows deep down that he would make the same choice again if he had to. No matter the cost.

---

Azula witnesses one of these reunions on a rare visit to the Lesser Hall. One moment Zuko is being lifted into the air, wreathed in Zhao’s praises, and the next he’s making eye contact with his sister from across the room.

Where Azula’s normally careful to keep her image as pristine as her reputation, her hair is now badly brushed, and she’s foregone her usual makeup for a bare face that makes her look terribly young. She fixes them with such an ugly scowl that Zuko immediately thinks, *She knows* . It’s as if those furious golden eyes can see right into their skulls, pinpointing the origin of their affection on that rainy night out on the palace lawn. Their happiness must seem like a mockery to her.

Yet for once, Azula holds back her vitriol. All she says is some sisterly thing (“Would you *move* this gag-worthy display somewhere more private?”) before trudging off down the corridor like a nature spirit - there one moment, gone the next, impossible to prove her presence. To compare Azula to such a spirit is the best way to capture how reclusive she’s become, as she not only avoids the Lesser Hall, but has stopped venturing out of her room altogether.

Although they haven’t been close in years, seeing her this way tugs at some long-buried brotherly impulse in Zuko’s chest. She wasn’t *always* his rival; there was a time where they were each other’s only playmates. Yet to talk to her directly is too much of a risk. Knowing Azula, she would just take advantage of his affection to needle the truth out of him, so Zuko decides to take a more indirect route by talking to his uncle.

Predictably, Iroh beams when Zuko asks after his sister’s health. “Thank you for asking, Zuko. Your sister is wounded, yes, but I assure you she just needs some time to regroup. From what I can gather, she is feverishly planning her next move.”

Ah, of course. Silly of him to think one little defeat could knock her prone. “I’m glad she’s confiding in you again,” Zuko admits. “I’d have thought she was still furious about the Avatar.”

“Yes. Among other things.” Iroh gives him a surreptitious look, then glances around as if in need of a servant. They are totally alone. “Zuko, your sister recently criticized me for my... lack of vigilance.”

Zuko frowns at the insult. Trust Azula to dig her knife into a flaw you didn’t even know you had. “What does that mean?”

Here Iroh pauses, as if carefully choosing his words. “Well. She thinks that I’ve been quick to accept when you tell me things are okay.” Then, hurriedly, as if shooing away the specter of their last fight, “Now, I told her that I merely trust your word - after all, I once broke your trust in *me*, and I want to rebuild that as best as I can. But she insisted to me that you’ve been putting on a brave face and that I would be letting an important opportunity go to waste if I didn’t at least ask you if everything was alright.”

Zuko thinks back to the last time he really talked to Azula, and has to resist the urge to touch his eye. “In what way does Azula think I’m putting on a brave face?”

Iroh opens his hands. “I suppose she means all of it. The departure of your friends. *My* departure.” He hesitates. “And though you seem happy, no marriage is easy all the time, let alone those which are arranged. Zuko, I want you to know that you never have to minimize your pain for my sake. You can talk to me about anything.”

His uncle is reopening old wounds, but with such a loving desperation that Zuko doesn’t have the heart to be mad. His uncle’s hands hover over his, not touching, not reaching, but near enough in case he needs to take them up. Zuko stares at his knuckles, gnarled with age, and suddenly can’t resist the urge to reward him for his kindness.

“I’ll admit things were… tougher than I was letting on,” Zuko says. “Like you said, I didn’t ever think marriage would be *easy* , but I didn’t expect it to be like… like…”

“Like what?” Concern knots Iroh’s brow.

Strangely, Zuko isn’t thinking of the moment Zhao hit him. Or the punishing sex after their fight about Ty Lee. He isn’t even thinking of Zhao pressing him against the wall, his grip on his upper arms hard enough to bruise. Instead, Zuko thinks about the aftermath, and all he had to do to clean up afterwards. The struggle to cake enough powder under his eye. Burning the sheets in the garden. The rare triumph of coaxing Zhao down from a fury.

“It’s a little bit like firebending,” Zuko admits, softly. “You can make fire do what you want, but only within certain bounds. It’s the only element that seems to have a mind of its own. Likewise, you can’t… control people. You can only do your best to understand why they do the things they do.”

Iroh catches his gaze, anchoring him back to the present. “...One small hole in your metaphor. You can’t reason with fire. But you can reason with people.”

“Right.” Zuko shakes his head to banish the heavy memories. “So we had a rocky start. But things are going well now.” He remembers the mantra. “Better than well - they’re *amazing*. I couldn’t be happier.”

“That’s good,” Iroh says. He smiles as his eyes roam over Zuko’s face, the search going unnervingly long before he remembers he should probably break the silence. “I’m glad for you. I hope that if anything happened, though, you *would* tell me.”

Zuko gives a stiff smile. “But nothing *is* wrong. So we don’t have to worry about that.”

Iroh hears the testiness lurking in this reply, and relents. “Of course, Zuko. I’m very happy for you.”

---

When Zuko’s bruise turns a mossy green and shrinks to the size of a thumb, Zhao suggests they attend a party being thrown by the wife of a fellow war council member. The way Zhao specifically phrases it is, “Now that you’re feeling better, we should get out of the palace for once,” as if Zuko’s been indisposed by a mysterious illness of no particular origin.

Zuko’s immediate reaction to any mention of a party is to resist. He can already picture himself trailing after Zhao like a decorative shadow, dragging down raucous bouts of laughter with delayed, tight-lipped smiles. His teacher Aloki used to say that while some omegas have the sort of ruthless wit that will allow them to excel as political, not just romantic partners to their mates, Zuko is of the camp better off perfecting arts like grace and composure, which require no wit at all. Zuko knows when to shut up, but lacks the wherewithal to know when he’s supposed to break form to laugh or smile without seeming thick, which is a roundabout way of saying he hates people and he hates parties.

But Zhao’s sole regret coming out of the Avatar incident is the fact he lost a chance to drink in a large group with the cancellation of the banquet, so he says, “Come on - it’ll be a chance for me to forge some important connections.” And when that draws a deeper grimace from Zuko, “Weren’t you just saying you miss your friends? Make some new ones.”

It’s not like Zuko can deny Zhao anything he wants; still, he tries to wheedle out one last time, saying, “Won’t it be suspicious if we’re celebrating this close to the Avatar’s escape?”

Zhao scoffs. “If anything, it’ll be more suspicious if we *don’t.* What self-respecting royalty doesn’t take at least a little pleasure when the people preceding them in the line of succession fail?” (*My* *uncle,* Zuko thinks.) “No, people will be expecting us to jeer at Azula at least a little. We’ll seem spineless otherwise.”

“Well… so long as word doesn’t get back to my father. It’s not *just* Azula’s failure we’d be celebrating.”

Zhao waves him off. “Of course, of course. We’ll be tasteful about it.”

So they go to the party. The home where it’s being held is a few miles outside the capital and very lavish - Zhao remarks that if palaces weren’t all Zuko had ever known, he’d be impressed by the size of it. It’s protected behind a tall wooden gate, despite the fact there’s not much outside to threaten it aside from some sparse shrubbery and an empty road. Zuko can hear the roar of voices even as they come through the gates, held back by the grand double doors like a flood waiting to drown everything in its wake. His distaste must show; Zhao tells him to stop pouting.

To Zuko’s horror, Zhao abandons him almost immediately after they greet the hosts and grab their drinks. Zhao doesn’t even have the courtesy to slip secretively off into the crowd, actively *chiding* Zuko as he removes his hand from his arm. “I want to go talk to the other council members. Go mingle!”

“I’ll try, but I don’t think I can do it myself the *entire* night,” Zuko confesses. He hates how clingy he feels, but the prospect of even an hour of this is making him sick to his stomach.

Zhao’s responding laugh is genuinely amused, which makes Zuko feel more embarrassed, but less nervous. At least Zhao isn’t annoyed. In fact, he’s been fantastically cheerful since Zuko let the Avatar escape, which is maybe why Zuko is daring to disagree with him at all. He’s grown used to this friendly side of Zhao. So much so that he’d rather not leave its familiar warmth.

“I *promise* it won’t be the entire night. It’s not like you’re going to make friends with your husband hovering over your shoulder. Besides, if you’re nervous, I have an easy solution.” And Zhao takes the hand Zuko’s using to hold his drink, gently raising it closer and closer to his face.

With remorse, Zuko watches his husband stride across the room and make some booming, jocular greeting to a severe-looking man three times his age, who throws his arms open and absorbs him into a fatherly embrace almost immediately. Come to think, the ages at this party are all over the place. Zhao is by far the most fresh-faced of the council members, with most of the men showing at least a hint of gray in their beards. The wives are generally older than Zuko, but by how much varies. There aren’t any omegas his age, but there’s a gaggle of skinny, perfectly coiffed women who don’t look *terribly* older than he does. He doesn’t have to rely on scent to designate everyone’s status; there is a clear divide between the austere shoulder spikes, chest guards, and bracers of the military alphas, versus the silken, draping fabrics and wide-sleeved robes of the omegas. As the room divides by sex, it does so by color, too, with the alphas in dark grays, blacks, and maroons, and the omegas clad in springier shades punctuated here and there by various gold accoutrements. If there are betas here, they are either dressed to blend in, or are amongst the plainly-dressed servants fetching drinks.

Speaking of which. Looking around, he has yet to see another omega he can definitively say is male; staring into the bustle of shoulder pads, he comes to the realization that there is also only the one female alpha at this party in his eyeline. Her name is General Mazeli, and he has met her before, having spoken to her on his father’s request several times. Actually, now that he’s really looking around the room, he recognizes more of the alphas at this party than their mates for a similar reason. He glances at the group of youngest-looking wives again, hoping this time he sees someone he recognizes, maybe a classmate of Ty Lee and Mai he’s bumped into before, and catches one of the women looking pointedly in his direction. She whispers to the woman next to her, who then *also* turns to look at him. Do they seem mad, or is he just nervous about being here? He turns away because not looking at them anymore is the fastest way he can think to eliminate this anxiety, second only to inhaling his glass of shochu, which he also does.

Zuko naturally gravitates towards the wall as he sizes up the crowd, not quite intoxicated enough yet to drift comfortably from group to group. He’s been watching the liquid in his glass steadily drain, willing himself not to spiral into sad-drunk, when he lifts his face to find he’s no longer alone.

The man at his side is deviously handsome and somewhere in his fifties, with a finely groomed goatee. He catches Zuko’s eye and smiles, and with a start, Zuko recognizes him as Huo Keohso *-* *the man who drove Ty Lee into hiding*.

Does Zuko’s disapproval show? He can’t tell; Huo just beams at him, as if they’re old friends who have no reason to be anything but thrilled to see each other. “Prince Zuko,” he says, “a pleasure to meet at last.” He bows low, and Zuko gathers himself enough to give the responding polite nod of acknowledgement such deference usually earns. Once he bends out of his bow, Huo’s eyes sweep his form, as if sizing him up.

“I’ve been told you and my fair Ty Lee were very good friends,” he says, and Zuko does not imagine the glint in his eye. “It’s so terrible, how she disappeared. Her mothers are worried sick.”

“You keep in touch with them?” Zuko asks.

“Yes,” Huo says, and it’s unfair how easy-going his smile appears. “After all, they’re family, now. Or will be, in time.”

Zuko’s stomach twists. Huo hasn’t given up on finding her. It’s for both the sake of her safety and his own selfish loneliness that he asks, “Do you have any leads?”

“No,” Huo says, all bright, straight teeth. “Do *you?* ”

“No,” Zuko says, wishing he were lying like this man probably thinks he is. The eyes flicker across his form again, once, twice, and then Huo is leaning back to admire him as one might a painting they’ve initially stepped too close to.

“They’re right, you know,” Huo says, cryptically. “You have a very - *arresting* aura.”

His word choice is indicative of Ty Lee; to hear this ism torn from her mouth makes Zuko want to punch a fiery brand against Huo’s.

Huo takes Zuko’s silence for an imperious refusal, and raises his hands in a laidback self-defense. “Pardon me for being too forward with a prince, but I simply had to comment on it... it’s as if it’s pulling me in.” He twirls one hand in a circle. “You’re like a… a whirlpool. A sensual whirlpool.”

He seems terribly pleased with himself for this simile, smiling so widely Zuko can see the sharp points of his canines. *No*, Zuko thinks, *absolutely not, no, no,* and without so much as a goodbye, he turns on his heel and escapes into the nearest cluster of people.

Huo doesn’t seem to follow him, but Zuko refuses to look over his shoulder like a creature hunted. Instead he keeps an eye out for Zhao. He spots his husband fairly quickly from across the room, laugh audible even over the general noise of party conversation. Seeing that he’s surrounded by other alphas makes Zuko nervous to approach, and so he finds himself watching his husband from afar as he interacts with other people.

It’s a strange experience: Zuko often feels he is locked under Zhao’s gaze, but for once he is the one to observe, although in secrecy, which gives the act a tinge of guilt. Still, he observes the boisterous way Zhao elbows the man next to him, then gestures widely, a burst of laughter following whatever he says from the group surrounding him. From the way the others fold around him, pawing at him in jest, trying to draw his eye, it’s clear that Zhao is the center of these men’s attention. Zuko isn’t sure why the notion that his husband has friends is such a surprise, but he’s just such a… a solitary homebody most of the time, clinging to Zuko as often as Zuko clings to him. If he’s capable of talking to others, of being this popular sort of person, then why doesn’t he engage in it more often? If Zuko found enthralling a crowd as easy as Zhao seems to, he wouldn’t despise parties so much. Maybe Zhao doesn’t do this sort of thing often for Zuko’s sake. Maybe Zuko’s been holding him back.

Zuko’s social anxiety could perhaps abide if he were a normal person, drifting from group to group, before being passively absorbed into the proceedings. Unfortunately, as royalty, his presence must be acknowledged; when he approaches people, their spines snap straight, then carve forward at impossible angles as everyone competes to be the most respectful towards his title. It makes him uncomfortable. What was a social crack in the mud becomes a chasm, potential friendships stumbling over the edge and into the abyss. This was all easier when they were children and stupidly oblivious of the social divide, a thought that makes Zuko miserable because he wasn’t any good at making friends back then, either.

Still. He eventually has enough alcohol in his body that he can stomach approaching a non-intimidating cluster of women. He’s chosen this group specifically because they are neither so boisterous that he’d be afraid of interrupting longtime friends, nor so icy that their demeanor puts him off entirely. When they spot him, they immediately stop what they’re doing to bow in greeting, smiling and composed, although he does notice a couple strands of hair fly out of the topknots of two women to his left, their cheeks rosy from drink.

It seems he’s walked up just as they’re talking about children. “What about you? Have you been trying?” asks a woman named Ai, and suddenly the eyes of the group are on him.

“We are,” Zuko replies. It’s a timely question, considering his next heat’s starting in a matter of days. He’s not sure if that’s a detail that would be inappropriate to divulge; is it fine because they’re all omegas, or is it completely rude to discuss in public? It probably doesn’t help that he doesn’t know these people well, so he lamely finishes, “No luck, yet.”

Ai smiles politely. “That’s fine. You were only just married a few months ago, weren’t you? It rarely happens the first time.”

“It did for my cousin,” says a freckled lady named Suzuna. “It’s supposed to be harder for boys, but he got pregnant in a heartbeat, so I’m sure you won’t have too difficult an experience.”

Ironically, it’s only because she’s said that this common knowledge he’s never heard of is untrue that he starts to feel anxious about it. Zuko is painfully average; if most male omegas struggle to get pregnant, then he most likely will, too. He thinks he sees Ai shoot Suzuna the briefest of annoyed looks before focusing back on Zuko. “Do you have a preference whether you have a boy or girl?”

“No,” Zuko says, honestly.

When he doesn’t elaborate, Ai fills the silence. “That’s a good attitude to have. You’re sure not to be disappointed.”

“I’ll bet your husband wants a boy - better chances of getting an alpha, then,” Suzuna supplies.

“He hasn’t expressed a preference, either,” Zuko says, although he thinks she’s probably right.

Because his responses are so minimal, eventually they stop prodding him and move onto other topics. They’re discussing the best way to ensure beta children don’t feel left out once the household starts to shift around their siblings’ presentations, when another woman steps boldly up to the group. And “bold” truly is the best way to describe her approach, as well as everything else about her. Many people at this party are wearing red, but she makes it into a statement with a blindingly bright shade that almost hurts to look at. Everything about her is big, from her hair, to her smile, to her tits *-* Agni, they are practically falling out of her dress. When she bows, Zuko can’t help but to divert his gaze in terror of witnessing the sort of accident that could grind the party to a halt, but when he dares look at her again, her wardrobe has not malfunctioned.

“It is such an honor to meet you, Prince Zuko. I’ve always heard you were quite pretty for a boy, but the stories haven’t done you justice, for you *are* a vision to behold!” She thrusts a heavily ringed hand towards him. “My name is Makamae, jewel of Ma’Inka, wife of that horrid curmudgeon you know as Commander Lei. Isn’t it a funny coincidence our husbands are both commanders in the navy? I’m sure your Zhao will outrank my Lei in a matter of years. Lei’s been stuck with the same fleet for damn near a decade - although lucky for me, he’s been on shore leave since he injured his back. Unlucky for him, of course, but I’d kiss that damn dirtbender who crippled him if I could, I’m so happy to have him home! You’d think this war was eternal. If only there was some way we could just raze everything to the ground without the expense of our own, then we could finally have our boys home where they belong.”

“Makamae, you’re scaring the hell out of him,” says a tall, knifelike woman to her right. Her name escapes Zuko, but she has a deadpan delivery that reminds him somewhat of Mai.

“Oh, I am *not,* Li,” Makamae huffs. She pulls out a paper fan that Zuko somehow didn’t notice, distracted by everything else about her intense entrance, and begins fanning herself with it. The folds in the paper warp the image of the tigermonkey from ferociously snarling to recoiling in terror of her. “My dear, how *are* things at the royal palace? Are you all holding up okay? It’s such a *shame* about the Avatar.”

The mere mention rattles him. Zuko hopes it doesn’t show. “We’re devastated by what happened. My sister was very careful in her preparations.”

“Evidently not careful enough,” Makamae says - pouting, not sneering. She ignores a side-eye from Ai and an elbow from Li, saying, “All things happen for a reason, though - I’ve heard this little jail break has given your husband the opportunity to invade the North? Such an ambitious feat!”

“Yes, it’s a small consolation to gain from an otherwise terrible tragedy,” Zuko replies stiffly. He practiced a few different responses in anticipation of this topic, not trusting himself to think of anything in the moment. Considering how much he’s had to drink tonight trying to psych himself up to talk to strangers, he’s doubly grateful for the script.

“Obviously we *all* agree the Avatar’s escape was such a tragedy,” Makamae agrees, “but a part of me isn’t exactly surprised things went south… Our honorable Fire Lord cannot be faulted, but your sister has been a little off-kilter lately, hasn’t she?”

Zuko takes the bait, sluggish to notice what’s being dangled in front of him until he stupidly snatches at it. “Not at all. Why would you say that?”

“ *Well,* ” Makamae says, voice dropping into a conspiratorial stage-whisper, “In all honesty, I never understood why a bright girl like that aligned herself with old General Iroh. Wonderful man, honorable man, but surely there was a reason his father’s dying wish was for him *not* to take the throne? It just seems like if Princess Azula wanted to invite good luck, she’d have partnered with someone else, or gone alone. As it is, this humiliation with the Avatar stands to be… *her* Ba Sing Se.”

“ *Makamae,”* Ai says in a warning tone. Perhaps she sensed the flare in Zuko’s temper the moment Makamae brought up his uncle.

“Oh - this topic is so dreary,” Suzuna whinges. “Let’s talk of something else. A Fire Nation *victory*.”

“That’s what I was trying to do - the invasion of the North Pole *will* be a victory, won’t it, Prince Zuko?” Makamae insists. “So long as your Zhao can conquer what hasn’t been claimed in a hundred years of war - but you have faith in your man, don’t you?”

*Stay quiet,* shouts a voice that sounds like Aloki. *Don’t make a scene.* Still, alcohol tugs on Zuko’s self-control with greedy fingers; he cannot resist levelling Makamae with a glare, even if it is a silent one. The sight of it makes all the color drain from the other omegas’ faces.

“Come on, now, Mae,” Ai says, voice wavering. “We were discussing our children when you walked up. How’s your son, Tetsu?”

Makamae brightens as one only can when someone is asked about their children. “He’s doing just *wonderful*. Did I tell you he’s the best bender in his cohort? His master says he’s even beaten a few alphas when they’ve done mixed classes.”

Zuko barely follows the rest of the conversation, simmering quietly as he sips his drink. The alcohol probably isn’t helping him keep his cool, but he needs something to occupy his mouth before he says something he’ll regret. Agni only knows that this woman is some indispensable political ally, or perhaps Commander Lei has access to resources Zhao will need in the near future.

Speaking of Zhao. Zuko can see him on the other side of the room, talking to General Mazeli. The hope that the youngest member and only female council member might be building up some sort of solidarity crumbles as he observes the sour expressions on their faces. General Mazeli’s brow is furrowed, her lips pursed into a thin line, and he certainly knows that stiff-jawed look on Zhao. Zuko *would* worry about that, except this is a party packed full of people whose respect they absolutely need. Surely Zhao wouldn’t start an argument here.

&#46;..Like how he absolutely wouldn’t fight War Minister Qin in the middle of a banquet. Zuko is starting to think he needs to walk over there and de-escalate things when a snatch of the group’s conversation throws him entirely off guard.

“I’d constantly wake up to him already inside me,” Makamae says, gesturing with her glass in a way that would be alarming, had she not sucked it dry. “You wouldn’t know it to look at him, now, but that man was a *dog* in his youth. You could not beat him off me with a flaming dao!”

Ai scoffs. “Makamae, don’t exaggerate*.* ”

“I’m *not*,” she insists, getting heated. “You realize all of our children were conceived while I was asleep? I told him to cut it out, but that man never listens to a word I say, so I stopped bothering.”

“That’s just awful,” Suzuna says, looking queasy. “How do you allow that sort of behavior?”

Makamae rolls her eyes. “It is all about picking your battles, and that one was not getting me anywhere. Honestly, after a while, you sleep right through it!”

From how badly she’d made her first impression, Zuko would’ve never dreamed he’d have anything in common with this woman. He isn’t so much unsettled by the topic itself as the way the other women are looking at Makamae, pity mixed with disgust, like this is just about the saddest and cruelest thing they’ve ever heard of a husband doing.

*What children*, he thinks. *What overgrown children.*

“Maybe this isn’t the best topic for the current company,” Li says, eyes flickering over to him.

“What? Why on earth would you say that?” Makamae looks at him as if she knew very well he had heard her and did not care one bit. “Prince Zuko isn’t *such* an innocent flower. I’m sure your husband does things that absolutely floor you all the time, doesn’t he?”

Over her shoulder, Zhao explodes, giving Zuko the perfect excuse not to answer. He watches his husband let loose on General Mazeli, finger jabbing into her face as he shouts. Snatches of his rant can be heard even from across the room, but that may be because the noise of the party has died down to better listen in.

“I need to go check on that,” Zuko says faintly. He pulls free of the group without pausing to see how anyone is reacting to this absolute embarrassment. Probably more disgust and pity.

Curiously, the closer he gets to his husband, the less of the fight he can hear, the sound of his own blood roaring so loudly in his ears that it drowns everything else out. Instead he watches the shape anger forms in Zhao’s mouth, curling sharp and hungry. There’s a mean glint in Mazeli’s eye as she glares down the finger pointing at her, as if she’s only moments from biting it off. Zuko finds him stopping a distance away, as if hitting an invisible wall; one more step, and one or both of them may finally notice him. He’s not sure anymore if that’s a good thing.

In the end, Zhao storms away, still not noticing Zuko as he reluctantly trails after him. On his way out, Zuko glances around to determine exactly how much of the party has turned to… ah, yes. Literally every eye in the room follows him and Zhao as they disappear down a back hallway.

Only when his blood has calmed enough that he can hear his own footsteps on the hardwood floors does Zuko call out, “Zhao.”

Zhao waves him off without turning around.

“I know you’re upset, Zhao, but if you want to talk-”

Zhao rounds on him, eyes blazing. “*Don’t*.”

Zuko obeys the warning instantly, halting where he stands. Zhao throws open a nearby door and stomps out into the darkness of the yard. Zuko can hear the chirrup of cricket-cicadas in the pitch blackness; from the lack of noise and light, it would seem the party doesn’t really extend to that part of the property.

Zuko steps up to the door, hesitating on the threshold as he watches his husband get swallowed by the night air, the only sign of him his angry footsteps crunching in the grass. If Zuko wanted, he could probably get some real privacy with Zhao out there, but the thought of following him where no one else can see sets him on edge. (Although surely it’s paranoia. Zhao wouldn’t do anything to him now that they’ve made up. And certainly not with everyone just inside?)

No, he isn’t going to follow Zhao out there. Better to let him calm himself down. Zuko shuts the door and turns around, the empty hall seeming to lurch at an angle when he considers the possibility of rejoining the party. Warm light touches a doorway at the end of the hall, loud laughter beckoning him back into the arms of jackals - no, he isn’t going there, either.

There’s another door on the opposite side of the hall that’s cracked open; in an instant, he’s pushed his way inside. It looks like a drawing room of sorts, laid out with a series of cushy couches and chairs. He sits down, lighting a small candle that waits on a table beside him. It does little to chase away the all-encompassing darkness.

Too late, he considers how invasive it is to invite himself into a space deliberately closed off from the rest of the party; he resolves not to snoop around the shelves, at least, for fear of seeming nosy. Unfortunately, that leaves him with little to occupy himself except his own thoughts. He dwells over every embarrassing moment that has elapsed over the evening: his slow responses to conversation, the things he could have said instead (he’ll probably be both arguing with and defending Makamae in the back of his head for months to come), and finally, the scene Zhao caused. Zuko should have gone over there before things escalated. He should be outside with Zhao, now, deescalating things. He feels pathetic for how afraid he is of his own husband, knowing they’re trying to rebuild their trust in one another; things are supposed to be good between them now, yet here Zuko is, hiding in the dark by himself instead of putting in the work.

A few minutes later, the door to the drawing room creaks open. General Mazeli steps inside and shuts the door softly behind her before she notices Zuko there; when he stands to greet her, she jerks back from him in surprise.

Her eyes harden the moment she recognizes him. Still, she affords him the manners owed royalty, bowing stiffly. “Apologies for walking in on you, Prince Zuko. I thought this room was empty. I’ll leave you to it.”

“No,” he says, “You stay, I’ll leave. I’m sure I’m the last person you want to see right now, given the grief my husband has caused you. The least I can do is give you space to relax.”

For once, he hasn’t said the wrong thing. Instantly she seems to melt, a warmth creeping into her voice as she says, “No. You aren’t the last person, by far.”

“You don’t have to say that.”

“I mean it. You and Zhao are two different people. I won’t hold you responsible for his actions.”

“Good,” Zuko says, sincere. “I’ve always liked you, Mazeli. It’d be a shame to lose your respect.”

Even in the low light of the candle, he thinks he sees her cheeks color. She sits down, leaving a chair between them.

“Do you mind if I ask what you were arguing about?” Zuko asks.

“That you’re unsure gives me hope we weren’t loud enough to disturb the entire party.” She waves off his concern, not meeting his eye. “Truthfully, everything and nothing. I wouldn’t bore you with the details.”

“I’m happy to listen, if you want to talk,” Zuko says mildly. He turns his legs towards her, and after a moment, she angles herself towards him, too.

“...It was small, but. Zhao was saying he hates the way the senior naval officers in the war council are quick to dismiss his opinions. I said I didn’t remember him being brushed off terribly often, and he brought up a… an example from just this morning, a tiff with Commander Lei. You know me, Prince Zuko; I’m painfully honest, even when people might not want to hear it, and I agreed wholeheartedly with what Lei had said. Your husband is very talented for his age, and very ambitious, but that doesn’t replace experience. I told him so, and that’s what started the shouting.”

“Oh, no - I’m so sorry,” Zuko says, hand landing on his chest.

Mazeli grimaces. “Well, let’s give Zhao *some* credit - I didn’t say it so articulately as that. I was a little irate with drink, so really I told him to stuff his whining, because he could stand to learn from others.”

Zuko’s horror must show on his face, because she lets out a bark of a laugh. “I know, I know. Talking like that to the Prince of Self Control. I must have a death wish.”

Zuko blinks. “Pardon?”

“Oh, er-” Mazeli *definitely* blushes deeply at that fumble. “It’s a nickname. A, er, sarcastic nickname. For your man.”

He takes a moment to process. Then, “That’s… a bit cruel.”

“Maybe. But it’s accurate, isn’t it?” Mazeli scratches her neck, averting her gaze. “He has a rotten temper.”

“He has his faults,” Zuko admits. “Still. I don’t think the nicknames are necessary.”

“Right,” she says. “Sorry. I’m sure that wasn’t what you wanted to hear.”

“No, it’s - I understand.” Because he does. Perhaps better than anyone.

They talk for some time like this, sitting in the dark. They keep their voices down not because they’re afraid of getting caught, but because the silence seems to demand it. As his eyes adjust, Zuko traces the familiar lines of her weathered face, the wide shoulders, the squarish jaw. At times her responses are nearly shy, and she blushes away from him like a schoolkid from a crush. Which, most likely, she has. Zuko spent nearly two years sidling up to every alpha Ozai asked him to. Nothing ever *happened*, but he knows what his purpose was, and he knows that if he did in fact see the wives of these alphas glaring at him, earlier, it’s not without reason.

At any rate. Given Zhao’s complete resistance earlier, it’s nice to talk to someone who *wants* to be soothed. Zuko has always liked General Mazeli’s lilting voice, so he keeps her to himself for a while, all the while privately wondering what it would be like to be married to her. It’s a fantasy borne of curiosity, not lust or intent. She’s much older than him, even more than Zhao. They talk until whatever bad blood may have been spilled between her and Zhao is completely wiped away, then they find their way back to the party.

They find Zhao has already beat them there. When Zuko spies him across the room, his shoulders are still a little stiff, but he’s smiling as he talks to a uniformed woman (Mazeli isn’t the only one, after all). As if sensing Zuko’s eyes on him, Zhao glances up, and from a distance, meets his gaze.

Then pointedly frowns at him. Zhao says something to the woman in uniform before stalking - *walking* towards Zuko, who has to resist the urge to step backwards into the hallway behind him.

“Prince Zhao,” Mazeli greets when he’s close enough to hear. “About earlier, I want to ap-”

“Why are you two together?” he asks. Zuko shrinks from the question.

“Your husband was just talking me off the ledge,” Mazeli says, tone light. “Speaking of which, I was thinking we should put this whole thing behind us.”

Zhao ignores her olive branch, looking at Zuko. “Have you two been alone together?”

“Yes,” Zuko admits.

“How long?” Zhao asks.

“I assure you he was totally safe with me. It was just a few-”

Zhao cuts Mazeli off yet again with a raised hand, not even looking at her as he does it. “Have you two been talking since I left, earlier?”

“...Yes,” Zuko admits, after some hesitation.

“You’ve been together this *whole* time?”

Zuko frowns. “Yes. I’m sorry if that bothers you.”

The funny thing is, he’s being sincere; no one has to convince Zuko that anything and everything is worth apologizing for. But his tendency towards flat tones and his poor word choice make him sound sarcastic. Mazeli throws him a look before she clears her throat and tries, yet again, to wrap this conflict up. “Look, Zhao - we both said some very hard-headed things tonight, but that’s what happens when you give a couple of firebenders too much booze, right? There’s bound to be some heat. I say we forget the whole thing.”

There is a solid second where Zhao watches them both through narrowed eyes. Zuko holds his breath, awaiting the fall-out.

Then a smile oozes across Zhao’s face, thick as blood. “Sure. We can put this behind us.” He takes the offered hand for the curtest of shakes. “I do apologize for my temper earlier, Mazeli; I may simply be exhausted.”

His eyes slide over to Zuko. “Are you ready to leave?”

Zuko nods dumbly. He’s wanted to leave for the better part of the night, so he should be grateful. Yet something about Zhao’s bearing gives him pause. His husband offers a few goodbyes to his fellow officers but is mostly silent as he carves his way through the crowded bodies.

To Zuko’s surprise, Ai, Li, and Suzuna catch him by the arm right before he steps out the door, taking the time to bid him goodbye and ask if he’s going to be at the next event, some birthday for so-and-so he hasn’t met. Despite having said almost nothing the whole night, the women seem to be eagerly awaiting his answer. He supposes as a prince, his company is inherently valuable, even if it isn’t all that enjoyable. The thought depresses him.

His nerves remain tightly wound as he steps into the carriage and finds himself alone with Zhao. They only coil tighter as the carriage pulls away from the house onto a dark road without any sign of a tantrum yet to pass; and tighter still as they journey longer into the night. Zhao doesn’t lose his temper on him, but he doesn’t talk, either, staring silently out the window. Zuko tries and fails several times to catch his eye.

It’s not until they’re riding through the palace gates that Zhao heaves a dramatic sigh. Although it’s testy, Zuko can’t resist the need to placate, instantly jumping at the chance to ask, “What is it?”

Zhao sucks his teeth. “I’m just thinking about how you weren’t even there when Mazeli and I had our disagreement, so there’s no way you even knew what it was about. You saw me miserable and thought the best move would be to go to *her* and comfort *her* .” He crosses his arms, making hostile eye contact with Zuko through his reflection on the window.

“I wasn’t comforting her,” Zuko replies.

Zhao looks disgusted, then. “Really? What else would *you* even have to talk to a decorated general about?”

One would think humiliation an emotion capable of providing instant sobriety, but heat floods Zuko’s face and makes his response fumbling, lacking confidence. “I - know Mazeli.”

“ *How?* ” Zhao asks, disbelief plain in his voice.

“From those assignments my father used to give me.”

Zhao’s eyes sharpen to the quick; Zuko’s gaze falls as quickly to his lap as a child’s face behind a blanket, convinced not looking is as good as banishing the monster. When Zhao doesn’t say anything for a while, words spill out of Zuko in the hopes of extinguishing all that fury before it can burn him away.

“I’m sorry,” Zuko says. “I didn’t mean to - to hurt your feelings. I was sick of the party, so I went off into a room by myself. General Mazeli happened to come into the same one by chance, and I know her and I like her, so we talked a little bit - it wasn’t anything inappropriate.”

Zhao scoffs. “Obviously. I would *hope* you’d have the restraint not to cheat on me in the middle of a party.”

Even as indirect as it is, the accusation grates on Zuko’s nerves. “Zhao, don’t. I wouldn’t *ever* .”

“And I’m not so crass to say that you *would* , but I’m sure you had plenty terrible to say about me.” It’s not a large compartment, but Zhao *is* a large man, so when he leans forward to grip his spouse by the knees, he forces him to rear flat against the back of his seat. “You really didn’t say a single word about me? You’re pretending I didn’t come up at all?”

The the physical contact is making Zuko nervous. “You - yes, of course you did, but we weren’t saying anything bad, just-”

“Just *what?* ”

“Just *nothing,* we only mentioned you for a second, and the point wasn’t to talk behind your back! I just wanted to calm her down because I was nervous if she stayed mad at you it’d hurt your career, and I wanted to help…”

Zuko feels like he’s babbling, stupidly drunk, and Zhao only turns up the heat of his humiliation by rolling his eyes. “Well, thank you for single-handedly *saving my career* .”

The carriage lurches to a stop. Zhao neglects to hold the door, storming off into the Lesser Hall without a glance backwards. By the time Zuko has gathered the many stifling layers of his robe and hopped down (thankfully without stumbling over and scraping a knee; he is *definitely* still wobbly with drink), he has to run to catch up, nearly tripping up the steps to the entrance.

Zhao is pacing their room like a caged animal when he enters. “It’s not even just the reminder of how your father whored you out to every fucking alpha in the royal court while I was risking my life for this country-”

“Leave my father out of this-”

“-it’s the fact that you went after *her,”* Zhao says, voice rising. “You went after another alpha instead of me. You spent *the whole night* comforting someone who isn’t your husband-”

“I would have followed you, but you brushed me off,” Zuko insists, shutting the door behind him. It hasn’t been able to close all the way since Zhao broke it in a rage, so he has to lift it, slightly, to get it back on the track and properly block their noise from the hall.

Assuming Zhao doesn’t break out into full-fledged shouting. Even as he’s keeping his anger quiet, he jabs an accusing finger in Zuko’s face, making him take a step back against the door. “You… you ran away from me. You’d rather spend your time with her than you would with me, that’s what you were saying with that.”

“I was *not* ,” Zuko says, almost in a whine. He’s frustrated. This argument keeps going in circles. “I wanted to spend the night with you, but you didn’t want me around.”

“Oh, it’s *my* fault,” Zhao rants, “ *I’m* the asshole for pushing you away. I’m the fucking worst human being on earth, never mind everything I’ve sacrificed for you, never mind the fucking *secret* I’m keeping for you-”

Immediately, Zuko shushes him, afraid of being overheard. Predictably, Zhao doesn’t like that. He takes a wobbling step backwards from Zuko, hand flying to the bedpost to steady himself.

“I could *out* you,” he spits, “but I haven’t. Because unlike you, I’m fucking *loyal* .”

Maybe it’s the alcohol spurring him on, or perhaps it’s merely the fact that what Zhao’s said is bald-faced slander, unable to be tolerated even by someone as well-behaved as Zuko. He finds himself shedding his meekness enough to retort, “You think I’m not loyal? Are you forgetting *why* I did what I did? Are you forgetting *why* we’re sharing that secret in the first place?”

Zhao glares at him, the effect softened by his inability to focus his eyes for all that long. He gives an irate sigh and sits (falls and catches himself, really) on the end of the bed.

Zuko takes a brave step towards him. Then another. “Are you really implying I’m not loyal?”

All he gets in response is a burning scoff. Not even eye contact.

There are many things that could be said of Zuko’s relationship with Zhao. He may not have always been honest with him. He may not love him as deeply as he wishes he could. But disloyal? After everything Zuko has sacrificed to keep Zhao here with him? After everything he’s done to preserve their privacy, the lies he’s told to the people he *does* love most in the world?
