The very rice paper windows and wood panelling that had made the Lesser Hall so understated also spelled its end; once the blaze caught, it raged on unfettered by glass or stone. There were foundations of the building left over, vestiges of blackened wood that mapped the borders between rooms, but for the most part, nothing was salvageable. All that remained of the garden stood out in bright green against the devastation that surrounded it. Looking down on the Lesser Hall from above, one could compare it to the charred skeleton of a massive creature that in its last moments had chosen to curl itself protectively around the turtleduck pond.

In recounting the moment Prince Zhao emerged from the fire, a maid described how she’d seen a dark figure rising from hundreds of orange tongues of flame, face twisted not in fear, but an ugly, potent anger. Limp in his arms was Prince Zuko, the delicate storybook prince being carried off to a fire ogre’s dungeon. It was an unusual way to describe a rescue; perhaps it was because of how Zhao spoke to Zuko when he finally opened his eyes.

“Do you see what you’ve done?!” Zhao thundered.

Zuko blinked up at him, gaze unfocused. “What?”

“Because of you, our home is destroyed! We could’ve been *killed* . Do you have anything to say to me?”

They were several meters away from where the Lesser Hall smoldered, Zuko laying on his back in the dirt with Zhao kneeling over him, cradling his head so he could better shout down at him. The staff who had escaped the burning building stood far enough away to respect the princes’ royal status, yet near enough to hear their argument and be disquieted by it. (Although to call it an argument was generous; Prince Zuko’s replies were too feeble, too lacking in conviction.)

“What - happened?” Zuko asked. His fingers reached clumsily for his temple.

“What do you mean, what happened? *You* happened,” Zhao said sternly. “You tried to win an argument by *bending fire* at me!”

Zuko squeezed his eyes shut, hand coming up as if to block Zhao’s voice from hammering down on him. He turned his face away, saying, “I don’t… I wouldn’t have it. It’s not… it’s not that.”

Zhao frowned, confusion blotting out his anger. “What the hell are you talking about?”

“It’s-” Zuko stopped, struggling for words. “I’m saying…”

He wasn’t making eye contact with Zhao, but it wasn’t a deliberate avoidance, as from fear or guilt. The older man grabbed him by the chin and turned the boy’s face this way and that, meeting no resistance. Zuko’s pupils slid around in his skull like egg yolks.

“Hey,” Zhao said, fear creeping into his voice. “How many fingers am I holding up?”

Zuko squinted at them, then squeezed his eyes shut again, neglecting to answer. Zhao seemed to finally appreciate the gravity of the situation; he sat up and shouted orders at the first guard to meet his eye.

“You - run to the Great Hall get us a carriage, now!”

The guard, his features blackened by smoke, balked from Zhao’s command. “I-I’d like to help, Prince Zhao, but some of us are badly burnt here, and-”

“ *And* it sounds like you could use a doctor as well as we can. So *find one!* ” Zhao shouted. Nearby, a maid that was cradling her likely injured hand in her apron flinched and turned away.

While they waited for a doctor, Zhao had Zuko put up in the emerald room. Truthfully he wanted something deeper in the Great Hall with more privacy, but the advisor who came to their aid insisted that the old bedrooms once held by the other royal family members had long fallen into disarray, with Ozai ordering them to be used for storage; it didn’t mean they couldn’t be cleared out, but in the meantime, there was little else available. Zhao was floored that they couldn’t even find a spare bed for Zuko, having to put out the sort of bedroll a servant would sleep on. The Fire Lord himself had yet to make an appearance and comment on this outrage; he was dutifully taking meetings, as though an entire building of his palace hadn’t hours ago burned to the ground.

When a doctor finally got her hands on Zuko, Zhao hovered incessantly. He watched the doctor poke and prod his mate while he took this treatment like a lifeless doll, eyes glassy and distant, limbs limp. The lighting certainly wasn’t doing him any favors; with the greenish hues coming off the walls, he looked deathly ill.

Eventually the doctor sighed and sat back on her haunches. “Prince Zhao. Please leave me to examine the patient in peace.”

Zhao bristled. “I’m not leaving his side. He almost *died* .”

Most people, especially those who were smaller than him, would waver instantly when pushed. The doctor merely levelled him with a stern glare. “I appreciate your worries, Prince Zhao, but I assure you the patient is safe with me. Now you *must* let me work, or I won’t be able to treat him properly.”

After a glaring match failed to make the doctor bend to his will, Zhao got to his feet with a muttered curse and stormed out of the room, slamming the door on his way out. He thought he heard another, louder sigh on the other end.

Iroh chose this moment to finally appear. With all the chaos, Zhao had all but forgotten the old man existed. His face was stricken as he ran up. “My nephew - where is he?”

“With a doctor,” Zhao responded curtly, nodding towards the door. Then, when Iroh reached out to slide it open, “No one’s allowed in there, right now. She’s still trying to figure out what’s wrong with him.”

Iroh stepped back from the door as asked, ringing his hands. “Is he badly burned?”

“Nothing like that,” said Zhao. “I thought I’d carried him out of the worst of it, but then he was babbling nonsense and completely unable to make eye contact.”

Iroh frowned, hands slowing. “...You don’t say. Does the doctor know what it could be?”

“Not yet. She’s taking her damn time,” Zhao huffed. “Anyway. Good to see you’re safe. Where were you when it started?”

“In the east wing. I was preoccupied helping people get out safely.”

Zhao glanced down. Now that Iroh’s sleeve had slid down his arm, he saw his wrist was bandaged. “...You saw the doctor first.”

“What?” Iroh followed his gaze down to his wrapping. “No, I did this myself. I wanted the doctor to focus on the others. There was a maid whose hand...” He shook his head. “It takes a lot to burn a firebender. But that blaze was *fierce* .”

Zhao’s lip curled. “Just so we’re clear: you’re telling me *servants* got to see the doctor first. Before Zuko.”

Iroh frowned. “It wasn’t out of spite, Zhao; there are some very serious injuries amongst our staff.”

Zhao breathed out hard through his nose. “No. I suppose you’re right. More important to see to a few commoners than your own flesh and blood. Never mind that we have no idea what’s even *wrong* with Zuko, that it could be more *dire-* ”

To his absolute fury, Iroh lay a soothing hand on his arm. In grandfatherly tones, he said, “I know you’re worried, but it will be alright. The doctor has him, now.”

It was no use fighting someone so relaxed; he’d only look like a madman in comparison. So Zhao swallowed his reply and let it fizzle, sour in the pit of his stomach.

“Speaking of hands…” Now that Iroh was close, he saw Zhao had been injured, as well. He gently lifted one of his sleeves to get a better look at the white, blistered flesh that trailed up his wrist. “That looks painful.”

Zhao yanked out of Iroh’s grip, shoving both his hands under his arms. “It’s nothing.”

“You should get those looked at.”

“Maybe when the doctor’s free,” Zhao said, curtly. “No use telling her now.”

While he waited outside the door of the emerald room, Zhao sat on a chair that an uninjured servant had brought for him. He pointedly didn’t offer it to Iroh, who didn’t ask to take it; instead the older man elected to kneel on the floor.

At long last the doctor emerged, shutting the door behind her. She waited for both men to stand before addressing them. “General Iroh - good of you to join us.” Her eyes flickered downward. “I don’t remember dressing that. You must let me look at it, later.”

“Nonsense,” said Iroh. “I’m not worried about myself right now - how is my nephew?”

The doctor’s already papery lips thinned. “That depends on what’s wrong with him. If you don’t mind,” and here, she turned to Zhao, “I’d like to ask you a few questions about what happened.”

“If it’ll help Zuko, then I’d be happy to,” he said, straightening his posture.

The doctor nodded. “Good. By your estimates, how long were you in the fire before you escaped?”

Zhao searched his memory. “About fifteen minutes. Give or take.”

The doctor’s eyebrows arched. “That’s quite long, considering. How thick was the smoke around you?”

“We were at the source of the fire, so it was fairly thick.”

“The source?” the doctor echoed.

Zhao nodded. “Zuko set the fire.”

Iroh’s mouth fell open. “What! Why on earth would he do that?”

“He was furious,” said Zhao.

“Zuko would *never* .”

“Why didn’t you try to put it out?” the doctor asked Zhao, ignoring the interjection.

Zhao tossed an irritated glance Iroh’s way before he addressed the doctor in measured tones. “I was trying to calm him down before I attempted anything else. I realize now this was a mistake, and take part of the blame for what happened to the Lesser Hall.” He cleared his throat. “What does this have to do with Zuko’s condition, though?”

“I’m getting there,” said the doctor. “Now - you say you were arguing.”

Zhao’s eyes narrowed. “I said *Zuko* was angry.”

The doctor’s gaze didn’t waver. “Were blows exchanged? Perhaps in self-defense?”

“What’s the meaning of this?” Zhao asked, voice dangerously low. “What are you *implying?* ”

Iroh blanched. “This - this *is* an alarming turn,” he told the doctor. “Maybe if you clarified what your theory was for us, we could help you better?”

“Very well.” The doctor removed her glasses, and began to fastidiously polish them with one wide sleeve of her robe. “Some of Prince Zuko’s symptoms are conclusive with smoke inhalation. He’s disoriented enough that he cannot string more than a few words together, and when he does, he tells me only that his head hurts. He has trouble standing and shows signs of nausea. He doesn’t have the cough that you’d expect to come along with it, but his voice *is* raspy-”

“His voice is always raspy,” said Zhao. Iroh nodded in agreement.

“I see.” The doctor placed her glasses back onto her face. “In any case, we can’t do anything to treat smoke inhalation other than give him fresh air and hope for the best.”

“Bullshit,” Zhao spat, just as Iroh interjected, “That doesn’t really explain the questions you’ve asked Zhao. Do you have another theory of what happened?”

The doctor nodded. “Yes, well. Although it’s certainly possible Prince Zuko breathed in smoke, that’s not generally a cause for alarm for firebenders. I think the real problem is that he has a concussion. Not that the treatment will be all that different. He’ll just need lots of rest and regular monitoring to ensure his condition doesn’t get any worse.”

“Oh.” Zhao’s eyes lit up. “You think he hit his head.”

“Precisely,” said the doctor. “Which is why I ask. Your fight…”

Zhao shook his head. “It wasn’t like that. Zuko was angry, but we didn’t lay a hand on each other. The most violent it got is that Zuko tried to - well, this is arguably worse, but he tried to burn me.” He paused, expression troubled, not really meeting their eyes. “There is one thing, though - I told you we stayed in the fire a while. We were caught up in our shouting match, so I suppose we didn’t notice the place burning down around us. When we finally made our way out, enough damage was done to the building that a beam fell from one of the doorways - it hit him in the head and knocked him briefly unconscious. I had to carry him from the Lesser Hall.”

A deathly quiet filled the corridor.

“Prince Zhao,” said the doctor. “Why didn’t you offer this information sooner?”

He only scowled at her in return. “It was a traumatic experience! And in my defense, you were so roundabout with your questions, I wasn’t sure what details you even wanted.”

“When dealing with a doctor, a list of known injuries is generally a start,” she replied, dryly.

Iroh saw Zhao rearing up in response and stepped in between the two, hands raised. “Now, now - I know we’re all anxious about Zuko’s condition, but all this hostility isn’t helping.”

The doctor sighed, crossing her arms over her chest. “I apologize,” she said. “It’s merely that I take the wellbeing of my patients very seriously, and I want to give the best care I possibly can. That means getting all the information I possibly can.”

Zhao nodded swiftly and took a step back, although he continued to glare down his nose at the doctor. He reached for the door, bristling when she threw out a hand to hold it shut. “You-”

“Prince Zuko cannot see *anyone* right now,” said the doctor. She levelled her gaze upon Iroh, who seemed surprised that he, too, was included in this mandate. “Social stimulation will only confuse and distress him further. Not a soul but myself goes into that room until he makes his recovery.”

“How do I know you can be trusted alone with him?” Zhao asked, lip curling back from his teeth.

“You are perfectly welcome to wait outside the door when I go in to monitor him,” the doctor acquiesced. From her sardonic tone, one could tell she had no patience for accusations that she was abusing her duties, and littler patience still for temperamental men like Zhao. Alpha bravery, or beta indifference? Iroh subtly tipped his chin upward, trying to detect the doctor’s scent, but there was only the smell of smoke. He wasn’t sure if it was a beta absence or his senses temporarily dulled by the fire.

Iroh scratched his beard, frowning. “If I must, I suppose I can leave my nephew alone while he recovers. But we’re not leaving him in that ghastly emerald room, are we?”

Zhao sighed in frustration. “Believe me, I want better for him. But the Fire Lord’s advisor told me this was the best they could do on short notice.”

Iroh mulled this conundrum over, perking up when he found a solution. “Azula isn’t here - we could move Zuko into her room for the time being.”

“She left the capital without you to chaperone her?” Zhao asked.

Iroh cleared his throat. “She expressed to me that she needed some time alone.”

A strange look passed over Zhao’s face. “Alright. Azula’s room it is, then.”

After some convincing, the doctor allowed them to move Zuko, giving them their last glimpses of him for the rest of his recovery. The bottom of his robes were blackened, as were his sleeves, but otherwise there was no sign that he’d been in a fire, his skin smooth and free of burns. When they greeted him, he squinted up at them as if he couldn’t quite make out the features of their faces; it wasn’t until Zhao leaned towards him that his eyes widened with something akin to fear. Zhao stopped where he was, arms frozen as they reached towards Zuko, who had broken out into a violent tremble.

“I-” Zuko’s voice wavered, and suddenly, his eyes were brimming with tears. “I’m sorry. I’m so sorry. I didn’t mean to.”

The depth of the guilt in his voice toyed with Iroh’s doubts; for all his suspicion, it seemed Zhao had been telling the truth about Zuko’s part in the Lesser Hall’s destruction. Watching his spouse crumple into sobs, the apologetic refrain lost to the echo of his cupped hands, the tension seemed to drain out of Zhao’s body. “It’s okay,” he hushed the younger man, his voice syrupy. “I forgive you. We all forgive you.”

When he finally lifted Zuko into his arms, the younger man buried his face in his husband’s chest, tightly clutching the fabric of his shirt. Saddened by the sight, Iroh whispered to the doctor, “It’s unusual for him to cry so openly.”

“This is typical for head trauma,” the doctor murmured back. “He may be emotionally volatile for a few more days.”

They made their way quickly across the palace to Azula’s room. For a fearsome little warrior, she had quite the mountain of pillows and blankets on her bed. Zhao laid Zuko amongst the nest of soft things, pausing to watch him settle in, his expression complicated.

Although by now Zuko’s sobs had all but disappeared, Iroh had taken hold of his nephew’s hand to soothe him. Zuko rolled onto his side and pulled it closer to his chest, forcing the old man to extend his arm uncomfortably. Iroh chuckled at the affection of the gesture.

“I’ll need that back,” said Iroh, voice gentle. “We have to go.”

“No,” Zuko groaned, eyes squeezed shut. “Stay with me.”

“You need your rest,” Iroh chided. The doctor was hovering closely now, pressuring them all to move on, and so Iroh reluctantly pulled his hand from the boy’s grasp. Zuko didn’t protest again; his fingers curled over empty space, his red, swollen eyes drooping shut.

The three made their exit. Eventually the doctor split off on her own to return to the other patients; she muttered something about needing another doctor as she made her way down the dark corridor and out of sight.

Now that Zuko was safe, Iroh wanted to know more about the incident that had led to the fire. He searched Zhao’s face for evidence he was calm enough to have this conversation; he certainly had one of the most sensitive tempers Iroh had ever encountered, second only to his younger brother. For some reason, the comparison made him heave a great sigh.

Zhao turned to him, frowning. “What?”

He might as well come out with it. “This is unusual behavior for Zuko. I’m struggling to imagine what could have made him angry enough that he would do such a thing.”

Zhao sucked his teeth. “It’s not that unusual. He told me he almost burned the reception room down, once.”

Iroh shook his head. “That was after he’d suffered a terrible humiliation. He was only a teenager.”

“He’s still a teenager,” Zhao pointed out.

At that, Iroh swallowed a great many retorts he could make about age. “What was he angry with you about?”

He had hoped that resisting the urge to frame it as a fight or an argument would coax the truth out of Zhao, but the young commander remained stubborn. “That’s not really any of your business, Iroh.”

Iroh snorted. “Considering it resulted in the destruction of my home…”

Zhao shot him a venomous look. “How do you know we weren’t arguing about *you?* You’ve been a frequent topic of strife in our marriage.”

Iroh severely doubted the argument had been about him, given the young couple hadn’t even seen him for a week, but the comment was hurtful nonetheless. He resisted the urge to deny or escalate, meeting Zhao’s aggression with another weighty sigh. “You have made your point. I won’t pry anymore.”

They came out into the foyer. By now most of the servants and guards who had been milling about had been spirited off elsewhere, perhaps to heal, most likely to keep them from offending the eyes of civilized society. Here both men paused, unsure where they were supposed to go now that the Lesser Hall was gone.

Zhao cleared his throat. “No one was - killed. Were they?”

“No,” Iroh affirmed. He glanced at Zhao’s face and was unable to catch hold of his gaze.

“Good.” Zhao gave a stiff nod. “I know Zuko would feel terrible if someone had.”

Iroh was about to ask Zhao what he meant to do now, when the quick percussion of approaching footsteps drew their attention to another hallway. One of Ozai’s aides ran up to meet them, her face as grey as the morning after a heavy rain.

“Thank goodness I finally found you,” she said. “The Fire Lord needs to see you both in the throne room, *immediately* .”

---

For some time, all Zuko knew was that it was dark and his head was throbbing. He couldn’t sleep on his back without aggravating the pain, although he was restless otherwise - every time he turned over to try to get comfortable, the room spun violently around him. Once or twice, he thought the vertigo would make him vomit, but he closed his eyes and breathed through his nose until the feeling passed.

He knew he wasn’t in his own bedroom, but he couldn’t remember precisely why; only that something had happened, and he was hurt. Bright orange flames flickered across his mind, reminding him that there had been a fire without revealing the finer details of how it started or the extent of its destruction. He ran his hands clumsily over his body, tracing his abdomen, his face, in search of wounds. There were none. Perhaps he’d be tempted to think there was no fire, after all, if not for the spectre that loomed in his mind. He saw a face cast in yellow and orange rise amongst the billowing smoke. The face twisted, ugly as a theatre mask with its sharp maw poised to bite him. He rubbed his forehead as if to banish the thought, and it slipped beneath the anxious waters of his memory.

The scent of Azula surrounding him should have made his disorientation worse. Yet as he drifted in and out of sleep, it was easy to believe he was merely curled up in his sister’s bed in the hope that their combined forces could keep the nightmares at bay. (How had they ever been surprised that he presented an omega? He’d been so sensitive even back then, the big brother seeking out his baby sister for comfort.) When he woke up, he patted what he thought was Azula’s sleeping body, and was surprised when she seemed to morph into a pillow, the blood red fabric simply the quilt, not her clothes. She was - she was abroad, he remembered. She was hunting the Avatar again.

Every few hours, Zuko opened his eyes and saw a woman with glasses sitting in a chair next to his bed. There was no chance to mistake her for Ursa; this woman was far older than he’d ever seen his mother, and sometimes the light would catch her glasses so she looked like an owl staring at him in the dark. The woman would ask Zuko questions like, Do you remember how old you are? What’s the name of our current Fire Lord? If you add five to seven, what number do you get? He felt a pang of pain at the mention of his father, but these were easy questions, and the woman with glasses nodded approvingly at all his answers.

Then came the harder ones. How did you hit your head? Do you remember the Lesser Hall being burned down? How did the fire start?

Another image appeared into Zuko’s mind, searing so painfully he was forced to touch his temple to brace himself against it. He saw his bedroom door wreathed in fire. He was walking towards it when his vision went black.

“I couldn’t breathe,” Zuko whispered. “And then I bent fire, and - and I could breathe again.”

“So you *were* firebending?”

Zuko labored through his memories as if through thick mud. “I… yes.” He remembered how Zhao had shouted at him when he woke up. “I think… I think it’s my fault the Lesser Hall burned down.”

“I see.” The woman with the glasses sounded disappointed. For good reason; no one, a prince especially, should be so reckless with their bending. “What about the rest? Do you remember anything else?”

It wasn’t merely that those memories were unavailable to Zuko; even as he tread carefully in search of them, one foot would lose balance and go hurtling through the air, forcing him to stumble back or risk falling into a terrible, throbbing fear. He shook his head, and knew when she sighed that he had disappointed her again.

“Is my uncle alright?” Zuko asked, voice trembling.

“He is,” the woman with the glasses confirmed. “Do you remember seeing him? He helped bring you here.”

Zuko shook his head, unsure where “here” even was. Faltering, he asked, “My - husband. Where is he?”

“Elsewhere in the palace. Would you like me to bring him to you?”

Zuko did not reply for a very long time. Eventually, the woman with glasses said, “In your condition, I wouldn’t have too many visitors. You should rest a little longer.”

Zuko nodded eagerly in agreement, wincing as the movement made the room surge beneath him like a wave-tossed ship. “Yes. I… think I need more rest.”

He hesitated then, the wheels of his mind turning slowly over the realization that he had asked this person to keep his husband away. The woman with the glasses was ready to leave by the time Zuko reached out, sluggishly taking hold of her sleeve.

“Please, though, I - I don’t want Zhao to be. Insulted,” Zuko said.

Given how his vision swam and the added barrier of the glasses over her eyes, it was hard to tell if she got Zuko’s meaning. But she spoke in an assured voice. “Of course. I’ll be careful, Prince Zuko.” She took the boy’s hand into her own and held it gently until he let her go. Then she made her exit, leaving Zuko alone in the dark once again.

---

Despite all the misfortune they had befallen by fire, Ozai still hid behind his wall of flame in the throne room. Iroh usually found it unbearable to face his brother under these circumstances, the demonic visage seeming like a ridiculous parody of what was only a mortal man. But given how Ozai now ranted and raved at them, Iroh was beginning to think the outward monstrousness wasn’t so warped a reflection of who his brother had become.

“Do you understand the *smear* this has left on the royal family’s reputation, on *my* reputation, that the very palace is crumbling around us? The reconstruction of the inner court in the wake of that earthbender nuisance has barely begun, and now *half* *my palace* has been reduced to smoldering ash!”

If the Fire Lord’s intimidation tactics were working on Zhao, he didn’t show it, meeting this vicious display unblinking. “My lord, it was an accident. Zuko-”

“Of course,” the Fire Lord scoffed. “Tell me what my son did, this time.” Iroh watched Zhao’s eyes narrow dangerously before he got a hold of himself and rendered his face suitably blank again.

“I’m not certain,” said Zhao. “We were arguing, so I left the room to cool down. The next thing I knew, the Lesser Hall was on fire.”

Iroh frowned. That didn’t match the story Zhao had told earlier. He didn’t voice this, waiting to see if there was some missing detail that would make it all fit together.

Ozai’s fist slammed down on one arm of his throne. “This is unacceptable, Zhao. It is *your* responsibility to keep your spouse in check. If that weren’t enough of an insult, you’ve now converted what remains of my royal palace into a *hospital!* ”

“That was me,” Iroh interjected. “The people who work in the Lesser Hall are our loyal subjects. I couldn’t simply turn them away-”

“Do you understand what a *shock* it was for the Minister of the Interior to see that chaos when he stepped from the council chambers?” Ozai snapped. “You may as well have dragged a circus into our halls. I sent them away immediately.”

“Away where?” Iroh asked.

“ *Away* ,” said Ozai. “As we no longer have a need for their services or room to house them, I terminated their employment. They were escorted off the palace grounds half an hour ago.”

So they had not merely been relocated. Even knowing it would be of no use, Iroh was moved to plead, “You can’t just put those people out on the street!”

“I am the Fire Lord, and I will do whatever I please!” Ozai shouted, his voice reverberating off the dark walls of the throne room like thunder. “ *Furthermore* , Zhao, no one gave *you* permission to occupy the Great Hall - you and Zuko will leave *at once* .”

At this, Zhao clenched his fists. “With all due respect, *your* *son* is gravely injured. I’m not moving him until he’s recovered.”

“If *my son* wanted to stay in the royal palace, then *my son* should have known better than to *destroy it* ,” Ozai spat. “He can recover elsewhere!”

“Ozai, *please* ,” Iroh said, stepping forward. “I’m begging you to let Zuko stay where he is. We’ve moved him out of the emerald room so he is no longer taking up needed space. Both Zhao and I can stay somewhere off the palace grounds, if that helps.”

It felt ridiculous, to plead for space in such a grand palace. No doubt it could house all the displaced staff and the entire royal family twice over. But Ozai did not operate in reality; he would twist things as he decided to see them, and it was up to those who would debate him to follow the spiralling halls of his logic.

There was nothing but the crackling of flame for some time. At a loss, Iroh hunkered down to his knees, then bowed onto the floor.

“ *Please* , brother.” With his face against the floor, he couldn’t see if Zhao joined him; but he heard a sigh, followed by the sound of the other man shifting position. Whatever he did, he did not punctuate it by verbally begging.

Still, it seemed to be enough. Ozai decided, “You may stay until Zuko is recovered. But you will remove him the moment he is able.”

---

Zhao spent the next day busy making arrangements. First, he hastily wrote a letter to an old friend in the colonies requesting his help with a nasty little problem, padding the envelope with yuans to ensure its comfortable journey abroad. Next, he had to prepare his family’s summer home in the capital; a new key had to be mailed, given that his old one was buried amongst the ashes of the Lesser Hall.

Then he set about finding a suitable household staff to ready the place for them to live. Iroh urged him to hire the displaced staff of the Lesser Hall, and though Zhao took this idea with a tight smile, he wriggled out of the obligation by saying, “We’ll see - I wouldn’t want to impose while they’re all convalescing.”

With all the fuss to attend to, he wasn’t able to keep tabs on the doctor or Zuko as desired. The doctor’s insistence that Zuko not see anyone for two days would buy him some time, but he knew he needed to align stories with Zuko as soon as possible, or suffer a disastrous repeat of the black eye incident. The next time he was able to stop by and the doctor refused to let him in, he relented; but not without bargaining.

“That’s fine - but when Zuko is ready to talk, I *will* be the first to see him.”

“Is that so?” came the terse reply. Despite the wrinkly little prune’s testiness, she seemed to comply with Zhao’s wishes. At the end of the third day, the doctor let him into the room with monotone promises that he was, in fact, the first to see Prince Zuko that day, other than the doctor himself. Zhao rushed to his spouse’s side, taking one slim hand in his. Zuko squeezed back with a weary but not incoherent smile, his eyes able to focus on Zhao’s face.

Zhao glanced over his shoulder at the doctor. “Can we have some privacy?”

To his annoyance, the doctor ignored him to instead fix Zuko with a look, waiting. The young prince nodded his consent. “It’s alright. I feel up to it.”

With a bow, the doctor left the room. For a moment, Zhao brought Zuko’s knuckles to his lips, not quite to kiss them, so much as to feel. He’d often thought of Zuko as delicate with a caveat, never forgetting the broad shoulders, the lean muscle, the long fingers. Growing up, his father had often sung the praises of male omegas for their “sturdiness,” insisting that after having been married to both, he could confirm that males were capable of enduring far more than their sensitive female counterparts. Yet seeing Zuko now amongst the mountain of blood-red sheets, he looked like a gray smear of a ghost, deathly pale and barely corporeal. Zuko neither pulled his hand free from Zhao’s grasp, nor did he lean into his touch. He was letting his husband do as we wished with his body; nothing more, nothing less.

“I-” And Zhao had to stop to gather himself, for how thick his voice became. “I’m furious at you.”

All at once, Zuko looked exhausted. “I don’t remember why you would be,” he said.

Zhao’s lips thinned into a line. “You bent fire at me.”

Zuko closed his eyes. For a moment, Zhao wondered if he hadn’t recovered that much; or maybe this was some childish way of ending the conversation by refusing to go on. But eventually Zuko opened his eyes again, and the look he fixed Zhao with was as raw as an open wound.

“You were hurting me,” he said. “I didn’t know what else to do.”

Zhao’s blood shot through his veins, propelled by fear and anger in kind. “Yes,” he admitted. “I admit I put my hands on you in anger. But you made things *deadly* when they didn’t have to be. You could have thrown me off. You could have fought me with your bare hands.”

“I couldn’t. You were too-”

“You didn’t have to try to *burn* me,” Zhao urged. “Look at this-” He thrust his hands out, showing Zuko the blisters around his wrists, the scratch marks. They were fainter than he expected.

Normally, Zuko would have rushed to his apologies. Now he merely said, “I thought you were going to kill me.”

Zhao flinched. In the dark of the room he couldn’t see his face reflected in Zuko’s wide pupils, yet he could imagine a full second where his terror was laid bare, before he summoned all the fury in his body to shout, “Don’t you *ever* accuse me of that ever again!” Remembering there could be people outside the door, he lowered his voice, hands shaking from the effort. “I would - I would *never.* That is a disgusting, *cruel* thing to say.”

Eyebrows knitted, Zuko lapsed back into silence. Zhao got the sense he was preparing an answer, and realized this was the source of the long pauses; Zuko often spoke as though picking his words was a laborious act, and the concussion had left him even slower than usual. Zhao could win this conversation simply by talking faster and louder.

He said, “Do you remember how the fire started?”

Zuko shook his head. “No, but I - I started it, didn’t I?”

Zhao released a breath he didn’t know he’d been holding. “Yes. You did. And thankfully no one was killed, but some of the servants of the Lesser Hall were *very* badly burned.”

At this, Zuko bit his lip, sealing his mouth shut.

“I know you might not remember our fight in its entirety,” Zhao said. “I’ll admit we *both* said some terrible things. What’s more, we failed to keep all that anger just between the two of us, and as a result, we share the blame for all the terrible things that happened as a result - the destruction of our home, all those servants cast out without work, your uncle’s burn…” He watched as each of these details landed like stabs of a knife, Zuko’s eyes growing wider and wider.

“I’m willing to put it all behind me if you are,” Zhao said. His grip on the pale hand tightened. “Because I love you. And that’s more important than who was right or wrong.”

He could see Zuko blinking harder, now, the subtlest twist to his lips. “Zhao…”

“What you did was - I won’t pretend it didn’t have repercussions. But I need you to know that more than anything, I’m happy that we’re both alive. I wouldn’t be able to live with myself if anything happened to you.”

Even before Zuko could summon a word, he returned Zhao’s grip, squeezing their clasped hands. For some time he kept trying to form a reply, lips moving soundlessly over the shape of consent, only to abandon it in place of a vehement nod. Satisfied, Zhao reached up to touch Zuko’s unblemished face, swiping his tears away with his thumb.

---

Iroh approached Azula’s bedroom to find the doctor posted outside with a pair of guards. “Is Zuko ready for visitors?” he asked, hopeful.

“Yes,” said the doctor. “Unfortunately, you can’t see him just yet. Prince Zhao requested a few minutes alone.”

Iroh tried not to let his disappointment show. He was anxious to see his nephew in good health; he could only imagine how Zhao felt. He could wait a few minutes more to give the couple space. “I’m glad he’s making a quick recovery. Does he seem like he’ll be back to normal, soon?”

The doctor shrugged. “He should bounce back once he’s able to reintegrate with his regular schedule. Of course he shouldn’t push himself, but stimulation is the best way to get the mind back in top shape. He’d do well to spend much time with his loved ones; reading might still be a strain on his eyes, but the challenge of a little pai sho could do his problem-solving skills well.”

At that, Iroh fell into a deep silence. “You seem to have something on your mind, General,” the doctor said, eventually.

“...Forgive me. I was thinking that earlier you told me Zuko was in need of isolation, but that wouldn’t make any sense, with what you just said.”

The doctor crossed her arms over her chest. “No, you’re correct. I did say that.” She studied his face, as if waiting for more. When the general wouldn’t push her, she offered, “It was a matter of rest, for one. Your nephew was awfully fatigued, and I wanted him to have peace. I’ll also say that the worst possible thing for a concussion is a lack of…” She paused, glancing at the guards before she chose her wording. “...Caution.”

“Caution,” Iroh repeated.

The doctor spread her hands. “I take the recovery of my patients seriously, especially when they are royalty. I wanted to diminish the chance Prince Zuko’s injury could be exacerbated.”

Iroh’s lips thinned. “You’ve made many veiled comments since you arrived here. Given their gravity, you had better believe in every single one.”

To his surprise, the doctor merely narrowed her eyes at him. “You needn’t be insulted on *that* man’s behalf, General. He hasn’t earned your defensiveness.”

Although the floor did not rush up to greet him, Iroh was assaulted by the peculiar sensation that he was falling. In staring back at the doctor, he no longer saw her face. Only Azula from two weeks before.

*Family has always been your blind spot.*

Then the door to her bedroom opened. And Zhao said, “Ah, Iroh. Excellent timing. You can see Zuko, now.”

---

It was something about the way Zhao said, “I love you.” He’d said it with the exact tone fitting for a love confession. His voice had swelled. He’d looked at Zuko like he was the most important thing in the world.

Yet something about it felt off. Like that wasn’t the way he was supposed to have said it, because Zuko had already heard him say it in a completely different tone.

Like fragments of a broken mirror, the disjointed memories of their fight started to fit back together. While Zhao clutched Zuko’s hand and told him everything was his fault, Zuko remembered the night of the fire with more clarity than he’d been able to before.

*Zhao was choking him. Zuko struggled in his grip, clawing at his hands, but no matter what he did,* *Zhao wouldn’t let go. The longer he struggled, gasping for air against a windpipe that wouldn’t* *yield, the darker his vision became. It was a horrible, jerking pain, the lungs reeling from their* *inability to perform their most basic function. He heaved in and in and in and there was nothing to* *take in and no way to remove the hands and he was certain, absolutely certain, that he was going* *to die.*

*Without the trappings of form, the proper stance, Zuko wasn’t bending, wasn’t indulging in an art* *so much as he was reaching into some deep, untamed place for protection. Fire spewed out of his* *hands without thought or direction, and Zhao cried out as he leapt back, releasing him. All at once* *air rushed back into Zuko’s lungs, and he gasped in heaving breaths.*

*When his vision cleared, he looked up to see Zhao watching him with a wild-eyed expression he* *mistook for hurt. Remorse raced to Zuko’s tongue.*

*“I-I’m sorry if I hurt you, but I couldn’t breathe! A-and you wouldn’t let go-”*

*“Sorry?” Zhao repeated. “You think you’re sorry, now? I’m going to* ***make*** *you fucking sorry!”*

*His expression twisted into a parody of an oni mask as he fixed his husband with a look of utter* *hatred. He didn’t remotely regret what he’d done to Zuko.*

*He was angry. He was angry Zuko had dared to disagree with him. He was angry that Zuko* *wouldn’t just lie there and take whatever treatment he decided in the moment he deserved, even if* *that meant choking him unconscious. And now, a deadly ember was roiling in the palm of his* *hands, ready to punish Zuko for the crime of defending his own life.*

*Zuko felt his blood turn to liquid fire in his veins. Zhao might be angry, but Zuko was suddenly* ***furious*** *enough to burn all of Caldera to the ground. It had no logic to it, no argument, no words -* *this was a primal fury, and the breadth of its power shocked him as it burst from some secret place* *deep in his chest. The painted powder keg had remained sealed and ever-burning for long enough,* *and it was time for it to explode.*

*Zhao hurled an arc of fire at him that Zuko easily dodged despite the cramped space of their* *bedroom, rolling and then leaping to his feet to punch a hot burst of fire back. Zhao raised his* *arms to block it, bracers taking the heat so his skin wouldn’t have to suffer. For a moment, his* *expression was one of surprise that Zuko had fought back; yet it quickly devolved back into a snarl* *as he levelled another burst of flame that Zuko only narrowly escaped.*

*It was a distortion of their spar, now made deadly as they launched flame after flame without care* *as to where it caught. Zhao would thrust forward with his arm and Zuko would duck down,* *shocked by the realization that he recognized a pattern, knew the rhythm of how Zhao fought. He* *lashed out as unpredictably as he could, aiming low to break his root, but Zhao was wary and* *wouldn’t be toppled. They never got close enough to make skin-to-skin contact.*

*As their vicious fight continued, so did its devastation. The Avatar research, essentially a pile of* *kindling, caught quickly. Soon the map was aflame, and the bedsheets, the window pane. In* *dodging one another’s attacks, Zuko realized they also had to take the environment into account,* *careful not to tumble directly into another flame’s path. What’s more, his robes were becoming a* *hazard. The loose fabric billowed behind him as he dodged, and there was one instance where he* *had to roll into his landing to put out a flame that had caught the ends.*

*Although he was still angry, Zuko knew he had to set it aside for the sake of their safety. “We need* *to stop,” he panted in between strikes. Zhao didn’t answer, narrowing his eyes as he thrust* *forward. Zuko avoided one flaming fist and took the opportunity to aim a kick at Zhao’s exposed* *abdomen. There was no fire to it this time, but Zhao didn’t realize that; he leapt back to avoid it,* *crashing into the bedside table, knocking the metal box that held the old engagement gift onto the* *floor. The sight of it made Zuko’s chest ache fiercely - only days ago he had presented it to Zhao to* *calm his ravings. It was evidence that they were capable of tenderness with one another, once.*

*“Zhao, I mean it!” Zuko hollered. “Stop!”*

*The other man hauled himself upright using the edge of the table, watching suspiciously with one* *hand bent in preparation to defend himself. Zuko shouted, “I know we’re angry, but this has gone* *too far! We need to get out of here before we’re really hurt!”*

*There was a look of hesitation on Zhao’s face. He couldn’t deny the curl of smoke in front of their* *faces. When the shouts of servants in the hall drew their attention, he finally nodded and relaxed* *his stance. Zuko released his as well. There was no more time to waste. He turned away from Zhao* *to make his escape.*

*It was just as Zuko reached out to slide the door open that he heard an object scrape along the* *wood floor, and Zhao said, “You should know better than to turn your back on me.”*

*And before Zuko could turn around or ask what he meant, something heavy slammed into the back* *of his head.*

*An explosion of pain blistered and burst in Zuko’s vision even as darkness swirled in to claim it. He* *collapsed to the floor, and the last thing he saw before he went unconscious was a demon looming* *over him, sharp maw cast in the flickering yellow and orange of the surrounding blaze.*

“Zuko,” Iroh called out. “Zuko, can you hear me?”

It took some time for Zuko to tear himself away from the memory, so entrenched in the orange light and roiling smoke that he could feel it burning his lungs, and he gasped and gasped with the effort to breathe through it. His hands leapt to where his uncle had taken him by the shoulders, his face a picture of concern. Seeing him, Zuko felt a rush of comfort unlike he’d ever experienced before.

Until a voice in the doorway dashed it all away. “For spirits’ sake, Iroh, don’t *shake* him.”

Zhao stood so that the light at his back cast him in a dark silhouette. At the sight of him, so like that demonic visage from his memory, Zuko cowered back against the pillows. He remembered everything, now. He remembered how Zhao had raved against their Fire Lord, choking Zuko when he refused to see things his way. He remembered their fight, the origin of the fire that consumed the Lesser Hall. And he remembered that the moment they’d come to a truce and Zuko had turned his back to leave, Zhao had hit him hard enough to knock him unconscious.

“Zuko,” Iroh pleaded. “Are you okay?”

Overwhelmed, Zuko struggled to speak. He didn’t want to say anything damning with Zhao so close, yet he needed to warn his uncle in some way. He reached up and held onto one of the wrinkled hands that gripped him; Iroh misinterpreted the action and let go of Zuko altogether.

“I’m sorry, my boy,” he apologized. “You were panting so hard. It was like you couldn’t even see me.” He turned to the doorway. “Do you know what set him off?”

“He was fine when I left,” Zhao said, voice testy. His eyes slid towards Zuko’s face; the young prince flinched and looked away, as if his gaze alone could harm him.

“I think he’s had a little too much stimulation for one day,” came a voice from the hall. The doctor. Zuko was grateful when Zhao disappeared from the doorway, but the fact Iroh began to pull away, too, made his chest hurt.

“Uncle,” he finally managed.

Iroh turned back to him with a smile. “It’s alright, Zuko. I will always be here if you need me.” Right. Right; Iroh had always been there, just around the hall, and Zuko had neglected to use him. He’d told himself things were alright, that it was better to maintain his and Zhao’s privacy than to vent in a way that might misconstrue their issues and make his uncle worried. But maybe it was time Zuko confided in his uncle. After all, they lived in the same palace. Surely they could find some time together to talk in private.

---

Hours before Zhao and Zuko were to depart for their new home in the capital, Ozai pulled Zhao into an alcove and said, “Governor Darah is dead.”

Zhao’s eyes widened with shock. “How? What on earth happened?”

“He was killed,” said the Fire Lord, expression impenetrable as stone. “There will be a thorough investigation into the culprit. My best guess is that it was one of those anarchists. Hopefully you won’t be nearly so stupid as to try to reason with them, Zhao; I’ll be appointing you as governor of Kirachu in the interim.”

All at once, Zhao felt he understood his spouse’s condition. His vision distorted like the view from a porthole before sliding back into focus. His lips moved soundlessly over his response. The Fire Lord watched him as if he very much expected this reaction.

“Generally, the proper response to a promotion is to show gratitude,” said Ozai.

Zhao managed to summon a weak nod as his military career slipped and shattered out of his grasp. “Right. Thank you, sir.”

---

“You don’t have to do this.”

As the words left Darah’s mouth, he knew they were pointless - trite, even. Both terrible things for last words to be, but they so often are. He was backed into a corner, hands raised in front of his face in more of a loose shield than a proper fighting stance. Even as a bender, he knew he lacked the skill to win against the man who loomed before him now.

Darah’s chest seized with the familiarity of his killer’s face. Darah had watched him grow from a laughing boy who chased his father’s ankles to the assassin who now looked coldly down his nose at his prey, light flashing off his roundish glasses.

“The Fire Lord sends his regards,” said Wei. Then with an upward thrust of his hands, he sent a ball of flame hurtling into the governor’s face.
