### Text

Zuko’s guilt towards the destruction of the Lesser Hall could fill oceans. It isn’t his burden alone to bear, but he is, between himself and Zhao, the one who will readily feel remorse. So he feels enough for both of them, and then some - every burn suffered, every rumbling stomach of the guards and servants cast from the palace, every ounce of humiliation the royal family has been forced to endure as this story breaks free from the ramparts and spreads through the capital. And he only feels guiltier still for feeling sad over what he’s personally lost, for it must be so inconsequential compared to the rest.

But Zuko can’t help it. He thinks of the hours spent compiling information on the Avatar, the stories, the evidence, rare editions of books and scrolls - all reduced to ash. Most of all, the loss of the airbender scroll and the prayer beads weigh heavy on his heart. The few surviving artefacts of a culture destroyed are now lost forever themselves. It was wrong for him to ever own them, but it’s far too late to correct that mistake now.

It is the small hours of the morning, and they will be leaving for Kirachu any minute. Iroh isn’t here to provide guidance, but in reflecting on his teachings, Zuko wonders if meditation will calm his mind. For years, Iroh has tried to instill in him the importance of its regular practice, the benefits of calming the chi and the mind. It could make his next course of action all the clearer.

The problem is that Zuko just isn’t terribly good at meditating. On the surface, he’s told he looks very composed; on the inside, however, his mind and his chi spiral off in perpetuity. Still, he isn’t sure what else to do. The shame of his failure burns in his chest. He wants to do anything he can to seek atonement for his failure to protect these sacred objects.

Zuko performs a cursory search of Azula’s bedside table, and finds a few sticks of incense buried in her drawer, along with a censure. For some reason, Zuko can’t reconcile the sight of it with the idea that Azula may have put it there herself, automatically assuming it must be a gift from Iroh. Once it’s set up, Zuko reaches out to light it so he can begin his meditation.

A terrible, white flash robs him of his vision. He startles, hand flattening to the bedside table to catch himself before he collapses to the floor.

*What was that?*

When he catches his breath, he tentatively extends a hand to light the incense again. Not only does he fail to produce a flame, but it *hurts,* a vicious and searing pain that sends him physically reeling backwards onto Azula’s bed. It feels like the very blood is boiling in his veins, his body curling in on itself to brace against the sensation.

*No,* Zuko thinks. *Not now*. He wants so badly to try again, but the memory of the pain frightens him into inaction. He stares at his hand in horror, trying to tell himself this is only temporary, that this will pass -

What if it doesn’t? There’s no way Zhao will let him seek treatment for this. There’s no way he can even let Zhao know this is *happening*. Bending was his only means of self-defense, and it’s now gone.

At this, his blood goes cold. Perhaps this is his punishment. This is the price he must pay for all that was destroyed with the Lesser Hall.

---

Firebenders traditionally rose with the sun, but Iroh forced himself onto his feet before daylight. He feared that if he didn’t appear at Azula’s door as early as possible, Zhao would have spirited his nephew off to Kirachu without granting them their goodbyes.

Yet as he entered the corridor, it was clear that all his planning had been useless from the outset: Zhao was already there, slumped up against the bedroom door. Iroh would think he was knocked out and left for dead if not for the way he stirred at the sound of the older man’s approach, blinking blearily awake.

“Maintaining a vigil?” Iroh asked. Zhao nodded, rubbing his eyes.

“Doctor wouldn’t let me in,” he said, voice thick with sleep, “but I couldn’t stand the thought of Zuko waking up alone, scared. He’s already prone to nightmares, and I’m sure the fire’s only made it worse.”

Before all this, Iroh would have rushed to the usual praise. *How protective! How thoughtful!* Now the words felt bitter on his tongue. He had been treating Zhao civilly for Zuko’s sake, but how deeply had he hurt his nephew by playing along?

Hands clasped, he entreated Zhao: “Would you mind if I stepped inside to see my nephew privately, for a moment? I promise we won’t be long.”

The dark circles under Zhao’s eyes rendered his smile about as pleasant as a two-headed rat viper’s. “Sorry, but I’m still feeling a little rattled after everything that’s happened - you’ll understand if I can’t bear to let him out of my sight.”

Iroh nodded despite the sinking feeling in his stomach. “Very well. I only wanted a chance to say my farewells - I’m feeling a bit overwhelmed by the prospect of an empty nest, with Azula gone, too.” He chuckled sadly with a hand over his heart, hunched to accentuate how very old and innocent he was, in the hopes it would get Zhao’s guard down.

Zhao’s smile didn’t quite reach his eyes. “Tell you what. I haven’t had a chance to say good morning, either. You can come in with me and bid him your farewells right now.”

“Wonderful,” Iroh said, although it was anything but.

Zhao didn’t bother to knock before he opened the door. They found Zuko leaning against the bed at a strange angle, as though he had fallen and caught himself. When he heard them come in, he wiped a thin sheen of sweat from his brow. He was dressed, but disheveled, with several strands of hair coming loose from his half-top knot.

“Are you alright?” Iroh asked.

Zuko nodded, albeit woozily. “Yes. I just… I’m dizzy, still.”

“A shame,” said Zhao. “I’m sure the boat ride won’t help.” He didn’t bother coming much deeper into the room, standing with arms crossed like a sentry by the door.

Thus Iroh and Zuko were forced to say their goodbyes under Zhao’s watchful gaze. Iroh took his nephew’s free hand in his and tried to imbue his touch with every ounce of love that he had in his body. “Kirachu is a beautiful island with a rich culture; I’m sure you will love it there. If you ever need me, please don’t hesitate to write.”

“Thank you, Uncle,” Zuko responded, the slightest upwards tug at the corner of his mouth. He looked so forlorn standing there that Iroh decided he didn’t care what Zhao thought: he pulled his nephew into a tight embrace. The boy wrapped his arms around his uncle and inhaled his familiar scent, jasmine and ginseng and something else, buried amongst all the tea leaves. The familiarity of it brought a tear to Zuko’s eye.

Zhao cleared his throat. “I will remind you both that we’re not going to the colonies. We’ll only be a few islands away.”

Iroh hoped Zhao was ready to live by those words. At the slightest sign of trouble, even if it was merely a foreboding dream, Iroh planned to be in Kirachu. Again, he hoped he was communicating this as he squeezed his nephew in his arms. No matter what silly fights they may have had. No matter what mistruths have been exchanged. Iroh was always going to be there for him when needed.

Judging by Zuko’s reluctance to let him go, he understood perfectly well. When they separated, Iroh wasn’t too proud to openly scrub the tears from his eyes.

They approached the departing carriage together. There was one trunk waiting by it, which a pair of footmen lifted up and started tying to the roof while Zuko openly stared. Iroh thought he was merely watching them work until he said, “That’s all we have left, isn’t it?”

“Yes.” Zhao’s tone was clipped. “There’s a change of clothes for each of us. The rest we’ll need to restock once we’re in Kirachu.”

Zuko nodded, face pale, but said nothing more. Iroh could guess what he was thinking. He took his nephew by the hand and said, “I have been aiding in the clean-up of the Lesser Hall. If any of your possessions are in decent condition, I will send them to you.”

Before Zuko could thank him, Zhao swiftly cut in: “If you find the dao swords, please don’t bother. I think we’ll be entertaining less dangerous hobbies from now on, won’t we, Zuko?”

The snipe flared in Iroh’s chest like fuel tossed on dying embers. Although Zuko’s responding look was grim, he acquiesced. “Yes, of course. You’re right.” He turned his attention to Iroh. “Uncle, if it’s possible, there *is* something I’d like you to find for me. If you have any paper, I can show you what it looks like.”

He did not, which meant Zhao was forced to wait impatiently as a servant fetched some. In the meantime, he stalked closer to the carriage to have words with the driver. It was a poor excuse for the privacy Iroh desperately wanted with his nephew; Zhao was still near enough that certain questions, even whispered (or perhaps *because* they were whispered), would not go unnoticed.

When Zuko finished drawing, he mimed the dimensions for his uncle. “It’s a metal box, about this big. Because of the materials it’s made of, I’m hopeful it survived the fire.” He ran his finger along the zig-zags he’d drawn. “This is a latch, you see, embedded in copper.”

Iroh nodded as he took the paper, eager to help his nephew in some small way. “Of course, Zuko. But what’s inside?”

Zuko went quiet again, eyes flickering towards where Zhao was barking orders at the servants. “...It’s something Zhao gave to me, when we were first engaged. A small token.”

In truth, Zuko didn’t know why he wanted it. After all that Zhao had done to him, it seemed wrong to want to cling to those small, tender symbols of their early affection. A week ago, Zuko had trotted out the same token to calm Zhao down from a rage; perhaps he was seeking some similar end, now. Perhaps he just wanted to know that at least one precious possession had survived the fire.

Iroh was not privy to the details of his nephew’s internal turmoil, but he could sense it from the way the boy’s eyes darkened. Seeing Zhao turn towards them, no doubt to signal the end of their goodbyes, Iroh could not resist yanking his nephew into one last embrace.

---

It doesn’t hit Zuko until they pass through the Great Gates of Azulon. He’s been through these ramparts dozens of times on the way to Ember Island, but there’s something so final about turning around in his seat to watch them grow smaller in the distance, knowing he won’t see them again for a long time.

For all that the royal palace has been his cage, it is also the only home Zuko has ever known. It is where he was born and educated and married, where he met his husband and Mai and the Avatar. It is where he was loved and where he was punished. For every hardship endured there was a fond memory, and panic squeezes his chest as he realizes that where he is going, there will be none of that fond familiarity to stave off any hardship yet to come.

The ship they’ve hired is on the smaller side, making Zuko anxious at the prospect of being in close quarters with his husband. But Zhao seems preoccupied with micro-managing the sailors. He paces relentlessly on the bow, stopping every once in a while to glare at the clouds and mutter about castles in the sky.

Zuko sees more of the Fire Nation in the next seven hours than he has in his entire life. They sail past Shuhon, where Mai is, and past Roku’s Island, which is nothing more than volcanic waste. They sail past Makamae’s old haunt, Ma’Inka, and Hing Wa, every island taking less time to traverse as they progress through the chain, until finally there it is, rising in the thin mist that has settled over the water: Kirachu. It looks like every other island they’ve seen today, stretching out in a thick green expanse over a jagged skyline of mountains. Just off the starboard bow, Zuko can make out a beach littered with volcanic crags. It’s all very beautiful, true, but it does little to lift his spirits.

“Can we see any settlements from here?” Zuko asks. It isn’t addressed to any one person; any of the sailors who have come along will do, but Zhao comes up beside him to grip the railing. Even as he stands at a healthy distance, it sends Zuko flinching imperceptibly away.

Ignorant of his reaction, Zhao points into the distance. “There’s a village there, right in front of you.”

Zuko squints, leaning against the railing, and thinks he sees brown thatched roofs peeking out from behind the many layers of palm trees. They blend in as if they’re only more vegetation.

“Home, sweet home,” says Zhao. He sounds about as miserable as Zuko feels.

---

This village is nothing like the capital. The roads aren’t paved, meaning the carriage ride is nauseatingly bumpy as they go over rain-thrashed mud. There are no grand apartments, no closely leaning towers; every building looks as though it was cobbled together from the materials least safe to house a people known to emit fire from their bodies. Everywhere Zuko looks, he sees unkempt, barefoot children. They run in packs like little animals, and it isn’t that there are no adults around, but none that seem to be supervising them; what adults crowd the streets have eyes only for each other, barely flinching as the carriage goes past. Zuko’s actually a bit astounded by how *close* people get to the carriage without acknowledging it, most of them fanning out in the middle of the road.

The ramshackle buildings fall away as the carriage takes to a path winding along the side of the mountain. They maintain their steady ascent into the air, until Zuko can see over the tops of the thick jungle foliage to the great blue sea beyond. What a privilege it would be to fly through the fluffy mounds of clouds with the colorful birds he can see even from this distance, their tailfeathers trailing like streamers in their wake. The longer Zuko stares out the window in silence, the longer he can ignore the cramped confines of the carriage ride, and the feeling of hateful eyes latched onto his face.

Eventually they pull onto a side road, away from the precarious ledge and into the expanse of trees. They follow a path to a large, walled estate. With all this protection, it looks less like the entryway to a home and more like the ramparts of a fort that expects to come under siege. The doors of the gate open, pulled by guards stationed at either side.

If Zuko had to describe Zhao’s childhood home in one word, it would be *tacky*.

Granted, it belongs very much to its environment, rising from the jungle foliage in bright, tropical shades. It’s a wide, two-story building, with the roof composed of multiple layers, punctuated by three twisting spires decorated in flame-like tiles of red and gold. On the veranda, there are pillars that end in draconic faces, sneering as they maintain the integrity of this not-so-humble abode. The closer they get, it’s easier to see the entire house is on a raised platform, with wide stone steps leading up to the front door. It is so strange, and yet eerily familiar; Zuko realizes, with a start, that it is a parody of the royal palace.

As their carriage draws near, three figures come to stand out on the veranda. Zuko takes for granted that these are the members of Zhao’s family: there is a diminutive figure in wide-sleeved robes of white who must be Ama, his mother, and a thickly built man with the typical Fire Nation beard, the younger brother, Yan. It isn’t until they’ve made their way up the steps that Zuko realizes the last person is actually a stranger to him, likely a servant of the household, judging by the drab gray of his clothes. As if noticing this too, Zhao frowns deeply at him, then asks, “Where is Wei?”

“He has business to attend to in the village,” Yan answers.

While the brothers greet one another with suspicious scowls, Ama breaks away to approach Zuko, tipping forward in a low bow. Although his face is blank, the picture of omega composure, his voice drips with emotion. “We are humbled to have a member of royalty in our home. I hope we are able to make your time here very comfortable.”

“That’s very sweet, but I don’t need special treatment. I’m-” Zuko almost says, *I’m not worth it*, meaning the urge to walk on tiptoe, or the respect, or the adoration, any of it. He catches himself before he can make his self-loathing a scene. “We’re family, now.”

Ama straightens and says, with a warmth that is almost eery when contrasted to his lack of expression, “Of course we are, dear. But this is as fine a household as you will find in Kirachu, and here, we know to treat our royalty with respect, kin or not.”

“Ma,” Zhao says, voice petulant, “*I'm* royalty.”

Ama glances at him. “So? I’m not going to bow at your feet. I made you.” At this, he reaches up to give his son a patronizing squeeze of the chin, his expression softening. “Still. I’m happy to have you home. I have missed you dearly.”

Zhao pouts. It’s not a great look on a grown man. “I wish I could’ve returned under different circumstances. Darah’s funeral?”

“Family-only,” Yan says, lurching forward. He walks with a cane half as gaudy as the house, hand clasped around the faux-gold head of a tigermonkey. What is with this family and tigermonkeys? Zuko turns to look out into the thick jungle foliage beyond the gates of the estate, suddenly nervous that they might be endemic to Kirachu.

“Good,” Zhao says. “Now at least it won’t be a political statement when I don’t go. Did you send anything to his family?”

Ama’s lips become a tight line. “Yes. But Rio returned with every yuan. Evidently, they are not interested in our condolences.” The servant hovering close behind him gives a slight bow of the head; Zuko takes it that this solemn young man must be Rio.

“Fuck them,” Zhao says, decisively. “We tried to be civil. We don’t owe them anything else.”

They head inside, Ama eager to give Zuko the full tour even as Zhao sighs and glares impatiently. The walls of each room are painted with elaborate depictions of wildlife, and it is in this way the family identifies them. On the first floor, there is a large drawing room with a magnificently snarling tiger-monkey painted across the doors. The face is at child-height, perfect for scaring away toddlers looking to bother their parents when company’s over. (At this colorful description, Zhao leers at Yan, who blushes and scowls at some private childhood memory.) Then another parlor painted over with a forest of bamboo reeds, “the reed room,” or the reed-ing room, as Ama cheekily calls it. They don’t go into the kitchen, but Zuko imagines it is terribly plain in contrast to the rest of the house, if only because nobility does not tread there.

On the second floor, the paintings on the bedroom doors are less focused around a singular creature or motif, becoming more sprawling and ambitious: the master bedroom has a bonsai forest littered with thin grey clouds; there is another door with a solitary crane, standing amidst cattails and dragonflies in a marsh; then there is another door where a mountain range is circled with birds that at first glance look like distant V’s, but upon closer inspection, have enough detail to distinguish them as messenger hawks. Each painting fades into the next, so it is like walking from one fantasy realm to another as they proceed down the hall.

Ama sighs, voice wistful. “I have moved my possessions into the cherry blossom room. It’s a bit tight, but I’ll manage. Royalty such as yourself deserves the master bedroom.”

“Thank you,” Zhao says, before Zuko can get in a word.

“Of course. I would sacrifice anything for my children,” Ama sniffs. “Even the very best bedroom in the house, where I’ve lived for years.”

“If you’d like to keep it, I don’t think it’d be too much trouble,” Zuko says, earning a glare from Zhao. Luckily for him, Ama becomes insistent.

“No, no. You’re two people. You need the space. Besides, that sprawling, empty bed reminds me of my late husband. I will only stop wallowing if I force myself to move on.”

“About time,” Yan mutters under his breath. If Ama hears it, he pretends not to.

They enter the master bedroom, and Ama leads them to the window, where he points out smaller structures on the estate. “Those are the servants’ quarters, and those are the stables. I wouldn’t advise riding the dragon moose, they are better-suited to carriage work.”

“Thank you, Ama.”

“Yes. And the baths, I’ll remind you, are-”

“*Thank* you, Ama,” Zhao says again.

His mother shoots him a look, before gathering up Zuko’s hands in his. “If you need anything, anything at all, do not hesitate to ask.” His hands are smooth and soft, covered in fine lines that reveal his age. Zuko is seized by the urge to drag this motherly stranger into a hug, resisting because it would, of course, be a ridiculous thing to do. They barely know one another - although Zuko has a sneaking suspicion that with all his reverence for royalty, Ama would probably let him if he tried.

Then the doors slide shut, and it is Zhao and Zuko, alone together for the first time since Zuko regained his memories. This time, there is no doctor or uncle waiting just outside the door. As he looks around the room, the paintings of dense foliage fail to distract from the lack of personal effects. He feels he is alone in a strange wilderness.

When Zhao finally leaves his perch at the window, Zuko jumps and backs away from the path Zhao makes towards the bed, eyes on the ground so he doesn’t have to see how his reaction might annoy him. Rio has left their sole trunk by the door; Zuko makes his way over and begins to unpack, for something to do. One uniform and a set of armour, a fine omega robe that Zuko doesn’t really recognize, some stray shirts... While he puts everything away, Zhao lays on the bed, an arm thrown over his eyes, saying nothing.

The scent of smoke wafts up from a shirt as Zuko folds it, and he is wholly unprepared for the effect it has on him. Suddenly, it’s as if he’s back there, in the roiling smoke of the Lesser Hall, orange tongues of fire licking at the walls. He is panting, he cannot breathe - is it the smoke? The physical exertion as he dodges and dives across the room? Or is it the fingers that are curled around his throat?

“Hey, are you alright-?”

That voice. Zuko whips around in anticipation of violence, both hands raised in fists. Zhao raises his hands, too, but in more of a conciliatory gesture, palms pointed upwards to show he means no harm.

Zuko realizes that while he’s panting like a cornered animal, his body stiff with terror, Zhao - Zhao is calm, neglecting to reach out and physically comfort (control) him. He says in that low, sonorous voice, “Zuko. Relax. Let’s not burn my parents’ house to the ground.”

“I-I’m sorry,” Zuko says, breathless. He lowers his hands, but doesn’t drop them completely. “I just, I thought I was back there, and we were still fighting, and-”

Something flickers in Zhao’s expression. “Why would we be fighting?”

In his panic, Zuko realizes he forgot the story they agreed on before. He’s let the fact he knows the truth slip. “I don’t - I don’t know.” There’s a pause of only a few seconds, which feels so weighty Zuko could choke on it. He fumbles, “You - you said it first. You said *let’s* not burn the house down. Both of us.”

For an instant, anger mars Zhao’s face. Zuko thinks, *This is it,* tensing in anticipation of a blow, but Zhao gets a hold of himself, smiling in a way that is meant to be a comfort despite its resemblance to the wildcat leering on the wall downstairs.

“You’re still recovering,” Zhao says. He sounds like he’s just decided something. “You’re bound to have some memory problems for a while, hm?”

“I - yes,” Zuko agrees, voice soft. He’s only cautiously relieved that Zhao has maintained his temper. It could change any moment, now.

The smile his husband fixes him with is polite and distant. “We’ve had a long day. Why don’t I let you get some rest?”

Zuko, who has wanted to be alone since Zhao came to get him nine hours ago, nods so frantically in agreement he thinks he might actually aggravate his head wound. His husband gives him a curt nod before heading for the door.

“I’ll get you when it’s time for dinner,” Zhao says over his shoulder. Then he’s gone. Zuko waits until he’s down the hall to rush forward and shut the door. It’s not that he feels unsafe with it open, he just - he needs to shut Kirachu out as best as he can. He slumps with his forehead against the closed door for a moment afterwards, eyes shut, trying to calm the buzz of his own blood.

For years Zuko has taken what he’s dealt and packed it neatly away, all the while telling himself that he provoked it, that there was a reason he was punished and steps he could take to improve himself so it didn't happen again. He let himself grow unrecognizable, a tiny, voiceless nothing that forced itself to become even less every time the great sum of his worthlessness earned him more heartbreak.

Zuko wants to forget all that happened in the Lesser Hall. But as he stands in the cool half-light of this foreign bedroom, illuminated by what little sunlight can break through thick foliage outside, he makes himself remember Zhao’s fingers around his throat. He makes himself remember the fire in his hands, how Zhao struck first.

He makes himself remember how hard Zhao hit him when his back was turned.

When Zuko opens his eyes, the paintings on the rice paper door slide into focus. Amongst the gray clouds and bonsais is a single bird, pinned under his hand. He lifts his fingers as if to set it free.

---

They eat dinner late. Ama tries to engage Zuko in conversation, and when he fails, fills the silence endlessly with inane stories about various schoolmates Zhao hasn’t seen in years. When his son tries to shut this down - “Ama. I’m tired. Can you not?” - Ama chides him, saying, “This is *important*. You’ll need to know the current state of things if you’re going to govern Kirachu.”

Wei doesn’t come home until it’s dark. When he passes the open door of the parlor, he is like a spirit of death, face pallid, black hair and robes billowing out behind him as he heads towards the stairs without a single greeting. “Wei,” Zhao calls out to him. Then, once he’s disappeared from sight, rises to his feet and shouts again, “HEY - WEI!” When the oldest brother does not reappear, Zhao stays standing, glaring at the door.

“That boy’s been acting so peculiar,” Ama sighs. “He’s out at all hours and I hardly ever see him. I miss having him here with me.”

“I think it’s been good for him,” Yan says, stabbing at a hunk of fish Zhao’s left unprotected on his plate. “All this mysterious bullshit is better than the moping he did before. Sit down already, you idiot.”

Zhao doesn’t offer a retort to his younger brother, but once he’s sat back down, he does steal a piece of pickled radish off his plate. Yan tries to grab it back, earning an elbow in the face.

“Don’t act like animals,” Ama admonishes. “We’re in the presence of royalty.”

“That warning better not be for me,” says Zhao.

“It’s for both of you.”

“Zuko is my spouse, we don’t have to act special for him. If anything, everyone should be treating *me* with respect. I’m head of the household, now. I'm the head of *Kirachu*.”

Yan snorts. “Please. You haven’t even been here in, like, ten years.”

“That doesn’t change anything. Being head of the household isn’t a consolation prize for wallowing around at home without a plan, it’s earned by status and birth order.”

“It’s *incidental* to status and birth order,” Yan snipes. “Words like *earn* imply you’ve actually done something, which you haven’t. You didn’t even earn your stupid governor title. The Fire Lord just gave it to you because you’re married to his son.”

“I doubt that,” Zuko says.

As quiet as they are, his words halt the bickering at once.

Yan blinks. “Uh, no offense, but how do you figure that? You *are* the Fire Lord’s son, and you *are* married to my brother, so the shortest line between point A and point B...”

“Whatever Zhao has been rewarded by the Fire Lord, it’s not due to me,” Zuko says, solemnly. “My father doesn’t believe in nepotism. Even his own children have to earn his respect.”

Yan flounders with this information. “That’s, that sounds, um…”

“It’s ruthlessly fair,” Zuko supplies for him.

Ama nods emphatically in agreement. “Yes. *Ruthlessly fair* is an excellent way to put it. Although they’ve all been divinely chosen, I *do* think Fire Lord Ozai is the best we’ve ever had.” He lays a hand on Zhao’s arm, looking at him as though the very sun rises at his behest. “We are so blessed that he remembered our family’s friendship when he sought your spouse, Prince Zuko. We’re terribly honored to have been chosen.”

“Yan thinks Ozai is the worst Fire Lord,” Zhao tells his mother. The comment, which makes Ama go positively rigid, reeks of tattling. For some reason, Zuko can’t help but picture his husband at ankle-height, tugging at the ends of his mother’s clothes, *Mommy, Mommy, Yan said...*

Yan huffs, blushing at his plate. “I never said that he’s the worst. Objectively, the Fire Nation is flourishing under Ozai’s reign.”

The tenseness seeps from Ama’s shoulders. He even chuckles. “I never thought I’d hear *you* admit that. Ozai must really be the best Fire Lord we’ve ever had, if even men of *your* beliefs are so impressed.”

“Well.” Yan pops a vegetable in his mouth, chews thoughtfully, swallows. “He’s great for the economy. He’s just also a dirty, rotten tyrant.”

Zuko doesn’t get a chance to go on the offensive because of how quickly Ama explodes. “How *dare* you speak of our Fire Lord in that way, and with a *prince* staying in our home!”

“Look-”

“No, *you* look,” Ama snaps, leaning over the table. He’s going to get sauce on his sleeves, but he doesn’t seem to notice or care, hell-bent on shouting at his adult son. “All your petulant whining may impress the other layabouts at your silly little social club, but it’s not going to be tolerated here! Your brother is of *real* importance, and you will not ruin his career with your capricious slander!”

Yan slams both his hands on the table, rattling the plates and silverware as he fixes his mother with a look of pure spite. It’s returned in kind. Zhao, meanwhile, wears a smile that is positively grimy as he watches the proceedings. It’s the happiest he’s looked since they disembarked from the capital.

“This isn’t about your patriotism,” Yan shouts. “This is about your favorite son. You wouldn’t be nearly so defensive right now if things were the other way around!”

The roll of Ama’s eyes in response is quite devastating; it’s a wonder Yan survives it.

Zhao scoffs, “Things wouldn’t ever *be* the other way around. You’re terminally lazy. You’d never have a career for me to endanger.”

Yan’s face turns the color of a lychee. “I’m not *lazy,* I’m injured! There’s a difference!”

Their bickering provides the soundtrack for the rest of Zuko’s meal, not even winding down by the time Rio clears the table. Zuko starts to help him for an excuse to escape, but Ama catches him by the wrist in the middle of lifting a saucer and begs him to leave it for Rio. Considering this whole fight started with Ama telling them to behave themselves for Zuko’s sake, they all seem quite comfortable shouting themselves hoarse in front of him. Zuko wonders with a sinking feeling whether they’re like this all the time, or if tensions are merely high because Zhao’s home.

After dinner, they all retire to the reed room, Ama leading the way. Zuko casts small, surreptitious glances at his husband as they take their positions, waiting to see if Zhao will approach him or continue to keep a distance like he did at dinner.

“Embers are burning low,” Yan remarks, poking at the hearth. Looking around, he must notice there’s no servant with them, as Rio is still in the kitchen cleaning up. His gaze settles on Zuko. “Hey - you’re a bender, aren’t you? Could you help me re-light the hearth?”

Zuko stiffens at the prospect. Thankfully Ama has taken up a role as his advocate. “Don’t order the prince around like he’s your servant.”

“I’m not ordering him around,” Yan whines. “I’m asking *politely.”*

He looks at Zhao, who leers back. “Don’t look at me. I’m a prince as well.”

Yan huffs irritably as he stomps out of the room, probably going to get some matches himself. Maybe a blanket. In any case, with his limp, his exit looks like a painful one. Zuko wishes he could have spared him the trouble, but unfortunately, he has a secret to keep.

“That boy,” Ama sighs, draping himself on a jungle-green divan. “I thought I raised him right. Evidently I wasted my best work on my oldest.” And he smiles, pointedly, at Zhao.

The comment throws Zuko off. “What about Wei?”

Ama touches a scandalized hand to his chest. “Do I look old enough to be Wei’s parent?”

Zuko feels the heat rush to his face. “I-I’m so sorry, I just assumed because you two looked so much alike…” Not to mention Zhao had never once implied Wei was a half-brother.

Ama waves him off, nonplussed. “You’re not the first to make the mistake - we do bear a resemblance, although it’s incidental. It's said that I look *extraordinarily* like my husband’s previous wife, so much so we could’ve been twins.” He takes on a sneaky smile, then. “Assumption of age aside, it isn’t such an insult. I quite like Wei. More than my own boys, at times. He behaves himself for me, which is an extraordinary thing, considering how quickly his father and I got together after his mother fell ill. By then he was ten years old. He could’ve given me hell - after all, his father wanted his blessing before we married, so he could’ve stopped our union in its tracks, had he wanted to - but Wei never saw me as the wicked stepmother. And for that, I’ll always be grateful.”

Zuko offers a small smile, relieved he doesn’t seem to have insulted Ama after all. “Wei probably appreciated that you *weren’t* a wicked stepmother.”

“Oh, that hardly means anything,” Ama sighs. “You’ll learn when you have children of your own that it doesn’t matter *what* the reality of the matter is - once they decide something’s true, it becomes true.”

A presence appears at Zuko’s side. He looks up to see Zhao, standing about three feet away.

“Can I borrow you for a moment?” he asks.

Although they don’t know one another that well yet, Ama’s deep respect for the royal family has instilled in Zuko a sense of safety. He’s reluctant to leave that behind, but Zhao gestures to the hall. Perhaps if they stay within earshot, it will be fine. Zuko nods and follows his husband out of the reed room, trying not to feel instant regret once the reed-covered doors are shut behind them.

Zhao clears his throat before addressing his cupped hand; “Once again, I find myself apologizing for my brother. He seems to find an opportunity to slander your father whenever you’re near.”

Zuko chews the inside of his cheek, debating with himself. He is faced with a choice, now. He can either go along with everything Zhao says. Nod and agree and lie as he so wishes him to.

Or.

“Yan was out of line, but I’m not upset with him,” Zuko says. “To be fair, you’ve said far worse about my father.”

Zhao sucks his teeth. “I thought we agreed to move past our… disagreement,” he says, eventually.

Zuko cast his eyes on the floor. He had nodded when Zhao suggested it, didn’t he? But that was before he remembered all that happened. That was before he realized that the Lesser Hall truly *wasn’t* all his fault. Now that he knows Zhao’s part, he wants - he wants *something,* some closure, but he’s afraid to ask for it lest he lose his temper.

There’s a weighty pause. Zhao’s eyes flicker to the door to the reed room, then back to Zuko’s face. “What do you remember from that day?”

Zuko sighs despite the sour drop in the pit of his stomach. “Zhao, I don’t want to fight…”

“We’re not fighting, Zuko,” Zhao says, a contradictory warning in his tone. “We’re having a discussion. I’m concerned about your recovery, and I want to know what you’ve remembered.”

Right, recovery. Zuko severely doubts that’s actually what his husband is afraid of. He crosses his arms over his chest. “I remember us fighting about my father.”

Zhao scoffs, crossing his own arms. “Well, yes, we just established that - what else? What had you panicking in the bedroom, earlier?”

This feels dangerous. “Are you saying that there’s more for me to remember, Zhao?”

Zuko’s waiting for the moment his husband grabs him and physically wrestles the truth out of him. It’s not here, quite yet; Zhao maintains his distance, eyes raking over him as if he can find the truth simply by looking. But he can no longer keep the anger from sharpening the edges of his features.

“Describe our fight,” Zhao says, voice rising. “Tell me *how* it went.”

Zuko wonders if he shut his eyes, banished the vision of his furious husband from his sight, if he’d have an easier time recounting what happened. At least his voice wouldn’t tremble so thoroughly. But he looks his husband in the face as he speaks.

“You... spoke out against my father. We argued.”

“About what?”

“I’d rather not rehash it.”

“*Try,* ” Zhao says, testy.

Zuko swallows back the bile in his throat. “You. Said my father didn’t love me. And then admitted you wanted to depose him. I tried to leave. You... *choked* me. I threw you off me-”

“You *burned* me off you,” Zhao says, standing close, now. Crowding him.

“I burned you off me,” Zuko amends, voice rising along with Zhao’s, “and then *you* attacked me with fire-”

“Because *you* had-”

“-And *we* fought and *we* burned the Lesser Hall,” Zuko says, voice now a shout, “and when *I* tried to stop us, when I tried to end things so we could get to safety, you *hit me* over the head-”

“That’s fucking ridiculous,” Zhao scoffs. “It wasn’t me, it was a *beam*. The Lesser Hall had lost its structural integrity-”

“*You* hit me,” Zuko repeats, standing his ground. “*You* hit me over the head after we *agreed* to walk out of there together.”

“That is fucking horrible,” Zhao grounds out. “Why the *fuck* would I do that to you? Why would you *ever* think I’d do something so psychotic?”

“I heard you say-”

“What, as you were falling unconscious?”

“You *said*, you said something before you hit me-”

“I did *not* -”

“You-”

Zuko is cut off when Zhao’s clenched hands jerk in the air, as if yearning for the moment they finally get to close the distance and throttle him. Yet there’s an invisible barrier Zhao is refusing to cross. Even now, wild with anger, he does not lay a hand on Zuko.

“How would you even *know,* Zuko?” he shouts. “You have a fucking *concussion*! You don’t know *anything* that happened!”

There’s a knock at the front door. Their shared, furious panting stands out starkly in the otherwise silent hall. They look at one another - then, repulsed by what they see, turn to the door instead. They wait, as if expecting someone else to materialize and open it, and when the knocking continues, Zhao finally steps forward to answer it.

There’s a man holding a scroll. He’s wearing what looks like outdated military armour, with large swatches of bright orange and bone-white spikes littering the padding. He does not bow when he sees them, going straight to business. “Sorry to disturb you all so late, but this message came by hawk from the royal palace. I didn’t think it could wait until morning.” He holds a scroll aloft, and indeed, it bears Ozai’s personal seal.

Upon seeing it, Zhao nods; there’s a few strands of hair loose from his topknot that flop in his face, breaking the illusion of calm he’s trying to project with the tone of his voice.

“Very good. I’ll take that,” Zhao says, extending a hand.

The guard shakes his head, retracting the scroll. “Apologies, I should’ve specified - this message is for Master Wei.”

The hand extended clenches into a fist. “There is no *Master* Wei here. I’m the head of this household. Give it here.”

“I’m sorry,” says the guard, “but this message bears the Fire Lord’s seal. It’s strictly confidential.”

“Whatever business my brother has with the palace, it has to go through *me*,” says Zhao. “If the Fire Lord doesn’t like it, then he doesn’t need to know.”

There’s a snarl in Zhao’s voice, the excitement from their fight transferred onto this new, innocent party. Zuko cannot resist the urge to sidle up behind Zhao, ready to de-escalate things.

“I will return when Wei is available,” the guard says firmly. He starts to take a step back, but in a flash, Zhao has grabbed him up by the front of his shirt and hauled him up so the toes of his boots only just scrape the ground beneath them.

In this moment of blinding terror, all Zuko can feel are the threads of an imaginary fire. He siphons them desperately, picturing them cooling under the airless prison of a bell jar. “This is a misunderstanding,” he says, practically vibrating at his husband’s side with anxiety. “Let him go, Zhao.”

Zhao won’t even look at him, shaking the guard in his grasp as if to threaten him. At this, Zuko’s hand flies up and touches Zhao on the arm, not necessarily to wrench him off the other man, but because pure instinct tells him to do *something*.

At once, Zhao flinches under the smaller man’s touch, eyes flashing to where his husband touches him. Zuko expects his expression to be one of fury, but with those wide eyes, that stiff jaw, Zhao looks almost -

Frightened? Why the hell would he be *frightened?*

Before Zuko can process it, a new, much calmer voice calls out, “This is all unnecessary.”

Wei stands at the far end of the hallway, expression impassive behind the glare of light on his spectacles. Yan stands behind him, eyes nervously darting between Zhao and the guard. As Wei moves towards them, the light on his glasses refracts, and Zuko thinks he sees that cold gaze fixed on *him*, of all places.

Caught in the act, Zhao releases the guard, who stumbles back, holding the scroll at a distance so Zhao can’t grab it away.

Wei’s eyes flicker to the newly freed guard. “I have nothing to hide from my brother. You can hand over the letter, Kasem.”

The guard looks stricken by this decision. He doesn’t hand the letter to Zhao so much as he stands there, stunned, as it’s snatched from his hands.

Zhao breaks the seal with a vengeance, skimming the contents with furrowed brows. When he’s finished, he swears, then stalks up to Wei to shove the letter into his hands. “You and I need to talk. Now. Upstairs.”

“Of course,” Wei replies, even-keeled. He has the most impressive poker face Zuko has ever seen. It doesn’t give even a twitch of emotion as he follows his younger brother out of the room.

In any case, with Zhao gone, Zuko is able to relax for the first time all night. As he shuts the door behind the retreating guard, his mind returns to the look of fear he saw flash across Zhao’s face moments before. It seems crazy to think, but… Zuko *did* hold his own in their fight, a few days ago. Is Zhao being distant to avoid Zuko’s possible backlash?

“Fuuuuck,” Yan groans at the end of the hall, startling Zuko out of his thoughts. He’s raking his hands over his face like a man at wit’s end. “I wanted Wei to light the hearth for me…”

Zuko avoids eye contact, sneaking off before Yan can ask him for help again. There’s no way he can let *anyone* in this house find out that his bending is blocked. If it gets back to Zhao, all that skittish distance and care he’s paid to Zuko will disappear in an instant.

---

Iroh’s legs were beginning to ache from being crouched down for so long. Yet he refused to take a break, sifting through the rubble and ash like a man possessed. This had long ago stopped being solely about helping the palace staff clean the remnants of the Lesser Hall, although he still felt that duty keenly. Now his primary goal was to find something for Zuko.

In the days that followed the fire, those few supporting beams had gradually collapsed and fell, meaning it was more difficult than ever to enter the remains of the Lesser Hall, let alone tell what room you were standing in. Much of the work wasn’t based in discovery, but in hauling materials away. The capable young men who labored beside Iroh chuckled that he would be physically fit in no time. Others nervously suggested he give it a rest.

Nevertheless, he toiled. That day, he was accompanied by a servant named Shouji, who had worked for the royal family for many years. He usually announced arrivals and escorted visitors across the grounds, but this effort called for as much help as possible. Not that this temporary reassignment bothered Shouji; although he served the entire royal family, he genuinely *liked* General Iroh. The old man was courteous and patient. He would’ve made a fine Fire Lord, had he ever been given the chance.

After a great deal of burnt debris was cleared, Iroh unearthed a metal object about the size and shape of a long novel. He rubbed the soot away with his elbow, and saw that underneath was a zig-zagging pattern set in copper. Instantly, he dug into his pockets and compared the box he held with the drawing Zuko had given him.

It was a match. Iroh doubted the fire had reached the contents, but nevertheless decided to check. He had seen trick latches like this one before, and opened it in a matter of seconds.

Inside was a belt. Nothing about it seemed particularly valuable, which didn’t match the protective container it was kept in. Something pungent rose from the velvet lining, and Iroh lifted it to his face, puzzled. There was something familiar about the scent. Was it merely the fact it smelled like Zhao? Or was it something else? Curious as to what he’d found, Shouji came over to inspect the belt, shrugging when Iroh offered it up to smell. “I’m a beta,” he said. “All I can tell you is that there’s loads of smoke. No pheromones are getting past here.”

“Well, we’ve found Zuko’s room, at least,” Iroh said, looking around the wreckage as if he could now see the old layout of the room in ghostlike outlines around them. “Let’s keep searching here.”

As nice as it would be to send something more back to his nephew, there was little sign of the Avatar research. Iroh had figured that would be the case, but it still saddened him. Over the years, he’d watched as a previously sunny, outgoing boy became more withdrawn and silent. Zuko’s obsession with the Avatar’s return had been one of the few things to imbue him with a sense of purpose. Looking up at the sky between the charred and collapsed remnants of the roof, Iroh saw he had a few hours left of daylight; he decided he was going to find some proof of his nephew’s work, if it was the last thing he did.

There was a section of wall that had collapsed inward, with only the smallest opening close to the floor that he could fit his hand through. Iroh reached inside and knocked against something, hearing it roll out of his grasp. Even straining his hand as far as he could, he was not able to lay a finger on whatever he’d knocked out of the way. He called Shouji over to help him, and together they lifted the collapsed debris so the opening was wider, and he could get the top half of his body inside to grab whatever it was he’d touched earlier.

It was a metal tube, the sort usually transported by messenger hawks. Without a thought to privacy, Iroh twisted off the cap and found a thick roll of parchment inside. When pulled free, the topmost letter read:

*Dear Zhao,*

*Sorry to write again so soon, I just really wanted to share something.*

*I think the Avatar’s heading for the North Pole. I’ve been mapping the places where he’s* *supposedly been spotted, and it’s not a straight path, but if you draw a line of best fit, he seems to* *be heading north. I guess he’d be fairly safe there. We’ve never figured out how to invade it, at* *least.*

*Do you think he’s still in training? He’s probably looking for a waterbending master. That would* *support the rumors that he’s a kid, since he still has a lot to learn, but I still don’t understand how* *there can be an airbender so young. They were all wiped out generations ago.*

*Best,*

*Zuko*

Iroh ran his thumb along the scratchy edges of his nephew’s handwriting. So these were letters Zhao had kept over the years. He shouldn’t read any more deeply than this.

He glanced up at Shouji, expecting to find a guilty look on the other man’s face. Instead, he gave Iroh a hesitant smile and said, “I won’t tell if you don’t tell.”

So Iroh thumbed through the other documents. There were a few written in his nephew’s hand, but Zuko wasn’t the only person who had written Zhao. There was also a puzzling message from his older brother.

*Zhao-*

*Color me shocked you actually bothered to write. I had to check the signature three times to be* *sure I wasn’t imagining it.*

*Yes, I have heard about Ozai by now. How fortuitous for all of us. Perhaps it’s trite to say, but I* *knew he was destined for greater things than mere princehood could offer him even when we were* *children. It’s satisfying to see he’s finally risen to the station he was always meant to hold. I’ve* *enclosed a receipt for his coronation gift; I’m assuming it passes your muster as sacred arbiter of* *our estate, so I’ve already forged your signature in approval, as per usual. Better write me back* *quickly if you expect me to return it.*

*Camelephant oil seems like a hare-brained solution to me. Although I for one trust Ozai’s word, it* *would be unfortunate if our entry into the royal family were marred from the outset. Do what you* *can to protect our interests and let me know if things go awry. I’ll personally regret if your* *engagement must be annulled, but Yan could use the laugh.*

*Take care to write home more often. Ama worries.*

*Wei*

There was something sinister lurking behind the fine penmanship of this missive. The mention of camelephant oil in relation to Zuko, in relation to *protecting their interests* made an awful dread rise in Iroh’s throat.

“I have a confession to make,” Iroh said. He was talking to Shouji, but also to any ear, earthly or otherwise, that would listen. “I’ve long been biased against this man my nephew married. Many times I’ve worried I’m merely looking for trouble where there is none, but reading this, now, I’m filled with unease. I only wish I had more details. Then perhaps I could be sure.”

Iroh looked at Shouji with a sad smile, but the other man wasn’t looking at him. He was still silently reading the letter, brow furrowed with what Iroh assumed was confusion until their eyes met.

“...General Iroh,” said Shouji. “I too know something about Zhao that puts me at unease. I don’t know what it means, exactly - or I haven’t ever known what it meant. Now, reading this, I fear I’m putting the pieces together.”

There was a beat where Iroh expected him to elaborate, and when he didn’t, urged him, “Tell me, Shouji. Please.”

Shouji’s eyes shone large and glassy with guilt. “I’m not blameless in this story, General Iroh. I’m afraid that by telling you, you’ll lose your good faith in me.”

“Know that whatever actions you regret, I will never disapprove of your honesty,” Iroh said, searching his face. “Please tell me what you know. I fear my nephew’s safety relies on it.”

And so Shouji told him how, two years before, Zhao had offered him a bribe in exchange for a very simple task: he was to write to Zhao as soon as it was officially confirmed that Prince Zuko had his first heat.

Initially this revelation only puzzled Iroh. He didn’t understand what Shouji meant, because he didn’t understand why Zhao would need to bother. He had been under the assumption that Zuko had presented as an omega *before* his engagement to Zhao, because Zuko had already done so by the time Iroh arrived in Caldera.

Then Iroh remembered how Azula had been identified by an exam years earlier, and realized the same could have been done for her brother. Shouji confirmed; “Everyone at the palace knew, but I don’t think it was widely known otherwise. It’s possible Zhao realized the prince wasn’t officially an omega and panicked.”

“He felt a need to protect his interests,” Iroh whispered, a cold sweat breaking out across his skin. He remembered something else from his return to Caldera: the fact Azula had seen Zhao at an herbalist. Iroh had looked into it, and at the time, the lead had seemed like a dead end. Now he looked down at the box in his hands and realized he knew what that faded scent was that had seemed so familiar.

It was camelephant oil, just as Wei had mentioned in his letter. A potent substance that, when administered over a long period of time, proved excellent for bringing out characteristics commonly associated with alphas. In a large, singular dose, it had been used to treat alphas with potency problems. To give it to an under-aged omega before they presented *could* theoretically trigger a heat, Iroh supposed. However, there were real risks to consider, and the thought it had been administered without Zuko’s permission terrified him to consider.

“What date did my nephew present?” Iroh asked. “A-and when did Zhao first reach out to you? I know it was a long time ago, but anything at all you can remember would help.”

“I actually remember it right down to the day,” said Shouji. “It was the same day Lady Ursa went missing and Fire Lord Ozai was crowned.”

“Which do you mean?” Iroh asked impatiently. “Zhao’s request, or Zuko’s presentation?”

“Both,” said Shouji. “It all happened in one day.”

Too many threads were trying to connect at once, the web becoming more and more tangled. Iroh was sure of only one thing: he needed to go to Kirachu at once. He didn’t know what he would do once there, but he knew he needed to be there for his nephew. He simply couldn’t wait.

That night, Iroh hastily packed what little he had left in preparation to disembark in the early hours of the morning. But as he was preparing for bed, a servant stopped by to tell him that Azula had sent word for him. The tiny envelope he was handed seemed to weigh a thousand pounds. He almost forgot to thank the person who brought it to him before closing the door.

Iroh was being forced to choose between his children. Guilt festered in his stomach at the prospect. He missed Azula and wanted a chance to make amends, but with all he was discovering, Zuko’s situation was clearly the more dire of the two.

Not that he would ignore her entirely. He opened her letter so he could properly devise a response, and was struck dumb by the words he found:

*Uncle,*

*I have much to tell you, but given that I just survived an assassination attempt, I don’t think it’d be* *wise to discuss over missive.*

*If this letter manages to make it to you, please meet me at our usual place.*

*Best,*

*Princess Azula*

---

Later, when they’re getting ready to retire for the night, Zuko happens upon Wei in the hall. He waves somewhat hesitantly.

“Um - hi,” says Zuko. “We haven’t really had a chance to meet, properly.”

Wei only cocks his head, as if puzzling through the details of a riddle. “That trick you used, earlier. Did Ozai teach you that?”

Zuko blinks. These are the first words Wei has said to him since his arrival, and they make absolutely no sense. “What trick?” he asks.

Nothing in Wei’s face belies his cryptic meaning. After a pause, he decides, “You didn’t even know that you were doing it.” Then before Zuko can ask what he means, sweeps past him down the hall and out of sight.

### Text

When Wei’s mother scowls, she gets these terrible shadows under her eyes. If he had to, he could pick out her skull from a thousand others, knowing only the shape of her sockets. Her sunken eyes swivel towards him as she asks, “How is my replacement doing?”

Wei never knows how to respond when she takes that tone. He shifts in his chair at her bedside and mumbles, “He’s not replacing you. No one can ever replace you.”

The dying woman isn’t touched by this comment; she takes a breath, chest rattling like a bag of coins, and says, “He’s the poorest excuse for a nurse I’ve ever met. I don’t know who your father thinks he’s fooling. Certainly none of the neighbors will-” She stops to cough, once, thrice, five times. “-will approve. Are people talking about it?”

“I don’t know,” Wei says honestly. At ten, he’s not exactly privy to the gossip that passes between adults. Especially since “neighbors” is a generous description for nobility who live dozens of miles away from their secluded mountain-top estate.

Wei’s home has always seemed a lonely one, but as of late, the isolation has become worse; no one wants the boy with the ailing mother to come play, fearful of the illness he may bring, and no one wants to visit for similar reasons. He doesn’t even get to see other children at school - all his tutors come to the estate instead, to the chagrin of his father. He probably would have shipped Wei back off to boarding school by now if it had not been his wife’s dying wish to spend what little time she had left with her son. Wei is grateful not to miss a moment of it, but he’s also keenly aware that she is his only companion, and he is rapidly losing her.

Well - there is one other person who makes for a potential ally. The male omega who has come to care for her at the end of her life. Ama, the doppelgänger. In fact, when he first stood in their foyer, Wei hadn’t realized he was a stranger, heart quickening as he wondered how his mother had managed to find the strength to get up and walk down the stairs all by herself.

Then Ama opened his mouth. That tenor voice had dispersed any illusions about Wei’s mother ever making a full recovery.

“I can’t stand that terrible, honking voice of his,” Wei’s mother spits. She never used to spit her words. She used to be a lovely, happy person, but that was before she lost half her weight in blood and sputum hacked from her lungs, before her husband shamelessly took a lover while she was confined to her deathbed.

“I hate it, too,” Wei says, because she expects him to.

“And he never stops using it. Does he at least say anything incriminating to you, something we could throw in your father’s face to have him sent away?” Wei’s mother asks.

In fact, that morning, while Ama cooked breakfast, he told a very age-inappropriate story about propositioning his former landlord. Having lost his sisters and his mother to the same illness now wasting Wei’s mother away, he’d struggled to pay for a place that had historically cost five incomes, and was looking for alternative solutions… but the landlord wasn’t interested.

As the eggs burned and stuck to the pan, Ama lamented, “He actually told me if one of my sisters had offered instead, he’d think about it, but because it was *me,* it was a no-go. Then he made some charming observation about how the wrong siblings had died. Thank Agni your father rescued me - otherwise I would’ve made a career out of men like that.” All the while he talked, he went through a cycle of such vivid gestures and facial expressions that Wei felt like he was watching a one-man play.

Back in the present, he decides not to recount this tale to his mother, if only to save her blood pressure. “No. He just says a bunch of pointless stuff about his life.”

Despite his illusion-killing tendencies, Wei actually finds Ama’s company to be a relief, at times. At least he never has to think up anything to say; Ama talks for him, as if he understands Wei’s need to listen without sharing - or perhaps he’s just really, really self-absorbed. Wei can’t quite tell, but he does like this stranger, who wears his mother’s face with a warm smile, and sometimes lies to his father about how long Wei’s been studying, so he can be permitted to stop earlier.

Wei’s mother narrows her eyes as if divining his treacherous thoughts. “Well. I know I can’t stop your father from remarrying, but I forbid you from ever loving that… imitation. *”* As a rule, she never says Ama’s name. “I don’t want you to forget about me after I’m gone.”

“I won’t,” says Wei, gut twisting at the reminder of her imminent loss.

She fixes him with a steely eye. “I am serious, Wei. Promise me.”

“I said I *won’t*,” he repeats, and although she doesn’t push the point further, her responding look is disappointed. He hasn’t any idea what more he could say to please her, so he says, “I love you,” because he knows it’ll make her eyes soften.

And they do. She takes him by the chin, her nails biting into his skin as she says, “And I love you *most,* Wei. I love you more than anyone else ever will.”

---

Days after Wei’s mother is lowered into the ground, an officiate from the royal palace comes to privately marry his father and Ama on the estate. The reason for the discretion isn’t merely the bad timing: Ama is very obviously pregnant, his stomach as gigantic as a ripe melon. The officiate’s eyes linger rudely over it for the duration of the ceremony.

Wei doesn’t have any other formal robes, so he wears the ones they got him for his mother’s funeral. He wants to believe she would like that he’s dressed in mourning whites for what’s supposed to be a happy occasion, but she would probably prefer that he throw cow-chicken’s blood on Ama and demand his father renounce him. Since Wei is not keen on being beaten to death, this smaller rebellious gesture will have to do.

---

A month later, Wei’s new baby brother arrives in the world, so furious about his eviction from the womb that he cries non-stop. Wei doesn’t ask to hold him, although he stiffly complies once Ama offers. He’s not allowed to love Ama, but it’s worth it to still try to get along, if only to have one adult in his life who is on his side.

Ama shows Wei how to cradle the baby’s head, fuzzy and a little bit misshapen, like an overripe peach. It’s not a particularly thrilling experience. All babies look alike, and this one is no more special simply because it’s related to him. Zhao wiggles and fusses in his brother’s arms, his tiny voice issuing short, abrupt sobs the entire time he’s held.

“He wants *me,* ” Ama sighs, hiding how pleased he is under faux exasperation. The moment the baby is bundled back in his arms, he stops moving and goes quiet, nodding off almost instantly. Wei ponders the fact Zhao’s brain is essentially an unmolded lump of clay, a tiny speck of nothing, yet he still inherently knows he’s safest in his mother’s arms.

(He is shocked by the jealousy he feels at this realization, welling up inside him so powerfully that it scorches his throat. Perhaps he won’t betray his mother, after all. It’s suddenly so easy to hate Ama, and his newborn son, to boot.)

For the first month of the baby’s life, Wei does everything in his power to avoid being alone with the beatific mother and son duo. No one seems to object to this, and he hopes it is less because everyone’s tired of him and more because he’s quite civil about it, all things considered. He’s not his father’s son, throwing a screaming tantrum every time he doesn’t get his way. Instead he spends most of his time alone in his room. Perhaps it’s normal for a boy his age; a contrary part of him is annoyed no one has nagged him about it.

By chance one day, he walks into the reed room just as Ama is waving something that looks like a wadded up napkin in front of the baby’s face. Zhao seems interested in everything but the prize his mother is offering up, eyes sliding around the room without purpose. He pushes himself up onto his elbows for all of three seconds, before he topples over onto his stomach. Unperturbed, he sucks his hand. Not exactly a prodigy, this one, but Ama carries on in gentle earnest, whispering his son’s name and lightly shaking the bundle near his face.

When Ama’s eyes flicker up to meet his, Wei realizes he’s been standing on the threshold for quite some time now, staring at them. Heat rushes to his face. Hopefully there was no hint of yearning in his gaze, or he might die of embarrassment.

“What is that?” he asks as a distraction, pointing at the thing Ama keeps waving in Zhao’s face.

The omega holds it aloft. “Cotton and bark, dipped in oil. Fatimah showed it to me the other day; you can use it to determine if a child will firebend. Supposedly even newborns can light it.”

“Makes sense you’d want to find that out as soon as possible, to avoid the baby burning the house down,” says Wei. He tries to remember if his mother ever did something like this with him. She must have, when he was too small to remember.

“I can’t get him to do it, though,” Ama huffs, waving the bundle again. “I do wish I’d asked Fatimah more questions about how this works. My mother never told me about these things. I don’t think she would’ve even *known* to tell me - my oldest sister was the only member of our family who could firebend, and my mother always said she got that from her father, whoever *that* was…”

Ama trails off. Wei hums, rocking on the balls of his feet in the doorway. “...Well. Maybe Zhao’s not lighting it because he can’t bend, either.”

“Of course he can bend,” Ama responds, scowling. “His father can bend, and he’s just as much a part of him as he is of me.”

He jerks the bundle of kindling this way and that in front of the baby, who merely lays on his side and stares at it. After moments, he is bored with this new toy, and looks up to his older brother standing in the doorway. He burbles and reaches for him, showing off his gums with a wide smile.

Which seems to give Ama an idea. “Hey, Wei… All I can do is shove this in his face, but maybe if you firebend for him, he’ll figure out what he’s supposed to do.”

Honestly the last thing Wei wants to do is help orchestrate some mother-and-son moment of triumph, but something about the hopeful look Ama has fixed on him propels him across the room. He sits on the floor next to the couch, and from where he’s toppled over inches from Wei’s face, Zhao swats him on the nose. His hand isn’t as disgusting and moist as usual, but Wei still ducks backward, out of reach of the next swat. When there’s a wobble of hurt on his baby brother’s face, Wei shoves his remorse down deep, reminding himself that it’s safer to put distance between them. No use letting the stupid baby burn himself during this demonstration.

Wei summons a single candle-sized flame, balancing it on his pointer and index. This, unlike the wad of kindling, has Zhao rapt with attention; Wei watches the way the fire reflects orange in his wondrous gaze, his lips spreading into another gummy smile.

Wei makes the flame disappear, and sees the baby’s face transform with confusion, sparse eyebrows knitting together, mouth slack. Then, with a laugh, Zhao slams one tiny palm against the corner cushion, setting it on fire.

Ama gives a shriek of panic and triumph. There’s thankfully a blanket he can use to smother the fire, which he and Wei do, frantically.

“Did you see that!” Ama exclaims. “He didn’t even *need* the kindling. He set a fire without any help at all.”

*He had some help*, Wei thinks, getting to pout for only one ridiculous moment before lithe fingers thread in his hair, tipping his head forward so cool lips can touch his forehead. Ama seals in his utter devotion with one shamefully basic phrase: “You’re a good big brother, Wei.”

The effects of this motherly kiss are immediate: Wei is filled with a boundless affection that is quickly doused by a sickly guilt. He feels like he is spitting on his mother’s grave.

He pulls out of the embrace, muttering, “I have to go,” leaving his step-parent alone to deal with the fact that he has helped a creature with no impulse control learn how to burn everything in grasping range. Wei can’t be bothered to worry about that now; he is too busy burning himself from the inside out.

---

Wei catches a glimpse of something he doesn’t understand. Through the crack of a door, he can see someone’s naked back, the pale expanse of skin webbed and warped by old burn scars. There is a series of fresh blisters trailing up one side, and it is around this locus of agony that the rest of the body seems to seize.

It is his mother’s back, yet not; the breadth of the shoulders tell him this is Ama. He kneels, his back to the doorway, shivering with pain instead of running away. He’s waiting for a cue, maybe. An order. Frightened, Wei doesn’t hang around long enough to see his father’s eyes hanging like two stars above him in the dark.

---

When Wei first slipped a casual mention of his prestigious new friend into conversation, his father barely noticed. He didn’t even nod, engrossed as he was in some treatise or another that he’d laid out on the kitchen table.

But Ama noticed. There was a clatter as he turned so quickly to his step-son that he knocked a glass placed too closely into the sink. “Did you just say Ozai?”

“Why, yes I did,” Wei replied.

“As in *Prince Ozai?* ” Ama repeated, hand to chest. Trust him to give you the dramatic emphasis you were looking for. Wei nodded, making his step-parent gasp. “I knew he was your age, but not that he was in the same class! How exciting!”

Wei tried not to preen when his father finally raised his head and looked at him. “I’d imagine a prince would be highly sought after,” he supplied dully. “I’m sure most children in your year are scrambling to say they’re friends with him, but which of them are, really?”

The implication that Wei had exaggerated their closeness stung. Ama scowled as openly as he wished to. “Weren’t you listening to what he said? He made the prince laugh. They ate together. That’s a real connection!”

His father gave a noncommittal shrug before shutting them both out again to resume his work. There was a shine in Ama’s eye - could it be jealousy, that the first wife’s son could make such famous friends, while his own was barely old enough to teethe?

Ama swept over from where he’d been perched by the window, spying on the gardeners, to pull a chair up beside his step-son. “What you’ve come across is a once in a lifetime opportunity, Wei,” he said. “You have been blessed by Agni with wit and humor for this very purpose.”

“And here I thought the most they would earn me were late detentions,” Wei breezed.

In the time since his official entry into their family, Ama’s expressions had become markedly less dramatic; he saved his smiles for rare occasions, as though allotted only the few. Now, as he bestowed one of these rare, close-lipped smiles upon Wei, the result was jarring - he saw, in an instant, his mother’s face, years before her death, when she’d been in good health and good spirits.

“Tell me - what was the prince like?” Ama asked.

Gathering his wits, Wei answered, “Oh, you know. For royalty, he’s really very ordinary.”

Which wasn’t entirely true. Ozai had something of a dour aura about him that put off their peers. He was always standing just beyond the crowd, the upward lilt of his chin and eternally bored expression telling the rest of them what they could already intuit on their own: that he was not some bashful creature, but all too good for their company. Truth be told, he was somewhat disliked, but in that covetous way the powerful always are, with every peer who scorned him secretly yearning for his favour.

All Wei had done to garner Ozai’s attention was raise one gangly leg to trip a teacher onto his fat face. Ozai had a front seat to the whole thing, and emitted the most unprincely *squawk* of laughter that a prince had ever squawked. It was simultaneously the most awful and the most beautiful sound Wei had ever heard. It stopped him in his tracks, so that he failed to make his getaway before the old man on the floor started shouting and spewing fire in his direction.

He’d had his lunch taken away and been forced to do twenty straight minutes of horse stance outside the classroom. Ozai snuck out midway through his punishment to eat in front of him with a wry smile, breaking off one solitary piece of his pork bun after considerable whining and puppy dog-eyeing on Wei’s part. It was as if they’d been friends for eons before that point. They simply clicked.

(“Just think: any other boy would be punished alongside me for the crime of egging me on, but royalty gets off scot free! I’m essentially taking your punishment for you.”

“Mmm, I don’t think you’re being punished for me laughing, I think you’re being punished for tripping a very old man.”

“Well, it brought you joy. Pay a pittance to your lowly jester, will you?” And Ozai had, pressing the bit of pork bun directly between Wei’s parted lips. Wei was as floored by the gesture as he was smitten.)

In recounting the tale, Wei left out the part where he’d injured a teacher and gotten in trouble, instead claiming he’d lost his lunch because he’d dropped it in a pond. There weren’t any ponds on the school grounds, but it’s not as though his father knew that. He hardly gave enough of a shit about what Wei was saying to ask any questions that would unravel his lie.

Ama, on the other hand, was rapt. “You *must* continue to develop a friendship with this boy,” he said fervently.

“Of course I’ll try, but I don’t want to force it,” said Wei. “These things need to happen naturally, right?”

“Only to an extent,” Ama insisted. “Relationships are like orchids. You must cultivate them obsessively, fastidiously, even, or they’ll die over the slightest mistake. Think, Wei. A friend like that could be a lifelong advantage. What if you have opposing presentations? Court Ozai successfully, and you could one day be a member of the royal family!”

Across the room, Wei’s father released a gust of a sigh. Without looking up from his papers, he said, “For spirit’s sake, Ama, they’re *twelve* .”

*Thirteen, actually,* thought Wei.

For someone trying to cultivate an impassive persona, Ama sure had an arsenal of stares, this one being particularly withering. “So? That doesn’t mean we can’t plan ahead. Alliances forged in youth are some of the strongest there are.” Wei realized then that the shine he’d see in Ama’s eyes hadn’t been jealousy. It was ambition; he was making plans for Wei’s benefit.

There again they were, twisting their way up Wei’s throat and making it difficult to breathe: those twin sensations of affection and guilt. He wished at times that Ama wouldn’t make liking him so easy, but really, when it came to paying Wei a little attention, who did he have to compete with? A dead woman, or in the case of Wei’s father, no competition at all.

---

Fast forward a few months, to his next break home from school. Wei was trying and failing to focus on a series of equations, too excited about Ozai’s impending visit to get anything done. Wei had casually dropped the idea on one of the last days of class, and the other boy had agreed right away. With mere hours to go before the young prince’s arrival, Wei abandoned his homework, resolving to either finish it all the last day of break or make a mad dash in the minutes before the teacher collected it.

His plan was to get out his energy by practicing his firebending forms in the yard, but from the moment he opened his bedroom door, he could hear his younger brother crying louder than probably any other child alive.

It wasn’t a sad cry; there was a sharp edge to it, an almost vicious anguish that made Wei’s hair stand up on end. Having known him since he was fresh from the womb, Wei was confident that he could tell Zhao’s cry of genuine need apart from his cry of spite. And this, most certainly, was a cry of spite.

Wincing to himself, Wei descended the stairs, reluctantly moving towards the source of the noise. The closer he got, the more sounds he could distinguish; there was a barrage of thumps, likely tiny limbs being flailed in all directions. Wei couldn’t resist popping his head into the reed room before he headed outside, if only to confirm that at least *one* adult was apprised of the situation.

He was greeted by the sight of Ama, tambour frame in hand, embroidering something while he steadfastly ignored the screaming three-year-old at his feet. It seemed impossible that the creature sitting on the divan was capable of producing that little monster; where everything about Ama was delicate and muted, almost to the point of appearing sickly, Zhao was a squarish, ruddy child, teeming with piss and vinegar. He didn’t seem to notice that his older brother had entered the room, tiny fists scrubbing over his eyes as he yelled his lungs out.

“Fussy today,” Wei quipped from the doorway.

“What?” said Ama.

“I said - fussy today?” Wei repeated, voice raised.

“Oh, yes,” Ama agreed, just as loudly. They nearly had to shout to be heard. Not to be outdone, Zhao tilted his head back and screamed as though his limbs were being torn from his body. For a creature so small, he really had a magnificent set of pipes on him.

It wasn’t like Ama to let Zhao cry on and on like this; in fact, he usually rushed to fulfill the little bugger’s every whim. Every teardrop was sacred and every impulse had to be rewarded. It drove their father crazy. Since Wei had been home, his father had given no less than three rousing speeches about the fact that *he* was master of the house, and would under no circumstances relinquish this title to a mere infant. The amount with which he viewed a helpless baby as his sworn rival for Ama’s affections was, in Wei’s opinion, frankly batshit.

Just as Wei was starting to feel sorry for the brat, a new stage of the tantrum began: Zhao raised his little fists and began *furiously* smacking whatever parts of Ama’s legs he could reach. It was a two-handed assault carried out with every ounce of power in his small but compact body. Still, his mother ignored him, unmoved by his tantrum even as Wei could hear the impact of fists on flesh.

“Doesn’t that hurt?” Wei asked, somewhat alarmed.

“He’s just so *little*,” Ama replied, which wasn’t really an answer.

“Right. Why are you letting him scream like that, though?”

“He’s self-soothing,” Ama explained, then repeated, when Zhao’s screaming drowned him out.

“I think the absolute last word I’d use to describe this is ‘soothing,’” said Wei.

“I know,” said Ama, voice straining, “but your father is fed up with me coddling him, and you know how he is once he decides we need to do something his way.”

As if summoned, they heard the familiar heavy footsteps take to the stairs. All at once Zhao shut up, fussy screams fading into a few last, pitiful whimpers. In a last ditch effort for attention, he tugged the ends of Ama’s robes, blubbering tears, before turning his snotty face towards Wei.

It was the first time they’d looked at each other head-on since Wei had come downstairs, which made it the first opportunity Zhao got to show off the enormous bruises over the right side of his face. The sight of them turned Wei’s veins to ice.

Zhao had long stopped by the time his father stepped into the room, but he couldn’t suppress one last, tiny hiccup. He may as well have continued his tantrum in earnest, for how their father’s lip curled in disgust. “For spirits’ sake, *stop* with the dramatics,” he said, already gruff voice taking on an edge, and immediately Ama’s hands lighted in Zhao’s hair.

“Um,” said Wei, “I just want to remind you all that Ozai is coming today. So, you know. A member of royalty will be here. In our house.”

All faces turned towards Zhao.

“You’ve got to be kidding me - you’re supposed to *warn* us,” his father snapped.

Wei felt his face go hot with shame. “I did, I said a few days ago-”

“Are you going to take care of this?” his father interrupted, addressing Ama. He gestured vaguely to Zhao as he said it.

Ama’s lips became a thin line. “I don’t know what you want me to do. Turn back time?”

“Just get him out of here. Take him to your friend’s.”
