Wei thought he could see the faintest ripple of disgust twitch Ama’s upper lip. “Fatimah may not be royalty, but I’d rather not show her our shame. Besides, she’s in Ma’Inka this week.” He reached down to lift Zhao into his lap, but in total contradiction to his earlier fuss, the three year old smacked his mother’s hands away. Ama sighed before straightening back up. “We’ll keep him in the master bedroom. Tell the prince he’s sick, if he asks.”

“Won’t that scare him away?”

“Not *deathly* sick, Wei. Just a little sore throat we don’t want spreading to the Fire Lord.”

The preparations for Ozai’s visit became a mad scramble. Nariya, their servant girl, had to rush into town for the makings of a prince-worthy dinner. Wei tidied his room obsessively, rearranging stacks of books as if such tiny details even mattered. And Ama did what was probably the most important job to complete before the prince’s arrival - he got to work calming his husband down.

By the time Ozai arrived, everything was squared away. As he often did in front of polite company, Wei’s father transformed into a jovial person, the sort of ruddy-cheeked man who complimented you as he shook your hand too roughly, who laughed in an infectious and ingratiating way. Ama gave his deferential greetings before dashing off to see to Zhao, who somehow didn’t scream and pound on the door for the entirety of Ozai’s visit.

All of Wei’s tidying hadn’t been entirely for naught - after a brief spar on the lawn (where he graciously lost to the prince on purpose), they spent most of the visit in his room, trading mean commentary about other students. For someone who rarely deigned to engage with their peers, Ozai loved nothing more than to talk about how awful they all were. Wei didn’t necessarily agree with all his observations, but if he was good at anything, it was taking Ozai’s cruel comments and spinning them up into something much funnier, even if they were no less mean. Ah, well. So long as it kept those charming squawks of laughter coming.

Although Ama had very much encouraged this friendship from a purely political standpoint, Wei wasn’t in it solely to get a prince to like him. Yes, that was a cool side effect, but Wei had quickly found that he was infatuated with Ozai, specifically. And there was no ignoring the fact that this strange, prickly boy had likewise chosen *him*. Nobody ever did that.

It was a seamless visit. The only hiccup happened towards the very end, when Ozai was on his way out. They left Wei’s bedroom as Ama was standing outside the master bedroom, straining to shut the door. When the boys approached him, he spun around, jarred by their appearance, and momentarily lost his battle with the door. It pushed open a crack, just enough for a tiny Zhao to shout,

“Let me go!!”

Ama shooed him away, pushing the door so the crack thinned enough to hide any incriminating details. But he couldn’t shut it all the way; one stubborn, chubby hand latched itself on the frame at the last second, and Ama was not about to break his son’s fingers.

With an apologetic smile at the boys, he said, “Don’t mind the baby, Prince Ozai. He isn’t feeling well, so we’re trying to keep him cordoned off.”

Wei glanced down at the crack in the door and saw one baleful little eye - thankfully, not on the bruised side - glaring up at him.

“I want to play,” Zhao said, voice about an octave below its usual shout.

“You and I can play as much as you want when I come back upstairs,” Ama said placatingly.

“I want to play with *the boys* ,” the three-year-old insisted. And his little eye swiveled to look up at his brother’s companion. Wei thought he saw a cringe pass over Ozai’s lips in response. Which was perhaps the first time he’d done something that secretly annoyed Wei; it wasn’t his little brother to be repulsed by.

“We’ll play later, brat,” said Wei. “Ozai has to go home now.”

He only got to hear rather than see the stomp of a tiny foot in protest, but he’d seen Zhao pout enough times to picture how he must look. The chubby hand disappeared from the doorframe, and the door was yanked shut from the inside. Ama looked ready to faint from relief.

Outside, Wei lingered by Ozai’s carriage, not overly eager to say goodbye. Would it be childish to suggest a sleepover next time? Or suspicious, since they were brimming with teenage hormones? Ama would probably faint from joy if Wei asked, but he had no idea if the Fire Lord would be keen on allowing his son to stay in some lowly noble mansion. Perhaps if they sent a phalanx of guards along.

Ozai cast one of his skull-burrowing gazes upon Wei. It was difficult to divine his thinking in these moments; sometimes he would lapse out of these silences and say something terribly cruel, and sometimes not. Perhaps this day had been a bust, after all, and he was about to end their friendship with a single, devastating word. (Once, Ozai had stared at him ominously like this for thirty seconds, then only asked, “How tall do you think you are? Taller than me?”)

But what Ozai said was, “You should ride with me to port.”

Wei nearly laughed with relief. “That’s like thirty minutes, one way. You want me to take a whole hour out of my day for you?”

“As your prince, I command it,” Ozai said, complete with a haughty little smirk. Wei wanted to lick it off his face.

And as it turned out, Ozai *also* wanted him to do that. Since the prince’s personal guard sat up with the coachman, the boys had the compartment to themselves. Wei later remembered it all being far greater than it could possibly have been; with no other experience to compare it to, the fumbling of a middle school kiss was transformed into pure perfection. Wei didn’t even have the wherewithal to be terrified about what this plunge into the world of adult things would do to their friendship, too preoccupied with the sound the prince made when he licked a stripe up the shell of his ear.

When the carriage stopped, Ozai sank his teeth viciously into Wei’s lower lip before releasing him. Maybe it was supposed to have the same effect as dousing him with cold water. In actuality, Wei gave his last goodbyes without leaving the privacy of the compartment, legs crossed to maintain some discretion.

So it began.

---

A crash, late in the night. Sharp, infantile cries.

“Don’t touch him, don’t - don’t *touch* him! *Stop* it-!”

Skin to skin impact, followed by a wordless shout. Then whimpering. It went on for a long time, animal-like excepting the snatches of words he couldn’t hear under the baby. Crying, still.

Wei pressed his covers over his ears and didn’t sleep.

---

“Who wants to come up to the board to solve this problem? How about you, Prince - sorry, not prince. Wei?”

They had become one entity. Teachers and peers alike mixed up their names or called upon them in tandem, Prince Ozaiandwei, as if the prince had absorbed his friend overnight.

Wei wasn’t popular, per se, but he had early settled into a role of classroom jester and smartass, which meant he was well-liked by his peers. It helped that he antagonized mostly teachers, not other kids, although that slowly started to change with Ozai calling the shots. Cruel but funny observations shared in private became weapons used liberally in public, first by Ozai, then eventually by Wei himself, who wanted credit for all the clever things he’d thought of. Ozai was just as content watching Wei tear other people to shreds as he was stealing his ideas to do it himself. It was probably a sign of weakness on Wei’s part, that he would sink to such levels for Ozai’s approval, but he did *so* like hearing that pointy little laugh the prince had.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, Wei found his once plentiful casual acquaintanceships falling away. People now looked to him as they did Ozai - as an unpleasant but immensely important person. The pair was invited to all the big gatherings, the prestigious parties, but none of the smaller and more intimate hang-outs. Ozai was Wei’s first *best* friend, but he wasn’t his first friend; for years, Wei had spent his summers with other sons of nobility at the estate of a boy named Rhe, who owned a veritable fleet of sailboats they’d commandeer all summer long. But this year, there was no invitation for Wei. Rhe and the others wouldn’t even wave to him in the halls.

Ama brushed off his concerns. “You don’t need to be loved by everyone. Isn’t it better to have one profound friendship rather than a hundred cursory ones?”

Wei didn’t confide in his father because he knew it’d be fruitless to, but he was in hearing distance. The old man looked up from whatever work he was doing long enough to grunt: “You’ve become best friends with a prince. That’s not good enough for you?”

And so, in the way infatuations run when left unchecked, Wei threw his entire being into Ozai, and lost himself there.

---

Within the walls of the Kirachu estate lay a grassy knoll shaded by a canopy of leaves. Unless they shouted, they couldn’t be heard from the house. This was where they spent much of the time they didn’t waste in Wei’s room, grappling with their fire, getting grass on their uniforms. As they’d gotten older, they replaced their sparring sessions with other activities that set Wei’s heart thumping for the thrill of being discovered.

On one such outing, Ozai turned to him and said, “I’ve discovered something. Do you want to try it with me?”

Wei hummed where he sat in the grass, long legs taking up an extraordinary amount of room even folded over one another. “Will this discovery leave me sore in a good way, or a bad way?”

Ozai cocked his head. “Why do you assume I’ll hurt you at all?”

Why assume water is wet? “Your love is vicious by nature. You squeezed me like you wanted to break off my blood supply only this morning.”

He received the blank weevil stare for this, so named because of how it burrowed into Wei’s skin. “Lay back,” Ozai asked (commanded, really). Wei complied, arms folded behind his head so that he at least gave his marching orders his own unique flair. One long leg swung through the air over his waist, and in moments the prince was in his lap, straddling him.

“Oh?” Wei asked, faux-inquisitive eyebrow bouncing up his forehead. He smirked as he lifted his hips to close that unconscionable space between his crotch and Ozai’s ass, but the prince’s hand insistently pushed his hips flat against the ground.

“You have to stay still for this,” said Ozai, which had the immediate effect of fixing the smile on Wei’s face into a doubtlessly idiotic look of glee. He was a month shy of fifteen, with his best friend (boyfriend? they avoided romantic labels like they avoided other people) in his lap, staring at him, concentrating very hard on something.

Ozai hovered both hands several inches over Wei’s face. So he wouldn’t have to see the stupid smile, perhaps? Wei was about to break the awkwardness with some feckless comment when a strange sensation came over him. Like heat wafting over his face, but without the actual heat. An energy, almost, that set his skin tingling.

“Is that your chi?” Wei asked. The movements of his mouth seemed to warp and dissipate it, so it rolled over his lips like steam.

“Don’t talk, either,” Ozai said, brows knitted together. He tilted his hands, trying to carry on.

“Wait, though,” Wei said, reaching up to cup the prince on the back of the neck, tugging him downwards. “Try it this way…”

He meant to copy Ozai with a dirty twist, threading his chi into the kiss; he didn’t really feel his chi move as he wanted, though, ended up concentrating so hard he really just kissed Ozai very roughly. The prince pulled off him with a scowl. “Do you want me to go home?”

“Apologies,” Wei replied, nipping Ozai’s lower lip to distract from the hot flush of embarrassment racing across his face. “Continue. Please.”

When Ozai tried again, this time he aimed for a less sensual target. The effect was the same; he concentrated, letting his chi emanate out over Wei’s chest, eliciting a pleasant, warm-but-not-warm sensation. The flow of energy seemed to call out to his own, nipping where it lay dormant, curling like tongues of fire in the places where they touched. It made Wei want to drag Ozai into a tight embrace, but he resisted the temptation, knowing he’d irritate the prince if he interrupted his experiment again.

After a while, Ozai sat back on his haunches, breathing as if he’d executed a few swift but easy katas. He only narrowly missed brushing his ass against the tent in Wei’s pants.

“I found some writings in my father’s private collection,” Ozai explained, once he caught his breath. “There’s so much more you can do with chi than our teachers ever let on.”

“ *Clearly,”* said Wei. He let his hands light on Ozai’s thighs, not pulling him closer so much as resting there, appreciating the heat of the other boy’s skin even through the crisp material of his uniform pants. “What were you doing, anyway? Pushing your chi on me?”

“Sort of,” Ozai replied. Then a long pause paired with a burrowing stare. In times like those, Wei could have sworn Ozai was trying to literally read his mind.

“Yuan for your thoughts?” Wei said, to break the silence.

“What did it feel like?” Ozai asked.

Wei blinked. “Um - tingly.” His eyes darted away, and he felt nervous about the next bit, as if it was embarrassing to get so graphic with a boy he regularly sucked off. “And, honestly? It was… quite hot. Not physically hot, but like. It’d make for excellent foreplay, I think, if we could both figure it out.”

Strangely, this response seemed to vex Ozai. “Really?”

Wei shrugged as best as he could while lying on his back. “Yeah.”

After studying his face a little longer, Ozai leaned in again, hands raised over Wei’s torso. “I want to try something else.”

And Wei waited for him to do so, for thirty seconds. A minute. Two. Time kept ticking by, but nothing seemed to happen.

“You doing okay, buddy?”

“Shut up,” Ozai groused. “I’m trying to concentrate.”

“On what?”

“ *Your* chi. I’m trying to find it.”

“I imagine it’s all over,” Wei responded, dryly, but that was the last lip he gave. Ozai’s responding look was so ferocious Wei let him be. He decided to wander off into his own head while Ozai did his thing.

Wei’s eyes slid to a nearby ash banana tree. Some of the lower leafy branches were broken off. He remembered being half to blame for that, Zhao being the other guilty party. They’d raced one another to see who could climb to the top of their tree the fastest. Zhao had been victorious, the little rat-weasel, but in his triumphant laughter lost his footing and fell.

That had been one of the most terrifying moments of Wei’s life - the snap of wood, the blank look of confusion on Zhao’s face, then empty air. Wei had clambered back down the tree so quickly he nearly lost footing himself, convinced he’d just watched his younger brother die. When he got to the ground, he’d found Zhao not bleeding to death, but laughing up a storm, thrilled by his own survival. They’d made a pact to keep the incident secret from Ama until the event of their actual deaths.

Wei was so lost in his thoughts, he’d all but forgotten the strange exercise of Ozai’s. But now he felt a twinge. He frowned, wondering if it was just one of those things, heartburn or some other mysterious bodily effect, but then there it was again. He felt it deep in his chest, like somehow Ozai had reached deep inside, wrapped his fingers around his heart, and *squeezed*.

A bone-deep cold washed over him - not a physical cold, but the cold of terrible understanding. He tried to speak, but something reached into the spiritual well where his fire lived and *pulled*, and now, *now* he was physically cold, trembling as the very wellspring of his bending power was unspooled from his body-

“What the *fuck?* ” gasped Ozai.

Wei looked down at his hand, and realized that in an instant, everything had changed: he was standing over Ozai, who had fallen on the ground - been *thrown*, most likely by Wei, although he didn’t really remember doing that. And the terrible, pulling sensation was gone. Still, he rubbed his chest, as if chasing away the ghost of that touch.

Wei’s voice was as hard as stone as he said, “Don’t you *ever* do that to me again.”

It didn’t go as expected. There was no welling of guilt or hurt in his friend’s eyes. They lit like lumps of coal ablaze, crushed to a spiteful distortion under sharp eyebrows.

Ozai leapt to his feet. “How *dare* you order me around? Who do you think you are, to tell me what I can and can’t do? I discovered a technique that probably no one’s used for a hundred years, and you’d stop me from mastering it?”

Wei’s hand was still pressed flat over his heart, as if protecting it. “I’m not trying to hold you back. It’s just that it hurt, and-”

“If you felt something, then it *worked*,” Ozai hissed. “I succeeded. You should be congratulating me. You should be proud to have been a part of it. You could have continued to be a part of it. I would’ve taught you too, you know.”

“Ozai-”

“What good is a right hand man who isn’t willing to stay by my side, for better or worse?” The prince demanded. “Is it always going to be like this? Are you always going to fight me when things don’t go perfectly your way?”

Perhaps it was due to the disorienting technique Ozai had tried on him moments ago; Wei found himself feeling particularly unbalanced by the direction this conversation was going. “No. Ozai, stop. I’m on your side.”

As Ozai stepped into his space, a peculiar image flashed into Wei’s mind. It was of his father’s boot. He could remember reflecting, in the moments before it hit his face, on the hole near the big toe. The placement of the scuff marks. The way the light hit the leather and showed off all that texture. Now, in the same way, he was swallowing the cursory details like stones. The way Ozai’s nose crinkled while he scowled. The smattering of acne near his hairline. The tremble of his clenched fist.

Time jumped ahead again, and Wei found himself in the middle of an apology. “I’m sorry for snapping. I guess I overreacted.”

“Whatever.” Ozai’s gaze stayed sharp. “Just don’t defy me like that again. I could replace you in a heartbeat, if I wanted to.”

It wasn’t unusual for Ozai to be pernicious and selfish, wielding his status as a weapon; it had just so rarely been used against Wei. It hurt almost as badly as whatever that bending trick had been.

---

Ama’s second pregnancy was not as smooth. He haunted the house, lurching from room to room with his spine bent and a hand on his stomach long before he gained any weight. The sheer angle of him was unbearable to watch, how he jackknifed his body to fit the mold of his pain.

He spent a lot of time in bed, which meant their father spent a lot of time on the threshold of the master bedroom, hands on his hips, berating Ama as though he was doing this purely out of spite. “The boy needs you,” he would say, sometimes meaning Zhao, sometimes meaning Wei; he would continue this habit even after Yan was finally born, of treating his sons as a single whining, needy amalgam.

Ama’s increasing absence forced Zhao to become a free-floating agent of sorts, scrambling between Wei and their father for a level of attention only Ama could possibly give. As cool older brother and non-psychopath, Wei was the superior choice, but he was gone at school more often than not. So at six years old, Zhao started to build a relationship with a father who, up until this point, had wanted very little to do with him.

Perhaps it helped that they each had the new baby to fear. Zhao and his father were covetous of Ama’s affections in that way only pure id could be. (“I hate the new baby,” Zhao told Wei once. “It’s stealing Ama.”) Or perhaps it was the fact that Zhao was at that age where children ape everything they see. He learned that if he only mimicked his father, he’d get all the approval he could ask for. For example:

“Fucking Zhang is giving me the run-around again,” their father groused across the dinner table. Zhao made a show of fake-gagging before he said, “Zhang! The worst.”

“The worst,” his father agreed, an amused smirk tugging at the corner of his mouth. “It’s as if he goes out of his way to be as incompetent as possible.”

Zhao nodded emphatically. “*Very* incompertent.”

“Yes,” his father agreed, “although it is pronounced in-comp-e-tent.”

Zhao screwed up his tiny brows. “Incompel-”

“In-comp-e…” The wick of their father’s patience was burning impressively long tonight.

Meanwhile, Ama had clasped a hand over his mouth in an effort to hold in his measly three bites of plain rice. When he gathered himself enough to speak, he whispered to Zhao, through barely parted lips, “Let’s not make gagging noises at the table, darling.”

Which prompted Zhao to immediately hack and gag again, which made Ama slap a hand to his mouth to hold in a *real* retch, making the six year old giggle with mean-spirited glee. Wei didn’t think it was guffaw-worthy, but their father threw his head back with such a laugh he honestly thought he’d missed something.

At the end of dinner, the servants took from Ama a plate left untouched, piled high with lukewarm vegetables and congealed sauce. The omega looked to his husband with sunken eyes and said, “I think there’s something wrong with the pregnancy. I don’t feel right.”

His husband scoffed. “It’s a pregnancy, Ama. Of course you don’t feel right. The little leech is sapping all your energy.”

Had his father talked about Zhao that way, Ama would have been furious. But no rebuke came on the new baby’s behalf. “This isn’t how it felt the first time,” said Ama. “I found more blood. You said if that happened again that you would call a midwife!”

Hearing the edge in Ama’s voice, Wei snuck a glance at Zhao to see how he was doing. Even at such a young age, he had already learned to stay out of things if their parents took on a certain tone. Where moments ago he’d taken up space, been exuberant in teasing his mother, he was now deathly silent, blank eyes fixed on his plate, his entire body tensed as if waiting for a blow.

Or to witness a blow. How many times had their father smacked Ama across the face, right in front of them? Now their father reached towards Ama, and Wei startled in his seat, leaning out of the way - but his father only smoothed his thumb between Ama’s eyebrows.

“There,” he said, casting his spouse with a paternalistic smile. “Do you feel it? Every time you fret, that’s where you wrinkle.”

Ama looked at him with a wide-eyed terror that suggested he, too, had been expecting a blow. “I - I can,” he affirmed, voice shaken.

“I’ll call for a doctor, but in the meantime, you must do me a favor,” his husband said. “You need to keep your face still. You can do that much for me, can’t you? I don’t want it to get ruined when you’re old.”

“Yes,” Ama uttered. It wasn’t the worst thing his husband had done to him in front of the boys; still, Wei couldn’t bear to watch any longer. He, too, bent his head for an excuse to look away.

---

There were times Wei could hardly tell the difference between touching Ozai’s body and his own. The pleasure was the same, and that expanse of skin seemed so intimately familiar. They’d run their fingers over puffy old scars and ask, how did you get that one? Your fire, or someone else’s? Kissing each other quiet when they didn’t want to answer, threading their chi with their tongues (a technique Wei had mastered after much dedicated practice). It was extraordinary how well they were matched, how in tune Wei felt with Ozai’s every impulse.

So this complete lack of response today was telling. Eventually Wei hoisted himself up off Ozai and wiped his mouth with the back of his hand. “Okay - you need to tell me what the hell’s bothering you, because while you’re not exactly the scream-and-alert-my-parents type, you usually give me *some* indication whether this is working for you.”

From flat on his back, Ozai glowered up at the ceiling. “I’m *fine,”* he said. Still, Wei couldn’t help but feel the plaster-melting look was actually meant for him.

“You are not fine,” Wei insisted. He clamored up beside the other boy, noting how little room there seemed to be in his bed for the both of them these days. They had started on their growth spurts, Wei destined for great heights with his large hands and ever-shrinking sleeves, Ozai keeping a more graceful pace beside him. If anything, they were both nearing the end of puberty - which was, doubtless, what had Ozai in such a snit.

“You’re not worrying about your presentation again, are you?” Wei drawled.

Ozai’s eyes narrowed ever so slightly, implying yes, that’s absolutely what he was thinking about. “I learned something today. It changes absolutely everything about my place relative to the throne.”

Wei cocked an eyebrow, settling his head into his hand. “What, is Iroh the bastard child of a Water Tribe chieftain, or something?”

Ozai’s lips pursed into a tight line. Wei hated that look. It always meant a tantrum was coming on. “I can’t tell you the specifics. It won’t matter if I’m not an alpha.” His eyes narrowed. “I *need* to be an alpha.”

“You and every teenager in the Fire Nation,” Wei quipped. He reached out a hand to pat the other boy, but Ozai rolled onto his side, his knobby spine facing his friend. Wei huffed. “Are you really not going to tell me this big secret revelation?”

Ozai didn’t respond, continuing his brooding towards the wall. Wei was a little wounded by this; Ozai wasn’t big on talking about his feelings, but he usually told Wei everything. Even the alarmingly classified stuff he probably shouldn’t.

Weary of his friend’s mood, Wei set about agitating him back to life. “Y’know, Ozai, it’s not what you want to hear, but you’re probably going to be an omega. I mean, considering the way you always *beg* me for a finger-”

Wei stopped, narrowly dodging one sharp elbow.

“Don’t patronize me!” Ozai hissed. “Becoming an omega would be worse than death.”

“Oh, come on,” Wei huffed. “It’s not that bad.”

Ozai pulled a face. “And how do you suppose that? Not only is it a loss, but the most humiliating one possible. A fat fucking ‘You’ll *never* be Fire Lord, even if your brother dies childless’ fate. It’s the worst possible outcome. Literally what options would I have if I presented as an omega?” Wei picked at a loose thread in the comforter. “Have my children. Run Kirachu with me.”

“Shut up,” Ozai said, but he missed a beat, leaving a stark, mortifying silence between Wei’s half-joking offer and his own grumpy response. They elapsed into a deeply uncomfortable silence after that, and lay glaring with their gazes fixed in opposite directions. Wei was hyper-aware of the fact their pants were unbuttoned, dicks out in the open air, and couldn’t decide if that made this moment more humiliating, or just hilarious.

“You know,” Wei said, “if you were an omega, and I was your alpha, I’d find a way to get you on that throne.”

Ozai raised one condescending eyebrow at him. “Oh, would you?”

“I would,” Wei promised, the idea picking up more momentum once it was out of his mouth. “I’d start annihilating royal family members left and right, if you asked me to. Your dad? Pow, gone. He’ll be a trillion by the time we’re grown, so it’ll be easy, anyway. Just one heavy pillow while he’s taking a nap, and...”

Even though Ozai rolled his eyes, there was a smirk tugging irresistibly at the corners of his mouth. “So you’d kill Iroh? The beloved crown prince the people are practically begging to see on the throne?”

“Without even a second thought.”

“Spare me.”

“No, I mean it, Ozai. I’d kill the shit out of Iroh for you.”

Ozai’s expression was disbelieving, as if this was a real discussion and not some bed-time banter. He said, “My brother has slain dragons. He conquered half the West.”

Wei shrugged, full of teenaged spitfire. “So what? I’m not scared of him. I’ll kill that old fart, make my first and last decree as Fire Lord that only omegas can rule the nation, and boom - you got the throne.”

Ozai’s lips twitched at that one. “*Really?* You’d give up the title of Fire Lord for me?”

“Baby, I’d do anything for you.” And he punctuated this with a patronizing peck on the nose. Ozai shot him a bitchy look, but didn’t fight him on it. He rolled onto his side so they lay with their foreheads pressed together.

After a while, Wei asked, “So - do you approve of my vision? Have I successfully argued the benefits of becoming an omega?”

“Sounds better than being a beta, I suppose,” Ozai muttered. “There’s literally *no* *point* to being a beta.”

“Aw, c’mon. Betas can do pretty much anything.”

“If they *claw* their way for it,” Ozai huffed. “I’m not interested in fighting for recognition. I don’t have it in me anymore.”

“*Anymore?* What are you, some wizened veteran?”

Ozai’s gaze flitted away. “You know how my father is.”

And indeed, Wei did. He had plenty of father troubles of his own.

Eager to change the subject, he said, “So it’s decided. We get married and rule the Fire Nation, or we give up on life entirely. Either way, it’s you and me.”

He missed a few outcomes in that neat summary he gave, and there was an annoying glint in Ozai’s eye, like he might push the issue. But he didn’t. He just pulled Wei’s hand towards his mouth to kiss the knuckles. Then graze them with his teeth.

Wei watched him hungrily. “Would you like to put something else in your mouth?”

---

The boundless energy of youth brought them from the privacy of Wei’s bedroom out onto the white Kirachu sands for a day of sailing. With the coachman and Ozai’s personal guards as witness, they were forced to be discreet in their fun; but then, wasn’t the most special part of their relationship the fact that it was all their own? Loathing the politics that might get involved, they’d hid the more intimate details from their families for years. And so they set out on the water with a chaste distance between them. (Excepting a brief moment when, far from the shore, Ozai brushed his hand over Wei’s, bringing with it that familiar prickle of chi. The other boy nearly capsized his father’s dinghy from the distraction of it.)

By the time they made their way back to the house, their hair was tangled with salt spray. “We should get cleaned up,” Ozai said, giving Wei a once-over. “Unless, of course, you think someone might drop in...?”

Wei grinned. “As a matter of fact, the baths are *exceedingly* private.” He pointed across the estate, to a smaller building set behind the main house. He was giddy with good fortune; he could have floated across the lawn, had things not taken such a turn.

As the boys were making their way across the grass, the front door of the main house opened, and Zhao emerged. Because that was exactly what this sensual outing needed - a six year old.

*Don’t follow us,* Wei thought, *Go back in the house*, but Zhao nonetheless started to hurry over. He seemed more coltish and stumbling than Wei had ever remembered him being. Still, he groaned audibly as the younger boy drew nearer. He could just imagine all the hollered protests he would get when he told the kid to beat it, but he wasn’t in the mood for a third wheel.

Zhao came to a stop about a foot away, eyes darting between the two older boys. Wei scowled. “Spirits, *what?* ”

Zhao’s eyes flickered to the house, then back to Wei’s face. “Ama needs you.”

“Right now?” Wei asked, allowing an edge to creep into his voice.

His brother shifted, looking at Ozai. There was something unusually large and shiny about his eyes. “Yes. Just you, though.”

That was weird. Normally Zhao liked to torture them in tandem. “What’s going on?” Wei asked.

Zhao’s mouth hung open as he deliberated his response. Wei glimpsed amongst the many gaps in his teeth the tiny, sharp edge of an adult tooth that had just breached the gum.

“Ugh, come *out* with it, already,” Ozai snapped.

“I-I don’t know,” Zhao stuttered. “It’s important, though-”

“And it can’t wait?” Ozai asked, tone impatient. “We’re in the middle of something.”

While Zhao struggled again to come up with an answer, apprehension took root in Wei’s mind. His younger brother wasn’t ever this fumbling. Everything about Zhao was loud and overly-confident - to see him speaking in such a hushed tremble spelled something seriously wrong.

There was a nasty look on Ozai’s face. “Look, kid, if you don’t go away-”

Wei cast a disarming smile on the prince. “Now that I think about it, Ozai, we’ll need a change of clothes and something to dry off with, right? Why don’t you head to the baths without me, and I’ll make sure to bring something on my way back. It’ll be five minutes, tops.”

The prince looked less than pleased with this turn of events. With the exception of their argument over chi-bending a year or so ago, Wei *never* talked over him. Nonetheless, after a stormy pause, he waved the brothers away, heading off in the direction Wei had told him to. From the moment Ozai’s back was turned, Zhao’s hands were on Wei’s sleeve, tugging him towards the house with urgency.

Mere seconds seemed to stretch on forever; Wei’s heart was in his throat by the time he entered the house. Zhao hadn’t said a single thing on the run over, and now all but shoved him through the foyer, around the corner towards the stairwell and the door to the tigermonkey room.

Ama lay crumpled at the bottom of the stairs. He wasn’t moving, and with his face covered by a tangle of dark hair, Wei couldn’t even tell if he was breathing.

The weight of his terror locked him to the spot, as though the longer he kept his distance, the longer he didn’t have to know the truth. He didn’t move until Zhao curled his hand in his and asked in a voice that was awful and small, “Wei - what do we do?”

Right. He had to get his bearings, for little brother’s sake. He squeezed Zhao’s hand, then released him to approach Ama.

He crouched down beside his step-parent. Something about the bulge of the pregnant stomach only made the scene that much more vile; Wei pointedly avoided looking at it, reaching out to hold a hesitant hand in front of Ama’s parted lips.

Air tickled his fingers. Wei leaned in to listen to Ama’s chest and heard a heartbeat. Okay - unless his own heartbeat was pounding that loudly in his ears, Ama was alive, still. Wei wondered if there was a way to assess the same for the unborn baby, and almost lay his head on Ama’s stomach. He stopped himself at the last second, electing instead to brush Ama’s hair out of his face.

He looked over his shoulder at Zhao. “Did you try to wake him up?”

The younger boy nodded, ringing his hands. “I yelled but he wouldn’t get up.”

That wasn’t good. Zhao had a shout that could raise the dead. Wei patted Ama’s face, speaking his name in a whisper, then a command. He pulled one eyelid up, not really knowing what he’d be able to see if he did, only for Ama’s eyes to flutter open.

Relief lapped over Wei. He didn’t know what he’d do if that hadn’t worked. Pray, maybe. “Hey. Ama, what happened to you? Is it something with the baby? Did you faint when you were coming down the stairs?”

“Wh…?” Ama blinked sluggishly, barely able to keep his lids aloft. Wei was cradling his head, and his entire weight remained slumped there, not an ounce of muscle in opposition.

Wei asked again, more slowly: “Ama. What happened?”

Ama mumbled something that could’ve been “I don’t know” and brought a hand to his forehead. The wide sleeve slid down his arm, and Wei was dizzied by the number of bruises he saw.

“It wasn’t the baby,” Zhao whispered.

Wei chewed his lip. A good big brother would ask, but he didn’t want to know more. “Okay. Well, whatever happened, we need to...”

“Dad was angry,” Zhao said, voice thickening.

Wei’s heart quickened in his chest. “He’s angry all the time, I’m sure he wouldn’t-”

“He *punished* Ama,” the six year old insisted, tears prickling in the corners of his eyes.

Wei’s vision tunneled. He shut his eyes briefly and breathed; he had to hold it together. No one else would.

“I’m getting - someone,” Wei decided. A servant, maybe. A guard. Those people were always disappearing in moments like this, either by design or by chance. He stood on wobbling feet and tried the tigermonkey room first because it was the closest one, barely hearing as Zhao called to him, “Wait, don’t go-!”

Wei slid the door away and saw his father sitting at the desk. He was holding a small clay cup aloft, inspecting it with one rheumy eye, lips bent in their usual sneer. The fact he’d been nearby the whole time threw Wei farther than it should have.

“Hey,” Wei said to his father, before he could stop himself. “What the fuck are you doing?”

People often described Zhu Han as striking: he was the source of his oldest son’s towering height, and was fit even in middle age, his body muscled to rival any military recruitment poster. His eyes were light, as intense as a flash of fire when kindling is just tossed over it.

There was something about this man, though, this towering man with rakish eyes and a mean-spirited smile, that made people loathe to call him handsome. Strangers who had only glanced his way could immediately tell there was something off about him; perhaps his striking features were out of balance with one another. Perhaps his meanness simply permeated every one of his features, sullying them.

Wei's father raised his cup to his mouth, downed it in one swallow, then leaned over the desk to pour out more. His gaze, when it finally settled on Wei, was nearly as unfocused as Ama’s.

“You think you can speak to me that way?” he asked. It wasn’t a warning tone. It was full of the good humor of a jaguar-lion on a branch, fangs bared: *Try it again. I dare you.*

Wei wrestled with the terror in his stomach. Pushed on despite it. “S - sorry,” he said, hating himself immensely for it. “But Ama is - Ama is injured.”

“Is that so?” His father’s tone was nonchalant. He took another sip before fixing his son with his nastiest smile. “I suppose you’d better do something about it, then.”

How funny that only hours ago Wei claimed he could assassinate the royal family in order to impress a prince. Now he was standing before the greatest monster he had ever faced, who terrorized his home on a regular basis, and he wasn’t even going to talk back. Somewhere behind him, his little brother was trembling on the ground with his half-dead parent, and even they weren’t enough to make Wei stand up against his father, because he was too much of a coward.

He couldn’t waste anymore time. Wei slid the doors to his father’s study shut, then went back to where his family needed him.

Ama hissed in pain when they tried to move him. Wei wanted to hoist him up into a carriage and send him to a doctor in town, but what if that only made his injuries worse? Plus even if he managed not to hurt him, there was no way Wei would be able to carry Ama all on his own. He would have to bring a doctor back here, instead. There was also the matter of Ozai; they needed to get him off the estate before he caught on to what was happening.

Wei turned to tell Zhao what he intended to do, chest tightening when he saw how his little brother’s face had contorted to hold in his anguish. There were tears streaming down his face, holes in a dam that couldn’t be fixed, but all in all he was suffering in silence. At a loss for how else to comfort him, Wei laid a hand in his hair. He wanted to tell him it’d be alright, but he wasn’t sure it was true, and he wasn’t sure it would do Zhao any good to lie to him. So he focused on what he could control, and said, “I’m going to get help.”

Moments later, Wei found himself racing across the lawn again, a bundle of clothes and a towel in hand. He felt terrible for leaving Zhao alone with Ama (with their father), but he didn’t know what else to do.

When he opened the door to the baths, steam hit him full in the face, fogging his glasses. There was a muttered, “Finally,” the sloshing of water, then the prince was standing before him, naked, tilting his head in that way he did when he wanted Wei to praise him or kiss him.

Wei thrust the bundle towards the prince. “Dry off. You’ve got to go.”

Ozai’s surprise lapsed into irritation. “Why?”

“Baby stuff,” Wei said immediately. “Ama’s not feeling well. I’m going to get a doctor for him.”

Ozai’s scowl deepened. “Why does he need *your* help? Make a servant take care of it.”

Wei swallowed. “I just - I need to do this, Ozai. It’s kind of a big deal. I can explain later. I can get our best guards to take you to the port...”

It took some begging and earned him a week’s worth of frostiness following his departure, but Ozai did eventually leave. Wei didn’t help things, sinking into the quiet dark of his mind the whole ride back to the port. He just didn’t have the energy to do the usual work of tending to Ozai’s overly-fragile feelings, lost in his own anxieties.

He barely cared that the prince didn’t even attempt a kiss goodbye before slamming the door in his face; he was too relieved that the fucking *trudge* of it all had finally ended, that he could demand the driver race to the doctor and back up the mountain where he was needed. Wei swore Ozai had gotten dressed as slowly as possible solely because he could tell how agitated it was making his friend.

---

Ama survived the incident with a broken pelvis, a shattered elbow, and several sprains, including a particularly nasty one to his neck. It was months before he could get out of bed again, and longer still before he moved comfortably.

Miraculously, the baby made it. So Ama spent those bedridden months nauseous, and fatigued, and surrounded by hundreds of get-well-soon plum flowers. Purchased, of course, by his dearly devoted husband.

The story was that Ama had slipped. So they told the doctor, and the friends who stopped by, and the boys, even though they knew otherwise.

“But Ama, I *saw* him,” Zhao piped up, only to be hushed with a gentle hand on his cheek.

“No more,” said Ama. “You’re going to hurt your father’s feelings.”

Bedridden, unable to even eat on his own, Ama was still terribly preoccupied with Zhu’s feelings. Was Zhu sleeping well enough, with Ama confined here? Was Zhu sure he didn’t need Ama to wrangle the help? Did Zhu need help straightening out the boys? And when turned down with the tenth paternalistic smile and kiss of the hand, Ama seemed to melt; “But I’ve *neglected* you so of late. Let me make it up to you. Please.”

“When you’re feeling better,” his husband acquiesced, petting him on the hand. Watching the two of them coo at each other made Wei want to scream himself mute. It was worse when Zhao joined in, giggling along with the silly nothings spouted by a man who had tried to kill his mother right in front of him.

“I do hope Ozai wasn’t upset by all this?” Ama asked. His voice swelled with worry; his face was as placid as a windless lake.

“He’s fine,” Wei said. In truth, they hadn't talked in a week. He would begin to grovel in earnest back at school, but for now, he could care less about Ozai.

Ama didn’t seem convinced. “He didn’t see or hear anything…?”

“We sent him home,” Wei insisted. “He has no idea what happened.”

With so many severe injuries, Ama must have been in agony. Still, his relief was palpable, as if it was coming off him in waves. “Oh, I’m so pleased. It’d be such a shame if I traumatized a prince.”

---

In the days that followed, Ama called Wei back into his room to chastise him for “having an attitude” with his father.

“I *know* you are only trying to be protective, Wei, but for all of our sakes, you must be a little more light-hearted when you’re around him. It makes him *so* upset when we’re unhappy.”

Wei sat at the end of the bed where he had watched his mother die and listened as a nearly-dead step-mother begged him to be kind to the man who had put him there. Eventually, Wei couldn’t take it. In his coward’s way, he took out all his anger on Ama, rather than the man who actually deserved it.

“Do you really not want anything better for yourself?” Wei snapped. “You’re happy, being treated worse than a fucking dog?”

Ama shrugged. It was such an indelicate gesture, while he was lying on his back with no range of motion. The splint around his neck meant he had to address the ceiling as he replied: “There’s nothing better out there for me, Wei. Without your father, I’m less than nothing.”

“That’s crazy,” said Wei. “Literally anything has to be better than this.”

Ama sighed. “You have an incredible future ahead of you, abound with options. But we can’t all be friends with a prince. There’s only one path left for me, and it ends here, in this house. So please make my sad little life easier, and play nice with your father, hm?”

---

“Can you bend somebody else’s fire?”

It was a beautiful day on the Kirachu estate. Agni in all of his glory had doused the lawn in golden light, creating the perfect conditions for a firebending lesson. Unfortunately, Jeong Jeong wasn’t sharing these conditions with the perfect student.

He cracked open one eye to appraise Zhao. The seven year old was lying on his side in the grass, not at *all* in the meditative posture he’d instructed him to adopt. The governor’s husband had spoken so glowingly of this child when persuading Jeong Jeong to come on as a teacher, but thus far he was unimpressed by what he saw. This was certainly a far cry from training naval recruits.

“Straighten your back,” he ordered. “And resume the exercise.”

Zhao pouted and rolled onto his stomach, but didn’t make an effort to push himself up.

Jeong Jeong sighed. “Get back into form, and I will answer your question.”

That earned him one last pout, but the kid at least complied this time. He mimicked his teacher’s cross-legged pose, albeit in a clumsy way.

Jeong Jeong held out his hands, cupping them in front of his chest. “Remember. We are starting small. The fire that you summon should only be about the size of your fist.” And a small, perfectly round flame began to bloom in his palms.

The boy reached out, too far from his chest, already anticipating a flame too big to control. Then he looked at his hands with intense concentration.

“Don’t forget your breathing,” Jeong Jeong admonished.

The child shot a scowl at him before resuming his concentration. As feared, Zhao’s fire came out in an over-sized burst, forcing him to fumble his hands further apart or risk a burn. But the added space only made it grow, harkening back to why Jeong Jeong had chosen this exercise in the first place: Zhao’s utter inability to keep his flame controlled.

When the third attempt nearly burnt his teacher’s eyebrows off, Zhao hurled the ball of flame at the grass with an angered cry. “This is stupid! Just teach me something useful, like a flaming kick!”

Jeong Jeong stopped himself short of calling the kid a snot-nosed brat. Instead he pinched the bridge of his nose and counted to ten.

He hated children. He hated teaching. In his mind’s eye, he saw a past lover insisting he’d like it more if he were only a little more choosy about the students he taught. But unlike certain men of his past, Jeong Jeong didn’t have generations of inherited wealth to fall back on while he got picky about his students. He had to earn a living, and the navy paid like shit. Having regretfully devoted his best years to honing his killing instincts over his studies, this was essentially all he could do to stay fed while on shore leave.

“Since you *tried*, I’ll answer your question,” Jeong Jeong ground out. “Yes. It is possible to bend another person’s chi. No, I don’t know how. No, I don’t advise you try it.”

“Why not?” Zhao whined.

“Because,” his teacher replied. “It’s considered a torture method.”

Even Zhao could not resist slipping into a reverent silence at this admission. For a moment, nothing permeated the humid air but the chirping of distant birds.

“Huh,” mused a new voice. “I thought chi-bending was a sexual thing.”

They were sitting at the base of a small, grassy hill, and looked up to find the oldest boy standing at its summit.

Seeing the dubious looks on Zhao and his tutor’s faces, Wei realized how incriminating his statement had been, and proceeded to turn lychee red. “I mean - not that I’ve tried it,” he fumbled. “I just figured, y’know, if it’s illegal, maybe it’s a perverted thing. Or something.”

Jeong Jeong coughed. “No, it - you’re correct. When done carefully - and on a *consenting* recipient - bending chi can feel…” Spirits, what was he even allowed to say, here? “But that’s not why it’s outlawed. When enacted in rage or when used for violence, it’s a terrible sensation. Old accounts describe it as if your veins are being pulled straight through your skin.”

“Cool,” said Zhao, grinning.

“It is not cool,” Jeong Jeong said severely. “It is cruelty, and besides, it’s impractical for battle. Finding another person’s chi requires immense concentration; redirecting it is nearly impossible when an opponent is in motion. You’d be better off learning where to physically hit a bender to block their chi entirely.”

“Or burning their face off,” Wei supplied. “Hard to fight back when your eyes have melted in their sockets.”

“Yeah!” Zhao cheered, both arms thrust in the air. “Teach me that one!”

“Absolutely not,” Jeong Jeong groused. “Aiming for your opponent’s face is dishonorable *.”*

The esteemed naval officer continued to try to wrangle his student’s attention, but the introduction of the older brother made it impossible. Despite his protests, the older boy sat down with them, and instead of setting a positive example, he proceeded to wind up Zhao even more thoroughly, just as Jeong Jeong had so righteously feared. Eventually the lesson devolved into a competition of who could do the most impressive flaming cartwheel, with him as de facto (unwilling) judge.

The whole thing filled him with a strange disappointment, although he was unsure why. It must be the glasses. They made Wei look scholarly and inspired unrealistic expectations regarding his maturity. Or maybe the fact he was the size of a grown man; he was, after all, nearly seventeen, drawing closer and closer to manhood. Had he been born to a less fortunate family, he would have already enlisted in the military, and been shipped off somewhere in the Earth Kingdom.

“Enough of this,” Jeong Jeong harrumphed at the end of the hour. “Time is up for the day.”

“Aw,” said Zhao. “That was just getting good!”

Jeong Jeong would like to have ditched them both then and there, but if he didn’t go back to the house, he wouldn’t be paid for this time wasted. So he followed the boys up the hill, keeping his distance as they bounded and stumbled like drunken puppies.

Upon entering some sort of gaudily-painted sitting room, there was at least one parent present. The governor’s husband, A-something, was arranging books on a shelf, while yet *another* child, this time a baby, tangled itself in his feet.

“For spirits’ *sake*, Yan, get *out* from underfoot,” the governor’s husband - Ama! - huffed. “If I drop something and hurt you, it is going to be all your fault!”

The child at his feet burbled in reply, too young to talk, or, frankly, move out of the way all on his own. Still, Ama sighed as though the child was out to inconvenience him.

Jeong Jeong cleared his throat. Ama glanced his way. “Oh - you. Had enough of our Zhao, have you?”

From the way his voice swelled, he was clearly being facetious. Jeong Jeong had early learned that the governor’s husband was suffering under the delusion that his son was not only some sort of firebending prodigy, but a pleasure to be around. Without waiting for an answer, he stepped away from the shelf to grab Jeong Jeong’s payment, the baby reaching desperately for his foot as he went. He gave a rough shake to free his foot from the baby's grasp.

Ama moved through the room in a stilted, painful-looking way. The part of Jeong Jeong perceptive enough to pick up on the limp felt sympathy, but the larger part of him, which hated this family, wondered if it hurt *so* badly that Ama couldn’t hurry it up. Surely no matter the ailment, the governor’s husband could get some rest afterwards on his gold-embroidered, silken sheets.

Wei and Zhao had long since gone off to do their own things, barely pausing to say goodbye or thank you for his time. Simmering with irritation, Jeong Jeong was pulled out of his thoughts by a tug on his pant leg. He looked down and saw the littlest one, hand in mouth, staring up at him with wide black eyes.

He heaved a sigh. He might as well ask. “The little one. I suppose he’ll be needing a tutor in a few years, too?”

“Not at all,” Ama scoffed as he made his way over, envelope of money in hand. “Yan simply doesn’t have his brothers’ talent.”

They probably thought the little brat unlucky. Jeong Jeong had always thought firebending was over-glorified, though; it was a terrible responsibility to yield, yet it seemed every moron and thug across the country wielded it with impunity.

He thought again of that old lover. Surely he shouldn’t be the only one to suffer with the governor’s sons. “I have an old friend who specialized in swordsmanship. When the kid’s old enough, I could introduce them, if you like.”

---

They’d been having sex from a young age - too young, honestly - so Wei couldn’t tell you what about this incident was so special. All he knew was that one moment they’d been grinding up against one another, then the next, Ozai was in rut. By design, Wei couldn’t scent the difference, but he felt it physically, when there was a girth there hadn’t been before.

When he realized what was happening, Ozai clenched Wei’s wrists so hard his hands went instantly numb. Ozai was delirious with joy; inconsolable. Out of his mouth spewed a steady stream of self-praise: I knew it. I knew it would happen, after all. I don’t know why I ever doubted it. Finally. *Finally.*

Somehow, Wei wasn’t happy for him.

No one asked what he and Ozai were doing when it happened. No one seemed surprised about that part at all. Wei thought they’d hidden their relationship so well over the years, but they’d been easier to read than a children’s primer.

Ama wrote a discreet letter to the royal palace to explain why they were keeping the prince longer than usual, and four days later, when Ozai’s first rut subsided, he went home.

Sitting at the kitchen table mere minutes after his departure, Wei asked the open air, “That’s it, isn’t it?” He turned his face this way and that, looking for someone he could beseech, and settled on Ama. “If I was going to present, then a rutting alpha should’ve been the thing to do the trick. But I didn’t present with him. So I’m never going to.”

Ama had soothed his worries on any number of occasions when he was afraid he’d done Ozai wrong. *Don’t worry, darling, we can fix this*, he’d say, and he’d tell Wei all the ways he could prostrate himself to win his difficult friend’s heart back.

Now he merely sighed and patted Wei’s hand. “Yes. Such a shame; our family got so *close* to the throne-” one more lugubrious exhale, “-but it simply wasn’t meant to be.”

Wei’s stomach sank. It wasn’t logical, it was literally the ruling of old folk wisdom, but he had to wonder. All those maxims about how feminine little boys grew up into omegas, and daring girls became alphas, and so on and so forth - had Wei's cowardice stunted him so thoroughly he’d become a beta? Had he spoiled his reproductive potential to hell by refusing to stand up for himself?

He didn’t have any answers. Only questions, for years and years more.

---

In the moments before his father’s fist hits his face, Zhao has an epiphany.

It’s brought on watching the way his father winds up to punch him, elbow snapping back at angle, an *upwards* angle, because Zhao is no longer a knee-height toddler tangling himself in his father’s legs as he scrambles to get away; no, at sixteen years old, Zhao is the tallest member of his family by far.

So when his father’s fist hits his face, Zhao doesn’t cower. He doesn’t rub his jaw and pout. He spits the blood from his mouth and punches back.

Zhao’s father, a decorated Major General and multi-term governor of Kirachu, has not held onto his power by hesitating in the face of difficult decisions. When his son strikes him, he lashes out again, catching his fist on his son’s teeth. They are stubborn fighters cut from the same fire-red cloth, and so neither one is willing to stop, leaving the rest of the family frozen at the borders, inert as statues as their fight unfolds into pure savagery, fists swinging and mouths snarling and bodies in motion beyond what anyone watching is willing to follow except to avoid getting caught in the crossfire.

Zhao’s father wins; Zhao may be tall, but his father has about fifty pounds on him and years more practice at being cruel. He subdues his son with one sharp elbow to his spine, bone grinding on bone, forcing a shout between Zhao’s lips. Yet as he breathes in the grass and the dirt and the blood that has forged a slick path over his teeth, he feels as though he’s won. Or is perhaps soon to win: he arms himself with the newfound knowledge of his size, his power, and bides his time until the next fight.

When he comes to clean him up, Ama is cross. “I can’t believe you would hit your own father.”

*You’re just jealous you could never get away with hitting back*, Zhao thinks petulantly. The mean remark is on the tip of his tongue until his mother takes his face in hand and touches a wet cloth to his face. The contact is so soothing that the retort dies in his mouth.

Ama continues to chide him, his words in complete contrast to the gentle way he continues to clean the blood from his son’s face. “After all your father’s done for you to clean up this mess. This is how you repay him?”

“I didn’t ask him to clean it up in the first place,” Zhao mutters. Then, when his mother fixes him with a withering look, “I had it handled.”

Ama scoffs. “If that were true, we wouldn’t have to send that boy to the doctor.” He shakes his head, lips fixed in a jagged line of irritation. “He was my *favorite* servant, Zhao. Now I have to find someone who can polish silver just as well as he can. You never think of anyone but yourself, do you?”

Ama gets to work spreading a medicinal balm over the open wounds on his son’s hands. Zhao bites his cheek to keep from hissing.

After a while, Ama says, “I have spoken with an old army friend of your father’s. She has graciously offered to find you a spot in a regiment she’ll be standing up in the Si Wong Desert. Her ship is disembarking from the capital next month.”

Zhao stiffens. “I’m supposed to be leaving *tomorrow.”*

“Yes, well. You gave up that opportunity when you decided to attack your father.”

His heart quickens treacherously in his chest. His escape has been aborted: it’ll be another month here. In Kirachu.

“That’s not *fair*,” he says, hating the petulant edge to his voice.

“Fair?” Ama reaches into the basket at his side and grabs a roll of bandages. “Would it be fair for you to leave looking like this? What do you think people will say about our family when they see your face?”

“Nothing they wouldn’t have a right to,” Zhao snarls. He tries to pull himself out of his mother’s grasp, but Ama resists. He obviously doesn’t have the strength to keep his nearly-grown son tethered there, but while Zhao has gotten a taste for the use of force against his father, he can’t do that to Ama, who has never raised a hand against him. So that gentle tug on his hand binds him to the spot.

“If the possibility of people seeing the black eye is what’s got you so upset, then may I remind you who put it there in the first place?” Zhao mutters.

Ama shakes his head. “That was you, Zhao. *You* put it there with your own bullheaded stubbornness.”

Despite its location in the heart of Agna Qel’a, this cove was almost as balmy as a Fire Nation night. The air weighed heavily upon Azula, almost as if she had entered another world entirely.

“Can you feel that?” Iroh had said, when they first stepped inside. “This place is steeped in spiritual energy. The line between our world and their world is thin here.”

Azula didn’t answer, cataloguing the details of the place. Across the water lay a small island of grass with a pond in the center. She squinted at it - had she seen something moving inside? - but the sounds of approach made her duck into the shadows, yanking Iroh along with her.

“I hate this place,” complained one of the Avatar’s companions. It was the little earthbender, for sure. Azula would know that whine anywhere. “I *have* to wear shoes, or I’ll freeze. All the earth’s hidden under a bajillion layers of snow. Why the heck am I even here?”

When she came into view, she was clutching the waterbender by the arm. The older girl looked much the same as always, lips fixed in a motherly pout: “Toph, you literally *begged* us not to leave you out of the ‘spirit shenanigans.’” This last phrase was accompanied by some fierce air quotes.

“I’m sorry. I promise we’ll be there soon,” said another, unfamiliar voice. Glancing carefully out from their alcove in the wall, Azula caught a glimpse of another Water Tribe girl, but with bright white hair. A wise woman of some sort? No; her face was too young and pretty. Azula’s research told her the elaborate hairstyle and the furs indicated someone important; the princess, then?

That curiosity could wait. Azula saw, sticking out like the sore thumb amongst the trio of diminutive women, the lanky form of the Avatar. Considering the siege going on outside, he looked nonplussed, gaze idly wandering as if he had all the time in the world to take it in. The party crossed the bridge to the oasis, none the wiser to the enemies observing them from not-so-afar.

Azula pondered the conditions. The Water Tribe warrior was absent, meaning they were lacking a tactical element; she had long since observed his role as strategist, and without him, knew the group was very powerful, but also very impulsive. The warmth and the grassy island in this cave meant there was certainly more unfrozen earth here than you’d see anywhere else in the North Pole - there the little earthbender was now, throwing off her boots, cheering as she kneeled down to kiss the grass - but this place was clearly sacred. They would not let her bend the earth for fear of upsetting it. In watching them all, Azula couldn’t tell if the maybe-princess was a bender or not, although she was leaning towards no; the girl had a gentility to her that spoke of a life spent indoors, allowed to do very little aside from looking pretty. Besides, the Northern Water Tribe was known for its resistance to cultivating battle-worthy skill in omegas. Perhaps it was instinct alone, but even being too far to scent her, Azula would swear on her mother’s grave that maybe-princess was an omega.

The maybe-princess kneeled down, glossy hair falling over her shoulder. “This is Tui and La,” she said, gazing reverently into the water. “The embodiments of the moon and ocean.”

The Avatar’s brows shot up. “You mean those are the *actual* moon and ocean spirits? Right here, in front of us?”

“They took on mortal forms so they could always be with one another,” the girl explained.

The waterbender fixed her with a puzzled look. “No offense, Yue, but I don’t really get how Aang’s supposed to get help defending the North Pole from a couple of fish.”

The Avatar didn’t comment right away. Instead he stood at the edge of the water, eyes tracing the movement of the spirits round and round. “...I don’t think I’m meant to talk to them here,” he said, after a while. “I think this place is just the border I have to cross to get into the spirit world. Then I can talk to them for real.”

As they watched the Avatar hunker down into a meditative pose, Azula whipped her head to look at her uncle, eyes communicating her silent glee. He gave her one firm nod in response: the Avatar would be incapacitated in mere moments. That was when they would strike.
