“Come on,” Zuko whispers, desperation leaking into his voice. “Come on, stay with me, *please* .”

In the center of his cupped hands is a flame so weak he cannot risk holding it near his face, or his shallow breaths might put it out. In the month and a half since they arrived in Kirachu, it is all he can manage.

If he concentrates, he can keep the flame alive. So he does, cursing quietly to himself all the while, stubbornly weathering the litany of terrible images ( *hands throat fire smoke* ) that flash through his mind every time.

As with most weights, there comes a point where Zuko can no longer carry it. He lets the flame die, shivering with revulsion as he does so. His very veins seem electric, but he already knows he doesn’t carry that coveted royal gene; rather, it’s merely the painful sensation that appears whenever he tries to bend. He’s not sure if it’s improved or if he’s simply learning to endure it. Frustrated, Zuko rubs his face, the lingering warmth on his hands reminding him he isn’t a complete and utter failure. Perhaps if he tries again later… but it took weeks of sheer stubborn force just to get this much out. He wonders if he’ll have to wait a lifetime before he gets the rest of it back.

Downstairs, the front door slams open, reminding him that he doesn’t have a lifetime to wait.

He is used to fearing the sound of doors; growing up, he could track the proximity of his father by counting the seconds between slamming doors, like claps of thunder down the hall. Zuko had been shocked the first few weeks of their marriage when Zhao *didn’t* throw an absolute fit every time he returned from the Great Hall. How he would instead treat the sight of Zuko like a blessing, the relief palpable on his face. Lately Zuko has found himself looking back on those early moments of their marriage with a mournfulness that part of him knows is deluded; but given the sheer chasm that has opened between them in the wake of the fire, it’s hard not to miss what he thinks of as easier times.

The footsteps make their move. Their dresser is lined with the various tinctures Zuko uses to maintain his princely image, and now every bottle and jar rattles in unison at Zhao’s approach. Zuko’s body is rigid as he listens, waiting-

Then there’s the unmistakable sound of footsteps mounting the stairs. The bedroom gives Zuko the privacy to work on his bending, but he has cornered himself by hiding here. For a moment, he considers leaping towards the closed door and turning the lock; if he did that, though, he has no doubt in his mind Zhao would only burn his way through.

By the time Zhao flings the door open, eyes blazing, Zuko has sunk in on himself, as if by making himself smaller Zhao will have to greet him with less force. He doesn’t immediately berate Zuko upon seeing him, but that’s almost worse; the younger man has to wait for him to make his rounds, to storm over to the dresser, slamming drawers as he removes his armor, tossing pieces to the ground without a care. While his husband is muttering to himself under his breath, Zuko casts a desperate look at the path to the bedroom door, technically clear, and wonders if he can make it to the stairs before Zhao shouts at him to come back (or worse - chases after him). He feels, without knowing for sure, that the common rooms are protection. They have the servants, and Ama, and Yan, and sometimes even Wei, multiple pairs of eyes to serve as witnesses.

When Zhao makes his greeting, it is no hello, no how are you, but in media res: “A fishing vessel went missing from the northernmost port of the island this week. I said, why the fuck am I being called in about one missing ship? Doesn’t the governor have anything more important to do? But I played along. We sent out word to commercial vessels nearby - and then my assistant, he got a hunch, so we expanded our communications to military ships. A week ago, this was. Finally, today, we get word that a Fire Nation vessel outfitted in Kirachu orange was spotted all the way over in *Chameleon fucking Bay* . And when they intercepted it, can you guess what they found on board?”

In the silence that follows, Zuko turns to see his husband is leaning forward with both hands on the dresser, talking to the floor. A nod won’t do; Zuko has to brave a tentative, “What?”

“Fifty-three of the most finely forged swords the Fire Nation has to offer.” Zhao takes one of the many tinctures in hand, palming it like he might a fireball as he locks eyes with Zuko’s reflection. “A common fishing vessel. Outfitted with enough blades to arm a fucking platoon.”

He’s shaking, now, the tincture in his hand looking more and more like a potential weapon. “They’re getting off the fucking island,” he says. “All that we’ve been precariously containing here has finally breached. They’re *smuggling weapons to the Earth Kingdom.* ”

With that, Zhao violently slams the tincture back onto the dresser’s surface; and again; and again; when it doesn’t break, he lets out a furious roar and sweeps the many bottles littering the dresser to the floor. Every *crash* of skittering glass sends a jolt through Zuko, and he watches with baited breath as Zhao pounds his fists onto the dresser’s surface, once, twice -

Then just as suddenly as he began, he is inert, panting as he leans on fists and elbows like a drowning man who has pulled himself onto the nearest dock. Zuko is on his feet now, although he doesn’t remember standing. Seeing him in the mirror, Zhao spins around to jab a finger in his direction: “Whatever the hell you’re about to do-”

“I’m not doing anything,” Zuko says, not sure if he’s lying, having moved on pure instinct. His eyes dart to the strands loose in Zhao’s topknot, then the broken glass littered by his boots, then where his hand is thrust towards Zuko - the side of his palm streaked with blood.

“You’re hurt,” Zuko says, almost surprised. And in the befuddled silence where Zhao follows his gaze, adds, “Let me look at it.”

Zhao still has the air of a wildcat cornered, but he lets Zuko approach, stiffly offering his hand once beckoned. Turning it over, Zuko is strangely relieved to see there’s no glass embedded in the flesh. He must have caught the edge of something sharp when he swept everything off the surface.

“I could… clean this for you,” Zuko offers. “I-I don’t have anything on hand I can use, but…”

Something shifts in Zhao’s expression. His brows soften out of their sharp arches, and with them, the rest of his features seem to slump with defeat. In a matter of moments, he seems to age years.

“Fine,” he replies, hoarse from shouting. “Go get it, then.”

Zuko nods, then makes his unsteady exit, pace lurching as he struggles to escape without looking as though he’s doing so. Once at the foot of the stairs, he seriously considers asking Rio to return in his stead.

Then the sight of Zhao’s face from moments before comes to him unbidden. There wasn’t any fear there - only defeat. Yet Zhao had still stopped himself short of enacting that rage physically on Zuko. Wasn’t that progress?

So Zuko gathers up the bandages. Gets water from the well out back. Finds a balm that will soothe the pain. Then he walks back up the stairs and brings it all to Zhao himself.

When he reenters the bedroom, he thinks he sees the ghost of that old relief on his husband’s face. Zuko joins him on the bed, and in the quiet space that follows, dresses his wound.

Just as Zuko has cleaned the last of the blood, Zhao says, “I don’t deserve this.”

“It’s already done,” Zuko replies, trying to keep his voice light. He drapes the bloody, wet rag over the side of the small pail of water at his feet.

Zhao shakes his head. “I don’t deserve your sympathy. I’m a failure. A complete fucking failure.”

Something like hope leaps into Zuko’s throat; he bites his lip to keep his mouth shut, gently spreading balm along Zhao’s injured skin. Fresh blood is already beading along the cut.

“I can’t keep Kirachu in line. The minute word gets back to your father about the spread of this, he’s going to be furious. And have I told you about the utter shit show in the North Pole?”

“I thought you hadn’t heard from the frontlines in a while,” Zuko confesses, paraphrasing from Zhao’s last screaming tantrum. *That* had been an ordeal. Even Yan hadn’t had the nerve to shout back, disappearing with unusual swiftness for a man with a cane.

Zhao shakes his head. “We finally got word yesterday - it’s been nothing but a bloody stalemate for weeks on end. It seems the Water Tribe was ready for us. We barely breached the Northern Sea when their ships met ours.”

Guilt and relief both wrap their fingers around Zuko’s heart. He’s afraid to even remember that warning whispered to the Avatar, as if Zhao can see the truth right through his skull.

Of course he doesn’t actually notice Zuko’s betrayal; he’s lost in his own thoughts, muttering, “I should have told them about the moon spirit.”

“Even if they can’t breach the walls to touch it?” Zuko offers, hesitant.

“Maybe it wouldn’t make a difference. We’ll never know for sure now, though, will we?” Zhao heaves a sigh that seems to carry with it the weight of the entire world. “I feel as though I’ve let my country down. I’ve let myself down, I’ve let-”

His hand closes around Zuko’s, and cowed by the implied or imagined remorse, Zuko lets their fingers entwine. The blood smeared between their palms feels like the makings of a pact.

“Thank you for listening to me,” Zhao mutters self-consciously, eyes falling away. “I know you don’t want to hear all my sniveling.”

“It’s not a problem,” Zuko lies. His face is dangerously close to Zhao’s, and there’s a feeling in his chest, a terrible, vulnerable feeling that threatens to crack him in half.

They resist as long as it takes to clean the blood from their hands and apply the bandage. Zuko barely has the last end tucked away when Zhao surges forward to kiss his throat.

In the forty-three days since they arrived in Kirachu, not a shred of violence has been exchanged between them. Even as Zhao has grown more agitated with the state of his career, he hasn’t laid a hand on Zuko in fury *or* affection.

And so. Just as desperately as Zuko has feared the potential violence of Zhao’s touch, he wonders if he has been missing this other half. They have been avoiding one another in the halls and after meals; they even sleep on the outermost edges of the bed to avoid contact. Zuko has no other outlet for physical affection, no source of comfort in this lonely and miserable time, so that must be why, when a tongue flattens against his pulse, he moans openly, wantonly for all the relief it provides.

What ensues is a tender, mournful act that leaves Zuko a thousand times more befuddled than before. It was easy, being frightened. Fear is a base emotion, the sort even animals understand. Now, as he lies skin-to-skin in the warm comfort of Zhao’s arms, he’s faced with the realization that he’s not ready to let this part go. He tries to snap himself out of it, to picture Zhao’s fingers around his neck… but can only see how they were intertwined with his only moments before.

Zuko thinks his husband has fallen asleep, until he hears him yawn. “Careful when you get out of bed,” Zhao says, voice drowsy and sated. “There’s still glass on the floor.”

---

Shortly after their rogue afternoon of intimacy, Zhao curtly informs Zuko that in a matter of days, he will be leaving Kirachu for a visit to the capital. Alone.

“Wait - I want to come along,” Zuko insists, tossing his scroll aside on the divan. He misses the capital for a myriad of reasons, chief among them the chance to see his uncle. His bending problem still hasn’t improved, and some privacy with Iroh would allow him to work on it. Not to mention they could be candid about certain topics. Like, for instance… the fire in the Lesser Hall.

But Zhao isn’t keen on letting him come along. “It’s for work,” he huffs, barely looking at Zuko as he fusses with his armor in one of the mirrors on the wall. “There’s an inter-island planning committee I want to attend. It’s not like I’ll be having any fun without you.”

Zuko casts a pleading look into the mirror even as his husband avoids his eyes. “I wouldn’t get in the way. I could spend my time with Uncle.”

The responding curl of Zhao’s lips is positively rotten. “Oh, he didn’t tell you? He’s not at the palace.”

“He isn’t?” Zuko asks, suspicious. “How long will he be gone, for?”

“The palace aide who wrote me had no idea. I’m sure it’s more alone time with his favorite niece,” Zhao says, leaning in to get a better look as he adjusts one bracer.

Zuko’s stomach twists. Zhao is probably lying, but it’s not as though he can accuse him of that outright. “Well. If not for Uncle, then it could be good to see my father…”

At that, Zhao rolls his eyes. Zuko surprises himself with the testiness in his own response, the flare of anger in his chest sudden and overwhelming: “ *What?* ”

Zhao raises an eyebrow at his intensity, throwing a glance across the room. When it’s apparent Ama has not noticed, engrossed in his embroidery, Zhao lowers his voice and says, “Do you not understand how furious your father is with you right now?”

*He only feels that way because he doesn’t know the Lesser Hall is both of our fault,* Zuko thinks spitefully. Steeling his temper, he grounds out an equally low-voiced, “Well. Then it’s the perfect chance to apologize.”

Zhao shakes his head. “There is no chance in hell he’ll be willing to talk to you.”

“You don’t know that for *sure-* ”

“He didn’t even come to say goodbye to you, Zuko. Doesn’t that strike you as even a little bit telling? Iroh came to say goodbye.”

“That’s just how Father is.”

At this, Zhao’s jaw twitches. Zuko can see the shadow of their last fight in his eyes before he wrenches his face back towards the mirror, gathering himself. When he looks at Zuko again, it is to say, “Your father wanted to throw you out when you were barely coherent. He didn’t want to let you stay in the Great Hall to recover from your injuries - *that’s* how mad he was. Iroh and I had to beg him to let you stay in Azula’s room.”

Zuko opens his mouth. It lays empty for a moment before he summons two petty, defensive words: “You’re lying.”

His husband is rapidly turning the color of his armor. Still, he maintains his cool as he hisses, “ *Ask* *Iroh* , if he’s ever back in the capital. He’ll tell you the same thing.”

Zuko crosses his arms, nails biting into his skin with the effort to calm himself. It isn’t just the continued slander against his father that’s rankling him; it’s the realization that Zhao is probably correct *.* From Ozai’s point of view, Zuko has down something atrociously stupid and destructive, an act that has smeared the royal family’s name in the mud. His father is angry with him because he doesn’t know the full story, and if he could only tell him the truth...

“You’re not coming with me,” Zhao says with finality. “You’ll only ruin any chances I have of settling things.” He casts his glare around the room, voice dropping even lower. “We’re frankly lucky he didn’t outright ban us both from the capital when he sent us to this shithole.”

Another flare of anger, like kindling in his gut. Zuko hisses, perhaps a bit loudly, “Dominion over a whole island isn’t a punishment, Zhao. You could show a *little* more gratitude for what my father’s given you.”

Predictably, this backsass does not earn Zuko a spot next to Zhao on the next boat out of Kirachu; instead, Zhao shoots him a look deadly enough to render him silent for the rest of the afternoon.

---

Despite what Zhao told him, Zuko writes to his uncle at the palace, keeping the damning details minimal while dropping hints that he’d like the chance to show his uncle around Kirachu. When this letter receives no response, he sends another, inquiring after the reconstruction of the Lesser Hall. By the third letter with no response, he stops trying.

Zuko also tries to write to Mai on multiple separate occasions. The issue here is not in the lack of response, but his own inability to finish a letter once he has started. He’s not sure how much he can tell her, not only because he’s unsure if someone here is reading his letters (is that what happened to the ones he sent to Iroh?), but also because he thinks she’d be incredibly disappointed in him if she could see him now. He imagines her responses, written in the familiar sharp brushstrokes: *So* *not only are you telling me you’re married to a lunatic, but you were actually willing to sleep with* *that lunatic after he beat you unconscious? Zuko, what the hell! You ignore me for months, and* *this is the news you finally bring me?!*

Despite this discouraging imaginary argument, he steels himself for his next attempt. At the desk in the tigermonkey room, with an enormous ream of paper unfurled in front of him, he writes:

*Dear Mai,*

*How are things in Shuhon? Does teaching suit you? I’m sorry I haven’t written until now, but I* *figured I’d better let you know I am no longer at the palace because*

He frowns at the page. How to sum up the turmoil that brought them here?

*my husband is now governor of Kirachu. It’s the same island where he grew up, you’ll remember,* *and the reason my father wanted us to get married in the first place. We’re supposed to be uniting* *the Fire Nation under us,*

He sets the brush back in its ink tray, hesitating over the next words. Well - he already added the comma. He might as well finish the thought.

*but things are not shaping up quite as nicely as we hoped. Trying to maintain order here keeps* *Zhao away for hours, sometimes days at a time. He misses the war council and the military in* *general, and worries often about the state of things in the North Pole. He put so much work into* *planning our invasion, and he wanted to go and fight on the frontlines himself,*

A realization.

*although he stayed because I asked him to.*

So the last two months could have been avoided, if he had only not begged Zhao to stay with him.

He doesn’t want to think about this anymore. Time for a change of subject.

*I spend most days stuck at home. There’s a village at the foot of the mountain, but I’ve only passed* *through once, on the way here. It’s several miles away, and often the family’s carriages are gone* *with Zhao and his brothers by the time I wake up, so there’s no means for me to leave.*

*I guess it’s pretty lonely here. I wish you*

Zuko crumples what he has written and starts over on a new sheet.

Zhao happens upon him while he’s hunched over the next draft. “You look like you’re puzzling over a real conundrum, there,” he comments, pausing to hover over his spouse’s shoulder. “What are you writing?”

Zuko doesn’t rush to cover what he has written; this time it’s a measly two words, *Dear Mai* , and then nothing. When Zhao reads it, he hums in recognition. “Ah, I didn’t know you two had kept in touch since she left.”

“We haven’t, really,” Zuko confesses. “Now that we’re no longer in the palace, though, I figured I’d let her know where I am.”

There’s a beat of silence before Zhao says, “Oh. Well. If you think that’s wise.”

His tone of voice is strange enough that Zuko feels compelled to turn and face him. “What’s wrong?”

Zhao shrugs, expression hard to read. “I don’t know, I mean… It’s been so long since she left, and you still haven’t reached out? Won’t it feel a little… arbitrary, that you’re doing so now?”

It isn’t that Zuko hadn’t thought of that - he’s an expert at imagining the ways his few friends secretly hate him. It’s just that he had finally convinced himself those fears were unfounded.

“I know it’s not ideal that I haven’t talked to her in a while,” Zuko admits. “But I mean… she hasn’t reached out to me, either.”

At that, Zhao outright *winces* .

“ *What?* ” Zuko asks, panic rising in his voice.

“Don’t you think that’s a sign?” Zhao asks, fixing his husband with a pitying look. “It’s normal to outgrow people. I don’t talk to any of *my* unmarried friends anymore.”

Zuko tries once more to write a letter to Mai, but soon abandons the attempts altogether. He’s content to wallow in his solitude until the letters he sent to Iroh return to him, unopened. A politely-worded note from one of the palace secretaries informs him that General Iroh left the capital some time ago, with neither word on where he was going nor when he would be back.

So Zhao wasn't lying about him being gone, after all. That soothes the sting of rejection, somewhat; of course Iroh wasn’t ignoring him, he was just. Off rekindling his relationship with Azula, somewhere. That’s great. Zuko is happy for them both. So happy he hardly notices how the ink runs against his palms, clutching the letters long after he’s stopped reading.

---

Although the prospect of not seeing Iroh is extremely disheartening, Zuko is looking forward to a few days free from Zhao’s influence. Since they arrived in Kirachu, he’s been dreading the moment his defenselessness comes to light. At least if Zhao’s gone, that anxiety will leave with him.

But during Zhao’s absence, something strange happens to Zuko. It starts with a restless night’s sleep; he wakes multiple times to find his hands outstretched towards the other side of the bed. He’s always been a light sleeper, but he becomes even worse, jolting out of bed with every late night jungle noise. It’s Ember Island all over again, but without the warm body to latch himself onto when he startles awake.

Ama alone keeps Zuko company during the day. Wei disappears for hours at a time, and despite the family’s constant complaints about Yan “lazing around at home,” he’s rarely around, either.

“Ah, but he isn’t at any sort of work - he’s wasting time with his layabout friends,” Ama tells him, as they walk arm-in-arm across the estate. It’s a sweltering day, as most are in Kirachu, although the line of ash banana trees planted along the outer wall cast a cooling shadow where they walk. “Yan was always a little behind his brothers. Not in a way the baby of the family *should* be, mind you. I’m talking years behind. I was so relieved when he finally joined the army - at eighteen, of course, because most boys leave home at sixteen, and spirits forbid Yan do *anything* on time. Then almost as soon as he was overseas, he started up all this unpatriotic nonsense! He would write home about how the Fire Nation was so violent and evil - what did he expect, for war to be a cakewalk?”

Ama can talk for hours if left unchecked, but Zuko doesn’t mind terribly. He gets the sense the older omega has been lacking for friendship and stimulation. Partially because Ama tells him so.

“As you know, my husband passed away about six years ago. He was very old, and suffered a terrible fall,” comes the brief elaboration, Ama’s voice thickening as if this is all the detail he can manage without bursting into tears. “But what you probably don’t know is that a few months after the fact, my closest friend in all the world was getting ready to move to a different island. We were used to dropping by one another’s homes unannounced almost on a daily basis, and I was convinced that I’d die, having to now schedule time to see her.” Ama punctuates his story with a joyless laugh. “Then her ship wrecked off the coast of Ma’Inka, and I realized a little journeying was *nothing* compared to losing her completely. It was so awful. I really saw no point in going on. I think if Wei hadn’t been living with me at the time, I would have faded away into nothing.”

“Oh no. I’m so sorry,” Zuko says, because he’s not sure what else you’re supposed to say when your in-law tells you such a sad story unprompted.

Ama sighs wistfully, leaning his weight a little harder on their linked arms. “Thank you, dear. As you can see, I’ve come out the other side only lightly scathed.”

In any case, when Zuko isn’t listening to Ama fill the silence, there isn’t much else to do. He doesn’t know anyone else in Kirachu, and few of the books in the house strike his interest, all being nonfiction or a dry, sparse sort of prose.

And so, as the itch of Zhao’s absence grows, Zuko finds himself asking what his husband was like, growing up. Ama swoons, delighted to talk about his eldest child. “Oh, he was wonderful when he was little. So inquisitive about everything. He would’ve been a scholar, if he hadn’t been so skilled in combat. He was fearless, even at a young age - often to the point of injury, but his impulsiveness has had other uses! Has he ever told you that he saved my life?”

“Really?” Zuko asks, stunned. “What happened? How old was he?”

For once Ama’s face moves, and the resulting smile is positively radiant. “He saved me from the moment he was conceived.”

That’s - not really what Zuko expected him to say. He asks, “How so?” while silently hoping the answer isn’t simply, “because motherhood is a gift that saves you,” or something saccharine like that.

And it isn’t, although it’s still strange. Ama leans in conspiratorially and says, “Well. I wasn’t born so blessed, the way you were. I came into my noble status by luck, when the man who’d eventually become my husband plucked me off the street.”

Zuko’s mouth flies open. The same parents who wouldn’t let Zhao elope with a servant had met like *that?* “Really? I wouldn’t have ever guessed.”

Ama clearly isn’t making the same connection, going giddy with imagined flattery. “Why *thank* you, my prince. I have been a member of nobility long enough now that such manners must seem natural to me.

“Before my husband found me, my sisters and I used to clean house for some of the wealthier merchants in that little village at the foot of the mountain. We were comfortable, with the four of us and our mother chipping in, and I likely would have settled for that life if not for the illness that swept Kirachu that year.

“I was the sole survivor of my family. Worse yet, once I’d come out the other side with close to nothing, I struggled to find work; the families that had once employed me now shunned me for fear that the illness that had wiped out my sisters would spread to them. I lost my family, and then my work, and then my home. I would have starved to death, had the governor not found me and taken me in.”

Ama tosses his hair over his shoulder, glossy and thick, the rare gray strands glittering amongst the dark like constellations. “My best friend used to tease me over how I worshipped my husband. But considering the circumstances, I can be forgiven, can’t I? There I was, sitting on the street, miserably trying to figure out how I would earn my next meal. All I’d eaten in the last several days were my own fingernails, chewed to the bloody nub, and a rotten ash banana I had stolen from beneath a tree on a local family’s property. And in my hour of need, what should appear, but the governor of Kirachu’s carriage? I remember it being gilded and shining, like the sort of magical thing you might see in a scroll about an ancient dragon emperor, although I know that can’t really be the case. None of the carriages we’ve owned since look like that one in my head.

“My future husband was very direct. He looked me up and down, then, as if satisfied by what he saw, asked if I would like something to eat. Somewhat stunned, I nodded, and he offered me his hand. He didn’t have very big hands, for an alpha his size. I remember seeing how my fingers were longer than his, and thinking, *That won’t do. He won’t want to keep an omega as unwieldy as I am* *for long.* I didn’t realize, until he had me home, why I’d been chosen.

“He told me he wanted someone to care for his wife. She was sick with the same disease that had taken away my own family members. I tried to tell him I wasn’t qualified - I was a maid, not a nurse - but he insisted. Then he sent me into the master bedroom to meet her.”

Ama’s breath hitches, remembering it even now. “I nearly fainted away at the sight of that pale little ghost, propped up against the covers. Her face was *mine* . I could have sworn I was being haunted by one of my sisters. And she clearly saw the resemblance, too. Do you know what the first thing she said to me was?”

Zuko shakes his head, spellbound.

“She asked, ‘Are you here to replace me?’ So matter of fact! Of course I told her no - what else could I do in that situation? But although I was younger than I am now, I wasn’t stupid, and I wasn’t-” Ama coughs, eyes darting away. “I wasn’t naive. I saw her face and I knew very well that she was right.

“So I cared for her, to the very best of my ability. In a strange way, I also found myself filling a motherly sort of void in young Wei’s life. He was shy around me, but he let me talk at him, like you’re doing now, and sometimes, when his mother was too fragile for company, he would find me where I was embroidering and simply... sit beside me. Never touching, never talking, he’d come up with some little book or game and quietly entertain himself. He was seeking a detached sort of comfort, I think. I quite liked him. He was the ideal candidate for a stepchild, and, frankly, made me vastly underestimate what raising children would be like.

“Still, even having chosen me for my uncanny resemblance to his wife, even given how his son silently approved of me, this man didn’t belong to me. He was my employer. He was nobility. He was the *governor of Kirachu* . I could sense that I had to lock down a commitment from him in some form, lest I find myself back in that gutter, but I felt keenly that I had a disadvantage. Surely you know, being one yourself, Prince Zuko, but male omegas aren’t most alphas’ first choice. Whether it’s based in truth or stereotype, we’re seen as this… inferior choice, this...”

“Last resort?” Zuko supplies.

“Yes,” Ama agrees. “In particular, we are un-women, barren imitations thought to be less than our female counterparts in every way, including our fertility. That’s the stereotype I grew up with, at least; choose a male omega, and you may as well have said you don’t want an heir at all. So if I wanted to be more than this man’s concubine, I knew I had to prove I could be a worthy mate by giving him a child. And not just any child; the last wife had already given him a boy, a statistical *advantage* , a chance at an alpha. So I had to give him a boy, too.”

Ama takes on that beatific look again. “It might sound strange to you, Prince Zuko, but I knew from the moment that I skipped my heat that I had won. I knew that the child I carried would not only be a boy, not only be a firebender, but an *alpha* . I believed it so firmly that Agni saw fit to make it happen.”

When the story ends, Zuko feels changed, as he might after disappearing into an epic play for a few hours. The curtain goes up, and suddenly the light in the theatre is too bright, the details of the surrounding audience too vulgar, too real. When the silence has finally been punctured by the mournful whine of a cicada-cricket, he manages, “That’s... incredible. You’re very lucky, or I guess you have really good genetics? Both of your sons turned out to be alphas.”

“It is quite a feat,” Ama agrees, humbly. “My mother would have been deeply envious, had she lived to see it. She wanted an alpha so badly. I always felt she resented me for presenting as an omega; as the only boy in the family, I got a lot of special treatment, until I suddenly didn’t.”

“Oh. I’m sorry.”

“Don’t be,” Ama sighs. “Such is the dynamic between every omega boy and his mother, right?”

Not for Zuko. Before she left, Ursa had never shown the slightest disappointment with his presentation. His father, on the other hand, had not reacted so well at first. At least with time he had come to see the value in Zuko’s omega status.

Despite the many hundreds of miles between them, Zuko finds himself thinking about his father especially often these days. It’s hard not to; he is in Kirachu on Ozai’s decree, after all, surrounded by the ghosts of his past.

“I heard that my father and Wei used to be close,” Zuko says. He's not sure who is harder to picture as a teenager - the Fire Lord in all his larger-than-life glory, or the baleful Wei. “Why did that stop?”

“For the reason you’re probably thinking,” Ama answers. “Prince Ozai presented as an alpha. Wei did not.”

Zuko casts his gaze at the grass below, flattened by their last few laps around the yard. He’s reminded of Azula, Ty Lee, and Mai, and his father’s order that they keep their distance. It was cruel, but at least Zuko could see why someone might not want their teenaged alpha spending lots of unchaperoned time with omegas. A beta and an alpha, on the other hand, had very little chance for scandal.

“I don’t understand why they couldn’t have stayed friends regardless,” Zuko sighs.

Ama pats his hand. “Oh… Neither did Wei.” He brings them to a stop. Ama can talk on forever without pausing, but he seems to struggle to keep up with Zuko on their walks. It’s taken him a while to notice the slight limp to Ama’s cadence, particularly towards the end of the day; Zuko’s unsure if it’s the result of age or an old injury.

“You know,” Ama says, “There’s something about the end of a friendship that can be as heartbreaking as the end of a romance. Never mind a friendship with someone so *important,* so powerful. Although Wei managed to move on and chase his own political aspirations for a few years, he gave up on them quite abruptly.”

“What happened?”

Ama shakes his head. “He’d never tell me. Even though it was years later, I’ve always thought it could be traced back to his falling out with Ozai. It destroyed his confidence. I can certainly sympathize; had Zhu turned his back on me, I would’ve spent the rest of my life regretting all that I could have become by his side, and he was only a governor. To be discarded like that by a *prince…* ”

Zuko glances at the house as if he might see Wei at a window, staring back. A part of him wants to ask the beta someday, but finds the prospect daunting. It’s a delicate subject, and Zuko has never been delicate with words. It doesn’t help that Wei is about as easy to corner as a skittish cat, the sort even its owners only see in swipes of a paw out from under the furniture.

“Oh,” Zuko says, almost as an afterthought. “What happened to Wei’s mother?”

There’s a shine to Ama’s eyes. “She put up a valiant fight, but she passed a few months before Zhao was born. She wasn’t overly fond of me - nor would *I* be, if I were in her position - but I hope you believe me when I say I did everything I could to make sure she was comfortable in the end. Looking into her withered face was like watching my sisters fade away all over again. It was like watching a part of myself die.”

---

Spiritually exhausted by his own sorrowful memoirs, Ama decides to fill the rest of their days alone together with happier tales from Zhao’s childhood. He gets Zuko’s help retrieving a small wooden chest from a high shelf in the tigermonkey room, and from this he produces a series of mementos. There’s a fist-sized wooden carving full of awkward, jutting angles, apparently a small Zhao’s attempt at carving a dragon moose. A certificate from a firebending course, affirming he’d passed his lessons with honors. A bag of baby teeth - which Zuko must fail to suppress a shudder at, because Ama laughs at his reaction. “I know it seems grisly. My mother kept mine and my sisters’ mixed together in a drawer. I had a heart attack every time I went looking for a comb.”

Holding a tiny canine aloft, Ama tells how, in sprinting across the house at age twelve, Zhao tripped and fell flat on his face, causing the last of his baby teeth to fly loose in a torrent of blood. (“He didn’t even flinch! So brave.”) How, at seven, Zhao protested his father’s plans to sell his favorite dragon moose by refusing to eat any meals for three days, a tactic that had Ama in a panic, up until he found the snacks squirreled away in his room. How, at four, Zhao refused to do anything Wei didn’t do first, from wearing certain clothes, to eating vegetables, to going to bed on time. “That’s half the reason the boys call me by my first name,” Ama huffs. “Wei did it, so of course Yan and Zhao had to follow their big brother’s lead. It drove their father absolutely crazy - he thought it was so disrespectful! But I wasn’t about to *demand* the poor boy call me Mom when his real one had just died, and my own boys wouldn’t listen when I corrected them, so in the end, I let them all carry on.”

“Did you ever have to explain to Zhao that Wei was his half-brother?” Zuko asks.

Ama gives a quick, breathy sort of laugh. “Of course, but it didn’t stick. Whenever I tried to tell him Wei could call me that and he couldn’t, he would say, *Ama, he’s my big brother!* And I would say, yes, but he’s not *my* son. That about made him burst into tears. Spirits, he cried over everything at that age, my sensitive boy. I don’t think he really understood until he was six, and by then, the habit was impossible to break.”

Ama pauses, then, looking closely at Zuko’s face. “My prince - are you feeling alright?”

It’s as if some spell has been broken with this pause in monologue: Zuko touches his cheek, and is stunned when his fingers come back wet.

“I-” Zuko’s usual rasp is reduced to an embarrassing croak. “It’s so stupid, but I just keep thinking. Isn’t it strange, how we all start out that little? You and me and Zhao, and our parents, every soldier and peasant and lord, Fire Nation or not. We were all that little, once, and we-”

He takes a shuddering breath as he imagines that same child from the stories, who innocently mimicked everything his big brother did, who cried because he couldn’t bear that they had anything separating them… then growing up into the sort of man who would brutalize his spouse.

“-I’m sorry,” Zuko finishes, taking in gasping breaths, “I’m not normally like this, it’s just that I haven’t been sleeping very well.”

“It’s alright,” Ama soothes. “I find when we’re tired, we’re often in touch with our deepest feelings. I think what you said was quite lovely, really.”

---

It isn’t the last time Zuko cries in front of Ama that week. His tears always come on the heels of some sweet anecdote, souring it entirely (although Ama keeps assuring him that it’s fine). For someone so used to maintaining an image, Zuko’s newfound volatility presents a terrifying obstacle. And of course, agonizing over ugly feelings only makes them uglier; the stress seems to have given him some stomach trouble, so he spends many of the days apart from Zhao feeling queasy, unwilling to eat very much that’s put in front of him.

In private, his flame becomes even less predictable, a thumb-sized bastard he can only conjure occasionally in fits and starts. This, too, only rubs his feelings bloodier. His failure to maintain control is soon just as likely to make him tear up as it is to make him curse and storm around his bed in angry circles afterward, and more than once, he loses his cool on Rio and Yan for little foibles. He doesn’t scream and rave as his husband might, but the icy tone with which he tells Yan to stop fucking shaking the dinner table certainly earns him an hour of silence, a rarity on the Kirachu estate.

Ama may notice this change in demeanor, but does not comment. They continue their daily talks, walking in slow circles around the edges of the estate. Zuko is reminded of a story his mother told him about a ship trapped in a whirlpool, spiralling helplessly towards the deadly center. Eventually the sailors were rescued by divine intervention, a local spirit rising up from the briny depths to drag them to safety. They couldn’t have done it on their own; the current was too strong.

“I miss Zhao,” Ama sighs. “I know it’s only been a few days, but I feel like I *just* got him back after years apart, only for him to disappear on me again.”

“It’s strange, not having him around,” Zuko concedes.

Try as he might, he cannot slide by with non-answers. Ama prompts him: “You must miss him even more than I do.”

“I miss him,” Zuko answers, after a pause he knows says otherwise. “We haven’t been apart very much since we got married, although... For a while, I thought we’d be constantly separated, because of the navy. I thought he would leave for months or years on end, and I would have to wait at home for him.”

“I’m sure the expectation doesn’t make the reality any easier.”

“No,” Zuko agrees aloud, while silently ruminating on the lost opportunity. Would he and Zhao have worked out better, if they weren’t together so often? Or would it all be the same, their heartbreak unspooled over a longer span of time?

They go nearly half a lap before Ama starts up again. “Forgive me for prying, Prince Zuko, but I’m curious. How would you describe your relationship with my son?”

“I mean - he’s my husband. I love him,” Zuko says, too slowly.

“Yes, I’m sure you do,” Ama acquiesces. “However, if you don’t mind me making an observation, the two of you don’t seem terribly close. That’s not altogether unexpected for an arranged marriage of about four months, but I remember Zhao spoke quite glowingly of you when you were first married. I’m wondering if something has changed, recently.”

The reminder of how short their union has been cuts Zuko by surprise. It feels like he’s been married to Zhao for years longer than that.

In ruminating on Ama’s question, he feels himself being pulled in opposite directions; on the one hand, he wants to confide in someone. With their recent closeness and his experience being married, Ama feels like the perfect fit. On the other hand - he is, after all, Zhao’s parent. It may not be there, but Zuko can still hear the threat lurking in Ama’s question. He needs to be careful what he says next.

Zuko takes a breath, before grasping at a plausible-sounding lie. Or perhaps not a lie; just certainly not the entire truth. “I… I think this change has been difficult for us.”

“Kirachu isn’t to your liking?”

“No, I - I mean, not just this specific change. Marriage in general.” Not only the fire, but all that came before.

“Don’t I know it,” Ama sighs. “I’m sure Zhao feels similarly. You should talk to him about it.”

“I don’t always know how to talk to him,” Zuko confesses. “You know how he can be.”

Ama blinks. Then, each word spoken deliberately: “How *can* he be?”

Surely he already knows. Surely not even a mother’s love can’t blind him to it. Zuko gravitates towards a specific example, saying, “Remember a few days ago, when he was shouting about the silence from the North Pole?”

“He was upset,” Ama sniffs. “Wouldn’t you be? All that hard work, only to be shut out from the glory of it. Then to have to twiddle your thumbs, waiting, knowing *nothing?* ”

“Yes,” Zuko admits, “but I wouldn’t have thrown a plate at Yan because of it. *He* didn’t do anything.”

Ama huffs. “On the contrary, he was being unnecessarily combative by trying to engage in anti-empire rhetoric at dinner. He should know better than to antagonize his brother when he’s already stressed.”

“...What if Yan did the same thing to Zhao? Threw something at him for teasing him when he was in a bad mood?”

“It wouldn’t *be* the same because Zhao actually provides for the rest of us,” Ama replies, hotly. “He gives us so much, while running a whole island. The very least we can do is let him air his feelings.”

“Right,” says Zuko, “but he should still be nicer to his brother about it.”

“Niceness is overrated,” Ama scoffs. “It is more important to perform your role and perform it well. I know Zhao’s domain must look very small in comparison to what your father leads, Prince Zuko, but I assure you that your husband is deserving of your utmost devotion.”

Ama has never spoken critically of him. Zuko almost wonders if he has misheard, until his in-law continues, “I know my son is passionate. His father was the same way - it is an intense experience being married to a man like that, for sure, but men of their sort are put on this earth to burn brightly, and who are we to extinguish them?”

“I’m not looking to extinguish him,” Zuko says, carefully measuring his words against his fraying nerves. “I just… would like him to be a little more patient. Sometimes.”

When he turns to look at Ama’s face, it is as blank as ever. He wonders if the corners of his mouth are as taut as Zuko thinks, or if his imagination is putting the strain there in absence of any other hints.

“Have you ever been homeless?” Ama asks, suddenly.

Zuko thinks, briefly, of the destruction of the Lesser Hall. That surely doesn’t count, when he had his sister’s lavish room and then an entire estate to relocate to. “No.”

“Have you ever starved, Prince Zuko?”

Zuko blinks. The very presence of his title within that question immediately renders it rhetorical. They both know the answer. He says it anyway: “No. I haven’t.”

Ama exhales through his nose. Reminds him, “I have. I wouldn’t wish it on anyone. Maybe a worst enemy, but that is because I’m spiteful, not because it isn’t a terrible experience. I’ve never lived through anything else quite like it, and in all my life afterwards, I think my sole focus has been on never going back to that place again.”

“That - makes sense,” Zuko says, lamely. There’s a terrible feeling in the pit of his stomach.

Ama nods, still not looking at him, eyes fixed at some unseen vantage point in the jungle foliage. “Sometimes I think we all need to have a little perspective.”

“...By remembering that there are people who have it worse?” Zuko asks, tensely.

“No,” says Ama. “You need to remember that it could be very much worse for *you* .”

His words stun Zuko into silence. Ama looks him over with a critical eye before continuing: “I know you are royalty. I know that it is unlikely you will ever starve or be homeless. But in the event this does not work out for you, there is a great and terrible unknown waiting. Take it from a person who has lived through tragedy, Prince Zuko - stability *should* be a right, but it isn’t. Not really. And so you must pay whatever price you can to keep it.”

It seems they’ve been pacing the yard for hours. Stomach now seizing, Zuko stops to breathe through his mouth, ignoring the gaze boring its way into the side of his head as he struggles not to retch into the bushes.

Ama doesn’t have to tell Zuko to fear the great and terrible unknown, because he already does. After all, isn’t fear of that unknown what kept driving him back into Zhao’s arms? How could he possibly risk asking his father to reconsider his engagement, when he was the only parent Zuko had left to please? Who else would be his companion when Ty Lee and Mai were lost to him? Even Azula and Iroh had seemingly forgotten him in the mad rush of their own lives - who, then, would be Zuko’s family? It was Zhao. Time and time again, all he had was Zhao. Zuko had spent the early days of his marriage frantically trying to keep him, terrified of what lay before him if he should lose this man. And now, in the face of the terrible violence that passed between them -

What could he do about it, really? Was this, as Ama implied, merely the price he had to pay for a little stability?

Eventually, the fervid waves in his stomach calm down, sparing him the embarrassment of vomiting in front of his in-law. At some point, he must have bent forward; now he straightens up, avoiding Ama’s gaze by scrubbing the tears from his eyes.

He asks the open air, “Can you tell me again what he was like when he was little?”

The change of topic is too late to spare his feelings. But Ama gladly goes along. “Of course, my prince. What would you like to know?”

“Anything. A happy story.”

Ama’s eyes soften, smooth voice lilting as he begins: “How about this one…”

---

Two more days of family stories coupled with terrible sleep leave Zuko feeling deeply out of sorts. He has a splitting headache and frayed emotions by the time that Zhao gets home, so when the other man looks at him with an affection that’s been missing for weeks, and reaches out to embrace him, Zuko allows himself to be swept up in the moment. The fondness in Zhao’s voice when he greets him, combined with the *I missed you* whispered flush against his ear, almost sends him into another round of tears.

Until he feels Zhao groping his waist. The older man pulls out of their embrace to look Zuko over with a frown.

“Have you gained weight?” Zhao asks.

In an instant, every affectionate feeling that’s been building in his absence is fried in the inferno of Zuko’s fury. He’s actually speechless with anger, left staring knife-eyed at his husband while being sized up like a piece of meat.

“You have,” Zhao decides, smiling in ignorance of how dearly the young prince wants to kill him. “The robes hide it, so I hadn’t noticed when I first saw you. Maybe if we adjust your diet now, we can stop it before your lovely face turns to pudding.”

The light of Zuko’s rage is comparable to that of Agni in all of his glory. Before he engages himself in a physical fight he absolutely cannot win, he wrenches himself from Zhao’s grasp, marching into the house without a word. He misses Zhao’s reaction, knowing only that he muttered something in the moments before Zuko slammed the door shut behind him.

At dinner, instead of everyone grabbing their own portions, Rio gives them each a readily-arranged plate, with Zuko’s noticeably leaner than everyone else’s. He stabs at the meager serving of meat with enough force to crack his plate. The only upside to having lost his bending is that he’s not involuntarily spewing fire all over the table.

“Don’t put up a fuss,” Zhao chides him. “You’ll be grateful when you’ve lost some weight.”

On the other side of the table, Yan scoffs. “Are your eyes broken? Zuko isn’t overweight.”

Zhao’s responding glare is reminiscent of the one he’s given every guard in the royal palace since he and Zuko married. With one lip curled, he says, “Stop being a suck-up, Yan.”

“I’m not being a suck-up,” Yan retorts. “If anything, Zuko should be super thin because he’s been picking at his food since he got here. It drives me up a wall, because I *really* want the leftovers, but I know Ama would absolutely freak if I asked.”

“Have at it.” Without a second thought, Zuko shoves the plate at Yan. His only consolation for being given so little food is the fact the smell of it makes him want to hurl; not that Rio is a horrible cook, but something about the sheer strength of that meat scent is not sitting well.

Despite the lustful way he looks at Zuko’s plate, Yan holds fast, pouting. “Hey, now, don’t give up dinner just because my brother’s being an ass…”

Zuko shakes his head. “I seriously don’t want it. I’m not feeling well.” Every time he blinks, he sees stars, and he’s not sure if it’s from the now three-day headache or his anger manifesting. He closes his eyes, rubbing his temples vehemently.

The next time he opens his eyes, he notices Ama watching him closely. It’s as if the other man is seeing him for the first time, taking care to deeply study his features.

“...Rio?” Ama calls out, not once taking his eyes off Zuko. “Can you pick up some fresh barley from the market tomorrow?” The servant seems to materialize from the doorway to affirm this wish, before sweeping out of the room with a handful of dirtied bowls.

Yan’s brow furrows. “What are you going to make with that?”

“A pregnancy test,” says Ama, popping a dollop of rice into his mouth.

All activity at the dinner table halts, the clattering of silverware against plates silenced as all eyes turn onto Ama.

“Excuse me?” Zuko asks, voice strangled.

“It’s an old trick my mother taught me,” Ama says, with a nonchalant wave of his chopsticks. “If you’re pregnant, the barley will flower when you-”

“No, no, no, start at the beginning,” Zhao cuts in. “You think Zuko’s pregnant?”

Ama shrugs. “That’s what the barley’s for. I don’t know Prince Zuko terribly well, but for the last few days, he’s seemed a little... weepy. I thought it was nerves from moving...”

“And lack of sleep,” Zuko says, quickly. “I’m not sleeping. That’s probably all.”

Ama hums. “True. But you keep saying your head hurts - I had *terrible* headaches when I first got pregnant with Yan.”

“Couldn’t that just be my concussion?” Zuko asks doggedly.

“Not unless you have a permanent brain injury,” Zhao huffs. “You recovered weeks ago.”

“And your nausea is telling,” Ama adds. “Contrary to the ‘morning’ part of morning sickness, I don’t think I could eat for - oh - the first trimester of either of my pregnancies. It was awful. I gagged so often over dinner that Zhu made me eat alone.”

Zhao brightens considerably. “And pregnancy would explain the weight gain!”

“I suppose. Although *I* personally don’t see it,” Ama says, diplomatically.

The table kicks up with an energetic chatter. Somewhere in the middle of juggling inane questions and trying not to vomit (from terror and general nausea both), Zuko finds himself honing in on the sight of his own flesh peaking out from behind the fabric of his sleeve. He wonders when his fingers got so long and so delicate-looking. There’s no longer evidence of those late night sparring sessions with Iroh. That might as well all be a distant memory, now.

Somehow, he manages to smile on cue when Zhao catches his eye, lips splitting almost mechanically as he thinks, *Maybe we’re all just being paranoid* . After all. Stress makes people gain weight. Stress makes people cry. Stress gives people headaches and nausea and all the rest. It’s probably not time yet. Not really.

---

Zuko’s uncle had subjected him to countless superstitions over the years, insisting he light this incense or drink that tea in order to please the spirits. Never had these ministrations inspired said spirits to appear in a puff of smoke and say, “Good job! You did the right thing.” Nor had anything else nearly that obvious ever happened. It was all vague interpretation. The hope you’d done enough, with no certainty.

However, now Zuko knows the color of certainty is a rich violet-blue that stands out against the barley plant’s stems and leaves. He didn’t even know before today that barley *could* flower.

The room tilts, and to steady himself, he presses his hand against the wall, guiding himself down until he is crouching next to the sordid bouquet that has sealed his fate.

He doesn’t have any friends in the village. There’s no one he can trust that he can ask. There might not even *be* anything that can help him there; he’s seen that Kirachu is far from the shining metropolis of progress the capital was. Whatever he finds in that little village at the base of the mountain might not even get the job done. It might disfigure him, or worse - word of his intent to rid himself of this pregnancy could easily get back to Zhao.

Zuko takes mental stock of the house, searching for alternatives. Alcohol. If he drinks himself blind, will that do away with the problem? He thinks of the child being born in agony because he failed to kill it all the way and finds himself fighting back tears. He wants to be rid of the problem - but he doesn’t want to risk hurting this child in a way it has to live with.

The stairs. A character in a miserable play his mother used to love had lost her child after the villainous step-mother threw her down the stairs. Maybe - maybe he could do that. He could fall. It would be an accident, so he could avoid suspicion while taking care of the problem. Except if that doesn’t work, then Zuko could be seriously hurt, or he could die, and he doesn’t want to die. He doesn’t want to die, does he?

Even as he tries to maintain control, he feels his face twist just as any muscle may seize in response to agony. With a wet, gasping breath, he bends forward over his knees, hands over his eyes to dam the torrent.

Weeks ago, this was exactly what he’d wanted. A chance to prove his worthiness to his father. A chance to prove his worthiness to *Zhao,* to produce something that was the perfect combination of the both of them, something they both wanted, something that would unite them. While he still desperately wants some of those things - there again is the terrible image of Zhao’s hands around his throat. Even as he shoves it away, clinging to the hope he can salvage this, that he can thrive in the political marriage his father chose for him, he cannot shake the terror he feels when he tries to bend fire.

Ama is infinitely polite for waiting so long outside the bathroom door. But given that Zuko’s sobs are now audible, he lets himself in. He pauses, glancing at the barley before he offers support.

“Oh - but that’s good news, my prince. The flowers mean you *are* pregnant.”

There hadn’t been any doubt to dispel, but Zuko cries all the harder, voice mournful and unfamiliar even to himself.

Gentle hands card through his hair, and Ama says, “I know it’s overwhelming the first time. You feel so young and so unprepared. It could be worse, though - imagine having a baby at fourteen, fifteen years old! If you had been born in that little village down the mountain, you would’ve been married off the moment you presented.”

“I was,” Zuko sniffs, wiping his eyes on his sleeve. “Father just gave Zhao an assignment that bought us a little time.”

Ama muses over this. “It doesn’t seem to have done you any good. You’ve got delicate nerves. There’s nothing worse an omega can have.”

This chastising fails to calm Zuko down; another torrent of sobs bubble their way out of his throat, as involuntary as bile. Ama sighs. “I suppose I shouldn’t judge you; I was twenty when I got married, so I was a fully-formed person. I’m sure I can’t imagine what you’re going through. How old are you, again?”

“Ei-eighteen.” Although his nineteenth birthday is fast approaching, a thought that curdles his stomach.

Ama’s eyes soften. “Well! That’s plenty old.” He reaches into one wide sleeve and pulls out a handkerchief, shoving it into Zuko’s hands before he can say he doesn’t need it. “Spirits. Eighteen. If you were an alpha or a beta, you’d have enlisted two years ago, and if you’re old enough to die for your country, you’re old enough to have a baby. You know, people have been giving birth for eons without any trouble - well, *some* trouble, but you’re not just *some people* . The light of Agni is on your side. You will get through this with ease.”

Although the attempt is clumsy, Zuko gets the feeling that Ama’s desire to soothe him is sincere. The older omega has become something like a friend or a mother figure, and if neither of those, then at least an ally.

To think that the *one person* he can turn to in all of Kirachu is his husband’s parent. Zuko wants to be grateful to have anyone at all, but every gentle gesture on Ama’s part only fills him with a more profound sense of loss. He can’t reconcile this person next to him with the son he raised.

Ama continues to sit with Zuko while he calms down, petting his hair and not quite looking at his face, sparing him the humiliation of eye contact. By the time the sobs have receded into quiet, trembling breaths, it’s more due to the fatigue of it all rather than the tears having actually run out.

With one last squeeze of the shoulder, Ama excuses himself from the bathroom, leaving Zuko to ruminate alone.

What Ama said before holds true. People have been having babies for eons. He doesn’t know how old his mother was when she had to do the same thing, but she’d done it, and in an arranged marriage, like him. And long before he learned that, he knew that she loved him with all her soul; although painful to remember in her absence, she used to tell Zuko all the time that he was her life’s greatest accomplishment.

&#40; *The fortress of blankets was far from the protection they needed, a wall of yarn where only stone* *and solid metal could possibly do. Yet it provided some irrational comfort. In a nest of soft things* *in the center, cradling a bruised wrist:*

*“Do you hate him?”*

*Then the reply, almost too quickly;*

*“He gave me you. I would never take that back.”)*

Zuko presses his face into the borrowed handkerchief until the embroidered flowers leave pits in his cheek. Red and white peonies. Did Ama sew it, or his mother before him? Zuko wishes more than anything that Ursa were here. He has suppressed such tender feelings towards his mother for years and years, so now that he finally acknowledges his longing, the force of it is enough to crack his ribs. He lets one more pitiful sob into the silk darkness before he hears the door open.

The steps are too heavy to be Ama. Zuko goes stone still and keeps the handkerchief over his eyes, as if by doing so he won’t have to acknowledge the newcomer’s arrival.

He hears Zhao clear his throat. “Well - congratulations. Although you don’t seem terribly pleased about it.”

There’s a thump on the tatami next to him, the sense of a person filling space. Zuko is struck by the unpredictable effect of fear on tears - this time, they dry up in an instant. The next time, he might only cry harder.

With a voice as tender as rotten fruit, Zhao tells him, “This is a good thing.”

Now Zuko lifts his face from the handkerchief, looking at the blurred mass beside him in disbelief. The circumstances have forced Zhao to finally forsake the polite distance they’ve been keeping all this time, allowing Zuko to really look at him closely. Although his face is relaxed, Zuko can see the constant scowling has left a permanent line between Zhao’s eyebrows, hardening his expression even as he speaks with a measured calm.

“Ama asked that I talk to you.” He pauses to chuckle, then corrects himself: “Really, he *demanded* that I come in here, saying you were scared out of your wits, that it was my duty as your husband to comfort you. Of course I didn’t understand what had happened that you were so upset in the first place, but as soon as he told me the news, I felt this... overwhelming relief.”

He sweeps his arms out, conjuring within them all that lies just beyond the estate. “Everything has been going wrong, lately. I’ve been sleepless over Kirachu and the North and the growing sense that your father is trying to push us out of the royal court - still, it all seems so insignificant now, knowing that we’re going to bring life into this world. It all seems *worth* something.”

He reaches out to touch Zuko’s face, pretending not to notice when the younger man flinches away. He says, “You asked me to stay and raise a family with you. We can do that, now.” He searches Zuko’s face, expression growing more and more troubled the longer the younger man doesn’t respond. “Do you not want that anymore?”

“It’s not that, I…” Zuko twists the handkerchief in his hands, his words bubbling wetly out of his mouth. “We *fought* each other, Zhao. We des… we destroyed our home, and we h-hurt each other, we can’t. We can’t bring a child into that.”

The look on Zhao’s face is dangerously close to one of pity; he thumbs at the streak of tears on Zuko’s cheek, which only spreads the wetness further. “It’s no accident I haven’t touched you since then, Zuko. I don’t want things to ever get that bad again. I didn’t want to risk the chance of losing this,” he says, gently curling a hand around Zuko’s waist.

At this touch, Zuko immediately breaks out into a tremble. He cannot name the emotion at its origin. Is he afraid? Is he relieved? He says, “You - you hate my father, and you want to overthrow him, and-”

Before he can say another word, Zhao is shushing him, one hand cradling the back of his head as he pulls him into an embrace. “Zuko, I was speaking in anger back then - you were right. You were always right, it’s better if we do things fairly. Think how *pleased* your father will be about this baby. If we end up with a healthy firebender, an alpha, this could be a way back into his good graces. Show him that even if your role is different, you can be just as useful as Azula.”

It’s tempting. It’s so, so tempting. In his mind’s eye, Zuko sees tiny hands curled around a makeshift carving. Bloodied hands entwined with his. Hands around his throat. Hands clasped in his own, trembling as their bodies move in tandem. Holding him down. Holding him close. Pulling his hair-

He flinches again, but Zhao isn’t pulling, he’s stroking. For much of this embrace, Zuko has neither refused nor returned Zhao’s affection, leaving his hands crumpled between their chests, toying at the wet ends of the handkerchief. But now, desperate for comfort, desperate for the pain to *end* , he relents, curling his arms around his husband’s neck.

“This is a good thing,” Zhao says, lips flush against his ear. “I’m telling you, this is the answer to all our prayers. We’re going to be fine.”

Zuko isn’t happy with the circumstances. He’s not - hopeful for better, or dreading the future, even, he’s just. Numb with the realization that this is happening. He tries to tell himself that all Zhao has done to him is... not justified, precisely, but in the very least ordinary. His mother would have felt the same way when she was pregnant with him.

(And what other choice is there? To forge ahead alone, as vulnerable as he is? To rob his child of their rightful place in the royal family, or worse - to do as his mother had before him, and abandon his child after it is born, while he selfishly seeks freedom for himself? What freedom even is there, for a person who is forced to leave behind their life and all they ever loved? Staying isn’t easy, but leaving seems impossible.)

In any case, Zhao’s embrace is a gentle one. Zuko gives him exactly what he wants because he doesn’t know how else to ensure it stays that way.

In hindsight, Azula could see where it had all broken down. It was as if each moment was stationary, a series of wood block paintings laid side by side in her mind.

Between the two of them, they should have been able to subdue a group that comprised of one master bender and a whole lot of dead weight. In reality, it became complicated: the earthbender was scrappy even when she couldn’t rip up the oasis to fight, calling chunks of earth from the surrounding mountainous archways as if the distance were nothing to her. The waterbender, clearly, had been studying, and fought with twice the vicious power she ever had before. To top it all off, Iroh had ruined it all by-

No. *Azula* had ruined it all. She was so eager to prey upon an enemy’s weakness, she failed to account for how it would affect her own. In the mad scramble to protect the Avatar, there was also the mad scramble not to upset the oasis, the precious spirits of Tui and La. Trying to get the upper hand, Azula had lobbed a bolt of lightning at the pond, hoping to distract the party.

Here then was where it all slowed down; where she could watch the lightning slice through the air; watch the waterbender and the earthbender and the princess turn their heads, a bouquet of horror blooming across their faces as they realized the consequences of this act, their helplessness to stop it.

And then Iroh had leapt in front of the pond.

Azula hit him with the full force of her power, unable to stop herself in the microseconds that elapsed between her initial decision and this development. Iroh absorbed her lightning as best as he could, one hand cast to the sky and spewing it upwards and away; when the flashing lights stopped, there was the distinct smell of burning flesh, and he stood tall for mere moments.

Then he crumpled, body falling limp at the mouth of the pond, not even flinching as he hit the water. Then screaming. Screaming and screaming and screaming, rending Azula’s throat like blades.

It was over. She had failed in her mission worse than she had thought possible. Her hands were now drenched in the blood of the only person who had ever really loved her.

### Text

As Yue entered the dungeons, a shiver wracked her frame. Even being used to the arctic weather, the people of the northern tribe were careful to insulate the spaces where they lived and worked. Human beings, even ice benders, can only endure so much cold before hypothermia sets in. The dungeons were kept much colder than the rest of their dwellings for the sake of punishment, and today, one would suppose she should be especially thankful for that. She had seen what their current prisoner could do at her strongest. The cold was perhaps the only thing standing between her and a face full of fire.

Yue approached the bars of Princess Azula’s cell with caution. She watched the other girl for signs of hostility, too cautious to even touch her mitten to one frozen bar if the princess so much as twitched.

But she didn’t. She didn’t even acknowledge Yue’s presence. She just did what she’d done since she’d been imprisoned here, which was lie on her cot, inert, with her back facing the bars of her cell. Her hair had come loose from its no-nonsense bun ages ago, which Yue understood to be a big deal to the people of the Fire Nation; yet the princess had let it go without so much as asking for a new ribbon to tame it with, instead hiding her eyes behind the great resulting tangle.

Enough sympathy for a villain. Yue cleared her throat, willing strength and resolve into her voice. As of late, her father had been looking to her as a more capable adult than he ever had before. She wanted to prove to him that omega or not, she could be a leader to their people. That she could interrogate the enemy princess. And so she said,

“Tell me everything you know about the invasion.”

Now, that had sounded quite imperious. Yet the only reply was the sound of her own words, echoed back at her from the icy walls of the dungeon. So she steeled herself again. “Do you hear me? I am your captor, and I asked you a question.”

More silence. The only evidence the other princess was alive was the minute rise and fall of her shoulders as she breathed.

Yue scowled. “In the very least, tell me how you found the spirit oasis!”

“Go away,” the alpha girl finally said. She spoke in such a pitiful whisper that Yue wondered if she was even talking to the right person. She had seen Azula’s fierceness first hand, the assured way she’d fought the Avatar and his friends…

&#46;..And she had also borne witness to her unravelling. Despite herself, Yue felt a twinge of pity for Azula as she remembered how she’d broken down into screaming tears following the old man’s injury. She hadn’t seemed like such a frightening monster then. She’d seemed like a scared little kid.

Yue sighed, eyes dropping to the ground. She knew what would rouse the princess from her stupor. So she said,

“Your uncle is alive.”

Suddenly the Fire Nation princess was on her feet, dashing towards the bars of her cage. Yue startled backwards out of her grasping range, cowed by the desperate look in the other girl’s eyes.

“Don’t just dangle that information in front of me like it’s nothing,” Azula said, lips curled back from her teeth like a sabermoose baring its fangs. “ *Prove it* .”

Yue composed herself, saying, “He’s alive and he’s stable, but he’s unconscious. He can’t come to see you, yet.”

Azula’s grip on the bars visibly tightened. “Then let *me* go to see *him.* ”

“You think I’d set you loose in the healing huts?” Yue asked, incredulous. “You’re out of your mind.”

Azula gritted her teeth. “It’s called *leverage,* you child. You can chain me up to take me to him - make me wear a *muzzle,* if you want - but if you let me see him, then maybe, just *maybe,* I’ll talk.”

Her condescending tone made a furious blush rise to Yue’s face. She had been *getting* there. Pakku and her father both had advised her to use General Iroh’s condition against Azula. It just seemed like an awful thing to dangle over someone’s head, Fire Nation scum or not.

Still, Yue raised her chin and said, “You’ve got it backwards. *You* talk. And if we’re happy with what you tell us, you get to see him.”

Azula narrowed her eyes. In her silence, Yue realized she was studying her, yellow eyes moving with fervor as they scanned over her face. When she’d had her fill, she smiled as if she’d seen all there was to Yue, and found it pathetically lacking. Bizarrely, the sight of Azula scheming filled Yue with relief. At least she seemed alive, this way.

“I’m not about to further humiliate myself by showing you all my cards,” Azula sniffed. “Bring me updates of my uncle’s condition, and if you can prove he’s really fine, then maybe I’ll see about rewarding you.”

Here was a girl who knew how to talk like a leader. Even as she irked Yue, she made for a fascinating subject of study. Yue held out her mittened hand, half-expecting Azula to yank her forward or squeeze her hard enough to bruise; instead, they ended up sealing their agreement with a brief clasp of the hands. Then Azula was away from the bars of her cell, her back turned to Yue, shutting her out once again.
