Becoming an omega had always meant losing familiarity with his own body. Zuko had long come to the conclusion that puberty was less a stage of growth than it was decay; where he’d been strong in childhood, following his kata daily, he found his strength waning the more he strayed from his training in the months leading up to his engagement. Seeing the soft, lean outline of his own limbs in the mirror had seemed like the worst way the transition to adulthood could manifest.

Until he got pregnant.

Weight began to sit on him in places it hadn’t before. It started in his hips, a previously unseen curvature made more pronounced, followed by what he could only describe as a *billowing* of the thighs -

Being in the first trimester, he hadn’t really gained that much weight. The change would have been imperceptible to anyone who wasn’t him. But it was his body. He knew it intimately, or he used to. Now it was changing in ways that made him sick to look at himself.

Lying in bed, running his palms over the terrible, excess flesh, Zuko dreaded how Zhao would feed into this insecurity. There was something so horrendously sensual about the shape of him, something soft and feminine in the preamble to childbirth that made him shudder down to the very bone - would Zhao be able to resist pawing at him? Would there always be hands grabbing at him, reminding him of how he was no longer the same?

It turned out to be the opposite sort of humiliation. Zhao hadn’t been kidding when he’d dreaded Zuko’s imagined weight gain; although he was now forced for the good of his heir to let Zuko eat his fill at dinner, every beneficent smile was paired with a steel eye that lanced the places where he was growing out of control. Zhao no longer hid from him on the edges of the marital bed, but he didn’t embrace him, either. Always that telling look, head to toe, then a chaste kiss on the forehead: Good night. Rest well.

Zuko couldn’t even rest when there *wasn’t* the discomfort of life growing inside him, let alone now. Kept awake at hellish hours by nausea, he took to haunting the halls at night, keeping his footsteps silent with the concentration of someone who knew his physical safety depended on it. To his credit, he never woke Zhao.

He always felt the sickest after dinner, a potent mix of anxiety and genuine, hormonal discord propelling him across the darkened estate to the separate building where they kept the toilets. (A journey made all the more difficult by his firebending problem. When on the second night he failed to light his lantern on his own, he scoured the kitchen for matches, and stole what must have been Rio’s stash.)

One night, as Zuko was trudging back into the house with a sour taste in the back of his throat, he saw a ray of light spilling from a crack in the tigermonkey room’s doorway. He was careful to keep quiet as he passed it by, not wanting to disturb anyone inside. Before he could take to the stairs, this is what he heard:

“-supportive of you, for the record, even if you’ve sided with a vicious autocrat. I'm glad you’ve found your purpose again,” said a grating voice. Definitely Yan.

Then came the toneless scoff of the oldest brother. “Don’t change the subject.”

“I’m not! I feel like I’ve been telling you for years that I’m happy to be the one to hold down the fort if you want to actually *live* your life again,” Yan said. “You’re not obligated to babysit us.”

“Evidently I *am* , given how you’re flaunting your bullshit in Zhao’s face,” Wei hissed. “He may not know Kirachu’s political climate as well as you or I, but he’s going to catch onto what you’re involved in sooner or later.”

“Tch. I’m not scared of *Zhao* .”

“Maybe not,” Wei conceded. “But he always has something to prove, so I can guarantee he won’t let you off as easily as I am now.”

A noise of frustration, perhaps a curse garbled below audible levels. “Haven’t you listened to Ama? I’m too *terminally lazy* to be up to anything.”

The creak of wood, as if someone had stood from a chair. Fearful of being caught like a child out of bed late, Zuko dashed up the stairs and back into his room. Once the door was shut behind him, he leaned with his ear pressed against it, waiting and listening.

There was the unmistakable creak of light footsteps on the stairs. He could hear the *tamp, tamp,* *tamp* of a purposeful approach just outside his door.

Silence again. It went on so long that Zuko began to wonder if he had imagined that pursuit, if Wei and Yan had remained seated in the tigermonkey room, if perhaps the old house merely creaked and groaned at random.

But then there they were again. Slow, but purposeful. The light *tamp,* *tamp, tamp* of a single set of footsteps leading away from the door. The cadence was unbroken, purposeful, lacking the punctuation of a thudding cane.

---

Rio stood by his master’s side with an enormous armful of flowers and a nose that had turned redder than a war banner. He sniffed every few seconds, tilting his head back to keep from inhaling the pollen or dripping all over the flowers. Zuko felt terribly sorry watching him suffer, and entreated him with hands outstretched: “Could I hold those for you…?”

Although the question was directed at Rio himself, Ama was the one to wave it away, eyes fixed on the vase of flowers before him. “He’s fine, Prince Zuko. Besides, you’re pregnant.” He plucked a flower from Rio’s arms and went about adding it to his arrangement.

Zuko raised a brow. “Is it bad to breathe in pollen when you’re pregnant, or…?”

“Maybe, maybe not,” Ama replied, cheerily. “You simply don’t have to do *anything* you don’t want to do when you’re pregnant. Your body is already doing such terrible things to you, you might as well have everything else your way. Hold your arms out, Rio, so I can more easily reach the peonies, they’re all bunched up against your chest.”

“It’s not that bad, yet,” Zuko mumbled, hand reflexively going to his stomach.

“Oh, give it time! It’ll get there.” Ama placed a pink peony amongst a nest of fire lilies. “And to think that when it’s all over, you’ll do it again. Funny how we subject ourselves to this torture, but it’s in our biology. You can’t change that.”

Zuko was still coming to terms with the one child. “I don’t know about that. I didn’t come from a large family myself, so…”

“You don’t want to gamble on just the one baby, though,” Ama said. “Considering the redundancy, *I* should have, but heat does ridiculous things to your critical-thinking skills.”

Zuko frowned at the slight, clearly directed towards Yan. Having only one child would certainly prevent the chance that more siblings would be brought into the world only to be pitted against each other. No heartbreak over favorites when there was just the one to favor.

“It’s not like you *knew* you’d have two alphas,” Zuko pointed out.

“Yes, I did,” Ama insisted, adding another bundle of flowers to the arrangement. “Well, at least I knew Zhao was going to be an alpha.”

“Yeah, but you didn’t really *know* .”

Ama huffed. “I did so. Agni himself gave me that vision. I didn’t *guess* that Zhao would be what he was, I *knew* .”

“Then what about Yan?” Zuko asked. “Did you know about him ahead of time, too?”

Ama sighed, taking another flower from the miserable Rio. “There was no such premonition for Yan. I didn’t even know if the pregnancy would last, it went so roughly. If I had to guess what I’d end up with based on family history, my mother had four girls and me, one beta and four omegas… but I *clearly* did not take after her. Maybe if I knew her lineage a little better, or my father’s, I’d see where this wellspring came from...” His ministrations slowed as he considered the details. “Do you have any aunts and uncles you can look to, Prince Zuko? Maternal grandparents?”

“I don’t know much about my mother’s side,” Zuko mused. “It’s probably bad to admit, but I don’t even know if she had siblings.” She would have mentioned them, wouldn’t she?

Ama glanced up from the thicket of vibrant petals. “You know, there wasn’t much the public knew about Lady Ursa, either… We all thought your father would be wedded to a noble, someone of standing, and there were many people his age who were interested… but then your mother seemed to come from nowhere.”

Zuko felt a twinge of something akin to annoyance. It was strong enough it inspired him to defend his mother’s right to her title, saying, “She was part of Avatar Roku’s bloodline. That’s why she was chosen for my father.”

Ama’s hand fluttered to his chest. “Spirits. That’s certainly difficult to compete with. I suppose that explains Princess Azula’s incredible prowess. With a pedigree like *that,* perhaps your little one will make for a master lightning-bender, too, someday.”

Zuko’s face burned; he knew it was foolish to expect to be mentioned in the same breath as an alpha sibling, but it still hurt, to be reduced to the vessel for *next time,* lacking potential otherwise.

Ama changed the subject, eyes once again on his arrangement. “Speaking of Avatars. What was it Zhao was so upset about, this morning?”

Zuko breathed through his teeth. “The Avatar hasn’t been spotted in upwards of a month. At first they thought he was merely being kept safe, but why exclude an asset like that from battle? They’re beginning to worry he’s left the North Pole altogether.”

“Don’t they have a fleet of warships up there? How could he have snuck past them all?”

Although pulled from the unscholarly source that was *Caress of the Moon Spirit* , Zuko held fiercely to the image of Agna Qel’a in his mind’s eye: an icy fortress surrounded on all sides by tundra. To a foreigner, the blizzards, the icy black waters, and the unforgiving landscape would seem like a deathtrap; but to someone who knew those conditions intimately, was there a chance to help the Avatar escape without a hitch?

In secret, Zuko hoped so. Out loud, he said, “I’m sure it’s a rumor. And even if it’s true, it’s not as though the sole purpose of the invasion was to capture the Avatar. Your son will still go down in history.”

Ama scoffed. “I’m certain of *that* . It was all part of the vision, after all.” He plucked a dead leaf from one of the stems in front of him to punctuate his point.

---

Wei stood on the threshold of the tigermonkey room, a splotch of black in an otherwise colorful landscape. His robes and fastidiously tied hair were set in monochrome against his pallid complexion. There was a coldness about him, brought about by his utter lack of expression, and when he spoke, it was with about as much gusto as a corpse:

“Ozai just requested that I set out to the colonies in search of his daughter.”

Zhao glanced up from the document he’d been reading, fighting to keep his expression as equally unmoving as his older brother’s. “Oh,” he said. “What a shame it’s come to this.”

“I don’t think it’s a shame,” Wei responded, flatly. “We have no reason to believe she has come under harm.”

All the while fixing him with that burrowing gaze. Zhao shifted. Not uncomfortably - in a normal and unsuspicious way, he shifted his weight.

“But if you’re being called in, I suppose that means Iroh couldn’t find her?”

“Iroh has not reached out to the palace in as long as Azula. I have been tasked with finding them both.” Wei paused. “Although there is less urgency to *his* recovery.”

The oldest brother gave nothing away. His eyes did have that impersonal cast these days, not yellow like a living fire, but yellow like fire reflected from the polished face of metal.

Eventually Wei had had enough of watching his younger brother squirm. He turned his gaze to the reeds painted on the walls and said, “Of course. While I’d like to help, I did tell Ozai my stunted career has left me lacking in connections outside the Fire Nation. I’m more useful here, in Kirachu.”

“Spying on me?” Zhao drawled.

Wei didn’t respond to the accusation. Instead he said, “You have contacts in the colonies, don’t you, Zhao? Perhaps you could look into it.”

“If I have time. Running an island keeps me busy,” Zhao replied. He reached over to pick up a brush and dip it in the ink stick, more to make a point than anything. He didn’t have anything to write, but he wanted his brother to think he was busy and to leave him the hell alone.

Wei seemed to take the hint, although he couldn’t resist one last, ominous comment. “Consider this a courtesy. Or a warning - whichever you like.”

It was a tidy sign-off, and would have made him look quite formidable, had he not run straight into Zuko on the way out of the room. The omega balked at the sight of the oldest and most inscrutable of the brothers, before he gathered himself, bobbing his head in a curt bow. “Sorry, I wasn’t looking where I was going.”

“Were you listening outside the door?” Wei asked.

Zuko blinked, confused. “No, I only just entered the hall.”

“Not now,” said Wei. “Were you listening outside the door last night?”

Zuko didn’t so much as twitch a lip, but he didn’t need to; his face went white as death. Wei saw his guilt, and looked upon it with an expression that reminded Zuko unnervingly of his father.

“I - didn’t mean to,” Zuko managed, at last. “I didn’t really understand anything I heard, anyway.”

Wei seemed unmoved by this explanation. “There are so few of us in this house, Prince Zuko. We should do what we can to get along.”

He surged forward, so Zuko had to flatten himself against the wall to avoid being knocked against it. At times like these, Zuko still felt like a visitor, skirting away from the true masters of the house. He wondered when that feeling would finally disappear.

From the open doorway, Zhao sighed. “Charming, isn’t he? I swear he wasn’t always like that.” Gripping the doorjamb, he peered down at his spouse, still clinging to the wall. “Do you need me for something?”

“Yes.” Zuko straightened himself. “Ama and I wanted to head into town for a few things tomorrow. We’ll need funds.”

He resisted the *If that’s alright with you* , trying not to so obviously beg for the right to go. Although he regretted his reticence when Zhao took the time to mull it over; Zuko could imagine him coming up with any number of excuses to keep him sequestered away. Zuko had grown to like Ama, but the thought of another day trapped inside with him, talking non-stop about the impending baby, was too dreadful to bear. Even if all they would do in the village was talk about the baby while they shopped, Zuko needed *some* outlet, *some* change of scenery to cushion the awful drudgery of his daily life.

So he crumbled. “Are you fine with us going on our own? I could ask one of the gate guards to accompany us.”

“You don’t need to resort to making me jealous for not answering right away,” Zhao sighed. “No, guards aren’t necessary. I was just wondering how much I was willing to spare; if you come inside, I’ll write you a money order you can cash in town.”

Apparently Zhao hadn’t let go of his irrational hatred of guards. Before Zuko could retort that he had no intent to slight Zhao, he was waved into the room. He followed his husband over to the large desk in the back corner, where he proceeded to write up a money order, signing and stamping it so the bank tellers knew they weren’t a pair of errant omegas trying to steal from the family vault. Zuko watched Zhao toss the stamp he’d used into a drawer, which he then locked.

When the money order was finally passed over the desk, Zuko was surprised at the relief he felt, like he was holding the paper equivalent of freedom. (Was it enough to pay for a seat on the next boat out of Kirachu? A place to stay the night? A start to a new life? He was so disconnected from the real cost of things, but his gut told him no.)

“Thank you,” he murmured. He felt pathetic for being excited about a quick trip to town, but there was so little to ever look forward to in Kirachu. Hopefully this could break the monotony.

---

The next morning, Zuko awoke to find the dragon moose stables empty. At a loss, he circled the grounds three times, but there was nothing to find. There were usually three carriages and just enough dragon mooses to pull the lot of them - today, though, they were all gone. All that was left were the tracks leading out of the front gate.

“How odd,” Ama said, when Zuko finally came back inside and explained the circumstances. “They said they’d leave a spare carriage, but they must’ve forgotten. I suppose we could wait a few hours, see if someone comes back.”

Two hours crawled by at an excruciating pace, during which Zuko ruminated. Each carriage needed two dragon moose to pull it. Yan had to take a carriage because it was easier on his leg. The other brothers had fewer excuses; the family owned enough dragon moose that both of them could have ridden into town and still spared a means for Zuko and Ama to leave. But that was just it: today Zuko finally had a chance to get out of the house, which meant something had to go wrong. Surely this was all Zhao’s fault; surely he had taken a carriage just to spite him. Had Zuko not thanked him for the money with enough reverence in his voice? Had the mention of the guards made him so furious he had to issue a punishment? Or was it merely fun for him to know Zuko was suffering, not just from carrying his spawn, but by having his few pleasures taken away?

By lunch, the yard was still empty. “What should we do?” Zuko asked Ama, for maybe the third time that day.

The older omega didn’t seem to think this was a crisis. He cast an almost bored glance out the window where Zuko was looking. “Perhaps we won’t go at all today. Truth be told, I’m not feeling all that well, so it’s probably for the best.”

Zuko stared forlornly out the window at the stables. Even knowing they were empty, he felt the compulsion to get up and look again, as if a dragon moose was something easily lost behind a bag of grain. “It’s just such a shame…”

“The village will still be there tomorrow,” Ama said, a slight scold to his tone. “Besides, we can have a nice day right here. We haven’t even talked about what you’re going to name the baby! Now, my husband’s father’s name was Xunzi, and I always thought that was such a stately name for a man...”

Zuko opened his mouth to respond, but he couldn’t make a sound. It was like the air was being syphoned from the room. He could feel the urge to pant coming on, to pull as much oxygen as he could into the shallow space in his chest, but if he panted he was going to go into a full panic attack. He clenched his jaw shut, only to feel as though he was suffocating.

Whether it was on his husband’s cruel whim or due to the carelessness of one of his brothers-in-law, Zuko was confined. He was confined yet again, and after days and days and days of just the same, talking about babies and watching his body transmogrify beyond his control, he was about to have *more* of the same, as he would tomorrow, and the day after that, until finally the baby arrived, and if he thought the terrible hollow of *this life* wasn’t bad enough-

“I’m walking,” said Zuko.

Ama didn’t even look up from his embroidery. “What was that, my prince?”

“I’m walking to the village,” Zuko repeated.

The needle slowed mid-air. “The village is an hour’s walk away, at least.”

“I can do that,” Zuko said. He used to run a few miles every day when he was training with Iroh. Even if he was out of practice, it wouldn’t be impossible.

Ama glanced up from the divan. Even without moving a muscle in his face, Zuko could see the judgement in his stare. “...And you’re thinking about the walk home, as well? Back up the mountain?”

Zuko shrugged. “I could use the exercise.” If he didn’t leave the estate, he was going to fully lose his mind. There was nothing, absolutely nothing Ama could say to him to convince him to stay, short of informing him that man-eating tigermonkeys were, in fact, endemic to the jungles surrounding the estate.

And Ama seemed to pick up on this. He turned away from Zuko’s desperation to resume his needlepoint. “Alright, my prince. Please do not feel too embarrassed to turn around and come back home if you find you can’t make it down the mountain, after all.”

---

The sun sat at its zenith for the hottest hour of the day. In retrospect, Zuko probably should have waited for it to cool down before walking to the village, but once he’d made up his mind, he couldn’t be kept for a moment longer.

There was something surreal in his march across the estate, like it was happening to someone he was watching from afar. He felt this even as he passed through the front gates, then again as he broke free of the jungle and came onto the wide dirt road winding around the mountain.

It didn’t feel real until about twenty minutes in, when Zuko turned to look out over the edge of the mountain and saw the village in the distance. He could just make out the thatched roofs of buildings, but no people. He cast his gaze upwards, upon the clear blue sky, and formed a private smile.

So he wasn’t helpless. He had two fully-functioning legs, and they took him the whole way down the mountain. He was panting by the time he’d reached the bottom, and absolutely drenched with sweat; once he stopped, he raked his fingers up from the base of his neck through his hair, letting as much air as possible get through the sweaty strands.

What a burden. In hot weather like this, he often wished he could take a knife to his hair, slice it to the quick, but of course that was only a fantasy. It was unseemly for anyone in the Fire Nation, especially an omega, to wear their hair so short. He might as well sever a limb, for the stares it would earn him. (To think he’d worried Zhao found him ugly just for gaining a little weight… If he so much as cut his hair above his waist, Zhao would *certainly* lose it.)

Setting out into the village, he couldn’t believe he’d looked at it with such apprehension when they first arrived in Kirachu. Now it was positively vibrant, bursting at the seams with life. People he didn’t even know were wishing him a good morning before telling him to get the hell out of the way. It seemed everyone was in a hurry, although to go where, he hadn’t the faintest clue; eager to savor his day in the village, he followed the flow of the crowd and soon ended up in an open-air market.

It wasn’t much, compared to the treasures of the capital. It was a lot of fruit, and kitschy things, the sort of rough hewn jewelry and quaint animal carvings commonly foisted upon tourists. But it was exciting when compared to the absolute nothing of his daily life. He drifted from table to table, giving apologetic nods and slipping into the crowd when merchants made eye contact with him and dialed up the aggressive requests to come, buy, please!

Eventually he came upon a table that was less intimidating, as it wasn’t surrounded by an enormous crowd. Once he got close, he could see why; it was draped high with fine fabrics, the sort an ordinary person would be unlikely to afford themselves. Although he knew very little about how to tell the quality of fabric, he could read a price tag, and he could see the shimmer of light that belied this as silk, or an imitation close to it. Would it be rude to touch it and see? This was why Ama had wanted to come to the village in the first place. Perhaps Zuko should’ve asked him more about what he was looking for, so he could pick it up in apology for storming off in the middle of the day… but then, that would have required him to remember to bring the money order along.

Zuko was so lost in thought that he didn’t notice the piercing look the table’s owner had fixed him with. When he finally looked up, he was too enraptured to flit away from the table, for there was a male omega with his hair shorn as short as a child’s. It wasn’t even long enough to permit a topknot. Zuko immediately wondered if he had been dishonored in some way.

Once their eyes met, the other man’s gaze seemed to intensify. He was older than Zuko, in his late twenties, perhaps early thirties. It wasn’t as obvious in the face; he had large, almost boyish eyes, but his neck and hands showed the slightest signs of age.

“Are you Prince Zuko?” the omega asked, in a clear, tenor voice.

He was at a loss for how this stranger had identified him, until he remembered the golden flame that marked him as a prince. He’d continued to wear it even in isolation, just as he never went without his topknot. It was a tradition so ingrained he’d forgotten it. The people of Kirachu hadn’t much helped him remember, either; plenty of strangers had bumped into him today, with plenty more blocking his path or demanding he move out of theirs. He wasn’t exactly getting the princely treatment.

“Yes,” Zuko confirmed, taken aback when the omega’s eyes immediately narrowed.

“So you’re married to the governor, *Zhao* . How is that?” Spoken as if he couldn’t bear to keep the words in his mouth any longer, bitter as they were.

His hostility threw Zuko. Rather than answer the question, he asked, “Who are you?” He hadn’t even considered that it may not be worth it to engage this person. For all he knew, he was about to be plunged into the petty politics of Kirachu.

The omega straightened himself. “Toru Kanegawa. Have you heard of me?”

Zuko searched his memory. There was something familiar about the name, but he couldn’t place exactly what. Perhaps he was a well-known tailor, in these parts. “I’m sorry, I don’t think I have.”

The brusque stranger breathed very hard through his nose. “When I was a teenager, I worked for the family. I was Ama’s personal servant.”

Suddenly, it clicked into place. A former servant. A person who, upon discovering Zuko’s identity, noted his marriage to Zhao with nothing less than open disgust. Zuko realized that he was standing in front of his husband’s first love, the omega he’d impregnated as a teenager, the same one his parents had forbidden him from marrying.

Zuko was momentarily speechless. Had this man stayed this close to the family’s Kirachu home this whole time? How had he been able to bear Zhao’s return to the island? How deeply did his chest ache at the sight of him?

“I - I’m sorry,” Zuko managed, hand rising to his neck as if to cover his mating mark. “I’m sure you hate seeing me here. I should go. Or buy something. But I don’t have any money - still, next time I could buy something, if you think that seems right?”

Toru stared at him as though he was speaking in tongues. Zuko amended: “I feel as though I owe you.”

At that, Toru’s nose crinkled. “I don’t have anything against *you* .”

“You don’t have to lie,” Zuko said. “I’d be upset if I ran into my ex’s new husband.” Spirits. What would he do if Mai got married? The thought made his stomach lurch. Was that how she’d felt, the entire time she was at his wedding? Or did normal people let their feelings go and move on?

Despite his insistence that he didn’t hate Zuko, Toru’s gaze sharpened like he very much wanted to see the other side of his skull. “Prince Zuko. Are you under the impression that your husband and I-” he paused, lip convulsing, “- *dated?* ”

“I don’t know the full story, but I-”

“You clearly don’t,” Toru interrupted. “Zhao wasn’t my boyfriend. He *raped* me.”

Zuko flinched from the word as if it was a knife held to his throat. He wasn’t given a chance to recover. Mouth jagged, Toru said, “He didn’t even have the mercy to do it only once. It didn’t stop until it became literally impossible to hide what was going on.”

His hand went subconsciously to his stomach, reminding Zuko of the child that had been lost. Or perhaps “child” was the wrong word - the *potential* child. The *potential* older sibling of the child Zuko carried now. He felt a strange guilt towards it, despite the fact this had all happened years ago, without his involvement. Or maybe guilt wasn’t quite it - there was something that scraped at Zuko, leaving his chest raw and sore.

With a start, he realized it was jealousy. He was jealous of Toru’s loss the way a starving man was jealous to see his master’s plate piled high with food. He made himself swallow the terrible feeling before he spoke: “Why didn’t you tell anyone sooner, get help?”

The question seemed to offend Toru. “You think anyone in that house was interested in helping me?”

“Surely Ama-”

Toru cut him off by barking the name: “Ama! He was the worst of them, next to his awful son! He *terrorized* me when he found out, saying all this shit to anyone who would listen about how I was an opportunistic gold digger, preying upon noble teenagers-” Toru bristled at the memory, momentarily mute with anger. “Which, for the record, I was only a couple years older, and Zhao *still* overpowered me, easily! But that isn’t the version that gets told.”

Toru blinked, and all at once he was composed. Not calm - but he was held together by a threadbare composure.

“I’m sorry. Was that shocking?” In the depths of his flattened gaze was a simmering fury. Zuko recognized the look; he’d seen it in the mirror every day for the last two years. “I hope it was shocking. I hope he treats someone as highborn as you more carefully than he did me. It doesn’t make me any less angry about what happened. But if it ended with me-” He swallowed. “I think I can stop wishing Zhao dead if it ended with me.”

Zuko stood as still as a prey animal trying to escape notice, heart hammering inside his chest. He didn’t want to contend with this. He had just made peace with his lot, and now this stranger was ruining all of that. He was just coming to terms with the fact he was having Zhao’s child, just letting himself believe that the worst of it was over, that the rest of his life would be drudgery but not torture.

Some of the fire seemed to be extinguished in the seconds Zuko spent debating his reply; Toru’s shoulders slumped as he spoke. “I’m sorry if I startled you, my prince. I suppose I’ve been holding all of that in for a while.” Something wry tugged at the corner of his mouth. “Maybe I thought it would magically fix everything if I got to yell at someone. Or maybe I just wanted to warn the next closest omega.”

“I don’t need your warning,” Zuko managed, voice torn between anguish and anger. “You knew him a long time ago. He’s a completely different person now.” One who had promised to change.

For a moment Toru stared at him without answering. With each passing second, Zuko feared the hateful response that might fly from this stranger’s mouth. Toru’s eyes kept moving over his face, like there was something tangible he could find there.

Then Toru asked, “Does he find every excuse he can to touch your throat?”

“Wh-what?”

He amended: “Do you wonder why he finds every excuse he can to touch your throat? Or do you already know? Has he already choked you?”

Rage tore its way through Zuko’s body at such a fearful speed, he expected his fire to come back in excess, spewing from his mouth. As it was, all that made it past his lips was the furious shout: “ *Fuck you!* ”

Zuko turned on his heel and headed blindly into the village streets. He half-expected this angry stranger, this person his husband had raped over and over again, to follow him down the street, shouting abuse after him. He would’ve had every right to, but he didn’t. It was Zuko alone to contend with the awful truth.

There was that siphoning sensation again. No longer content to burn his lungs, it now glittered at the corners of his vision. Hearing a smattering of laughter from nearby strangers, Zuko knew he needed to be alone before he fell apart. He ducked onto a street that looked less crowded, then another, then another, not paying attention to where he was going so much as he was doggedly seeking privacy wherever he could find it.

When he finally stopped running, only one thought managed to push its way to the forefront of his dizzied mind: *I didn’t learn anything new* . Perhaps this was somewhat new information about Ama (or was it? Had he already seen that glint of fangs before?), but this was the same thing it always was with Zhao. Another terrible secret, another terrible revelation.

Only Zuko couldn’t afford to doubt Zhao anymore. They were about to raise a child together. A potential Fire Lord.

Zuko resisted the urge to sink to the ground, instead leaning all his weight against the nearest wall. He could imagine how he looked. Disheveled from the walk to the village, eyes wild from the revelation. Aloki would spit at the sight of him, but he wasn’t around. So for a few moments, Zuko allowed himself to unravel.

---

Eventually Zuko gathered himself enough that he was ready to leave the village. But in his blind panic, he hadn’t paid much attention to the way he came. He knew to head towards the mountain, yet with every turn he took, he only seemed to get more lost, unsure where on earth the entry to the road back up to the estate could possibly be.

The stench of strange alphas hit him before he even saw them. He had stopped to rest by a longer, wider wood hut, and now turned around to find that he was surrounded on all sides by strangers. Two men and a woman. Each eyed him like he was a ripped bag of gold coins lying prone in the street. He glanced behind him, hoping to see movement inside the hut, but the windows were all boarded over.

“Need help finding something?” asked the closest stranger, hair pulled into a ratty phoenix tail. Even as he spoke, the other two closed in, further blocking Zuko’s escape options.

The young prince glared at them, holding himself tall. “I was just looking for my husband. Maybe you’ve heard of him.”

At least one snuck a surreptitious glance at the golden flame in his hair. But the one with the phoenix tail, their designated speaker, only smiled. “You must’ve been looking for a while. We’ve seen you running around half the day, not a guard in sight. Surely you know it’s dangerous to go out alone?”

“If you’re looking to rob me, you’re out of luck,” Zuko scoffed, sounding braver than he felt. “I don’t have any money. So you might as well leave me alone.”

The woman cocked her head, then looked at their leader, as if Zuko wasn’t even worth addressing directly. She said, “What do you think the dissidents will pay, for the chance to hold the governor’s mate hostage?”

Phoenix tail scratched his chin, pretending to consider. “I wonder if they’ll even ransom him. Things are really heating up now; they might torture him to death to teach Zhao a lesson.”

A thrill of fear went through Zuko’s chest at the mention of the growing unrest in Kirachu. He hadn’t even considered the danger this might pose when he’d come to the village today; he’d assumed, perhaps foolishly, that the anti-crown sentiment was directed mostly at his father.

Still, this told him that it was now or never. Zuko planted his feet firmly into the ground as he concentrated on that inner spark. He imagined it running through his body to the tips of his fingers.

“Get back!” he shouted in his most threatening voice. Something flashed in each of their eyes, and in the split second during which Zuko raised his hands to ready an attack, they almost seemed to reconsider this gamble. Zuko held his position, praying desperately for protection.

No fire came. As the seconds ticked by and nothing happened, the strangers allowed themselves to chuckle at his misfortune.

“Here,” said the leader. “Try it like *this* .”

And instantly the alpha’s fist was encircled with flame. Teeth gritted, arms still raised in defense, Zuko took a step back, then another as the strangers drew near.

“C’mon,” drawled the other man, “don’t make a whole scene. Just come along with us nicely.”

The leader leered. “We don’t want to burn your pretty little face off.”

“I agree,” said a new voice. “It seems totally unnecessary to burn anybody right now!”

Trading confused frowns, the alphas turned to see that someone else had apparently joined the fray. The newcomer had a shock of dark hair and no topknot. Zuko didn’t get very long to study the newcomer’s face, still apprehensive of his aggressors, but he was youngish-looking, and wore what looked to be a naval academy uniform. Whoever he was, Zuko knew at least that this newcomer wasn’t Toru; he was much too tall.

“Fuck off, kid,” snapped Phoenix Tail. “This doesn’t concern you.” The others glared in kind. They didn’t seem threatened by the fact a member of the military was standing before them, student or not.

The smile plastered on the newcomer’s face didn’t move an inch. “On the contrary. The fact you’re harassing somebody who’s clearly defenseless concerns me quite a bit.”

A loyalist, then. No use trying to persuade him any longer. With a ferocious shout, the female alpha lobbed a handful of fire in the newcomer’s direction. He swiftly ducked out of its way, inviting yet another flaming punch from the man on his left. He was light on his feet, as if unhindered by the laws of gravity; the ends of his headband fluttered in the wind as he quick-stepped backwards, before sweeping a leg out underneath the man to his right, making him trip and fall onto his face in the dirt.

Despite it being three against one, the newcomer dodged the oncoming blows as if he knew the attackers’ every intention. Zuko supposed it had to do with how sloppily these alphas fought; they weren’t exactly master firebenders, and this man, whoever he was, was taking advantage of their poor coordination. With his quick maneuvering, he managed to turn their impulsive attacks against one another, so the leader accidentally burned the other man in their group on the shoulder. He clutched it, shouting, and stayed where he fell on his knees in the dirt. Then it was just the two willing to carry on. Their faces twisted with fury as they continued their onslaught, not at all ready to give up.

In a matter of moments, the newcomer had managed to corral the attackers, so he now stood between Zuko and the rest of the horde. In gazing upon the broad expanse of his back, Zuko was struck with the strangest feeling of deja vu. As if feeling his gaze, the newcomer glanced over his shoulder with a lopsided smile.

“Are you hurt?” he asked. There was something about the warmth in those gray eyes… Before Zuko could puzzle out what was so familiar about them, he saw over his protector’s shoulder that one of the alphas was surging towards him.

“On your right!” Zuko shouted.

With impressive dexterity, the newcomer landed a blow on the female alpha’s arm to redirect the blast of the fire away from him and Zuko. This was when Zuko realized the newcomer had spent the entire fight evading and defending; this parry was the closest this man had gotten to using physical force.

Managing to leap backwards and put some distance between himself and the female alpha, the newcomer squared his stance. The jut of his arms and legs seemed so unnatural on him that the female alpha faltered, as if unsure if he was butchering his technique, or simply on the verge of a seizure. Zuko, skin abuzz, wishing desperately he could join in the fight, found himself leaning imperceptibly towards the newcomer; if he was a bender, too, that would really add to the excitement.

With an uncomfortable grimace, the newcomer raked his hands upward through the air, bringing with them a wide enough column of dirt that the female alpha had to scramble backwards to avoid hitting her chin and breaking all her teeth.

It hadn’t looked like it’d come to him easily, but it was surprising enough of a move that it caught all of them off guard. The leader gawked a full five seconds before he pointed the newcomer’s way and screamed: “ *Earthbender!* ”

“Fuck,” said the newcomer. He grabbed Zuko by the wrist and, with a few clumsy movements, managed to drag from the ground a series of dirt-pillars meant to block their attackers’ onslaught before the two of them started booking it. He hadn’t exactly summoned walls of stone; Zuko looked over his shoulder and saw the attackers burst through the pillars in a blaze of dirt, looking pissed off.

“Did you really just *earthbend?* ” Zuko shouted as they ran.

“Yep!” said the newcomer. He didn’t even turn to face Zuko, focused on leading them down convoluted side-streets.

“You blew your cover!” Zuko shouted. If this guy was some sort of foreign rebel coming to raise hell in the Fire Nation, he’d just outed himself. “Why the *hell* would you do that?!”

Even running as they were, his rescuer replied with a booming laugh, his lung capacity a force to be reckoned with. “Well, I figured it’d be an even *bigger* blow to my cover if I bent air, so earthbending it was!”

Now it wasn’t merely the mad dash to safety stealing the breath from Zuko’s lungs. He realized now why this young man looked so familiar, and yet not - they’d met once before, but he hadn’t had hair, back then.

“Wait,” Zuko called out. “It’s *you* .”

As if in confirmation, the Avatar flashed that ever-familiar grin over his shoulder. “Yeah - you only just now figured that out?” He let out another triumphant laugh. “Sokka is going to eat his words - my disguise is *amazing* .”

Zuko balked. “What are you even *doing* here?”

“Rescuing you!” the Avatar shouted back. “C’mon - this way!”

If Zuko had thought the trip down the mountain was rough on his lungs, this was something else entirely. He was so exhausted he could barely breathe, yet the complete oxygen deprivation seemed to fill him with a lightness, a giddiness, because here was the Avatar. The Avatar was *here* , holding his hand, laughing like they were a pair of children up to no good.

They had long broken the village’s edge, and now darted towards the jungle treeline. There would be cover under the canopy of leaves, a place they could hide while they rested up. They stood panting, Zuko hunched over his knees, the Avatar flopping back against the nearest ash banana tree with arms splayed.

Eventually, Zuko gathered himself enough that he could actually get a good look at his rescuer. His eyes went to his face immediately, still not quite believing his incredible fortune, that the Avatar, the *real* Avatar, would actually manage to save him. He still had the lightest shadow of a beard, too trim to provide cover amongst Fire Nation norms.

The dark hair suited him, but it was understandable why Zuko hadn’t recognized him. The Avatar had taken pains to hide his iconic arrows from view, donning long sleeves, and tying a headband across where it dipped onto his forehead - wait, *was* that a headband, or the cloth belt from the Kirachu home guard uniforms?

Zuko’s hand shot to his mouth to hide his smile as he carried on his appraisal. There was a clear similarity between the Avatar’s physique and the tree he was leaning against: long and lean, curved like a bow. Not exactly exuding gravitas.

The Avatar caught Zuko staring and drew himself up to his full height, in a less slovenly pose. He cleared his throat, perhaps to disguise the flush of embarrassment that rose to his cheeks. Zuko found the effect humanizing.

“Are you alright?”

“I’m more than alright,” Zuko replied. “Thank you for saving me back there.”

The Avatar’s lips split into a grin. “It’s no problem! I mean, I owed you from before, right?”

Warmth spread through Zuko’s chest. Even as he had yearned for it to be true, it had seemed fruitless to hope that the Avatar had saved him for *him;* it had to be a happy accident, not a product of recognition.

And yet. “You remember me?”

“Literally how could I forget you?” asked the Avatar. “It’s not everyday someone saves my life.”

His gentle gray eyes met Zuko’s, and the young prince felt, however absurdly, like this stranger saw him more clearly than anyone else had in ages. Although improbable, fate had once again brought him face to face with the Avatar. This was Zuko’s chance to ask him all the burning questions he hadn’t been able to before, and all the others that had crowded his mind in the months since his escape.

“You have hair,” was what he blurted instead.

The Avatar’s smile rippled as he fought back laughter. “I *do* have hair.” He scratched it, as if suddenly self conscious. “Does it look okay?”

Instead of reassuring him, Zuko said, “I miss the arrow,” apparently lacking a filter today.

The Avatar heaved a gust of a sigh. “I miss it, too. It’s not exactly low profile, though, so...”

The Avatar’s grace in spite of Zuko’s fumbling replies put him at ease. There seemed no pressure to get it perfect; the airbender exuded patience, as though he would wait eons for Zuko to collect his thoughts.

“What are you doing in Kirachu?” he finally asked.

“I could ask you the same question. Needed a break from the palace?” The Avatar cast the usual wide grin Zuko’s way, but it faded, seeing how the prince’s expression clouded over.

“A few weeks after your escape, the palace was destroyed. Part of it, anyway. So we were sent here.”

“We?” the Avatar repeated, one brow raised.

Zuko chewed the inside of his cheek. “Me and my husband.”

Something unreadable flickered in the airbender’s gaze. “Makes sense!” he said, in a too-chipper voice that Zuko could have sworn bore a grating edge. “Totally makes sense you’d move here with him. That you would move together with your husband, because you’re, uh. Married.” The Avatar cleared his throat. “Well, not to brag, but I’ve mastered all the elements-”

Zuko’s lips quirked. “Are you sure about that? Remember, I *saw* you earthbending.”

The Avatar went red to the tips of his ears and laughed, “It’s more earthbending than you can do! Alright, so I’ve *dabbled* in all the other elements, and now I need to learn fire. That’s why I’m here.”

Zuko’s good humor faded quickly. “But why would you willingly come to a country where you’re public enemy number one? That’s crazy behavior!”

The Avatar met his intensity with a shrug and helpless smile. “There just aren’t that many firebending masters outside the Fire Nation.” He gestured widely. “We chose this island because we figured, y’know, It’s pretty far from the capital. I didn’t expect to run into royalty here.”

“You’re lucky it was me,” Zuko huffed.

“Right. I should be counting my blessings your sister’s not around.”

But Zuko wasn’t talking about her. If Zhao found out about the Avatar’s presence in Kirachu, he’d be positively thrilled. What incredible luck it would seem after the abject failure of the Northern campaign, to turn around and find his prey had wandered right into his own backyard!

When Zuko emerged from his troubled thoughts, he saw that the Avatar was watching him closely, head cocked.

“You wouldn’t happen to know someone who could teach me to firebend, would you?” he asked. “And when I say me, I of course don’t mean,” he gestured, vaguely, “ *the Avatar,* I mean *me,* regular old Fire Nation guy. I’m trying to do this as discreetly as possible. Hence the hair and the disguise…”

“And the earthbending in public,” Zuko teased. The Avatar scratched his neck, offering a sheepish smile in response.

Zuko sighed. “I’m sorry, but no. I don’t know the island that well. I can ask my husband’s family who here has the best reputation, if that’d help?”

“Any lead is a good lead,” said the Avatar. He lapsed into silence, his eyes moving over Zuko like he was following a rapidly moving object. But when Zuko looked down at himself, he didn’t see anything.

The Avatar chewed his lip. Then, “Alternatively. If *you* knew how to bend…?”

At first all Zuko could do was blink stupidly back at him, unable to comprehend what he was implying. When he realized that he wasn’t crazy, though, that the single most powerful entity on earth was looking at him with a semblance of hope, he felt like he had just fallen from a great and deadly height.

What a time to lose his bending.

“I’d be useless to you,” Zuko said. There was a plaintive wobble in his voice that made him feel ashamed; he looked away to gather himself, hoping he wouldn’t have to say more.

“Hey, it’s no worries,” the Avatar insisted, voice light, hands up in a gesture that echoed his sentiment. “I just thought, y’know, if you were able... But it’s fine that you can’t!”

Above them, the sun had begun to sink into an orange haze. If Zuko was going to get home before dark, he needed to leave soon. He folded his arms across his chest to ward off the imagined chill of the night air. “I better go.”

“Oh,” said the Avatar. The familiar smile was gone, now. “Well. Let me walk you home, at least.”

The idea sent a thrill of fear through Zuko. If Zhao got even the shortest glimpse of the Avatar and recognized him… “No. I’ll be fine on my own.”

“Okay.” The Avatar looked troubled, but he didn’t question Zuko’s decision. “If I wanted to see you again, how would I find you?”

It was as if he’d reached into Zuko’s heart and plucked one sweet chord; his whole chest rang with it. Face hot and avoiding his gaze, Zuko murmured, “I don’t know…”

The Avatar seemed to wilt. “I understand if you don’t want to see me again. I’m sure I only complicate things, with your family and everything, and…”

What he said wasn’t wrong, but it stirred something in Zuko, so he recovered fiercely: “You don’t understand - I *do* want to see you again. Undercover or not, I just worry it wouldn’t be safe for you to come by my home. I wouldn’t be able to live with myself if I was the reason you were endangered.”

A look of surprise crossed the Avatar’s face, before settling into something softer. He gestured towards the village and a landscape beyond that neither could see; in watching the movement of his hands, Zuko realized he was wearing gloves. More cover for the arrows.

“Starting in the village square, there’s a path down to the beach. If you walk west until you start to see volcanic rocks, you’ll eventually come upon much larger rock formations that stop you from going any further. Among these you’ll find a cave; that’s where we’ve been staying since we got here.”

Zuko self-consciously grabbed the neck of his robes. “Are you sure you want to reveal your location to me like that? You hardly know anything about me.”

A brief shrug. “I know we don’t know each other *well,* but we’ve saved each other’s lives - I think we’re beyond mere strangers, right?”

The last thing they did was trade bows. The Avatar didn’t get the hand gestures quite right at first, perhaps mimicking an old airbender custom. With a gentle, “Hold on… here,” Zuko used the excuse to touch his hands, carefully guiding them into the correct formation. They weren’t firebender warm, but there was still the promise of heat beneath the dark fabric of the gloves, a spark that seemed to prickle against his bare skin.

“Might as well blend in, right?” Zuko murmured, pulling his hands away. The Avatar didn’t reply, only nodding wide-eyed in response.

And they parted ways, Zuko up the mountain, the Avatar back towards the village. As Zuko watched the shadows of nearby trees warp and wave over the path before him, he realized there was a chance he wouldn’t be able to fulfil his pact to see the Avatar tomorrow. For all their desire to meet again, fate could just as easily intervene, driving the other man into hiding, or Zuko into isolation, or-

Or Zuko could tell someone what he’d seen today. With a few words, he could earn the love of his husband and his father tenfold. The only price would be the Avatar’s freedom. Zuko realized he should have taken better advantage of this time with the other man. He should have asked more questions, learned more about his purpose here while he had his trust. It’d be easier than forcing the truth out of him later. It’d spare him the torture.

Zuko was feeling the threads of an unnameable emotion, something that threatened to unravel him as he started the long climb to the top of the mountain. He realized he’d forgotten to ask the Avatar the most basic detail of all. He turned around, hoping he wasn’t too late -

And there was the Avatar, right where he’d left him. He stood at the base of the hill with his eyes locked on Zuko.

The young prince couldn’t help it; his lips split into a wide smile at the realization that he hadn’t lost his chance. Even from this distance, he could see the Avatar’s expression mirroring his. He cupped his hands to his face and called up to the prince: “Forgot something?”

“Yes!” Zuko shouted back. “I didn’t ask for your name!”

“Aang!”

Zuko knew as soon as he heard it wasn’t an invention, another layer of the disguise. It so perfectly suited him. Zuko cried back down the hill, “That is very much an airbender name!”

“What?” Aang called back, a hand raised to one ear.

“Your name - you’re going to need a new one while you’re here!” Zuko shouted.

Aang paused to consider his choices. Then: “I was thinking Kuzon!”

*Kuzon?* Zuko crinkled his nose. “That’s an old man’s name! It doesn’t suit you at all!”

He thought he saw the shape of a laugh in the other man’s gesture. “Well, what’s *your* name?”

“Zuko!”

The wind carried his name across the open air. He saw the moment it reached Aang’s ears, the glitter of recognition in his eyes.

“Nice to meet you, Zuko! Now stop shouting and go home!”

They waved like mad before he turned around again, the frantic departure of two schoolchildren who would see each other again after summer break, dreading their separation in the meantime. Contrary to how Zuko had worried, the walk back up the hill wasn’t a labor at all. A burst of giddy energy carried him the whole way home.

---

Azula was getting sick of the sight of her own breath. Every sigh, every scoff, every word was punctuated by a puff of vapor in mid-air. It was too cold to concentrate on her thoughts. Too cold to firebend. She was pretty sure this kind of cold counted as torture even to the tribespeople; why else was the princess so meticulously bundled up every time she came to see Azula?

And she did come to see Azula often. It was fucking annoying.

On cue, the door to the icy dungeon opened, and Azula watched as Princess Yue once again made her entrance. She looked less and less afraid every day, the little fool, no doubt using these meetings as a stepping stone for some stupid inner journey. Six more conversations with the raging fire bitch, and she’d be a worthy chieftess for her people! Or so Azula imagined. When that cool blue gaze fixed on her, it was like being doused in freezing water. It made her skin hurt.

Truth be told, Yue did not match her assumptions of what a water tribe princess should be. Azula expected a costume of bones and fur and teeth adorning a feral she-beast, but the young woman who visited her day in and day out was exceedingly composed. With her demure shyness and gentle beauty, she’d fit in shiningly amongst the omega nobility of the Fire Nation.

Even hugging her knees on the floor like a grounded toddler, Azula couldn’t resist the urge to shoot a glare at the other princess. “You might as well send in the real warriors to torture me. I’m sure they’re sick of your pet project and are just dying to flay me alive.”

“Maybe in your country, you do that to prisoners. We don’t do that here,” Yue insisted. Her words weren’t enough to distract from the fact she’d given the barest flinch of disgust at the thought. Weakling.

Azula rolled her eyes. “Seems like a missed opportunity to me. You could get creative with all the options ice bending offers; just think what sorts of classified information I might confess if you made me walk barefoot over thousands of tiny, freezing needles!”

Rather than flinching or fretting, Yue ignored the bait, drawing closer to the bars of Azula’s cell. The alpha pondered the length of chain tethering her ankle to the wall; it would be easy to lunge for the bars, grab a hank of hair, but she’d have to time it right. Meanwhile, the other young woman was kneeling down to her level, fixing her with that gaze that was as blue as spoiled ginger.

Smell didn’t exactly thrive in this arid, freezing environment, but that didn’t stop Azula from catching the faintest whiff of something delicate and omega. Interesting, to catch it after all this time; Azula imagined Yue, in all her virginal innocence, had been struck by her proximity to true alpha virility. She was slick enough to scent, thighs quivering at the very thought of how the Fire Nation princess would ravage her, should she be let loose from her chains. How frightening to entertain, and yet so tempting! Perhaps she fantasized about giving Azula a key while she laid back in her royal igloo at night. Azula pictured her fondling herself through the many layers of fur, too inexperienced to even touch her bare pussy.

Yue fixed her with a damnably tender look, unaware of her prisoner’s disgusting machinations. “The healers say your uncle is coming along nicely. Any day now, and he should be waking up.”

Every lascivious feeling Azula ever had left her body at once, dashed away like smoke in a vacuum. What rushed to fill that empty space was anger.

“You keep *saying* that,” she snapped. “But if he was coming along, wouldn’t he be awake by now? How long can he possibly stay under before he’s-?”

A humiliation, how her lip wobbled, forcing her to shut her mouth against it. She whipped around to face the wall, feeling the tears at the corners of her eyes already starting to freeze. A mercy; they wouldn’t leave tracks on her face.

“I know you’re worried about him,” Yue said, and she was right. She had watched Azula in her utmost humiliation, screaming like a fucking baby in anguish after her uncle’s mis-

No. After her own, *stupid* mistake.

“Well, thanks for the lack of news, as usual,” said Azula flippantly. “You can leave, now.”

After a few minutes where she’d stayed stubbornly facing the wall, she didn’t hear movement. She sighed loudly to herself. “I’m *serious* . I know that somewhere in your hopeful, naive little heart you think that if you just come here and talk to me enough, treat me like a real *person* , I’ll become oh so nice and accommodating, maybe switch sides. It’s not going to happen, though, so you might as well save your breath.”

She wondered what sort of face Yue was making. If her painted lips were fixed in a pout, or if she was merely watching Azula with that watery gaze.

“I have a question,” said Yue.

“I don’t want to give an answer,” Azula quipped. “But I’m sure you’ll ask, anyway.”

She swore she heard Yue scoff. “Do you seriously think I want to be your friend after everything your people have done to mine? Have done to the *entire world?* ”

Azula paused to think of a response. In her silence, Yue continued: “Are you *that* narcissistic? Or do you just think that lowly of me?”

“Well-”

“I’m not here to be your friend,” Yue interrupted. “I’m here to figure out how you found the spirit oasis, how you got in, and how to ensure that never happens again.”

Again, the mention of that place where they had met, the “Spirit Oasis.” Azula thought back to that day, to the explanation she had overheard this girl giving the Avatar’s party. It was clearly a delicate, sacred space, but Azula hadn’t heard of it before that moment. Her only goal had been to find her target and take him out. Yet the fact she’d found it had clearly rankled Yue.

A slow, predatory smile stretched Azula’s lips. “Oh… you’re scared that there are hundreds of firebenders just waiting to use the same path as me. If only you knew where I got in, perhaps you could fortify your defenses, but alas...”

She turned around, eager to see the other princess’s reaction. A wrinkle of annoyance appeared on the ice princess’s pretty little face, rendering it no less pretty or little.

“Fine, yes!” Yue huffed. “Just tell me how you got in, already!”

Azula sighed, inspecting her nails. “I wasn’t going on any intel, or whatever you may think. *I* found a natural vulnerability in your walls, then *I* followed the trail the Avatar’s incredibly loud friends were leaving.” She chucked to herself for the effect. “The truth is I came in without even planning ahead, and your defenses were shoddy enough that it didn’t matter.”

She was acting cool, now, but she remembered her own desperation from the moment they departed the Earth Kingdom to the moment she was hiding herself away in the spirit oasis. (“ *I* *can’t let Zhao get to the Avatar first, Uncle. Not after he tried to kill me. I want to rip this victory* *right out from under him, just like he did to me back at the capital!”)* It had not been easy to find the way in that she had. She had torn through the snow with the same confidence that prey, cornered, snaps and bites at a predator that far outmatches it. There was simply nothing else she could do.

“Oh,” Yue said, pulling Azula out of her thoughts. She was probably devastated to think their defenses could be so easily toppled. How mortifying for her to be outdone by Azula this way! How-

“Thanks for finally cooperating,” Yue said. Her smile wasn’t anywhere near mocking enough. It was tiny and genuine, emanating a warmth that made Azula want to lean towards her.

So she leaned away, and scoffed, “It’s a pittance. One small morsel to convince you to let me see my uncle.” She huffed, crossing her arms over chest. “There won’t be any others if you continue to drag your feet.”

To her absolute chagrin, Yue *giggled* . “Whatever you say, Azula. I’ll see you tomorrow.” One last smile, cast from beneath thick lashes, and she was gone, footsteps trailing up the dungeon steps. Azula did not crane her neck to watch her go.
