## Chapter 33

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Zuko meets the Avatar's companions.

### Text

The first thing Zuko did when he got home from the village, before he even stopped to say hello to Ama, was bathe. He told himself he wasn’t delaying the inevitable, even as he dallied at the well, and then took his time in the warm water of the baths, scrubbing until his limbs turned raw and pink. He wasn’t washing away the evidence of the Avatar’s visit, because he fully intended to tell someone what he saw. He just needed the chance to scrub away the day’s exertions.

Once he finally returned to the main house, flushed from the steam, hair dripping wet, Ama only laughed briefly at his need to tidy up. “My prince, I *am* impressed you managed to walk all the way to town, but you do know that level of exercise is frowned upon when you’re pregnant? No, don’t fret, it was just the once, after all. It shouldn’t hurt if you don’t make a habit of it.”

That was the last he mentioned it; he didn’t ask what Zuko had done in the village, and Zuko didn’t volunteer any information. By the time Zhao arrived home, Zuko’s hair had dried, as if the last traces of his meeting evaporated all on their own.

Zuko truly meant to tell Zhao about the Avatar. He had made the decision several times while walking up the mountain, and again while lying in the bath, and again as he toiled away the hours awaiting Zhao’s return. He considered it now, as Zhao walked in the door, and later, when they sat down for dinner, and later still, when they finally laid down in bed together.

&#46;..And every time, Zuko argued himself out of it. Despite his many failings, despite how he’d been taught his sense of judgement would always be inferior to that of his father and husband and sister, his silence came down to two inarguable facts: the first was that, for years, Ozai had tasked Zuko with winnowing information from men and women of the royal court. This belied a certain level of skill even his father couldn’t deny. The second was that Zuko had spent just as long gathering information on the Avatar. While Zuko was no bending prodigy, no military genius, he an irrefutable expert on the Avatar, to the point that Zhao had even admitted to using his findings to justify a renewed search for him at the North Pole. Thus, armed with these skills, Zuko decided to show his family his full worth by figuring out the Avatar’s plans before they did.

See, Zuko was well on his way to earning the Avatar’s trust. He could ask him any number of questions, get to know his secrets, all without laying down a single torture implement. The others would absolutely *rush* to torture - but the Avatar was too extraordinary to break immediately! It’d be weeks, maybe even months before they got anything out of him. And in the end, what would they have? Months wasted, blood wasted, tears and resources and troops wasted.

So really it was in everyone’s best interests if Zuko dealt with the Avatar by himself, in secret. They’d all thank him later.

---

The next morning, Zuko agonized over how he could find his way back to the village. It wasn’t just about transport, but the excuse he’d need, now that Ama had voiced his disapproval. He was buzzing with reasons by the time he made it downstairs, but he didn’t get a chance to say a single one.

Without looking up from his book, Ama said, “Good morning, my prince. I meant to tell you, I spoke to Wei about everyone monopolizing the carriages. He took only his favorite mount and left you a means of transport for the day, if you’d like to go back to the village.”

Zuko was struck by the thoughtfulness of the gesture. He’d thought Ama wouldn’t approve, but it seemed that so long as he wasn’t endangering his health (or really, the health of his grandchild), Zuko was allowed to have this outlet.

Toru’s angry face flashed briefly in his mind, but Zuko pushed that thought away; he couldn’t afford to question Ama’s kindnesses. Ephemeral or not, he would take what he could get.

“Thank you for talking to Wei,” Zuko said. Then, because he loved to make things hard for himself, “Will you join me this time?”

He nearly cursed himself for the slip. Luckily, the older omega shook his head. “No. My hips are sore today. I think it’s best if you go on without me.”

---

Toph could tell from the impatient tapping of Sokka’s foot against the cave floor that he was livid, the wet echo of his anger reverberating off the spacious walls. As he got up to move, perhaps pacing agitatedly, she wondered who would be on the receiving end of his impending talking-to, and snickered at their misfortune.

Until his footsteps stopped in front of where she sat, and he addressed her in a warning tone. “ *Toph* .”

Damn it. “What?”

More pissy foot-tapping. “I heard an interesting rumor while I was in the village today. Apparently an earthbender was spotted on the island.”

Her eyebrows shot up. “There’s another earthbender here?”

Sokka let out a humorless laugh. “Ha, ha, Toph. I know it was you!”

She scowled in the general direction of his voice. She wouldn’t be slandered this way. She meant to respond with a list of irrefutable evidence, but perhaps due to exhaustion was reduced to a simple, childish protest: “It was *not* .”

“Was too!” Sokka replied, meeting her childishness in kind.

“Nuh uh, I’ve been behaving,” Toph insisted. “Tell him, Sweetness.”

Sweetness did not come to her rescue. There was a wobble of uncertainty in Katara’s voice as she said, “Are you *sure* you didn’t bend in front of anybody, Toph? It could’ve been anything. Even a little trick you thought no one would notice.”

The earthbender’s mouth fell open in shock. What betrayal! “ *Katara,* you know I’ve been in this stupid, boring old cave all day!”

Sokka huffed. “Yeah, but the earthbender was spotted in the village yesterday and - ugh, it doesn’t matter! Guys, we *cannot* blow our cover here.”

“You’re right. We can’t,” Toph replied, stiffly. “Which is why *I’m* not stupid enough to bend in public.”

Sokka gave a noise of frustration. “Toph, literally who else could it have been?”

There was a nervous cough from the other side of the cave. “Um.”

“Aang, what?!” Sokka shouted. “We’re in the middle of something!”

The Avatar made his sheepish entrance, hand fixed to the back of his neck. He always rubbed his neck when he was feeling guilty or embarrassed about something. “Don’t be mad at Toph. The person who got caught earthbending in the village was me.”

Sokka’s mouth fell open in disbelief. Then, “You *willingly* bent earth?”

“It’s not *that* surprising,” Aang pouted.

“It is, though,” Katara said, joining in on bullying the Avatar. “It’s your least favorite element. Must’ve been the teacher you had!”

Toph could just hear the smarminess in the other girl’s voice. Scowling, she reached out, and the omega waterbender fit easily into the curve of her arm, fingers lighting over Toph’s own. “You’re lucky I like you, Sweetness,” Toph grumbled.

Sokka groaned, rubbing his face. With Toph straggling at the end of the line, they were all technically adults, separated only by a smattering of months. Yet those months made all the difference; Sokka constantly felt like the sole adult amongst a horde of unruly children.

“Aang, why the hell would you blow our cover like that? You know we’re trying to lay low here!”

“I did it for a good reason!” Aang insisted, gloved hands raised in defense. The gang looked at him expectantly, waiting to hear what could possibly be so important it was worth giving away their presence in enemy territory. Oh, boy. He had maybe not entirely thought this through, but honesty was always the best policy, so he forged on ahead.

“Do you remember when Azula’s brother saved me, a few months back?” Aang asked. He didn’t wait for any nods or flicker of recognition, plowing on before anyone could interject. “He’s here, in Kirachu. I walked up just as he was being assaulted, and I couldn’t *leave* him there, after what he did for me. I tried not to do any bending, but the situation got dire, and I figured, y’know, earthbending would be suspicious, but not nearly as bad as airbending or even waterbending…”

The sheer heroism of his gesture seemed to go right over his friends’ heads; they gawked at him in horror.

“Did he recognize you?!” Sokka asked.

“Well. Not initially, no.”

Sokka seemed to deflate with relief. “So he’s none the wiser? We’re safe?”

Aang winced. “I kinda… told him who I was?” he admitted. Sokka responded with mouth agape, followed by a frustrated smack to his own forehead.

Next it was Toph’s turn to fret. “One of the reasons we chose this place is because it’s so far from the capital. Were we stupid enough to land smack-dab in the middle of the royal family’s vacation spot?”

“No, it’s just Prince Zuko *,* ” Aang explained, waving his hands. “Well - Prince Zuko and his husband. Who apparently runs the island.”

Katara’s hand flew to her chest, aghast. “So half the royal family knows we’re here?”

“No!” Aang shouted, growing more and more frustrated. He really should have gotten ahead of this yesterday, but he’d been in such a good mood after everything that happened... “Zuko wouldn’t sell us out like that, he told me outright that he didn’t even want his husband knowing we were here, so we’re totally safe, and why are you all looking at each other like that?”

Katara and Sokka were trading worried looks. After a brief, silent battle, it seemed Katara won the role of arbiter, and addressed Aang with soft eyes and a voice dripping concern: “Aang, I know you feel you owe this person for helping you escape, but he’s a complete stranger - a *Fire Nation* prince. Do you really think it was a good idea for you to reveal yourself to him like that? Think about our safety, here.”

Aang opened his mouth, ready to counter-argue, but Toph spoke up first: “Yeah, Twinkle Toes, we still don’t even know *why* he helped you escape. It could’ve been out of the goodness of his heart, but it could’ve also been a political thing, or him just fucking over his evil sister.”

Aang frowned. “First of all, enemy or not, I’m not fond of calling Azula *evil* .”

“So you’ve said,” Katara muttered.

“Secondly, I’ve talked to Zuko. I’ve looked him in the eye. He seems honest!” Again he was met with quiet grumbling, and couldn’t help but wilt in the face of it. The others were quiet for only moments afterwards, but in such uncomfortable silence, those moments stretched for eons; agitated, Aang asked, “Can you just tell me what you’re thinking, so I can stop assuming the worst?”

“...Truthfully? I think this is Azula in the ruins of Taku all over again,” Sokka muttered, rubbing his brow. “Look, Little Buddy, I know you want to see the best in people…”

The memory Sokka had dredged up brought with it a potent flash of pain, against which Aang bristled. “Don’t ‘Little Buddy’ me. I’m not childish for believing people can change!” He addressed them all now, hand over his heart as if in a pledge. “Yes, what happened with Azula in Taku was bad. I’ll even admit it was fully my fault. But just like we survived that, we will survive whatever happens as a result of me trusting Zuko!”

His words dropped heavily in the space between them, weighing the air down. Only Toph was eventually brave enough to speak.

“...Kinda’ just sounds like you’re admitting this is destined to go badly.”

Sokka and Katara seemed unable to meet Aang’s eyes. He could feel a defensive curl of anger twisting up inside his chest, and with effort, he made himself untangle it, made himself breathe through his passion and address them logically.

“Guys, Zuko is *from* here. There’s so much to gain by having him on our side. Like, yesterday, he showed me I was bowing incorrectly. That’s the kind of stuff that can help us blend in better! Not to mention he could hook me up with a teacher who won’t blow my cover, which is our entire purpose for coming here.”

Sokka considered this with a hand on his chin, no doubt weighing what he’d said carefully. Meanwhile, Katara viciously chewed her cheek in that way she did when she knew she couldn’t convince someone further, but desperately wanted to keep arguing, anyway. Toph raised a hand to rub her waist, beckoning the stiff muscles of discomfort to uncoil; unable to watch, Aang’s gaze flitted away from them.

Although the cave provided much-needed privacy, it was filled with the roaring of waves. When added to Appa’s soft grunts and Momo’s constant chittering, they were lucky if they were able to detect even the approach of a shrieking seabird outside the cave. Yet in listening closely, Toph thought she could hear something else: the faint cry of a person’s voice, calling out a familiar name.

Her eyebrows shot up. “Um, Aang? When you met up with your princely savior, you didn’t happen to tell him where we were, did you?”

Aang was an awful liar. Rather than deny it, his lips immediately split into a sheepish grin. Both Water Tribe siblings went rigid with horror.

“ *Aang-* ”

“Sorry!” he said, running to the mouth of the cave. “I’m really, really, *really* sorry, but it’s my fault for telling him, not his, so please try to be nice to him, okay?”

Without waiting for an answer, he ran to the highest vantage point he could in order to survey the sands. Having hair was incredibly annoying; even at this length, it whipped in the wind, distracting him as he scanned for signs of Zuko. He spotted him by the long, dark hair and wide-sleeved robes, each billowing erratically in the wind. Between this and the minefield of sharp volcanic rocks, Aang would think his visitor would have struggled through his approach, but he seemed to move with grace and agility, eyes focused on his feet.

When Zuko finally looked up, he spotted Aang waving, and raised a single, shy hand in reply. In place of the plain white robes he’d worn the last few times they’d met, he was wearing a set in the classic Fire Nation reds and grays, with a pair of hakama underneath. There was a boxy obi cinched around his waist to pull it all together, which must’ve been tight if it managed to so valiantly fight the ocean winds’ attempt to strip him. Aang bounded over, offering a hand to help him step over the rough-hewn landscape. Despite how easily he’d done it on his own, Zuko took the proffered help, smiling in greeting.

Time had slowed so sweetly for the moment of their reunion. But then they were back inside the cave with Aang’s companions, who gave a less than enthusiastic reception. They didn’t openly glare at Zuko, but they stood a distance away in a frosty clump. Only Momo seemed eager to approach, sniffing at the newcomer’s hands in the hopes he’d brought a delicious treat. No such luck; the first attempt Zuko made to awkwardly pet his ear, he fled back to the group, scurrying up the Water Tribe warrior’s shoulder to safety.

Aang smiled through the discomfort, hands thrown akimbo to present Zuko to his unwilling friends. “Everybody, Zuko! Zuko, this is Sokka, Momo, Katara, Toph, and Appa.”

Zuko fixed the clump with a quiet, intense stare as he struggled to commit the many new names to memory. Had the Avatar pointed at the Water Tribe man or the lemur on his shoulder, when he’d said Momo?

“Um - welcome to the Fire Nation,” he said, at a loss for how else to broach the tense silence. “Are you… enjoying your stay?”

“No,” said the waterbender, without elaborating. She crossed her arms over her chest.

Aang was wary of how icy those blues were turning, and eagerly changed the subject. “Zuko, you said yesterday you might know of a firebending master I could learn from?

“Yes,” said the prince, eager to prove himself. “I actually know of a few.”

It hadn’t been the easiest task, getting that information from his husband and his family. When Zuko asked at dinner the night before, Zhao had fixed him with a suspicious eye in return.

Zuko’s heart had thundered in his chest, convinced it would all go to hell, until Zhao asked, “Are you looking to fill your days...?”

Zhao thought he wanted the firebending training for himself. Relieved at the misdirect, Zuko said, “No, of course not. I’m just thinking about our children’s future.”

He thought it was a smooth lie, but Zhao stayed frowning.

“My father trained me, so I will train our children in kind,” he sniffed. Across the table, Zuko watched Yan roll his eyes.

Later, when dinner was cleared and Zhao retired to the tigermonkey room, Yan approached Zuko to set the record straight: “Our father was way too concerned with his work to have time to train my brother. He had a private tutor to teach him bending, instead.”

It was a strange thing to lie about, but Zuko couldn’t waste time being annoyed at his husband’s dishonesty. He was on a mission to gain the Avatar’s trust, and helping him find a teacher was clearly the first most important step. “How would I get in contact with him?”

Yan sighed. “He’s not… with us anymore.”

Zuko tried to keep his personal disappointment out of his voice. “Oh - I’m sorry for your loss.”

“Yeah. He was a good man. He deserted, you know - he couldn’t stand the shit the Fire Nation was doing overseas, and I don’t blame him.” Yan swallowed past a lump in his throat before soldiering on. “Still. If you’re looking for another option, there’s a firebending school in the village.”

Zuko took down the information Yan had on the bending school, although he rebuffed the offer to go further in depth about all the ills of the Fire Nation’s foreign agenda. It seemed Yan knew a master or two on the other islands, too. For a supposed layabout, he had amassed quite the network of allies, so that at a certain point Zuko’s paper was thoroughly scribbled over with suggestions.

“If none of *those* work out, just let me know,” said Yan. “There’s more where that came from.”

Later, as he was getting ready for bed, Zuko would remember that Admiral Shu had once told him about his husband’s tutor, the traitor Jeong Jeong. It made him look over the list Yan had given him with a more critical eye. Surely he wouldn’t be foolish enough to fraternize with other men labelled as traitors, not when both his brothers were employed directly by the crown?

&#46;.. *Well,* thought Zuko, *if these men are radical in their views, the Avatar might be in less danger of* *discovery, in their hands.*

Back in the present, he didn’t volunteer this additional layer of information, given it was only a theory. However, he did hand over the list of names. The Water Tribe man stepped up to take it from him, eyes scanning the page.

Now that they were close, Zuko could catalogue the finer details of his person: the way the sides of his hair had grown out to an awkward length, almost as if they’d been shaved before. The sinew of his exposed bicep… The heady whiff of an alpha’s scent. It made Zuko realize how little he had noticed of Aang’s scent, which made sense. After all, he and his sister had talked a few months ago about how the Avatar was most likely a beta. The Avatar’s other two friends weren’t standing close enough for Zuko to get a read on them, and their clothes gave no indication of their orientation. Perhaps something he’d need to advise them on, if they hoped to blend in here.

Katara huffed. “How do we know the names on this list aren’t just people waiting to ambush us?”

“They aren’t,” Zuko protested lamely, unsure what he could say to cast suspicion away from himself.

Luckily, the Water Tribe man came to his aid. Clapping one large hand on Zuko’s shoulder, he said, “No worries. We’ll all tag along - that way if anybody’s waiting around for us, they’ll have to fight the full force of our party.” He then whipped out a *very* conspicuously Water Tribe weapon, a club made of some sort of animal bone, with a blue sphere fixed at the end, and the handle wrapped in hides.

But he recognized the issue immediately. His face fell as he regarded it as if for the first time, twisting it this way and that in his hands. Katara reprimanded him with a huff. “Sokka, put that thing away! You’ll only draw more attention to us!”

Ah - so Sokka was the man, and Momo was the lemur. Although by the cut of his jaw he looked more man than boy, the responding sneer he gave his sister de-aged him by about five years. “I *know* that, Katara, I’m not dumb!”

With some grumbling, Sokka headed across the cave and clamored up onto the bison’s back, returning a few moments later with a leather bag. Settling on the ground, long legs stretched before him, he began rooting around in the bag for a suitable alternative to the club. Zuko was grateful that the group - particularly Aang, whose orbit he was reluctant to leave - closed around Sokka to watch; he wanted to see what Water Tribe weapons looked like first-hand.

First came a knife lined with flat animal teeth. Then a blade bent at a peculiar angle - it didn’t look damaged, but deliberately designed that way. Lastly came a machete about the size of the tiny earthbender’s forearm. Zuko gazed at each item with a longing he hadn’t felt since he’d pulled Mai’s dao swords from their box. So many glittering, violent treasures, none of which he could ever hope to wield.

When they were all laid out, Sokka regarded his options somberly. “None of these really look like they’ll blend in…”

Zuko caught Aang smiling his way, gesturing subtly at where Sokka sat ruminating at their feet. Zuko took the hint and looked again at the options so he could formulate an opinion.

“...The big knife,” he advised, pointing at the machete. “It’s not considered normal to carry most weapons around in public if you’re not in the army, but there's a lot of jungle here. I’ve seen regular villagers with those things just for the purpose of clearing vines and underbrush away.”

Sokka held it aloft with a hum. “Yeah - that’s mostly what this guy is for, too. Of course, that means he doesn’t exactly have a ton of experience hacking and slashing at *people* , but he’ll have to do. At least until I figure something else out…”

Although Katara still wasn’t fond of the plan, they were now free to make their way out of the cave and towards the village, where Zuko’s recommendations awaited them. She agreed only on the grounds that they try the bending school first; although she was wary of the sheer number of people, she seemed to have decided it was the location least likely to be involved in an ambush, no doubt hosting a number of children. Surely even firebenders weren’t so evil as to put their children in harm’s way.

In observing the Avatar’s group, Zuko had picked up on the fact the earthbender was at least partially blind; he’d seen her fight, so there was no way she could be *completely* unaware of her surroundings, but she failed to respond to visual cues, and her eyes were light and unfocused. As they walked down the beach, Katara snatched her by the hand and dragged her to the front of the group, perhaps acting as her guidance. Meanwhile, Sokka hovered around the middle of the clump, and Aang hung back to walk along with Zuko - who, because of the frosty reception, felt it best to trail behind everyone else.

Zuko cast his eyes to the sand. “Your friends hate me.”

“I wouldn’t say *hate* ,” Aang said, scratching his neck. “But they don’t completely trust you. Nor would they really trust anyone Fire Nation without reason.”

“But you trust me,” Zuko pointed out. “Why?”

Aang looked to the sky. “Good question… maybe it’s because I can remember a time of peace between your people and the rest of the world. They’ve only known this war.”

A sour pit festered in Zuko’s stomach. The source of it was guilt, although not just for the decades of history the royal family and the Fire Nation at large had played a hand in; no, what had scraped the wound raw was a more immediate violence, of which he had been reminded as Sokka went through his weapons, with every cold look Katara flashed his way: Zhao’s murder of his former Water Tribe lover.

Of all the ominous signs Zuko now looked back on, this was the one that had rattled him the most thoroughly, making him question his safety in Zhao’s care even early on. But it wasn’t as if Zhao had only killed one person during his tour of the South Pole. He had probably threatened, maimed, or killed countless members of Katara and Sokka’s tribe. With growing horror, Zuko realized that if Sokka and Katara were as close to himself in age as he thought, then Zhao’s tour had probably taken place during their childhood. This was no distant, generational pain; this was a recent trauma. They had probably lost community, lost *family* thanks to him.

Although removed by hundreds of thousands of miles, there was also his impact on the North Pole to consider. It was thanks to Zhao the Fire Nation had even reawakened their aggression upon the isolated nation. And while he hadn’t gone through with it, Zuko counted Zhao’s desire to kill the moon spirit high on the list of crimes he’d committed against the Water Tribes, if only because it showed the lengths to which he’d go, the cruelty he’d resort to.

From Zuko’s vantage point, it was hard at times to comprehend the sheer impact his father and grandfather had had upon the world, especially when both men had always seemed so much larger than life itself. But Zhao had only ever been a man to him, and that man had committed countless atrocities against the Water Tribes. That was what truly curdled Zuko’s stomach, more even than the distant guilt he associated with the Earth Kingdom.

“I’m going to make it up to them,” Zuko decided, out loud.

“I don’t know that you can really ever do that,” Aang said, voicing Zuko’s fears aloud. The prince must have visibly wilted; he saw a certain softness enter the Avatar’s expression. Aang amended, “But I’m glad you want to *try* . That’s the real key - and with time, I’m sure the right opportunities will present themselves for you to prove yourself to them.”

They continued to make their way over the rock-strewn beach. While those ahead made their own way, Aang and Zuko alternated helping one another through the difficult terrain, although they hardly needed it. It was an act of goodwill, to show that the silence that had fallen between them wasn’t tense. It was merely silence. Perhaps even the comfortable sort shared by old friends.

After some time, Aang started the conversation up again. “I’m surprised you’re even admitting there was wrong done to them. Last we talked, you seemed convinced your country was at war for a reason.”

Zuko sighed. “My country isn’t *evil* . We don’t do things merely to terrorize people. I still think there’s a reason we go abroad as we do, a goal of advancement.”

Aang raised his eyebrows. “But…?”

“ *But,* ” Zuko acquiesced, “we’ve lost our way, in a lot of respects.”

The beach was getting easier to walk on, with nothing but wide open white sands as far as the eye could see. Sokka glanced over his shoulder at the couple holding up the back of the procession, and slowed his pace until they were matched. Locked into his gaze, Zuko was filled with a sudden and intense anxiety. Had Sokka heard what Zuko was saying? Was he about to confront him on his views, or rage against the crimes committed against his people?

But all that Sokka said was, “You’re the Fire Nation expert. How suspicious will it be for a ripe old man of eighteen to seek out firebending training?”

That was a good question, actually. Zuko pondered it for a moment, thinking of the Avatar’s scentlessness, of his own brother-in-law, Wei. “It might not be suspicious simply because he’s a beta.”

Sokka and Aang traded raised eyebrows. Perhaps the cultural difference had caught them by surprise.

“Don’t worry, it’s not illegal for betas to learn to bend, here,” Zuko clarified. “I don’t know what it’s like where you’re both from, but in the Fire Nation, the role of a beta is to look out for the best interests of the family. Sometimes that means training up and joining the army, but it’s also really common for them to stay home well into adulthood in order to take care of immediate family. Old people, sick people. Sometimes kids.”

At some point, it seemed even the women at the front of the pack had slowed out of curiosity, to see what it was they were all talking about. Toph chimed in now: “Take care of the family? That sounds like an omega’s job.” Katara elbowed her, forcing her to amend what she’d said. “Ack - I meant if we’re talking traditional gender roles, and all that crap! Not how things *ought* to be.”

Zuko shook his head. “It’s not quite the same. You want omegas to get married and start their own families. But if you need additional support, that’s usually what betas are for.”

“Can you give an example?” Aang asked, frowning.

Zuko looked around. Now that they were close, he could detect even through the whipping ocean winds the fact that the earthbender girl was also an alpha. No scent seemed to come from the waterbender, though.

“Sokka,” Zuko said. “If you and your mate had lots of children, and they felt like they needed support, you would have a right to ask Katara, as a beta, to move into your home and support them.”

Katara scowled. “What if I was busy?”

Zuko shrugged. “Ideally, you’d drop what you were doing and come help, anyway.”

Sokka hummed. “I think I get it, but in the Water Tribe, it wouldn’t be required so much as freely given, and it wouldn’t necessarily be gendered? You could probably ask any family member for help.”

Katara snorted. “So says you. I think girls would most definitely be pressured to help more than boys would.”

While they debated this point, Toph gave a hum of understanding. “I see, though. We could say Twinkle Toes put off his firebending because there was a death in the family, so he had to, like, care for his siblings, or something.”

“Exactly,” said Zuko. He turned to Aang. “You had to work from a young age to provide, so you never put time towards more than the basic fundamentals you’d have learned in primary school. As for when you stopped learning - how much do you currently know?”

“Uh.” Aang scratched his neck. “Nothing?”

Okay. *That* would be suspicious. “You can’t know *nothing* . You’ve summoned fire, at least?”

Aang hesitated. “I mean… yeah. Once.”

Zuko’s brow furrowed. “Why only the once?”

“It didn’t go so well. It… came out too big.”

As if suddenly done with the conversation, Katara yanked the earthbender by the hand, surging ahead of the pack again. Toph flailed a moment before allowing herself to be dragged away. Sokka watched them both go with a somber look.

“...You guys hang here,” he said. “I’m going to check on her.”

He picked up the pace, lightly jogging towards his sister and the other alpha. Zuko was unsure what had passed between the group in the last few moments, but when he turned to the Avatar, his gaze was downturned, troubled. Perhaps it was that Katara was against him even learning firebending. Or perhaps this spoke of a firebending accident; Zuko had had enough of those to know the terrible guilt that came along with them. He brushed his fingers against Aang’s, stopping short of grabbing his hand, and began the frantic rambling of a person who had no idea how to provide reassurance, but desperately wanted to.

“You may be a little old, but you’re not the only firebender incapable of controlling himself. That’s what the teacher’s for - to help you learn.” Then, when that failed to lift the weight that bowed the Avatar’s shoulders, “You know, I used to struggle to keep my fire small, too, but now I *wish* that was the case. I pretty much have the opposite problem, these days.”

Finally Aang caught his eye. “I thought you couldn’t bend at all.”

Zuko shook his head. “I could, once. But now I can only make the smallest fires, and only if I concentrate really hard on them.”

“If only I could give you some of *my* fire,” the Avatar said with a chuckle. This seemed to have sufficiently distracted him from whatever bad firebending memory had brought him down; his hand brushed against Zuko’s, returning his brief, comforting touch.

“Maybe you need this teacher, too,” Aang said, excitement entering his voice. “We could learn together.”

Zuko colored. “No - I couldn’t.”

“Come on!” Aang implored him. “It could be fun, learning with a buddy. You don’t want me to have to do this all alone, do you?”

Zuko chewed the inside of his cheek, remembering the suspicious eye Zhao had cast him with at dinner the night before. “I can’t be seen with a firebending master. As an omega, I’m not...”

He trailed off. But Aang had been to the North Pole. He had seen how people in repressive families lived.

“You’re not allowed, are you?” he supplied.

Zuko knew he should clarify; it would be a lie, to imply it was entirely illegal for omegas to learn firebending. Still, he couldn’t summon a word, only nodding in reply. For a while, there was nothing but the fluttering of their clothes in the wind and the crunch of the sand beneath their feet as they carried on towards the village.

“You know,” said Aang, “bending is deeply emotional. When we feel fine, it all comes so easily. And when our emotions are in conflict, our bending is in conflict.”

Zuko gave a quiet laugh. “Yeah. That sounds about right.”

He hadn’t even realized he’d dropped his gaze until he raised it, now, and saw how closely the other man was watching him.

“It’s not forever, Zuko,” Aang said. His gray gaze seemed unusually serious. There was no laugh to cushion his words. “If you’re honest with yourself about what you’re feeling, you can begin to untangle your fire.”

“I’d imagine it’s not as easy as the other elements,” Zuko murmured. “Air doesn’t actively hurt you when you struggle against it. Neither does water or earth.”

“Yeah, but it’s not about struggling against the elements,” Aang said. “It’s about working with them.”

The maxim reminded him of Iroh. Not for the first time, Zuko found himself wondering where on earth his uncle was. He’d probably love to be a part of this conversation, and Zuko wished he could tell him about it. But Iroh’s repeated alliance with Azula made Zuko unsure if he could ever trust the old man with this sort of thing ever again. Those quiet afternoons in the Lesser Hall spent poring over Avatar stories seemed like ancient history.

The Avatar coughed, pulling Zuko out of his thoughts. “If you want to talk about it…”

Zuko stared ahead. “I see my mount coming up here, where I left him.”

They were coming upon the village, now, the sand fading away amongst the yellow beach grasses. Up ahead, grazing at them listlessly, was a dragon moose. Its fin-like protrusions twitched at the group’s approach, and once the prince was in scenting distance, the creature raised its head to look at them.

“I will never get over the freaky animals on this island,” said Sokka. “What the hell is that thing?”

“That’s mine,” said Zuko, quickening his pace. The animal was tied off on a makeshift wooden fence, which served less to keep anything out than it acted as a lazy boundary between the beach and the dirt road leading to the village. Zuko took the creature’s muzzle in his hands, stroked the short fur behind its proud antlers. “Maybe I should get going. I’m lucky no one nabbed this guy while I was gone.”

“Sure, abandon us to face hostile Fire Nation strangers all by ourselves,” Katara scoffed.

Zuko frowned. “Then I’ll come along?”

That possibility only made her grimace harder. Although she couldn’t have possibly seen her expression, Toph cocked her head as if she’d detected a change in Katara’s bearing.

“Uh, not for nothing, Sugar Queen, but you’re sending some mixed signals, here. You want the Good Prince to stay, or leave?”

“I don’t *know* ,” Katara huffed. “I just - whatever he wants, I want the opposite. I don’t trust him!”

Although a litany of discomforted looks flashed over everyone’s faces, no one immediately jumped to Zuko’s defense. His stomach twisted violently in the short silence that followed.

“...I don’t think it’ll hurt if Zuko heads home for today,” Aang said, diplomatically. His decision would have stung, if he didn’t immediately fix Zuko with a soft smile and say, “We can always see each other again another time. I’m sure I’ll be dying to tell you how my training went.”

Zuko gave a stiff smile in return. “Yes. Of course.”

“I mean it,” said Aang. “Come back as soon as you can.” He didn’t take Zuko’s hand, but he tangled his own, briefly, in the dragon moose’s mane, so they gripped the creature affectionately on either side of its head.

This time, Zuko’s responding smile came more easily. “I’ll try my best.” He leaned forward in a bow, floundering somewhat when the gold flame in his hair, loosened by the ocean winds, nearly fell off his head.

His departure was somewhat less arctic than his reception; Sokka and Toph bobbed their heads in acknowledgement of him, at least. But there was the polar blast of Katara’s gaze, reminding him of the fact he very much did not *deserve* their affection in the slightest. She occupied his thoughts for much of his ride back up the mountain, save those moments he wasn’t gazing at the rustle of branches in the wind, wondering what it would be like to bend an element like air.

---

Azula isn’t sure when her uncle became so small. In her childhood memories, he was as big as his laugh, a hardy man who filled the room with his mirth. Perhaps it was Ba Sing Se’s fault, or perhaps, more specifically, it was Lu Ten’s fault; he went and died, and suddenly, all she could see was how Iroh seemed to stand a head and shoulders below her father, how age had hunched him over.

And now. Without his laugh to fill the air, without those big gestures to project him beyond his physical form, her uncle is even smaller. She sees him laid in that nest of furs and immediately wants to bolt, but the guards that have escorted her here block her in. Even with her hands bound in steel, there are ways to subdue them so she can make her escape, things she could do to damn herself with the Northern Tribe forever while saving her the pain of this specific moment. She considers them very seriously.

Then a hand lands on her shoulder. It’s not the meaty paw of a guard; she looks up and sees Yue’s sympathetic gaze, and all at once, Azula remembers how many times she demanded this opportunity from her. It would look incredibly foolish if she threw it away. With a violent roll of the shoulders, Azula throws Yue’s hand off, and marches across the healing hut to where her uncle lays.

She has decided she can hold it together long enough to ensure his slumbering breaths look normal - once she’s sure he’s really alive, she can permit herself to take leave. But when she kneels down next to him, he stirs, and blearily opens his eyes.

Iroh smiles at her, and all at once she is six years old and lost in a crowd during the Fire Festival, completely unaware of how unmoored and how frightened she was until she saw a warm and familiar face. She wishes she could take hold of the hand resting over his heart. At least it is bigger than hers, although his skin is loose and has gone blue with cold.

“Uncle,” she says, terse. In an effort to hold herself together, she has made her voice harsher, worked her expression into one of iron and stone. It is a familiar shield, one that can keep just about any threat at bay.

Iroh’s smile wilts and goes sad at the sight. “Azula,” he croaks. “I’m sorry.”

All she can do is blink at him. Of all the nonsensical things he could possibly say, he has chosen to apologize. He is apologizing to her while *bedridden* from an injury *she inflicted on him* . She clenches her jaw to hold in her anguish.

The sight clearly wounds him; she can see the concern crease his face deeper, even, than age. He explains himself. “After all the Water Tribe princess said about the spirits, I knew I had to protect them. I jumped while only thinking of them, and in doing so, I nearly left one of the people I care about most alone in this world.”

She understands his decision, split-second though it was. Still, her lips wobble so hard she almost cannot respond. “You fucking - *fool* ,” she grinds out. “You *scared* me. I thought you were dead!”

“I know. I’m sorry,” he says. “I’m sorry I frightened you, by risking my life. I’m sorry I haven’t always been honest with you about how I feel about these things. I know you feel I’ve only ruined your plans time and time again.”

“Uncle-”

He interrupts her as firmly as he can, with his voice wavering so. “But I want you to know, Azula. I don’t *ever* regret this time spent with you. Even when I don’t agree with you, I care deeply about you. You are my family. And at times, though I know you may not feel the same, I think of you as my… as my...”

Too overcome to finish the thought, he reaches out, arm shaking with the effort to be held aloft. Finally she feels tears spill in messy globs down her cheeks. It’s pathetic. She could say it’s the torture of the cold and flimsy prison meals and her complete lack of sleep - but that’s all just an excuse. She is weak and has allowed herself to be broken by this.

His arm is still hanging there. He won’t close the space between them without her permission, even now, so she does it for him, pitching forward so she can sob into the front of his robes. She feels his fingers light in her hair, stroking gently.

The front of his shirt smells like the awful fermented things they eat here, paired with the distinct aroma of tanned animal hides. Yet even under the alien miasma of the Northern Tribe, Iroh’s scent is comforting and familiar. Gemsbok oil and patchouli… but the litany of herbs he’s always used to mask his scent has dulled. A brief flash of panic goes through Azula when she remembers how deeply he relies on these scent-changers. She worries how he’s faring without them, what could happen to the privacy he’s worked so hard to cultivate, how this secret can be used against him by their enemy… until she remembers again how old he is. Just as children start on neutral ground before they present, he is at the age where such divisions have fallen away again. Unless the healers examined him much too closely, no one should suspect anything. His lifetime secret can remain one.

Azula wishes she had her hands free for any number of reasons. But she especially wishes she could bury her fingers in her uncle’s shirt, have the assurance of physical touch to assure her that she can hold onto him, that she can keep him right here with her for as long as she needs.

“Stop apologizing,” she says, words muffled into his shirt. “You were right about everything. You didn’t even want to come along in the first place, but I made you come.”

“Azula, you nearly lost your life. I came because you needed me.”

Although he can’t see it, she glares into the dark thicket of fabric and fur. “You came to the Earth Kingdom because I nearly lost my life. Then I used that guilt to get you *here* . You told me that following the Avatar to the North Pole in the middle of a seige was desperate and stupid, but I wouldn’t listen. It’s not your fault you got hurt.” She swallows. “It’s *mine* .”

“Azula. You didn’t hurt me out of malice. It was I who...”

“Let me be sorry!” she snaps, anger muffled against his chest. “I can carry the blame - I’m *strong* enough. Let me carry the blame...”

She’s certain she can hear the rueful smile in his voice when he says, “It’s not yours alone, Azula. We’ll carry it together.”

His insistence on carrying the blame piques her interest. For all her uncle’s apologies, a part of her suspects that, if faced with the same decision, he’d make the same one all over again. He’d protect those fish at the risk of his life. He’d be sorry about it, but the fact of the matter is, leave her alone to protect spiritual balance, the natural order of things.

Azula isn’t so sure that she’d do things the same way, though. She has turned those slow motion moments around in her mind a thousand times, criticizing her choices, seeing, in hindsight, all her many faults. She doesn’t say anything about that, though, focusing instead on the way her uncle’s fingers feel as they weakly card through her hair, letting their audience intercept her silence however they wish.

Their time doesn’t last forever. Azula hears the guards move from the doorway and doesn’t let them drag her off her uncle, instead standing and walking out of the room with as much composure as she can muster. She has missed her usual facade of makeup during her imprisonment, but at least without it her lack of poise isn’t further emphasized by streaks of mascara across her red-rimmed eyes.

The guards walk a respectful pace behind her, Yue at her side. When they’re no longer within hearing distance of the healing huts, she says to Azula, “Your uncle’s sacrifice wasn’t for nothing. He protected the moon and ocean spirits.”

“Whatever,” Azula mutters, gaze fixed forward. She wants to get as far from this incident and her feelings of guilt as she possibly can.

“I’m serious,” Yue says. “Had he not stepped in, it would’ve been chaos. Seas drying. The moon going dark in the sky.”

“The end of the world,” Azula says. “Or at least, the end of waterbenders. You wouldn’t be so useful without your precious moon, hm?”

There is a sharp intake of breath from one of the guards behind them: the princess has just let a crucial detail slip in front of the enemy. Even if she is their captive now, should she ever go free, this information could be useful to the Fire Nation. They could be facing an onslaught of soldiers and spies whose only goal is to destroy the spirit oasis.

“So you superstitious brutes *assume,* anyway,” Azula huffs.

Yue narrows her eyes. “Excuse me?”

“I’m sure you’ve just chosen to worship the first unusual pair of pretty fishies you’ve ever seen in this wasteland of a country,” Azula sighs, turning up her nose.

“Tui and La are real,” Yue starts to argue. “You were *in* the spirit oasis - couldn’t you feel their energy?”

“Not at all,” Azula says. “I don’t believe in silly spirit stories like the one you’ve told, and neither does my father. When I go home - and I do mean *when,* not *if* - I won’t burden him with the details of this particular leg of my adventure. It’s been nothing but disaster, anyway.”

Something like shock flashes over Yue’s face. Azula walks a little faster to escape the questions that may follow, and as predicted, the guards close in behind her, pushing her along, widening that gap between her and the pretty little idiot.

Like she said before - they’re *not* friends. If things were reversed, Azula wouldn’t have let Yue visit with her own ailing uncle. She’d use that fear for the old man’s life against her, then execute them both.

There was a time Azula would have called Yue’s mercy a sign of weakness. She would have said that everyone else’s compliance with this visit was further proof of the Northern Water Tribe’s inherent inferiority to the Fire Nation’s ruthlessness. That they simply didn’t have the stomach to do what needed to be done.

Now, though. Now Azula’s not so sure.

### Text

Sokka wasn’t sure what the hell it was with men who could bend, but none of them seemed capable of manipulating their given element with a shirt on.

Back at the beginning of their journey, he’d thought that the love of toplessness was solely an Earth Kingdom trait. Now that he’d observed a firebending school in action, Sokka realized this was simply the way it was done, regardless of age or nationality. Honestly, the highborn snobs in Pakku’s tutelage probably would’ve bended shirtless, too, had they not been working in subzero temperatures. Sokka supposed he had the North Pole to thank for not having to look at half-naked man-children for a solid month.

Sadly, those days were over. They were in the balmy Fire Nation now, and despite their many repressive gender roles, when it was time to blow fire around, everyone shed as much clothing as humanly possible. Aang had long resisted this macho impulse, but in an effort to blend in, here he was, waving his arms around with his shirt distinctly not on his body. Bizarre to think that there was a time Sokka would’ve jumped at this opportunity - but ah, well. That was all ancient history.

“Thank La for the cave blocking all that ocean wind,” Aang laughed. “Otherwise I think I’d burn my face off, practicing here…”

“Or *my* face off,” Sokka grumbled. He didn’t particularly want to be here, but Katara had rushed out pretty much the moment Aang started practicing, and where she went, Toph went. It was distinctly unfair, how much his sister hogged Toph’s attention these days. What did Katara have that he didn’t?!

…Okay, there was a very obvious answer to that question. But were the bonds of romance really *so* much stronger than the bonds of platonic toilet humor? Even with her in close proximity most of the time, Sokka missed Toph to death. They should be getting into shenanigans like the old Earth Kingdom days, wreaking good-humored havoc across this dinky little village. But one rogue love confession, and now it was just Katara and Toph all the time. It made him miss his closeness with Toph.

It also made him miss Yue.

God, what he wouldn’t give to be cuddled up with Yue instead of feeling useless while Aang leapt around half-naked. What could he even offer Aang, right now? Guardianship? The Avatar could take care of himself. Sokka supposed if anything terrible happened, he would just… witness it, or be swept along in whatever terrible fate befell Aang, because again, useless. Sokka was really going to have to do something about that, soon, because the longer they stayed in the Fire Nation, the more he felt like dead weight.

And the more he regretted leaving the North Pole.

It wasn't until he was looking up at Aang from the ground that Sokka realized he had essentially melted like a puddle in his listlessness.

The world’s last airbender fixed him with a sympathetic look. “You okay down there, bud?”

“Not really,” Sokka sighed. “I’m just really missing Yue. Among other things.”

Aang hunkered down beside him, bandy legs folded. “Speaking of... Could I ask you something about her?”

“Maybe,” Sokka said. “Shoot and we’ll see.”

Aang picked at a loose thread on his pant leg. “You love her.”

“Not really a question, but yeah.”

“So why did you leave her behind?” Aang asked

Sokka was asking himself that over and over these days. But he’d had a reason - a really good reason.

“You don’t have to answer if you don’t want to,” Aang said, ever generous.

“No. I do, I just-” Sokka heaved a sigh, relieving the tension in his body so he finally went limp against the cave floor. “You remember my mission. While you were in the spirit oasis.”

Aang nodded. “Sneak on and take control of the ship at the head of the fleet.”

“And you know how Hahn… didn’t do so well.”

Aang grimaced. “He got captured *immediately* , didn’t he?”

“Yeah. Well. After I got things back on track, freed him and whatever, even if he was a piece of shit, I wasn’t going to rat him out. But the other guys on the mission talked up his failure, and I guess I got misconstrued into this big hero-”

“Sokka, you *were* a hero,” Aang huffed. “Taking down Admiral Choi literally changed the tide of that entire battle.”

Sokka raised one arm into the air and wiggled it dismissively. “What *ever* . The point is. Not only did Chief Arnook beg me to stay. But he, uh. He offered me Yue.”

Aang blinked. “Wait, what do you mean, he offered you Yue?”

Sokka gestured grandly. “As a reward for my work, he offered me Yue.”

“Like her hand in marriage?”

“Yeah.”

Aang’s eyes were the size of dinner plates. *“Really* ?”

“I thought you knew this,” said Sokka.

“I knew you and Yue were together, but not *legitimately,* ” said Aang. “I kind of thought you left because you didn’t want to see her marry someone else.” Aang stopped, realizing something. “Wait. So what about Hahn…?”

Sokka grimaced, draping a hand over his eyes. He wasn’t losing sleep over taking Yue from Hahn. But that wasn’t all there was to lay awake at night agonizing over. “I mean, this probably doesn’t mean much, coming from someone who hated him, but… I feel sorry for Hahn? He essentially went from golden boy who could do no wrong to just… completely losing his standing with the chief.

“Anyway, pitiful rich boys aside, the point is that Arnook offered me his daughter on a silver platter, and it made me sick to my stomach, because she wasn’t a prize to be won. She’s the person I love.”

Aang blinked. “Yeah, but regardless. You loved each other. Why wouldn’t you just get married anyway, regardless of her dad’s reasoning?”

“Do you really not *get* it?” With a sudden surge of energy, Sokka pushed himself up onto his elbows. “Chief Arnook didn’t give Yue a choice in the matter. He literally gave her the news *after* *talking to me about it* . I *watched* her learn that she was engaged to me, and I just couldn’t stop thinking about the fact that - that she never got to be her own person! She just got handed between these men who thought they knew better for her, her dad and Hahn, and then me - she never got to *choose* for herself.

“I talked to her about it. I talked to her and Arnook both - I said, more than I want Yue, I want her freedom. That should be my prize. She should get to choose whatever she wants for herself - and if that means marriage, to me or somebody else, fine. But if that means she just wants to be by herself, to try something new, well… it’s her choice.”

Aang was enraptured by Sokka’s passion, jaw agape. “Wow - so what happened?”

“Arnook said he could agree to my terms.”

“And Yue?”

Sokka cast his eyes downward. “She said she wanted to be on her own for a while.”

“Oof,” said Aang. It was more an involuntary reaction than a conscious response. “That’s rough, buddy.”

“Hey - I *wanted* this,” Sokka said, half to himself. “I’m happy for her. She didn’t even say she didn’t ever want to be with me, she just - doesn’t want to be married to me right now.”

“Yeah, still. Ouch.”

Sokka inhaled for five long seconds before he released all his anguish in one quick gust of a sigh. “...Yeah. I know.”

That wasn’t even the entire story. The truth was, days before their departure from the North Pole, Sokka had asked Yue if she wanted to come with them. She had told him once that she wished she could see the world beyond her kingdom; that she could experience a real summer, go swimming in the ocean, go on *adventures* like the ones he described. “You’re lucky, Sokka,” she’d told him. “Your duty called you to the Avatar.” He had assumed that when given the chance, she’d jump to join him.

But she hadn’t. She’d laid her hands on his and said, “I appreciate what you’re trying to do. Marriage or not, though, I have a duty to my people.” She’d given him a sad-eyed smile. “Besides - won’t it be easier to break through the siege if it’s just the four of you?”

“Appa’s a big boy - he can handle carrying one more person,” Sokka had insisted, but Yue had once again declined. He tried not to take it personally, but it was hard not to. Maybe if he’d offered to stay in the North Pole in her place, free her from the awkwardness of travelling with an ex, she’d be able to live out her life’s dream. If he hadn’t thought of that literally mid-air over the Mo Ce Sea, he would have done that for her.

And now he was here, dragging all of Team Avatar down with him.

“That was incredibly brave of you, Sokka,” said Aang, getting to his feet. “You did the right thing for a person you loved, even though it meant you’d be separated.”

“It’s not brave,” Sokka muttered. He sat up, swiping sand off his cheek. “It’s the bare minimum.”

Aang flashed him a cheeky smile. “Still - who would’ve thought the guy who *railed* against the idea of a pair of omegas going out all on their own to save the world would turn into such an egalitarian?”

“Hey - I’ve grown up!” Sokka said, pouting. “I haven’t been that guy in a long time!”

Aang grinned, ready to tease him again, when a familiar figure stepped inside their hideaway.

---

Zuko didn’t expect to be able to make it back to the Avatar so soon. But Wei left a mount for him again the next day, and Ama still wasn’t feeling that well, so he rode down through the village alone again.

When he arrived at the mouth of the cave, he was struck by the sight of the Avatar’s bare back, a line of blue cutting from the dark hair at the nape of his neck all the way down to the waist of his pants, where it disappeared. Again, he was surprised by the width of the shoulders, the tasteful definition in the muscles of his back. He was unused to seeing someone else’s naked body aside from his husband’s, and though there was a power about him, Aang wasn’t so overly muscled the way Zhao was; he reminded Zuko more of himself in peak condition. In looking at the Avatar’s body, he was unsure if he was jealous of the freedom he had to build himself up as a bender and a soldier, or if he was feeling something else entirely, some unnameable emotion that sat soft and warm in his chest… even as it was tinged with guilt.

Aang turned, and before Zuko could be embarrassed for ogling the Avatar, he was struck by another novelty.

“Your beard is gone!” he exclaimed, ever one for stating the obvious.

Thankfully, Aang was too polite to mock Zuko for his lack of social skills. He rubbed his chin, smiling ruefully. “Yeahhh, I got kinda self conscious, being the only student with a beard yesterday.”

“He was *way* older than everyone there,” Sokka piped up.

Zuko startled, whipping around to face him. “I didn’t see you there!” Yet Sokka was only a few feet away, sitting on a rock. Zuko must have been too wrapped up in Aang to notice.

A smile that spoke of evil intent crept its way onto Sokka’s face. “Hey, highness, maybe you can settle something we were talking about before you came in.”

By the way his brow furrowed, Aang wasn’t sure what Sokka was about to say, but Zuko nonetheless offered his help. “I’d be happy to help - what is it?”

That sly smile on Sokka’s lips split into a white-toothed grin. “Is the Avatar cute without his beard?”

Zuko’s mouth flew open. “Excuse me?”

“Is he cute enough to pass for sixteen, I mean?” Sokka asked. He gave a flutter of the eyelashes that was the opposite of innocent.

Aang shot him a scowl. “Sokka, shut *up* .”

“I’m sure he blends in better without it,” Zuko replied hurriedly, avoiding looking at Aang too closely.

“But is he *convincing?* ” Sokka pressed. “Or does he look naked without it, as he’s been whining all day?”

Zuko stole a glance at Aang’s face with the hesitancy of an innocent maiden peeking behind the curtain of a men’s bath. True, it did make him look younger. But it wasn’t as though Aang was unbearable to look at with facial hair.

“You look fine either way,” Zuko said.

“Gee, thanks.”

“I don’t mean it half-heartedly,” Zuko huffed, channeling all his energy into bending the heat away from his face. “Beard or no beard, you have a nice face.”

Aang grinned, reddening in kind. “ *Aw.* So I’m not hideous.”

“Not at all. In fact, it's nice to see your bare face somewhere other than a wanted poster, for once.”

Aang clutched his chest. “ *Ow* . Spirits, Zuko, if you wanted to spar, why didn’t you just say so?”

The boys had a knack for getting absorbed in the moment. Zuko didn’t realize until Sokka gave a very fake-sounding cough into his hand that he’d inadvertently shut him out of the conversation - in an effort to focus on Aang, Zuko had entirely turned his back on Sokka.

Aang shot his friend a look over Zuko’s shoulder. “Hey, Sokka, didn’t you say you wanted to head out to the beach for a second?”

The older boy only blinked back at him. “No?”

“Yeah you did,” said Aang. “You wanted to… gather up some grass. For Appa to eat.”

At the sound of his name, the bison exhaled a gust of air that sent their bedrolls and packs tumbling across the cave floor. Sokka’s lips twitched. “Oh *yeah* . I did want to get some beach grasses for my good, good friend Appa.”

He stood up, dusting himself off. “I’ll see you two crazy kids later. Don’t do anything I wouldn’t do.” On his way across the cave, he gave Appa a series of hardy pats on his side, which earned him an unimpressed huff from the creature. His hands practically sank inside the thick coat of fur; Zuko wondered how soft it was, and found his fingers itching to bury themselves in it.

“A creature his size must feel cooped up in here,” Zuko mused, watching Appa settle down with his massive head on his paws.

“Definitely,” Aang agreed. “But we can’t let him graze. He sticks out too much.”

“True. How did you even get him on the island without…”

Zuko trailed off, having turned to find the Avatar standing only inches away from him, still very much naked from the waist up. With such a direct view, Zuko couldn’t help but notice there were no tattoos on his chest; just a glisten, brought on by a sheen of sweat or ocean air, both, rivulets caught in the sharp slope of his lower abdomen. There seemed to be something sacrilegious about ogling the Avatar, so Zuko made himself stop literally navel-gazing to make eye contact, instead.

“I wanted to show you something,” Aang said, holding out both hands in front of himself. “I think it’ll help with your bending.”

Zuko raised an eyebrow. “I know you’re the Avatar, but are you really trying to teach me something after *one* firebending lesson?”

Aang playfully rolled his eyes. “This isn’t something I learned *today* . It’s actually something I learned when I was very young, just starting my airbending training.”

He kept his hands aloft, palms facing downward. “In every human being, there’s a spiritual energy known as chi. This is what benders harness every time we manipulate the elements.”

“I know that,” Zuko huffed. Truthfully, he had only known chi was the source of a firebender’s power; he hadn’t been sure if other benders used it, too.

Aang smiled patiently. “Good. Then you know if there’s an issue with your bending, your chi might be at the root of it?”

“So I’ve been told,” Zuko sighed, “but that hasn’t helped me. I’m bad at locating my chi, so I have a hard time untangling it.”

Aang paused to look him over, as if he could see it. “Interesting that you call it tangled. That’s exactly the impression that I’m getting from you.”

Zuko blinked, surprised. “You can feel my chi?”

Aang nodded. “Faintly.”

“Do *you* know how to untangle it?” Zuko asked.

“I was getting to that. Here, hold your hands under mine; don’t touch them, though.” Zuko did as Aang said and was rewarded with the lopsided smile he’d seen so many times on paper - to think he now got to see it so often in person.

“Breathe with me,” came the smooth-voiced instruction. Zuko obeyed immediately, eyes fluttering briefly shut as he focused on the rhythm of Aang’s breathing.

This seemed familiar, so far - after all, breathing exercises were crucial to firebending. Perhaps an airbender would understand that better than any other bending master. Zuko cracked one eye open, and saw their chests rise and fall in perfect tandem.

“Good,” Aang said, the simple praise setting off a small flutter of contentment in Zuko’s chest. “Now, I want you to try to find *my* chi.”

Zuko frowned. “Not my own?”

“Not your own. Try to feel my energy. Concentrate on the space between our palms - can you feel me reaching out to you?”

Even the cave seemed to breathe around them, inhaling and exhaling sea air as they focused on the task before them. Perhaps it was an illusion, but soon, Zuko thought he felt a concentrated swirling of air, or - not a physical wind, but something adjacent, spiralling invisibly between their palms.

“I think I… I think I feel it,” Zuko said.

“Good,” said Aang again. His voice was soothing, and the ease of his praise made Zuko’s skin prickle. He’d make an excellent teacher. “Next, I want you to do what I’m doing. Try to fill the space between our hands.”

“What about your chi?” Zuko asked. “Won’t it be in the way of mine?”

“Let them mingle,” Aang answered. “Don’t try to move my chi or take it. Just let them both flood together, until you can’t even tell them apart.”

Zuko nodded, dazed. They returned to their synchronized breathing, and in doing so, he found himself deeply embedded in the moment. There was no Kirachu or Fire Nation beyond. No war, no royal family, no obligations looming; it was just the two of them here, in this space, performing an exercise that probably hadn’t been done in as long as the airbenders had been gone. The thought of sharing in this with Aang was exciting, it was - an honor, to be trusted like this.

The longer Zuko concentrated, something strange happened. He had never had an easy time detecting his own chi, but he imagined now that he could feel it spilling from his palms to spiral in between their hands. It tumbled in that liminal space between them, every once in a while crossing into Aang’s space. But that was alright; Aang’s chi didn’ seem so perfect, either, dragging along the skin of Zuko’s palms like the tongue of a cat. It filled Zuko with a heat-but-not, brushing against him with the laziest of touches.

He knew when he’d finally succeeded in mixing his own chi because he heard the sharp intake of Aang’s breath, followed by, “That’s it.” Spurred on by his encouragement, Zuko tried not to lose his momentum, concentrating as he had in the dark of his bedroom, trying to summon a flame.

Yet this exercise was so different from that. These last few weeks, when Zuko tried to summon his flame, he was rife with internal conflict. Amongst a thousand other terrible feelings, he was furious at himself, frustrated and ashamed at his impotence. It seemed fitting in the most unfair way, that he should struggle his entire life to bend, then lose it entirely as soon as he needed it most.

However, with Aang, Zuko didn’t waste time on self-flagellation. Nor was he galvanized by any of his other anxieties; he felt little save for a deep inner peace. There was little room for anything in his mind but the task Aang had set before him.

Aang swallowed. It was loud in the quiet that had built between them. “Now,” he murmured, slipping his hands under Zuko’s. “See what you can do.”

Zuko twisted his wrists so his palms faced upwards. Then he produced a flame.

It was small and weak. But it was steady; it didn’t flicker and fight him, instead standing with all its brilliance for as long as he held it.

When Zuko looked at it, he wasn’t filled with fear, nor giddy excitement; again, he felt peace. Like everything was going to be okay.

He didn’t realize he’d brought the flame in his palm closer to his face, nor did he realize Aang had leaned down towards it until he raised his eyes to look at the other boy, the warm glow flickering across his face. Their gazes met, and Zuko could see the movement of their shared fire reflected in the slate gray of Aang’s eyes.

Aang’s lips curled, then split into a small, triumphant grin. “Hey,” he said. “Look at *you* .”

Zuko felt his own lips curl in turn, but before he could respond, there came a commotion from the mouth of the cave.

“Toph and Katara are back!” Sokka shouted from the mouth of the cave. The mention of his sister’s name filled Zuko with an instant guilt, like he’d been caught doing something he shouldn’t, and the fire disappeared. Aang looked so disappointed; Zuko felt as though he’d let him down.

Katara managed to control her temper when she saw Zuko, suppressing all her hatred into the spasming muscle of her left eyebrow. “Oh,” she ground out. “ *You’re* back. And spending time with Aang unsupervised.” At that, she shot her older brother a poisonous look. He only shrugged in reply; curiously, he didn’t seem to be carrying anything. The girls must have intercepted him before he got a chance to gather food for Appa.

Toph grinned from behind her floppy bangs. “So that’s the Good Prince I feel over there? Welcome back!”

Despite himself, Zuko was relieved to be met with approval from one of Aang’s companions. “Hello, Toph,” he greeted. “Hello, Katara.”

Katara didn’t respond, instead pointedly turning away with an audible scoff. Toph smirked in response; “C’mon, Sweetness, he can’t be all bad. His recommendation yesterday turned out to be good.”

“So far,” Katara replied, chin in the air. “He could be playing the long game for all we know.”

Toph snorted. “If his long game involves letting the Avatar master firebending, then he’s a pretty rotten spy.”

A ripple of hurt made its way through Zuko’s chest, but it was entirely undeserved. Katara was right, after all. Zuko *was* playing the long game. The entire point of him making nice with the Avatar was to ultimately gain information from him. Somewhere between the estate and the mouth of this cave, he had forgotten all about that. By introducing Aang to a firebending master, he had inadvertently added another challenge to his mission: he now had to race to get the information he needed before the Avatar finished mastering the last of the elements.

Zuko turned to Aang, doing his best to sound casual. “Um, sorry I didn’t ask, sooner. How did your lessons go, yesterday?”

Aang scratched his neck. “They were fine, I suppose. The master *did* say I was one of the best beginner students he’d ever coached."

Before Zuko could make an effort to fawn over the other boy’s progress, Toph interrupted with a snicker. “I would *hope* he’d say that. You’re five years older than the next youngest student *and* you’re the Avatar.”

“Yeah, but he doesn’t know that I am,” Aang huffed, sounding surprisingly defensive. “He just knows what he sees, and what he sees happens to be a model student.”

Zuko couldn’t help but find the flare of pride charming. For a moment, he could imagine Aang was just another teenaged boy learning to firebend, excited that he’d already shown some prowess. He was allowed to celebrate the little triumphs without worrying about how fast he was moving, about the international fate that lay on his shoulders.

“Prove it,” Sokka shouted, pointing at Aang. “Show us some fiery poses!”

“They’re called *drills* , Sokka, not *poses* ,” Katara said, with more disgust than necessary. Probably some excess steam at Zuko escaping, there. Really, in the Fire Nation, they preferred to use the term *kata* , but Zuko worried that if he corrected her, she might send an icicle through his chest.

“Ugh, I don’t know. I’ve only had one lesson, after all…” Aang said, avoiding their eyes. This earned him a litany of boos and hisses from Toph and Sokka.

Zuko gave him a hopeful look over folded hands. “Please? I want to see what you’ve learned.”

The Avatar seemed to get a little taller, at that. “Since someone asked nicely, I guess I can show you all a thing or two.” He struck a few stances in quick succession; to an unpracticed eye, they would have seemed smoothly executed. But Zuko caught sight of an error in his footing.

When finished, Aang fixed him with a triumphant smile. “Well?”

Zuko fumbled, voice going a tick too high. “Oh, that was good!”

Toph cocked her head. “I feel like the Good Prince is holding something back,” she said.

“I’m not,” Zuko insisted, but Toph had made up her mind. “C’mon, out with it!” she teased. “You’re not all that impressed by Twinkle Toes’ fancy footwork, are you?”

“Guys, stop embarrassing Aang,” Katara said, tossing a warning glare Zuko’s way. It *almost* deterred him from talking.

Almost. And then Aang struck the worst cat stance Zuko had ever seen.

Zuko’s protest was immediate and instinctive, coming from the very depths of his chest. “No, no, Aang - watch your center of gravity!”

Aang blinked at him. Then shifted his hips slightly.

Zuko released a breath he hadn’t realized he was holding. The result was a somewhat strangled noise. “Not like *that* , just-”

He couldn’t resist the impertinent urge to physically readjust the Avatar. With one foot, he reached out and slid one of Aang’s legs further outwards from his body. Then he grabbed his arms, pulling them into the correct positions. Flustered by the turn of events, Aang let Zuko do as he pleased, but his resulting pose was much too stiff.

“Looser,” Zuko commanded. “It’s not called cat pose to be cute. You’re supposed to feel agile. It’s all about getting you ready for quick, agile movement - that should be your forte as an airbender!”

Aang’s mouth fell open with surprise. “Wait, so there *is* a point to the name?” He slid into position, and the result was much closer to the intended outcome. Zuko nodded in approval.

Toph threw her head back to laugh. “Man, Aang, you thought you were *such* hot shit, and he put you in your place!” Beside her, Katara was an ominous, simmering quiet, her arms crossed over her chest. Zuko got the impression she wasn’t thrilled about Toph getting friendly with him.

Sokka approached Zuko and Aang, scratching his beard as he inspected the Avatar’s stance. “Why do you know so much about this, Zuko?”

“He’s a firebender, too,” said Aang, smiling.

“Was,” Zuko tried to insist, but he was drowned out by the sheer force of Sokka’s excitement.

“You’re a firebender?!” he exclaimed. “Then why are we even bothering with this bending school for babies? *You* should be teaching Aang!” Zuko tried to interject, but it was difficult to get a word in - Sokka’s words were coming out in excess and at mach speed. “I was really worried at first, but you seem like a cool guy! I mean, all we *really* know you is that you’re a member of the royal family, and yeah, that’s a strike against you, but you were willing to *save the Avatar’s life* , so even if we don’t see eye-to-eye on everything, that still makes you way cooler than most firebenders we know and in our circumstances you’d can’t just abandon an ally who shows that - ooh!”

Sokka clenched his hands with excitement, getting a little too deep into Zuko’s personal space for his comfort. “Can you teach Aang the lightning thing Azula does? She’s tough enough of an adversary already, but that’s the one trick that makes her, like, *deadly* . Man, if Aang could lob a bolt of lightning right back at her, that would really level the playing field! He’d be the best bender in the *world* just for that.”

It was the reminder of his inferiority to Azula that did it. Almost without thinking, Zuko lashed out. “If you’d stop talking for *one second* , you’d know that I can’t teach Aang anything! I can’t bend anymore!”

Sokka looked startled by the force of his response. “I didn’t even know that could happen!” Then, guilty but unsure, “I’m… sorry for your loss?”

At some point, Zuko had clenched his hands into fists at his sides. He flexed his fingers, now, forcing the blood flow back into each useless appendage. “It’s barely a loss,” he muttered. “I wasn’t ever any good. So even if I regained my power, I couldn’t pass anything onto you, Aang. Nothing of use. The closest I can even get is…”

He lowered a hand with the intent of miming what his uncle had once taught him, about how to absorb a lightning blast by bending it carefully through one’s own body. Instead, the moment his hand touched his stomach, he remembered its occupant.

The cave seemed to grow thousands of feet taller, so that Zuko felt as though he was standing at the bottom of a jagged grave.

What was he even doing here, with the Avatar? His role in the royal family wasn’t to fight. It wasn’t reconnaissance, to play soldier or spy or whatever he was doing. It was to remain married to Zhao, for the unity of the Fire Nation. It was to have this child, to hope that however they turned out, that they, too, could be of use to the needs of their country.

“Zuko?” Aang asked, voice soft. “What were you going to say?”

Zuko chewed his lip. “The closest I can even get is a complete mess,” he said, tucking his uncle’s trump card away. “Just… fire in all directions. I can never get it to the right temperature.”

The look Aang settled him with was unbearable to behold; would he feel any of that pity, that patience, if he knew the truth of Zuko’s intentions?

The Avatar gestured towards the other side of the cave, away from the rest of the group. “Hey - I know you just said you don’t have much to pass on, but can you help me with my cat stance, again? Using it to dodge, I can see, but I’m not sure I understand how that’s supposed to transition into a kick or a punch…”

Zuko deliberated. No doubt helping the Avatar hone his firebending would be a mistake. But… if he resisted this late, wouldn’t it be all that more suspicious? What would Azula do, if she needed to infiltrate a group and learn their movements, their plans?

It would be best to continue establishing trust. Besides, it wasn’t like Zuko had any skill to pass on; his father had told him his entire life that he was an embarrassment of a bender. A bitter part of him even wondered if instructing the Avatar would help weaken him, ultimately.

“Okay,” he agreed. “I’m not that good, but I’ll show you what I can.”
