Aang and Zuko went off into their own corner of the cave to spar, while the rest of the group sat on their bedrolls at a respectable distance, close enough to see and hear, but far enough to avoid the crossfire of their faux fight. Over the course of an afternoon spent sending nosy glances in their direction, Sokka watched as the cultivated image of the Fire Nation prince unravelled.

It started with the top half of Zuko’s outfit; the long, flowing sleeves weren’t conducive for sparring, so he rolled them up as best as he could, only to find that concentrating that enormous bulk of fabric around his upper arms did little to help his mobility. With a frustrated huff, Zuko shed the long robes to reveal the naked chest and high-waisted hakama pants underneath. Before anyone could get a good look, though, he transitioned into a fervor of punches and kicks that kept Aang duly distracted from the skin he’d exposed. Perhaps unlike all the other Fire Nation men, he was unused to being shirtless in public - an omega thing, Sokka supposed.

Next came the crown (or whatever the gold flamey thingy he wore in his hair was technically called). It flew off enough times that Zuko became visibly frustrated, then threw it onto the bedrolls with a clank. Then came the hair itself; Tui and La, if Aang had gone red-faced and dopey when Zuko took off his shirt, this was magnified by approximately a *thousand* when Zuko untied his topknot so he could gather his hair into a simple tail instead. There’d been a moment when Zuko held the tie in his teeth while he lifted the thick mass of night-black hair up off the back of his neck, where Aang had wobbled sea-sick on his feet, as if on the verge of fainting. As far as Sokka was concerned, only a monk could find the nape of someone’s neck a more erotic sight than their bare chest.

Sokka was so distracted by the effect Zuko had on Aang, he didn’t notice the scar until his sister pointed it out. She had been trying and failing to ignore those two, shooting them hateful glances in between stilted attempts at conversation with Toph and Sokka. But when Zuko pulled his hair up, she caught sight of the mangled bite mark on his neck.

Sokka knew for a fact that the expression that initially flickered over Katara’s face was one of concern. But she quickly hid this behind a veneer of disgust, lip curling, finger pointing as she called out to the prince, “What is *that* on your neck?”

Finished tying off his hair, Zuko cocked his head, drawing more attention to the scar in question. “You mean my mating mark?” For a man being demanded to explain a physical injury as though it was a revolting character flaw, he was surprisingly calm. Beside him, Aang had gone blank-faced, lips pursed in a tight line.

Katara’s eyes narrowed. “Is that exactly what it sounds like?”

“I guess. Every alpha leaves one on their omega partner when they’re… married,” Zuko said, substituting his choice of words at the last second. He seemed able to tell by Katara’s scowl that his explanation hadn’t cut it. With a curious look cast her way, he wondered aloud, “Do you not do that, in the South Pole?”

Katara shook her head, neglecting to mention that for the last several years, there hadn’t been a single alpha in their village except for Sokka. In a lot of ways, they had lost touch with what was considered normal for mating rituals even amongst their own people. Yet another thing lost to the war.

“That looks like a pretty deep scar. Didn’t it hurt when he did that to you?” Katara asked.

“Yes?” Zuko answered. “But it’s nothing to be worried about. It’s just an alpha acting on biological impulse. I’d think every nation would know how this worked.”

“Some little villages in the Earth Kingdom still do that,” Toph interjected, “but it’s not considered to be, like, civilized behavior.”

Although the prince tended towards impassivity, he couldn’t hide the twitch of his eyebrows when she said that. Sokka wondered if he was insulted, or just rethinking the things he took for granted as true.

“...It’s nothing,” Zuko repeated, voice skeptical. “My mother had one, as did her mother before her. It’s how you can tell taken omegas from single ones.”

“I’d think the scent change was enough,” Katara insisted, frowning. “That, or you could just *ask* a person what their marital status is. Why the hell would you ever need to scar somebody you supposedly love? And where everybody can see it! What, you’re so insecure about your ownership over your partner, you have to publicly injure them?”

Zuko’s face went beat red, and *now* it was obvious he was pissed. “I’m sorry you evidently don’t have sex education in the South, but biting is a normal response for an alpha during sex. There’s no fucked up deeper meaning to this scar. It just means I’m married.”

“Then why don’t alphas have to get one?” Katara challenged. “Admit it: it’s just a socially acceptable way to brutalize omegas!”

Now that the conflict had evolved, Aang snapped himself out of his stupor. “Katara, it’s a cultural difference, same as the spicy food. Let it go.”

“It’s not the same,” she insisted, fingers clenched over her knees. “Food is food, but this is *cruelty* . Don’t you see how ridiculously evil this country is? No wonder they’re storming across the earth, insisting this war is about progress - they don’t even know what healthy human relationships look like! It’s all about domination and submission with them!”

At that, Zuko’s face went positively rigid with anger. Ready to retort, he clenched his hands into fists at his sides, only to be derailed by an intense burst of orange light. Sparks jumped from his hands, where they landed sizzling in the small puddles that littered the stone floor of the cave.

Then just as quickly as it had appeared, Zuko’s fire fizzled out. A look of clear shock contorted his features; he lifted his hands to look at them, as though he hadn’t expected that response.

Katara crossed her arms over her chest. “I thought you *lost* your fire.”

“I did,” Zuko insisted, lowering his hands. He wasn’t looking at anyone as he walked across the cave, brow furrowed as if lost in thought.

“Then what was *that?* ” Katara piped up. “So you can’t summon your fire to train Aang, but you can summon it when you’re pissed at *me?* ”

Zuko didn’t reply. He approached the semi-dry corner where he’d left his robes and began pulling them back on.

“You’re not leaving, are you?” Aang asked him, stricken.

“I’m not going to stay where I’m not wanted,” Zuko said. Without meeting anyone’s eye, he made his way towards the cave’s entrance.

Aang followed after him, not sparing so much as a glance at his other friends as he passed them by. “Wait, Zuko, hold on…”

Katara almost stood to follow them, but Toph’s hand lighted on her shoulder, gently holding her down. “Let ‘em go, Sweetness.”

“Aang’s not thinking clearly. He’s about to step outside with his tattoos visible,” Katara groused.

“You’re not thinking clearly, either,” said Toph. “I understand not trusting Zuko. I even get that you think me and Sokka have been way too laissez-faire about him. But all that stuff you said, about his scar, about his relationships? That was a personal attack.”

Katara’s entire body tightened, and for a moment, it seemed that she, too, would start spewing fire. But then she slumped forward, burying her face in her hands. “I must be losing it if *you’re* being the voice of reason right now.”

Toph didn’t rise to the bait to tease or bicker as she normally would. Instead she just rubbed Katara’s back in small, comforting circles.

Sokka leaned back on his hands, musing. “Y’know, Zuko seems to have a de-aging effect on this group. He’s turned Aang into a lovesick teenager, and *you* into a finger-pointing toddler with no filter.”

He expected his sister to become furious with the revelation of Aang’s crush. Yet when she dropped her hands from her face, her expression was calm. “Aang’s only eighteen. I know it’s easy to forget when he’s the Avatar, but he *is* a lovesick teenager. Which is why I worry about him getting taken advantage of.”

Toph whistled. “Man. Lovesick barely cuts it. Their hearts go freaking *wild* when they’re around each other. And it’s been, what. Two days? Not even?”

“That’s what I’m *saying* ,” Katara sighed, frustrated. “We don’t *know* Zuko. A couple of kind acts don’t redeem him. He’s a member of the royal family. He has a direct line of power - he could stop this all if he wanted to, and instead he’s running around with the Avatar in secret!”

Sokka had to give her that. He’d also found himself wondering what on earth Zuko’s motives were. Was this a calculated political move? Or perhaps just a rebellious phase?

“...I don’t think it’s that simple,” Toph said after a while. “Royal family or not, I don’t think he actually has that much power to yield. Otherwise wouldn’t he have done more, like you said? Would he even *need* us?”

Katara huffed. “I don’t pretend to understand it, but there’s no way Aang’s… *fixation* could be good for us. Even if Zuko does turn out to be our ally, he’s married to a man who almost definitely isn’t.” She turned to her brother, eyes pleading. “Sokka, can’t you talk Aang out of this? For obvious reasons he can’t hear it from me *,* but he respects you. Maybe if you say something…”

Sokka raised an eyebrow. “Putting aside how impossible it is to talk anyone out of a crush. You want *me* to give Aang a speech about *not pursuing married royalty* ?” He crossed his arms over his chest. “Even if I *was* a hypocrite, he wouldn’t hear it from me.”

Speaking of Yue. Perhaps Sokka now understood why Aang had been asking about her earlier. He had to admit that if Aang was starting to develop feelings for Zuko, that was a cause for concern. Aang couldn’t even stay unbiased when dealing with Azula, and he’d only wanted to be her friend. Bringing romance into it would only further complicate things.

Not to mention there was a world of difference between competing with someone’s fiance versus their *husband* . The few whispers they’d heard about Zuko’s governor-husband had been… ominous, to say the least. Katara was right; the sort of man who was working to raze the island bare of the slightest hint of anti-empire rhetoric was not the sort of man who would protect them, should their secret come out. Or should the Avatar take what was his.

Maybe Sokka should talk to Aang, after all.

Zuko didn’t make it very far before Aang managed to catch up, using his airbending to carve his way across the beach, sand flying out of his way as he went. With a burst of speed, Aang maneuvered himself in front of Zuko, stopping the other boy in his tracks.

“Zuko, hold on. Let me say goodbye, at least!” he called out, spraying the other boy with sand as he came to a halt. Zuko only just barely raised his arms in defense, blocking most of the sand.

“...You cheated,” Zuko eventually answered, lowering his arms. “You used your bending to get ahead of me.”

“Only because I’m desperate not to leave things like this,” Aang said, exasperated. “You’ve got me airbending in plain sight just to get one last word in. So will you hear it, please?”

Zuko chewed the inside of his cheek as he deliberated. Then, “I’m… I’m sorry I’m not someone else.”

Aang blinked at him. “What?”

“I’m sorry I am who I am. I wish it could’ve been a palace guard to save you that day, or a servant, or ideally some - some earthbender revolutionary, who came to bust you out. I wish I wasn’t royalty; I wish I was someone less culpable.”

Aang didn’t seem mollified by this speech; only bewildered. “Zuko, I don’t want you to apologize for being you.”

“Katara does,” Zuko muttered.

“No, she really doesn’t.”

“Then what *does* she want?” Zuko demanded. “I don’t know what I can possibly do to make her stop hating me!” He punctuated this with one angry stomp in the sand, the muted impact and the petulance of the act serving only to embarrass him further.

Aang was clearly frazzled, his headband askew, his arms flung out in askance as he said, “Zuko, I don’t think even she knows. I mean, it’s not even just about you - she’s furious on behalf of everything she has seen, over everything the Fire Nation has done in her lifetime.”

They still hadn’t told him all that many details of their prior adventures; Zuko didn’t know what could possibly be *so* bad that Katara should have to form such a deep hatred of an entire country. He sniffed, turning away. “If it’s not about me, then she shouldn’t take it out on me.”

“I said it’s not *just* about you,” Aang said, exasperated. “It’s about you, and it isn’t about you! I get that it feels unfair, and - I get that just now, what she said was personal, and that was over the line. I’ll talk to her about it, I promise. But I followed you out here because I needed you to know that she’s coming from a good place, so it shouldn’t discourage you from coming back.”

Zuko reddened at the prospect. He hadn’t considered even for a second that he’d never return. He just couldn’t stand to be here right now, when someone so openly reviled him.

He cast his eyes aside. “You want me to keep coming back? But I have so little to teach you.”

“Are you kidding?” said Aang. “I’m going to blow my sifu away tomorrow, with how much you’ve fixed up my cat stance. At this rate, I’ll learn twice as fast.”

Zuko shook his head. He needed to shut this line of thinking down, for both their sakes. “You can only go so far playing around with stances. Eventually you’ll need to work with fire, and so long as I’m blocked, I’m going to make a terrible partner. You’re going to outpace me in no time, Aang.”

“You say that like you’ve lost your fire forever,” Aang said. “But you haven’t. You just need to practice. I mean, you did great with the chi work, earlier!”

“I did not,” said Zuko, rolling his eyes. “I barely held my flame for thirty seconds.”

“Well, for someone who hasn’t been able to summon their flame for a while, you were great,” Aang insisted. “Just like I thought you would be.”

He fixed Zuko with a smile; although he didn’t get one in return, he saw the corner of Zuko’s mouth wobble, slightly, like he was tempted.

“Please,” Zuko scoffed, and there was that smile, rueful though it was. “My chi’s pathetic. It’s always been weak, and it always will be.”

“Uh. Weak?” Aang’s brows shot up under his headband. “Zuko, you have an *excess* of chi. I was shocked when you told me you weren’t a bender; when we first met, I thought you were deliberately reaching out to me.”

Zuko frowned. “Reaching out to you?”

“Yeah. It’s like you have so much chi, it’s bursting out of you, reaching for anything and anyone around it. But I’m guessing you don’t do that on purpose.”

“No, I don’t…”

Musing over this new information, Zuko fell into silence. Aang spotted a few grains of sand glittering in the frontmost locks of his hair. He reached forward, brushing it out of his face, trying to ignore the way Zuko’s skin seemed to scorch his hand.

“I know my friends are a lot,” said Aang. “But you’ll get to know them, and we’ll get to know you, and eventually, we’ll build that trust. Just please know that you’re welcome here whenever you want.”

For the second day in a row, the Avatar was begging him to return. And with everything he still hoped to accomplish, who was Zuko to tell him no?

## Chapter 35

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

As he gets to know the Avatar and his friends, Zuko is forced to confront his views on his father as a ruler.

### Text

Someone keeps leaving a mount for him, so Zuko continues to ride down to the beach to see the Avatar. He and Aang talk for hours without even trying, and Zuko quashes the guilty feeling that rises up in him when he finds himself drawn in by the Avatar’s orbit by reminding himself that he is, after all, on a fact-finding mission. He needs to find out what sort of threat Aang poses to the royal family, and that means every detail he can get is critical.

So Zuko indulges himself in the long, private conversations exchanged, panting, in the aftermath of a good spar. Slick with sweat, casting tentative glances at Aang’s naked chest while they discuss intimate details of his past, Zuko is reminded of those first conversations with Zhao in their marriage bed. A getting-to-know-you phase conducted in heady proximity, too shy to look one another in the eye even as they spend most of their time together in states of undress.

Aang does not let on about his larger plans for the Fire Nation, but he does explain the mystery that had bothered Zuko the most since his reappearance: how an Air Nomad could be alive today. Shockingly enough, it turns out Aang was born almost twenty years before the attack on the Western Air Temple. He is over a hundred years old, predating the war itself.

“We were totally innocent of what was coming,” Aang says. He has been guided into a stance by the older prince, chest to back, their heartbeats parallel. “I came to my destiny fairly late. Brings a whole new meaning to the idea of ‘presenting,’ let me tell you, to expect only to show a second sex, and suddenly start shooting fire out of your hands.”

“How old were you when you found out you were the Avatar?” Zuko asks.

“About sixteen,” Aang answers.

Zuko whistles, watches how his breath makes the tiny hairs on Aang’s nape stand at attention. “Wow. That *is* late.”

Aang’s shoulders bob up and down. “The elders at the temple technically knew for a while. Because it was a time of peace, they had this idea in their heads that the only thing in need of protecting was my childhood.” He chuckles; it’s not a happy sound. “It all seems so pointless, now. Maybe if they’d have taken my childhood from me sooner, I could’ve come much further in my mastery of the elements. Maybe I could’ve stopped-”

With an exhale, Aang slides into his next stance, pivoting his body so his profile is finally visible again. He looks contemplative. “Never mind. All the ifs about what kind of Avatar I could’ve been back then are moot, now.”

Zuko watches the muscles in Aang’s back flex as he goes through a series of motions. He comes back to the question that started this musing: “How did you get here, then?”

Aang’s stance tightens. “While I was… traveling, I was caught in a storm. There was no visibility and the winds were too strong, so Appa ended up in the water. The last thing I really remember was being afraid of drowning, then just this… white light. I think the power of all the past Avatars came to me then, to protect us both.”

“The Avatar state,” Zuko supplies. He has done his reading.

Aang seems to relax at that. He lets go of his stance, fully turning towards Zuko with a small, careful smile. “Yeah. I froze us in the ice, then next thing I knew, it was a hundred years later, and Sokka and Katara had found us.”

It is an unbelievable story, but Zuko accepts it without question. After all, the supposedly extinct airbender tattoos are staring him in the face. He has seen Aang bend all four of the elements. And who else but the bridge between mankind and the spirit world could survive a century frozen in ice? No, Zuko doesn’t doubt the Avatar’s honesty even for a moment. Instead he thinks of the century separating their births, the thousands of miles between their homelands, the circumstances that lead them each to this place, to this moment.

It’s remarkable that they ever chanced upon one another at all.

Zuko’s lips quirk. “So *that’s* why you were convinced Kuzon was an acceptable name.”

Memory had shrouded Aang like a dour fog, and now Zuko’s teasing pulls him free. With a sunny smile, Aang insists, “Hey, when I was a kid, it was the most popular boys’ name in the Fire Nation.”

“Oh, really?”

“I personally knew a Kuzon!”

Zuko crosses his arms over his chest. “And is Kuzon the one who told you it was acceptable to tell everyone to *flameo?* ”

“Yes!” Aang’s grin is lost in an instant as he regards Zuko with a suspicious look. “Wait - don’t tell me that’s offensive?” He gasps, both hands flying to his mouth. “Have I been telling everyone to *fuck off?* ”

“No,” Zuko chuckles, “but you still haven’t made a very good impression regardless. It’s total gibberish.”

Aang brings a hand to his chin. “What about calling fellow firebenders ‘hotman?’ Is that a real thing?”

“What about *what?* ” Zuko squawks.

“Hotman!” Aang repeats. “It’s like a title, or maybe just a country-wide nickname?” He gives an exaggerated bow, addressing Zuko in a lower tone. “Good day, fellow hotman. How are your flameos?”

“That is *not* a thing,” Zuko insists. “Not even an old-timey thing. I think Kuzon may have hated you.”

They tease one another, eyes meeting and flitting away like birds in a dance, unable to hold one another so long as they want to keep the momentum in their wings, yet still desperate to meet with the barest brushing of feathers as they pass.

The fact they don’t touch is what retains the fantasy that this isn’t a flirtation. Not that they don’t feel moved to, hands naturally gravitating towards shoulders, fluttering backwards at the last second before the electric contact of skin to skin can bring the innocent illusion crashing down. (Zuko is unmoved by late night thoughts, burying them so deep during the day that all they breathe is dirt.)

Some time later, when they’re resting between spars, Zuko clears his throat. “Now that I’ve educated you on proper Fire Nation greetings… Maybe you can tell me a bit about the Air Nomads.”

Aang’s lips curl around the mouth of his canteen. “Yeah? What do you want to know?”

Zuko thinks of the airbender scrolls, heart giving a painful lurch at the remembrance of their loss. He supposes now is the time to test their authenticity. “What was your airbender training like?”

Aang thinks deeply for a moment. “...Well, there’s a lot of breathing exercises, like with firebending. Which means a lot of meditation.”

Zuko’s least favorite. “Did you have sparring sessions like this?” he asks, trying to lead the conversation towards airbender styles of combat.

Aang grimaces, shrugs. “No, not really.”

Zuko frowns. “Not even for the sake of learning evasion?”

“There are other ways to work on evasion that don’t involve fighting your peers. Like for one, we work on our speed, in general. Can’t get hit if they can’t catch you.” Aang’s eyes light up, suddenly. “Oh, and there’s the obstacle course!”

“Obstacle course?” From what Zuko’s been told, the Fire Nation army is sometimes trained using an obstacle course. There’s a pit full of spikes you have to leap over, a giant wall slathered with grease you have to try to climb up, a number of fights with higher-ranking recruits you must win to move on…

Aang holds his hands aloft, palms flat. “There’s a series of wooden panels set up on spokes so they turn all around you.” He twists his palms, demonstrating. “Try to barrel your way through the course, and you’ll *definitely* hit a few panels on the way. Instead, you need to master spiraling motions with your airbending. The only way to find a clear path through the panels is to find the right rhythm of movements that will push the panels out of your way while you simultaneously move carefully around them. Those spiral patterns are one of the core tenets of airbending.” Aang scratches his neck, grinning. “I got *walloped* on my first few tries, let me tell you.”

It was a clever, nonviolent means of training. Typical for a nation that supposedly valued every breath of life, to the point of refusing to eat animals.

Zuko hesitates before posing his next question, perhaps knowing the answer will sink low in his stomach like a stone. “So if your people avoided violence even in training your benders… How did it train its army?”

Aang gives a brief, quiet laugh; all air. “We didn’t have an army.”

“You’re sure? They didn’t even start one after you left?”

Aang scoffs. “For an entire people to change their view on violence, in a matter of the few short years between my disappearance and the war’s start? There’s no way. Never.”

Zuko thinks he couldn’t possibly know for sure. But there’s such conviction in Aang’s eyes.

The sinking feeling worsens.

---

It is just the two of them alone in the cave for much of the afternoon, but eventually Katara and Toph return, Katara’s expression souring the moment she sees Zuko. He directs his greetings at the less hostile of the two. “Hey, Toph. Is Sokka not with you?”

Sokka is personable in general, but he also has a keen handle on his sister’s moods. Zuko feels he needs all the allies he can get, although upon self-reflection, he feels guilty for thinking this way; after all, Katara is just one woman. He shouldn’t need an army of reinforcements to deal with her, but of the rest of the group, she is the only one to cut straight to the treachery in his heart. She even scowls at Zuko now, as if divining his thoughts.

“Sokka’s off doing his own thing,” Toph answers.

Zuko frowns. “Are you sure it’s a good idea for you all to split up like that? You’re in enemy territory, after all, and he’s the only nonbender.”

“Well, that’s partly why he’s learning to…”

Katara clicks her tongue, a clear *shut up* , and Toph trails off. So whatever Sokka is off doing, they definitely don’t trust Zuko enough to tell him. Fine - he won’t press.

Zuko and Aang try to get back into the momentum of training, but it’s harder with an audience. Aang is easily distracted, wanting to make conversation with his friends, and Zuko is unsure how to keep him focused without seeming like a hardass, so he lets him go. He isn’t Aang’s real teacher. He doesn’t have true authority over what he learns and how fast he learns it. If anything, Zuko should be welcoming the distractions. The Avatar improves in leaps and bounds; he’ll be a real threat to Zuko’s father any day now.

They gather in a pack, Zuko and Katara putting as much acceptable distance between themselves as they can without being cut out of the conversation. They’d love to ignore each other as much as possible, but Aang, perhaps anxious for his friends to like each other, says to Katara, “You know, I think Zuko’s a better teacher than Sifu Shang down at the school. I feel like everything makes more sense when Zuko explains it.”

“That’s nice,” Katara says, flatly.

Toph flashes a grin into the void. “Would you say Zuko’s a better bending teacher than Katara?”

The question makes everyone visibly uncomfortable. Not looking at any one particular person, Aang hems and haws. “Oh, well, they’re both good. Just in different ways.”

“Yeah, but if you had to rank us,” says Toph, impervious to all glares and alarmed looks that might be thrown her way. “I don’t really care about any of the old guys, but of like, me, Katara, and Zuko, who would you say is the best and the worst?”

Katara and Zuko’s body language has gone positively jagged. “You’re all amazing teachers,” Aang placates, hoping they’ll relax.

“Yeah, yeah.” Toph waves dismissively. “But of our super high caliber, who’s the *best* of the best? It’s totally me, right?”

“Sure, Toph,” Aang relents, sighing.

She thrusts her fists into the air in triumph, and Katara quips, “He only gave it to you because you wanted it so badly.”

“He still gave it to *me* , sweetheart, so I’ll take it!”

Toph doesn’t push the subject on who is the worst teacher, and everyone eventually relaxes again. Aang fills the silence with some interesting things he has noticed in town. Apparently on his way to his lessons today, he witnessed two women challenging each other to an Agni Kai. He’s already somewhat familiar with the concept from that troublesome Kuzon, but he doesn’t know much beyond the fact it’s some sort of honor duel.

“It seemed like an insane reaction to what happened,” Aang says. “I mean, you’re really going to fight someone to the death just because their dragon moose knocked over your fruit stand?”

“Sounds like a macho pissing contest,” Katara huffs.

“True,” Aang agrees, “but honestly the weirdest part was who started fighting - like, the omega guy was clearly the one driving the cart, but then his mate essentially *leapt* on the owner of the fruit stand the moment she demanded reparations. It was like the omega just faded into the background of the alphas fighting.”

“I’m sure that alpha thinks of that omega as her property to defend,” says Katara, mouth slanted in disapproval. For a beta, she seems very preoccupied with omega rights in the Fire Nation.

Zuko shrugs. “Acts of aggression are gendered in this country. Omegas are supposed to be… not peacemakers, because they’re supposed to support their mate’s decision to fight, but they should be docile above all else. They’re not even permitted to participate in Agni Kai. Usually if they commit some wrong, an omega’s mate will fight for them.” Zuko pauses, looking nervously at Katara. “But it’s, um, still all macho pageantry. Totally a pissing contest, like Katara said.”

He can’t tell if she approves; he expects her to be impressed by his position, maybe even surprised, but she's hard to read, her face betraying no emotion. “Weird,” is all Toph says.

The conversation moves on to other idle things. It’s almost as though Toph waits for the exact moment Katara looks loose and relaxed before she starts to stir shit again.

“So - Sparky. Not to slap the camelephant in the room on its hindquarters, but what *is* your deal, anyway?”

It takes Zuko a moment to realize “Sparky” means him. “Sorry, what camelephant?”

Toph gestures vaguely. “Well, you know. You’re the son of the enemy, but you’re helping us. What’s up with that? Like, what’s your angle?”

All at once, Katara’s expression hardens. Zuko looks to Aang, perhaps a bit desperately, and finds the Avatar gazing somewhat thoughtfully at the wall opposite.

“…Not that I don’t appreciate all your help so far, but I can’t say I’m not curious as well,” Aang admits.

Zuko should have prepared an answer for this question ages ago. He fumbles for a lie, his voice sounding stupid to his on ears. “I mean, I… I don’t have a real reason, I just…”

When Zuko trails off long enough without elaborating, Aang gently leans in; “It’s okay - I know you’re one of the good guys. You’ve sided with us, after all.”

“Yeah, but like, to what end?” Toph asks. “Are you looking to show up your sister, or gather power for yourself?”

That’s an easy answer, at least. Zuko shakes his head vehemently. “I don’t want power for myself. Omegas can’t rule.”

“Anyone can rule if they drum up enough support,” says Toph. “Coups aren’t legal, but they happen, and they work.”

Zuko shakes his head again, heart thumping wildly in his chest at the prospect of such upheaval. Is that what *this* group is planning? A coup? “That’s not my aim.”

“You really don’t want *anything* from us?” Toph crosses her arms. “Call me skeptical, but you’ve gotta’ have more motivation than that.”

Zuko fumbles, looking at Aang. He gazes back with those gentle gray eyes, head inclining with the slightest nod of encouragement. Looking at him, it’s easier to shut out Katara’s insistent glare, Toph’s probing questions. Zuko feels much safer held in Aang’s gaze, and it is in this safety that he is able to think clearly.

“I believe in the Avatar,” Zuko says. “I believe there’s a reason he’s here with us, now. I believe that if he disappeared again, it would be a terrible loss. So I want to keep him as safe as possible and I want to help him in any way I can. Even if I don’t know entirely what he aims to do, I. I want to help him do it.”

Aang’s resulting smile makes Zuko feel lit from within. It would be the perfect moment, if only they were alone to share it.

“Are you kidding me?” Katara asks. She looks between Aang and Zuko questioningly, as if waiting for some revelation. “Aang. You can’t be blindly falling for this?”

Katara looks Zuko dead in the eye. “You talk about changing the world, but do you understand we’re out to depose *you* ?”

He feels as though she is staring at him so deeply as to see the blood slosh inside his veins. She’s talking about his royal lineage. His bending. His race.

“You’re not deposing *me* , specifically,” Zuko protests. He isn’t the one with the power.

“Fine, then!” Katara snaps, arms crossing over her chest. “Not you, but *your* nation. *Your* family. *Your* *father!* What they’re doing to the rest of the world is evil, and we’re going to stop you.”

“I’m not with them in the capital, am I?” Zuko points out, perhaps defensively. “I’m here with you all. I’m helping you all as best as I can.”

“So you’re ready to fight them, if need be?” Katara counters. “What if you had to imprison Azula?”

At that, Aang looks as shocked as Zuko feels, his eyes going wide, face white as a sheet. When the prince is too flabbergasted to give an answer, Katara presses on: “What if you had to let Aang kill your father?”

Zuko’s heart races in his chest. Here it is. His worst nightmare realized; the Avatar is plotting his father’s end. He has no idea how to respond to this without giving his true aims away.

Luckily, Aang steals the spotlight, his face now alight with anger. “Katara, we’ve talked about this. I’m not killing anyone!”

He punctuates his point by standing, and the effect of his height over hers is alarming. Zuko has never seen the Avatar like this, so physically intimidating. Yet Katara glares up at him like an equal, the air between their locked eyes nearly electric. How many times have they had this argument? Do they regularly discuss brutalizing Zuko’s family members? What could drive them to consider such savagery?

Katara looks away first, trembling with frustration. “We’re not arguing about that right now, Aang! Spirits, *whatever* we do to remove the Fire Lord from power, Zuko needs to get it through his thick skull that there’s a real cost to this! We can’t afford to keep him here if he’s a weak link who will chicken out and betray us for his family at the last second!”

Zuko fights the heat of embarrassed anger that rushes to his face. “I’m not going to betray Aang,” he says, but it feels like a lie.

“Not even for *family?* ” Toph asks. She isn’t coming in as hot as Katara, but the skepticism is clear from her arched brows. “No matter how deeply you believe in Aang, you might have to directly oppose them. That’s not easy for anybody.”

“And there’s no alternative?” Zuko asks.

“Not unless you think we could reason with him,” Aang says. He says it seriously, with no small amount of hope. It’s clearly a prospect he has suggested before; Toph openly grimaces, while Katara narrows her eyes.

Zuko tries to picture it. It would be ideal to find a solution where neither the Avatar nor his father has to come to harm. But to think of Ozai letting Aang speak, rather than locking him up the moment he crosses the throne room threshold…

“…I don’t know,” Zuko murmurs. “Maybe, with the right argument. I don’t really have all the answers.”

Toph scoffs. “No offense, Aang, but I don’t think we’re talking our way out of a hundred years of war. You don’t reprogram that kind of thinking with one conversation.”

“Exactly,” Katara agrees, looking pointedly at Zuko.

Much of Aang’s anger has already dissolved. His eyes are still hard, his posture sure, but he seems more consumed with determination than anything. He holds out his hand, staring into his palm as if his lifeline contains all the answers he needs.

“I know it’s a long shot,” Aang concedes, “but I have to believe there’s a better way. In the meantime I’ll prepare for the worst case,” he says, a flame flickering to life in his hand, “while keeping the alternatives just as ready.”

Katara shakes her head, mouth rigid. “Even if he’s willing to be reasoned with, the Fire Lord should be punished for what he’s done. He might not not have started the war, but the Earth Kingdom has continued to be torn apart under his reign. He should suffer for that, and for every other parent, child, and loved one killed in the name of *progress* .”

She sits with her back straight, her fists on her knees. Kneeling there with such regal confidence, draped in reds, she oddly enough resembles one of the female Fire Lords painted in the Great Hall.

“He’s - he’s culpable, but he didn’t do all that killing himself,” Zuko says, lamely. “Doesn’t any responsibility lay with his armies, for their own decisions? He’s only been in power for two years. Maybe he doesn’t know the extent of it. What he’s contributing to.”

Katara looks at him with a terrible fury burning in her eyes. Zuko almost expects her to explode, the air growing tense and silent as they all wait for her to speak. When she finally does, her words, although heated, are controlled.

“It’s all so far away to you,” she says. “Men in boats sailing to other countries. Little skirmishes. The losers pouting, then learning to live with it, making peace with, or even *marrying* the enemy, and using his technology to make life *better* . We saw that propaganda all over the Earth Kingdom.” Her face lights up in a mockery of joy as she parrots the many flyers: “‘The Fire Nation brings progress!’ ‘Clean water and steam power and order!’”

Her expression clouds back over, voice darkening in turn. “I need you to understand that that’s not the reality. Sokka and I grew up with *nothing* . We don’t have any great cities in the south. How could we ever build one? Our people were massacred to prevent the next Avatar from appearing. All those wonderful inventions - steam-powered transport over land, made into tanks to trample our villages. Armored boats to attack our shores. Everything you people touch becomes a weapon.”

“My father couldn’t have known-”

“ *Our mother died to protect me* ,” Katara snaps, not letting Zuko talk over her, voice filled to the brim with pain and longing and fury. “ *My* father left us when we were young to try to help the resistance. We could’ve spent all that time together, but instead he threw it all away to fight for a better future for us all.”

When next Zuko is brave enough to meet Katara’s eye, her expression no longer seems frightening to him. It’s not that her expression has changed at all; there’s still that hardness, those narrowed brows and mouth set in a firm line. The difference is that now Zuko sees Katara more clearly. Sees at her core a child who has lost her entire life to violence, a violence she fears will never end. She is angry, yes, but at the core of that anger is an immense pain.

“Countless lives are impacted by decisions tyrants make thousands of miles away from them,” Katara says. “So I frankly don’t give a shit if your father realizes the extent of his actions or not; what he has done is untenable, and he needs to answer for it.”

And she looks, now, at Aang. “ *That* is why Ozai shouldn’t be reasoned with. It would be spitting in the face of everyone who has died in the past hundred years.”

Aang’s lips become a thin line. “I know. I’m not suggesting we become his friends. But to repay blood in blood… The Air Nomads don’t believe in putting more violence into the world.”

“We’re not getting into this right now.” Katara stands and brushes herself off with finality. “But I’ll say it again: sometimes to prevent more violence, you need to kill a killer.”

---

Katara marches off, shortly followed by a stumbling Toph. Embarrassed, Zuko buries his face in his hands.

“I know she can be intense,” Aang starts, ready with a million excuses, but he quiets when Zuko raises a hand, asking him to stop.

“It’s not that,” he sighs. “I just…”

His stomach is in knots. This girl has professed hatred for his father, a desire to see his reign and his life end *,* and still, Zuko feels bad for *her* . He keeps thinking about what she said about her mother, about the naked desperation on her face as she told her story, and he can’t shake the feeling that he is doing something terrible.

What is the point of Zuko toying with the Avatar like this? Perhaps this will ultimately benefit the empire. Perhaps he will prove to his father, to Zhao, to Azula his worth, but does that change how Zuko has snaked his way into Katara’s friend group? Does that change the fact he is torturing this girl just by being here?

“I feel so *bad* ,” Zuko admits plaintively. He flings his hands from his face with palms upwards, as if beseeching Agni for answers. They cannot see the sun for the ceiling of the cave, but that’s no matter, because another deity answers his call.

Aang grabs his hand and squeezes it reassuringly. Zuko fights with himself only for an instant before he gives in, squeezing back, chest fluttering when he feels Aang’s heartbeat in the soft flesh between thumb and pointer. Zuko’s hands are by no means small, but Aang’s dwarf even his.

“It’s going to be alright,” Aang says, soothing.

Zuko shakes his head. “You should hate me. All I do is say stupid, heartless things to your real friends.”

“Everyone makes mistakes,” Aang insists, and it’s as though his small burst of defensive anger earlier didn’t even happen. “I know you weren’t speaking out of cruelty. You can always apologize later, if you like.”

There can’t be such a simple answer to these tangled and painful feelings, yet Aang says it with such confidence that Zuko almost believes it’ll be enough. He doesn’t say anything back; he just enjoys this feeling, this moment, this physical contact.

---

There are good days, when Zuko gets to the village without incident, and is able to spend a whole afternoon with Aang. It is a time of delusion, for sure, but a happy delusion, where Zuko is able to forget the limitations placed on him, on his body.

Then there are bad days. Days preceded by nights spent bent in half, retching until his ribs are sore. Days where he can barely keep anything down, let alone sway pendulously atop a smelly animal for miles down a mountainside with the sun beating on his back. Days where reality comes rushing back to greet him, to remind him of the impending baby.

All that anguish at Aloki’s hand seems to have been for nothing, because Ama can read Zuko with a single glance. This morning when he sees him, he tuts, “You’re positively green! Is the baby giving you trouble?”

Zuko wants to deny it, but in the face of such motherly fuss, it’s hard not to feel sorry for himself. “I couldn’t sleep, it was so bad,” he says, and Ama coos and dotes.

“Oh, how awful! I was just like that when I was pregnant with Yan.” A cool hand is pressed against his forehead, more a reflexive, motherly gesture than one with purpose. “You must stay home with me, Prince Zuko.”

Zuko wants nothing less. He stands, eager to leave, protesting, “No, it’s fine…” Then the floor seems to pitch beneath his feet, another wave of nausea rolling over him.

Ama chides Zuko, all but man-handling him back into his seat by the window. “You can’t go riding in this condition! I *insist* you stay here.”

Zuko turns his face away from Ama to hide his disappointment. With a sigh, he settles an elbow on the window pane and fixes his gaze on the grounds outside, not really seeing them so much as imagining the beaches that lay far beyond.

It’s early enough that the light coming through the window is a pure white haze, casting the reed room in stark contrast. Wei lurches down the hall, half his face black with shadow as he approaches his step parent.

“I’ve made arrangements for the day. I still need to be in and out around lunch, but otherwise if you need anything…”

Ama waves dismissively at his step-son. “You don’t have to stay home on my account, Wei. I’m feeling much better.”

Something akin to worry knits Wei’s solemn brow. “You were in a bad sort last night. I’d really rather not leave it to chance.”

Zuko was awake all night, but he was across the grounds, in the building that houses the baths, so he missed whatever it is they’re talking about. He asks, “Are you alright, Ama?”

“I’m fine, both of you, really,” Ama says, rolling his eyes for an excuse not to hold anyone’s gaze. Now that Zuko gets a good look at him, Ama looks gaunt and sullen, his eyes nearly bruised by the dark bags beneath them.

Wei must see it too, because he presses: “Are you *certain* you’re alright?”

“I know I seem very delicate, but I’ve endured terrible hardship all my life. A little back pain won’t end me. Besides!” Ama places his hands on Zuko’s shoulders. “Prince Zuko is rife with baby pains today, so I will be wallowing in good company.”

Until now, Wei hasn’t paid Zuko any mind. Once he has looked the young prince over, he evidently finds him lacking, his lip giving the slightest ripple of disgust. “Given Rio’s absence, I’d feel safer if the both of you had a chaperone. What if you find yourself immobile again, Ama? Zuko can’t possibly have the strength to get you back to bed.”

This last comment is pointed sharply at them both - an indictment on the fact Ama is standing in the middle of the reed room when he should be in bed, and an indictment on Zuko’s physical capability as a pregnant omega.

Ama scoffs and comes to his son-in-law’s defense. “Prince Zuko is quite strong, actually! He can walk for miles without collapsing.”

“Can he,” asks Wei, unenthused.

“He can,” Ama insists. “In fact, he has walked all the way down to the village and back - and he’d probably do that every day if given the chance!”

The admission causes the hair on the back of Zuko’s neck to prickle with uncertainty, an animal sensing danger. Wei must know he has been venturing out of the house, given the fact he keeps leaving a mount for Zuko to use. But that doesn’t mean Zuko is overly open about what he’s doing in the village. He avoids mentioning it to the family in the hopes Zhao won’t find out and react adversely to this little slice of freedom.

“…I’m sure Zhao would be so thrilled to hear that,” Wei says, his dry words sending a thrill of fear through Zuko’s chest. “In any case. I would feel better looking after you myself, Ama.”

Ama gives a hell of a sigh before taking one of Wei’s hands in his, squeezing it. “Well, if you *must* , I won’t stop you. Better you than Yan, at least. That boy hovers incessantly.”

Zuko is already anxious enough that he is missing the Avatar’s company for the day, but to do so under such unusual scrutiny…

If what Yan does is hover, then Wei can only be said to lurk. He does not stay in one place for long, but he darkens the doorways of the house like a shadow, casting meaningful looks Ama’s way until he relents to being helped up to his bedroom. (Zuko notices him rubbing his lower back incessantly before that, bracing his knuckles against the base of his spine once he’s finally forced to make his slow ascent of the staircase.) Zuko hopes once Ama is gone, Wei will haunt the second floor to remain close to him. But when Zuko has again wretched the contents of his stomach and returned to the house, there Wei is, reading in the corner, a fixture.

Zuko doesn’t want to hide in his room. He’s sick of feeling like a prisoner in his own home, so he drags a chair out onto the veranda to mope in the fresh air and sunshine. And, confirming Zuko’s suspicion that he’s being followed, Wei gradually makes his way outside, too. Like a fog, he spills from the open door, drifting towards Zuko without ever getting too close. He barely disguises the fact he has no reason to be outside; he just grips the railing of the veranda and stares blankly out into the trees.

Zuko would be determined to ignore Wei if he didn’t otherwise feel like death. The book in his hands is doing little to distract him, the tiny text jumbling across the page as his nausea grows worse. So he says to Wei, “It’s, uh. Really nice of you to stay and look after Ama.”

“It isn’t nice,” Wei says.

Zuko isn’t sure if he’s just being contrary, so he replies, “Sure, it is.”

“It isn’t. I’m merely fulfilling my duty as the only beta son.”

Zuko considers this. “But is it really your duty, if Ama isn’t your real parent?”

That verbal fumble earns him quite the glare. “Ama may not be biologically mine, but he is in fact a *real* parent. He cares for me more than my own father ever did.”

Zuko looks away, sufficiently cowed, although he knows little of the heat beneath Wei’s words. With the exception of Iroh’s late wife having been married once before, the royal family is very traditional. While many past Fire Lords had children on the side with lovers, had an entire second family that was spoken of in whispers and treated as less than their legitimate ones, Zuko’s father had no interest in paramours. Even after Ursa left, he refused to remarry, to have more children legitimately. So Zuko doesn’t know what it is like to have to blend two or more families together. That a family could be fraught by bloodlines, or stranger yet, not follow them at all… the thought is alien to him.

“But you don’t even have to do any of this. Yan is willing to take care of Ama for you,” Zuko protests. He realizes a second too late that he probably shouldn’t be using this line of reasoning, considering he only knows this because he eavesdropped on the brothers late at night.

If Wei notices the misstep, he doesn’t care to comment on it. “Yan has childish notions about everyone’s place in the world. He would call himself progressive; I would say he’s throwing away a gift.”

This response only confuses Zuko. “A gift?”

There is a dragonfly so large it seems to make the air hum with its approach. Wei watches it jerk towards them, then away, spiraling up and up until it’s lost in the canopy of leaves.

Wei says, “A secondary sex is a gift. Alphas and omegas get to participate in society. Your romantic affairs are the hinge upon which entire political movements turn. Find the right partner, and you’re unstoppable. Find the wrong one…”

He trails off. Zuko almost expects Wei to fix him with a judgmental look, to imply that *he* is the wrong partner for Zhao, but Wei seems to have forgotten he’s not alone. He just keeps staring up at the patch of trees where the dragonfly disappeared.

“Being an omega doesn’t feel like a gift,” Zuko says. “More like a weight. I was born with a thousand rules and expectations in place, and now I have to keep them all above the tide without drowning.”

Wei heaves a sigh. “You omegas are always sniveling about your lot in life. But you don’t realize the value of what you have. When I was finally getting used to the idea I’d never present, I of course used to wish I’d become an alpha. Perhaps I could’ve served by Ozai’s side as his right-hand man. His… general, his servant, whatever he wanted of me.”

Insulted by Wei’s dismissal, Zuko jumps on this line of logic. “That’s stupid - you don’t need to be an alpha to do any of the stuff you just said! You can do all of that *now*, as a beta.”

To his surprise, Wei nods at him. “That’s exactly it, Prince Zuko. I wallowed for years before I realized that the odds were always stacked against me. My life wouldn’t be any better if I were an alpha, because your father has no use for an alpha. A business partner can be easily disposed of, as can a servant, as can all the rest.” He looks at his hands, eyes angry, eyes sad. “A spouse, on the other hand. The mother of your children. There’s no casting that aside.”

Zuko has spent his time in Kirachu thinking of Wei as an ominous, menacing figure. In meeting that cold, almost metallic gaze now, he realizes he was wrong. Zhao’s oldest brother isn’t frightening. He is mourning a friendship that died decades ago. He is jealous for a life he thinks he should have had, a life he has entirely made up while wallowing in solitude.

Wei isn’t menacing. He is pitiful.

“You’re wrong,” Zuko utters. Wei looks up at him as if confused why he is even talking, and Zuko takes this opportunity to admit something to himself he has never said aloud. “My father cast my mother aside without a second thought. When she went missing, he hardly cared. He didn’t fight to get her back.”

For once, Wei drops his usual glare for a round-eyed look of surprise. Zuko swallows, carrying on before he loses his nerve. “No one is important enough to my father to be invaluable. He always finds some fault, eventually.”

“Or you all fail him, eventually, and deserve whatever vitriol you get.” Wei’s lip curls back from his teeth in a full-blown snarl. “ *I* wouldn’t have made whatever mistakes your mother did. No doubt you inherited all your sniveling from her.”

Strangely, the slight at his mother doesn’t hurt Zuko’s feelings, nor does it anger him. He feels like he’s arguing with a child. Wei’s words are too far removed from reality to make a real impact.

Zuko feels a twinge in his stomach. Wincing, he lays a hand on it, rubs soothing circles. “Then I guess *you’ve* made plenty of mistakes. He abandoned you for years.”

Wei bristles. “You f-” He stops himself short of lobbing obscenities at a prince. Fury rangled, he says, “Regardless of the past, I’ve been awarded a second chance. I know how precious that is. I’m not going to squander it!”

“You’re only back on speaking terms because my marriage to Zhao made you useful again,” Zuko says, flatly. He’s too busy staring out into the yard now to see Wei’s face, but he feels how stiff his body gets, sees the jerky retreat out of the corner of his eye. By the time Zuko looks again, the specter is gone, and he has the veranda to himself again.

---

Sokka finds it painful to watch Aang on days like these. This is the third or fourth time Zuko hasn’t been able to make it out to spend time with them, but the experience hasn’t made it any easier. Aang stands several yards from the mouth of the cave, half-heartedly making his way through his kata with loose limbs, neck forever craning this way and that in search of Zuko’s approaching dragon moose. It never appears on the horizon, and Aang’s kata only get worse. He barely lifts his arms and legs to move. It’s like watching the saddest dance in the corner of the emptiest party.

After some vicious elbowing from Katara, Sokka agrees to talk to Aang, on the condition that she and Toph go somewhere else. It’s bad enough they won’t just do this themselves, but the fact they want to micromanage *how* he does this is unbearable. Once they’re on their way, he sidles up to Aang and throws an arm around his shoulders.

“Feeling alright, bud?”

“Huh? Yeah, I’m fine,” Aang says, distractedly. Still watching the horizon.

Sokka can’t fight the fond smile back from his face, as inappropriate as it is. Is this what he looked like when he was mooning over Yue? It’s cute. Annoying, but cute.

“I take it Zuko didn’t come today?”

“What?” asks Aang. He then gives a mawkish performance, looking around the cave, pretending to only just gather whose absence it is that Sokka’s talking about. “Uh, no. I guess I hadn’t noticed.”

Sokka gestures to the mostly empty cave. “Hey, drop the half-hearted training. All your teachers are gone. Let’s hang out, maybe go for a walk in town.”

Aang shrugs, casting another look at the horizon. “Uh huh. We can hang out here, though, can’t we?”

He probably just wants to stay on the minuscule chance that Zuko’s still coming. Fine; Sokka can work with that. At least if they don’t go to the village, they won’t bump into Toph and Katara on their date, which means they won’t continue to tell Sokka how to broach this conversation.

Sokka’s not going to get Aang to move from the best vantage point on the beach, so he compromises. He grabs some blankets for them to sit on, as well as Aang’s shirt. “Put this on for me, will you? It stresses me out when you run around with your tattoos out.”

“Right. You’re just still secretly in love with me, and can’t stand to be so close to all *this* ,” Aang says, gesturing at his naked torso. Sokka makes a go of a sputtering, indignant denial, but he’s somewhat relieved about the teasing. It means Aang’s got enough pep left in him that this talk shouldn’t be a total downer.

“Nope, nope, the days of crushing on every omega that crosses my path are far behind me!” Sokka insists, raising his hands in defense. “As for *you* .”

Aang blinks. “As for me?”

Okay, there had to have been a smoother way to work this in, but sometimes once Sokka’s mouth starts running, it just has to finish the marathon. “Well, *you* don't seem to be over your falling-for-every-other-omega-you-meet phase.”

Aang’s mannerisms are usually loose and willowy; now he snaps straight as a matchstick and says, “I don’t know what you mean.”

“Really?” Sokka presses. “You don’t know about Zuko? Omega prince of the Fire Nation? Lustrous dark hair, cheekbones for days, Katara’s mortal enemy? He comes here fairly often, I’d think you two would’ve met.”

Aang's face flushes with color. “ *Obviously* I know him. I’m not in love with him.”

Sokka startles. “I didn’t say *love* , Aang. I thought this was still a baby crush, like, squashable by a bad haircut or a stern talking-to. Are you in *love* with him?!”

“No!” Aang protests, but he’s red all the way up to his hairline. Oh, they are completely *fucked* .

“You can’t be in love with Zuko!” Sokka all but shouts, panicking now. “You know he’s-”

“The Fire Lord’s son,” Aang sighs, going boneless as he falls to the blankets. “A foreign prince from an enemy nation. I *know,* Sokka.”

“I was going to say *married* , but all that other stuff is pretty valid, too.”

Aang is looking red-faced and miserable. This is already a disaster, so Sokka might as well dive in. He flops onto the blankets beside Aang.

“You know *I’m* supportive of true love and all, but like, it’s not going to look great to all the other countries if you show up to the world council with a Fire Nation prince on your arm. You think Katara is hard to convince? Just wait for a whole horde of disapproving old men to see your little love affair.”

Aang raises an eyebrow. “World council?”

“ *Obviously* we’re going to have to start some kind of international summit after you save the world, to maintain peace past the first few months,” Sokka huffs, arms crossed. “Anyway, if you hook up with the Fire Lord’s son, people are really going to question how clear-headed your diplomacy skills are, not to mention the near-term danger that’s gonna put us in… You think this governor sounds like a psycho *now?* Wait til he hears the Avatar’s been romancing his husband behind his back!”

Aang rubs the bridge of his nose. “...Romancing implies it’s mutual, but it isn’t.” A watery pause. “And even if it was. I *know* it would never work out. For all the reasons you gave and then some.”

Sokka notes the heaviness of Aang’s voice with very little triumph. After all, unrequited love is nothing to celebrate. He gives Aang a brotherly pat on the shoulder. “It’s okay, buddy. Join the royally broken hearts club.”

In any case, Aang has proven that even though he does have feelings for him, he’s not thinking of romancing his firebending tutor (for now), and that’s really all Sokka needs. It’s time to switch to other topics.

Sokka flings his hands out, pointing to the distance beyond which the village lays. “I didn’t see you leave for your training once today. Are you so obsessed with Zuko that you forgot to go?”

Aang rolls his eyes, but it doesn’t stop his blushing. “I’m beginning to think that I should switch teachers. Sifu Shang got me onto the basics, but I feel like I’m quickly outpacing the class. I’ll need a private tutor so I can go as fast as I need.”

Ah. The part of this journey they were all somewhat afraid of. When it comes time to put the safety of the Avatar into another stranger’s hands. At least thanks to Pakku and Zuko, they have a list of candidates.

“Okay. Well, between the two lists we have, we’ve got to be able to find someone trustworthy, right?” Sokka says.

Aang casts his eyes downward. “I know it’ll piss Katara off, but I don’t want to use Pakku’s list.”

“Uh, why?” Sure, the old fart was obstinate about training a pair of omegas, but Katara and Aang *had* won him over in the end, and Sokka didn’t think they still bore him any ill will.

Aang shrugs. “The North Pole has been closed for so long. Even if all those guys were once Pakku’s friends, there’s no way his recommendations are up-to-date.”

“You’re worried they’re all dead?” Sokka asks, scratching his neck. “I guess they’d be pretty old.”

“…Or imprisoned,” Aang considers, wincing. “Either way, I don’t think it’s worth it.”

“I could ask Master Piandao if he has any recommendations? He’s pretty cool,” Sokka says, but Aang waves him off.

“It’s fine. I’ll reach out to the first person on Zuko’s list.”

At the mere mention of the prince, Sokka heaves a sigh. Katara will definitely see this as favoritism for her sworn enemy. However, the firebending school was Zuko’s suggestion, and that worked out fine. Aang just has to be extra careful to conceal his identity in close quarters, now.

“Okay,” Sokka says. “Before we totally rule out Pakku’s guys, let’s at least compare the two lists. If they happen to overlap, those will be the absolute safest choices to start with, since they’ll have double the glowing endorsements.”

Aang agrees, and they return to their encampment inside the cave. It takes them a few minutes to find the lists, one crumpled up deep inside Katara’s pack, and the other carefully folded inside of Aang’s belongings. Sokka reads names off Pakku’s list and Aang adds a checkmark to Zuko’s if there’s a match.

“Minoru Takaki of Kirachu.”

“Shit - Zuko’s list doesn’t have locations,” Aang says. He takes a while to scan the names. “I do see Minoru Takaki here, though.”

“Nice.” Might as well go through the rest, especially if Pakku’s information on where they live has become outdated. Sokka reads on, sure he’s butchering the pronunciation of each name. “Shoji Izanagi of Ma’Inka?”

“Nah, not-” Aang stops himself, eyes locked on a name. “Never mind, here!”

“Kyou Hayashida of Kirachu?”

A pause. Then, “Here.”

Sokka frowns. Three in a row is a pretty weird coincidence. But not impossible, right? “Ren Xueqing of Capital Island?”

Another pause. Then Aang says, “Here.”

“Tang Yuan of Shuhon?”

“...That’s also here.”

They look at one another for one perplexed beat, before holding their lists up right next to each other so they’re easier to study.

At first glance, they couldn’t look more different. Pakku’s handwriting is neat and precise, laying everything out in two orderly columns, while Zuko’s writing is cramped, written on a slope. But aside from an illegible entry and a couple names on each list with no match, there’s no mistaking it.

Zuko and Pakku’s lists are identical.

## Chapter 36

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Zuko gets a chance to prove himself to the Avatar and his friends.

#### Chapter Notes

Trigger warning for domestic violence...

### Text

“Want to play a game of pai sho with me?”

Zuko looks up from where he’s been bent over the veranda railing to see Yan, and wonders how long he’s been standing there. Zuko has been listlessly hanging over the railing for quite some time now, hoping the breeze on his face will afford him some respite from his morning sickness. On the grass below is his breakfast, but he can’t look at that, or all his attempts to break his nausea will be for nothing.

Perhaps it is a good day for Yan. He has addressed Zuko in a cheery voice, and seems not to lean so heavily on his cane. Under the opposite arm, the pai sho board is tucked. Zuko is almost impressed he’s able to carry it out here himself, but then chastises himself for this thought; Yan is disabled, but not helpless. While unwieldy, the board is not so impossible for a grown man to carry.

“I’m terrible at pai sho,” Zuko remarks, self-consciously wiping his mouth with the back of his sleeve. He’d never have used his clothing as a napkin a few months ago, but pregnancy is just one indignity after another.

Yan shrugs. “Regardless, I could use a new opponent. Ama’s sick of losing to me.”

“What about Wei?” Zuko asks.

“What about him?” Yan asks. Does Zuko detect a flicker of that old defensiveness returning to his voice?

“Where is he?” Zuko clarifies. His eyes flicker to the gaping doorway behind Yan as if he expects the eldest brother to materialize in the darkness there. Truth be told, Zuko wouldn’t be surprised to learn Wei is deliberately avoiding him. Not after the talk they had yesterday.

Yan shrugs, and in the gesture Zuko cannot read whether his older brother has ranted to him about what a wretched harpy Zhao has married. “Who knows anymore? Wei’s probably out hunting resistance members for our brother.” Then, head tilted in thought, “No, nevermind - probably out hunting resistance members for *Ozai* . Which I’m sure has Zhao irked, not because he’d do any different, but because he wants to be the one calling the shots.”

It hasn’t occurred to Zuko before now that Wei could be devoting his spare time to such pursuits. It’s enough to distract him from his nausea. He stands up straight, fixing Yan with a look.

“Do you know if he’s been successful?” Zuko asks, all the while wondering if it will give him away to ask. Surely as Zhao’s spouse, as the Fire Lord’s son, it’s not suspicious of him to want to know?

There’s a tug at the corner of Yan’s mouth, like he already knows what Zuko’s hiding and finds it funny, how obvious he’s being. “How should I know? That guy doesn’t tell me anything.”

They set up the board inside because Zuko’s embarrassed by the thought of his bile steaming in the grass behind them while they play. However, Zuko finds he still needs to throw the doors and windows open to let in a breeze, as the fresh air is all that can ward off the nausea when it crashes over him. Yan is amenable to all this, and soon enough, they have a game going.

It isn’t quite like playing pai sho with Iroh. Yan will mull over his next move for a moment or two, but he never takes as long as Iroh does. In fact, he’s nearly as reckless a player as Zuko, changing the direction of his siege on a whim. Where Iroh sometimes gains the upper hand by wearing down Zuko’s patience, Yan relies on quick wit. It lets him corner Zuko often, but he isn’t as good at thinking through all the holes in his defenses.

“Shit, that was tight!” Yan exclaims, grinning over the maneuver he so narrowly avoided. “You nearly got me. You’re good!”

“Not really,” Zuko says, scanning the board. “I haven’t beat you once.”

“Still - you’ve come close!”

It’s true. That would never happen with Iroh, but Yan doesn’t play like Iroh. If anything, he reminds Zuko of Lu Ten - barreling ahead into the fray, full of flashy trick plays.

“Was that a Smothered Mate?” Zuko asks, recognizing an old favorite his cousin used to play.

Yan laughs heartily at the suggestion. “Yes, it was! See, you act like you don’t know the game, but you know it inside and out!”

Perhaps because Zuko isn’t as easy an opponent after all, Yan takes at least a little longer than usual to ponder his next move. In the quiet moments that pass, Zuko feels his stomach lurch ominously. His hand flies to his waist. He has soldiered through a few faint moments during their game, but this feels significantly worse. Maybe if he breathes through his mouth…

Yan’s eyes flicker from the board to his face. “Are you alright?”

“Yes, I-” Another ominous lurch. Then Zuko is on his feet and running for the veranda, hand pressed tightly over his mouth.

He finds himself on his knees, head thrust between the banisters as he wretches what amounts to little more than acidic spit. How cruel, that he doesn’t even have anything left in his stomach to vomit, and *still* , his entire body heaves like he’s filled to the brim with poison. Maybe he’s not even carrying a real human baby; maybe Zhao has implanted him with some horrid parasite that’s just killing him from the inside out. Zuko wretches again, a curtain of dark hair falling in his way, only to be surprised as it’s pulled away, as if of its own accord.

“Shit,” Yan says, holding the dark strands out of Zuko’s face, crouching uncomfortably, “fuck, sorry, I couldn’t keep up with you. You definitely, um, got some on your hair, here.”

Is that the burn of embarrassment, or nausea? Zuko’s body feels like it’s a thousand degrees. He lets go of his last shred of dignity to place his cheek against the stonework of the porch and lay, panting, while the violent tides in his stomach stop crashing, subside.

“Sorry,” Zuko mumbles, eyes shut, because he has no idea what else to say to his brother-in-law for interrupting their game of pai sho to be disgusting. “You didn’t have to hold back my hair.”

“Well, I felt bad,” Yan says, voice trailing like he might say more. He doesn’t. This silence is one too awkward for even Yan to fill up. Zuko battles now and again between the need to get up and compose himself and the need to simply *rest* - perhaps it’s the added burn of embarrassment, but this last bout of morning sickness has taken every last drop of energy from him. So he remains on the veranda, counting the acrid breaths that whistle past his lips.

Eventually, Yan clears his throat. "I don't suppose you want to play more pai sho?"

He’s still got Zuko’s hair, so the young prince pushes his hands away, breaking the link between them. “I don’t.”

“Ah.”

Still, Yan doesn’t leave. “I’m fine now, thank you,” Zuko says. He hears a noise as if Yan has stood up to leave, but when he opens his eyes, his brother-in-law is still hovering there. Yan and his gaudy cane both, with the brass tigermonkey head at the handle, seem to be watching him with concern.

"What do you normally do for fun around here?" Yan asks. Zuko doesn’t answer right away, put off by the sudden switch in topic, so Yan has to press him. "I’ve been told that when you’re not barfing your brains out, you like to go down to the village."

Yesterday Wei also made a judgmental comment when Zuko’s excursions to the village were mentioned. Is this how he’s retaliating against Zuko’s slight? By spying on Zuko? By getting all the brothers in on it? Is everything Zuko says next going to be dutifully delivered to his husband with an incriminating veneer? The thought should frighten Zuko, but it just makes him incredibly angry, that he shouldn’t be allowed even the smallest pleasures, the simplest privacies.

“So what if I’m going to the village?” he says, hotly. “It’s not illegal for me to leave the house!”

Yan is a portrait of gnarled, unkempt hair, beard and eyebrows both grown unwieldy. Those wild eyebrows knit together now, nearly inseparable in his confusion. “Who said anything like that? I’m just trying to figure out if you've put down roots on Kirachu yet!”

Zuko sits up, intending to leave, when his stomach gives a pang of protest. He leans against the railing instead. “I’ve got all of you, haven’t I?”

“I mean *outside* our family. Have you got any friends?”

Aang’s face immediately flashes through his mind. Zuko sniffs, turning away as if to hide the thought. “So what if I have? Do all my friends need to be approved by my husband? Do they need to pass *your* muster?”

“No, of course not,” Yan huffs. “But according to Ama, you’ve been cooped up more than you’re used to, lately. I’d imagine whoever you’ve been hanging out with, you miss them.”

Zuko pictures hands entwined with his own. A gaze as gray as storm clouds. Banishes them both with a gust of a sigh.

“Yeah. I guess I do. I hate having to cancel plans like this, but I wouldn’t be any fun to talk to, anyway.” And he lays a hand on his stomach.

Yan pouts. “I’m sure they understand, though. You’re not gone for no reason.”

Aang doesn’t really prod about the reasons Zuko stays away some days but not others. Nor do any of his friends push this question, although it is a fear that goes through Zuko briefly every time. He’s not ready to admit to himself why he might be afraid to tell them all that he’s pregnant.

Why he’s afraid to tell Aang.

“I’m not trying to be overbearing or nothing,” Yan says, shrugging. “I just want to make sure you’re not lonely.”

He sounds genuine, but Zuko has no idea what Wei may have told him. What Zhao may have asked him to do. It’s better to just keep Yan at arm’s length for now.

“You don’t need to babysit me,” Zuko says. “I’m fine on my own.”

Yan doesn’t linger this time, hand aloft in a gesture of *okay, you win* . “Alright. But if you need someone to hold your hair or beat you in pai sho, I’m only a holler away.” And he retreats back inside the house.

---

“Of all the firebenders!”

“I know.”

“Of all the firebenders in this *entire country!* ”

“I know, Sokka.”

“Of all the firebenders in this *entire hostile country!”* Sokka shrieked, throwing his arms into the air to emphasize his point. *“* Your boyfriend is telling us to go see the same guys Pakku is! Of all the people in the world that they trust to teach the Avatar, it’s the *same* group of guys! *They run in* *the same social circles!* ”

Aang pinched the bridge of his nose, choosing to ignore the “boyfriend” comment. “I *know,* Sokka *.”*

“I don’t think you do know,” Sokka huffed, planting his hands on his hips. “If you did, you would be freaking out!”

“Freaking out about what?” Toph called out. The boys looked up to see she and Katara had returned from their outing. As they stepped inside the cave, they fixed their companions with puzzled looks. Sokka dashed over and caught them up on the situation - that they had been comparing Pakku and Zuko’s list of recommended firebending teachers for Aang, and there had been an enormous number of similarities.

“That… *can’t* be,” Katara ground out. “Zuko probably found Pakku’s recommendations and copied them to gain our trust!”

“How?” asked Aang. “They were buried in your things.”

“Well, maybe he was snooping!”

“What, and you think I wouldn’t notice?” Aang asked, a touch of frustration creeping into his voice. “All the times Zuko’s been here, I’ve never once let him out of my sight.”

“I’m not doubting *that* ,” Katara grumbled, turning away. “But maybe you were *distracted* , all things considered.”

Aang’s brows narrowed. However, before he and Katara could get too wound up, Toph dropped another revelation. Crossing her arms over her chest, she declared, “I’m finally understanding why that guy seems so *cagey* .”

Sokka was taken aback. “Cagey? What do you mean, Toph?”

She rocked on her heels, pointing down at the solid dirt floor of the cave. “I’ve been trying to get a read on Zuko’s heartbeat since we met, but it’s been tough. It’s not an exact science, and the guy is inconsistent, to boot. Sometimes he seems like he’s hiding stuff - scratch that, sometimes it’s clear he’s *definitely* hiding stuff - and other times he’s being totally honest.”

“What kinds of things has he lied about?” Aang asked, dread creeping into his voice.

Toph shrugged. “Nothing crazy, which is why it’s been hard to pin him down. Like, he’ll lie about why he’s here, but then he’ll be a hundred percent earnest when he tells us he cares about you and wants to keep you safe.”

While fighting off a blush, Aang felt something click into place in his mind. Up until a few days ago, Toph had been fairly unbothered by Zuko’s presence. But the last time they’d seen him, she’d switched on a dime, grilling him about his intentions with their friend group. She must’ve been reading his responses through the reverberations of the cave floor the entire time. Aang supposed she had every right, and she’d used her skills to protect them before, but - for some reason, the thought bothered him. This seemed like a violation of privacy. She’d been looking for signs Zuko was lying without telling anyone else about it, least of all Aang.

And worse, it seemed she’d found something worth being suspicious of.

Katara’s hands clenched at her sides. “Toph, why the hell wouldn’t you tell us Zuko’s been lying? Don’t you think that information might be useful to us?!”

“Knowing that somebody’s lying isn’t the same as knowing the whole truth. And with how you are about him, I wanted to know more before I started jumping to conclusions.” Toph cocked her head. “Besides, I think this incident shows Zuko’s not necessarily cagey for evil reasons, but for something else.”

“Like?” Aang prompted.

“Like maybe he’s tied to a local anti-empire cell, and needs to be secretive about it,” Toph said. “This island is crawling with resistance rumors, after all.”

Katara frowned. “Wouldn’t we be supportive of that, though? Why not tell us that at the outset?”

Toph’s brow furrowed as she pondered the answer to that. “For one, as royalty, he definitely has to avoid any rumors about his wavering loyalties getting out there. But for another, not all anti-empire groups are going to have the same methods, right? Maybe this one’s kinda intense, and he doesn’t want to scare us off. He wants to build trust with us, first, so we don’t write him off.”

Sokka nodded emphatically. “Right, I get what you mean! Even Jet showed us a completely different face before he revealed what his actual aims were.”

All the color drained from Aang’s face. “Oh no. You don’t really think this is another Jet situation, do you?”

Early in their travels, before they had even met Toph, Aang and the others had encountered Jet in the colonies. He was a young man who had built a community filled with the offal that couldn't serve in the Earth Kingdom army: children too young to fight, the old, the injured, and outright deserters who opposed the army’s methods. At first introduction, Jet had made it seem like his community was solely a place of refuge.

Then he’d let Aang and the rest come along on a “mission.” They’d discovered that Jet and his people had been attacking nearby Fire Nation colonies - not guard outposts, but places where omegas and children resided, too. He’d been about to destroy a reservoir and flood an entire town. Thankfully, Aang and his friends had managed to hold off the flood long enough to evacuate the town to safety.

It seemed impossible to Aang that someone as careful and gentle as Zuko could be wrapped up in such militancy. But then, wasn’t he essentially training Aang to fight?

Aang shook his head, banishing his doubts. There was no use endlessly speculating. “We need to ask Zuko directly.”

---

It seems like the first time in more than an age Zuko has felt well enough to come down the mountain. It’s only been a few short days, yet the urgency of his absence lights in his limbs, making the long, overly-cordial breakfast with his brother- and mother-in-law almost unbearable. By the time he has escaped their well-wishes, their many overly sweet congratulations for his recovery, he nearly leaps onto his dragon moose. The crack of the reigns signals his freedom, and joy sweeps over his whole being as the jungle greenery passes by in a blur.

Since there are no paved roads on this island, Zuko could just as easily navigate straight to the beach. In spite of this, he makes a point to ride through the village every time he visits the Avatar. Crowds used to fill him with dread, but after his long isolation in Kirachu, it seems thrilling, if not vital to his very wellbeing, that he be surrounded by as many people as possible.

There’s also the matter of Toru. As the crowds ebb and flow around him, Zuko searches for people lacking topknots. Of the few he spots, they are never diminutive, boyish omegas with their hair shorn short. A part of Zuko wonders if he dreamed up that encounter just a few weeks ago. Perhaps all he wants to do is confirm it was all real - what would he even do if he saw Toru again? Call out to him? Act all *friendly* , after how he screamed in Toru’s face?

No. Zuko couldn’t imagine doing anything. He’d be damned to inaction, watching from afar, then leave before he was spotted. The only one who would even know they’d crossed paths again, the only one shaken by the encounter, would be Zuko.
