The buildings in this village are slapdash, arranged in a broken spiral around an open space in the center. This is the closest it can be said to have a “town square,” although Zuko is unsure whether any of these buildings are municipal in nature. If he had to take a guess, he’d say these are a mixture of storefronts and residences. None of the careful city planning of the capital can be found here.

As Zuko approaches the center, the crowd thickens. One of the few people riding a mount, he makes his way through easily enough, but as more and more people close in tightly around his dragon moose, he’s forced to wonder: why has everyone gathered? From his vantage point atop of the crowd, he doesn’t see anything out of the ordinary. Only people standing, stopped, all around him. Their faces are pointed towards the empty square, as if waiting for something.

Before the question can prey too greatly on his mind, Zuko’s eye is drawn to another shock of dark hair with no topknot, and in place of the omega he’s been searching for, he sees the Avatar and his friends. Aang’s hair aside, the group has gotten much better at blending in. Thanks to Zuko’s suggestions, their clothes align properly with gendered expectations, the shoulders on Sokka and Toph’s outfits leaning more severe, Aang and Katara’s clothes markedly plainer to indicate their beta status. So long as no one ever looks too closely, no one would ever suspect a thing.

Zuko is deliberating whether it would draw too much attention to call out to them when Aang looks up, smiles, and waves him over. The rest of the group then notices Zuko, too, and while the receptions vary, he figures he might as well approach.

When he has finally waded through the thick mass of bodies, Zuko dismounts his dragon moose and asks, “Do you all know what the crowd’s for?”

“I think there’s going to be some kind of an announcement,” Aang replies.

“That’s well enough, but why are you here for it?” Zuko asks. “You should be making yourselves scarce.”

Even with every inch of Aang’s arrows covered, Zuko is anxious to see him out in public. The Avatar responds to his concerns by smiling them away. “Hey, I’m just trying to get to my lesson. It’s the crowd’s fault I’m trapped.”

Zuko frowns. “Here? But you’ve passed the training school.”

“I switched teachers yesterday,” Aang explains. “The training school wasn’t quite enough for me anymore.”

Sokka nudges Aang in the side, and the Avatar’s expression shifts. His smile when he turns back to Zuko is weak. “On that topic, Zuko, it’s good we ran into each other. I’ve been meaning to ask…”

“Not here,” Toph says, suddenly.

Aang blinks. “What?”

“Not here,” Toph repeats, frowning. “There’s too many people here.”

“We could talk back at your encampment, if you want,” Zuko offers, curious what they have to discuss that’s so secretive, but there is a commotion at the front of the crowd before any of them can move.

A carriage thunders through the crowd of people, making its way to the center of the village where all eyes are pointed. Some armored soldiers at the front, previously blended into the crowd in their silence, now make a show of ordering people to shut up, to move, to listen. As the carriage halts to a stop, Zuko has the creeping realization that he has seen it before. He doesn’t even need to hear the shouted introduction of the soldiers at the front to know who is about to step from its depths.

A heavy boot on the mounting block. Then a familiar pair of wide shoulders crowding the carriage doorway. Instinctively, Zuko ducks down so as to not be seen through the throng of people. He can’t see his face, but he hears the familiar booming voice.

“Citizens of Kirachu,” Zhao shouts. “Ten days ago, signs of earthbending were found in this village. In response, we put up posters asking for information. We offered rewards.” He pauses, letting those words sink in, all the while raking the crowd with a glare. “Yet not one person has stepped forward to report the perpetrator. No one has so much as described what this earthbender looked like. Can you really claim that *none* of you saw them, when the evidence left behind was so obvious?”

Next to Zuko, Aang also shrinks down to blend better into the crowd. It is much less convincing at his height.

“Who the hell is this asshole?” Toph mutters.

Katara’s gaze is steely. “That’s *Zhao* . The governor.”

“ *What?!* ” Sokka hisses. “ *That* guy is married to Zuko?!”

And Zuko doesn’t see what kind of scowl Katara throws his way, because he can’t even bear to look at her. He can’t bear to look at any of them, he feels so ashamed. It’s like they’ve seen the ugliest parts of him laid bare.

Meanwhile, Zhao surveys the crowd with a stern eye, a father figure disappointed by his inept charges. He sighs, pacing as he addresses his subjects once more. “Fine. I should know by now you are all insubordinate, since you also refuse to cooperate in matters involving rebel cells that have appeared in the area. Involved or not, you’re all quite desperate to protect your loved ones who have gone astray. However, encouraging this kind of delusion isn’t constructive to our great empire, and you don’t seem to realize that this makes you just as culpable.”

“Is there a point to this?” a woman near Zuko mutters under her breath.

“Yeah,” says someone else, louder. “What’s with the lecture?”

“We don’t know what you’re talking about!” shouts a man across the crowd. “We’re all patriots, here!”

The crowd breaks out into murmurs, and becomes unruly enough that the soldiers at the front shout for silence, taking a threatening stance with their hands ablaze. That shifts the mood of the crowd considerably - there’s a tensity to everyone’s stances, a fear and a fervor that violence may break out at any minute. It’s unlike anything Zuko has ever seen; these people are shouting at a member of Fire Nation royalty. At their *governor* . Such defiance is sure to get them killed, but in their vast numbers, they seem wholly unafraid of the possibility. Perhaps they trust in one another, that they will protect and in turn be protected. They certainly stand against their leader like a wall, their scowls and glares defiant.

“There’s no need for things to get out of hand,” Zhao cries out, one large hand extended towards his guards. “I have an offer for you all that I think you will like: whoever can deliver information leading to the earthbender’s capture will be granted *full immunity* for any anti-empire activity they’ve engaged in, provided it does not continue.”

Sharp cries of surprise and murmurs of interest. Zhao gives his sleaziest smile.

“Generous, I know. But let me be even more generous: anyone with information on activities conducted against the empire will be granted immunity for themselves *and* any family members they wish to protect. So I encourage you lot to over-report. *Anything* suspicious you see in town is worth mentioning, and has the potential to be handsomely rewarded.”

Moments before, the crowd had seemed united against Zhao, an immovable stone wall protecting its own. But this news travels through it like a hairline fracture. Zuko watches as glances around them shift and fall, the confidence from before shaken. Perhaps these people are all evaluating now. Who truly matters to me? Is it worth trading my neighbor if it means I can protect my son? Are my friends going to turn me in - or should I try to beat them to it?

Zuko may imagine the turmoil in these people’s minds, but he doesn’t imagine those nearby who now turn and look at their group with a critical eye. As of late, Zuko has forsaken the gold flame when he comes out to the village, and while people may look to him as a newcomer, a stranger, the fact is that his golden eyes and other Fire Nation features protect him from suspicion. Aang’s group, on the other hand… They’ve learned to blend in, but there are certain details in their appearance that fall apart under scrutiny.

An older woman with a slash in her eyebrow frowns deeply at them. “You’re not from around here - I don’t think I’ve seen any of you before.”

Katara looks back at her, startled. “Oh, no, we’ve been in the village for a while! We’re-”

“How long?” the woman interrupts. The sharpness of her tone makes another person nearby turn to look at them. Zuko sees this stranger size them up, eyes sweeping their forms.

Zuko grabs Aang by the elbow. “Take my dragon moose. Leave.”

He tries to press the reins into Aang’s hand, but the Avatar brushes him off, whispering, “No need to panic. We just have to…” And he smiles, raising his voice as he steps forward, hands aloft in a gesture of no harm. “Hey, we’re citizens of the Fire Nation, same as you. We’ve just settled in Kirachu after we got tired of all the capital city noise…”

The strange man who’d turned to scrutinize them scoffs so hard, his mustache flutters with his indignation. “Is that so?”

“It *is* so,” Sokka sneers. Attention caught, the old woman steps closer to him, staring right into his face. Her eyes widen at what she sees.

“Hey - your eyes are *blue!* ”

From deep in his throat, Sokka releases a high, garbled noise that can only be fueled by panic. Frustrated, Toph grabs him by the elbow, pulling him close to her side. “Hey - leave my guide alone! You wouldn't bully an innocent blind woman and her friends, would you?”

“Ma’am,” cries out the old woman, pointing uselessly at Sokka. “He’s tricking you! This man has blue eyes! He’s a *foreigner!* ”

“Surely there’s some kind of mistake, here,” Aang laughs, sweating bullets. “Our whole group grew up in the Fire Nation. His eyes are blue because he’s…”

“He’s got an eye disease, and he’s losing his vision, just like me!” Toph says, clutching him for dramatic effect. Meanwhile, Katara shades her own eyes, hoping no one will notice her while she searches for a path out of the crowd.

“Or they’re blue because *he’s* the earthbender *,* ” the old man proclaims.

It doesn’t matter that there’s no logic to that argument; the moment *earthbender* hisses past his lips, several more people in their vicinity are turning to see what’s going on. Zuko tries to crane his neck to look past these nosy strangers, but there are too many bodies blocking his way. If he wants to figure out whether their group has been spotted by guards, there’s only one thing he can do. Zuko grabs onto the saddle of his dragon moose and hoists himself up onto its back. From his high vantage point, he can see where Zhao is, scrutinizing the crowd, expression hard as he searches for any weakness that he can prey upon. It doesn’t seem like he has caught wind of the commotion at the back of the crowd where Zuko and the rest are, but if he does, he’ll no doubt approach.

Then Zhao turns his head. Zuko sees the moment he is recognized, his husband’s eyes narrowing before bulging in shock. Zuko curses himself; he should’ve known better than to make himself stick out like this. No doubt Zhao will have questions for him. No doubt he’ll *come back here* .

There’s really only one thing Zuko can do, now. He snaps the reins, urging his dragon moose forward. He hears Aang somewhere behind him calling his name, asking, “What are you *doing?* ”

“Go *now* ,” Zuko replies, not turning to look at him. He leans forward over his dragon moose, and it picks up the pace, people dispersing in its wake.

“Doesn’t he realize he’s going to draw attention?” Katara hisses, barely whispering for the mounting panic in her voice.

“That’s the point.” Sokka grabs his sister by the wrist. “He’s buying us time. Let’s *go* .” And with Katara in tow, he begins to shove his way out of the crowd, the rest of the team following suit. Aang spares one last glance towards where Zuko’s head bobs along in the crowd, a silent *thank* *you* on his mind, but the prince knows better than to cast one last look their way.

At the front of the crowd, Zhao stands flabbergasted as his mate emerges from the throng of bodies. “Zuko?” he calls out. “What on earth are you doing here?”

“Kirachu is my home, too,” Zuko blusters, willing the terror in his throat not to latch onto his voice. “Aren’t I allowed to explore it?”

His snippy tone elicits a hideous crinkle in Zhao’s lips, foretelling the temper yet to break. At least for right now, though, they are surrounded by curious onlookers, citizens itching to see royalty behaving badly. Mollified by the need to save face, Zhao holds back any pernicious reply he might be forming in his head.

Now that he’s here, Zuko realizes he has absolutely no plan for how he’s going to keep Zhao’s attention occupied. He’s not even sure how long he’ll need to do this before the Avatar and his friends have gotten away safely. So Zuko scrounges for the first thing he can think to say. “What’s going on here?”

The hideous crinkle deepens. “Surely you heard me just now? An earthbender’s been…”

Zhao is interrupted as a woman shouts out, incoherent but clearly angry, from the direction Zuko came. Zhao and another nearby guard turn their heads towards the source of the noise. Knowing only that the commotion might be due to Aang’s escape, Zuko acts without thinking: he jams his heels as viciously as he can into the sides of his dragon moose.

The beast lets loose a cacophonous bugle, rearing up onto its hind legs before thunderously landing back onto all fours. Its massive head swings side to side in a panic, the sharp horns sending several people - Zhao included - leaping out of its path. Zuko only just manages to hold on for dear life.

“Easy!” Zhao shouts, snatching at the reins. “Easy!”

This ruckus succeeds in distracting Zhao (and, so it feels to Zuko, quite possibly the entire village) from anything else. It takes quite a while to calm the creature down, and by the end of it, Zuko’s palms are burning from clutching so tightly to the leather reins, his thighs wretchedly sore from trying to hold himself to the saddle. He doesn’t have to pretend to be harried when the animal has been calmed down again and Zhao fixes him with an incredulous look, asking, “What in the hell happened?”

“It’s - it’s these crowds!” Zuko gasps out. “She’s scared of all the people - some *idiot* probably bumped into her.”

Bewildered, Zhao shakes his head. “In any case, this animal clearly isn’t tame enough for you to be riding it in your condition. Come down, and you can wait for me in my carriage.”

He extends a hand towards Zuko, who hesitates. He isn’t sure if his work protecting Aang is done; is he giving up too soon if he complies with Zhao now? Besides, there’s something ominous about the thought of getting off his dragon moose. It feels like surrendering his autonomy. He won’t be able to leave without Zhao.

“What will become of my mount?” Zuko asks, stalling.

“I can ask one of my guards to bring it home later.”

Zuko hesitates again, then takes Zhao’s hand. Short of kicking his mount again, Zuko’s not sure what to do to keep Zhao busy, and there’s no doubt he’d be caught terrorizing the animal this time around. He manages to get both his legs on the same side of the saddle, but still hasn’t gotten down when one of the soldiers aiding Zhao in crowd control catches his eye.

Zuko stares back at the soldier, silently willing him to come over. The soldier glances at the crowd, then back at them, but evidently a fresh-faced prince proves more interesting than a crowd full of belligerent villagers. He makes his approach.

“Prince Zuko, are you alright?” the soldier asks. “I can hold fast to your mount, so it doesn’t panic again.”

“Yes, please,” Zuko insists, watching from the corner of his eye as Zhao’s lip curls in annoyance. The soldier busies himself taking the reins, shushing the creature. It has long since calmed down, but Zuko can feel the nervous tremble to its every breath, and is remorseful for injuring it.

Even with a tug of his hand from Zhao, Zuko is too afraid to budge from the saddle. He clears his throat. “It’s - it’s awful to hear about the earthbender. If I'd known there was such a danger running around this island uncontrolled, I’m not sure I would have come to the village today.”

“Then we’ll get you someplace safer,” Zhao says, tersely. “Step off the dragon moose, now.”

Zhao looks ready to get back to work. Zuko will have to try harder if he wants to really hold his attention. He wets his lips, then says, voice straining over the cruelty of it, “You once spoke so poorly of Darah and how he let this island get out of control - but you don’t seem to have any better handle of it yourself.” He waves, vaguely, around them. “I mean, look at all this.”

“It’s not so much of a mess as you're making it out to be, *darling* ,” Zhao replies, fury lurking in the eaves of his voice. He tugs Zuko’s hand once again, only for Zuko to hold firm.

“But it is - this crowd hated you, only seconds ago. You didn’t seem to command any respect of them until you bribed them. Perhaps my father made a mistake after all, entrusting this island to your care.”

They’ve all gone very still; the soldier, Zuko, and even the animal underneath him all seem to have slowed their breathing. There is a dark look growing on Zhao’s face, storm clouds that foretell a tempest.

The soldier clears his throat uncomfortably. “Governor-”

“ *Prince* ,” Zhao coldly corrects. The soldier swallows.

“Prince Zhao. I could help Prince Zuko down and keep an eye on him so you can continue your patrol, if you’d like.”

All at once, the fury vanishes from Zhao’s face. He smiles placidly at the soldier. “No need. I’ll take care of this.”

And with that, he shoves his hands under Zuko’s legs and bodily lifts him from the saddle of the dragon moose. On instinct, Zuko clutches at his husband’s neck, afraid of falling from his grasp. He is swung around and carried bridal style to Zhao’s carriage, where he is unceremoniously dumped inside.

“We will talk about this later,” Zhao hisses, and before Zuko can get a word in, the door is slammed shut in his face. Muffled through the wood, Zuko can hear Zhao giving someone the order to keep watch over him, which means at least one less person will be terrorizing villagers into confessions. Zuko just hopes he has stalled long enough to let his friends get away.

---

It was hours before Zuko saw Zhao again. Hours spent locked in the carriage, fearing the worst. His mind was filled with visions of Aang and the others being ambushed on the road, in the jungle, in their encampment on the beach. He felt simultaneously that he was powerless to do anything and a failure for not doing more.

They arrived at the estate after dark. Zhao didn’t even accompany Zuko on the ride home, electing instead to use the errant dragon moose. When he eventually came to let Zuko out of the carriage, his face was as tense with anger as it had appeared hours before.

This time Zuko stepped from his ride the moment he was bidden. “Did you find the earthbender?” he asked.

Zhao’s hand only squeezed his in reply. No. They hadn’t.

His ominous silence made the walk from the carriages to the house stretch on like an endless shadow. The entire time, Zuko’s skin prickled with anticipation of their arrival. Surely once they were inside, Zhao would let him have it. What had Zuko been thinking, acting so defiant? Apparently nothing but the fact Aang and the others' safety was on the line. Thanks to how he'd behaved, he was now the one whose safety was at stake.

Inside the house, Zuko noticed there was light spilling out from under the reed room’s door. He made a desperate beeline towards it, hoping there would be at least a few people in there who could protect him from the full extent of Zhao’s wrath.

He thrust the door open and found, to his immense relief, that the entire family, including Rio, had gathered in the reed room. Everywhere he looked, there were eyes. Witnesses. Safety.

Ama raised his head from his embroidery. “Prince Zuko. Welcome back.”

“Good evening, Ama," he replied, hearing the shake of relief in his own voice.

The older omega set his embroidery down, the most imperceptible ripple of worry showing on his brow. “You sound out of breath, my prince. Is everything alright?”

Before Zuko could answer, a hand closed around his shoulder. He looked up to see Zhao sanding behind him in the doorway, eyes blazing.

“How often do you go down to the village?” Zhao asked.

“I’m not sure,” Zuko lied, deflecting.

“ *Guess* .”

The sharpness of his command caught Zuko by surprise; they were in front of other people. Zhao should be scrambling to compose himself, but he only seemed to be getting angrier, the grip of his hand visibly tightening.

Perhaps it was the presence of those who knew better. Perhaps it was fear; Zuko gave an honest answer. “I - if I had to guess, I’d say I go every other day.”

He could actually see the vein on Zhao’s forehead throb. “I see. And what if something had happened to you while you were in the village?”

“Nothing ever has,” Zuko said. Meanwhile, he was trying not to think about the encounter with the firebenders just a few weeks ago, when Aang had rescued him, lest his guilt show on his face.

Zhao scoffed. “Nevermind the myriad of other dangers in the village, I watched you nearly get *thrown* from your dragon moose today.”

“But I’m fine!” Zuko reached out a placating hand to Zhao, intending to close the distance between them, but Zhao leaned out of the way, revulsion warping his face.

“It doesn’t matter that you’re fine *now* ,” said Zhao. “You’re my spouse. You’re *royalty* . Any ruffian could see that and make you the target of their abuse.”

Zuko hated that Zhao was technically right. But what he couldn’t possibly know was that the world’s greatest protector was on his side. “Zhao, it’s *fine.* ”

“It isn’t. You deliberately put our unborn child in danger.”

“Not deliberately-”

“Then *selfishly* , thoughtlessly,” Zhao interrupted, eyes narrowed. “I can’t believe you. Do you have anything to say for yourself?”

Zuko turned away from Zhao to the others, silently searching for help. He found none. Everyone was making a point to avoid his eyes, expressions ranging from blank to uncomfortable. When Zuko made eye contact with Wei, the oldest brother merely raised a single bored eyebrow, as if to say, *Well, what did you expect to happen, when you looked to us for help?*

It’s not as though Zuko could tell Zhao the truth. That he had been going to the village because he was lonely; that he felt trapped in the walls of this estate and this marriage alike; that he had met the Avatar, and found in him a genuine friend, a chance at redemption with his father - and perhaps even some greater destiny he was still sussing out.

Zuko stayed where he was on the threshold of the reed room, mouthing excuses without getting a single one past his lips. Eventually Zhao got tired of glaring at him and redirected some of that energy towards where Ama was lounging on the divan. “And *you!”*

Ama touched a scandalized hand to his chest. “What on earth did I do?”

“You let him go, and you *definitely* know better!”

Ama met his son’s intensity with as much enthusiasm as was needed to flick lint off a shirt sleeve. “It’s not illegal for him to want a change of scenery, Zhao.”

“No, but it is a danger to our child, *your grandchild,* to let him go riding that animal day in and day out!” Zhao shouted. “What if he fell? He could have killed my heir, then that blood would be on *your* hands!”

It was a ridiculous escalation, but Zhao’s urgency and fury made Ama wilt. Wei tensed in his seat, and Zhao fixed him and Yan both with a vicious glare, as if daring them to defy him. Neither said a word.

With one last scoff, Zhao stalked away from his family, returning to where his spouse lingered in the doorway. He made a point to stand chest-to-chest with Zuko so he could look down his nose at him, looming with all the height Agni had given him. “I still haven’t heard an apology from you.”

Zuko’s face burned at the prospect. Suddenly the others felt less like witnesses and more like an audience to his suffering. “I…”

“With *feeling* ,” Zhao said, chastising him before he’d even begun.

Zuko worked his jaw, prying the humility from his gums with vicious force. “I’m sorry, Zhao.”

“You’re sorry for *what?* ”

He willed himself to look into Zhao’s eyes, to avoid the gazes burning a brand into the side of his face. “I’m sorry for worrying you.”

“And?”

“And for endangering myself, as well as the baby.”

“And?”

“And for being… rude, back at the village.”

“And?”

“And…” And *what the hell else* could there possibly be? Zuko hesitated, as if by elongating the word, he could make the answer materialize in his mouth.

“ *And* for interrupting me when I was in the middle of governing. *And* for making a scene in front of my subordinates. *And* for deliberately disobeying me.”

“Disobeying…?” Zuko blinked. “You mean when I wouldn’t get in the carriage?”

“I mean when you started sneaking off to the village in the first place,” Zhao snapped.

“But you never said I couldn’t go!”

Zhao cut off his answer with a wave. “It’s the *spirit* of the thing, Zuko. Just because there isn’t an explicit rule doesn’t mean you weren’t still acting insubordinate. Now apologize.”

The tiniest of sparks lit in Zuko’s chest. “I’m sorry I upset you and I’m sorry I did something so bad for the pregnancy, but I’m not one of your cadets, Zhao. You can’t order me a-”

Zhao grabbed him by the jaw hard enough to bruise. Even if he hadn’t physically interrupted him, the shock of it would’ve made the words die on Zuko’s tongue.

“You’re right, Zuko,” said Zhao. “You’re not one of my cadets. My cadets would know better than to talk back to me.” He emphasized this by giving Zuko a shake that threatened to pull his jaw loose.

Zuko’s eyes darted to Ama. Surely he wouldn’t allow for this treatment, not to royalty, not to someone who might be carrying the future Fire Lord in his womb? But no matter how desperately he willed it, the other omega wouldn’t even meet his gaze, his glassy stare fixed on the wall instead.

Zhao shook Zuko again, forcing his eyes back on his face. “Now - how about a proper apology?”

“I’m sorry for disobeying you,” Zuko said, voice hitching. He felt hot tears spill over his cheeks. Zhao seemed vaguely irritated by the sight of them, lip curling reflexively.

Of all of them, it was Yan who spoke up. “Hey, give it a rest, already. He’s apologized a million times.”

“Stay out of this,” said Zhao, gaze never once leaving Zuko’s face, all the more painful and humiliating because of how he took in all the details of Zuko’s discomfort, his unraveling.

Perhaps to escape it, Zuko dared to glance Yan’s way. His expression was unbearable to behold - it reminded Zuko of how those women of the palace court had looked at Makamae, with a potent mix of pity and disgust. The thought only seemed to increase the flow of tears from Zuko’s eyes; he felt his face crumple. He saw Yan watching it all, feeling worse for him, and wanted to melt into the floor.

“Being pitiful won’t get you absolved,” Zhao said, glaring down at Zuko. “You know what you did was wrong.”

“Would you fucking knock it off!” Yan actually stood from his seat *.* Wei reached for his sleeve, perhaps to tug him back down, but Yan swatted his hand away.

In turning to level a glare at his brother, Zhao’s attention was divided; his grip loosened. Zuko didn’t care about the consequences - dying to get away, to break down in private instead of in public, he yanked his face out of Zhao’s grip.

One moment, he was turning, intent on running towards the door. A stream of dark hair trailing in his wake. Sliding between Zhao’s fingers.

The grip in his hair tightened, and Zuko let loose a whimper as he was dragged back towards Zhao.

“L - let me *go-* ”

The hand in his hair twisted and pulled him flush to Zhao’s chest, hot breath borne so close to his naked ear he could feel the moisture of it: “What are you going to do about it? Are you going to burn me? Huh? Or are you determined to play the victim now that you’re in front of an audience?” Zuko struggled blindly in Zhao’s grasp, more certain than ever that anything could happen to him. It wasn’t enough to be witnessed. There was no safety in numbers. Zhao was going to grievously injure him, and he would do it in front of his own fucking mother if Zuko didn’t get away.

He snatched desperately for his last line of protection. “Zhao, careful, the *baby-* ”

Zhao's lips curled. “So *now* you care about the baby. I’ll tell you, Zuko - I can do plenty to you without hurting the fucking baby!”

Thick fingers wrapped around his neck. Zuko’s legs went numb, then limp, as if his body no longer saw any point in resisting even as his mind still screamed with fear.

&#40; *Are you still wondering why he finds every reason he can to touch your throat?)*

“I’m sorry,” Zuko chanted, shaking uncontrollably every time those fingers so much as slid across his skin. “I’m sorry, I’m sorry, I’m sorry…”

“Enough.”

Zuko felt Zhao stiffen around him, and looked up from the wild tangle of his own hair to see that Wei had laid a steadying hand on his brother’s shoulder. Zuko’s mouth fell open in shock; of all the family members he expected to defend him, Wei was the absolute last. The conversation about Zuko’s father had been their first extended interaction, and Zuko had thought it’d gone terribly, all things considered. Yet here Wei was, anyway.

Wei’s touch had done its part for a moment in calming Zhao down, but the longer Zhao glared at the hand, the more he seemed to return to himself. “Get the fuck away from me,” he snarled, throwing a shoulder to loosen his brother’s grip. Wei let him go without a struggle, taking a step back for good measure. Zuko realized that Yan, too, had crossed the room, and was hovering just over Wei’s shoulder, looking like he wanted to throw himself bodily into the fray.

“You’re upsetting Ama,” said Wei. “Either stop, or take it somewhere else.” His gaze was trained on Zhao and would stray nowhere else, no matter how tear-streaked and disheveled those other sights may prove.

That was what really deadened Zuko’s last remnants of hope. *Stop or take it somewhere else* . In other words, it didn’t matter if Zhao hurt Zuko or not. If he ripped his hair out by the scalp, or slammed his face into the floor until it turned black and blue, or if he strangled him until he was dead.

Across the room, Ama shaded his eyes as if from the sun.

Zuko went limp in Zhao’s arms, expecting to cry, and found himself too thoroughly drained. No room for anguish. No room for fear. No more room for anything. Zhao had to haul him up the stairs so they could continue their one-sided fight in the privacy of their marital bed.

---

Zuko didn’t awaken until Zhao finally unlocked the door. He sat up groggily in bed, looking around the room and seeing mostly darkness, with only the faintest shape of Zhao moving through the room. His movements and his footsteps were unhurried, without bite, suggesting he wasn’t as agitated as before.

As he waited for his husband to join him in bed, Zuko ran a hand over his right shoulder, wincing at even the gentlest touch to the tender flesh. He had to sleep on his left to avoid agitating the injury; the pain was deep, as if he’d torn the muscle lifting something far too heavy.

Then his fingers strayed to his stomach. He imagined there was a heartbeat pulsing under the pads of his fingers, but that was only fancy; it was too early to feel kicking. At least he wasn’t nauseous. No dinner meant there was little to throw up.

He heard the dresser doors close, and several footsteps later, there was the weight of Zhao sinking into the bed beside him. After a long silence, Zuko laid back down, too. He moved slowly and carefully, afraid the barest movements could draw Zhao’s ire.

It must not have worked. Zhao spoke into the dark. “What the hell are you going to the village for, anyway?”

Zuko took one long, shuddering breath. “Not - not much.”

“Nothing at all?”

Zhao’s tone sounded like a threat. Zuko felt himself start to shake, and tried to think of a way he could answer honestly without revealing the truth. “Sometimes I just like to walk around and look. And I, uh, like talking to new people. Getting to know them.”

“Like who?”

“Like-” There was an easy answer, here. Many pounds of flesh he could extract to sate Zhao’s hunger.

But he wouldn’t do it. Not yet. Maybe not ever.

“Like… Toru.”

The dark seemed to tremble around them. Zuko’s shoulder throbbed where Zhao had struck him, as though it was anticipating the next blow.

If it was possible for the sound of bed sheets being pulled in a particular direction to be spiteful, this was it. “Go to sleep, Zuko,” Zhao muttered.

Of course, Zuko couldn’t sleep. Not with Zhao lying beside him, body jagged with agitation. So Zuko laid on his back in the dark, staring at streaks of window light on the ceiling, waiting for the sound of Zhao’s breathing to calm down so that he could feel safe again.

At least Aang and the others had gotten away, he thought. Zuko figured he was destined to bear pain at Zhao’s hands for the rest of his life. At least this time, something good came of it. Maybe that was all he could ever hope for; for this pain to have a purpose.

(Strangely, he thought of his mother again. In the nest of pillows and blankets.

*Do you hate him?*

*He gave me you.*

Cradling the wound she’d sustained protecting him. She’d sworn to Zuko that there’d never be a repeat of the beach house. And to her credit, while she’d never succeeded in ending the violence, Ozai hadn’t injured Zuko that severely ever again. She’d made sure to bear the worst of it herself.)
