### Text

Seeking physical comfort is unforgivably childish. Azula remembers the exact moment she began to spurn such frivolities: she’d been about six, walking along the dunes in Ember Island, and a misstep had sent her tumbling down into the sand. She can still remember the look on her father’s face when Azula had reached out for her mother’s outstretched hands. Ozai was so disgusted at her moment of weakness, nose crinkling as if he was looking at some rotten, dead thing.

Right away, Azula dropped her hands to her sides, and forced herself to stand up on her own. Her feet wobbled beneath her, and there were grains of sand stuck painfully in the skin of her knees, but her father had stopped looking at her like she was repulsive. Somehow, whatever crestfallen look Ursa must have given her was not so nearly as burned into her memory.

In the years since, Azula has allowed very few people to touch her. Ty Lee used to be a hugger, but one fierce zap to the hand had cured her of that habit. For the last few years, Iroh has been the sole person allowed to embrace Azula, and only sparingly.

And now. It’d be easy for Azula to pull away from this touch, to retreat to the corners of her desolate little cell. But she doesn’t; she remains here, pressed up against the bars, her hands in the grip of the Water Tribe princess’s.

There’s something a little foolish about how Yue has taken off her gloves to hold Azula like this. Azula wonders vaguely if this whisper of body heat can give her the spark she needs to light a fire, then does nothing with this thought, letting that initial burst of warmth from their grip gradually fade.

“You know,” Yue says, “you remind me of a baby polar leopard.”

Azula purses her lips at this indignity. “I assume you’re referring to the fact that I’m a near-perfect killing machine in a deceptively small package?”

If Yue’s touch cannot get Azula to spark, her laugh certainly will. She pulls one of her hands away to cover her glee, as a polite omega princess always must. “No, silly! I mean we tame them, sometimes, to keep as pets. But you need to get them young, and you need to expose them to human touch at a very, very slow pace. One wrong move, and you either frighten it away or lose yourself a finger.”

Is that what Yue thinks? That she has tamed Azula? A burn would cure her of that delusion, but while Azula’s hands twitch in her grasp, they do not pull away. “It is impossible to imagine *you* out on the tundra, communing with wild animals. You’re too soft for it. That’s warrior’s work.”

Yue scrunches her nose like she takes offense to that, but she doesn’t voice it. Instead she returns her gaze to their hands. She turns Azula’s hands over in hers, looking at the palms, touching more incidentally than with purpose.

Up until she strokes her thumb down Azula’s lifeline, that is. The sensation is so pleasant, so unexpected that Azula has to jam her tongue up against the back of her throat so she doesn’t moan.

“You have such pretty nails for a warrior,” Yue remarks. She’s not even seeing Azula’s hands in their full glory; Azula doesn’t exactly have the resources to keep her nails tidy in this dungeon, so they are jagged from being ripped or chewed away. Meanwhile, Yue’s nails look closer to what Azula’s used to, perfectly manicured ovals of a pearlescent pink. Seeing the contrast, Azula thinks what a distorted mirror view they must present to anyone watching. Yue is the picture of civilization, with her clean clothes, hair painstakingly coiffed into an elaborate updo. Meanwhile Azula wears drab prisoner garb, her hair tied in the same messy lob atop her head since she was imprisoned; she’s pretty sure it’s so tangled by now she wouldn’t be able to pull the tie free.

Yue presses the pad of Azula’s pointer finger, watching the blood that gathers there chase away the bluish tint the cold has brought to her nail. “The tips are so white, and the shape is so… dainty.”

Azula narrows her eyes. She is not dainty. She is compact. She is spritely. But never all the waifish delicacy that comes with a word like *dainty* .

“They’d be much prettier if you gave me the means to tend to them,” Azula huffs. “I’m not asking for much - a file, maybe a pair of scissors? Frankly, my hair is getting unruly, too, and I’d like a chance to cut it.”

Yue’s expression goes grim, her hands stilling in their gentle ministrations. “I don’t think we trust you with sharp objects yet, Azula.”

Azula leans back against the bars of her cell with a faux-petulant sigh. “I don’t know what I could possibly do to anyone with a nail file, but *you’re* the captor, and I’m the prisoner, so I suppose I must deal with it.”

*Yet* . The glimmer of hope in that single word keeps Azula going.

She will bide her time. Play nice when the princess offers her pretty little hands to hold. Let herself be treated as a wild animal to be tamed. Yue is right to make the comparison, to be cautious, but she forgets. Both people and animals can be dangerous. But an animal is not smart enough to conceal its intentions.

She looks to Yue, only for all her silent plotting to be chased away by the softness of the other girl’s smile. “I know hair is very important in the Fire Nation. Maybe I can convince my father to let one of my maidservants wash and cut it for you. You’ll have to behave, though.”

What a wild spark, that *behave* sends through her. Azula tells herself it’s annoyance. She scoffs to sell the myth further. “I’m not your pet. You needn’t *groom* me.”

“You’re the one who brought it up,” Yue says, shrugging. She drops the subject from there, content returning to their idle hand touching, their bickering, the strange comfort they now share.

---

As Yan makes his slow, difficult ascent, he curses his family several generations back for subjecting him to this indignity. Who builds a multi-story building outside of a city? It’s unnecessary!

He puts all of his weight on his cane as he lifts the stronger leg to the next step, before then using its strength to propel the rest of his body upwards. Every mistake in his maneuvers is rewarded with a sharp, electrical pain, which starts from the heel of his weaker leg and shoots upward through his hamstring. When he finally makes it to the cherry blossom door, he stands with both hands on his cane, his eyes closed, breathing as though he can ever truly banish the sensation, like fire burning up the wick of his nerve endings.

Once this has subsided to a less severe ache, Yan enters. Ama is lying in bed with his back facing the door. Seeing him prone in the dark like this evokes a powerful series of childhood memories for Yan. He remembers many afternoons, blurred into one and the same: his father letting him inside the room; having to be very quiet as he crawled through the blankets to lay with Ama, lest someone shout at him to settle down, or sent him away; lying in the dark for what felt like hours, a heartbeat against his cheek. It used to be the only way they could spend any time together, when Ama’s pain was at its worst.

“Close the door, Rio,” Ama says languidly, voice muffled by the quilt.

Yan shakes his head, dispelling the memories. Given how easily he moved around the house yesterday, he doubts Ama’s bad feelings are physical. Instead, what he’s suffering from are feelings of guilt.

“It’s me,” Yan says. “I’ve come to ask if you want anything, or if you’d just prefer to wallow in your room all day.”

For a while, Ama doesn’t answer. Eventually Yan continues, saying, “You know, if you talked to Zuko…”

A weary sigh, muffled by the quilt. “Yan.”

“I’ve seen how close you two are,” he says, quickly, before Ama can talk over him. “If you’d stop being stubborn and talk to him, maybe even apologize…”

“Apologize for *what?* ”

Yan fumbles. He thought it was a given, that they were all culpable in some way. “Well - you know. Maybe not an apology even, but like, some show of sympathy. Some sense you care.”

Ama’s voice flies out of the dark, sharp as a knife. “Don’t chastise me. I’m not *your* child.”

“Fine,” Yan grumps. That angry, motherly tone has deflated a lot of his bluster. He shifts uncomfortably. “So, *do* you want anything?”

“Is Wei here today?” Ama says after a while.

“Nope. He’s back at it in the village.”

“Then no. I don’t want anything from *you* .”

At the top of the stairs, Yan hears a door open. He turns back around, wondering if Ama’s had a change of heart, but it’s the master bedroom that opens, a red-eyed Zuko emerging from inside. For a moment, almost without thinking, the two trade deep stares: Yan, looking for signs of violence, and finding only a single smudge of black-blue on the underside of Zuko’s jaw, easily mistaken for shadow. Zuko, eyeing the leg that hangs nearly-limp at Yan’s side. It almost doesn’t bother him anymore, the way people look at it.

“Would it be offensive of me to ask if I can help you in some way?” Zuko says. “You look like you’re struggling.”

Yan’s gut response is to refuse. But his left leg shrieks out for relief.

“...Sure. Let me throw an arm over your shoulders.”

While Zuko makes his approach, Yan has a brief fantasy of him pausing at the top of the stairs, then landing a kick square in the middle of Yan’s chest. “And that’s for not ripping my shit head husband off of me last night, you fucking coward!” Zuko might shout, as Yan goes toppling down the stairs.

In reality, Zuko goes out of his way to help Yan, supporting him by locking arms with him. It’s an awkward way to go about it, but when Yan tried to throw an arm around his shoulders, Zuko had *winced* , teeth clenched, air hissing between them. And because this is about minimizing pain, they try something else, something that doesn’t work as well, but hurts the both of them the least.

The whole time Zuko is helping him down the stairs, Yan keeps replaying the same moment from the night before over in his head: Zhao’s hand in an escaping Zuko’s hair, the wordless shout of terror he gave as he was dragged back into the room. Yan had long suspected things weren’t good between Zhao and Zuko, given how rarely they spoke to one another around the house. Still, actually seeing the extent of it last night had been beyond shocking.

Yan feels a significant amount of guilt for his part in what happened. But for all he tried to lecture Ama about the importance of repairing things with his young friend, he finds himself completely unable to say a word. What *can* he even say? *I’m sorry I just stood there and watched my brother* *throw you around like a rag doll. I can’t begin to tell you why I froze like that, because I should be* *numb to that kind of shit by now.*

“How are you, uh, feeling today?” Yan asks instead.

Zuko doesn’t answer. He’s a real high society omega; graceful, quiet, eternally blank-faced. One of the many reasons it was so awful to see him in Zhao’s grip last night, screaming and crying like that. When they reach the bottom of the steps, Zuko releases Yan and walks away. Yan hesitates, watching, before he heads in the same direction.

He doesn’t miss the way Zuko’s footsteps stutter on the threshold of the reed room. It’s obvious what must be running through his head. Once the fear has subsided, Zuko darts into the kitchen instead. Again, Yan hesitates before following Zuko inside.

Zuko spins to face him, eyes hard. “Ama’s right. You *do* hover.”

Not like Yan hasn’t heard that before. He should be pouring out apologies right now, but he just stands there like an idiot, eyes darting between Zuko and the floor.

Yan fumbles. “I’m - I wanted to say-”

“What?” Zuko asks, impatient. His voice sounds raspier than usual.

“It’s - do you, uh - do you want me to give you a ride to the village?”

Since Yan’s not so great with words, he figures a gesture will have to do. Zuko stares at him, then lets out a sharp sound that, he realizes, must be a startled laugh.

“Oh,” Zuko says. “You’re serious? You think that’s a good idea, right now? After Zhao-” He swallows, hard, unable to finish the thought.

“Well - fuck him,” Yan says. “Right? He’s an asshole.”

Zuko seems to be working over the trade-offs in his head. He’s really analyzing Yan, eyes darting all over him as if signs of insincerity are always so easily divined. “And you won’t tell him?”

“No, of course not.”

“And Ama?”

Yan feels something clench in his chest. “I sincerely doubt Ama will say anything to him.”

“How can you be so sure?” There’s something a little too cracked, a little too vulnerable about Zuko’s voice. It makes Yan want to avert his eyes.

“Well… Ama let you go for ages without ever saying a word, didn’t he?”

---

When their carriage arrives in the village, the first thing Zuko notices is a higher number of soldiers than usual. He wonders if Zhao has instructed them to keep an eye out for him, or if they’re solely focused on stopping suspicious strangers, in the hopes of finding the earthbender. This will certainly make Aang’s trips into the village less safe, which is worrying.

Zuko turns to Yan, sitting opposite from him. “Are you going to follow me around today?”

Yan seems startled by the question. “Oh. Um, no.”

“Good.” Zuko shoves the carriage door open.

“Wait - hold on!” Yan says. “Shouldn’t we work out a plan to meet back together, so we can ride home?”

Busy looking for an alley he can slip into that’s not bustling with soldiers, Zuko barely turns around. “Sure. Same place, three hours from now. Goodbye.”

And he heads out into the village. The only reason he doesn’t look to see if Yan’s following is because he doesn’t want to draw unwanted attention by looking paranoid. He makes a point to take a twisting, convoluted route to the beach, even walking through areas where the thick jungle foliage hasn’t been cleared away. By the time he actually does pause to look behind him, he is definitely alone.

---

During the long walk up to the Avatar’s encampment, Zuko’s chest thrums with terror at the possibility his distraction was all for nothing. He keeps picturing the cave empty. The sea air running through the hollowed stone, its wet gasp the only denouement, all other evidence of Aang’s presence gone without a trace.

But even as Zuko gets close, he hears their voices, and from the moment he lights in the mouth of the cave, he is surrounded by bodies, by cheers, by joy. A number of arms fling around him, and while the impact of a small but compact Toph on his bad shoulder makes Zuko clench his teeth, he is swept away by everyone’s smiles.

Aang grabs Zuko’s hands, grinning brilliantly. “I thought we were going to be hauled off by guards yesterday! But you kept things from getting out of hand. Thank you.”

“It was no problem,” Zuko says, gripping Aang back just as tightly. He wants to stay here, in the spotlight of the Avatar’s attention, but the rest of the group is jostling pretty hard for *his* . Sokka, of all people, squeezes Zuko into an affectionate hug with some face-nuzzling. (Is the scrape of his beard what has Zuko heating up, or is it that look Aang is casting Sokka’s way, the irritable twist of his mouth?)

“Our savior!” Sokka croons.

Katara scowls, but it’s not meant for Zuko. “Can’t you see you’re suffocating him, Sokka?” She grabs her brother by the ear and hauls him off of Zuko, earning a litany of dramatic “OW”s and pleading for mercy. Toph does not get the same treatment, although she moves, lessening the weight on Zuko’s bad side.

“Anyway,” says Aang, angling himself between Zuko and the Water Tribe siblings. “I’m really glad you came back! We were all worried you might disappear for a few days.”

“I don’t think anything could have kept me from coming to see you today,” Zuko says, nervously meeting Aang’s gaze. “Even though Zhao didn’t say they’d captured anyone, I didn’t see what happened to you all, afterward. I wanted to make sure you were okay.”

“How’d you end up distracting him?” Aang asks.

“I, uh, whipped my dragon moose into a frenzy.” The group laughs and smiles at this, which catches Zuko somewhat off guard. Right; it had all started somewhat absurd, before it escalated.

“Quick thinking,” Sokka says, smiling. “Did your man seem suspicious at all?”

A quick succession of memories from the night before renders Zuko momentarily mute. He shifts into a smile he hopes looks more natural than it feels. “He - was surprised to see me. But he didn’t notice you all, and that’s what’s important.”

---

Given the news about the increased patrols, it’s decided they should all lay low for a while. They debate over who should go into town if they need something in the meantime, versus who should not. Everyone is most anxious about Aang’s safety, but his lack of topknot isn’t nearly as conspicuous as the Water Tribe siblings’ blue eyes. Toph could technically go on her own - she confirms Zuko’s suspicions, explaining that she’s more independent from the others than one might think, because she can use her earthbending to determine where objects and people are. However, there are limits to this sixth sense, and she’s sure that running around the village by herself will only raise questions.

“What do we even need to go into town for?” Sokka asks, holding his boomerang blade aloft. “We’ve got all the food we need within our reach! We just have to go hunt it down.”

“Or gather it,” Aang adds, reminding them all of the importance of vegetables. Especially for someone who eats no meat.

“We could still be spotted if we get too close to the village,” Toph huffs. She throws herself onto her back on the ground, head landing squarely in Katara’s lap. Katara rolls her eyes, before getting to work gently running her fingers through the alpha girl’s hair. Zuko’s fascinated by their closeness, at times; they seem more than ordinary friends. He’s never heard of a beta and an alpha romantically involved, but nothing’s outside the realm of possibility…

“Plus my sifu’s in the village,” Aang points out.

“Oh yeah,” says Toph. “Our whole reason for being in this lousy country to begin with. No offense, Zuko.”

“None taken.”

Sokka points at Zuko with his boomerang. “I know I’ve said it once before, but I’m gonna say it again: why aren’t we relying solely on Zuko for firebending training?”

“I’m not good enough for the Avatar,” Zuko says. He doesn’t flinch, but Aang does. Not wanting to upset him, Zuko amends: “I’m not being hard on myself. It’s just a fact, especially when compared to the rest of my family, who you’ll probably have to fight.”

Not to mention there’s no guarantee Zuko can make it to the cave every day. He isn’t even sure how he’ll get here tomorrow, if he feels well enough.

“Oh, I just remembered!” Katara smacks her open palm with her fist, drawing everyone’s attention. “There’s something else we need from the village. We’re running out of suppressants!”

The question of what a beta would need with suppressants is followed by the realization that Katara is not, in fact, a beta. Zuko feels all at once surprised and vindicated - of course! How could he have not seen it before? Katara’s such a champion of omega rights, and so critical of alpha hegemony, in the Fire Nation especially. Not to mention that Zuko had once theorized the Avatar was traveling with an omega. It must be her. Which means…

He sneaks a glance at where the alpha girl lays with her head in Katara’s lap. Suddenly Katara and Toph’s closeness makes sense… while also coming across all the more scandalous. Perhaps things are different abroad, but in the Fire Nation, the way Katara runs her fingers through Toph’s hair is an intimacy best left to the utmost privacy. *Are* they a mated pair? From her protests before, Katara definitely wouldn’t let Toph leave a mark on her neck, and with her natural scent suppressed, Zuko has no way of determining whether their scents have become mingled or not.

Toph sucks the air between her teeth. “Yikes. No clue how we’re finding those here.”

Katara frowns down at her. “It’s not a big deal. This place sucks in a lot of ways - again, no offense, Zuko - but at least it’s warm. I’m sure silphium grows in excess here, unlike the North Pole.”

Toph cringes. “You’re forgetting what the Fire Nation and the North Pole do have in common, Sweetness. Rigid-ass gender roles. Suppressants are illegal here.”

Suddenly, there is a tightness to Aang’s bearing that wasn’t there before. He seems to go rigid where he sits beside Zuko.

“It’s fine,” Aang says. “Illegal doesn’t mean impossible to find. We just have to brush up on our shadier sources.”

Zuko is waiting for him to make surreptitious eye contact, to ask if he, as a local omega, can help them find what they need, but those gray eyes remain fixed straight ahead. Instead it’s Sokka who asks, “You wouldn’t happen to have a connection in the village…?”

Zuko casts his gaze aside, pained by his last memory involving silphium. His voice shakes as he answers. “In the capital. I don’t know anyone here, though.”

Sokka doesn’t seem to pick up on his discomfort. He insists, “You could have your source mail some, right? I mean, what’s a minor felony to a member of the royal family?”

Zuko must be visibly pale at the thought. To his surprise, it’s Katara who speaks up in his defense. “Sokka, there are probably a million eyes on him. There’s no way he could get it without it being a huge scandal! We’ll find it ourselves.”

Then she casts a nervous glance at Aang. “Well,” Katara says, voice straining to take on cheer, “things aren’t dire, yet. We have at least a week before we’ll be forced to fight for the last-”

She stops abruptly, hand leaping to her mouth. But it’s too late; Zuko whips his head around to look at Aang, to confirm that what Katara said means what he thinks it does. He’s not at all thinking of the fact this was hidden from him, not at all thinking of why Aang might be avoiding his eyes-

“Aang, *you’re* an omega, too?” Zuko asks, incredulous.

The Avatar is lacking his usual relaxed looseness. He scratches his neck, mouth drawn in a tight line. “...I. Guess?”

His response doesn’t make any sense to Zuko, who can only blink in reply. Sokka loudly claps his hands and tries to change the subject, but Zuko doesn’t really hear what he’s saying. He’s focused on how wholly Aang has closed himself off, his entire body turned away, eyes desperately avoiding Zuko’s no matter how hard the prince stares. And Zuko realizes he *is* staring. It’s probably rude, but he’s just so incredulous.

This should be an exciting revelation. One of his oldest theories about the Avatar has been proven. Hell, Zhao had *laughed* at the idea of an omega Avatar, it seemed so impossible.

And here the omega Avatar is, looking less than thrilled about the revelation. This seems like the perfect opportunity to relate to one another. Is he worried Zuko is going to use this information *against* him, somehow? There can be no other reason behind his discomfort.

So Zuko hovers, waiting for the right moment. It takes a while; the group bickers a little longer about the necessity of going to the village, and of the possibility of relocating to the other side of the island, hours away from the village (an idea Aang vehemently rejects). Eventually, the rest of the crew makes their way outside to lounge around on the beach, and in this solitude, Aang is able to meet Zuko’s eye again.

“Should we spar?” he asks.

A spar sounds perfect to Zuko. He stands and stretches, ready to voice his agreement, only to abort whatever he was going to say in a painful wince as he pulls his injured shoulder.

Aang sees his distress. “Are you alright?”

“Yeah,” Zuko lies, other hand coming up to rub it, “I just… slept on it weird. Give me a moment, and I’ll…” He tries to move into a defensive position, but he pulls it again, the resulting wince as deep as the last.

“Are you sure you’re okay?” Aang asks, brows crumpling with worry. “You didn’t get thrown off your dragon moose yesterday, did you?”

“No, I-” Zuko stops himself, realizing the opportunity Aang has handed him. “Wait. Actually, I do think I might’ve strained it trying *not* to get thrown off. I whipped her into a real frenzy.”

Seeing the utter trust and sympathy in Aang’s face, Zuko tells himself that what he has said isn’t entirely a lie. No doubt one of the reasons the shoulder hurts so profusely is that it was somewhat overused even before Zhao doled out his punishment.

Aang steps a little closer with hands raised, which makes Zuko think he might try to touch him. He doesn’t; he just ends up looking more closely at the shoulder, at Zuko himself. Zuko fears Aang can see beneath the layers of red silk to the black and blue galaxies of bruised flesh beneath, and averts his eyes.

“I hate that you got hurt on my behalf,” Aang says.

Zuko summons the bravery needed to look at Aang’s face, heart quickening when he realizes it’s only a gentle twist of the head’s distance from his own. “It’s fine, Aang. I’d do it again.”

“I wouldn’t ask that of you.”

“Well, I’d do it. Without question.”

They’re alone, and close enough to steal one another’s breath. Aang watches him, a certain heaviness to his lids, head tilting-

“Why didn’t you tell me you were an omega?” Zuko whispers, inches from his lips.

There it is again. That profound discomfort sharpening the edges of Aang’s body. Suddenly Aang is pulling away, mouth a jagged line, and Zuko knows that he’ll begin to pace and put more and more distance between them, so on instinct alone he grabs Aang’s hands and tugs them towards him, brushing his thumbs over the knuckles - smooth to the touch. These haven’t been bloodied and torn by battle.

Anchored to the spot, Aang sighs, lets the rigid lines of his body soften with each movement of Zuko’s fingers over his. “I think I didn’t tell you because… I don’t really see myself that way.”

Zuko doesn’t understand, but he doesn’t interject, getting the sense Aang’s trying to gather his thoughts. He’s usually so quick to fill silence, to joke and laugh, but whatever it is he wants to say now, he wants to say it right.

“I’m still getting used to this world I woke up into,” Aang admits, “where everyone’s second sex matters so much. When I was growing up in the Southern Air Temple, it didn’t… it’s not that it didn’t matter at all, but it wasn’t such an obstacle. For one, we weren’t as opposed to suppressants the way a lot of countries are. If anything, we encouraged their use.”

Zuko can’t suppress his surprise. “Really?”

Aang nods. “It was highly advised that anyone living in the temple should stay on suppressants and scent blockers.” He says the next part hurriedly, like he’s used to people assuming the worst: “It wasn’t about shame! It’s not like we thought we were making anybody hide their ‘true nature.’ It was more about… about transcendence. Because how can you ever really focus on your spirit, how can you ever connect to your body and make it flourish, if you’re a - a slave to it? And so to make it fair, we just… equalized everyone. Started from the same clean slate.”

“What if you wanted children?” Zuko asks. “Were you allowed?”

“It was always a choice,” Aang assures him. “If you wanted to mate, you could. You had to leave the temple to do it, but you could do it.”

“Really?”

“Yeah. I’d even say a majority of Air Nomads, the people who left our temples, were pursuing those kinds of lives. The option was *there* . It’s just that a lot of people chose to go back on suppressants and return to their spiritual duties after it was all said and done with.”

Zuko’s response is born of anxiety. “What happened to their lovers when they did that? Their children?”

“What do you mean?” Aang asks, head cocked. “They were all welcome back home. You weren’t supposed to enter a heat or a rut on sacred grounds, but there were no other rules against sex or romance. Meanwhile, kids were pretty much raised by the whole community, so whether you wanted to raise a family or not, you had an option to fall back on, if you felt the nomadic life wasn’t safe enough for your little ones.”

“That can’t be,” Zuko murmurs, shaking his head.

Aang’s smile goes terribly sad. “I suppose it all sounds insane, by today’s standards.”

“No, it-” Zuko sighs. “It sounds too good to be *true* . Like you were all living in an impossible utopia.”

Surprise registers on Aang’s face, his brows leaping beneath his headband. When he recovers, it’s like seeing the sun dawn, his smile is so sincere. “You know, your reaction is the opposite of Sokka and Katara’s? They were horrified when I told them air acolytes suppress their heats. They saw it as fighting nature.”

Zuko remembers something. “You said Sokka and Katara found you - does that mean you woke up in the South Pole?” Then, when Aang nods, “What was *that* like, given how differently they see sex?”

At least this time Aang’s look of discomfort is somewhat comical. His eyes practically bulge out of his head at the memory, and he lets loose a torrid exhale to bring himself back down to center. “Ugh… that was probably the rudest awakening of my life. I find out I’m alive, at least, but a hundred years of war have passed, so everyone I’ve ever known is dead. And to top it off…” Aang coughs, averting his eyes with a blush. “I, uh. Went straight into heat.”

Zuko can’t help but go red himself. “No! Seriously?”

Aang grimaces into his nod. “I’d really only had one heat before, my very first heat before I went on suppressants. It was short, probably as average as they come. I don’t know if it was all the years I spent without suppressants, and my metabolism caught up when I thawed, but… the heat I had after waking from the ice was - *long* . And really, really intense.”

Zuko covers his mouth. “Since you hadn’t had one in a while. I’ve heard that can happen.”

“Yeah. At least the people of the Southern Tribe handled it with grace. They have these structures where you can go for privacy during your heat, so I stayed there the whole time, really only seeing other people when they sent, like, clean water and food, and changes of clothes.” Aang scratches his neck, growing redder at the memory. “Katara, uh… Katara was actually. The person who brought those things to me, which was supremely mortifying. Like, here was this pretty older girl, the savior who’d pulled me out of the ice, and she was immediately seeing me at my worst.”

It’s not at all the point of the story, but Zuko finds himself irked by the way Aang talks of Katara. With those wide blue eyes peering out of her delicate face, she certainly is pretty, but not in a way Zuko’s particularly taken notice of… or that he thought Aang would take notice of.

Zuko forces a laugh. “Wow. I always wondered about some of your earlier adventures. And there were some I wished I’d gotten to see up close - like when you stopped the flood in the Hu Xin Provinces! But I suppose it wasn’t *all* adventure.”

Aang laughs along with him. “Ugh, *no* , it really wasn’t! Like, no silphium grew in the South, and trade was blocked by the war, so that wasn’t the last shitty heat we endured.”

“I knew it!” says Zuko, pumping a fist into the air. At Aang’s dubious look, he dampens his elation somewhat, saying with a nervous smile, “Sorry. I saw the pattern early on, so I figured you were at least traveling with an omega.”

Aang’s smile has a curious ripple to it. “So somebody *did* notice… Yeah, I mean, even once we got our hands on some silphium, it was hard to convince Katara to go on it. So the early days weren't all fun. And that’s not even addressing all the dumb, hormonal teen drama over who liked who…”

Zuko feels a flash of something white and hot he can’t quite name, and thinks again of Katara, *pretty* Katara. He turns himself somewhat away from Aang to hide whatever this… bitter feeling is, and summons all the casual indifference he has in his body to say, “Oh? I guess it makes sense. You’re all teenagers. Crushes were bound to happen.”

He thought he was being subtle, but Aang’s eyes widen, and he immediately goes on the defensive, saying, “No, I mean - that’s all in the past, though - ancient history! I don’t know why I even brought it up. Nobody even returned anybody else’s feelings, so it was kind of a bad time for all of us, and we had to learn to just be friends, and…”

He’s miming shapes with his hands, getting more and more frazzled. “Anyway - I don’t think Sokka was *really* in love with me, so much as I was the - well, that was the first whiff of heat he’d ever gotten. So he got kind of obsessed.”

The shock of this revelation, that *Sokka* once liked *Aang,* is enough to pull Zuko out of his jealous pouting. “Sokka? And *you?* ”

“Hey, I wasn’t into him!” Aang insists, waving his hands wildly. “He’s so not my type! And now he’ll tell you I’m really not his type, either. He prefers the really femme-y omegas. Women, mostly.”

Zuko chews the inside of his cheek. He’s trying to focus on this funny revelation, but… “And. Those were the only crushes in your group? Did you and Katara ever…?”

Aang goes scarlet. “Again - ancient history!”

“...Who liked who?” Zuko asks. He despises the sound of his own voice - plaintive, forlorn.

Aang swallows. “I uh. Well. It was a misunderstanding, I’m sure. Spending your heats together is, like, a normal, platonic thing for omegas to do in the Southern Tribe, I guess. But afterward, I couldn’t get the sight of her out of my head. Or the scent of her…”

He searches Zuko’s face, and suddenly stops this line of talk. “But she’s, y’know. Normal. So even when I told her how I felt, she was just… She didn’t get it. She was cool about it, of course! Which is why we’re still friends…”

“Do you still have feelings for her?” Zuko asks. (Who is this person, with the audacity to grill the Avatar on his romantic history?)

Aang outright blanches. “ *No,* ” he says, scandalized. “ *Hell* no. Even if Katara wasn’t one of my best friends, Toph would kick my ass if I made a move on her.”

So Katara and Toph *are* an item. Zuko’s chest floods with relief, and he can breathe easier now. He feels a particularly idiotic smile threatened to stretch his face, and is forced to fight it down. He coughs into his hand, starts to talk just to change the subject.

“I never realized the other nations were so different, when it came to this sort of thing. I mean, I had a feeling. I was told a little bit about how they do things in the South. That they’re more… egalitarian. But the Air Nation’s way of doing things is even more surprising.”

Aang shrugs. “Yeah. I mean, I wish I had a Southern Tribe attitude, sometimes, that I could just see heat as another bodily function. But I don’t. I just… I hate it.”

That certainly catches Zuko’s interest. “What do you hate about it?”

Aang scoffs. “ *Everything* . I hate sweating out of my skin. I hate the idea of getting pregnant. I hate the way every single nation except mine thinks about omegas. I just hate it all.”

There’s a rawness to his voice that Zuko finds intimately familiar. He realizes he’s never had the chance to commiserate with another omega in this way. Even those bitter words his teacher, Aloki, had spoken to him long ago had been more resigned than defiant.

“I don’t think I know a single omega that loves being an omega,” Zuko admits. “I think it’s more just a role you accept because you have to. Isn’t it?

Aang laughs softly. “You’d be surprised.” Something passes over his face, darkening his expression. “I feel more conflicted about it than usual, now. Because my people are gone, I feel an obligation. I should have a family to make up for it. But the thought of giving birth just… turns my stomach.”

Zuko feels as though his lungs have gone shallow. He’s looking at Aang so closely, studying the turmoil in his face, praying the other boy won’t meet his eyes, because then he’ll be forced to look away.

“I know about obligation,” Zuko whispers. He would leave it there, but Aang watches him in gentle silence, leaving ample room for him to go on, to explain himself. So he does. “Zhao was… picked out for me, by my father.”

“You didn’t choose him.”

Zuko doesn’t think this is accurate, and wavers. “I was told there were important political benefits to marrying him. The chance to help repair the nation. I could have turned him down…”

Aang shakes his head. “But then, how could you, with stakes like that?”

Zuko doesn’t deny him this. After a pause, Aang asks, “What would you have done if you could’ve chosen for yourself?”

Zuko gives the smallest lilt of the shoulders. “I really don’t know. That’s like asking what I would’ve done if I was born with wings. It’s just such an impossibility, why even entertain it? Even if I’d been born an alpha, I’m sure my father would’ve picked an omega for me. To be a beta would be a shame. It’s all about continuing the family line.”

Sadness weighs Aang’s features down. “That’s… not fair.”

“That’s how it is in most nations,” Zuko says. “You’ve been living in a dream.”

“No, I haven’t. It was all real.” Aang speaks not with anger, not with defensiveness, but with a touch of sorrow. “Now that my people are gone, I… I think all the nations left tend to focus too much on sex for reproduction. Obsessing over bloodlines. Most people think of betas as inherently asexual just because they can’t reproduce, but overwhelming evidence shows they aren’t. They’re just as capable of sexual intimacy, of desire. Likewise, so are we all, even without heats or ruts. And I think, you know, there are probably tons of omegas and alphas who really don’t want all of this as much as they think they do. That with or without bodily cycles, they’d be fine without a family, or without marriage, or without both.”

“But we’re made for it,” Zuko says, without feeling. “It’s what our bodies were made to do.”

Aang shakes his head. “We tie everything to the body, but just because something fits, does it make it destiny? They change so drastically halfway through our lives - doesn’t that mean we’re dynamic beings? That we’re made to *change?* ”

He pauses, eyes running over Zuko’s face. Then, “There’s a bruise on your jaw.”

Zuko has to suppress his reaction. He feels the old mask slide into place, the one he was taught to wear as a proper omega coming up in Fire Nation society. “Is there? I had no idea.”

Zuko raises a hand to cover the bruise, but he realizes he doesn’t know where it is. Instead, he presses his hand over his scent gland. Feels the heat of his own palm.

“It’s so strange to think we’re the same,” Zuko murmurs. “I genuinely don’t think of you as an omega. Which I think you prefer, anyway, right?”

Aang nods. Zuko smiles somewhat sadly. “I’ve only ever known you as scentless. I don’t know if it’s bad of me to say, but I can’t help but wonder…”

It’s as if a light goes on in Aang’s eyes. “You know scent-blockers aren’t perfect, right? You could probably detect it, if you got close enough.”

Zuko is utterly struck by the notion. “Is… that alright?” he asks, recovering. “Would you be comfortable with me doing that?”

As if in answer, Aang leans down, baring his neck to Zuko. The prince can’t resist the prickle of heat he feels rise to his cheeks as he arches up, face inches from Aang’s skin, and inhales.

“It’s… faint. I can’t…”

“That’s alright,” Aang assures. “Take as long as you need.”

With this proximity, Zuko finds himself clasping his knees, Aang’s hands hanging rigidly at his sides - both of them fear what will happen if they make contact, yet can’t bring themselves to move apart. Zuko hovers there, waiting, breathing, heart thundering in his ears.

Then there it is. Zuko gently inhales, feeling the air pass inside him, light in his throat, in his chest. Aang’s scent. He doesn’t know how to describe it, precisely - an image passes through his mind of roiling clouds heavy with rain, darkening the sky the night they met. It’s a bodily scent, but a clean scent. Breathing it in, Zuko feels something inside him flutter and clench.

Aang swallows, and it’s so loud at this proximity. “Have you… have you caught it?” he asks, voice cautiously low, like one might speak in order not to scare away a frightened animal. Still, the sound of it frightens Zuko out of whatever trance he’s in, makes him rear back, face flushed.

“I - yes,” Zuko says. “It’s - you’re -” He bites back a compliment, floundering over how else to fill the silence instead. “I never realized scent blockers were so imperfect. But I should’ve realized, since false scents also aren’t, um, perfect. Not that I have a ton of experience with either, I just…”

There’s noise at the mouth of the cave, and Zuko sees something akin to disappointment flash across Aang’s face. He takes a step back, rendering the distance between them socially acceptable as the rest of the group files back inside, alive with chatter. Sokka waves emphatically to them, completely unaware of the intimacy that transpired while he was gone.

“Hey Aang, I talked to Piandao about that thing! Turns out he knows those guys, too. Thinks fairly highly of them.”

Once again, Aang’s brows shoot up beneath his headband. “Really?”

“Yeah! I have a lot to tell you about that.” Sokka looks at Zuko, perhaps surreptitiously. “Uh, later, later. I don’t want to interrupt your training.”

Perhaps it’s the reverberation of their voices on the walls of this cave, but the switch from such stolid intimacy to such noise and crowding makes anxiety shoot through Zuko like a bolt of lightning. As little as he wants to return to the estate, he doesn’t want to be here anymore.

“I should go for the day,” he says, somewhat breathless. In grasping to appear normal, he flutters a hand in goodbye, swings it so awkwardly that it lands on Aang’s arm, makes contact with warm skim.

Before he can pull away, the Avatar places a hand over his own, gives it the tiniest squeeze. “Wait. Before you do, I remembered something…”

From the crisp lines of his pilfered naval academy uniform, Aang pulls a piece of paper. “This list of recommendations you gave me. Do you know these people personally?”

Pinned under the gentle warmth of Aang’s hand, it takes Zuko a moment to come to earth, to understand what the paper is and where it came from. He shakes his head as if clearing a fog. “No, that… I don’t know anyone on Kirachu that well. My brother-in-law helped me make it. Why - are you worried if those men are trustworthy?”

Aang blinks. “No. Actually, I trust them all quite a lot.” He unfolds the paper, showing Zuko the names. “This list of names actually matches one given to us by another friend.”

“Oh,” says Zuko. “I didn’t know you’d made other friends here in Kirachu.”

“That’s just it,” Katara says, approaching. “We haven’t. Our other list is from a man who tutored us in the Northern Water Tribe.”

That doesn’t make any sense. Why on earth would Yan run in the same social circles as a waterbender, let alone one living thousands of miles away?

Truth be told, Zuko was torn between fury and affection for Yan only that morning. Yan may have stood up for Zuko briefly, but it wasn’t like he had charged up the stairs after the two of them that night. He hadn’t prevented what came later, when Zhao had Zuko alone.

…But what could he have done? Zuko remembers Yan’s difficulty ascending the stairs. Yan is a capable adult, but he isn’t all-powerful. And he had tried so hard to ingratiate himself to Zuko today, even bringing him to the village.

Zuko shakes his head, clearing his thoughts. “...He’s anti-empire, and speaks out against my father’s policies every chance he gets. If he has chosen to associate himself with these men, it’s likely they feel the same way.”

“That’s good,” Toph says, but Katara looks stricken beside her.

“You haven’t told him about us, have you?” Katara asks, a hint of that old, angry fear towards him creeping back into her voice.

Zuko shakes his head. “I wouldn’t give you up even for my own flesh and blood. But I do think you can trust Yan’s recommendations.”

And maybe Zuko himself could trust him. Albeit tentatively.

---

They meet back in the village, just as they said they would. Zuko drops some of his moodiness from earlier, meeting Yan’s wide, nervous smile with a muted one of his own. At first they don’t say very much, feeling the reverberation of the carriage wheels on the road. Yan doesn’t ask Zuko what he was doing, although he does eventually ask, “Did you have a good time?”

Zuko nods. Yan melts into the stiff cushions surrounding him, face slack with relief.

“Fuck,” he says, “thank Agni. I felt so sorry for everything, you know, last night. I figured this was the least I could do.”

There’s a beat. Something closes off in Zuko’s expression, like a door sliding shut.

“What do you have to be sorry for?” he asks.

Yan has struggled to put all of this into words, and Zuko’s unyielding stare isn’t really making it any easier. “I don’t know,” he says, honestly. “Maybe I could’ve done more.”

Something quivers in Zuko’s expression, but he grabs hold of it, remains composed. “I’ll admit I was short with you this morning, probably because I agreed with you at the time. But I’ve thought a lot about it since then, and I’ve realized there really wasn’t anything else you *could* do.”

Yan hesitates. “I mean. I could’ve fought him on it…”

Zuko shrugs. “Then what? You fight him every time, and he wins, because he’s a trained soldier, and you’re disabled? So the two of us end up sharing in the misery?” Zuko crosses his arms defensively over his chest. “I don’t want that, Yan. I’d rather be the only one.”

Yan isn’t sure what to say to that. Zuko seems so sure that someone is always going to get hurt.

Eventually, Yan mutters, “I’m a trained soldier, too, y’know.”

“Right. I suppose I forgot,” Zuko says. “You’re so anti-empire. How did you ever end up enlisting, anyway?”

An obvious change of subject. Yan taps the golden tigermonkey head on his cane, considering his reply.

“Honestly? Because I didn’t want to live in the same house as my father anymore.”

“Oh.” That single word, threaded through with a hairline fracture of emotion, is all he gets out of Zuko. They sit in the carriage with their blood thrumming, eyes not really meeting.

Yan has always hated silences. When things went quiet back home, it meant something bad was about to happen. So to chase away the apprehension, he starts filling the air. “I joined the army late, you know. Wei was out of the house before I can even remember, and Zhao left pretty much the second he was allowed.”

“That sounds like him,” Zuko says, distantly. His eyes are on the window. He’s probably thinking about Zhao’s obsession with glory, in general. Yan agrees it’s just like Zhao, to leave first, but a part of him has always secretly thought it was selfish. Like he was saving his own skin.

“Yeah. After Zhao left, it was just me and Ama at home for a really long time. I was terrified to leave him alone there, so much so I missed the recruitment cutoff a couple years in a row. But after a point, I couldn’t take it anymore. So I left, too.

“I really liked swords as a kid. I thought because I won a few tournaments that that would translate into army skill, but it didn’t. You can’t come into a real battle expecting to parry and dodge the whole time, because the other guy wants you dead. He slashes at your throat, and you move just in time, but now you need to slash *his* throat, and his buddy’s, and all the rest of them, or they’ll retreat and get earthbenders, and you do *not* want to fight an earthbender.

“Just by the nature of the bending they do, the landscape’s really ripped up out there. And it has these unexpected consequences. Like, when it rains really, really hard, there are these mudslides in the hills. I literally watched as fifty, sixty men were…” Yan swallows, struggling even now, years removed from it. “As they were buried alive, under all that. And that was the last straw, for me - it was bad enough killing people, it was bad enough fucking fighting for my life every day, but it was like even the *land* didn’t want us to be there.

“So I deserted. Right there, next to a heap of mud and silt where my comrades were entombed - I had started running, to avoid being caught, then even when I was clear of the mess, I just kept running. I ran all night, barely able to see in front of me, just listening to snapping branches, hoping I wouldn’t trip and break something.

“Eventually I collapsed from exhaustion, and I pretty much figured that was the end for me. Until I woke up in this nice little house. Apparently some family found me and took me in. I wasn’t even in the colonies; it was obvious, looking at my eyes and the color of my civilian clothes, what I was. But the dad, he’d seen me lying out there in the field, and he didn’t think it would be right to leave me, so he brought me into his own home and let me get the recovery time I needed.

“It wasn’t just him. The whole family was good to me. To each other, too. They had so little to eat, but they shared it with me. They barely had enough beds, but they made the kids share so I’d have a place to sleep. They didn’t ask me a thing about where I was from, and in return I’d do whatever chores they asked, like they were my neighbors or something.

“It was fucking mindboggling. I’d been told we were in the Earth Kingdom fighting savages, right? Mud slingers who needed to be civilized. But these were decent people. Better than the ones I left behind! Fuck, there was this one moment - the youngest boy dropped this jug, shattered it. It was the only water they had saved up. Here I’m thinking, I’m about to see this kid get beaten. He starts sobbing, which only stresses me out more, but then his dad is like, ‘It’s ok, kid! Accidents happen! We’ll be more careful next time.’ Then he helped him sop it all up, like it was nothing. It didn’t matter if it was an accident or not; my dad would’ve given me the belt over something like that.”

Yan realizes he’s incessantly tapping on the head of his cane, but he can’t stop. He’s anxious. He keeps talking, hoping to chase the feeling away.

“It didn’t last forever. Eventually the whole family left to try their chances at the gates of Ba Sing Se, and I headed back west, only to get picked back up by another Fire Nation unit. I served in the army until I got the injury that sent me home, but in all that time, I never stopped thinking about those people. I’d never seen a family up close like that other than my own, so it’d never really occurred to me that it wasn’t normal to be scared of your own dad all the time. I didn’t realize most people walk around their whole lives without ever once thinking their dad’s going to kill them, or their mom, or their brother.

“And weirdly, you know, the more I realized I’d been living this… closed off, narrow point of view, the more I started to question other stuff. It wasn’t such a jump from questioning the violence in my family to questioning the violence in my home country. It felt eerily familiar, and when I think back to the kind of stuff my dad would say and the stuff they’d say in school, I don’t know why I didn’t see it sooner. Always doubling down on the excuses, always telling you that when you’re hurt or it looks unfair, that’s just because *you’re* the one who’s wrong. Always, ‘We’re doing this for your own good.’ Oh, yeah? If it’s so good, why am I so fucking scared for my life? Why the fuck are these good people so scared for their lives?”

It is on this tangled train of thought that Yan finally runs out of oxygen. He pauses to catch his breath, eyes nervously flitting to Zuko and then away, afraid to see his reaction. But there isn’t much to see; instead, the only sign he is listening is the smallest, most imperceptible shake of his head, back and forth. Even as Yan leaves space for a response, Zuko doesn’t fill it.

Perhaps Yan hasn’t made as much sense as he’d hoped; he’s never been good with words. Embarrassed, he shuts up for the rest of the ride back up the mountain.

---

When Zuko gets home, he takes to the stairs, flitting up to his room, where he shuts the door behind him faster than Yan could possibly pursue.

The weight of his thoughts pushes him towards the bed, bids him lay on his side and stare at the images painted on the door. The bonsai forest. The birds in flight. Just a few months ago, he had leaned against that same door, and grappled with the severity of his husband’s violence. That was weeks before he’d found out he was pregnant. He hadn't known that any revelations he’d had were about to become useless, that his fate was already sealed.

As Zuko lays curled on his side, the still imperceptible bulge of his stomach seems gargantuan, billowing under the folds of his robes. There is a human being growing inside him. Most days he still can’t wrap his head around the thought. Eventually, though, it won’t matter that he can’t picture this child, or Zhao in fatherhood. It’ll be the reality.

He wonders if someday their own child will fight abroad just to escape this house, or if there’s something more he can do to protect his child from Zhao.

Zuko’s mind returns to Aang. It is a shame he doesn’t want children. With all the joy and patience he possesses, he’d make for an incredible parent. Not that Zuko blames him for wanting to avoid pregnancy - he has spent most of his own pregnancy dressing in layers, avoiding mirrors, hiding his body from himself. He dreads the day he can’t ignore it any longer.

Fingers loosely bunched in the silk sheets now tighten their purchase in remembering how easily the Avatar had bared his neck to him only hours before. He was hiding that scent to protect his status, and still, he’d let Zuko detect it. Scenting may be a common means of identification, but Aang’s complicated relationship with his second sex made the act seem much more intimate.

And it had been such a *good* scent. Zuko blushes to even admit to himself how he’d wanted to remain there, breathe it in again. He remembers Aang towering over him, the anticipation in those empty moments before he finally found the scent, how difficult it had been to keep his hands still, how badly he had wanted to surge upwards and… and…

And what? Lay a kiss on the Avatar’s neck? Surely Aang wouldn’t have allowed it. To have your neck touched was so - vulnerable. So omega. When Zuko goes to kiss him in this next fantasy, the Aang in his mind tilts his head down at the last second, captures his lips. (Is that head tilt familiar? Had Zuko seen Aang do something like it today?)

Maybe the Aang in his mind stops Zuko short. Maybe to not be an omega means to lean more alpha.

A hand in Zuko’s hair prevents him from laying a kiss at the last moment. The grip twists, softened by a gentle chuckle inches from his mouth - *Eager, aren’t you?*

It isn’t like before, when he had to watch his hands, lest they betray his desires. Alone in his room, Zuko closes his eyes and lets his hands start to inch downwards, careful to avoid touching any part of himself that could ruin this fantasy. Body curled like a crescent moon, he pulls the many layers of clothing out of the way, outer thigh jerking in surprise at the coldness of his own touch.

The house is quiet. He cannot hear any voices, nor creaks of footsteps, nor even the hint of birds outside. In this quiet, he is able to tumble deeper into his fantasy, images coming to him almost unbidden, like a dream. It happened in the span of moments.

A guard outside Azula’s cell was trying to look threatening, twirling a knife in his hands. It was small, which of course she commented on, so he blushed angrily and told her all the animals whose throats it had been drawn across, beasts much bigger and more threatening than *you,* kitten, and he twirled it in the air, passing it from hand to hand.

Maybe it was her lack of interest he found so unnerving; maybe it was the sudden slam of the dungeon doors as someone else arrived. But the guard fumbled and dropped the knife.

Azula was across her cell like a shot, and before the guard could drop to the ground to recover his knife, she’d snatched it up, then fled to the opposite side of her cell. There, she crouched on her bed and clutched the pilfered weapon to her chest, her eyes never leaving the barred door.

The guard was shouting abuses at Azula through the bars of her cell, which earned him a ferocious glare from the normally composed Water Tribe Princess when she finally arrived.

“What is going *on* here?” she demanded.

The guard stepped back from the bars so he wouldn’t be unguarded within stabbing distance, and pointed accusingly at the girl inside. “The prisoner got her hands on a weapon.”

“The prisoner picked up a knife *you* dropped right in front of her,” Azula huffed.

Yue frowned at the guard. “Is this true?”

“Well-”

“He was doing tricks,” Azula tattled. “Trying to intimidate me. It was barely entertaining.”

The guard went beet red. “No! That’s not what happened!”

Yue calmly absorbed Azula and the guard’s versions of the story, babbled frantically over one another, converging and diverging until the truth left them as quiet as chastised children, watching her urgently for her final word. When everyone had finally quieted, Yue walked right up to the door of the cell and stuck her arm through, despite the nervous protests of the guard.

“Give it here, Azula,” she said.

Azula looked at the outstretched hand, the same one she’d held in her own that morning. Slowly, she stood from her cot and made her way closer to the princess, stopping just shy of her reach. Still, Yue held her hand out expectantly, but she did not retreat. It would be easy for Azula to lash out, to draw a wretched red line across the unbroken skin of the princess’s palm.

Azula moved swiftly. She saw Yue and the guard flinch, frozen in place when they realized she wasn’t lashing out at the princess. Azula had grabbed hold of the loose ponytail piled at the back of her head, and with gritted teeth, she sawed the knife through the tangled strands.

A shower of black hair fell to the cell floor. Yue’s mouth fell open. “Your *topknot* . But why…?”

The gravity of the gesture wasn’t lost on her, then. Azula wanted to praise Yue, but she didn’t trust herself not to inject malice into her voice, to say it in a way that was cruel ( *There you are, I knew* *you were smarter than the rest of them,* an implicit jab at her beloved people). Azula had a silver tongue that was forked. She knew that most of what she said was dishonest or outright hurtful, but she also didn’t know how to correct it, how to speak… gently, as Yue did with her.

So rather than speak, she chose to gently lay the knife in the Water Tribe princess’s hand.

### Text

Even in a strange place like this, Iroh can sleep like the dead, unmoved to consciousness even as Azula violently shakes him atop his bed of furs. She imagines the tinctures lined along the walls of the healing hut are rattling with the force of his snoring. When she wakes him, the peace and quiet will be more suspicious than any sound they could possibly make.

Still. She dumps her waterskin on his face, then clamps her hand over his gasping mouth, gesturing at him to *shush* before he can alert the guards.

Iroh does not shush. “Azula? What are you doing here? How are you free?”

“The princess has granted me a favor,” Azula hisses back. “Let’s cash it in before she changes her mind.”

To Iroh’s credit, he tries to hurry as best as he can. But even the weeks of rest and recuperation haven’t brought him to full strength, and he’s huffing and puffing by the time they make their way down the dark, snowy path towards the docks. Azula looks behind her and sees how his great heaving breaths fog up the air around his head, and wonders if she’s making a mistake, if she’s risking his safety all over again.

They make their way to the waterfront, where the strange wooden ships of the Northern Water Tribe creak and groan like dreaming animals. Azula directs her uncle to crouch behind a ledge while she assesses the area. So far she hasn’t seen a single soul, not even a guard, but she knows better than to become complacent. For all she knows someone heard her approach and is now crouching in wait, ready to catch them by surprise.

She realizes a few minutes in that her uncle is shivering. *Audibly* shivering, because the man can’t resist vocalizing even the smallest actions. She tosses a scowl his way. “Use your breath of fire.”

“I’m - trying,” he manages through chattering teeth. He clutches and rubs his arms through his coat, and again, she wonders what she’s risking by bringing him here.

“Do - do you know how to sail one of those?” Iroh asks, preying on her doubts with a nod towards the solemn boats waiting in the harbor.

“A boat is a boat,” she mutters back. She has sailed before. Granted, not in arctic conditions…

She’s quiet for a long time, weighing all the possible consequences. For the past month, her escape has been the first thought in her mind when she wakes up in the morning and the last thought she’s held in those last fading moments of consciousness. She has pictured endlessly what little layout of the castle she knew outside the dungeons, imagined by the echoing footsteps of retreating and returning guards on rotation. She has mapped in her mind the most plausible architecture of a dungeon and challenged herself to imagine all sorts of pitfalls that may stand in her way so that she can be prepared to confront them. With her firebending subdued, she planned to use her own shackles as weapons, as well as some chi-neutralizing jabs she has observed Ty Lee do (although never attempted herself). She even convinced herself she was growing closer to the Water Tribe princess for the sole intent of catching her unawares.

However. Now that Azula is here in the frigid air, her escape route rippling placidly before her, it feels less like she’s been give a chance at escape and more like she’s living out an idiotic impulse.

Azula turns to her uncle. “Forget it,” she says, her defeat crystallizing in the air before them. “This is suicide. Let’s get you back to the healing hut before they realize you’ve gone.”

She starts to sneak past her uncle, to head back the way they came, but he grabs her by the shoulder and says, “No.”

She looks back at him, baffled. “What do you mean, no?”

“I won’t have your entire life wasted in a jail cell, Azula,” he says.

His conviction warms her heart, but it doesn’t quite change her mind. Crossing her arms insecurely over her chest, she mutters, “What about all you’ve gone on about, our crimes against these people? I have to pay, right? Isn’t that part of my growth?”

Iroh releases a noise of frustration. “Regardless of what we might have done to these people, regardless of what we owe them, we cannot pay it back when we are locked away from the world. Rehabilitation is best conducted out in society, where the good you do will matter.” He smiles at her, then, and the shadows that catch in his age lines cast him forward a decade or so. “Besides… I selfishly want to go home. I miss Fire Nation food. I miss my nephew…”

Azula cracks the smallest of smiles, trying without enthusiasm to add some haughty bite to it. “Fine, old man. Let’s go.”

There is a guard out on patrol, after all. But they manage to catch him by surprise, knock him out before he can alert anyone to their location. From there, they have to hustle. Iroh manages an impressive burst of speed as they vault themselves into the nearest vessel and unmoor themselves.

It’s a harrowing trip out of the port onto the open waters, Azula terrified out of her skin that she’ll knock into a row of boats, call the whole city outside to watch their escape, but eventually the parapets of Agna Qel’a fade into the distance, and they are really, truly free.

Azula turns towards the placid black waters. The sky is cloudless, so she can see the stars reflected in the ocean, as well as the moon, paving the path home.

For the entire night after his excursion to the village with Yan, Zuko’s heart was in his throat, waiting for Zhao to confront him. But the only words they exchanged in the hours following Zhao’s return home were right before bed, when Zhao asked him to turn off the bedside lamp. He didn’t ask what Zuko had done that day, even to check that he had obeyed him. He barely seemed willing to talk to Zuko at all.

So it seemed Zuko’s secret was safe with Yan, for now. It helped that Zhao was barely around to be on the receiving end of any snitching - in the days that followed, he began to stay out of the house well past dark. For all he complained at the dinner table about being appointed to Kirachu’s governor, he put ungodly hours into the work.

Maybe it was just Zuko being paranoid, but given the furtive way Zhao avoided his eyes whenever he was home, he was starting to think Zhao was not only using work to avoid the house, but to avoid Zuko himself. Perhaps he’d finally grown hopeless about Zuko’s repeated insolence. Or perhaps looking at Zuko was difficult for another reason. Zuko wondered if the reason for his husband’s sudden absence was because, deep down, there was some kernel of humanity left inside him, some small part that knew what he’d done the other night was excessive, cruel.

Zuko shook his head, bringing himself back to the present. Zhao’s reasons for staying away didn’t matter. It was all the more chance for Zuko to spend time with the Avatar.

---

Despite the growing trust between Yan and Zuko, the young prince’s loyalty was ultimately to Aang. And so on some days he left before Yan awoke, making a point to cut through the trees, avoiding the village, concealing his path as he went.

On one such day, as Zuko cleared the jungle, he saw a figure standing on the beach a distance away from him. He had an initial pang of fear that this was a patrolling guard, but then he realized the silhouette lacked the sharp jut of armor, the topknot.

Even from far away, Zuko could tell that was not Aang. The height and posture were all wrong, and the stranger’s clothes shone too brightly in the afternoon light, as if made of fine material.

Zuko approached with caution, since even a random villager could spell trouble if they stumbled upon the Avatar’s hiding place. The stranger didn’t look to be doggedly searching for anything along the beach, though; he was just standing there, watching the waves roll lazily in. Once Zuko was upon him, the sounds of his approach made the stranger turn, and he realized he was looking at Toru.

Recognition registered on the other omega’s boyish face. “Prince Zuko - it’s a surprise to see you here!” He bobbed forward, hands clasped in the symbol of a flame.

When he straightened again, there was a guilty look on his face. “What is it?” Zuko asked. “You look troubled.

“Truthfully, Prince Zuko, I’d like to apologize for how I accosted you when we first met. I’m sure my intensity was off-putting, when all you wanted was to shop in town.”

“It’s fine,” Zuko assured him. Then he hesitated; he’d long fantasized about seeing Toru again, but he was unsure how to take advantage of this meeting now. “...May I stay and speak with you?”

“Of course!”

Zuko dismounted his dragon moose. Even with no one around to hear them, to talk to someone from so high up made the conversation feel public. At this proximity, at least, Zuko could lower his voice. Having the enormous mount puffing next to him, shielding his body from any eyes that might be peeking from the treeline, also made him feel safer.

“What are you doing here?” Zuko asked.

Toru shrugged, glancing back towards the sea. “I find the water calming. And it’s private, here. It’s the perfect place to clear your head after a particularly frustrating day of work.”

The wind off the tides was chilly and wild, tugging at their hair like a mischievous toddler. Zuko held a lock of it behind his ear with his hand, and still the errant threads pulled free, whipping across his face with every breeze that came off the waves.

“What you told me back then did upset me,” Zuko admitted, eventually. “But I know you were just trying to be honest. My uncle actually - my uncle told me what Zhao did to you, once.”

Surprise registered on Toru’s face. Zuko wanted to look away, but he made himself maintain eye contact as he amended, “My uncle told me what he knew, anyway - which wasn’t much. Still, it made me so angry at Zhao. I confronted him immediately.”

“And what did he say?” Toru asked, expression unreadable.

“He twisted things around until I was convinced it was all a misunderstanding. He said that you two had dated, but been forced to end your relationship at his parents’ behest.”

Today, Toru had seemed much gentler than when they first met. Now, he gave a quick puff of joyless air, mouth shriveling with disgust reminiscent of that first encounter. “Of course he would say that. I’m sorry you were fed such an indulgent lie, my prince.”

Zuko shook his head. “I’m sorry Zhao did that to you.”

Toru turned his face so the wind off the water would blow his bangs out of his eyes, or maybe just so he didn’t have to look at Zuko anymore.

“I haven’t spent my whole life dwelling on it, you know,” Toru told the sea. “I’d mostly moved on. It helped that the merchants in town looking for employees didn’t run in the same circles as the nobility, so they didn’t care about the rumors Ama spread. Don’t get me wrong - it was a hardship. I had to start over, making far less money than before. But I got back on my feet, eventually.”

Toru heaved a titanic sigh. “I thought I’d made peace with it all. I figured I could even stomach Zhao never having to pay for what he did, so long as I didn’t have to see him around here anymore. Then he came back to Kirachu. I had heard about his marriage. I pictured you much smaller in my head; a teenaged waif. It wasn’t until I really saw you, this - this broad-shouldered boy, that I realized what danger you were in.”

And now Toru looked at him full on, his gaze so deep it was as if he saw to the root of him. “Because it’s always so easy to laugh off the violence against a male omega, isn’t it? I kept picturing him hurting you and getting away with it. I was consumed with this rage I hadn’t felt in literal years.”

Zuko looked at him wonderingly. “You felt all that for a stranger?”

There was a shift in Toru’s expression, a bashfulness that wasn’t there before, but Zuko’s comment wasn’t meant to admonish him. A part of Zuko was stunned by the kinship Toru felt; he had felt a similar protectiveness of Toru once, too, before he’d ever learned his name. All he’d known was that he was another person his spouse might have hurt, and he’d stormed off to find Zhao, filled with a protective bloodlust. If only he hadn’t been so easily misled.

Toru’s hands were clenched and shaking where they lay by his sides. Zuko almost reached out to smooth them in his own hands, when he remembered how little they knew each other.

Instead, Zuko turned towards the sea, letting the wind push the moisture from his eyes. “Toru…”

“What?”

Zuko hesitated, rolling the question around in his mouth, its sour weight staying his tongue. He could feel, even without looking, that Toru’s eyes were trained on his face. Perhaps reading the question straight out of his mind.

*When Zhao’s family forced you to end the pregnancy - where did they take you?*

“Never mind,” Zuko murmured. “It’s not a question you ask a stranger.”
