By the time he arrived at the Avatar’s hideout, Zuko felt shaken to his core by the unexpected meeting with Toru. He hoped Aang could distract him, but when he entered the usual cave, he only saw Katara, sitting against one wall, reading. Momo was curled up in her lap, asleep.

Of all the members of the group to be alone with, of course it’d be the one who’d liked him the least. Zuko jerked his dragon moose to a stop beside him, trying to make as little sound as possible. A childish part of him wanted to immediately turn around, maybe wait on the beach until the rest of the group came back. But his dragon moose had other plans, and let out a loud, frustrated whinny.

Katara looked up from her reading, and for a second, he swore he saw the same desperate desire to run flash across her face. She quashed it immediately, mouth stretching out into a smile that looked a tad too big to be genuine.

“Oh - *you’re* here!” Katara seemed to marinate on how that sounded, then amended, “Not that you’re not welcome here. It’s just - hello!”

“Yes. Hello!” Zuko matched her awkward smile with one of his own. “And you’re here! That’s great.”

“Great,” Katara agreed, and there was a solid ten seconds of agonizing silence that elapsed afterward.

“Um - are the others alright?” Zuko asked. Even Appa, dozing in the corner, would not be enough buffer to make this one-on-one bearable.

Katara visibly winced, as if thinking the same thing. “Everyone’s been gone a few hours. But they should be back soon if you want to wait here!” She patted the spot on the ground next to her, awaking Momo with a jolt.

“Oh, great,” said Zuko, although it was not very great at all. Still, he didn’t want to offend Katara, and he didn’t want to miss his chance to see Aang today, so after he got his dragon moose settled, he sat down beside her.

After some awkward small talk about the tides (“They’re, like, super high today!”), they fell into an equally awkward silence. Zuko could tell Katara was itching to get back to her book, but felt obligated to entertain him.

“You can keep reading, if you want. Don’t let me interrupt.”

“No *,* you’re not interrupting!” she insisted, waving her hand a bit too aggressively in emphasis. Still, she had little to say to him, and soon they were once again stewing in silence, their gazes darting every which way but towards each other’s faces.

With little else to distract him, Zuko’s mind returned to the chance encounter he’d just had with Toru. Why was it that every time the other omega showed up, Zuko had such a crisis about his pregnancy? Most days he was so preoccupied with Aang and the others that it was like the child inside him wasn’t even real.

Except, of course, that it was. And barring a tragedy, it would remain there, growing ever larger inside him, until Aang and his friends wouldn’t be able to help glancing at Zuko’s stomach. He’d already made a point to stop sparring shirtless, to let what little weight he’d gained hide in the many layers of his robes. But soon that wouldn’t be a viable recourse. And Aang would be sure to notice.

And then what?

“Do you want kids someday?” Zuko blurted. He regretted it immediately after; surely someone as progressive as Katara would be offended by the question. It would seem like he was only asking her because she was an omega, and she probably didn’t want to be tied down by such traditional gendered expecta-

“Yes,” said Katara, evenly.

Zuko didn’t conceal his surprise. “Really? Well - how many kids do you want?” He could see her having one, with all of her independence.

“I know it’s not common, but I want a really *big* family. I’ll settle for just two, if my partner doesn’t want a lot. But that’s my minimum!”

There was something uncharacteristically self-conscious about her response. Zuko blinked at her, waiting for the illusion to break. But Katara looked genuine. Her smile was warm, if a little bashful.

“Do you come from a big family?” Zuko asked.

“No - Sokka’s my only sibling. And to tell the truth, we were always the only two kids our age in our village. But there were a lot of much younger kids and babies, and I liked how close they all were. I always thought it’d be fun to have a bunch of my own.”

“Huh,” said Zuko, fixing a puzzled look on the cave floor. Growing up, it’d always just been him and Azula - and, for a time, Lu Ten. There’d been times when that felt fun, but also plenty of times that it… hadn’t.

“Do *you* want kids?” Katara prompted.

“I don’t know,” Zuko confessed. “I don’t know how you’re even supposed to know. Does it just… *feel* right? And how do you tell that apart from obligation, like - being told you’re supposed to want it?”

Katara hummed as she thought over her response. Zuko couldn’t help but think she looked far less anxious than she had moments ago, when he’d first walked into the cave. He wished he had the same ease when he talked about this sort of thing.

“Well, I don’t know that there’s one right way to figure that out,” Katara eventually said. “Maybe if you look to your own family. What are the parts that you want to pass on?”

Zuko had been sitting with his legs stretched out in front of him, but now he began to curl in on himself, knees coming up to his chest. “What if you don’t have that many good parts to look back on? Should you never have kids, then?”

Katara seemed to understand that there was something deeper at work there. She was silent for a while as she thought over her answer.

“When I was really little, and my mom was still alive, I felt incredibly safe and secure with her. Whenever I pictured myself having kids, I pictured what it would be like to pass that onto somebody else. Especially after she was gone.

“I think the worst parts - I think they can motivate you in a different way, like they’re showing you what not to do. But I do think you need a good foundation to go off of, too. Like you need to really be loved by somebody the right way, or love someone the right way, before you can pass that onto your kids. And I think I have enough of that good foundation from when I was little, before my mom died, and my dad left to fight.” Katara scratched her hands nervously. “At least, I hope I have a good foundation. I’m scared to bring kids into this particular world, where there’s so much war and hardship, but I don’t think there’s ever a perfect time or circumstance. So, to answer your question…” She paused. “I think I forgot the original question.”

Zuko laughed softly. “It’s fine. I liked what you said.”

And though her rejection stung still, he let himself think of Ursa, and how things had been before. Afternoons at the turtle duck pond. Reading old plays at bedtime. The protective nest of blankets after a fall or a push. Without her, those early years would’ve been unbearable.

“All my nicest childhood memories are of my mom,” Zuko said. “I feel like when you’re a kid, you take your mom for granted. All the injuries she soothes and the tears she wipes away seem so effortless. Like magic.”

“I know,” Katara agreed. “Sometimes I worry I won’t be as good a mom as mine was, until I remember that she was just a person, like you or me. There wasn’t any magic. She probably made plenty of mistakes, and we just don’t remember those as much.” She beamed. “My dad, too - I was lucky to have both of them, even if it was just for a little time. And if I ever get to see him again after all of this, I know we’ll be a family again.”

Zuko could certainly relate to having loved and lost a mother, but…

Although he didn’t say anything, Katara could clearly tell the mood had shifted. She hesitated, before venturing, “Do you and your dad… get along?”

It was quite diplomatic of her to ask this way, considering who his father was and how she felt about him. Zuko sighed. “He’s just always had such high expectations.”

“Parents often do,” Katara said, measured. “But I’d guess, being royalty, those pressures might be even higher?”

“Yeah,” Zuko said, allowing his voice to crack the slightest bit before regaining control of himself. “For Azula, it was no problem pleasing our father. But my whole life, it’s felt like I can’t do even the smallest thing right. He hated the way I did my firebending, and how I’d behave in public, and even the fact I turned out to be an omega. The only time I ever seemed to please him was when I accepted the proposal from my current husband, but even that didn’t last very long. He quickly went back to setting endless expectations - and worse, it felt like I had to somehow do all the work of making sure me *and* Zhao were meeting them.”

“That… honestly sounds impossible,” said Katara. “I can see why you’re not close.”

Hearing her admit it scared him back into the old excuses. He was curling in on himself, knees to his chest, arms over his head, as he told her, “He wants what’s best for me, though. He knows I can improve, and he’s trying his hardest to make sure my potential isn’t wasted. That’s what a father is for, right?”

Katara blinked. “No. I think fathers are just supposed to love you, and keep you safe. Children aren’t projects. You don’t have to be *made* into anything.”

She said it with her usual heat, a touch of righteous anger in her tone. And for once, Zuko wasn’t cowed by it - he was grateful. Even if he didn’t quite believe her, even if a small part of him still believed the way Ozai treated him was for the greater good, it was nice to imagine a world where the expectations just… stopped.

“What was your dad like?” Zuko asked.

“He was - is - a pretty sentimental guy. Which you wouldn’t know when you first meet him, because he’s kind of quiet. It’s like…” Katara tapped her chin, contemplating. “...One time, back when my mom was still alive, me and Sokka ate this entire basket of berries. She was furious when she found the basket empty - she had spent *hours* picking those berries the day before, and they were the very last of the season!

“So she goes searching for the culprit, and finds us. We were dumb kids, so we didn’t realize it at the time, but our guilt was pretty obvious - our mouths were smeared with juice, and we had it all over our hands and clothes. So she goes up to us, her hands on her hips, and asks us, ‘Do *you two* know where my berries went?’

“Sokka immediately starts fumbling over excuses, and I can tell he’s two seconds from fessing up - some partner in crime! - but I wasn’t going down that easily. So I yell at the top of my lungs, ‘Daddy did it!’”

Zuko snorts, pressing a hand over his mouth to stifle his laughter. “You accused a *grown man* ?”

“Shamelessly!” Katara admitted, grinning. “Anyway, when my dad got home from the hunt, my mom told him what we said. By this point, Sokka was shaking in his boots. He was sure Dad was going to catch onto our lie.

“But instead of exposing us, my dad just nods and says, ‘Yup! It was me! I ate all the berries!’

“So my mom goes along with it. She says, ‘Alright! As a punishment, you’re going to go to bed hungry. No dinner for you.’”

“And *then* you confessed?” said Zuko.

Katara shook her head. “No! Sokka wanted to, but I bullied him into keeping his mouth shut. We literally got the whole way through dinner without cracking. And to my parents’ credit, my mom didn’t give my dad any helpings, and my dad didn’t even try to eat a bite! Sokka couldn’t even keep a straight face. He was leaking tears.

“So later, when my mom leaves for a sec, Sokka’s all over Dad. He’s like, ‘Why aren’t you saying anything! You didn’t do it! You’re being *framed!’*

“But then Dad just smiled at us. He said, ‘I know you aren’t doing it to hurt me. It’s good for kids to get into a little mischief now and again. Just promise me you won’t blame something like this on one of your friends, or on each other.’

“Stubborn as ever, I said, ‘I don’t know what you’re talking about. But even if I did - why would you let us do that to you?’”

“And what did he say?” Zuko asked.

“‘I’m your dad. You can put anything you want on me, and I’ll take it, because I love you. I always will, no matter what.’”

“Wow,” Zuko said, because he was too choked up to say much of anything else. He was starting to understand what Yan must have felt back in the Earth Kingdom.

“I know!” Katara grinned. “So when my mom came back into the room, I immediately confessed to eating all the berries. Waterworks and everything. Sokka of course caved, too. Mom said she was glad we finally admitted we were wrong, and let Dad eat - although she told us she’d planned all along to give him a plate after we went to bed. She just wanted us to see that our actions could affect others.”

---

They were still on the thread of parenthood when the rest of the gang finally filed into the cave. Sokka was having a tense talk with Aang and Toph, but stopped mid-sentence when he saw his sister and Zuko alone together.

“Oh, shit,” he muttered. “Just what we need right now!”

“What is it?” Toph asked.

“Zuko and Katara were alone together, who knows how long. I’m sure they’re at each other’s throats…”

The three newcomers jogged across the cave to meet their friends, afraid of the worst. But Zuko and Katara were so deep in conversation that they only looked up once their friends were toe-to-toe with them, greeting everyone with genuine smiles.

“It’s about time you guys!” Katara teased. “We thought you’d gotten lost.”

“I mean, kinda. That’s the last time we take directions from Toph,” Aang quipped. “What were you two up to?”

Zuko and Katara traded conspiratorial smiles.

“We were just talking about family,” Zuko said.

Aang’s grin slid into a grimace. “Oh - so you heard?”

Zuko and Katara’s smiles died down. “Heard what?” she asked.

“Oh, er…” Aang and Sokka swiftly traded looks, but neither would answer Katara’s question. The longer they took to answer, the more Zuko felt his skin begin to hum with anxiety.

Taking mercy, Toph cut to the chase. “Azula’s back.”

“She’s - back?” Zuko repeated, not quite comprehending. It seemed years ago that she had set out abroad once again, with Iroh in tow. Zuko admittedly hadn’t noticed her absence, too wrapped up in what was going on in his own life.

“People in town were saying she showed up unannounced in Ma’Inka,” Sokka explained. “It’s the first time she’s been back in the Fire Nation since she was captured. You’d think she’d stop by the capital to say hi to dear old dad first-”

“Wait,” Zuko interrupted. “ *Captured?* ”

The same guilty look crossed every member of the group’s faces, their wide eyes darting to one another in search of guidance. An awful, anxious silence had fallen upon them, and no one was willing to be the first to break it.

Zuko shakily got to his feet. “Captured by *who?* ” The Fire Nation had plenty of enemies. He didn’t even know where to start his frightened fantasies.

“The Northern Water Tribe,” Aang admitted, much to the rest of the group’s chagrin. He was greeted by a litany of looks, ranging from annoyance, to disappointment, to fear. He rounded on his friends, insisting, “Zuko’s one of us - frankly, we should have told him sooner.”

*But you didn’t,* Zuko thought. He clenched his jaw, fending off the complicated emotions that threatened to seize his expression. “Are you telling me Azula was chained up somewhere this whole time? And my uncle - was he chained up with her? Was *he* in Ma’Inka, or is he still in trouble?”

“They were both spotted in Ma’Inka, so they must both be alright,” Aang soothed. His hands were raised without actually touching Zuko, like one might do to calm an animal.

“Knowing they escaped doesn’t tell me what they escaped *from,* ” Zuko shot back. “How do I know they weren’t being starved or beaten?”

Sokka frowned. “Because our side doesn’t do that?”

“Zuko, your sister and uncle weren’t captured for no reason.” Katara put a comforting hand on his shoulder, her voice earnest. “They snuck into the Northern Tribe and attacked Aang while he was in a vulnerable state.”

Zuko’s heart quickened in his chest at the thought of Aang’s life in danger - but he was not to be deterred. “That’s not the problem,” he said. “It’s Azula. Of *course* she did something awful.”

“Then what’s the big deal?” Toph huffed.

Zuko was only just coming to terms with the fact he was probably never going to turn the Avatar in. That his desire to learn the Avatar’s plans and gain his family’s favor had perhaps always been an excuse, an attempt to conceal how his urge to follow Aang was something deeper, as if rooted in his very bones. It had driven him time and again to protect Aang, to the point that he was beginning to realize he would risk utmost harm and humiliation for it. He’d let Zhao beat him again, if he had to. He’d stop trying to meet those impossible expectations, quit trying to please…

“ *What’s the big deal?* ” Zuko repeated. “You’ve been here for two months, and none of you told me before now! Azula and Iroh are my family. I have a right to know what’s happened to them, but you all hid this from me. And after we were all starting to trust each other!”

Without even meaning to, Zuko only looked at Aang as he spoke. There was so much hurt in those gray eyes, and Zuko couldn’t bear guilt being added to his inner storm of anger and betrayal. He shook off Katara’s hand and left the cave in a rush.

---

With Zuko gone, the tensity of the situation was released like a sigh. In its place, the Avatar and his friends settled into a slouch of disappointment.

“Just when we were finally starting to get along,” Katara sighed. “I knew getting him to turn against family was a long shot.”

Aang shook his head. He wasn’t meeting his friends’ eyes; his gaze was fixed on the blurry figure of Zuko off in the distance. He was standing right up against where the low tide hit the sand, his back to them.

“We should’ve told him about Azula sooner,” Aang said, resolute.

“What?” Toph scrunched her nose. “Did you not hear his reaction? Katara’s right. He’s not cut out for this. His loyalty’s to his family, not us.”

Aang shook his head. “You weren’t listening. He was upset because it was a matter of his family’s safety. Even if he disagrees with them, even if he’s working with us, he deserves to know what’s happening to them.” Something occurred to Aang. “And you *know* it’s unfair to lump Azula and her uncle together. Especially given what he did for us.”

While the rest of the group traded guilty looks, Aang was flooded with memories of all that had happened in the north, unease washing over him like a tidal wave. It’d been so long since he’d thought about Iroh. The man had been severely injured the last the group had seen him, and all this time, Zuko had been totally unaware.

Aang was pulled from his thoughts by something nudging against his arm, then a soft whinny, the exhalation warm against his skin. Zuko’s dragon moose had wandered closer to the group, perhaps anxious that her owner was out of her eyesight. After a calming stroke along her snout, Aang took her by the reins and guided her outside to her owner.

Aang didn’t have a chance to agonize over how he’d open the conversation, as the dragon moose announced their presence with a frustrated huff and a hoof stamp. Zuko looked up at her and briefly met Aang’s gaze. Even in that moment, Aang thought he could see the hurt in his eyes. Zuko’s expressions tended to be microscopic, the subtlest ripple of a brow or lilt at the corner of his mouth. But the more time they spent together, Aang was gradually getting better at reading them.

This was a begrudging smile. “Thanks for bringing her out to me,” Zuko said, eyes darting away.

“Of course.” Aang paused. He didn’t offer the reins, and Zuko didn’t reach for them, still watching the waves with his arms crossed over his chest.

“I’m really sorry we didn’t say anything sooner, Zuko,” Aang said.

“It’s fine,” Zuko muttered, still not meeting his gaze. “You barely know me, after all. No use trusting a stranger.”

Aang felt his heart lurch. “Maybe that excuse would’ve worked way at the beginning. You’ve saved my life more than once, Zuko. All you’ve done to guide me here in the Fire Nation - the bending you taught me, the connections you’ve had, and…” He searched for the right words, the ones that would communicate just enough, but not too much. “...I love talking to you. I consider you a real friend. The very *least* I owe you is honesty.” He squared his shoulders, bracing himself. “If you’re willing to hear me out, I want to tell you everything that happened with Azula and your uncle up north. I promise I won’t spare any details this time.”

It was a while before Zuko responded. Aang waited patiently for him, trying to calm his burgeoning nerves by listening to the sound of the waves and the dragon moose’s gentle breathing. All the while the sea wind whipped around them. Aang wasn’t sure he’d ever get used to having hair; the annoying sensation of it being tossed around his head, how his bangs flew into his eyes. He didn’t know how Zuko could stand it. In watching the dark, glossy strands moving in the wind, it occurred to him that the tips of Zuko’s ears were very, very red. Maybe from the cold.

“I consider you a friend, too,” Zuko said, softly. “I care about you. That’s why it hurt that you wouldn’t tell me this.”

Aang was grateful Zuko wouldn’t meet his eyes, still; that *I care about you* had made his face hotter than the sun, even given the context. “I know. I’m sorry.”

“Thank you. I want to know what happened.”

So Aang told him it all. About Azula’s attack during his spirit world meditation; about how she’d pivoted her attention once she’d realized her plan wasn’t working; about how she hit Iroh with her lightning bending by mistake, and her utter anguish at what she’d done. Aang even told Zuko how, in the end, they hadn’t bested Azula; she’d been so horrified by her own actions, she’d all but gone limp, letting them subdue her.

Over the course of the story, Zuko had hugged himself tighter and tighter. “What did they do with my uncle?” he asked, fingers white where they pinched the sleeves of his robes.

“The healers took him in. He still hadn’t regained consciousness by the time we left the continent, but he must be okay now if he was spotted with Azula in Ma’Inka.”

Aang told Zuko more than the rest of the gang probably would’ve liked. He wanted to honor what Iroh had done by leaping in the way of Tui and La, and the only way to do that was to be honest about how deeply their lives mattered.

For some reason, Zuko did not react to the news that the moon and ocean spirits had taken mortal forms as fish. Then he opened his mouth and shocked the hell out of Aang with a little honesty of his own.

“I already knew about Tui and La; my husband wanted to target the moon spirit during the siege on the north. He thought by destroying the source of the waterbenders’ powers, he could weaken their army.”

Aang felt the hair on the back of his neck stand on end. Up until now, he had made a point not to think much about Zuko’s husband. He was an obstacle in more ways than one, but even more than that, he had just seemed like a faceless cog of the royal family, yet another top-knotted stranger in armor who wanted the Avatar dead.

Killing the moon and sending the entire world out of balance, all to win a stupid war - this was the first time Aang had to reckon with just how individually evil Zuko’s husband could be.

“And why didn’t he?” asked Aang, faintly.

“I begged him not to do it,” Zuko said. “In the end, he decided not to go to the North Pole at all.”

“Would he have told Azula about Tui, so she could try in his place?” Aang asked.

Zuko shook his head. “No. They’re constantly competing for my father’s approval. Zhao would never hand her a victory like that. He wouldn’t even feed my father that sort of information, if he wanted to save the glory for himself.”

Aang didn’t need to call Toph over to verify this. He trusted Zuko’s word unconditionally. “Okay. Thanks for telling me.” He paused. “And thanks once again for saving the day. I suppose without you, Tui might’ve died for real.”

Zuko’s brows gave the faintest furrow, which Aang knew meant he was utterly incredulous. “I’m discovering that Zhao says what I want to hear more than he ever tells me the truth; for all I know, he chose not to go to the North Pole for some other reason. Maybe my father told him he couldn’t go.”

Aang frowned outright at that. A spirit-killer *and* a liar. Perhaps it wasn’t so selfish for him to hate this man as innately as he did.

Zuko sighed. “Now that I know my sister and Iroh are alive and untortured, I can see how bad this is. The last thing this group needs is Azula on our doorstep. I’m sure she’s furious she was captured and will be dying for revenge.”

***Our*** *doorstep* , Aang noted, smiling at the possessive. “Don’t worry. We’ll think of something.”

He hadn’t realized how much guilt he’d been holding onto, and for so long. The secret of Iroh’s critical condition; taking Azula into custody moments after such a heart-breaking display of humanity. Talking about it didn’t change things, but he felt lighter for having finally confessed to Zuko.

“Who knows,” Aang mused. “Maybe they’ll show up and tell us they’re on our side, now. Maybe our friends up north saw some good in them and let them walk.”

Zuko let out a dry, humorless sound. “Sure. And maybe my dragon moose will learn to fly.”

---

Hours later, Zuko stands in the front hallway of his home, a liminal space between violence and safety. Here he waits, trapped, listening to his husband shouting furiously on the other side of the shut door. Zuko cannot see who Zhao is shouting at, but by process of elimination, he supposes it must be their servant, Rio.

He should step in. If he was even half the person Aang thought he was, Zuko would storm into the room and demand Zhao stop. And yet he is keenly aware that the longer he stands outside the door, hand nervously poised over the handle, the greater the risk he will be noticed. The greater the risk Zhao will accuse him of lurking, of listening in. The greater risk he will become the target instead.

&#40; *Better him than me.* )

Zuko hates himself for thinking it. Nevertheless, he turns away from the cacophony of Zhao’s fury, and pads quietly down the hall and up the steps.

Ama is hanging halfway out of his bedroom door, hand laid flat over a cherry blossom, his head cocked as he listens to the fight happening below. He startles when he sees Zuko, then nods in acknowledgement. Zuko is about to retire to his room, until Ama makes a comment.

“Nasty, all of that. I’m sure it’s warranted, though.”

Zuko stops, momentarily uncertain he has heard Ama correctly. He looks at the other omega incredulously and asks, “Do you really believe that?”

“Of course,” Ama sniffs. “My son wouldn’t act that way if it wasn’t justified.”

Zuko stares at him wonderingly. He’d nearly forgotten he’d seen Toru that day, but Ama’s casual cruelty brings it all flooding back.

“Every time you defend him, you really believe every word you’re saying,” Zuko says, more to himself than to Ama. “Even with Toru. You would rather ruin somebody’s life than let Zhao face the consequences of his own actions.”

Ama’s nose gives only the slightest crinkle. “Who is Toru?”

A rush of anger flares in Zuko’s chest. “The servant Zhao impregnated when he was a teenager.”

Ama’s eyes bulge, no doubt horrified to find such a dirty family secret has made its way to the prince’s ears. But Zuko is well acquainted with all their family’s ugliness. As he comes to grips, Ama’s face relaxes into something more stolid; more resolute.

“Oh. That little whore,” Ama sighs. “You don’t *really* feel sorry for him?”

Zuko can feel heat in his palms. “I do feel sorry for him. His life was ruined by what you told people. He suffered for years without work - not to mention from what you made him do.”

Ama scoffs, hand batting the air as if to swat the idea itself away. “Please! How has he suffered so terribly? He didn’t even have to give birth to the little bastard! You know who has really suffered?” And Ama slams his open hand to his chest. Zuko expects the sound to be hollow, but it makes an impact. *Whump* . “ *I* suffered. I lost everything. I had no one. All I had left when my late husband took me in was my body and soul, and I was prepared to give it all to ensure my child would have a better life than I did. Am I supposed to negate all that suffering because my beloved made a simple boyhood mistake? You would begrudge a *child* a second chance?”

He has never seen Ama this way. The wildness about his eyes, hand clutching his chest, strands falling loose into his face. Zuko can imagine the unrefined young omega as he first appeared in the foyer below nearly thirty years before, neck craning, heart swelling with the possibilities opening up to him. Not content merely to watch over the lady of the house, but waiting to take her place. He had made the mistake of assuming Toru’s heart was the same shape as his own, and punished him tenfold for it.

Zuko doesn’t say anything. Perhaps cowardly, or perhaps resolutely, he turns and goes inside his bedroom, shutting the door behind him. He understands now why Zhao never thinks he’s wrong, and that the problem goes back further than they can possibly imagine, to a crucial period of development when he was a child.

Zuko pictures Aang following him onto the beach just hours before, the earnest look in his eyes, and knows that there’s no future where Zhao would ever apologize to him like that.

## Chapter 39

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

The Avatar disappears.

### Text

There was a small window in the door of the governor’s private office, and every time it darkened, Zhao could feel his blood start to boil. The person on the other side always wanted *something*. No matter what he had handed over and how recently, there was always the horde of open hands and expectant looks - the roads need money, the schools need money, the businesses that are failing need money. An onslaught of fucking beggars. It wasn’t like being the Fire Lord; that was met with some gravitas, some fear. The people of Kirachu treated their governor like a hissing snake that had curled itself possessively around a perpetual coffer. What a cruelty that Zhao wouldn’t let them shove their fat hands into it and scoop up coins whenever they wanted! It didn’t seem to occur to these people that wiping out the seeds of insurrection on this island deserved far more urgency than their little troubles might.

Still, even as he despised the work, Zhao found himself returning on days he didn’t have to. If the public hated him so fucking much, they couldn’t argue it was because he wouldn’t devote himself entirely to their safety. He worked every day of the week, scouring the island without a break, then he worked until the late hours of the night. Zhao’s overloaded schedule was the natural result of his impeccable work ethic, and nothing to do with the fact that he couldn’t stand being at home.

Even in his absence, Zhao sensed that there had been an irrevocable shift in his household’s climate. While Wei’s secretive activities hadn’t changed - if anything, he was around even less - Ama seemed to have retreated to his room permanently, to the point of taking meals in bed. And Yan and Zuko seemed chummier.

It wasn’t overly obvious. They knew better than to converse freely in front of Zhao. Yet there was something unforgivably soft about the way Zuko would offer to light the hearth for Yan, and Yan’s smile in return.

Zhao’s first instinct was to shout that deviance out of them, to threaten them until they dropped whatever alliance they were undoubtedly forming against him. But some sane fragment of his underslept mind told him that to throw around accusations when all he’d seen were a few polite exchanges would come across… perhaps a tad deranged. And so he settled for something more subtle.

He had few opportunities to get Zuko alone anymore. His spouse skittered from the room whenever he entered, so he had to wait for them to retreat to their bedroom for the night. It wasn’t until they were under the covers, the lamps extinguished, that Zhao addressed the dark:

“I know I’m the last person you’d turn to for comfort. But if Yan ever does anything that puts you off, just say the word. No matter what else is going on with us, I can put it aside to deal with him.”

His words hung there untouched for long enough that he was convinced Zuko hadn’t taken the bait. He was rolling the words over in his mind, wondering what to try next, when Zuko’s voice emerged from the dark, cautious and small:

“What do you mean?”

Zhao could hear the wobble of uncertainty in the question, and latched onto it with relish. “I know my brother. With his condition, he’s unused to kindness. When he receives even the littlest bit, he can become… overbearing. I noticed he’s hanging around the house a lot, and if he’s bothering you…”

“He isn’t bothering me,” Zuko replied. “He’s just nice to me, sometimes.”

“He’s always nice at the start,” Zhao said, doubling down. “But if I were you, I wouldn’t be alone with him.”

Again, Zhao’s words hung in the dark. He heard Zuko suck in a breath.

“You’re one to talk,” Zuko said, eventually. “You can’t even be left alone with servant boys.”

A wild flame of anger reared up inside him, and Zhao had to smother it under a bell jar of patience. When he’d caught his breath, he was impressed by the smoothness of his response, painting it with only the slightest sardonic hint of malice.

“Well. He is *my* brother, after all. Who’s to say we’re all that different?”

*Let Zuko turn* ***that*** *one over in his mind tonight,* Zhao thought. *See if he gets any sleep.*

---

When Zuko comes down the stairs that morning, he finds Yan has been waiting in the reed room with the door open, hands folded, watching the door. The moment he sees Zuko, he scrambles to his feet, fighting cane and chair to get upright fast enough.

“Zuko! You should let me give you a ride to town!”

It’s unusual to see Yan up so early; he has complained that rising with the sun is exclusively a firebender’s prerogative, and the rest of the country shouldn’t have to adhere to such ungodly early timetables as a result. What’s not unusual is that he has offered Zuko a ride, but it’s usually phrased as a suggestion, not a declarative.

Still, Zuko says, “Sure. Thanks for the offer,” because he has no reason not to trust Yan. Zhao’s nasty comment from the night before surfaces in his mind, a lurking catgator, but he shoves it back into the depths of his doubts.

Yan beams at him, raising one arm aloft in triumph. “Alright - let’s go, then!”

Zuko glances at the door to the kitchen down the hall. “In a minute. I wanted a bite to eat first.”

“Right - of course!” The arm awkwardly dips to Yan’s side. “Breakfast. Good idea.”

Yan is agitated all throughout their meal, his stronger leg shaking so restlessly the whole table shakes with it. His conversation is equally as harried.

“Looks like Wei left ahead of us, as usual,” Yan says, a tad unnecessarily, “but you never know if he’ll be back to get something. Ama could always get out of bed soon, too. And, well-”

He shoots a look at Rio once his back is turned. Remembering how Zhao had verbally abused him last night, Zuko turns to look the young man over as well. He doesn’t see any bruises or cuts, but that means little. Rio is wearing long sleeves and pants. Stuffy, for the weather they’ve been having.

Rio excuses himself to grab another towel from the linen closet, and the moment he’s gone, Yan lets out an anxious noise between a chuckle and a cringe. “I find nobility have a bad habit of forgetting that the help are, in fact, people. I mean it in the obvious ways, mistreatment, unfair living conditions, but I also mean that they aren’t careful enough with what they say around them. If you treat your employees really terribly, what’s to stop them from selling your secrets to the first enemy who asks?”

Zuko waits to finish swallowing his congee to speak. It’s not as good as usual, sticking like glue to the roof of his mouth. “Oh? Is there something you’re hiding from Rio today, Yan?”

It is at this moment that Rio steps back into the room, so in lieu of an answer, Yan winks at Zuko, then stands up from the table. “No worries. I’ll leave you to your breakfast - meet me outside by the stables when you’re done.”

When Zuko eventually makes his way to the stables, Yan doesn’t notice him at first, deep in conversation with their coach driver. From the shadow of the awning, Zuko watches as Yan slips something to the driver, palm-down so as to conceal it. The coach driver pockets it, then makes a gesture, to which the scowling Yan hands over several crisp yuans.

The exchange looks extraordinarily like a bribe, especially with what Yan was saying at breakfast. An optimistic part of Zuko hopes that was only the driver’s paycheck; plenty of people are paid in hushed whispers out of the eyeshot of the main house, aren’t they?

Things only get stranger as they’re ready to depart, when Yan insists on taking the seat that faces the back of the carriage. He then spends the next ten minutes of their ride *staring silently at Zuko*, fingers drumming incessantly over the head of his cane. It is one odd antic too far, and Zuko is forced to speak up.

“Are you alright today, Yan?”

“What? Yes,” Yan replies, only half-paying attention. His gaze is still ultra-focused, seemingly on the same point on Zuko’s forehead. Unease starts to grow in Zuko’s gut.

“Are you sure? Because you’ve been staring at me this whole ride.”

Yan laughs outright at that. “You! I’m not staring at you - I’m looking at the road behind you!”

Zuko turns, and sure enough, there is a window behind his head. The sight of it is somewhat of a relief. “Oh, of course. What are you watching the road for?”

There’s an easy answer there. *Oh, it’s where my eyes landed,* or, *Just want to watch the scenery*. But Yan’s mouth goes taught and stiff, like he has something to hide.

“I’m not looking for anything specific,” he says, defensively. “I mean, it’s not like I’m worried about us being followed, or something!”

Bewildered, Zuko asks, “Why would someone be following us?”

“I said they aren’t!” Then Yan pauses. “I suppose - it’s not totally outside the realm of possibility. People do things without reason all the time, and like, I suppose, with Zhao being the governor, and you being royalty, there’s probably more reason for us to be followed, but we’ve been careful, so-”

“Is something going on?” Zuko cuts him off. The unprompted mention of their lack of safety has him searching his mind for possible causes.

The last time Zuko saw Zhao in town, he was hunting insurrectionists plotting against the empire. And during his first encounter with Aang on Kirachu, a group of ruffians had recognized Zuko as a prince and been eager to hold him hostage. Blanching, Zuko asks, “Is there something going on with the insurrectionists? Are they after us?”

Yan’s eyes bulge wide at that. “Um! Well, you see, the thing about that is, I wanted to get a little further from the estate before we - but I guess we’re all alone, now, so there’s no risk of us being overheard by unwelcome ears…”

But before he can make his point, Zuko realizes the scenery passing them by has changed from jungle foliage to small wooden huts. “Hey,” he interrupts, flattening himself against the rightmost door’s window, “we’re in the village. This isn’t usually where we get out, is it?”

They must be long past the bustling village square. Zuko keeps looking around, hoping he’ll recognize something they pass, but the near identical buildings are starting to blur together. “Where are we?” he asks, panic creeping into his voice. “I’ve never been here.”

“This is a more residential part,” Yan explains. His hands are raised less in a soothing gesture than in a *don’t attack me* gesture. “You may not have seen it before. It’s pretty far on the edge of the village. Pretty soon, we’ll have left altogether!”

*That* sets alarm bells ringing in Zuko’s mind. Rather than demand why the hell they’re leaving the village, Zuko schools his fright, and says, as calmly as he can muster, “I don’t think we should go any further. My friends will be expecting me in our usual meeting place.”

“But you can’t go there!”

Yan shouts it like imbuing Zuko with a terrible fear will deter him from going; but even as Zuko’s heart thunders in his chest, his desire to escape will not be abated.

“Why not?”

“It’s not safe - they could be looking for us, too!”

The insurrectionists in Zuko’s wild fantasies are no longer content to kill only him; now they have the Avatar and his friends in chains. Zuko is officially past the point where he can ignore his dread, and says, with no little amount of strangle to his voice, “I don’t care. Let me out here.”

Then he reaches for the handle - only to be stopped shy by a hand around his wrist.

“Now hold on, there!” Yan cries out. “You’ll get yourself killed!”

Panicked, Zuko yanks his wrist towards the door, overpowering Yan with sheer surprise. It’s enough to get his hand free so he can twist the handle. Yan puts his hands on Zuko’s shoulders, perhaps to hold him there, perhaps to ground him in reality before he does something rash; bursting with adrenaline, Zuko throws himself bodily against the carriage door, sending himself tumbling into the street.

Zuko feels the battery of sticks and stones and road against his flesh only distantly, his panic numbing his skin. He doesn’t waste any time. Before the carriage can finish slowing to a stop, he stands up, barely hearing the shout of, “Are you alright?!”, perhaps from Yan, perhaps from a concerned stranger who watched him throw himself from a moving carriage. Zuko steps forward hesitantly, searching for the protest of a broken or strained bone, and when he feels only the dullest of aches, he darts towards the nearest treeline.

For all he knows, he could be leading the enemy right to them. But with his sense of safety rattled, his anxieties from the night before aflame, Zuko only wants to see one person, to know that he’s safe and sound where he left him.

In his panic, Zuko doesn’t bother to make his path difficult to follow. It doesn’t matter. When he arrives at the beach, lungs on fire, heart pounding in his chest like a wild bird caged, he finds his worst nightmare come true.

The cave is empty. He sputters, falling to his hands and knees in the sand, before begging himself for one last ounce of strength. He rises, grains sticking to his palms as he lurches forward, inside, so he can verify firsthand that what he’s seeing is real.

There’s no sign of them. Not a single bedroll. Not a footprint, nor a bison-sized pawprint, for that matter. Zuko scours the cave, his eyes seeming to pulse as they adjust to the low light. But there is nothing to be found. Aang and the others are gone.

Zuko falls to the hard stone ground, uncaring of the bruises sure to bloom all over his shins, only distantly aware of the seawater soaking the seat of his robes. Contorting his neck in terrible angles, he searches the ceiling of dripping stalactites, as if he will find the gang crouching there in the rafters. All that greets him is emptiness, echoing the roar of the ocean waves back at him.

He isn’t sure how long it takes, but eventually there are footsteps behind him, awkward, dragging, and still he looks to the cave mouth with hope, as if he’ll see anyone other than Yan there.

“You - you’re fast,” Yan pants, lurching towards him. “Fucking fast. Ugh.”

Yan makes his way over with difficulty, wheezing, leaning hard on his cane. Zuko will feel bad for this, later. For now, he is too numb to feel anything.

“I should’ve told you from the start. I’m sorry,” Yan says, sighing, drooping where he stands like a flower in the sun. “I should’ve just told you that he - that he moved.”

Zuko blinks. Then swivels his head to look at Yan. “He… moved?” he repeats, uncomprehending.

For the first time that morning, Yan says something that puts Zuko at ease. “The person you’re looking for is safe. Or I should say, they’re *all* safe. Give me a chance to catch my breath, and I’ll take you to them.”

Zuko’s world had been so small for so long, there were days he couldn’t imagine what lay beyond the governor’s mansion, let alone the village. When the jungle finally fell away to a wide, open mountain road, Zuko peeked out the window to observe their destination, and found himself at a loss for words.

Just ahead, perched on the edge of a cliff, was an enormous estate. A thick and vibrant moss clung to the cliffside and painted the great mortar walls in natural tones, making the whole thing look as though it had sprung naturally from the mountain side. As they came past the great stone walls protecting the estate, Zuko saw that there were a number of buildings on the premises, the main house being a large, multi-tiered building with one central tower that thrust up into the sky. “Feels like coming home,” Yan said wistfully. There was a glint in his eye Zuko hadn’t seen before.

Their carriage was paused at the gate by a guard. She came to the window, and Yan pulled something out of his pocket to show her. To Zuko, it looked like an ordinary pai sho tile. But it must have meant something to her; she nodded, then stepped aside so their carriage could move past.

Of course, now that they had arrived, they would need to settle in. The coachman would take the dragon mooses to the nearest stable. Yan would want to introduce Zuko to these people, and explain to him who they were and how they’d come to be here.

But Zuko couldn’t wait. He all but flew out of the carriage door when it was opened for him, startling a man who had come to greet them. As Zuko ran past the stranger, who was yelling for him to stop, he heard Yan call, “It’s alright! He’s with me!”

The yard was absolutely stunning, manicured to perfection - but Zuko didn’t slow down to appreciate it. In his haste, he ran past Sokka, who didn’t notice him, either; he was engrossed in a conversation with several older men, all huddled around a pai sho board.

Zuko ran past Momo, chittering happily amongst the ash banana trees on the premises; he tried to pilfer a bunch that was twice the size of his body, only to find the weight of it tested the strength of his wings, sending him plummeting to the ground with a squawk.

Zuko ran past a group of men doing sword drills on the lawn, several of whom paused to gawk at his flight, and past a phalanx of servants shoving enough hay to feed six stables’ worth of dragon mooses into Appa’s mouth. Zuko ran until the estate was a green blur around him, following the winding tiled path all the way up to the great manor on the hill.

As soon as Zuko got to the front door, he flung himself inside, nearly bumping into Katara and Toph in the process. He slowed, but didn’t stop, twisting to talk to them while he ran backwards through the foyer. “Is he-?”

“Upstairs, second room to your right,” Katara said automatically. Zuko barely stopped to thank her as he ran where he was told, hearing only Toph’s shout of encouragement fading into the distance behind him.

“Go get him, Sparky!”

It took a few doors, but when Zuko finally stepped into the right room, Aang turned towards him as if on a spring, the smile on his face warmer than the sunrise. “Zuko,” he said, his next words lost in an *oof* as the other young man seized him in such a powerful embrace, it pressed the air from his lungs.

There was a heart beating against Zuko’s, and fingers carding through his hair, and lips by his ear that breathed, “Zuko - are you alright? I didn’t scare you disappearing like that, did I?”

And Zuko had to drown the laugh that nearly forced its way out of his throat, because what was Aang doing, worrying about his feelings at a time like this? He had had to abandon the hiding place that had been his only refuge for months. He had had to move four people, a lemur, and an enormous flying bison, all without being noticed.

“Why are you asking if *I’m* alright?” Zuko asked, incredulous. “I should be asking *you* that!”

Aang gave a lopsided smile, although it was not the usual one. This was softer about the eyes. “I can’t help it, Zuko. I care about your feelings.”

Zuko couldn’t even chastise him. His heart was too swollen to say a single word against Aang. All he could do was wonder; who else could ever care about him like this?

“I want to show you something,” Zuko said. “If you remember nothing else of training with me but this one thing, it’ll all have been worth it.”

He was mortified by the gooeyness in his voice. Aang smiled down at him, reaching out with a thumb poised to wipe whatever errant tear had gathered at the corner of his eye, but Zuko ducked out of the way.

Just in time. The door opened, and the rest of the gang filed in, along with Yan, and a man Zuko didn’t recognize. He was tall and stately, with a graying goatee and a kind, sun-weathered face.

“So you found the Avatar?” he asked, his voice as smooth and amicable as his appearance. “Thank goodness. You scared quite a few people tearing your way through the grounds, Prince Zuko. At least it looks as though your reunion is going well.”

Although Zuko had batted away the hand that tried to stroke the tears from his eyes, he and Aang were still standing quite close to each other. They seemed to remember their place, and leapt apart, faces going scarlet.

“How do you know who I am?” Zuko asked.

“Your friends have told me a lot about you,” said the man. “I suppose I should even the playing field by introducing myself; I am Piandao. This is my home.”

He gave a bow, which Zuko hastily returned. “It’s nice to meet you, Master Piandao. Thank you for giving safe refuge to the Avatar.”

At his side, he could feel Aang getting bashful, scratching his neck in that nervous way he did. It didn’t draw Piandao’s eye; instead he was watching Zuko, smiling thoughtfully as he stroked his goatee. “How much has Yan told you?”

“He explained a little on the ride up,” Zuko said. “I know the group must’ve moved here for their safety, and I know that you must be one of the friends Yan’s always spending time with. But I don’t quite get how you all came to be connected.”

Yan scoffed. “I *did* explain more than that. You were just too anxious to listen.”

For the first time since he entered the room, Sokka piped up. “Our group knows Piandao because of me. I sought him out as a swordsmanship teacher. I wanted to contribute more to the group, and when I heard one of the best swordsmen in the Fire Nation was right here on Kirachu, I figured he’d be as good a start as any.”

Toph interrupted, raising one hand into the air. “I feel the need to point out that Sokka is the only one who thought he wasn’t contributing anything to the group. But you never listen when *we* say it, so, thanks to your master here for finally getting you to see your own worth. And now you’re a sword-fighting, master-planning, inventor-genius!”

Piandao gave a firm, proud nod. “Indeed he is.”

Sokka looked ready to gag from the praise. “Ugh - don’t change the subject! The *real* point here, Zuko, is that Piandao belongs to a certain organization that wants to see the Avatar succeed and slow the Fire Nation’s takeover. It’s the same organization our friend back in the North Pole belonged to, and it’s the same organization that Yan, your, uh…”

Sokka squinted at Yan, his hand fixed to his chin. “Who are you to Zuko, again?”

“I already told you - I’m his brother-in-law!” Despite his agitation at being forgotten, Yan was soon preening. “I’m also a former student of Master Piandao. He was one of the first people I turned to when I got back from my tour, and was more than willing to enable me when I confessed to my less-than-imperialist new viewpoint.” Yan spread his arms. “He introduced me to some of his like-minded friends, and the rest was history.”

Zuko was starting to make the connection. “So… what is this organization, exactly? You wouldn’t happen to be the same ones making trouble on the island lately, are you?”

Piandao steepled his fingers. “I object to the word trouble - trouble for who, exactly? The men in charge?” He smiled a sly and even-keeled smile. “But I suppose I should answer your question. We have been involved in the activities you are referring to, although we are not the total sum of anti-empire sentiment in the Fire Nation.

“We call ourselves the Order of the White Lotus. We have sects all over the world, and in times of peace, our main prerogative is simply scholarship. We believe in the sharing of knowledge and education for all.”

Zuko frowned. “So then why are you helping the Avatar?”

Sokka outright frowned at the question, and started to respond, but Piandao stopped him with a quiet hand aloft.

“Prince Zuko, I want you to imagine all that can happen when an entire people is lost. What happens to the culture they created? To all of their knowledge? If we don’t protect them - if, worse, we actively work to erase their way of life, either by killing them or forcing them to assimilate to *our* way of life - we’re at risk of losing that great font of knowledge forever. As the last airbender, Aang is his people’s only hope at preserving their way of life.”

“I think I see,” Zuko admitted. Out of the corner of his eye, he noticed Aang turn his gaze towards the floor, expression complicated. As subtly as he could, Zuko sidled closer to him, fingers brushing against the hand closest to his, gauging. Aang gripped him loosely back, and so they stood, fingers entwined, palms apart.

“We really can’t thank you enough,” Katara said, turning to Piandao. “We know it was short notice, but when we heard there was going to be a sweep of the island, we didn’t know where else to go.”

“Please, the pleasure is mine,” Piandao insisted, waving off her concerns. “I was horrified to learn my favorite pupil was sleeping out in the wilderness, and I’d be remiss if I didn’t do something to help him and his friends. The realization you were traveling with the Avatar was a welcome surprise.”

“That’s why we moved so suddenly,” Aang said to Zuko, by way of explanation. “A guard Toph buddied up with in the village tipped her off that they were planning to sweep the surrounding jungle. You know there’s a group in Kirachu that’s been stowing weapons to ship out to the Earth Kingdom resistance? Apparently their outpost was discovered in the middle of the jungle, totally by accident. That’s when the local guards realized they needed to stop focusing solely on what they thought were ‘habitable’ areas if they wanted to find insurgents.”

Piandao sighed. “It’s a loss, for sure. I worked briefly with that cell, and they were comprised of some fine men and women.”

Yan looked grim. “I wish I’d known what my brother was planning. Maybe I could’ve warned them before it was too late.” Piandao gripped his shoulder comfortingly. There was a weighty pause where they all seemed to consider these nameless strangers who had rebelled against the Fire Nation - and what fate they were now to befall at the hands of the Kirachu guard.

“Hey, Zuko.” Aang’s fingers pulled free of his grasp. “You said you wanted to show me something?”

“Oh - yes, I think I have something that can help you. Remember when you said you were worried about Azula’s lightning bending?”

Aang nodded. “And your dad’s, by extension. I thought you couldn’t bend lightning yourself, though?”

“I can’t,” Zuko confirmed, “but I can show you something else. Something my uncle taught me a long time ago.”

Even with an audience, Zuko found himself effortlessly slotting back into the role of Aang’s teacher. He reached out to adjust Aang’s limbs, and Aang obeyed him, until he was standing with a firm, wide-legged stance, one arm pointed into the air, the other pointed at Sokka, across from him.

Zuko explained, “If you’re attacked with lightning-bending, it doesn’t have to be a death sentence. You can actually take the flow of lightning and redirect it, using your own body as a conduit. The key is the path that you allow the lightning to travel through your body.

“With one hand, you take the blast, and absorb it into yourself.” Zuko pressed a hand over Aang’s chest. Even through the fabric, he could feel the other young man’s heart drum a steady beat against his fingertips. “You’ll be tempted to take the shortest path from one arm to another, but you should *never* do that - if you let lightning pass through your heart, the result could be fatal.” He lowered his hand over Aang’s abdomen. The muscles spasmed under his touch. “Concentrate the flow here in your stomach, instead.”

Moving in tandem with Aang, Zuko had brought himself right up against the other young man’s back, lips nearly brushing his shoulder with the effort to speak into his ear. That moment wherein he realized their physical closeness seemed to shine so brightly in his mind, illuminated by each place their skin touched; he almost forgot what he was doing, frozen as he was.

Then Aang let out a labored breath. “I see. Take it in, push it down, and let it pass through.”

“That’s right.” Zuko turned his head to give Aang a small, tender smile, only to find Aang had turned at the same moment - bringing their faces very close.

Then Sokka cleared his throat, ripping the moment to shreds. “You’re pointing one of his hands at his would-be attacker, but the other at the sky - couldn’t you technically blow that power back at your attacker, instead of releasing it?”

Zuko removed his hands from Aang’s body, taking a full step backwards.

It had taken Sokka saying it out loud for him to realize that what he was giving Aang wasn’t only a means of protection. It was a deadly advantage over his sister. Over his father. If he wanted to, Aang could easily-

“I’m not doing that,” Aang said, voice hard as stone.

Sokka’s brow furrowed. “Don’t discount it before you’ve seriously considered it. If the Fire Lord is attacking to kill…”

“Then it doesn’t mean I have to, as well. It’ll be enough to survive.” There was an unusual seriousness to his tone. Zuko had only rarely heard him speak with such finality.

“Still, we might as well know if it’s technically feasible,” Sokka argued. He addressed Zuko now, asking, “Would the changes I suggested work?”

Zuko shrugged. “Your logic makes sense to me, but I wouldn’t know. I’ve never used the move at all before.”

Shock ripped through the group like an electric current, faces falling one by one.

“Then how can we even trust it’ll work at *all?* ” Toph asked.

“We can’t,” Yan muttered.

Zuko narrowed his eyes at them. “Shall we test it, then? Find a lightning storm to stand in? Or should we call my sister here to zap at humanity’s last hope?” Yan cast his gaze away, his mouth a jagged line. Zuko went on, addressing them all. “This move isn’t meant to be used to gain the upper hand in a fight. It is a *last resort* . This is the difference between complete failure and being allowed to carry on for one more day. Of course I haven’t practiced it, because that could be fatal.”

Before anyone else could speak, a hand landed on Zuko’s shoulder and squeezed; he looked up to see Aang smiling fondly at him.

“Thank you,” he said. “I get the sense you’ve saved me once again.”

Heat rushed to Zuko’s face. “I haven’t done anything,” he muttered, casting his glance at the floor. “We don’t even know if you’ll get a chance to use it.”

“Let’s hope not,” Aang said. He gave Zuko’s shoulder one last squeeze before letting him go.

The sincerity of the question nearly sends a laugh bubbling out of him; Zuko suppresses it, not wanting its affection to be lost, its meaning misinterpreted. “Yes,” he murmurs, pecking Aang on the corner of his mouth. “Very good.”

“Good.” Aang chews the inside of his cheek. Then asks, “Was that… alright?”

He’s not asking about the quality of it, this time. The same person comes up again in Zuko’s mind, and he finds himself glaring at the ceiling, at the interruption of this peaceful and private moment by the guilt he feels towards a person who has done nothing but cause him pain.

“I don’t regret anything if you don’t,” Zuko says, resolute.

Aang takes him by the cheek, guides their lips together into a kiss. “No,” he says, when they’ve parted. “Not at all.”

Zuko sighs with relief, resting his forehead against Aang’s; somewhere under the hair, the headband, is his blue arrow. “Good. I don’t want you to feel guilty about that.” A pause. “He’s not someone worth feeling guilty about.”

“Do you want to talk about it?”

“No,” Zuko utters, without hesitation. And to Aang’s credit, he doesn’t press him. They lay there, damp foreheads pressed together, quiet.

After a while, Zuko says, “Where did you learn to ask those questions?”

“Which questions?”

“You know. All those questions, when we were…” Zuko blushes, pulls his face away. “Like when you kept asking if I was okay.”

“Trial and error?” He feels Aang shrug next to him. “I kind of… fucked up, early on. Not in a horrifying way, I - I kissed someone without asking, and it was a total mess, and… I don’t know. I found that being frank, just asking people what they wanted, seemed to work better.” Aang turns, looks at him fully. “Why? Was it weird?”

“Kinda?” Zuko admits. He snuggles closer to Aang. “But also… I don’t know. It made me feel safe.” He pauses, considering, as he always does, if he’s about to say something he’ll regret. But it is being here, with Aang, that makes saying it a little easier. “You’re good at that. At making me feel safe.”

Aang’s fingers intertwine with Zuko’s. “Funny. I was thinking the same thing about you.”

That afternoon, Zuko and Yan set out for home. Zuko waves goodbye to Aang until they cannot see one another, hand lingering on the glass long after Piandao’s estate has disappeared into the jungle. To Yan’s credit, he lets Zuko sulk for quite a long time, gazing into the distance like he might materialize Aang in their carriage through ache alone.

Eventually, though, Yan is the one to break the silence. “You realize this isn’t sustainable, right?”

Zuko doesn’t fully look at him; he’s angled away, one hand still pressed to the glass of the window, as if physical touch can stand in for his gaze. Ever since the Avatar confessed his love, Zuko has been as happy as a man on death row who has been told his long lost love will come to kiss him goodbye. It is everything he has ever dreamed of, even if it is utterly doomed to fail.

“Of course I know this is all temporary,” Zuko says. “I’m not delusional.”

Yan searches his face. “Have you told him about…?” And in lieu of finishing his sentence, gestures at his stomach.

Has Zuko told Aang his most damning secret? No - temporary or not, he’s been enjoying their love affair. And despite himself, Zuko is happy Aang invited him to leave Kirachu with him. Even if it’s an impossibility, he would like to let Aang live as long as he can in this liminal space, where Zuko might still come along - where he is *worthy* of being asked to come along, and not a weight that will slow the entire group down.

While he’s trying to summon the right excuse, Zuko’s eyes dart away. That’s telling enough. Yan sighs. “How far along are you, anyway?”

“Nearly three months.”

“Then you’re not going to be able to hide it much longer. You should probably tell him before he finds out, or he’ll be pretty upset.”

“Why can’t I put it off for as long as possible?” Zuko asks. “He’ll be upset, regardless.”

“Not necessarily. If you’re honest, he might be fine with it.”

*Right,* Zuko thought ruefully. *I was so upset with him for concealing Azula and my uncle’s* *whereabouts from me; if he finds out I was hiding* ***this*** *from him all along, that will be reason* *enough for him to never want to see me again.*

When Zuko fixes him with a disbelieving cock of the eyebrow, Yan amends. “I’m not saying it won’t be *jarring,* and I’m not promising that he’ll love the idea. But I don’t know - you two seem crazy about each other. He might be more fine with it than you’d think.”

It’s true that Aang is endlessly patient with Zuko. Somehow, though, being asked to raise another man’s child seems just a mite too far. Zuko is not exactly eager to find out whether Aang’s devotion can withstand that test.

“To what end?” Zuko asks. “They’re thinking of leaving soon, aren’t they? And who knows if this news will scare them into leaving sooner?” He fixes Yan with a rueful look. “Should you, as a member of the White Lotus, be encouraging me to chase the Avatar off before he has completed his training?”

Yan scoffs, both hands perched on the brass tigermonkey head atop his cane. “Oh, fuck off with the White Lotus bullshit. I’m saying this as your friend. I want to see you happy.”

Zuko has to blink at that. It’s strange to receive advice on his love affair from his brother-in-law. Nevermind the fact that they have their own relationship outside Zhao, a wholly fulfilling one.

“We’re friends?” Zuko asks.

“I’d *thought* so,” Yan replies, looking wounded.

“No - we are,” Zuko agrees, a touch of uncertainty to his voice. He’s been alone for so long. It’s strange to suddenly find himself with a solid group of real friends.

Yan takes advantage of Zuko’s stupefaction to change the subject. “You know how relieved I was when I found out what you’ve been doing in the village all this time? To think that tyrant’s son, of all people, has been tutoring the Avatar, hiding him from the government that would see him flayed. You’re a much better person than I thought you were when we first met.”

That cocky, uneven smile of Yan’s is so eerily similar to Zhao’s, even when it’s not being used for the same evil. Zuko grimaces at him, saying, “I’m not a good person.”

“I mean, you don’t exactly agree with our nation’s endless thirst for power, so I’d say you are.”

“I don’t know about that,” Zuko says. “I care about helping Aang, but I’ve never necessarily agreed to the rest of it.”

“Well, helping Aang is helping us,” Yan huffs. “Erego, you’re an honorary White Lotus member. And we only recruit the best people.”

“...Do the best people generally sleep around behind their husbands’ backs?”

Now Yan outright laughs. “Considering who my brother is, I think you can be forgiven, Zuko. I mean, look at the evidence. You know the location of the Avatar *and* the White Lotus. You could bring all the anti-crown activity in Kirachu grinding to a halt if you wanted to - one letter to your father is all it would take! But you won’t do that. Because deep down, royalty or not, misgivings or not, you’re on the right side.”

It’s much to think about. Watching his reflection against the blur of green, Zuko begins to put some thought to his future.

The skies of Ma’Inka are black with storm clouds. In the midst of an open valley, Azula crouches on hands and knees under torrents of pouring rain, her fingers squelching in the thickening mud, her tears of frustration lost in the downpour.

“Azula,” Iroh begs. “We must stop for now.”

“No,” she snarls through gritted teeth. “I can’t waste any more time. I know he’s here. I’ll comb every fucking inch of this island if I have to!”

Even though she’s only a few feet away, Iroh has to squint to see his niece through the gray curtain of rain. “It’s no use going on in this weather. We won’t find anything,” he tells her. He crouches down beside her, placing a ginger hand on her neck. “We can continue our search tomorrow.”

For a moment, all he hears is the rumbling of thunder in the distance and the relentless timpani of rain on the fields surrounding them.

When Azula finally speaks, her voice is small. “Fine.” She unfurls herself slowly, the wet hair plastered to her face hiding her expression. Iroh makes a point not to try to gaze into her face, focusing instead on getting her to her feet, before he guides her in trudging steps back to sanctuary.

It’s some time before they’ve made it back to their temporary lodgings, to sit dripping around the hearth in the center of the room. The shade pinned over the window billows erratically, but keeps a good deal of the wind and rain out.

Azula stares blankly into the fire, its reflection dancing in the gold of her eyes, imbuing them with a warmth she doesn’t have to spare. Without the layer of makeup she usually sports, she has a naked vulnerability about her that makes her seem several years younger - or perhaps simply her age. Iroh waits until the tea pot is half empty to ask the question; as with all things he says to her, it is ginger, as careful as the hand that cradles glass.

“How much longer do you want to search Ma’Inka?”

Azula’s shoulders bob in an approximation of a shrug. Iroh forges ahead with a sunniness he knows cannot make up for the harsh winds outside. “You know we need to search Kirachu, too; why not take the opportunity to move on?”

“I know you want to see Zuko,” Azula mutters. “But he has to wait.”

“In my estimation, he has waited a long time.” Iroh grabs the wet clothes they’ve crumpled in the corner, and begins ringing them out into a bowl that’s empty save the last grains of their earlier, meager supper. “We can look for the Avatar in Kirachu, and reach out to Zuko in the meantime. See if he needs our help, too.”

“He’ll slow us down, uncle.”

“Perhaps. But he’s family.” Iroh goes quiet as he concentrates, twisting the wet cloth in his hands. He watches the droplets fall into the bowl below, rippling in the stagnant thimble’s worth of water. “The three of us could go together.”

“Go *where?* ”

“Anywhere at all.”

“No, *where?!* ” Azula stands, the fire in the hearth momentarily surging up with the force of her frustration. “Back to the North Pole, so we can be locked up again? To the Earth Kingdom, where they despise us? To the capital, so my father can finally officially disown all three of us?”

“Azula-”

“There is no future for us anywhere if I don’t do this, uncle!” she shouts. “There is no peaceful ending allowed for us until *after* I make things right! Anywhere we try to run before that will just be a temporary shelter. And you want to pull Zuko out of his cushy mansion into *that* kind of life?”

Despite the force of her speech, she slumps back into her seat, shoulders hunched, looking tired and ragged.

“Zuko’s life may not be as comfortable as you think,” Iroh tells the floor.

Azula knows. Even in the palace, with pure silk sheets and goosefeather pillows, a phalanx of servants at his every whim, there had been foreshadowing of worse to come for Zuko. Still; she knows she cannot provide the safe harbor that her brother deserves. And for that reason she continues to refuse.

“At least he can count on a place to sleep. At least he has food and a roof over his head. *This* life,” she says, gesturing to their torn and soaking clothes, the empty bowls, the shabby lodgings, “would only make his situation worse; as soon as we’re discovered, we’ll be captured or killed or banished.”

The hand that swept through the air moments before now clenches into a fist. “No more of these half measures. I want to prove my worth, Uncle.”

Iroh takes a moment to hang the shirt he’s been ringing out on a hook on the back of the door. It’ll dry easier than way, even if it becomes terribly deformed. “Azula. I am immensely proud of you.”

The fire all but dies in the hearth, reduced to embers. She blinks at him, dumbfounded. “Wh-?”

“When you told me what you wanted to do, I was so deeply moved. I knew you had it in you all along to make the right choice, and you have. So believe me when I tell you that I support what you’re doing.”

As she sits there, blushing furiously, a child embarrassed by her family’s love, he walks towards her with arms open. She flinches back. He drops his arms, but smiles at her, still, gazes at her with all the love he can no longer give his first child.

“You are working yourself to the bone searching for the Avatar, Azula. Just as you have for months. Allow yourself to rest a little while, and when the skies clear, we’ll decide how best to resume our search.”

She watches him suspiciously, catlike in her caution. But eventually, she darts forward, squeezing him in the briefest, fiercest of hugs. She embraces like a child unused to physical affection, who doesn’t know that the wrong amount of pressure will suffocate the baby bird helpless in her palm.

And even if it’s a little hard on his old spine, Iroh is happy to receive it. She has come so far, after all.

---

*For delivery to the office of the venerable Fire Lord, from his most loyal son, Prince Zuko:*

*Dear Father,*

*I am writing because I have something important to tell you, and must do it quickly, before I lose* *my nerve.*

*I want to start by apologizing. I know that what happened was a terrible humiliation for our family* *as well as a danger to all who lived and worked at the palace. I am beside myself with shame for* *my wrongdoings and deeply humbled that you would bother to read this letter.*

*It’s been months since it happened, and I never got the chance to tell you more about that day.* *Although I admit my guilt, I am not alone in it. I’m telling you this not because I’m trying to shirk* *responsibility, but because I feel it’s my duty, as your subject and as your son, to tell you what* *really happened.*

*The afternoon of the fire that destroyed the Lesser Hall, Zhao and I were arguing. Why is* *unimportant. When I decided I wanted to end the conflict, I tried to walk out of the room, but he* *prevented me with lethal force. He tried to choke me unconscious, and when I could not break free* *with my bare hands, I used my bending to protect myself.*

*We proceeded to fight one another viciously, and it’s our firebending that’s responsible for* *burning the Lesser Hall to the ground. Without making excuses, though, I want you to know that I* *did come to my senses about the damage we were doing. Towards the end of our fight, I tried again* *to resolve things with Zhao in a peaceful way, and he even led me to believe that he wanted that,* *too; but when my back was turned, he hit me over the head and knocked me unconscious. That’s* *how I got a concussion; not a falling beam, like he told everyone.*

*Although I would hope this example stands on its own, it is not the first incident of violence* *between us, nor the most recent. I would like to spare you the details, but suffice it to say he has put* *his hands on me a number of times since then, even with knowledge of my pregnancy.*

*Father, I know I have no right to ask anything of you. But I want to do everything in my power to* *protect this life, your grandchild, that I possibly can. And so that is why I am writing to you, to ask* *that you give me permission to end my marriage to Zhao. I fear for our safety should I remain in* *Kirachu under his care.*

*Thank you again for taking the time to read this letter. Please let me know what you think about my* *request.*

*Your loyal servant and son,*

*Prince Zuko*

Exhaling a shaky breath, Zuko leaned back in his chair to reread what he’d written. These words had the power to change his life forever. The fire was still burning in the hearth; if he really wanted to, he could wipe them from existence and carry on, unchanged.

But Zuko didn’t burn the letter. He clasped onto the image in his mind that convinced him this was the right thing to do, and held strong. He wasn’t thinking about the hands at his throat, or on his face, or on his arms. He wasn’t thinking about an intimate moment turned into a nightmare.

He was thinking about a crooked smile first seen on a wanted poster. How badly he didn’t want that memory to fade back into illustration.

Zuko still wasn’t entirely sure what would come next. He just knew that if he could only appeal to his father, show him how deeply this was hurting him, maybe he’d convince him this marriage was a mistake worth ending honorably. And maybe - maybe once that was over with, the rest of it would fall into place. After all, if Ozai could see reason on this, then maybe he could see reason elsewhere. This could be the first step not just to a better life, but to a better world.

Rereading his letter, Zuko found himself once again wondering if he should tell his father of what, exactly, he and Zhao had been arguing about the night of the fire, about the designs Zhao had held on the throne - only to dash the thought. The safest thing would be to exclude it for now. If he laid all of Zhao’s secrets bare, there was no telling what Zhao would reveal about Zuko. His involvement with the Avatar’s escape from the palace was damning; he wasn't ready to test the bounds of his father's forgiveness just yet.

Once the letter was written, Zuko refused to keep it in the house long. He woke in the early hours of the morning, when the dew was fresh, to hand it to one of the guards posted by the gates of the estate.

He cast what felt like a shaky smile upon the beta woman before him. “A letter for my father, updating him on my pregnancy.”

The guard took the parcel with a warm smile. “I’d be happy to take this to the hawkery in town, Prince Zuko.”

She bowed, and he breathed a sigh of relief. It was only the first in a series of difficult steps, but he had taken it. Now to wait for Ozai’s response.
