There’s a mirror on the door of the wardrobe. It’s not quite long enough for Zuko to see his entire body in, so he has to take an awkward step back, crane on the tips of his toes to see if his waist is adequately swathed in cloth. He has taken to tying his robe higher on his stomach, creating something of an empire waist, but even that is starting to reach its limits as a method of concealing his pregnancy.

Lighting back on the soles of his feet, Zuko stares at his anxious reflection. Maybe if he wore a wider obi? But he only has the one really wide one left - it’d be perfect to flatten his figure, but it is also ridiculously formal. He can’t leave the house wearing that, not even if he uses it with a different robe than the one it was designed for. It’ll stick out like a sore thumb.

He flings open the wardrobe door, banishing the stressor that is the sight of his own face, and trading it for another stressor: the limpid silk jungle of clothes. Even now, after years of being worn day in and out, every article that hangs before him feels like a costume he must wear rather than a true reflection of himself.

Fingering a pair of pants, Zuko thinks about how the waistband would bite at his hips, and sighs. If he was talking to Ama, maybe he’d have clothes Zuko could try. Everything in the older omega’s wardrobe is exquisite, even if it is also about twenty years out of date. But the two of them were only just barely the same size before; with all the weight Zuko has put on now…

As if peeking around the corner at a bloodbath in progress, Zuko very gingerly tilts the door, allowing himself only the quickest of glances in the mirror, in the hopes it isn’t as bad as he remembers from only moments ago. Unfortunately, his imagination fills in the worst of the details, and he sighs again, resting his forehead against the edge of the door.

He is going to have to come clean soon. Yan is right that he cannot wait for Aang to notice, to come to him with utter betrayal in his gaze. If it’s not the weight gain, it’ll be the fact that, in all the time they’ve known one another, Zuko hasn’t disappeared for a heat.

Closing his eyes, Zuko challenges himself to visualize the ways this could possibly *not* go wrong. Maybe he could start by asking Aang how he feels about kids, and if he wants them someday? But he already knows the complicated feelings Aang has about childbirth, his sense of obligation and dysphoria.

Although, now that he’s thinking about it, feelings about childbirth are not feelings about children. Has Aang ever said if he wants children? If he likes them?

If Zuko had to guess, he’d say Aang would be really good with kids. He’s a bit like an enormous kid himself - he loves to play and has a great sense of humor. He’s patient, too. Zuko imagines the sorts of mischief children are bound to get into - swinging off banisters, pulling their sister’s hair, breaking all kinds of glassware - and can’t imagine Aang losing his temper over every little misadventure. He can certainly be stern when it’s something gravely important; Zuko had learned that whenever he’d seen others try to sway Aang to take a more violent approach.

That’s right - Aang is a pacifist. That means he probably wouldn’t be comfortable using corporal punishment at all, would he? Zuko can’t even imagine raising a child that way. But if it is such a precious aspect of airbending culture, he can’t possibly say no to preserving that…

Running his fingers along the grains of wood in the wardrobe door, Zuko allows himself to picture a child with golden eyes squealing with delight as they ride around Aang’s shoulders. How Aang would clutch the tiny legs around his neck, whooping and laughing. Zuko allows himself to imagine that his child could become their child, that he and Aang could be a family.

And he wants it. It’s a mirage in the desert, but he wants more than anything to crawl across the dunes until it’s within his grasp, to prostrate himself before this fantasy so that he might get even one sip before it disappears.

Zuko makes the mistake of letting his heart buoy. Of standing in his wardrobe with his eyes closed to the room around him, enraptured in fantasies of a different life with Aang.

There’s a knock at the door. Zuko opens his eyes and turns, just as Rio’s voice comes, muffled, through the door:

“Prince Zuko - there’s a letter here for you.”

---

They sit in stagnant silence in Piandao’s salon, waiting for their most crucial guest to arrive. Toph and Katara are joined at the hip, of course; but in choosing where to sit, they’ve kept their orbit unusually close to Aang, gravitating towards him because they think that, in a matter of minutes, he’s going to need their sympathy. Because this plan Sokka has, which he convinced Piandao will work, which Aang *always* hoped would work, is absolutely never going to actually work.

Neither Katara nor Toph are deeply against Sokka’s idea. That’s why they are all sitting in silence; they’ve all agreed to support one another. They won’t fight about it - they’ve voiced their worries, been summarily brushed off, voiced them again more urgently. Things did not devolve into an argument, precisely, but they got close enough that they’re all avoiding looking at each other now, and there’s an empty chair dividing where Piandao and Sokka sit, versus where the rest of them sit.

Although if pressed, they would all insist the garish, red-cushioned chair was left empty for Zuko.

Aang is drumming his fingers nervously on his pant leg, shooting glances at the window, then the door. Katara lays a gentle hand over his so he stops drumming, curing the symptom, but not the cause. She shoots him a sympathetic look. He barely nods in acknowledgement.

Zuko doesn’t say anything when he and Yan come inside, but Zuko is often silent. The rest of them don’t notice that it’s a different sort of silence, as all at once they drop their own, crowding the air with a desperate, faked hospitality.

“Come in, come in!” Piandao says.

“It’s good to see you two,” Sokka says. He stands, hands clasped, rubbing them nervously together.

“What’re we all gathered around for?” Yan asks, shrugging his coat into the hands of a waiting servant. He and his brother-in-law come closer to the group, taking seats across from each other. Zuko takes the seat next to Aang, but doesn’t return his smile of greeting.

“We wanted to talk to you,” Sokka says. “Well - not to both of you. Sorry, Yan. You as in Zuko.”

Zuko blinks owlishly, like he’s only just awoken from a nap. “What do you need me for?”

“I’ll explain. How well versed are you in the latest legislation your fathers’ officials are writing?”

The question has obviously caught Zuko off guard. He looks at Sokka, as if gauging whether this is a serious question, and then says, “Not at all.”

Sokka’s smile gets bigger and faker. “That’s fine! That’s totally fine. I’ll just catch you up on it. Right now they’re thinking about trade reforms. See, when you’re at war with the entire world, it doesn’t give you a whole lot of options in terms of business partners. In the case of the Fire Nation, they kind of just conquer and take. And for the most part, that’s a pretty one-sided, beneficial situation for them.

“*But*. This kind of endless exploitation isn’t, like, foolproof. In theory, it works, but in practice, it’s more complicated than that. For instance, where you win and lose your battles determines what *actual* resources you get access to. So you aren’t guaranteed to get access to everything you want. And if you aren’t careful, your means of transport can be eliminated; so, let’s say you conquer inland, where all those good good resources are, but then the enemy regains control of the best passages by sea. How are you getting those good good resources back to your country? Or to your *colonies*, if need be?”

He pauses there, as if realizing he has dumped a lot of information on Zuko, and giving him the opportunity to ask any questions he might have. He doesn’t voice any, though. He just continues to look at Sokka with a somewhat blank expression. Sokka clears his throat to shake the nerves from his voice, then dives back in with gusto.

“Anyway, the point of all of this - your father’s government officials are drafting emergency legislation that would reopen trade with certain parts of the Earth Kingdom. They’re doing this because the colonies cannot get any grain imports - the eastern archipelago has been once again seized by the Earth Kingdom, and the canal leading up through the colonies is swimming with angry earthbenders. They can’t get a single ship up there. The colonies are *literally* starving.

“Right now, the legislation they’re considering would put Earth Kingdom states that agree to cooperate under a certain level of protection from Fire Nation encroachment. Not total immunity mind you; and it’s likely only temporary. But if we strike at the right time, that shouldn’t matter; see, if we can send out members of our organization posing as grain shipments, Fire Nation banners and everything, we can get Master Piandao’s swords to some of the cells that have become more isolated. I mean, we could even ship *golden-eyed imposters* over there and start tearing up the colonies from within. Not to mention that there are short-term material benefits for the Earth Kingdom if trade is reopened!”

“Okay,” Zuko says flatly. “What does any of that have to do with me?”

Sokka seems pleased to have gotten any engagement from Zuko at all. With a cat-like grin of glee, Sokka says, “Well, Prince Zuko, while all the government officials are in favor of the new trade law, your father is against it. He doesn’t think they should be making any exceptions towards any of the Earth Kingdom states, and he doesn’t care if the colonies collapse in the process. We’d like you to talk to him and convince him otherwise.”

Zuko stares. “How would I do that?”

“Play up the colony angle! It’s a strategic area for him to hold onto, and if it gets reabsorbed in the Earth Kingdom, there will be hell to pay on the battlefield.”

“And what if that doesn’t convince him?”

“I can ply you with all sorts of strategic arguments, if you like,” Sokka says, waving him off. “Given your connections, I figure we might as well use them, right? I mean, you don’t just know the Fire Lord, you’re his son! I felt so dumb when I realized we haven’t taken advantage of who you are at all!”

Sokka’s voice rings out like a child shouting in the middle of a temple; stark and slightly embarrassing in the silence that follows. He purses his lips, looking nervously at the prince who refuses to speak. Then he casts a desperate look at Aang.

The Avatar clears his throat. “We’d really be grateful if you could try, Zuko. As a member of the royal family…”

“I’m sorry,” Zuko interrupts. He’s not looking at any of them, his gaze unfocused. “I wish I could be more useful to you all. But I could never be trusted to advise my father.”

“It wouldn’t have to be on an official basis; this could be more of a casual conversation, to sway-”

“That would never work,” Zuko emphasizes. “My view is far too narrow; I could never be trusted to bring a valuable opinion to my father, so no matter what I say, he won’t even blink at it. If he hears me at all.”

There is a quiet beat in which they are all too afraid to speak.

“Sorry,” Zuko says again. “It sounds like you worked really hard on your plan, Sokka. Maybe if I were Azula, it would work. My father trusts what she thinks. But I’m not.”

Then he stands and walks out of the room. Sokka looks crushed; Piandao stands and lays a comforting hand on his student’s shoulder. Realizing something must be wrong, Aang gets up and follows Zuko.

Zuko has left the manor altogether, walking with increasing urgency across the lawn. Aang cannot tell if he has a purpose in mind or if he’s just looking for solitude. He presents a morose figure, his back hunched, hands clenched by his sides as he marches on.

“Zuko!” Aang calls out, keeping a respectful distance. “Are you alright?”

Zuko slows until he reaches a stop. Aang takes this as consent to talk, and rushes to his side.

“You seemed really upset back there,” Aang says to Zuko’s hunched back. “I’m sorry, did we-?”

“I can’t leave Kirachu with you,” Zuko says. “I shouldn’t be seeing you at all.”

The sudden rejection nearly sends Aang staggering back. “What?”

“I’m sorry.” Zuko’s voice thickens; his shoulders shake. “I wish we could stay together forever. But I realize now that was deluded - I was running away from my duty as a prince. From my duty to my husband.”

Aang can’t help it. Maybe it’s the fist of grief clenched around his heart, sending his blood pumping through his veins in an angry burst. But he loses himself; he exclaims, “I don’t know very much about your situation. You haven’t wanted to tell me, and I’ve respected that. But I do know one thing, Zuko. I know that you don’t love him, and that’s reason enough for me to know that you deserve better!”

Zuko turns to face him. When most people cry, their faces crinkle and close, like their very features have collapsed inwards from grief. But even as fat globs of tears stream down Zuko’s face, there’s something very composed about his expression, as smooth and unbending as it is.

“Love doesn’t matter,” Zuko says. “Only people who don’t represent anything larger than themselves get to marry for love. I’m not a real person. I am a symbol of the Fire Nation, and I have forgotten myself.”

“No,” Aang says, forcefully. “It doesn’t have to be that way!”

Zuko doesn’t seem moved by Aang’s words. “Surely you understand. As the Avatar, you have to behave similarly. I’m no good for you; I’ll only drag your good image down.”

“We are not *symbols*,” Aang says. “We are real people. We have our own feelings. You have to know that matters!”

Zuko doesn’t respond, but the resolute set of his jaw tells Aang it doesn’t, actually, matter to him. Aang feels like all the air has been scraped from his lungs. His chest hurts.

“Don’t I get a say?” Aang asks, stepping close, hand clutching his own chest hard enough he feels the heartbeat through the fabric - that he is *real* , unlike Zuko insists. “Don’t I get a say in whether or not you’re good for me?”

“Of course. But it wouldn’t matter,” Zuko says. “Because I’m saying no.”

Aang bites the inside of his cheek until he tastes blood. The hard snap of teeth on flesh fails to save him from this terrible, dizzying moment.

“Did you ever feel the same way?” Aang asks. And he’s so wounded, Zuko can’t bear to lie to him. That stalwart look of his crumbles, lip wobbling as he turns his face away.

The only answer Zuko can muster is a short, sharp bob of the head. An affirmative nod. All at once, Aang feels joy and despair. If they want to be together, then they should get to be together - even knowing Zuko’s circumstances, he can’t understand this rejection. Does he just need more time? Could Aang convince Zuko he is loved if he just took a little longer, worked a little harder?

“Zuko, if that’s the case, I - I can *wait* for you to be ready. I can wait for as long as it takes. The White Lotus are happy to host us here-”

“They’re hunting for insurgents all over this island,” Zuko says. “They could find you any day.”

“We can hide from them! We can run, we can…”

“Aang.” He hates the way Zuko says his name just then, like it’s bladed. Zuko steps into his space, bravely tilts his face to look at the Avatar with all the anger he can muster while still crying. “You will not wait for me at the expense of your own safety.”

“But-”

“You will *not* wait for me,” Zuko grounds out. “I forbid it. You will not sacrifice the great life of the Avatar for a small, meaningless one like mine. If the time comes that you all have to leave Kirachu, you *will* go, and you will not turn and look for me even once, because if I slow your escape for even a moment, I will never let myself live. I would sooner *die* than be the cause of your doom.”

And if the single, shaky nod wasn’t enough, then this is it: proof Zuko loves him, wholly and entirely. The deepest despair of Aang’s life was when he had looked upon the ruined Air Temple, had found the remains of the closest thing he’d ever had to a father. What he feels now is not the greatest despair of his life, but it is the deepest despair he has felt since he set out on his quest to right the world. It all suddenly feels so impossible, now.

Aang leans down, eyes closed, to let his forehead rest on Zuko’s, and the prince doesn’t push him away.

“Fine,” Aang croaks. “I won’t wait for you. But I want you to know - if there’s ever a world where - where we ever see each other again. I will open my arms to you. No matter what.”

“Know that in a world where I am anyone else, I would have come.” Zuko tilts his head, kissing Aang briefly, his lips salty with tears. “I love you, Aang. Goodbye.”

---

*Son,*

*Do you know why peasants are allowed to marry for love?*

*It is because in the grand scheme of things, whatever they choose to do is meaningless. Regardless* *of whether they marry, separate, or die alone, it makes no difference; the world will move on,* *unchanged by their decisions. To be a member of the royal family is to make a mark on history. To* *bear the burden of the empire’s needs before your own.*

*Just as your union was symbolic, so too would be your separation. We have been working towards* *peace with our brothers and sisters in Kirachu, and you would selfishly undo all of that hard work,* *why? Because you still haven’t learned to keep your mouth shut? I will be the first to admit that I* *do not always see eye-to-eye with Zhao, but he is not my husband, and therefore it is not my duty* *to. Were you a little more agreeable, the fate of my palace would not have been dragged into this* *unsightly mess.*

*Do whatever you wish. But I hope it goes without saying that if you choose to step away from this* *marriage, then you are no son of mine.*

*Think hard on whether you want your child to be able to claim their birthright.*

*Regards,*

*Fire Lord Ozai*

The response arrived within twelve hours, crinkled from moisture:

*Father,*

*Forgive my lapse in judgment. I will be staying with Zhao.*

*Regards,*

*Prince Zuko*

## Chapter 41

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Zhao has discovered the Avatar’s location. Will Zuko’s intervention give Aang a means of escape? Or will it all end in tragedy?

#### Chapter Notes

and so continues zuko's habit of doing extreme stunts while pregnant...

The warnings on this fic have been updated. See end of chapter notes for trigger warnings, as they contain spoilers.

### Text

Despite barely sleeping the night before, Aang is up and performing kata at the break of dawn. From the moment those first silvery threads of light peer through the bamboo leaves and shower Piandao’s property in dapples of light, Aang goes through the motions, his gaze fixed solemnly on some imaginary point in the distance.

He wishes Sifu Jaa would arrive already. He needs something to take his mind off the day before. He carries on, summoning flames in whirling kicks and punches. The force of them is inconsistent; sometimes he summons only a flicker, and sometimes they erupt from his body like they are taking the shape of his grief, enormous and billowing, only to disappear in an instant.

When Sokka eventually finds him, he knows at least to stand at a safe distance. “Up and at ‘em early, huh, buddy?”

“Yeah,” comes Aang’s curt response. He doesn’t turn to Sokka, focusing on his relentless onslaught of an invisible enemy. He hears a sigh behind him.

“How are you holding up?”

“Fine,” says Aang. He wishes Sokka would leave, but he’s not sure he has the stamina to say more than a word at a time without his voice cracking.

After Zuko had run out yesterday, Aang had told his friends what had happened in lurching details, his voice flat, his eyes unfocused. In his disoriented state, he hadn’t thought to conceal his own stupidity, to leave out the part where he asked Zuko to come along with them.

But Aang didn’t get a chance to worry about what his friends would think of him making a big decision like that without asking. Katara of all people was the one to clutch her chest and say, “Really, Aang? That’s such a shame. It would’ve been great to bring him along.”

She’d turned to Toph, brows furrowed with worry. “You know what it’s like to have your family put such awful expectations on you. Maybe if you talked to him…?”

But before Toph could even respond, Aang had croaked out his refusal. “No - it’s Zuko’s decision. If he isn’t ready to leave, he isn’t ready to leave.”

Toph’s smile was gentle. “You took the words right out of my mouth. It can be rough, trying to force yourself into whatever narrow mold your family wants you to fit into. But you can’t make him see the situation for what it is if he isn’t ready yet.”

“This sucks,” Sokka had said. “His husband seems like a shithead - like, way worse than Hahn. I’m sure Zuko would have been better off with you.”

Which had the exact opposite of making Aang feel better about how things had turned out. Anxiety thrumming in his chest, Aang repeated, “It’s Zuko’s decision. I want to respect it.”

Which brought them back to the present, with Sokka lingering behind Aang, making his lousy feelings even worse. “Hey, Aang. Maybe you should take the morning off. Relax a little.”

“I thought you wanted me to train,” Aang mutters. “Make up your mind.”

Sokka ignores the hostility in Aang’s tone. “You’re going through a pretty rough breakup. It’s not a crime to take a little time for yourself.”

“But just a little,” Aang says, sarcastically. “I can’t mourn *too* long.”

“Aang-”

“I’m *fine* . Let me train in peace.”

He can almost hear Sokka’s nervous movement. He wonders if he’s rubbing his hands together (a habit he seems to have picked up from Piandao) or something else. “Alright, Aang. Just don’t forget to take a break.” A pause. “I’m here if you want to talk.”

Then the crunch of grass under Sokka’s sandals, getting softer and softer as he gets farther away. Aang glares at the empty space in front of him, slashes it with a particularly unforgiving chop of the hand. He stands there, arm frozen in the air, panting as he stares into the distance. From here, he can just see the hillside as it fades into the jungle.

When he first sees it, he wonders if sadness now has the power to cause hallucinations. But that glint of brass in the trees is real; eventually, a familiar carriage emerges from the jungle’s shade, rolling with considerable urgency towards the main house. Aang’s stomach drops; it’s probably Yan, alone. Still. It’s not like Aang wants to see him, either. He resolves to stay where he is, practicing at a distance from the manor.

But not long after he turns away to continue sparring with the air, Aang hears shouting.

---

Zuko awakes from anxious dreams. He doesn’t remember the contents, only aware of the terrible thrum they leave in his body. It isn’t unlike the days leading up to a cold; his eyes are raw and puffy, his throat is spent.

Gradually, his memories of the day before seep back into his mind, explaining away his current state. He shuts his eyes to the blue-gray sunlight bursting through the curtains, and thinks to himself, *You’re doing the right thing for you both. Even if Aang wanted you as you are, you’d only* *slow them down. Your pregnancy makes you a liability.*

He curls his arms around his stomach, reminding himself that this will be worth it. How many mothers have dreamed that their child could one day be royalty? How many have sacrificed their bodies and souls for a better life for their children, only for them to starve in the street? He would be spitting in the face of every parent not fortunate enough to have been born into this privilege if he turned it down. Of every Ama.

Slowly, the early dawn light begins to warm into a subtle, buttery yellow. Sleep has long left Zuko; despite how deadened his limbs feel, he knows he has to get up and face the day. With effort, he pushes himself from the sun-dappled sheets, and makes his way through his morning routine.

Zuko runs into Yan in the kitchen. He smiles, asking, “Oh, do you need a ride…?” before he seems to remember, wincing mid-sentence. “No, I suppose not. Sorry.”

Zuko puts on what he hopes is a brave face, and wishes he was so lucky as to forget. “It’s alright. Happens.”

They eat a quiet, awkward breakfast. Yan swallows his last bite of dumpling and shoves his chair out from the table in the same swift breath. “Well, I’ll be seeing you, Zuko. I’ll say hi to…”

Just then, the back door clatters open, and Zhao steps into the kitchen. Zuko and Yan both give a tiny jolt of surprise at the sight of him; he seems just as badly slept as Zuko, with his red-rimmed eyes and overgrown beard. Zhao doesn’t pay either of them mind, though, stomping past on the way to the front hall.

“...Our mutual friends,” Yan finishes, startled. He watches and waits for Zhao to be out of earshot, not talking again until he hears the slam of a distant door. “Why is he still here? He never leaves the house this late!”

Zuko frowns. “What was that he was carrying under his arm?”

Yan shrugs. “I don’t know. Looked like a hawkery tube, though.” He pats the table to get Zuko’s attention; he’d been staring off after Zhao, still, and Yan wants a chance for a proper goodbye with eye contact. “I’ll see you later, Zuko. Take some time for yourself to grieve, and don’t let him ruin the day for you, okay?”

The last part is spoken in hushed tones. Zuko manages a nod in reply, and Yan is off.

Zhao’s presence certainly makes Zuko uneasy. Still, as the minutes tick away with no sign of him, Zuko finds himself wondering, again, what Zhao is doing holed up inside the tigermonkey room. When he’s done eating, Zuko goes to the veranda with the wide window in the foyer; he tells himself it’s for the fresh air, but it’s a good vantage point to watch the door to the tigermonkey room.

No matter how hard Zuko tries to focus on the trees swaying in the breeze, the odd humming spider wasp that flies past, his attention keeps wandering back to that painted, snarling face. It is a distraction from his self-imposed anguish, at least. He lets himself stare at the tigermonkey room door, counting the teeth in its maw - until suddenly it’s sliding away.

Zuko makes himself look busy, leaning on the railing and gazing up into the trees, half-expecting Zhao to chastise him for spying. But Zhao doesn’t seem to notice Zuko at all. He marches down the front steps and around the corner, out of sight - perhaps finally heading for the stables.

Zuko slips back inside the house, pausing in the foyer. If asked, he couldn’t explain his curiosity. He only knows that something about Zhao’s presence is off. After glancing behind himself to make sure Zhao won’t reappear, Zuko eventually tip-toes onto the threshold of the tigermonkey room.

It’s cluttered. There’s a map unfolded across Zhao’s many papers, covering most of the desk while propped up by a lockbox which, judging by the way the lid hangs ajar, has been left carelessly unlocked. Zhao must have been here all morning because he was working on something, although what, Zuko can’t tell from the doorway.

After another paranoid glance behind himself, Zuko circles around the desk so he won’t have to read the map upside down - and finds it is a map of Kirachu. Of course. Zhao hasn’t left any overly-interesting notes on it; there’s an X over a big green patch of jungle, and another over an area he *thinks* could be mountainous, but he isn’t in the habit of studying maps.

Zuko gingerly lifts the flimsy with one finger, scanning the notes underneath. These are even less clear; Zhao seems to have written half of them in some kind of shorthand.

*3 men 1 woman? 2 men 2 women? Regardless, 4 total, as at palace*

And a little further down:

*Boat blade etchings match the 1s on Yan’s wall*

*Same blacksmith - P?*

And then, scrawled on the corner of the paper in a slant:

*Earthbender in village -&#62; headband, fire academy uniform -&#62; same group?*

Zuko’s skin starts to crawl. That sounds like a description of Aang.

He knows Zhao has been doggedly searching for the “earthbender” who once appeared in the village. Zuko began to dread that someone who’d seen them that day had finally come forward. And if Zhao’s investigation really was thorough, then there was no reason he couldn’t have questioned the students and the teachers at the firebending school. He could have connected the description of an errant earthbender to one of a mysterious new student at the local bending school. Aang would be sure to stand out; in addition to being an outsider in a tiny village school, he would’ve raced through his lessons, only to suddenly disappear when he and Zuko began to focus on private training.

Zuko reads over the first notes again. Now that he’s looking at them with this realization, he thinks the counting could be Zhao trying to figure out how many people are in the Avatar’s party. There might be plenty of 4-person groups, but the mention of the palace, where they had once pulled off an escape, is particularly damning.

Then the other note - something about some blades on boats matching something Yan owns. As he thinks about it, Zuko remembers Zhao telling him ages ago about a fishing boat smuggling fine swords out of the Fire Nation to insurgents abroad. The same operation Piandao had recently confessed his involvement in. Was he the P referenced in the note? And if Yan was a former student of Piandao… does he own a sword he forged? Has Zhao connected Yan to the sword shipment?

Zuko shoves the papers on the desk aside, the feeling of dread in his chest ever-growing. In his haste, he knocks a paperweight onto the floor. As he scrambles to pick it up, he finds a sheet of paper lying face-down on the floor. He has to dig his nails into it to peel it free from the flat surface.

It’s a letter. Perhaps the same one that had arrived by hawk that very morning.

*Estate of swordmaster Piandao is the new Lotus HQ.*

*They are not just harboring an earthbender, but the Avatar himself.*

*Hurry now, while you have the element of surprise.*

*-W*

---

Zuko bursts from the front door just in time to see Zhao’s carriage rushing out of the front gates of the estate. There’s no time to outfit the single carriage that’s left in the stables - Zuko climbs onto the back of his favorite dragon moose, and soon they are racing down the winding mountain road towards the village.

Zuko feels as though his mount is an extension of himself; that they are a singular creature moving towards a singular goal. The jungle disappears around them in a tunnel of green, Zuko’s sights focused on the imagined shape of Zhao’s carriage as he waits with every bend in the road for it to appear in his field of view.

And once he has rounded the bend, there it is, clattering on the road ahead faster than any carriage should move. Zuko leans forward, urging his dragon moose to pick up its already breakneck speed. It obeys with only a brief whinny of discontent, bringing them up next to the carriage door.

In the brief moment that they manage to catch Zhao unawares, Zuko swears there is a self-satisfied look of contentment on his face, so sure as he of himself. But then he glances at the dark shape filling his carriage window, locking eyes with Zuko. Zhao only lets his shock pass over his face for a mere moment before his expression narrows into a snarl, and he lunges towards the door.

Zuko yanks back on his dragon moose’s reins, slowing their speed so that when the door flings open, it doesn’t knock Zuko off the back of his mount. Holding the door ajar with considerable strength against the inertia of their descent, Zhao fixes his spouse with a look of utter contempt.

“What the hell do you think you’re doing?!”

There are months of context to provide. His secret dalliances in town, his growing friendship with the Avatar, his discovery of Zhao’s plans. Zuko settles for simplicity. He narrows his eyes and shouts, “Stop this carriage, or I’ll *make* you stop!”

Something passes over Zhao’s face. His golden eyes are wide and haunted, the line of his mouth jagged as a crack in an heirloom vase. Zuko doesn’t know if his betrayal is coming as a terrible surprise, or if Zhao is in the process of putting all the disparate shards of foreshadowing together at last.

Whatever the turmoil in Zhao’s mind, Zuko takes advantage of it. He bids his dragon moose to dart forward, bringing itself neck-and-neck with the dragon mooses pulling the carriage. He ignores the shouted question from the driver as he takes a deep breath, willing the inner fire that has proved so unreliable to do his bidding. He’s not sure whether it will work - but he makes himself believe in the roiling sparks of heat that build in the furnace of his stomach, until it is pouring between his lips.

Zuko leans over to blow a torrent of fire at the dragon mooses’ thundering hooves, and they bray in terror, stumbling and jerking away. The smell of burnt hair stings Zuko’s nostrils, but the animals, while scared, are still running; they must not be quite so injured, yet. The driver shouts again, words lost over the stamping of hooves and the roaring of the wind.

Zhao seems to come to himself, expression hardening as he tells the driver, “Faster! We need to outrun him!” and closes the carriage door.

The driver snaps the reins. The creatures try to match his demands, if only to escape the aggression of Zuko and his mount, but Zuko follows effortlessly. He builds his inner fire up in his stomach, stoking it by sucking air into his cheeks, then lets another burst of fire loose at their hooves. The dragon mooses hitched to the carriage stumble, hooves tangling together, eyes rotating madly in their skulls as they plummet to the ground in a cloud of dust and dirt.

The sheer weight and force of the two gigantic animals’ fall yanks the carriage onto its side and sends it skidding with centripetal force along the narrow mountain road. The driver topples from his seat atop the carriage, his shout lost amongst the frightened braying of the animals.

Zuko only narrowly manages to surge ahead of the commotion, stopping just ahead on the road so he can watch the carriage crash onto its side, windows rattling - except, in the moments before it slides into a tree, the door bursts open, and he sees a large shape dart from the carriage, rolling into the bushes.

Zuko hesitates only for a moment. Zhao is somewhere in that tangle of dark green leaves, crouching and waiting. He may be injured.

Or he may only be furious, waiting to strike back. Shaking off his concern, Zuko decides not to waste any time. With a snap of his reins, he bids his dragon moose into a gallop down the mountain.

---

When he finally arrives on the outskirts of the village, Zuko is vigilant, gaze darting around in search of possible obstacles to his journey to Piandao’s estate. Any moment now, guards could come sweeping down on him, but the streets seem remarkably bare.

Zuko yanks his dragon moose’s reins to drive her onward, and she gives a shrill, pitiful whinny. The pace he has set has been a cruel one, and now that they’ve made the mistake of pausing, her exhaustion seems to have overwhelmed her. He wants to comfort her, but they can’t afford to lose momentum by stopping completely. At most he can offer her a scratch behind the ears, before he is once again urging her to trot forward. Luckily she obeys, but she’s reluctant about it, her pace sluggish.

As his dragon moose carries on in her slower canter, Zuko can feel the blood sloshing through his veins, the *lub dub, lub dub* of a panicked heartbeat canceling out all other sound. He is on high alert for anything suspicious, for danger, for Zhao, for any sign that they have already lost.

Underneath him, Zuko’s dragon moose finally grinds to a stop. Just as he’s about to dig his heels into her sides and urge her forward, he looks up, and sees.

They are in front of a restaurant, the suffusive scent of steamed dough and roasted meat making his dragon moose pause with her snout in the air to savor it. Just outside that restaurant, parked on the street, is a familiar carriage with ornate carvings, one Zuko has ridden in himself countless times. And there, seated at the top, is Yan’s usual driver, looking bored as he waits. Zuko looks around for some sign of Yan himself, and is about to approach the driver when the restaurant door opens.

It feels like fate. Yan left the house quite a while ahead of Zuko, but now here he is, the dull thump of his cane against the packed dirt road acting as the metronome that will steady Zuko’s panicked heart. He sees Zuko and smiles, before realizing something’s wrong.

“What brings you here, Zuko? I was just having some lunch before I-”

“Zhao *knows* ,” Zuko interrupts, breathless from panic, if not the chase. “He’s going to Piandao’s estate right now to capture Aang and everyone else.”

Horror passes over Yan’s face. “You’re not kidding!”

“I left him behind on the mountain, but he won’t be long. You have to hurry!”

Yan rushes to his carriage, shouting up a quick order to his driver as he flings the door open. He pauses before hoisting himself up, turning to Zuko in askance.

“Do you want to keep your own dragon moose, or do you want to come with me?”

Before Zuko can reply, the sound of a veritable stampede catches his attention. When he turns to look at the end of the street, there must be at least fifty armored men on the backs of komodo rhinos clamoring there.

It’s as if every guard in Kirachu has gathered here for this purpose. Before now, Zuko has never noticed how wicked the Fire Nation uniforms look, with their sharp shoulder pads and skull-like face plates. But now he’s forced to see his countrymen as his new friends always have; as heralds of something terrible yet to come.

“You go ahead,” Zuko tells Yan. “I’ll hold them off.” He ignores the bulge of Yan’s eyes as he readies his dragon moose.

“How in the hell are you going to do that?” Yan exclaims. “We should just outrun them! Come with me, and…”

But Zuko cuts through Yan’s protests with an imperious tone: “There’s no guaranteeing you’ll be faster than them. If there’s any hope of us getting a warning to everyone, one of us has to stay behind and hold them off. So go *now!* ”

A chorus of voices at the end of the street urge their mounts onward, and Zuko knows that it’s time to go. Trusting in Yan to make it to Piandao’s and alert the others, Zuko starts galloping towards the throng of guards. Yan gives only a final, brief curse before hurriedly packing himself inside the carriage. He can barely watch the shrinking scene from the rearview window as Zuko races towards the guards, meeting them head-on at full speed.

“Stop what you’re doing!” Zuko shouts. “As your prince, I *command* you to stop!”

It takes considerable bravery to run towards an armed group riding horned giants, but the move pays off. Every single guard grinds their komodo rhino to a halt, yanking furiously at their reins to prevent trampling their prince. The komodo rhinos’ nostrils flare, their great horned heads whipping side to side in frustration. In their impatience, their gigantic clawed feet churn up a cloud of dirt from the road below.

“Prince Zuko,” says a guard towards the front of the pack. “Why are you stopping us?”

“Because you’ve left our people vulnerable,” Zuko snaps. He holds his head high, hoping that he can frighten them with eminence and body language alone. “I haven’t seen a single guard on these streets, and now you’re all planning to leave the village? What in the hell do you think you’re doing?”

“Governor Zhao told us this mission was a matter of great importance,” says the guard. “He said he needed all of us in order to accomplish it.”

“And did he say why?” Zuko asks, curious if the men gathered here know what their mission is.

“My apologies, my prince, but I’m not at liberty to say.”

While Zuko is scowling at the guard for his refusal to elaborate, the wheels of his mind begin to turn. When did Zhao have a chance to contact his guards? But then the answer comes bursting through the crowd on the back of a dragon moose.

“Why the hell have you all stopped?!”

There’s dirt all over his uniform, a nasty scratch on his face, and quite a few strands of hair have come loose from his topknot, but Zhao has clearly survived the leap from the carriage with no serious injuries. Before anyone can answer him, he sees the obstacle in his hateful-eyed spouse, and meets Zuko’s hostility tenfold.

“ *This* is why you’ve paused our urgent mission?” Zhao casts a caustic look at all the guards present. “ *I* am the official head of Kirachu’s guard - not some lowly housewife.” He jerks his head at a random guard. “You, nearest me - arrest him!”

Even with his face obscured by a helmet, Zuko can tell from the way the guard clutches at his reins that he is aghast at the thought. “Arrest the prince?”

“You heard me - he is impeding our mission,” Zhao snaps. “The rest of us will go on ahead.”

He waves to the other guards, and without a moment of hesitation, they take off. Zuko tries to block their path, but the village streets are wide, and there are just too many guards; even when Zuko bids his dragon moose swipe her horns at one rider, several others thunder past him, and soon the only ones left are Zuko and the guard ordered to arrest him. Zuko leans over his dragon moose with the reins clutched in his hands, glaring, refusing to back down.

“I don’t want to hurt you, my prince,” The guard says. “If you come along nicely, there will be no threat to you or the governor’s child…”

It is just about the most foolish thing the guard could admit to a person who is wholly unafraid of him. Zuko feels his fire in his throat, flames licking at his teeth to be set free.

Iroh would be proud to see his nephew finally put his signature move to use, as Zuko spits a stream of fire at the guard that’s as molten and fluid as lava. Utterly thrown, the guard and his komodo rhino rear back, and Zuko takes advantage of the momentary distraction to flee in the same direction as Zhao’s men.

It’s easy to follow the guards’ path out of the village. Even if they weren’t still visible in the road ahead, there are slashes left in the dirt left from the komodo rhinos’ claws and tails, not to mention the lack of crowds. Zuko is thankful most of the villagers are smart enough to clear out when a battalion goes thundering down the street, but there are a few fools who wander into his path, yelping and darting out of the way as Zuko surges forth, refusing to stop or slow down.

Zuko tosses a look over his shoulder at the guard meant to be pursuing him and finds he’s rapidly regaining the distance between them, a figure made ominous by his complete lack of expression behind the iron mask. Zuko turns back around, cursing as he just barely manages to dart around a man who has wandered into the road. When Zuko glances back again, the guard in pursuit of him is even closer.

Desperate to keep him at bay, Zuko sucks another font of air into his chest and lets loose quick, sudden bursts of flame out behind him, but his pursuer won’t be deterred. He dodges every one, and soon, his komodo rhino is neck-and-neck with Zuko’s dragon moose.

The guard does not retaliate with any bending of his own. Instead, a wide, gloved hand flies towards Zuko, forcing him to duck out of the way without falling from his saddle. He can feel his dragon moose growing confused by his movement, her canter stumbling to a slower pace, the guard and his komodo rhino effortlessly matching her. Once again, the guard lunges towards the prince.

Thoroughly winded from his repeated use of his fire breath, Zuko tries to elbow the guard in the face - but instead of knocking him off his mount, the guard snatches him by the arm.

“You’re coming with me!” the guard shouts, triumphant.

With their mounts still running forward at dangerous speeds, Zuko wildly tries to shake his arm loose, but the guard’s grip is firm. Zuko is afraid of being flung from his dragon moose, killing himself and his child in the process, and desperate for escape, his eyes wheel in search of an answer-

Only to realize another grave danger. Holding onto his dragon moose for dear life, Zuko yanks suddenly and forcefully on the reins, bringing them to an abrupt stop. With one hand still on Zuko, the guard is yanked backwards on the saddle, grip slipping as his komodo rhino goes barreling headfirst into the fruit stand parked right in front of them.

The guard and his mount land with a crash of splintering wood and splattered fruit. Zuko doesn’t pause to see if he’s alright, or to apologize to the furious owner now raving about his precious place of business. He races off to find the rest of the guards.

By the time he gets to the end of the street, the horde of guards are still in Zuko’s eyeline, but they are growing smaller and smaller as they gain distance. Zuko urges his own mount onward, all the while knowing it won’t be enough to catch up to the horde of guards: he needs to stop them from overtaking Yan’s carriage. But from back here, he can’t tell whether it’s already too late.

Zuko clears the last of the village, the verdant stretch of jungle rising like a wall before him. Seeing a narrow path up into a hilly, tree-thick area, he gets an idea. He has taken the trip to Piandao’s many times and knows it well. Due to its size, Zhao’s group will be forced to take the official roads, the areas cleared for mounts and carriages, but if Zuko is alone on his own dragon moose, he will have more options open to him. Now if only he can find the smallest break in the trees…

---

Zuko and his dragon moose almost lose speed when her horns catch in a thick snarl of branches, but with a powerful shake of the head, she is once again free and racing through the trees. Zuko can feel the wild timpani of her pulse against his legs; it’s as though she knows how important this is to him, how urgently she must succeed.

Through the breaks in the trees, he can see the guards thundering on the main road. Even if he weren’t leading the pack, Zhao’s dragon moose is much taller than the komodo rhinos, and with its great branching horns, makes Zhao stand out amongst his men.

Just a few hundred feet ahead on the road, Zuko can see Yan’s carriage. It’s moving too swiftly to see inside the windows, but Zuko can imagine the look on Yan’s face as he grips the seat and hopes desperately that his driver can outrun the horde in pursuit.

Trusting his mount to carry him onward, Zuko looks over his shoulder and blows a steady breath of fire onto the branches and thickets trailing behind him. They spark and catch light, spreading, creating new onus for his mount to carry on quickly. None of the guards on the road react, the blaze not yet big enough to notice from this deep in the trees, from the speeds they’re running past, so Zuko continues to spread his fire, until suddenly there are shouts coming from the middle of the pack, calls to go faster and escape the blaze.

Just then, Zuko and his mount burst through the trees, diving into the road between the carriage and the oncoming horde. Zuko has managed to cut them off, but he knows that standing in their way won’t guarantee that they stop. Remembering a movement he saw Katara make once, he lets go of the reins and uses both hands to create twin whips of fire that lash out, rippling towards the oncoming guards.

The entire line of guards skids to a stop. At the back of the group, guards caught unawares crash into the guards in front of them, creating a momentum that sends a few of the creatures on the frontline skittering closer to the fire than they’d ever voluntarily allow, their tiny gray ears swiveling, bugles of fear and frustration sounding from their mouths.

But there is still the fire spreading to their left, in the thicket of trees from which Zuko came. As it roars to life, the men and their komodo rhinos veer right - towards the wrong turn in the road.

“Quick, the road bends, we’ll come back out on the right path!”

“No, that’ll slow our arrival. It’ll be faster to go on!”

“But the fire!”

“Forget the mission, we should stop it before it spreads to the village!”

All the while, the carriage clatters down the road behind Zuko, getting further and further away. Zuko staves off the wistful feeling that grabs ahold of his heart as he listens to it fade. With a ferocious cry, he sends out another whip of fire, lashing out all along the frontline and into the thicket of trees steadily burning higher. As if flung there by spirits or the force of Zuko’s anger, a fiery tree comes crashing into the middle of the road, showering it with sparks and ash. Every pair of hands on every set of reins gives the same frightened jolt, the breathing of the komodo rhinos coming out in panicked pants. Now none of them will be able to catch Yan.

Zuko watches the reflection of his own fire twisting in his husband’s gaze. Somewhat to his surprise, Zhao is hesitating.

But resolve soon hardens his eyes. “You’re telling me none of you idiots can capture one rogue omega?” Zhao whips around to look at his men, cowering away from the flames that lick at them from the trees, their armor made to withstand spurts of fire, but not a forest fire. Despite this human show of weakness, Zhao scowls at them in disgust.

“Fine,” he says. “I’ll do it myself!” And he surges towards Zuko.

Zuko cracks another whip of fire, but Zhao’s movement is unpredictable, weaving side to side as he approaches. He’s faster than Zuko expects, too, and in microseconds he is upon Zuko, grabbing him by the front of his robes. He then yanks *hard* , using the terror of a threatened fall to startle Zuko into clutching onto him for support.

Zhao has the front of Zuko’s robes balled up in his fist just beneath his chin, their faces brought within kissing distance, forcing them to look into one another’s eyes as he says, “I *knew* you were up to no good.”

Zhao shakes him with a wild-eyed glare, but even as Zuko clutches him to avoid falling, he knows his own expression is completely devoid of fear, instead hardened with hatred. It only seems to make Zhao angrier.

“Do you even understand what you’re doing?” Zhao utters, voice rising with every word. “Don’t you know they’re just taking advantage of your status as a prince? Otherwise those radicals would never recruit someone as useless as you!”

“You’re the one who doesn’t know what he’s doing,” Zuko replies. He grabs Zhao deliberately by the wrist that holds his robes aloft. It’s been a while since he has touched Zhao in earnest, since he has used force of will alone to urge him down from a frenzy. He reaches deep for that thread that connects them, now, trying to soothe the flames before they grow out of control.

“If you go there and hurt them, Zhao, you’ll be making a huge mistake. Don’t you see it? All this fear we have of the Avatar coming to destroy the Fire Nation - it’s not because he’d ever dream of using such violence against us. It’s because we *know* , deep down, that what we’re doing is wrong, and one way or another, someone is going to have to stop us!”

Zhao’s expression undergoes a litany of transformations as he grapples with Zuko’s plea. The most recognizable of those emotions is anger - his entire body *heaves* with it. And yet, in the hollow stare of his eyes, there is also a certain fear. Zuko tries to bank on it, urging him with one long, ferocious tug at that thread of fate: “Please, Zhao - see reason!”

That storm of emotions quiets into nothing. The grip on Zuko’s robe tightens, and Zhao’s voice goes low.

“You really are a lost cause.”

Zuko scrambles in Zhao’s grip, trying to free himself, but Zhao snatches up his wrists and draws him close. Even as the wildfire burns ever greater behind them, Zhao takes his time, pressing his cheek against Zuko’s, speaking directly in his ear:

“You think you can go behind my back and plot to take everything from me?” His mirthless chuckle is wet against Zuko’s ear. “Now I’m going to take everything from *you* .”

Zuko sucks in a breath - a gasp, really - but anticipating fire, Zhao slams a hand over his mouth. For all that Zuko struggles, he is crushed to Zhao’s side, trapped in the spiral of his arms. With a forbidding wall of flame at his back, Zhao looks up at his men through the tangle of his loosened hair, and roars,

“The goal of this mission has changed! *Bring me the Avatar’s head on a pike!* ”

They may have lost the chance to overtake Yan, but there is still the long path to Piandao’s, and all at once, the crowd of guards goes rushing through the break in the trees. With what little air he can suck in through his nose, Zuko exhales hard, trying to burn Zhao’s hand - only for the grip over his face to tighten. He can smell Zhao’s flesh cooking as it’s pressed against his mouth, but Zhao perseveres, smothering his spouse’s fire with every ounce of his strength.

Helpless, Zuko feels hot, salty tears flow down his cheeks as he watches the enormous sea of guards funneling down the curve in the road, away from the fire that is reflected in ominous orange and yellow streaks in their armor.

---

By the time Aang jogged all the way down the hill to the entrance of the main gate, the rest of the household had also arrived to receive Yan’s carriage. Toph and Katara were arm-in-arm, expressions wrought. Sokka and Piandao had both moved to help a panicking Yan out of his carriage, but he swatted them away with his cane.

“Don’t waste your time helping me!” Yan shouted. “You should be packing your bags!”

Aang joined the group, nearly out of breath. “What - what’s going on?”

Before any of the others could pipe up, Yan pointed his cane right at him and exclaimed, “Zhao knows everything! About you, about the White Lotus - he’s coming here with his men *right now!* ”

A gasp went through the group like an electric shock.

“Can we - can we fight them off?” Aang asked.

“Maybe?” Katara looked worriedly at Toph. “We fought a pretty big group of guards at the palace when we broke Aang out…”

“We fought nearly twenty with just the three of us,” Toph boasted.

But Yan wildly shook his head. “You don’t understand - this is the entire Kirachu guard! Zhao must’ve had twice, maybe three times that many men with him. I’ve never seen so much armor in one place!”

Sokka looked ashen. “There’s no way we can fight that off ourselves. Yan’s right - we need to leave Kirachu.”

To hear the strategist of their group say it made it real to nearly every one of them. Aang could see the fear fall away from their faces, replaced only with determination.

“I’ll saddle up Appa with Toph,” said Katara.

“Good thinking - I’ll find Momo,” Sokka added.

“I need to warn the other members of the Lotus,” Piandao said, frowning deeply. “But who should I send a hawk to first? There are too many to warn…”

Everyone darted off in separate directions. The only one left lingering was Aang. After a moment of hesitation, he followed after Katara and Toph.

“Hey, guys,” he called out, quickening his pace. “I feel like we abandoned the plan to fend the guards off way too quickly. I’m sure if we just come up with a good strategy-”

Katara and Toph didn’t slow their pace to talk to him. “You heard Yan,” said Katara. “There’s too many of them.”

When they reached Appa, they set about getting him ready to go. Katara grabbed the saddle from one side and tried to lift it, despite the fact it absolutely dwarfed her in size. She struggled alone for about ten seconds before grinding out, “Can somebody help me get this up?”

Toph rushed to her side, but Aang only hovered. “But guys,” he said, “what about Zuko?”

“What about him?” Toph asked. She got into a low stance, and she and Katara were able to more effectively lift the saddle about a foot off the ground.

“You said it was his choice not to come with us, Aang,” Katara reminded him, wincing somewhat less now that Toph was helping.

“Yeah, but we don’t know if he’s okay, or if the governor knows his involvement,” Aang said. “Maybe he needs to escape as badly as we do.”

Aang heard the sounds of another approach. He turned, expecting to see Sokka, maybe Piandao, but it was Yan. His expression was terrible, as if it was manifesting all the fear the rest of them were burying for the sake of preparing their escape.

“You’re talking about Zuko?” Yan asked.

Aang nodded. “It just seems wrong to leave him…”

But Yan shook his head furiously. “He’s helping head off Zhao and the rest of his guards. He stayed back so you could all escape!”

That news sent all of them rigid. Katara dropped her end of the saddle, dust flying up in its wake.

“Zuko can’t fight off all those people himself!” Aang exclaimed.

“That’s why it’s important you *hurry* ,” Yan urged.

Aang flung his arms out. “But we don’t know if he’s okay!”

“Aang!” Katara shouted. It was sharp and abrupt enough that it felt like an order to back down, and by instinct alone Aang stopped talking.

He looked at Katara sullenly. Everything about her, from her rigid posture to her stiff voice, told him her patience was up. But then she surprised him by saying, “If you really think the four of us can survive this attack, we will stay.”

“Hey, don’t agree for me,” Toph grumped.

Katara carried on, ignoring her. “We *will stay*, because we’re your friends, and we trust you. But I need you to really think about this, Aang.”

She raised a hand to him, her serious tone subtly etched through with desperation. “The life of the Avatar is incredibly important. We can’t risk you being captured or killed before you’ve had a chance to change things for the better. I know you love Zuko, but he’s making this sacrifice *for you* . The best way to honor that is to make sure it’s not in vain!”

With a grunt of effort, Toph, too, dropped the saddle. She looked vaguely in Aang’s direction, her imagined gaze joining Katara’s and Yan’s. Aang realized that he was looking at three people from three different nations, all of whom had risked almost everything to keep him safe.

His hands trembled at his sides. He clenched them just to get some feeling back in them. “I… I think we should…”

---

The guards descend upon Piandao’s estate. There may be a wall around the perimeter, but with the entire structure perched on the edge of a cliff, it is too vulnerable to an onslaught the size of the Kirachu guard. The men do not waste time swarming the grounds, chunks of the once-immaculate lawn torn asunder beneath the claws of the komodo rhinos.

Once they’ve dismounted, Zhao thrusts Zuko towards a pair of guards, and each one grabs the prince by an arm. “Keep an eye on him while I search the grounds,” says Zhao. However, just as he’s turning away, someone approaches them from the main house, amidst all the pandemonium.

It’s Piandao. The sight of him fills Zuko with a heart-rending fear. Did he not escape in time? Did *none* of them escape in time? Almost without thinking, he jerks in the guards’ grasp, but they hold him back from his friend. Meanwhile, Piandao avoids Zuko's gaze, instead fixing Zhao with a stern look of disapproval.

“Governor Zhao. Would you care to explain why you and your men are destroying my home?”

With the flat of his hand, Zhao slicks back the hair that has fallen from his topknot, creating the illusion of composure. “You can drop the act, Piandao. You and I both know about your involvement with the insurrectionists on Kirachu.”

“I haven’t the slightest idea what you mean.” There’s not a twitch in Piandao’s expression; but then, perhaps that stillness is even more suspicious.

“Let me jog your memory,” Zhao sneers. “We’re here because you and your White Lotus brothers are harboring the Avatar.”

Zhao gestures, and soon another pair of guards have crowded on either side of Piandao, restraining his arms behind his back much like Zuko. After a brief struggle, Piandao relents, going still. He catches Zuko’s eye, and there is defeat in his gaze; but that doesn’t offer Zuko any clear answers.

Zhao and his prisoners move to the apex of a hill that once served as Piandao’s training grounds, where they can watch the rest of the men ransack the estate. Crashes echo through the yard as potted plants are overturned, followed by a shriek of fear from a servant as he’s thrown from the kitchen doorway onto the lawn, where he is bound and gagged to prevent any interference. The longer Zhao’s men search, the more Zuko’s stomach ties itself into knots of anticipation.

Piandao raises his head towards Zhao. “How did you find us?”

“Not playing dumb anymore?” The curl of Zhao’s lip is ugly. He tosses his head in an arrogant way. “You need to be more careful about who you invite into the sanctity of your home.”

Piandao’s brow furrows. “I would never consort with the sort of back-stabbing cowards that would give us up.”

“I suppose your friends are made of weaker stuff than you think.”

But Piandao won’t have it. “My friends wouldn’t talk. I know I’m facing execution for this - the least you can do is grant me my dying wish and answer me frankly.”

“Traitors to the crown aren’t entitled to dying wishes,” Zhao snipes, but he can’t resist the chance to wound Piandao. “I suppose you’re right, though - Jaa wasn’t *eager* to volunteer information to us. Thankfully, after a few broken fingers and some well-placed burns, my eldest brother managed to coax it out of him.”

Zuko sucks in a horrified breath, remembering how old and frail Sifu Jaa looked. “You fucking *monster* .”

Zhao tosses him a glare over his shoulder, then gestures sharply to one of the guards. “Shut him up.”

Zuko expects a gag, but once again a hand is shoved over his mouth. This one is gloved; he’ll have a harder time burning it.

Soon, a trio of guards emerges from the house with Yan in tow, and Zuko’s stomach lurches. Yan’s hands are free, at least, but the guard at his back keeps harshly jabbing at him to speed up.

When they’re within spitting distance, Zhao levels his brother with a glare. “I knew you were involved, but it’s no less disappointing to see you here.” He doesn’t give Yan an opportunity for a comeback, looking to the guards who escorted him here. “Status report?”

“This is the only person we’ve been able to find on the premises, Governor Zhao.”

Zhao’s lips give the most imperceptible twitch of annoyance. “Then tell the others to keep looking.”

“We’ve scoured the grounds again and again…”

“And now you’ll do it again!” Zhao snaps.

In the dreadful quiet of the pause that follows, Zuko almost lets himself feel hope. Maybe there’s nothing to find here, after all. Maybe Aang and the others have really escaped.

Then Yan clears his throat and says, “I’ll take you to ‘em.”

Zhao’s face whips around to look at him, his disbelief plain on his face. “Excuse me?”

“I know where they are,” Yan says, voice measured. “If you’ll all follow me, I’ll show you.”

He lifts his cane to point down the hill, towards where the main house looms at the back of the estate, flush against the cliffside wall. The color has drained from Piandao’s face. He looks just as shocked as Zuko feels.

A grin stretches across Zhao’s face, and Zuko’s surprised there’s no blood to be found in his teeth, no scraps of shredded flesh. Zhao says, “Good. Someone here has finally come to their senses.” And waves at all the guards to follow. He told Zuko he wanted to take everything from him - how better to deliver on that promise than to make him watch as he does it?

The group proceeds across the lawns, Yan leading, the trio of guards never straying far from his side. Zuko is staring a hole in the back of Yan’s head, but Yan doesn’t turn to look at him. The traitor probably can’t bear to meet his eye.

As they pass through, they bear witness to the destruction of Piandao’s home. All the doors are thrown open, all the valuables shattered on the ground or stuffed haphazardly into the pockets of greedy guards. On the top floor, the group eventually finds themselves at a pair of grand doors, and Yan throws them open, revealing a spacious parlor with a sliding door on the wall opposite from them.

Zhao pauses on the threshold to cast a frown around the room. Zuko immediately spots the reason for his confusion; save for a few couches and a table, this room is quite empty. Yan walks to the sliding doors, and a memory of this room niggles at Zuko’s mind - because isn’t that just a door to- ?

“Here they are!” Yan announces, gleefully sliding the door open to reveal a balcony. Zhao and the rest of the group immediately run to stand on it, perhaps knowing already in their hearts what they’re about to see.

Just beyond the cliff where Piandao’s estate perches is a canyon, punctuated throughout with spires of rock. There is a steep, deadly drop from the balcony down into the canyon, but save for the shadows hiding those deepest depths, the group has a clear view for hundreds of miles across this vast landscape.

And there. Out where none of them can follow, swooping and soaring through the air, wide tail fanning out like a manatee’s - Appa. And all the rest of them.

Zuko goes limp in the guards’ grasp. *They did it* , he thinks. *They escaped in time.* Zuko watches the undulating shape in the distance and feels his heart clench briefly in his chest, but - for another life, a life that he refused, a life he can now never claim for himself. He tells himself it is enough just knowing that they will live on. It is enough just knowing that Aang is okay.

Yan is delighted by his own misdirection, grinning ear-to-ear at a brother that won’t look him in the eye. Zhao stands at the railing of the balcony, gripping it hard enough that Zuko expects to hear the wood crack, the great mass of his muscular back heaving with fury.

Then all at once, Zhao whips around to snarl at the guards. “What are you all doing standing around?! Follow them!”

Yan snorts. “You’re delusional if you think you’re ever going to catch them on foot.”

For a moment, the guards stand there, rooted to the spot. Yan is right; Zhao is asking for the impossible. The path down into the canyon is many miles away, and they could never descend it in time to keep their eyes on the Avatar’s retreating party, let alone catch up to them.

But then Zhao roars - “Do you answer to him, or to me?! I told you to *GO!* ” - and suddenly no one cares that it’s impossible. All the guards rush from the room, taking Piandao with them, nearly taking Zuko until Zhao snaps, “Leave him here.”

Then it’s just Zhao, Zuko, and Yan left in the room. Zuko considers taking the opportunity to run, but even while Zhao seethes, ready to burn over, Zuko can’t take his eyes off the figure in the distance growing steadily smaller.

Yan doesn’t seem to care about the heaviness of the moment. He addresses Zhao with a mocking voice, his head held high. “You always told me I threw in my own with the wrong lot - well, who chose the wrong side, now? Our guys may have suffered losses, but a sacrifice or two is worth getting to put you in your place!”

“Shut up,” Zhao grinds out. Yan cannot see his face, but Zuko can. It is as still as though it was carved in stone, with angles just as frightful. Zuko casts a look at Yan, silently begging him to stop, but his friend doesn’t seem to notice. It doesn’t help that Zuko’s been struck silent by it all.

Yan carries on oblivious to the danger - or perhaps indifferent to it. Zuko can tell from the tilt of his head, his smug grin, that he is enjoying gloating. That he has perhaps been looking forward to this moment for longer than Zuko can even fathom. Yan sidles up next to where Zhao stands heaving in the center of the room, and says,

“This fuckup is going to cost you big time with the Fire Lord. He sent you to Kirachu just to get rid of you, and what do you do? Let the Avatar get away! So you exposed the Lotus, so what? You may’ve captured a few pawns, but we’ve still got our fucking king!”

Yan punctuates this by pounding his own chest once, twice. “Months, maybe even weeks from now, he’s going to bring down that Fire Lord that you worship - but no, no, who am I kidding? You were never devoted to the Fire Lord, Zhao. You were only ever concerned with your own glory, whatever you could reap from this shitty system the Fire Lord propped up.” He jabs at his brother, expression mean. “Well, the Avatar’s going to bring all of it crashing down, and you won’t even get to witness the end, because you’ll have been demoted so far underground, you’ll never see the light of day again! Ama was always going on and on about your big special fucking destiny, but you know what’s really in store for you, Zhao? *Nothing* . Because you’re a big fucking failure of a- !”

Zhao pivots so quickly Yan doesn’t even have a chance to step back before his older brother’s hand is wrapped around his neck. Shock flashes through Yan’s eyes for only a brief moment, then the hand that grips him immolates, causing those same eyes to roll back in agony, mouth wrenched open in a bone-curdling scream.

Zuko watches in open-mouthed horror as Yan claws desperately at his own throat, even as he is engulfed in flames, even as the eyes that have rolled back in their sockets lose their shape and collapse into a bubbling liquid, even as that scream is lost behind blackened lips that curl back from from exposed teeth, even as the shape of his skull bursts forth from its prison of flesh and hair, all of it burned away to reveal the angular bone that lay just beneath. The smell is ungodly, a strange meat cooking, and Zuko feels himself heave, bending at the waist with the force of his horror, too late to be spared a moment of Yan’s suffering.

The fire dies and Zhao lets go, Yan falling on the floor with a *THUMP* , followed by the clatter of his cane, followed by another *THUMP* as Zuko falls to his knees, an acrid spit in his mouth, shaking with terror, involuntary sounds escaping from the darkest hollow of his throat.

Zuko isn’t thinking clearly, finds himself reaching out to Yan, laying a shaking hand on the arm still bent towards the phantom pressure around its neck. With trembling fingers, Zuko touches the hand, flinching back when one curled, blackened extremity cracks, then falls away. Yan doesn’t flinch at this loss - the body that was Yan doesn’t flinch at this loss - and Zuko lets loose a wild, mournful sound, like a loyal animal being beaten within an inch of its life.

Zhao swiftly crouches down beside Zuko, and there is no room left for dignity - Zuko screams as he falls back, catching himself on his hand, the other raised in front of his face as he shouts, No, no, no, *please* , no! And Zhao’s hand wraps around the outstretched wrist meant to act as his shield, and yanks, bodily pulling Zuko -

Into an embrace. Zuko shudders hard, not quite understanding what’s going on and waiting for the other shoe to drop. But Zhao doesn’t crush him or hit him - he only holds him, one hand cradling the back of his head like a parent might hold a child.

And he can’t help it. Zuko still can’t resist the urge to curl his arms around those shoulders and weep. He hates himself for it, hates that he is seeking solace with his face mashed against the chest of the man who has terrorized him into this very state, but he doesn’t hate himself enough to drown out the terrible sorrow of Yan’s loss, his violent and painful end.

Zuko thought that Aang and the others getting out free would mean that everything would turn out alright. The worst would be having to die nobly to protect them. That seemed a worthy sacrifice to him - but he’d never accounted for this. He’d never dreamed Zhao would have the gall to lay his hands on his own family.

Nevertheless, Zuko cries in the arms of Yan’s killer, hard enough that his ribcage will be sore with it tomorrow. He cries so loudly he feels as though the flesh is being rent from inside his lungs. He cries with enough force to shove his heart up through his throat. And all throughout, Zhao holds him.

Eventually Zuko’s cries begin to quiet, his throat too sore to continue holding the enormity of his grief. Zhao strokes his hair once, then says, “Repeat after me. You have never heard of the White Lotus.”

“Wh - what?” Zuko croaks.

Zhao says it again, his voice as smooth as glass. “Before this raid, you had never heard of the White Lotus. You did not know Yan was a member.”

“I - I don’t…”

Zuko pulls back to look at Zhao, to better read his face. He looks calm, but that’s through the thick blur of tears. Zuko gives a loud, wet sniffle, and Zhao uses the seat of his palm to gently push the tangle of hair and tears back from Zuko’s left eye.

“Say it. So I know you’ve got it down.”

Zuko swallows. “I… have never heard of the White Lotus b-before. And I didn’t know Yan was a member.”

“Good.” The hand is still pressed there to his eye, as if cradling his face. Strangely, with only the one eye unobscured, Zuko feels he’s able to focus better on Zhao’s expression. There’s an exhausted serenity in it.

“Aside from Yan, you have never met any members of the White Lotus,” Zhao says.

“I have never m-met any members of the White Lotus,” Zuko repeats.

“You didn’t know they had the Avatar.”

“I didn’t know.”

“This was all Yan.”

“Yan…” Zuko can’t help it; he falters, voice cracking. Zhao carries on.

“That’s right. Yan did this. He had his minions attack you. I had no choice but to do what I did.”

Zuko didn’t think he had anything left in him, but a few soft, hiccuping sobs jump from his throat. Zhao is neither annoyed nor pitying; there is something dead about his gaze.

Zhao says, “How could I not kill him, after what he made them do to you?”

Zuko’s genuinely at a loss. “Do what to me?” he asks.

And in reply, the hand on his face begins to heat up.

## Chapter 42

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

As his convalescence ends, Zuko sets all of his energies towards hating Zhao. During a trip to the capital, a terrible realization sets him free.

#### Chapter Notes

the theme song of this chapter (particularly the end) is "give it to me," by miya folick

### Text

Zuko felt like Zhao had held that burning hand against his face for hours - but then, time expands around burns much as it does around grief. When all was said and done, the burn only lasted about thirty seconds. That burning hand was held against Zuko’s face only long enough to ensure that the lightly fire-resistant skin of a bender could be breached. Long enough to watch as Zuko’s face blistered and broke open. Long enough to make sure that Zhao was creating a permanent mark. To make sure Zuko would always carry a reminder of his betrayal.

The muddled timeline wasn’t helped by the fact that the *feeling* of the burn didn’t stop when Zhao finally pulled his hand away. It didn’t even diminish by the time they’d arrived home. That immense, ghoulish pain soothed and reared itself all through the night, so that Zuko only slept in exhausted snatches, crying all the while.

Then came the fever - had it come from pure exhaustion, or was the burn infected? Whatever the cause, the days followed in a watery blur, reality mixed with dreaming. Zuko didn’t remember very much of the ride up the mountain to the estate, nor how they came over the threshold - but he remembered Ama finding out about the death of his youngest, the terrible howl of sorrow bursting forth from his chest like a spirit trapped.

“How could you do that to your own *brother?!* You were supposed to *protect him!”*

Ama raged, pounding with both hands on Zhao’s chest like he was trying to break down a door that was barred from the other side. Zhao had the gall to look shocked.

“What’s the matter with you? All you ever talked about when he was alive was how useless he was! Why would you ever care now?”

Ama looked at his oldest son with such an intense, body-shaking anger, it was a wonder Zhao didn’t immolate, didn’t go out exactly like the fratricide he had apparently so justified in his mind. “In what world,” said Ama, “in what *world* would that excuse what you’ve done? You - you sick, selfish monster!”

Face wet with tears, Ama nearly spat in Zhao’s face as he shouted, “You and Wei promised me! You said no harm would come to him, no matter what he got involved in! You *promised* me!”

He buried his face in his hands. “My whole life - everything I’ve ever sacrificed - it’s all been *wasted* by you! All the hopes I had for you when you were conceived - if I knew then what kind of animal you would become, I would have run myself through with a knife - I would have killed us both!”

Zhao seized Ama with a fury Zuko had never seen a child extend to their parent. “You think you have the moral high ground? You think your slate is clean? You are the person who made me this way!”

It was obscene, for all that youth and strength to go towards battering a frail omega man; yet for all of his sorrow, Ama met Zhao’s ferocity with quite enough of his own. “Everything I did, I did to protect you, to protect our family! Yan was your *blood* . You should have *died* rather than let any harm come to him!”

And, as if possessed by this revelation, Ama began to scream it, over and over, with such force that Zuko could see the bulge of the veins in his neck: “ *You* should have died! You should have died! *You should have died!”*

The fingers wrapped around Ama’s upper arms shook with the force of their grip, and Zuko was frightened that Zhao’s reign of terror against his own family wasn’t over yet.

Then, as if his strength had suddenly drained away, Zhao let go. Ama crumpled to the floor, bawling, nails scratching at the wooden floors as if to unearth his own grave. His screams followed them up the stairs, and in dreaming later that evening, Zuko imagined that they’d echoed upwards into the trees, the fiery orange sky filled with the enormity of a mother’s grief.

---

Zuko eventually awoke underneath unfamiliar bed covers. He lifted his bleary eyes to the paintings on the walls, and rather than the bonsai forests of the main bedroom, he saw a flurry of birds painted as distant V’s circling snowy mountaintops. He swore he could see the birds’ wings flapping, the mist rising off the snowy peaks, a cloud drifting lazily from the panel of the door to the wall next to it. His mouth was dry and sticky, and his head felt like it was wrapped in a thousand layers of cotton - or bandages, as he realized when he lifted a shaky hand to touch his head.

The woozy movement of the paintings on the walls left Zuko unsure whether or not he was awake, until he rolled onto his side and saw Wei sitting in a chair at his bedside. He was soaking a compress in a bucket of water, focused on his ministrations until the bedsprings creaked and groaned, beckoning him to look. Behind Wei’s glasses were dark rings of exhaustion.

“You’re awake,” Wei said, the tiniest modicum of surprise coloring his voice. He wrung the excess water out of the compress.

Zuko blinked slowly, and when Wei didn’t disappear, he tried sitting up. A gentle, somewhat wet hand kept him pressed flat onto his back.

When Zuko settled down, Wei laid the compress over his injured eye. Zuko realized, dully, that it didn’t change what he could see of the room. Everything to his left was obscured in darkness.

“Do you know what happened to the rest of the White Lotus?” Zuko asked, his voice soft from disuse.
