“You’re not supposed to know who that is,” Wei replied. In the pause that followed, all Zuko could hear was the ringing of a spoon in a porcelain cup as Wei mixed some medicine into hot water.

“Please,” Zuko said. “If there’s anything at all…”

Wei sighed. “I’ve heard the swordsmith was resistant to naming names, even under considerable duress.”

“Good.”

Wei gave a tiny exhale - not quite a scoff, not quite an agreement. “Not really. It’s only a matter of time before they’re all found.”

While Zuko reflected on this, Wei administered the medicine, gently cradling his head with one hand, while tipping the cup to his lips with the other. Wei’s touch was gentle, but the position made Zuko nervous. He was entirely at Wei’s mercy. He didn’t feel safe until Wei had sat back again to prepare another cup, silver spoon ringing against the delicate porcelain sides.

“What will happen to Piandao?” Zuko asked.

The ringing stopped. “It’s already over. He’s been put to death.”

Zuko watched the ceiling blur, uncaring if Wei saw his tears. He was already seeing Zuko at his absolute lowest, so he might as well openly mourn. At his bedside, the sound of swirling water commenced.

“Why am I still alive?” Zuko whispered.

At first, there was no answer. Perhaps Wei hadn’t realized it was a pointed question, rather than a lamentation. Zuko pressed; “Is it because of the kid?”

“It would seem that way.” A pause. “I’m sorry for your loss.”

Zuko’s scoff was wet, lacking bite. “You’re sorry? Like you weren’t the one performing the execution?”

“Not that one,” said Wei. “Piandao was always… good to Yan. Even if he ultimately led him astray.”

“Piandao didn’t lead Yan astray,” Zuko told the ceiling. “Your brother was principled. He came to all those conclusions on his own.” There was a watery pause, wherein Zuko was sorely tempted to bite the inside of his cheek, latch his mouth shut. But he resisted, and said, voice wavering, “Yan was a good person.”

“Yes. Well.” Wei stared into the cup in his hands as if searching for more to say. He never seemed to find it.

A silence fell heavily over them both. Zuko closed his eyes, trying to banish the imagined moment of Piandao’s death, the witnessed moment of Yan’s. If Aang knew what would come on the heels of his escape, he would be furious. He would have stayed, and he would have fought, and he would have died.

*I made the right choice* , Zuko told himself. *If I hadn’t rejected Aang, I wouldn’t have stayed home* *that morning. I wouldn’t have caught onto Zhao. We all would’ve all been at Piandao’s that day.* *None of us would have known what was coming.*

Even as Zuko threatened to blame himself for failing to warn Yan, even as he pictured himself crying and pawing uselessly as the body on the floor, even as he hated himself for wasting away in this room while Piandao underwent interrogation - he made himself push all of that aside. There were people worthier of his hatred than himself.

*I’m not to blame for what happened,* Zuko told himself. *Zhao is the one who killed Yan. Zhao is* *the one who ordered Piandao’s death.*

And as Zuko laid there, repeating this to himself, a curious thing happened. There had always been a fire roiling low in his gut, an ever-burning anger that made his insides glow. Every moment of that awful training at the hands of his etiquette teacher had gone towards keeping that very fire contained. And ever since, all of his waking energy had gone towards sealing that flame behind a painted facade. Now, though, the fuel for that fire had changed, staking it higher and higher until it singed the back of his throat.

A not so painted powder keg, nearly ready to burst.

---

When Zuko was well enough to maintain consciousness for most of the day, Zhao came into the bedroom where he was recuperating and sat in Wei’s chair, utterly destroying the illusion that any room in this house could be a sanctuary.

“Tomorrow, we’re going to the capital to talk to your father,” Zhao said. “Ozai wants a report of what happened, and we need to have our stories straight.”

Zuko stared at him, but Zhao couldn’t see the judgment in it. His eyes were trained on the bedspread.

“You’ve already told me what to say,” Zuko said, dully. Zhao had literally burned the memory into him.

“Considering you were under duress when we first discussed it, I think we should recap,” Zhao replied. Zuko made to sit up, but that still didn’t draw Zhao’s eye; if anything, it seemed to repel it.

“Your father doesn’t know that we had the Avatar here in Kirachu, and I’d like to keep it that way. Instead, our mission was to expose a group known as the White Lotus, who were aiding rebellion efforts on the island. Having seized Piandao’s weapon stores and cracked down on the biggest hive of vermin, we’ve already seen a steep drop in anti-empire activity. So long as we do not let on about the Avatar, there is no reason to see this as anything but a victory.”

Zuko stared at him. “My face.”

“You were taken hostage,” Zhao replied, still. Not. Looking. “That’s what you get for being kind to a terrorist.”

“I thought you said I didn’t know what he was.”

“So you *have* listened,” Zhao muttered to the wall. “You didn’t know he was a terrorist. You *did* know he had a tendency towards anti-empire thinking.”

“As did you.”

He could see the skin of Zhao’s cheek impress as he bit the inside of his mouth against a response. “...In any case. To deter our pursuit, the Lotus burned a swath of forest and village. We’ve lost many businesses and homes, and while we suffered no casualties, the one doctor posted in the village is quite overwhelmed with burn victims. We are in need of aid right now, so. If only for the good of these people. I ask that you emphasize that point to your father.”

It took Zuko a moment to understand what Zhao was referring to. The White Lotus most certainly hadn’t set anything alight, but in trying to hold off Zhao’s men…

“I set that fire,” Zuko realized aloud.

“Yes,” Zhao confirmed, irritably. “Considering his fury over your last bout of pyromania, I figured we should conceal your involvement. No use getting you and, by proxy, my heir executed.”

Zuko swallowed his guilt, clinging to what Zhao had said. “So - that *is* why I’m alive. The kid.”

That calm, hateful gaze hazarded as close to Zuko as it would dare. But still. Wouldn’t meet his face.

“If you weren’t pregnant,” Zhao said, “you would be in the ground with Yan.”

---

From the moment they had identified his secondary sex, Zuko had been told there were few things he’d ever be good for. His father and his teacher had made it clear he was not a fighter, and even less so an intellectual. But in a rare stroke of luck, Zuko had developed a beauty that nevertheless charmed people in place of those shortcomings. From the beginning of his adolescence, Zuko had submitted himself to being stuffed into all manner of uncomfortable costumes, plucked and coiffed beyond recognition in order to harness that sole virtue - and it had all paid off. Alphas, betas, and omegas alike had looked to him with a stunned sort of admiration. The beautiful omega prince. Object of every eye.

When Zhao burned him, each tongue of flame had licked out a ridge of raw, pink tissue, so that the left side of Zuko’s face now looked like a snarling theater mask, a monster spirit sent from the wings of the stage to wreak havoc on the pretty ingénue. Zuko’s left eye was permanently narrowed into a glare, and much of the hair on the same side of his head was clipped down to the root or outright singed away. It didn’t matter what Zuko did to brush the longer black strands from the back of his head over the burnt, twisted knob of his left ear; it didn’t matter if he parted his hair so the curtain of black would fall over that now-useless eye. It was impossible to hide. The scar dominated his face. When he looked at his reflection, he felt like he was being glared at by a total stranger.

But that stranger was one of the only people willing to look him in the eyes anymore. As Zuko came downstairs that morning, prepared to leave for the capital, he heard Wei’s smooth voice chastise someone - “We can’t do that. We’d look like we were condoning terrorism.” - and the door to the reed room flew open, Ama storming down the hall without so much as a glance in Zuko’s direction. Perhaps his fury and hurt could be blamed for not acknowledging Zuko; but when the young prince stepped into the room, Wei became fixated on adjusting his own sleeves.

“What was that?” Zuko prompted.

“Ama wants a funeral for Yan,” Wei said without looking up. “As much as I’d like to, I can’t fulfill that wish. It would reflect too badly on us.”

Then came Zhao on the threshold. “Let’s all get going,” he told Wei, and the three of them filed out of the room. In the carriage, Zuko sat across from the brothers while they watched the windows, or stared at their laps. When the three of them got out at the docks, the driver came to the door to help Zuko out, his smile of greeting usurped by shock when the door opened, before he cast his gaze to the ground. Not looking at what he was doing, he held his hand too low to possibly help, and had to be prompted with a sharp direction from Zuko, which only earned a litany of stammers - “Oh, I’m so sorry, my - oh, here, my prince.” The sailors on the vessel they took behaved similarly. If Zuko ever looked at someone, he only saw their eyes sliding away from his face.

Zuko was used to being watched - ogled, at times - as a pretty decorative doll, a human symbol of royalty, a sex object. But now he found himself worse than ignored. He was the subject of a gaze lanced from the corners of eyes, a gaze that hurriedly ran away the moment he turned towards it. There were a thousand eyes on him, except when they could be caught.

Made anxious by this cold reception, Zuko drifted towards the bow, thinking he could turn his back on the rest of the ship while he watched the sea. But when he arrived, he saw that Zhao was already there, leaning with his back against the railing, all alone. He glanced up upon Zuko’s approach, quickly looking away when he realized who he was.

It made Zuko’s blood boil. Of everyone, Zhao had no right to look away. He had no right to act as though he couldn’t stomach the sight of Zuko. *Zuko* should be the one turning away. *Zuko* should be the one refusing his gaze, making Zhao feel too foul to behold.

For a moment, Zuko stayed there, his fists clenched by his sides. He didn’t know what he wanted to do. Step on Zhao’s foot, walking past? Mutter something nasty under his breath?

As if hearing his thoughts, Zhao snarled: “I can feel you staring at me. Either come out with it or leave me alone.”

And there it was; the same queasy fear he’d had when Zhao’s ominous silhouette had filled out the threshold of Yan’s bedroom. The left side of his face seemed to throb as Zuko slinked off, head low, hair hiding much of his face.

He hated himself for still being so afraid of Zhao. A part of him had fantasized about running towards him with hands outstretched, shoving him over the railing and into the sea - but what if he didn’t move fast enough? Push hard enough? What if Zhao reached out to snatch him by the wrists, held Zuko close to his body and crushed him there, as he had in the flaming vestiges of the forest?

As he gripped the heated metal of the ship’s railing, tiny sprays of water leaping up to soothe his face, it occurred to Zuko that he’d have to find a manner of revenge where Zhao would never get to lay a single finger on him.

---

It was bad enough watching people’s reactions when they beheld him, but seeing it over and over again, with each new set of servants and footmen who attended their arrival, was a nightmare. The polite smile always went stiff as iron, a brief touch of fear occasionally flitting across their face. Soon Zuko kept his gaze trained on the ground, if only so he didn’t have to see how others saw him. He was thankful there weren’t any children around; it was bad enough to be reviled and ignored, but he didn’t think he could stand the chubby hands pointing at him, the well-meaning exclamations, the open-mouthed curiosity.

“Why did we need to come in person?” Zuko murmured.

Their carriage was just entering the palace gates. At this, Zhao cast a stern frown in his general direction. “Because your precious father asked us to. Do you need another reason?”

“We could have sent someone in our place.”

“And entrust our story to someone else?” Zhao scoffed. “Don’t be an idiot.”

Zuko was surprised he still felt enough to be stung by the comment. “I guess I hadn’t thought of what an *elaborate* story it was.”

He hadn’t outright rebelled. And yet he felt the space between the seats closing up as Zhao leaned forward. The sheer shadow of his form fell over Zuko, and to his utmost shame, he found himself cowering in the corner, where the door met his seat.

“But I can trust *you* to tell it, can’t I, Zuko?” Zhao asked, smooth voice dripping with threat. “You might think it satisfying, to embarrass me in front of your father. But I can promise you that before I met my fate, I would make sure that you suffered for your betrayal.”

Zhao reached out, just shy of his face, and Zuko flinched away. “See?” Zhao said. “You already know what I’m capable of.”

Satisfied with himself, Zhao stopped crowding Zuko to sit back in his seat. When Zuko hazarded a look at him, making sure he had really moved away, he caught sight of Wei, where he sat just next to Zhao. Wei was stone-faced, as usual. But the hands perched on his lap were clenched so tightly, the knuckles had gone white. Zuko watched Wei, so distrustful of his own eyes that he wrote it off as his own delusion, and waited for it to dispel.

And gradually it did. By the time the carriage doors were open, and servants thrust their hands out to them in obeisance, those hands had relaxed, leaving Zuko alone with no allies once again.

---

Disgust marred every feature on Ozai’s face. “You look repulsive,” he said. “What happened?”

Azula could feel her uncle’s eyes boring a hole in her face, but she refused to look at him, lest it seem like she was looking for direction, or for comfort. She said to her father soberly, “I assume you’re referring to my lack of topknot?”

“It’s unsightly,” Ozai sniffed. “A blatant disrespect of our most ancient traditions. Why would you mutilate yourself in this way?”

It seemed that in the months they’d been apart, her father hadn’t managed to file down any of those terrible edges. Despite how long Azula had been away, Ozai hadn’t bothered to ask after her wellbeing. He hadn’t even allowed her to approach him face-to-face, instead forcing her to make an appointment through his aide - with his only opening taking place an entire day after she arrived in the Fire Nation. Yet even as Ozai wound her up so tightly she was afraid she’d burst at the seams, Azula found a small, ancient part of her was still desperate for him to show her some affection, just the tiniest smidge of approval.

She wrestled that part of herself into a headlock.

“I was deep undercover with our enemies abroad,” Azula said. “I had to gain their trust. It paid off.”

“It had better,” Ozai sneered.

They were interrupted by an attendant who rushed across the throne room to whisper in Ozai’s ear. The Fire Lord turned his gaze to the door, a frown settled deeply into his face.

“We’ll have to talk later, Azula. It seems Zhao’s time away from the capital has been more productive than yours.”

She narrowed her eyes at the mere mention of the name. “That’s difficult to imagine. What could he have possibly accomplished on that backwater island?”

“Wei has given me reason to believe they’ve located a major sect of the White Lotus.” Ozai looked down his nose at her. “Have you heard of them before?”

Azula had long beaten down her most instinctual tells, so that her response of, “No, I’m afraid not,” came out without so much as the tiniest tremor in her voice. She cocked her head at her uncle, her expression almost outright disinterested, and he responded with a dumb, innocent look and a shrug.

“Then your intel is lacking,” Ozai huffed. “They are one of my greatest nuisances - although perhaps, not anymore.”

The door opened, and in came Zhao, a tall and gloomy figure Azula vaguely recognized as his older brother, and Zuko. In contrast to his usually painstakingly crafted image, Zuko was disheveled, a hank of that once-lustrous dark hair draped like a ratty veil over his face. It drew Azula’s eye immediately, and as he came deeper into the room, the veil shifted, allowing her to glimpse the disfiguring scar hiding just beneath.

Even with her father present, she very nearly lost her composure, fire roiling in her stomach at the sight. She managed to stave off any visible response at the last moment - but her uncle was not as contained.

“Zuko,” he said, breathless with disbelief. “What happened to you?”

Zhao answered instead. “He was taken hostage by insurgents. We’re lucky he’s even alive.”

“I was talking to my nephew,” Iroh snapped, trading glares with Zhao.

Azula turned to her brother. “Is that what happened?”

Two eyes peered at her from under the ratty veil of ink blank. Strangely, it was the eye surrounded by scar tissue that she found more human. At least the warped tissue narrowed it into a facsimile of anger. The other was a dull, metallic yellow, like a coin passed between too many hands.

“Yes,” Zuko replied. “I sustained this injury trying to escape.”

It was difficult to tell if his voice was so hollow because the tragedy itself had left him fragile, or because what he’d said was a lie. Azula watched her brother’s face for even the slightest twitch out of place, but he was like a stone wall. It dawned on her that he was no longer the anxious little boy who went blurting the truth at any given pressure; at some point, he had drawn up an excellent mask, and spent all of his time hiding behind it.

“You see?” Zhao said, puffing up. “I can hardly be faulted. I’m the one who *rescued* him from those Lotus dogs.”

At that, Iroh rounded on Zhao. “Please; this is your fault!”

Zhao’s lip curled. “Are you going deaf in your old age? I said-”

“You should have protected him,” Iroh cut in. “It was your responsibility as his partner. How could you have allowed it to come to this?”

Anger contorted Zhao’s face, but before he could respond, their Fire Lord rose up with his face jagged with fury, and roared:

“ *Enough!* ”

Ozai’s voice shook the room like an eruption, echoing in the high ceilings. When he had stunned everyone else into silence, Ozai turned on his brother and cried, in an imperious voice, “Zhao did not come all this way for you to waste his time pointing fingers! He is here to deliver the facts of a mission that has proved far more useful to his Fire Lord than your idle traipsing across the Earth Kingdom. For the time being, I am ordering you and Azula both to leave my presence!”

Iroh seemed on the verge of belaboring the point, fists clenching at his sides, but a gentle touch on the shoulder from one manicured hand helped him recenter himself. He closed his eyes, breathed, then found the strength to bow to Ozai before he and Azula took their leave.

When the large, heavy doors of the throne room slid shut, Azula turned to her uncle and asked, “What ridiculous lies do you think Zhao is telling in there?”

“Who knows. Given the slander he spat in front of us just now, I do not have high hopes.” Iroh shook his head. “Your poor brother. I have failed him worse than I ever imagined. We have to move quickly.”

“It feels like we’re already too late,” Azula said, glancing at the sealed door.

Iroh cast his own heavy gaze towards it. “In some respects, yes. But we must move forward. So long as your brother is still alive, we can’t afford to lose any more chances.”

---

One day in Kirachu, when the morning light was still a hazy white, and Zuko, riddled with morning sickness, had been confined to the estate, he had sat out on the veranda and watched as a spider wasp wove her web. She worked with a strangely human attentiveness as she flew from one anchor to the next, fixing her thread in an intricate design. What a mesmerizing, if sickening sight it was, to watch that silken material unspool from her body. It was only at the end that Zuko could see what her design had been all along, as her vivid blueprint came to life, glittering in the rafters when the sun hit it just right.

Zuko was thinking of that spider wasp as he watched his husband tell his version of events. Zhao had fed the script to Zuko continuously leading up to their departure from Kirachu, and yet there was something about seeing it finally in action. The details he would artfully forget, only to clarify later. The little inklings of truth mixed in. It was artful. It was calculated.

It only made Zuko seethe ever more deeply. Yet it seemed that every time his hatred was in danger of revealing itself on his face, Zhao would turn and prompt him to add onto whatever he was saying. He never glared at Zuko, never cracked the facade of the concerned husband where the Fire Lord could see it. Yet there was an intensity to Zhao’s gaze.

It was the first time in days that he’d looked Zuko in the eye. There didn’t need to be an arched brow or a curled lip to make it a threat. And shamefully, Zuko cowered underneath that piercing gaze every time it swept over him in askance.

“And you didn’t know your own brother was involved in these sorts of activities?” Ozai asked, when Yan’s involvement with the White Lotus came to light.

“Not at all,” Zhao insisted. “There were no signs.”

“Interesting. Azula told me shortly after meeting Yan that she found him to be unsympathetic to the crown. It would seem the signs were there.”

Zuko imagined he saw the slightest spasm at the corner of Zhao’s mouth. “Well,” Zhao said, “maybe it *seems* that way in retrospect, but I assure you Yan’s beliefs were never radical enough that we thought he was out there blowing up ships. I mean, he was a member of the army, for spirits’ sake. He enlisted willingly.”

“And yet he was well within prime enlistment age when he died. Did he also leave willingly?” Ozai countered.

“Yan left the army because of a serious injury,” Wei explained. “At the time, he was aggrieved to have to return to the Kirachu estate.”

“He spoke of his time in the army fondly. It was enough to overlook the occasional incendiary remark at dinner,” Zhao added.

“You two are too close to the matter.” Ozai glanced at Zuko out of the corner of his eye. “I need some assurance that you aren’t just covering up for the embarrassment of missing such an obvious danger.”

Then came Zhao’s gaze. Zuko swallowed.

“I can attest that they had little reason to suspect Yan,” he uttered. “As mentioned, Yan had an injury from the army that left him with limited mobility. He wasn’t really capable of sneaking around and attacking civilians.”

“And his incendiary views?” Ozai prompted.

Zuko paused as if to consider, all the while fighting the knots in his stomach. “When I first met him, Yan’s political remarks often came across as insincere. He seemed to only voice them when he thought it would embarrass Zhao; when he got to know me well, he stopped mentioning them around me, maybe knowing it wasn’t a shock anymore. I assumed he was jealous and acting out, being the younger alpha male in the family.”

“Then you agree that there was no reason to suspect him earlier?”

Zuko ducked his head, hoping the curtain of hair would hide any sorrow that might flit across his face. “Had you asked me, I would’ve said Yan was incapable of the violence Zhao’s describing.”

He could feel the glare Zhao wanted to lob his way for that, but it was unwarranted. Zuko was playing along with his lie. There was merely a limit to the extent he was willing to sully Yan’s memory.

Zhao piped up. “My lord, you have every right to question us like this and ensure that the work we do in your name is worthy of it. But if I may defend myself, I have shown considerable loyalty to the crown by - stopping my brother for good.” Here, he seemed to falter, but he recovered quickly. “I was faced with the ultimate choice; my loved one, or my country? And I made the necessary sacrifice.”

Zuko felt his limbs go rigid. Hands twitching at his sides, he kept his face inclined, the veil of hair doing twice the work as before to hide the fury radiating off him.

“I don’t appreciate you speaking out of turn,” Ozai responded. “But yes, it is a boon in your favor that you didn’t let your feelings cloud your judgment.”

They carried on. Wei explained, in his usual flat tones, that he had long been hunting the insurrectionists on Kirachu, and came across the name “White Lotus” a few times before. The day of the incident, he had caught a man accused by several villagers of having openly radical views, and after a few hours of interrogation, this man had revealed the White Lotus’s connection to the weapons coming out of Kirachu, and given up a location for their base of operations. Wei then sent a messenger hawk to Zhao at home, in the hopes of helping him strike as soon as possible.

Here, Zhao cut in. “Wei didn’t realize - or perhaps even care - that Yan was also home at the time. Like I said, we were wholly unaware of his involvement. But Yan intercepted the letter before me, and it changed everything.”

According to Zhao’s story, Yan had not paused for even a moment before he grabbed Zuko, held a knife to his throat, and demanded Zhao back off, or risk his spouse’s death. When Zhao tried to talk him down, there was a struggle, and Yan escaped from the house with the hostage, hell-bent on warning his allies what was to come. Zhao pursued, and while fuzzy on the exact details, a fire had started up in the jungle surrounding the village, their best guess being that it was started by allies of the White Lotus to deter him.

When they touched on the origin of his injury, Zuko went faint. He turned away from them all, sick with terror at the memory, at the lie towards a beloved friend - but his turmoil only made the story that trembled its way out of his mouth all the more believable. Zhao had prepared Zuko to be cross-examined ferociously, to have answers for every possible question Ozai might throw at him. But in the end, they didn’t linger on this part of the story. Once it’d all been laid out, Ozai wanted to move on.

“What of the other members? Who is alive?”

“Jaa was a good enough resource that we held onto him a few more days, but the stress was a bit much in his old age,” Wei confessed. “I misjudged my force, and he died in custody a few days later.”

“The owner of the place they were operating out of, Piandao, wouldn’t talk no matter what we did. So he was put to death,” Zhao added. “Barely mattered. We got a lot of names out of Jaa, and Piandao had employees who, with some persuasion, were willing to talk to us. I’m confident we’ve wiped out the entire source of insurrection on Kirachu.”

Wei added a dose of realism. “At least, if there’s anything left, they’re unlikely to openly oppose us now.”

Zuko closed his eyes. He and Zhao had practiced these lies so many times over, but they never seemed to hurt any less. He could only hope that the woozy unreality of it outweighed the terrible tragedy of it. If he were to faint, he wouldn’t have to cry.

Ozai gave a brisk nod. “Very well. It seems your appointment to Kirachu has not proven a waste after all, Zhao. If the Order of the White Lotus are truly out of the picture, this could mean progress for our eastern expansion. Your nation thanks you.”

The three of them bowed before heading out into one of the courtyards adjoining the Great Hall. It wasn’t crowded, but amongst the usual servants, there were quite a few people in uniform milling about, and they all naturally turned towards the three of them as they descended the stairs. Zuko didn’t get a chance to comprehend whether he knew anyone there - that many eyes on him at once made him instinctively duck his head, the protective veil of hair once again falling over half his face.

Zuko could feel Zhao stretching to fit the space next to him, eager to soak up the same looks he was avoiding. “Did you *hear* that, Wei?” Zhao asked. “The fucking bastard wouldn’t thank us himself, but still - the *nation* thanks us. He couldn’t hide how pleased he was! This is my ticket back into the upper echelons of Caldera - *our* ticket!”

“Hn,” was Wei’s only response. Zuko didn’t bother hazarding a glance up at him; it’d be impossible to tell what he was feeling.

Zhao made an irritated noise. “C’mon, what’s with the attitude? You just brought great news to your beloved Ozai.”

“Forgive my lack of cheer,” Wei said, flatly. “You see, I recently lost my younger brother.”

“Don’t even start,” said Zhao, anger creeping back into his voice. “You think I wanted to do that? He was out of control for a long time, and you knew it. I did what I had to, and I didn’t take any enjoyment from it. It was no different than you tearing into that old man.”

“So you keep saying.” Zuko watched as Wei’s sandals cut quickly through the grass.

“Wei - hey, come on. Wei!”

But he wouldn’t respond to Zhao’s calls. Zuko glanced up just in time to see the dark shape of Wei flitting across the courtyard -

&#45; and to make eye contact with a stranger standing, glass in hand, gaping at him. Zuko quickly lowered his face, but the damage was done. Now came the simpering masses to gawk at their homecoming.

“Prince Zhao - Prince Zuko! How good to see you back in Caldera. Oh… but what *happened?* ”

---

Every time Zhao recounted to another person how he’d bravely saved Zuko from the menacing insurrectionists, Zuko swore he could smell his hair and his skin burning again, could feel an electric zap of pain run across the many folds of his scar.

Zuko had been expecting people to mob him with a suffocating pity. But once the minimum level of sympathy had been shown, they were glad to let Zhao hog the spotlight, while Zuko fell away into the background. Just as deeply as Zuko didn’t want to be seen, no one wanted to see him.

He kept his eyes trained on the steps leading up to the Great Hall. He had descended them hundreds of times before, but looking at them now, he recognized them for the same ones where Zhao had once been locked in a violent fistfight with another member of the war council. Zhao had humiliated Zuko in this place once, and now he was doing it again.

As he stood at a distance from his husband and the audience so eager to feed on his lies, Zuko saw the doors to the Great Hall open. Ozai emerged, then descended into the courtyard, heading towards a group a good distance away from theirs.

Zuko glanced at Zhao. He seemed enraptured by his own story, as did the people encircling him. They’d all shut Zuko out, showing their backs to him. Hesitantly at first, Zuko began to break free of their orbit. Once it was clear no one was watching, he set out swiftly across the grass.

All morning, Zhao’s fearful presence had kept Zuko from speaking the truth. But with Zhao occupied, Zuko would be able to tell his father what had really happened. He just had to complete the impossible task of pulling his father aside - a feat made all the more daunting by the fact that Ozai had walked straight into the center of a group of alphas decked out in armor. Experience told Zuko that his father would be furious to be interrupted, especially since these men looked to be some of his highest ranking generals. But Zuko steeled himself, knowing his father would be even angrier if he concealed the truth any longer.

Zuko drew close to his father’s side, and called out softly, “Father - may I speak to you?”

A few of the men glanced at him, but Ozai didn’t. He waved dismissively, and said to the man to his right, “What about the situation in the colonies?”

Zuko swallowed. “I wouldn’t dare to interrupt you, but this is incredibly important.”

“Not now,” Ozai said, sharply. “I’m in the middle of something.”

After a moment of hesitation, the man to Ozai’s right carried on, talking about the allocation of troops in some region or another. Zuko stood there, stomach churning, his instincts telling him that this was the time to run. But his heart couldn’t take it; he had been made mute for too long.

“It’s about what we talked about today,” Zuko said, a little louder, now. “Zhao isn’t what he seems.”

Ozai shot a brief, fierce glare at him. “Excuse me,” he said to the other alphas, before rounding on Zuko. It had been so long since they’d been in the same room, that Zuko had forgotten Ozai’s habit of snatching him by the back of the neck, and using this hand to steer him around. Ozai forced him some distance away, then pulled him close to glare into his face.

“Are you *still* fixated on this?” Ozai ground out. “I thought we’d agreed that you were going to respect your husband from now on.”

“I’m sorry, Father, but I can’t,” Zuko said. “And you shouldn’t, either. Zhao is lying to you about what happened. The White Lotus didn’t kidnap me, and they’re not the ones who burned me.”

Ozai’s face could never be said to soften; yet some of the hardness in his expression gave way to something like curiosity. Eager to appeal to him, Zuko carried on. “The White Lotus also weren’t responsible for burning down the jungle, and Yan wasn’t the villain Zhao made him out to be. There’s actually a critical detail Zhao’s hiding from you - the original goal of the mission wasn’t just to expose the White Lotus’s hideout!”

“Then what were they trying to do?” Ozai asked, scowling still.

Zuko opened his mouth to tell his father that the reason Zhao set out that day was to capture the Avatar, who had been hiding on Kirachu all along. After all, it was humiliating. It painted Zhao as a failure to the empire.

It would also reveal something of Aang and the other’s movements. Suppose Ozai questioned the men who had followed Zhao on his mission that day? Surely someone would talk?

Perhaps someone who had seen the direction that they were flying?

“I - I don’t know,” Zuko said.

Ozai gave a disgusted sigh, glancing back towards the group Zuko had separated him from. Frightened he would leave, Zuko blurted out the first thing he could think of. “Father - Zhao is the one who burned me!”

He succeeded in pulling Ozai’s gaze back on him, but his father only appraised him. He didn’t say anything about this revelation or even change his expression. Zuko repeated himself, as if unsure he’d heard. “Zhao did this,” he said, gesturing to his face. “He’s the one who disfigured me.”

Still, there was no movement from Ozai’s face. All of the anger and hurt that had propelled Zuko across the courtyard began to dissipate, and he was left with a terrible, hollow realization. With a certain hysteric grief rising up inside him, tears pricking his eyes, throat choked by a wet fist of defeat, Zuko began to beg. “Father, please. *Please* say something.”

Ozai let out a long, loud sigh. “Was the place Zhao raided really the headquarters of the White Lotus?”

Zuko sniffed. “It - yes, it was. But-”

“Did he really get information on their membership?”

“I think so, but I’m not-”

“And are the White Lotus really eradicated?”

“As far as I know, but Father-”

“Then I don’t care about anything else,” said Ozai. He turned and walked away, leaving Zuko exposed in the middle of the courtyard lawn, silent tears streaming down his face.

Zuko stayed where he was, rooted in place by humiliation. He buried his face in his hands, all while feeling the sting of dozens of imagined eyes boring into him, wondering, what was the ugly little prince doing, making such a scene in the middle of the palace courtyard? Wasn’t he afraid he’d embarrass his esteemed father, his husband?

Zuko’s breath began to come in harried, panicked pants. He pressed his palms hard against his mouth, feeling the wet slick of his own miserable cries stopped short, but - this was worse, wasn’t it? He was covering that terrible scar, so all that was left to gawk at was the spectacle of his public unraveling. He didn’t want to run - he wanted to immolate, to let the ash of his remains scatter in the wind.

He heard murmuring. He couldn’t make out a single word, but the imagined mockery was sharp enough to make him flinch, to make him peak between his fingers. Yellow eyes looked at him from all angles, and - they couldn’t see his line of sight, so they didn’t turn away. He could see the pitying looks, the cringes, the way they would lean over to one another to whisper, there he was, what a shame, he used to be such a pretty, graceful thing, not ever the talent his sister was, almost forgettable by comparison, but you’d have a hard time forgetting that face now, wouldn’t you? And no one was sniping at them to shut up, no one was running to his side to comfort him, no one was coming to save him because - because -

Because no one here had ever really cared about him, had they?

Whenever Zuko looked at his scar in the mirror, it had a hard, rigid look to it. But it was soft against the palm of his hand. Softer than any of the rest of his skin. Pink and satiny and newborn, it didn’t hold moisture quite like the rest of his face, didn’t bear back the weight of his tears quite like he expected. It was like touching the soft insides of his body, the secret, sacred parts meant to be shielded from harm.

Suddenly, Zuko felt he understood. Zhao had not ruined him with this burn. He had simply… pulled back the veil. He had shown Zuko that, beneath the perfect omega performance, no one really cared about him. Not Zhao. Not any of the members of the Fire Nation court.

Not even his own father.

Zuko lowered his hands from his face. Standing across from him on the lawn was General Mazeli. Zuko couldn’t help comparing the look of horror on her face to the tender look they’d once shared in a dark study, or the heated one she had passed him over dinner when he was about seventeen, and his father had wanted him to ply her for information on a political movement he wanted to quash. Zuko had once sat across from her and batted his eyes and ignored the hand on his thigh, and now here she was, at the same safe distance you reserved for a wild animal, an older woman who looked to be her wife hanging onto her arm. General Mazeli caught Zuko’s eye, and she seemed to jerk where she stood, caught looking too long to reasonably turn away, trapped like a wasp in a jar.

Mazeli’s mouth moved. And perhaps, if she had asked the question on her mind, things would have gone very differently. Had she asked if Zuko was alright, perhaps the young prince would have come to himself, said there was nothing, and scuffled away to mourn in private.

But Mazeli’s wife tugged on her shoulder. And after all that agonizing eye contact, Mazeli turned away.

Heat surged through Zuko’s limbs. And suddenly, for the first time since he presented as an omega, he didn’t give a damn about decorum. If everyone here wanted to treat him like a monster, then he would show them a goddamn monster.

There were three yards of naked grass between Zuko and the next nearest gaggle of court nobles. He walked swiftly, nearly gliding over the fine green blades as his jaws opened, and a torrent of fire poured out. People were so unwilling to look at a little scar, to be caught looking, that it was a moment before they let themselves turn towards the rippling orange glow, another moment before they instinctively clutched their faces and shrieked.

Zuko was a monster, but he had once been a prince, too, so the nobility didn’t know how to retaliate at first. He took advantage, attacking everyone within his range, lobbing fire from his hands until they went skittering back, arms up, eyes wide, their shock written like an epitaph on their faces. He didn’t follow them where they ran - his goal wasn’t to kill them or even to hurt them, but to corral them, to clear the way so he could stalk across the lawn, heading doggedly towards where his main goal loomed amongst sycophants.

Seeing the ugly brat charging towards the Fire Lord seemed to awaken a few of the onlookers. With determination, Mazeli charged Zuko from behind, but he knew her chi intimately. Sensing her approach, he moved deftly out of the way of one fiery punch, the next, then landed a swift elbow to her neck, stunning her momentarily so he could focus on the rush of chi coming from his right. He lifted a hand and all but caught the fire heading for him, tossed it aside so it hit the grass at its owners’ feet. Zuko was so deeply inured in the moment, it didn’t even occur to him how in tune he was with the sheer energy of the other firebenders, how easy it was for him to feel rather than see their every advance, all without ever taking his eyes off his true target.

The man coming from his right stumbled briefly when the flame fell at his feet, but he leapt over it, arms outstretched towards Zuko. At the last second, Zuko fell back from his grasp, leaving the man to fall straight into the barely recovering Mazeli. Another woman leapt out to stop Zuko, but he ducked out of her way, then out of the way of a fireball lobbed at his head, pausing in his dogged movement across the lawn to stand with both arms outstretched, away from his body.

Twin funnels of fire spiraled out from Zuko’s hands, bidding his pursuers fall onto their backs in the grass to avoid being just as viciously burnt as him. In that instant that Zuko stood there, flames pouring from his body, he finally met his target’s eyes.

Ozai did not avoid his son’s gaze. But that wasn’t a surprise; people avoided looking at Zuko because they did not want to be caught gaping in horror or disgust. Even if they didn’t care enough to ask how Zuko was, they cared that anyone, even he, might see them as cruel.

But Ozai wasn’t afraid to hurt Zuko. He looked right into his eyes with his lip curled back from his teeth. It made Zuko want to rush forward, hands blazing, and accept whatever death awaited, so long as he got to leave a mark first.

The fire spewing from his hands extinguished all at once, the unoccupied space of burnt lawn seeming to gape in its absence. With a ferocious cry, Zuko sprinted towards his father with his hands aloft, fingers curled like claws.

The war council was comprised of men who had earned their place at Azulon’s side after decades of service to the Fire Nation military. They were not in their prime - but they were not greenhorns, either. They enfolded their Fire Lord like a phalanx, and those at the front lunged towards Zuko.

There was a struggle. Zuko lashed out, looking to wound, to maim, but his fire died on the resistant armor, died against the sheer mass of the men who threw themselves at him. In the end, Zuko was not defeated by men whose chi he could sense like a second sight. These were men accustomed to holding their own amongst benders with nothing but the weapons at hand, and here, unarmed in the courtyard, they stopped Zuko by piling on top of him, smothering him like the unruly fire that he was.

Zuko thrashed in their grip, the noise of fury and frustration that escaped him not unlike the snarling of a trapped animal. His father was only inches away, and as if he could close that distance with words alone, he cried out, desperately, furiously: “*Father!* Why won’t you come here, Father? I’m not done talking to you! I still have more-!”

His words were arrested as a thick hank of rope was jammed between his teeth. He bit down as if to sever it, whipping his head as the man on his back tied the gag into place, another hastily binding his limbs. His father hadn’t moved even an inch, and was peering down at him with a look of distaste, like Zuko was something smeared on the bottom of his boot.

“That ought to hold him.” The man on Zuko’s back paused to adjust his own disheveled topknot, before addressing his Fire Lord. “What shall we do with him?”

“Lock him away.”

The man on Zuko’s back dismounted him and was preparing to hoist him up when a familiar voice cried out.

“Wait!”

Zuko looked up just as his uncle and his sister arrived on the scene. Iroh’s face was wrought with horror, and Azula -

“He was trying to say something,” Azula said, hand outstretched. “Take out the gag. I want to hear him speak.”

“He has clearly lost his mind,” Ozai scoffed. “Why should I give him another opportunity to heave fire on us all?”

“He was cooperating with you only an hour ago,” said Azula. “I want to know why he’s suddenly attacking you.” When Ozai scoffed at her, she doubled down. “It’s a matter of *your* safety.”

“You can easily interrogate him *after* he’s been thrown in a cell, Azula. For now, I want him out of my sight.”

But Azula marched over to where the war council members had Zuko subdued in the grass. “Azula, don’t bother,” Ozai cried out. Then, when she crouched down beside her brother, “*Azula!* ” “This could be urgent,” was all she said. There was a certain determination in her expression as she reached out and, with more gentleness than Zuko had ever seen her possess, untied the rope from his mouth.

“What were you trying to say just now?” she asked.

Zuko worked his jaw, already sore from the gag. He had no time to cast a soft look of thanks towards his sister; he had only eyes for their father. And they were not the eyes of a penitent.

“I wasn’t trying to kill you,” Zuko said, voice crackling with the fires of his loathing. “I was trying to get you to listen to me, for *once* in my miserable life! You wouldn’t hear what I had to say when I came to you civilly, so I figured that this would be the only way to get through that wall of stone you’ve put up!”

Ozai’s eyes were like fiery coals. “Tell me right now why I shouldn’t have you executed for attacking your Fire Lord.”

“I’m warning you of a much greater danger than myself.” Zuko turned to Azula, now. “Four months ago, when the Avatar escaped the royal palace. Did you know I’m the one who set him free?”

Azula’s eyes visibly widened. It was the first time Zuko had ever seen her at a loss. She mouthed a question that he heard whispered in triplicate, as every person in earshot reacted to the news.

Finally, the distance between Zuko and his father began to disappear. Ozai approached in long, angry strides, his dark robes sweeping out from him like the wings of a bat. He stopped his boots just short of Zuko’s face, and Azula moved out of the way to avoid being shoved.

Glaring down at his son, Ozai forced only a single word through his gritted teeth: “*Why?* ”

“Because I was told to,” Zuko replied, looking up into his father’s face. “Zhao didn’t come to the mainland to report to you. He’s here to usurp you.”

## Chapter 43

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Zuko finds some unlikely allies. Zhao fights the greatest battle of his life.

### Text

“He’s lying.”

Everyone turned. Just at the edges of the group, amongst the onlookers, stood Zhao himself. He was puffed up, as if trying to look threatening and angry, but the haggard, desperate eyes that peered out from his face gave away his fear.

He pointed where Zuko was subdued in the grass. “That little rat just attacked you in broad daylight. Why would you listen to a word he has to say?”

Zuko cast him a caustic glare. “Because you have terrorized me into silence for long enough. I’m not hiding this secret for you anymore!”

“I’m not terrorizing anyone!” Zhao thundered, body clenched and trembling. “You’re the one who’s-”

“Why do you think the rebellion in Kirachu got so much worse under Zhao’s reign?” Zuko interjected, loudly enough the whole courtyard could hear. “Why do you think he let a Lotus member live in his own house for so long? Didn’t know? About his own *brother’s* whereabouts? He’s not as clueless as he’d have you believe.”

“You little fucking-”

“-He was using the Lotus for his own gains, and when they realized his goals weren’t the same as theirs, that Zhao merely wanted to topple my father so he could take the empire for *himself* , they cut ties with him. Zhao eliminated the White Lotus - and his own *brother* - to prevent their involvement from ever coming to light. He brought us here for one last chance to get close to my father.”

Zuko was in awe of how quickly the lies flowed from his own lips. He remembered a time when he had struggled to keep up with Azula’s many falsehoods, when he had fumbled honestly in her wake, always getting into trouble where she wouldn’t. This must be what it had felt like to her. Almost like it was second nature.

Red-faced, Zhao tried to interject again. “I would never commit *treason-* ”

“He has a *history* of treason,” Zuko said, even louder. “Just ask his former superior, Admiral Shu. Back when they were stationed in the South Pole, Zhao conspired with tribesmen to commit a *mutiny* . What’s to stop him from doing the same thing a second time?”

He could now expertly weave truth and fiction into a seamless braid, and it was all thanks to the man now glaring at him in mute fury. Zhao certainly had no trouble meeting Zuko’s eye now, channeling all of his hatred and anger into his gaze.

Looking right back at him, Zuko said, “Zhao told me early in our marriage that he wasn’t satisfied just having an heir. He wanted to replace you himself, Father. He made threats against you and Azula, both.”

“You have no proof,” Zhao snarled.

With his hands bound, Zuko couldn’t gesture to his scar. But he could crane his neck, let the protective veil fall away from the left side of his face. “I feared how Zhao would punish me. He had a plan to kill you while we were here in the capital, Father, when your guard was down. Now you see why I had to act so rashly - when we spoke earlier, and you showed me how blind you were to Zhao’s true nature, I knew I had to do so much more to get through to you.”

Zuko was already being held with his chest against the grass, and now, in front of all these onlookers, he pressed his face to the ground as he said, voice dripping with humility, “I risked my life, the life of *our child,* for *your goals,* Zhao! I’m - I’m *begging* you to stop this!”

Zhao opened his mouth, but all that came out was a choking sound. Surrounding guards traded glances, then began to advance upon him. He stepped back, hands up -

“You - you can’t all seriously believe this! Obviously that burn didn’t just damage his skin - it’s driven him insane! I mean, what proof do you have? My story was corroborated!”

Zhao’s eyes lit up. “Wei - we need to find Wei! He’ll tell you that this lunatic is lying to you!”

After a pause, Ozai gestured to a few nearby guards, urging them to search the grounds. He was tired of the gawking from court nobles, and banished everyone save the guards that came to restrain the unhappily married couple, as well as Azula and Iroh. It wasn’t that those two were invited, but they managed to slip by, following the rest of the party back into the palace.

For the second time that day, Zuko and Zhao arrived in the throne room, no longer in triumph, but in chains. Zuko shook his wrists in their shackles, trying to get some blood flow back in them after being subdued for so long. All the while, he was ignoring the poisonous glares Zhao was throwing his way.

The mask Zuko had learned to wear as an adolescent omega was of use today, as underneath his impassivity, his stomach was roiling with nerves. He knew Zhao had traitorous tendencies, but much of his story had been thrown together on the spot, acting on desperation and fury-blind revenge. He had all but forgotten about Wei, and now anxiously awaited his arrival, which would undoubtedly end this gambit.

Ozai turned to Zhao. “Did you know that several months ago, when the Avatar escaped from the palace, it was Zuko who set him free?”

Zhao’s eyes widened. “I - well, I-”

Ozai’s impatience was becoming fiercer by the second. Where before Azula had been shocked when her brother told her, she now snickered behind her hand; “Oh, that was *both of you?* I never would have guessed!”

“It - my lord, I - yes, *Zuko* is to blame for that, but it’s not like I approved of it!” Zhao stammered.

“I’m just an omega,” Zuko said. “I don’t have anything to gain from a political move like that. Of course I did it for your sake.”

“Shut up!” Zhao snapped, his attempt to grab at Zuko aborted by the restrictive chains around his wrists. “You did it all on your own!”

“But if *you* knew, Zhao,” Ozai cut in, “then why didn’t you turn Zuko in? It’s clear to me you had something to hide.”

“I was only trying to protect Zuko! Given how he’s turning on me, though, I *should* have told you immediately. I’m sorry, my lord…”

Zuko was silently preening over Zhao’s misfortune. His father’s suspicions seemed to only grow by the second. But Zuko’s sense of triumph was soon snuffed out as Ozai lanced him with that vicious stare, and said, “Don’t think you’ve won yet. I know of your insolence towards your husband. If Wei says there is no proof of what you say, you *will* be sent to your death.”

As he was talking, the doors to the throne room opened, and Wei had entered, followed by one of the guards sent to find him. He took in the proceedings coolly, considering his brother was in chains. He stayed by the door, keeping some distance from where Ozai stood like a pillar in the center of the room. In contrast, Zuko and Zhao were being held by guards behind the Fire Lord’s dais, where they couldn’t easily escape.

“What’s going on?” Wei asked Ozai. “Prince Zuko’s to be punished? For what?”

“Interesting that you missed my son attacking me in broad daylight,” Ozai said, dryly. “Half the court saw it. Where were you?”

Wei’s eyes widened the most imperceptible amount. “I was in the gardens, my lord. I apologize for my absence; had I been there, I would have done everything in my power to protect you.”

Ozai did not look convinced. “Zuko told me that he attacked me on *Zhao’s* orders, as part of a bid to put himself on the throne. Zuko has also confessed to releasing the Avatar several months ago, as part of that very same plot. He says that your recent triumph is a lie, too, as Zhao intended to work with the White Lotus to rise to power, but eliminated them over petty disagreements. Lastly, he has said that there were plans to take my life during your visit to the mainland.”

“ *Hearsay* ,” said Zhao, through gritted teeth. “Not a word of what Zuko said has even an iota of proof. Wei, can you please tell these people the truth, that I’m innocent of this?”

Wei didn’t answer right away. His gaze slid from each person in the room, landing eventually on Azula. She and her uncle had been watching the proceedings in silence, Iroh stunned and Azula enraptured. Seeing Wei look her way, she tilted her head upwards to acknowledge him, one sharp eyebrow arched in question.

“Princess Azula,” said Wei. “You have spent several months abroad in the Earth Kingdom. While you were there, was there ever an attempt made on your life?”

“Yes,” said Azula. “A few months back, I was set upon by assassins in the colonies. I survived the attempt, but only by eliminating every one of them. I never learnt who sent them.” She cocked her head. “Why do you mention it?”

Wei bowed his head. “I’m sorry for the trouble, Princess Azula. I’m almost certain it was Zhao who sent them.”

Zuko was sure his mask slipped, his disbelief laid bare on his face. Wei was the last person he suspected would come to his aid, but there was no way he’d invent such a story solely for Zuko’s benefit. From the looks of it, Zhao hadn't been prepared for this revelation, his expression stone-still.

“I’ve long suspected Zhao, too. But I was never sure,” Azula admitted.

“It took some time for me to track the evidence,” said Wei. “But a money order was sent from our family’s bank account to the colonies. If we compare dates and locations, I think we’ll see a match.”

There was a murmur of disbelief from Iroh, the beginnings of a stuttered denial from Zhao, but all was cut through by Ozai’s thunderous voice as he rounded on Wei. “Why am I only just now learning of this?! In all your many reports to me, you’ve never once mentioned an attempt on my heir’s life!”

Zuko was also curious why Wei, in all of his devotion to Ozai, wouldn’t reveal this sooner. He looked past where his father loomed in the center of the room, nearly blocking Wei from view. It looked as though Wei was looking over Ozai’s shoulder, addressing Zuko himself, as he spoke.

“I suppose you could argue the signs were there all along. But I looked away because he was my brother, and I didn’t want to believe what he was capable of.”

And perhaps Zuko was imagining all of it. Perhaps he was imagining how Wei met his gaze over his father’s shoulder. Perhaps he was imagining the heavy remorse in his voice. But Wei seemed to look Zuko in the eye as he uttered, “From the bottom of my heart. I am sorry for what he’s done. For what I failed to stop.”

And though it may have been meant for his Fire Lord, Zuko could feel something shift and crack inside his chest, like a glacier drifting into warmer waters. He rapidly blinked back the tears threatening to cloud his vision.

“I’ve heard quite enough.” Ozai turned to his son. “You may have earned the right to live another day, but you and your husband both have endlessly disrespected my reign with these spectacles of yours. Your legacy has left a stain upon Caldera, and I will think of a befitting punishment for you both. For now-” He waved to his guards. “Take them away.”

Zuko didn’t take even a moment to reckon with his own fate; he only wanted to soak up Zhao’s reaction, to see the naked terror on his face. They were close together, could have touched if they were unchained, and as their guards started to haul them away, Zuko swore that he could see - not just Zhao, but something inside him, leaping up his throat every time a guard laid a hand on him, growing wilder and wilder still, even as it stayed bottled up inside him. Watching the feverish, desperate looks Zhao was casting around the room, as if searching for a lifeline - remembering those intense moments out on the lawn, when Zuko could feel the other firebenders coming for him before he even saw them - he got the distinct impression that if he just… *pulled* on Zhao. Lifted his fingers in a beckoning gesture, found the thread, and plucked -

Zhao’s voice exploded through the throne room.

“This is *slander!* ” Zhao struggled against the guards, his firmly planted boots sliding and screeching along the marble floors as he was dragged towards the exit. “You think one bank slip is enough to justify destroying a man’s life?”

He lunged towards Ozai, held at bay by the guards as he shouted, “I eliminated the White Lotus for you! I went to Kirachu for you, I left the navy for you, I married your son, I did everything you told me to, and you won’t even dignify me with the bare minimum of justice?! Are you even going to investigate what they’ve said about me?!”

Ozai wouldn’t even turn to look at Zhao as he said, “Whatever small successes you’ve brought to this empire are outnumbered by embarrassments. You have no use to me anymore.”

Slowly, the desperation on Zhao’s face gave way, so there was only an anger so fierce it made him ugly. “At least let me defend myself, you fucking coward! You honorless *fraud!* ”

*Now* Ozai turned around. “What did you just say to me?” he asked, in a voice Zuko had long learned to fear. Zuko found himself shrinking away even as Zhao stood even taller in his anger.

“You heard me!” Zhao shouted. “If you had a shred of honor left in your shriveled little brain, you’d give me a fair chance at defending myself!”

In one fluid motion, Ozai turned and marched up to where Zhao stood, his dark robes rippling at his feet as if he was gliding along the floor.

Zuko waited for the hellish fury to burst forth from his father’s steely gaze. However, Ozai remained chillingly composed as he reared up before Zhao and said, “Alright. You want so badly to defend your name? Then you can defend yourself from these accusations in an Agni Kai.”

The fear in Zhao’s gaze came and went in an instant. “Fine. I accept your challenge!” He struggled in the guards’ grip, if only to get an inch closer to Ozai, to snarl in his face: “If I win, I keep my rank, and you name my child as your heir over Azula!”

Ozai outright laughed at him. “You think you have the leverage to ask me for something like that? If you win, you get to live. Anything more is a privilege.”

And with that, the guards dragged Zuko and Zhao from the room.

---

After everyone had cleared out of the throne room, there were only two people left lingering in the adjoining antechamber. Wei was standing at a far wall, looking at something his body obscured from view. When Iroh approached, he saw it was a portrait of his own late father. He had never noticed it there himself; he had assumed Ozai had removed all images of Azulon from the palace upon taking the throne.

Iroh stood beside Wei for a moment, pretending to admire the image himself before he broke the silence. “I believe your testimony may have saved my nephew’s life.”

“I have been gathering intelligence for Ozai for months now. It was my duty to report to him.”

“Still - I thank you for speaking up,” said Iroh. “Given how long ago Azula was attacked, you’ve been sitting on this information a while. You must have struggled over what to do with it.” Wei didn’t respond. Iroh gently pressed. “Perhaps you thought you were protecting family?”

Wei scoffed. “What a delusion.”

He was still looking over the portrait with a steely eye when he said to Iroh, “Did you know that Ozai hated you growing up? He blamed you for leaving the capital to pursue your own glory in the army. He blamed you for leaving him behind with him.” Wei nodded to the image of Azulon.

Iroh blinked, not expecting to be chastised. Nevertheless, he paused to absorb what Wei had said.

“When I was young,” said Iroh, “and he himself was thus young… my father treated me with the utmost kindness. I cannot do justice to the depth to which he cared about my wellbeing. To the opportunities he let me have that many parents of his generation simply would not give their own children. So when he started to change, I was especially blind to it.”

Iroh shifted. “We hid it from the public, but towards the end, my father had issues with memory. He prided himself on his mind, and even the smallest of errors made him angry and ashamed. I didn’t realize, being as far from home as I was, that his condition had begun to erode his personality, as well. Had made him cruel.”

“You don’t have to justify yourself to me,” Wei said wearily. “I used to hate you on principle, simply because Ozai did. Until I left Kirachu to pursue my own career in politics.”

Wei was an angular, stern-looking man. Yet with a simple shift, those metallic yellow eyes lost their hardness. Suddenly Iroh was looking at someone who carried a terrible sadness.

“I left Yan as you once left Ozai. It was easy to; I was finally grown. I had always wanted to leave, because unlike you, I knew what my father was.” The breath Wei inhaled was delicate, wet. “Yan joined the army to escape our home. That is where he sustained his lifelong injury, and that is where he began to take on more radical ideas. Had I not abandoned him, had I - taken him along with me. Maybe things would have turned out differently. Maybe he would still be here.”

Caring for Azula had schooled Iroh as to the caution that needed to be exercised when offering physical comfort. But Wei struck him as a man who had rarely been touched; and so Iroh allowed himself to reach out and gently clasp one wrist. It was a wide, thick wrist, with bones that jutted out in sharp angles, as if to deter touch. Wei himself did not react, as if Iroh’s hand was meant to be there, and had been all along.

“The only person to blame for Yan’s death is the man who killed him,” Iroh said. “It sounds like you did everything you could.”

“No,” Wei murmured. “I could have done more.”

“Then we can say with certainty that you loved him. And that always makes a difference, even if that difference can’t save our loved ones from their fates.”

---

They held the Agni Kai later that same day, just as the sun was about to sink beneath the horizon, bathing the grounds of the royal palace in a hazy orange glow. Despite the short notice, the match drew much attention, and the arena was flooded with nobles curious to see how the headstrong prince commander would fare against their Fire Lord.

Zuko was seated in the front row, chained and flanked by guards. Even from his limited vantage point, he realized as he surveyed the crowd that he recognized a few faces. For instance, over there, on the other side of the platform, War Minister Qin was seated. His hair had since grown out from the shaved phoenix tail he’d been forced to bare immediately following his defeat by Zhao; no doubt he was praying for his downfall. And nearer by, a few rows to the left of Zuko, was General Mazeli. This time she did not make the mistake of gawking at him, keeping her gaze fixed firmly on the stage.

As nobles continued to pour into the stands, Zuko identified amongst them Makamae (arm-in-arm with a man Zuko had never seen before, but hated on sight); a disheveled-looking Admiral Shu, who may have been called in to testify; and countless alphas of the court Zuko’s father had once tasked him with - he could admit to it now, couldn’t he? - seducing for information. Watching these many familiar faces fill the crowd, Zuko was filled with a bizarre, almost static sensation, as if every nerve ending was thrumming, as if the air was awash with a spiritual power. He supposed what he was feeling was anticipation - for whatever happened next, his life was about to drastically change.

Iroh and Azula came, too. Although they were not allowed to sit right next to Zuko, they came as close as they were allowed, separated on his right by one guard. His uncle leaned forward to give him a smile just before the Agni Kai started, but the gesture puzzled Zuko enough that he only stared back.

Finally, the challengers came onto the stage. A hush fell over the crowd. Ozai and Zhao walked to opposite ends of the stage, where they crouched facing away from each other, the ceremonial shawls of the Agni Kai draped around their shoulders. A guard came out to arbitrate the match, and at his signal, the two men stood, letting the flimsy material flutter to the ground as they came to face one another.

Zhao was the first to lift his hands into an attack-ready position, squaring his shoulders as he faced down the Fire Lord. Ozai stared back at him, his own fists raised, unmoved by Zhao’s attempt at intimidation.

As the guard declared the terms of the match, Zuko closed his eyes. He could see the meager remains of sunlight shining orange through his eyelids, the tiny pulse throbbing in the outline of a vein. Without the distraction of the familiar crowd, he could imagine a world where this Agni Kai had been called weeks ago.

Zuko imagined his father gripping Zuko’s letter in his hands, momentarily paralyzed by anger, by fear, by shame. He imagined that his father never wrote back, seizing on the urgency of Zuko’s situation to send guards to Kirachu to safely extract him and bring him home - or perhaps Ozai would come to Kirachu himself. Perhaps the Agni Kai Zuko was imagining now would have been declared on the front steps of the estate. The first time the Fire Lord had stepped foot on Kirachu soil in decades, risking his image and the stability of the empire’s unity, all to avenge his son. It would be like something out of Ty Lee’s terrible novels, the ones set in ancient times, where alphas were always fighting Agni Kai for noble reasons, not just over any old slight.

When Zuko opened his eyes, he understood that to the two men standing across from each other on stage, he might as well be invisible. He didn’t need to keep his eyes open and look to know that neither of them had glanced into the crowd to search for him.

The guard’s hand came down, and he leapt back from the center of the stage as Zhao and Ozai lunged towards each other.

Their skill sets were completely different, but each of their fighting styles had a directness and a savagery that set them in comparison to each other. They fought at close quarters, their opponent moving so quickly in tandem that they never landed a blow where intended - although the audience in the stands could hear the impact of each block, the sheer force of contact a viable contender in place of a direct burn.

With a roar of frustration, Zhao sent a high kick arcing its way towards the Fire Lord, which missed its mark. Ozai dashed back, landing in a crouch, jutting both hands toward Zhao to bowl a sparkling ball of electricity his way. He had backed far enough away that, without their earlier close-quarters pressure, Zhao could easily dodge.

Even the guard to Zuko’s right leaned in, entranced by the battle. It seemed like it was going to be close. Steadily, the sun fell lower and lower, and even with the arena lit by torches, the fires of the Agni Kai glowed and burst and illuminated their snarling battle with an eerie contrast.

The moment things shifted was almost imperceptible. But, after all, Zhao was a man fighting for everything, and his desperation could only weigh him down. To Ozai, this was a paltry fight. He was the first to land a blow, grazing Zhao on the shoulder with a fiery hand, and while Zhao managed to leap back, to save himself from a deeper burn, that was the beginning of the end. His breath came in ragged pants as he watched Ozai, one hand clutching that shoulder, the other clenched, as if ready to defend him alone.

Ozai didn’t pause to wait for Zhao to recover. He darted forward, two hands tucked into his side to gather a swirling, fiery ball that he didn’t throw, but *thrust* at Zhao, who wasn’t fast enough, who stumbled back and fell to hands and feet, a single hand raised before him. Ozai speared down on him with two hands flaming, and while Zhao could keep one at bay, he couldn’t adjust his weight and free up his other arm fast enough to block the other hand, which came straight for the right side of his face.

Zuko felt rather than saw the way the crowd leaned forward as the flaming appendage gripped onto Zhao’s face, causing him to cry out in agony. Watching his father hold his husband down and burn him until the skin blistered and broke, Zuko felt a bizarre tickling in his chest. A levity. Ozai raised his hand above his son in law, now sputtering and incoherent, not even fighting back. There was a crackle of electricity, the sound like a thousand birds chittering in sync.

When the killing blow came down on Zhao’s heart, Zuko realized he was smiling.

---

When most of the crowd has funneled out of the stands and the guards are hauling Zuko off, he sees two men carrying a stretcher away from the stage, one arm hanging limply from its side. Even if it weren’t bloodless, even if it weren’t dotted with burns, Zuko would recognize the sinew of that muscle anywhere, would remember how that same arm had held him close and held him down.

With a burst of hysterical strength, Zuko darts towards the men carrying Zhao’s body away, breaking free of his guards in the process. He can hear them shouting after him, but he doesn’t stop - he *needs* to see for himself, to know that it’s really all over.

The men carrying the stretcher don’t obey Zuko’s command, precisely, but his shouted “ *Stop* ,” the sight of him running towards them startles them into dropping the stretcher to the ground, dust gathering in swirls around it. Zuko falls to his knees beside it and peers into Zhao’s face, getting one last look at the strong jaw and proud nose he had loved at a time that felt so long ago.

All along the right side of Zhao’s face is a gruesome burn. Zuko can smell the cooked flesh now that he’s close, and bids himself not to gag as he reaches out to touch. It’s not unlike touching his own face, and it’s warm enough that one could imagine Zhao is still alive, excepting his indifference to Zuko’s stare. Zuko can imagine how Zhao would jerk away from his touch if he could, the piercing look he would lance him with.

“Look at us,” Zuko murmurs, tracing the burn with his fingers. “A matched pair.”

He can imagine the hardened edge of Zhao’s jaw at that, even as he lays inert and slack-faced, strangely peaceful for the injury he sports. Zuko is searching his husband’s face for fine lines of stress, evidence he died in agony, when a shadow falls over him.

Zuko looks up, expecting to see the medical attendants or his guards. But it’s his father. He’s looking down at Zuko, and there’s something strange in his expression.

Zuko blinks up at him. “Congratulations on your victory, Father.”

Ozai ignores the praise, his eyes seeming to scan Zuko’s body. “Wei said he thought you miscarried from the stress of your burn. That he found blood.”

Zuko can feel prickling as the hair on the back of his neck stands on end. He gets up, just in time for his guards to close in and take him by the arms. His father continues to watch him with that catlike intensity, gaze never relenting as he says, “A doctor will be coming to examine you.”

And despite everything, Zuko lets relief wash over him. He says, “Father,” his voice foolishly soft, trusting that this man has ever wanted any good for him.

Ozai dashes that all away. “If you are in fact pregnant, I will do you the honor of raising your child myself. You’ve willfully risked its life enough today that you’ve proven yourself unfit to parent.” A pause. “You *do* remember the child, don’t you? You haven’t outright *forgotten* it, in all this spectacle you’ve caused?”

“Of course I do,” Zuko protests, even as he knows his father is right. In the past twelve hours, he hasn’t been thinking at all about the danger to his child - *or* to himself, for that matter. He’s only been thinking of revenge against Zhao.

Ozai tosses his head. “I’m sure that without your influence, your child will come of age as a worthier heir than you ever were. Regardless, *you* will be spending the remainder of your life exiled from the Fire Nation.”

Zuko’s misguided affection is cotton in oil, and Ozai has set it ablaze. Consumed with fury, Zuko lurches towards his father, but the guards are prepared this time, and manage to hold him in place. Not that it’d make a difference; Zuko is still immobilized by chains.

Even without meaning to, Zuko feels the heat rushing to his hands, feels the manacles become a searing hot brand on his skin. He doesn’t flinch away, staring at his father with the hatred of a lifetime suddenly coming to fruition.

“Careful,” Ozai says, primly, and for once, Zuko thinks of the lives that hang in the balance. So he doesn’t fight the guards’ grip. But they do have to drag him away.

---

Sonzehn isn’t sure if the boy recognizes him. To his credit, the boy surely has other things on his mind; the guards hauled him inside with no little force, binding him to the examination table so there would be no threat to the doctor’s life. As if that wasn’t enough indignity, they gagged him, too, although they assured Sonzehn this was a necessary measure - evidently, the boy had a habit of breathing fire when driven into a corner.

And what a corner. Even now he struggles against his bindings, head whipping back and forth as if the momentum could break him free. Perhaps Sonzehn should be frightened by the possibility, but he isn’t. He just feels sad for the boy.

He keeps referring to Prince Zuko as a “boy” - and while he is cloaked in a rich omega scent, while his stomach bulges so that even someone who isn’t a doctor could easily answer the Fire Lord’s question, while the anger in his face speaks of ages of hurt - isn’t he still only a boy, at nineteen? But Sonzehn supposes the moniker could come from the fact that he remembers Prince Zuko when he was even more of a boy, sixteen and mute with nerves, on the cusp of a coming of age. No matter how different they may look, Sonzehn cannot separate the shy child who had perched on the end of the examination table from the wild, wounded creature that thrashes before him now.

Sonzehn knows he has no control over the boy’s biology. Yet as his eyes trace over the terrible scar that mars that beautiful face, he thinks about how the boy’s only options are to be exiled or to be imprisoned, have his child stolen, and still be cast away. It doesn’t matter what Prince Zuko has done to their Fire Lord to deserve this - even knowing very little of the boy’s life, Sonzehn knows he had to be driven to this.

Sonzehn can’t shake the feeling that he was the one who set this boy on this path. Even though his work for the Fire Lord’s children did wonders for his career, he would give it all back if he could just give this child some peace.

So knowing Zuko still has a life ahead of him, Sonzehn makes a choice.

---

Despite the fact he had spent his entire life within the walls of the royal palace, Zuko has never come close to the dungeons before this. He has always known to avoid these outer limits of the caldera, where, amongst the barren landscape, there hides an entrance deep into the bowels of the earth.

As a child, Zuko had pictured a terrifying place with rivers of lava lighting the walls in an eerie red glow, torturers grinning maniacally as they poked red-hot brands at the prisoners between the bars. There are no torturers and no lava to be seen, but the walls are made of a black, shiny volcanic rock, jagged and fierce, and the heat of the place creeps upwards the deeper they go.

Zuko’s cell is at the end of an enclosed hallway. This block has eight cells, and could feasibly house many other prisoners, but it’s entirely empty. They can’t even hear the shouts of the distant guards once the door to the hall has been shut.

After the bars have been slammed over Zuko’s face, Ozai seizes upon the opportunity to hurt him one last time. “It seems Wei wasn’t lying to me, after all. The doctor has confirmed that you are no longer pregnant.”

It is one more tragedy in an unstoppable series of them. Yet Zuko finds there’s still something of him left to hurt. The realization sits dead in the center of his chest, scraping him hollow.

His reveries are broken by a languid sigh. “If a little stress has that much effect on you, I can’t imagine what use you’d serve for me again. Even if we managed to find a noble capable of withstanding the sight of you, your delicate constitution would make it a waste. Ah, well.” And with that, Ozai turns and begins to walk away.

“Hey!” Zuko scrambles to his feet. “How much longer am I going to be here? You said I’d be exiled!”

Ozai tosses a disinterested glance over his shoulder. “Right. Well - I was thinking I might keep you here instead. Call me sentimental.” Said with an unkind smile.

Zuko’s wrists are still chained to restrict his firebending, so he reaches out to grab a single bar and shake it violently in both hands. “So you’re going to let me rot down here? Hey - come back!”

Ozai retreats without so much as a wave goodbye. Zuko feels a molten rage building up inside him, and with nothing left to lose, he shouts,

“Like you’ve ever been sentimental about me once in your life! You pressured me into getting married when I was only a kid. The only time I ever pleased you was when I was manipulating people in the court, because that’s all *you* know how to do, is manipulate people!”

Ozai doesn’t turn, and he doesn’t offer any cruel or enraged quips.
