He’s nearly to the end of the hall, so Zuko rattles the bar harder, talks faster. “You’re a shitty father, and you’re only the Fire Lord because you killed your own shitty father, and probably your wife, too! You’re an evil, sadistic psychopath, and I hate you! *I fucking hate you!* ”

Zuko’s throat-tearing scream is punctuated by a slammed door, and he is left entirely alone. With gritted teeth, he glares down the door, willing it to open again, to no effect. Eventually he gives up looking, giving the bar one last ferocious squeeze before he bends forward, head resting against it, to glare at the floor instead.

He’s finally rid of Zhao, in every sense. He’d once wished that he’d lose the pregnancy - that instead of betraying him, his body could, for once, do something he wanted it to. So what in the hell is this anguish he feels, rattling around the hollow inside him?

Even as his anger dissipates, his face aches with the aftermath of it. He can feel everywhere he clenched with rage, as if the outlines of it are permanently carved there. He should be relieved. He keeps telling himself to be relieved. The kid won’t have to grow up with Zhao as a dad, and it won’t have to grow up with Ozai, either. It won’t have to grow up at all.

As if weak from his anger, Zuko feels his fingers go slack where he grips the bars, soon breaking out into a tremble. He feels foolish. He thought that so long as he got revenge on *someone,* the aftermath would be worth it. He had suffered and he had suffered and he had thought he could suffer more, but now here he is, lamenting the loss not of a life, but a potential life. Aang’s face flashes in his mind, and he thinks to himself that it wasn’t enough to love and lose - he wants it all back.

Zuko scoffs aloud to himself. He has grown so attached to the dream life he envisioned with Aang that he actually *wants* this kid now. He has convinced himself this is a chance at a do-over for himself, too, that he can have the nest of blankets without the danger waiting outside. How delusional is that?

Staring at the many cracks in the stone floor, he thinks, *It’s not like I’d even be a good parent. It’s* *like Katara was saying. You need a good foundation.* And his is rotten from the inside out, comprised solely of the man who has doomed him to this fate.

---

Hours may pass, but time is made meaningless by the lack of windows and a persistent dim light from the sconces lining the hall. Zuko sits slumped in the corner of his cell, his back where the cell door meets the wall. He’s staring at the far corner, counting the many clusters of vesicles in the igneous rock, wishing there was at least a spider wasp or a cockroach to eliminate the monotony of this place.

The door is sound-proofed, so he doesn’t hear an approach. Suddenly, there’s a growl of iron on rock as it opens, and he jolts, turning around to see who has come.

The figures who approach him are clothed in black with wide hoods that do much to hide their faces. Zuko tenses as he stands, expecting executioners. But there’s something familiar in these strangers’ gaits, and when they get close enough to his cell, they throw back their hoods, and he can see why.

It’s Iroh and Azula. Zuko stares at them, blinking as if they are a trick of the light that will disappear at any moment.

“You’ve actually come to see me?” he asks. “You’re sure Father won’t be furious at you?”

Azula goes straight to the lock on Zuko’s cell. From the folds of her cloak, she produces an iron ring of keys.

“We’re not visiting,” she says. “We’re getting you out.”

“Did Father change his mind?”

He’s seen that sympathetic look in his uncle’s eyes so many times. When he was a teenager, and they were living in the Lesser Hall together, it used to get on his nerves, and make him snappish with Iroh. Now, though, Zuko sees the love behind it.

“No, Zuko,” says Iroh, voice heavy with condolence. “We’re here against Ozai’s wishes.”

Zuko could perhaps understand his uncle acting against his Fire Lord’s wishes. But Azula? The golden child? Zuko watches her test each key, as if waiting to see her purposefully fumble one, or do something else to suggest her heart isn’t really in it. But she’s going about her work dutifully.

“Why are you doing this for me?” Zuko asks. “Father will be furious, even if it is you, Azula.”

She looks up briefly from where she’s hunched over the lock, meeting his eyes. “I’m sorry that you’ve been so thoroughly fucked up that you can’t conceive why someone would want to save your life.”

Iroh openly cringes. “ *Azula* .”

“Sorry. I didn’t hear how it sounded until it was out of my mouth,” she says, eyes flitting back to the lock. “I suppose I should apologize to you, Zuko, for my part in that disbelief. I haven’t always treated you well. I suppose I’m the last person you thought would bother to come to your rescue.”

The door swings open. Zuko hesitates before stepping out, perhaps expecting her to slam the door in his face. He keeps a buffer of space between them, guarded as he is. With a questioning look, he opens his mouth to ask Iroh again what is going on, only for his uncle to raise a finger to his lips.

“We’ll talk more when we’re in the clear. We need to move quickly.”

After they’ve freed Zuko from his shackles, the three of them make their escape from the dungeons. They move swiftly through the dark halls, and as Zuko keeps a lookout for guards, he makes sure to flex this newfound sense for other firebenders’ chi - but if it weren’t for the voracious glow of Azula and Iroh’s inner flames, he’d think it was shut off to him. He isn’t sure what his sister and his uncle did to clear the dungeons out so thoroughly, and he doesn’t ask.

Once they reach the surface, Zuko discovers that it’s the dead of night. Even with the palace burning brightly in the distance, it’s gruesomely dark out here, and he can make out thousands of stars in the sky. He tilts his head up, briefly, before Azula snatches him by the sleeve, bidding him to move.

They’re forced to walk the many miles over the dark, barren expanse of the caldera. But once they reach the south, and manage to slip free without detection, there’s a carriage waiting for them on a nearby street. When the door closes behind them, and the vehicle takes off, Iroh heaves a dramatic sigh, and fans himself. “I’m too old to be making these sorts of journeys!”

Azula snorts. “Don’t say that. You know it’s long from over.”

“Right, right.” He looks at his nephew. “How’s your arm strength? Did those shackles give you a good workout?”

“...Why are you asking me that?”

They arrive at the harbor. It’s dark and quiet, not bustling like in the daytime, but still they have to stop their carriage a few streets away, and sneak down the dock to a two man vessel. It’s fitted with a sail that’s been folded down tight. There are also two sets of oars.

“This is where I leave you,” Azula says, throwing a packed bag into the boat. “This has some essentials, including a little money. It’s a mix of Earth Kingdom tender and pure silver. The merchants in most small towns will try to barter you down on the silver, but you shouldn’t let them. It’s worth a lot. Stand your ground.”

So they’re sending him to the Earth Kingdom. “You’re not coming with us?” Zuko asks.

Azula shakes her head. “I have some things to take care of first. But I’ll join you later. I promise.”

“Don’t worry, Zuko,” says Iroh. “I’ll be coming along. We’ve had quite enough of leaving you alone.”

He smiles as he says it, but that dies down as Zuko fails to react, and Iroh seems to reflect on what he’s said. Zuko looks at the both of them, still as unsure as he was when they first appeared outside his cell. Perhaps the last few hours have all been the work of cruel spirits.

Before he can decide anything to say, Azula lurches forward - and to his endless surprise, he finds she has wrapped her arms around him in an embrace. Zuko stands there dumbly, not really returning the gesture and not really pushing her off.

He has awkwardly bent an arm, reaching up to pat her, when she removes herself, straightening up like she didn’t just do the most bewildering thing in the world.

“I mean it, Zuzu,” she says. “I’ll come back for you.”

He nods. “You’d better.”

Zuko and Iroh gingerly step down into the boat, which bobs under their weight. It’s the first time they’ve gone sailing together since Zuko was a little kid and the whole family would summer in the Ember Island home. Azula doesn’t dash away once she has helped push their boat off from the dock, standing and watching them row until they’ve gotten a safe distance away. Only then does she turn and leave.

They row for a long time. Iroh apologizes for the inconvenience, explaining that it won’t be safe for them to open the sail until they’re free of the gates of Azulon, and thus out of eyeshot of much of the capital. Zuko just nods, pushing and pulling, the swish of the water around their boat a soothing monotony against the wild thrum in his chest.

The slosh of the water can cover up most sounds, but soon, Zuko notices a ragged breathing rising above it. Without looking up, he tells his uncle, “You can stop for a while, if you want. I’ve got it.”

“We’ll move faster if it’s the both of us,” Iroh replies, stubbornly. He tries to repress the sound of his panting, but he still breathes, open-mouthed, sucking wind into his lungs with the desperation of a drowning man.

Zuko sighs. “It’s fine. I’m used to doing things alone.”

“That’s the problem,” Iroh grunts, pushing onward, still. “You shouldn’t have to be.”

His hard labor doesn’t make Zuko feel reassured. He just feels awful, to see someone strain themselves like this for him. “Uncle… You’re going to be the first person Father suspects. What if you can never go back to the Fire Nation after this?”

“The body of my oldest son lies under Ba Sing Se,” Iroh replies, grunting as he pushes his oar against the flow of the water. “Once Azula joins us, all three of my children will be in the Earth Kingdom.”

Zuko goes mute trying to wrangle the vulnerable feeling that rises up inside him. He breathes loudly in and out of his nose, and soon, his breathing is in sync with Iroh’s.

Eventually, the sky turns a muddy color, orange paint seeping into black. They can’t see the sun from where they are, the enormous stone statue of a past Fire Lord standing and blocking their view. Zuko starts to row harder.

At one point, Iroh clears his throat. “Zuko - I wanted to apologize to you. It shouldn’t have taken as long as it did for us to rescue you.”

“It was only a few hours,” Zuko replies.

“You know well what I mean.”

Zuko focuses on the lapping waters and the burning in his arms as he rows. His eyes are on the packed bag that sits between them. He’s thinking about every time he pushed his uncle away, or lied to him about what was going on. “How much did you really know?” he asks.

There’s a pause as Iroh considers. “A lot was intuition. Even if you had stories ready, some things didn’t sit well with me. But I never had proof. At least, not until the Lesser Hall burned down…”

Zuko expects his uncle to tell him that a servant saw him and Zhao fighting that night, or something related to the fire itself. But he doesn’t. Instead, Iroh tells his nephew about the aftermath, when he was salvaging the burnt remains of the Lesser Hall, and stumbled upon a letter and a metal box.

“Camelephant oil is a powerful hormone. If administered over a long period, it can change the presentation of an omega, stopping heats, changing their scent. But in acute doses, it can *lead* to a heat. It seems Zhao wanted to force you to present as an omega, in order to verify that you really were what your father claimed. He even bribed a palace servant to confirm it for him if you ever did present.”

“And I did present,” Zuko murmurs. “The day my mother disappeared, I…” He remembers how Zhao had appeared at the palace that day, the gift he’d given him. The comfort he gave.

Zuko stops rowing. Clutching the oars with a white knuckle grip, he says, “He… never cared about me. Even from the very beginning. He was always just using me.”

“I’m sorry, Zuko.”

Tears well in his eyes. He feels foolish, for crying over a man who burned his face. A man who’d knocked him unconscious, a man who’d battered him in a litany of ways. A man who’d comforted him when his mother disappeared, who’d marveled over his research, who’d been the first to tell Zuko he deserved more than what his father gave him. Zhao had been an awful person, and he had loved Zuko at one point in time, at moments in time, but then, maybe he hadn’t. Maybe those small affections, those jewels scattered in the sand, had been an illusion all along. And the fact that Iroh *knew,* but didn’t say anything *…*

Sadness isn’t the only feeling that rushes through Zuko. “Why didn’t you tell me sooner, Uncle?”

Iroh stops rowing, too, leaning over his oars to say, “Zuko, I’m so sorry. I wanted to come to you. Please, believe me when I say I did. But your sister wrote to tell me she’d nearly been killed. It was a dire situation, and only I knew where she was. I had to go to her.”

“You could have written to me!” Zuko shouts.

“We suspected Zhao’s involvement, and didn’t want to give your sister’s location away to him.”

“But after she was safe! You could have come after she was safe…”

Iroh hangs his head in shame. “...She was convinced she had to fight for your father’s good graces; we followed a lead and went to the North Pole to follow the Avatar. We found him, but we failed to capture him, and were imprisoned. We had no way of reaching you.”

So Iroh had held onto that knowledge for months. He had left Zuko in Kirachu, with a man who had tried to kill him, for *months.*

“Zhao may have abused me, but he was right about you,” Zuko says, voice cracking. “You *did* choose Azula over me.”

Iroh looks at him mournfully. “I’m sorry, Zuko. I had to spend a long time convincing Azula she was wrong about your father, about everything. That she needed to stop trying so hard to please him. It took so long to turn things around, but we finally changed objectives. That’s why we came back to the Fire Nation - we have been working to create a better life for all three of us. For the world, too.”

He isn’t denying anything, though. Zuko feels hot tears run down his cheeks. “You know he did this to me, don’t you?” And he doesn’t even have to name it, to gesture to it - Iroh knows he’s talking about the massive burn scar on his face.

When Iroh nods, Zuko lets out a wet, humorless laugh - “Exactly like you thought the black eye was him, too? If you hadn’t waited so long…”

Iroh is shaking his head. “I’m sorry, Zuko.”

“I don’t fucking forgive you!” Zuko screams back. He barely recognizes his own voice, can barely stand the way Iroh fails to meet him with any anger of his own, just looking at Zuko like that, with so much pity, with so much sorrow.

“I’m not asking your forgiveness,” Iroh says. He’s sliding his oars back into the water, arms pumping as he once again sets their vessel moving. “I’m paying my penance.”

Zuko watches him work, his own arms still, his innards boiling with anger and hatred. Most of it isn’t for Iroh - not really. But he has pent up so much towards Zhao, towards his father, and it has to go somewhere.

“You know what I think?” Zuko asks, starting out in a whisper. “I think you went with Azula because it was easier. You can relate to her more. After all, she’s the heir, you were the heir. She’s an alpha, you’re an alpha.” His voice is gathering some weight now, and some volume to go with it. “You avoided me because you don’t have any idea of what I went through. From the moment I was identified, it was like a switch was flipped. I was the same person, but suddenly everyone was treating me differently. Everyone has always been telling me what to do, but the pressure got even worse after I became an omega. Every step had to be perfect, not a single word could be misspoken, and it was easier sometimes to just shut up and do as little as possible to avoid everyone’s hatred. I’ve been taught to just - to just go along, and do whatever is wanted of me. And if I’d had even the littlest bit more leeway, if anyone at all gave a shit about what I wanted, I wouldn’t have been married to that psychopath, and I would’ve been able to leave Father all on my own.”

“I know, Zuko,” Iroh says, voice full of sorrow, and this display of sympathy only ignites Zuko’s furies further.

“ *No!* ” Zuko shouts. “You *don’t* know! You don’t know, you can’t even *imagine* what I went through, because you’re not an omega!”

They let it stew for a moment, Zuko glaring at his uncle as he gathers his words. He doesn’t look angry with Zuko, because why would he? He isn’t Ozai. He has always had patience for other people’s hurt.

“I’m sorry I didn’t do my part to alleviate your suffering,” Iroh says. “And you’re right - I don’t know what it’s like to be restricted so. I suspect you may even be right to say that misunderstanding influenced what I did, although I promise you, I did not consciously *choose* to play favorites. But you’re right; I don’t understand what it’s like to live as an omega, and I suppose that has always been my problem with the way your father chose to raise you.”

Iroh’s expression is complicated. “He was… so eager to restrict you to that role, even before you really presented. I’ve always suspected that it might be the fault of our own strained relationship. So I’m sorry for that, too, Zuko. I’m sorry your father used you as an outlet for his revenge.”

Zuko can feel his anger soften. His shoulders lower from their stiff, defensive posture. “What are you talking about, Uncle?”

Iroh hesitates. He pushes the oars another round, then seems to think the better of it, sliding them across his lap. The flat ends drip, drip, drip into the water while he speaks.

“My mother and father had issues conceiving. As I understand it, she’d had several miscarriages over the course of their marriage. When I was born healthy, they were both overjoyed, and I remember a happy childhood, filled to the brim with love and attention. They showered all of their affections on me. I never doubted their devotion for a second.

“When I turned fourteen, we were visiting the island of Ma’Inka. My father was there for business, but my mother and I were at leisure. We were sitting on the beach, watching the birds fly in, when I suddenly had the most peculiar feeling. I thought it was a fever; my entire body felt… molten. And I could barely breathe.”

Iroh laughs softly. “I’m sure I don’t have to tell you what a heat feels like. Once it subsided, my parents sprang into action. We had all been counting on my being the heir. My father and I used to stay up late into the night, talking about war strategies. I loved my firebending classes, and was at the top of them. I *begged* them to find a solution for me. To find a way that I could keep living my life exactly as it’d been planned.

“And they did. From then on, I started to take suppressants. I used various mixtures to hide my scent, and - in fact, I used camelephant oil, to achieve many of these effects. I had a few intense heats early on, and my parents did everything in their power to conceal them. But about a year in, the heats stopped altogether.

“My father… was willing to break his own laws to make me happy. I know he scoured the city for those answers. All I had to do was beg him, and he loved me enough to make it happen.” Zuko can see his uncle’s jaw working beneath the thick beard, trying to hold his emotions back. “Your father’s eventual birth and presentation changed nothing. My father felt I had a right to the throne. For years we kept things from Ozai, but I know he eventually found out, and he was furious. He thought I was taking his rightful place from him.”

Something in the depth of Zuko’s memory clicks. “So he usurped you,” he whispers. “He made all of that up about Grandfather’s last wishes.”

“Perhaps,” Iroh says. “But I think my priorities changed when Lu Ten died. I didn’t want to be Fire Lord anymore. I still don’t.”

Zuko hesitates. “And what about Lu Ten?”

Iroh chuckles. “Another thorn in Ozai’s side… you remember that I was not my wife’s first husband?”

Zuko vaguely remembers his mother telling him that his aunt was a widow when she met Iroh. “So Lu Ten wasn’t…?”

“Lu Ten is my son,” Iroh says, firmly. “But he is not my blood, no. Ozai was always furious at the possibility of ‘diluted blood’ on the throne, but our father didn’t care. Again; he loved me. I could have asked him for the moon, and he would have found a way to get it for me.”

With his anger dissipated, all that’s left is shame. Zuko turns away from his uncle, and says, in a quavering voice, “I’m sorry, Uncle. I didn’t…” He isn’t certain what he’s apologizing for. He’s sorry he lost his temper. He’s sorry he made assumptions. He’s sorry his uncle’s greatest secret had to be laid bare at his feet before he could calm down. “I-I didn’t mean to pressure you into telling me something so private.”

“It’s all right, Zuko,” Iroh says, his voice brimming with warmth. “I wanted to tell you. You’re family. We should talk to each other more about these kinds of things.”

What a thought; a family that can reveal secrets without the fear of them being used as weapons later. As Zuko stares into the horizon, where the first strips of orange light are starting to glow, he thinks that he finally understands what he’s been missing all this time.

“I told Father how I got this scar. And he didn’t care.” The strips of warm light on the horizon start to bleed into one another even more. “Not that he ever cared about me. But I thought, this time… For something like this…”

“Zuko.” And a warm hand lands on his shoulder. “Your father is a terrible man.”

A surprised laugh bubbles its way out of Zuko’s chest, past the tears. His uncle looks at him seriously. “I mean it. He is a fool for not loving you unconditionally, and I’m sorry for all the heartbreak he has caused you. Although you have lost much, you can rest now, assured that your life will be better without him in it.” All Zuko can do in response is nod, feeling tears slip from his cheeks onto the tattered robes he wears.

Once they’re free of the harbor, they finally put their oars aside, and set about the task of righting the sail. It takes both of them working together to unfold it and set it right, but once they have a good wind going, they are off, heading in the direction of the rising sun.

“It should be calm waters from here on out,” Iroh says, confident.

They stand side-by-side and admire the sail. Maybe it’s their sore limbs and sheer exhaustion from the escape, but the relief that washes over Zuko is indescribable. He turns to look at his uncle, at the lines of orange and yellow light that trace his features, and feels such comfort in the familiarity of those deep lines, the tranquil smile.

Before he can stop himself, Zuko surges out, snatching his uncle into his arms. Iroh wobbles, then laughs once he catches his footing, wrapping his arms around him in turn.

“Thank you, Uncle,” Zuko whispers.

“Of course,” Iroh whispers back, his beard damp with tears.

### End Notes

#### Chapter End Notes

In light of PPK soon drawing to a close, I wanted to talk about some of the stuff I ended up cutting from the fic! This’ll be long, so feel free to skip over it if it doesn’t interest you :)

1&#46; For a while I wanted to include a subplot where Zuko is the Blue Spirit, a la Dracze’s fic “Li.” In fact, the dao swords Mai gives as a wedding gift were included just in case I decided to go in that direction! but ultimately I decided this subplot would be too much in an already busy fic, and I cut it, later using the daos decorating the wall as a symbol of Zuko’s wasted potential, as he is treated by Zhao and Ozai both as largely ornamental.  
2&#46; In chapter 19, Zhao forces himself on Zuko after their argument about Ty Lee. I woke up in the middle of the night and wrote that scene all in one go, and the version you see does not differ significantly from that original draft - but there’s actually an alternate version of that chapter opening! I thought the story was escalating too quickly; per my original plot outlines, I wanted Zuko &#38; Zhao to have an argument where they were on more equal footing, that they then resolved (unhealthily) with rough, D/S sex - blurring the lines before their relationship escalated into more overt violence. But no matter how hard I tried to rewrite it, I liked the original better, so it stayed in the fic.  
3&#46; There’s a lot of flexibility in omegaverse fics re: who can get who pregnant. I spent a lot of time wondering if I wanted female alphas to be able to get pregnant, and if I wanted male omegas to be able to impregnate. There was an early plot involving Azula getting pregnant unexpectedly, and another where Aang impregnated Zuko… but that seemed like too easy of a way out of Aang and Zuko’s personal conflicts. Aang wouldn’t feel so much ambivalence about childbirth, and Zuko could just have Aang’s child rather than Zhao’s. I don’t really like easy resolutions, so I went for the more challenging option.  
4&#46; …The source of Azula’s unexpected pregnancy was going to be… upsetting. I thought about addressing incestuous abuse in this story, as many writers in this fandom have successfully re: Ozai. Ultimately I didn’t think I could do the subject matter justice, and I was worried, as with many plotlines I cut, that it would simply be Too Much. Maybe I’ll try to address those themes elsewhere some day.  
5&#46; When writing the chapter about Zhao’s family, I was originally going to have more from Ama’s POV. I actually have a few incomplete snippets where he meets his husband. But given that the fic is already from the POV of a male omega and Ama gets a lot of screen time, I wanted to give Wei a chance for some development, and pivoted. My only regret is that by cutting those scenes, I lost some ominous callbacks for Zhao’s treatment of Zuko vs. how his father treated Ama.  
6&#46; There was going to be a subplot where Iroh &#38; Azula visited Zuko in Kirachu and stayed at the estate a while. This was the most difficult darling to kill, because I pictured those scenes so many times, but they clashed with my planned ending so badly that I was forced to cut a lot of it. At least the most important stuff was salvaged elsewhere in the story.  
7&#46; I was going to cut the chi bending stuff a few chapters in! But a lot of you noticed it, so I kept it. I hope the result isn’t too messy; I’m mostly just trying to build a metaphor for relationships &#38; the boundaries that are either respected or disrespected (e.g., with Wei &#38; Ozai, there is a clear power imbalance, which is not solely due to Ozai’s station, but with the boundaries they fail to create/respect). The chi bending is highly influenced by Nele’s fics, but I’d also just read the Mistborn series, and the concepts of “Soothers,” who essentially bend and calm the emotions of those around them, also intrigued me.  
8&#46; I had this concept where I wanted Ama to be a firebender who couldn’t actually produce fire. He could only put them out. And it’d be this whole thing where Ama’s always swallowing his feelings / Zhao never learned self control because Ama was always cleaning up after him. Again, things got too busy. But it was a fun metaphor. 9. Kahno, the water tribe omega from Zhao’s past, has SUCH an elaborate backstory. I will probably never write it, but I have an entire outline sitting around. Hakoda plays a major role.  
10&#46; Not a cut scene, but I just want to say my biggest regret with this fic is not any of the torture I put the characters through or failing to get my plot organized sooner… it’s how I handled Zhao’s name! Truthfully, my least favorite fandom thing is when characters don’t have full names, so fans just Give them names, rather than writing around it. Not only did I perform one of my pet peeves, but in treating Zhao as his given name, I foolishly missed the fact Zhao is a surname….

## Chapter 44

### Notes

#### Chapter Summary

Zuko and Iroh arrive in the Earth Kingdom as refugees.

#### Chapter Notes

the theme of this chapter - and perhaps the song that finally convinced me to sit down and write this fic - is a little acoustic ditty from the 70s called "Haenim" by Kim Jung Me

&#40;...altho the verrry last scene is more of a "bike dream" by rostam vibe)

### Text

The morning they first arrived in Earth Kingdom waters, the water glittered like thousands of diamonds under the sharp rays of the morning sun. As they drew closer to shore, Zuko pored over verdant countryside and rolling green hills beyond, thinking to himself that at this distance, it didn’t look all that different from home.

Iroh began to rummage around in their bag. “Ah, I almost forgot. I wanted to do this before we arrived.”

Zuko shaded his eyes from the reflection of the sun in the knife’s blade. “What are you going to do with that?”

Iroh didn’t answer. He reached behind his head, one hand gripping his topknot, the other the knife. The blade dug into the thick gray bundle of hair, and there was a ripping sound.

When Iroh lowered his hands, he set his topknot, tie and all, down into the water, where it was quickly washed away by the ebb and flow of the tides. Zuko drew close, placing a gentle hand on his uncle’s shoulder to bid him turn, so he could get a better look. There were uneven spurts of hair bursting from the cap of his uncle’s skull.

“Here - you’ve got some stragglers. I can get rid of them.”

When he was finished, Zuko clasped the knife in his hand still, considering. “You don’t have to,” his uncle soothed. “You could just untie it, if you prefer.”

Since he had been designated an omega, Zuko had been wearing his hair at waist length. Even with the left side of his hair burned somewhat away, he had held onto the rest of it - not out of his own need to preserve a feature he loved, but out of habit. Obligation.

Although he had neglected it as of late, Zuko could picture hundreds of mornings spent combing and oiling his hair, all blurred together in their unremarkable way. For longer than Iroh had besieged Ba Sing Se, Zuko had spent his mornings in front of a mirror, weary, an hour or so of sleep lost for the sake of looking how others expected him. And what had he gotten out of it?

Zuko grabbed his hair around the base of his skull, and began to saw it away with the edge of the knife. When he had nipped every long, errant strand away and set it loose on the water, he looked up to find his uncle watching him. The look on his face was hard to read, and Zuko wondered if he was disappointed. He reached out to touch the ends of Zuko’s hair.

“It suits you,” Iroh said. He presented Zuko with his open palm. “I can’t promise how well I’ll do, but I can try to help even this up.”

It was, admittedly, not their best work. But no matter how choppy the result, when Zuko leaned over the side of the boat and saw his reflection, as wobbly as it was in the shifting waters, he was the most satisfied with the sight of himself he’d been since his burn.

“You did it perfectly,” Zuko said.

---

In the hours before they arrived on shore, Zuko had imagined what their journey in the Earth Kingdom could be like. In his mind’s eye, he and his uncle were always a pair of dots amongst an enormous expanse of green and brown. He pictured them trekking across vast, empty farmland, so ravaged by the onslaught of war that there was not a single laborer or crop to be found. He pictured them in a dark jungle during the rain, huddled under some makeshift shelter, shivering as a thumb-sized fire threatened to die in the onslaught of a frigid wind. He pictured the landscape itself repelling them with mudslides and monsoons, imagined that if they didn’t travel in the darkest, most isolated hours, that strangers would see their yellow eyes, and send them running.

And it wasn’t as though Zuko’s predictions had been entirely wrong. Those first few days had been difficult. After several failed attempts to catch a rabbit badger, Zuko had caught onto the fact that they could instead eat whatever plants they observed their prey eating, trusting that those plants weren’t toxic; but the handful of greens wasn’t exactly filling. While the first night they slept like the dead in the underbrush just off the sole road in the region, they had spent the nights following wide awake, worried about wild animals and bandits. And when they did first see a man with an ox cart on the road, and Iroh had tried to ask for directions, the man had muttered something under his breath about “mixed bloods,” snapped his reins, and driven away.

Then they happened upon the refugee encampment. They were drawn in by the fire light and the smell of food cooking, but hovered around the outermost edges, nervous to engage until a woman spotted them. She waved them brusquely over, and Zuko and Iroh ate their meager share of the meat in a frenzied, desperate way, leaving not even a scrap of skin or tendon on the bone.

Zuko had been convinced this was a fluke, and that when the sun came up and the others saw them for what they really were, they’d be left behind. But when it came time to depart, the same woman who invited them nudged them each awake and helped them pack up their things. When the dark hours of the morning finally gave way to sunshine, Zuko finally had a chance to get a good look at the others, and he realized he saw a whole litany of eye colors. It was mostly a sea of green and brown, but there were some golden eyes, and even one pair of blue.

He also saw many people with burn scars. There was a man with a mark running up his collarbone and over his chin. Another had a hand covered with angry whorls of damaged skin. When he looked down, Zuko realized the woman who’d invited them to join had a severe scar of her own running up the back of her calf.

The longer Zuko looked, the greater the rush of blood in his veins. He was anxious at the thought of being discovered as a firebender. He was angry that these people had had to suffer so thoroughly. And he was sorry. He was filled with such a bottomless sorrow that he didn’t know what else to do with it.

So Zuko worked himself to death trying to help the others in the camp. He was the first to wake and the last to go to sleep. Any task that needed doing, he jumped to volunteer.

Unfortunately, he was bad at everything they put in front of him. He had not led an easy life, but he had never had to take care of himself. He could barely pack a bedroll. If he tried to clean one of the cooking pots, he always left streaks of mess, or he overused what little water they had left for washing.

A few days in, a man in the group confronted him. Zuko couldn’t scent him, but the man was at an age where it might not matter what he even was anymore. There was a prickly layer of uneven hair over his chin, like he’d been shaving without a mirror.

“This stew is inedible,” snapped the man. He thrust his dish out, the contents sloshing over the edge and onto Zuko’s shoes.

Zuko felt his face heat up in anger. “Sorry to offend your delicate taste buds. I’m sure it’s better than nothing.”

“The hell it is. This rice isn’t cooked, and the bottom’s burned black.” The man dumped the contents onto the ground, a few flecks hitting them both.

“Hey!” Zuko cried out.

The man thrust his face close to Zuko’s “What you made was inedible. We worked our asses off to get these ingredients, and now all that’s been wasted.”

That reminder cooled some of Zuko’s irritation down to a smoldering guilt. Even if this man was being aggressive about it, he wasn’t wrong. Food was scarce even in the nearby villages. Their group survived entirely off whatever they could scrounge from the surrounding land.

“Well - fine,” Zuko said, crossing his arms over his chest. “I won’t volunteer to cook again.”

“It’s not just your shit cooking.” The man spread his arms. “ *Everything* you do around here, you fuck up! All the tents you put up collapse in *minutes* of people getting inside, and yesterday the bottom of Yuujin’s bag broke open because you over-packed it! Half the pots and pans are dented, now!”

Zuko was burning with anger and shame. “I’m sorry. If I’m really such a burden, then I won’t bother you all anymore! My uncle and I will leave first thing in the morning.”

He made what was likely the angriest, swiftest bow in the history of bows, prepared to storm off immediately afterward. When Zuko straightened up again, though, he was surprised to see all of the fury had drained from the man’s face.

“Kid…” The man scratched a smattering of coarse hair on his neck. “Look. I’m sorry for getting short with you. You don’t have to get out of here - I just want you to slow down and ask questions more. It’s good you want to help, but you’ve got to learn to help *right* .”

Zuko scowled at where his stew was quickly congealing in the dirt. “But I’ve fucked up so much at this point. Are you sure that…”

The man waved his words away. “What matters is that you’re willing to do the work.” He clapped Zuko on the shoulder. “You’re not always going to figure out the right thing to do all by yourself. You’ve got to listen and learn.”

After that encounter, Zuko did try to slow down. He managed to get his and his uncle’s bedrolls packed perfectly after asking the woman in the tent next to theirs how she did it. And at the next meal, he didn’t volunteer to cook, but he watched the person who did, asking them hesitant questions when he didn’t understand why they’d done something. They didn’t tell Zuko to get lost, answering every question with the utmost patience. But then, they had a little kid of about five hovering around them, so maybe they were used to lots of questions. Zuko had watched their gentle parent-and-child interactions with a certain wistfulness.

Zuko’s newfound patience was put to the test the next day. It had rained overnight, and for once he wasn’t the only person in the camp incapable of finding good kindling. After doggedly combing the woods, the lot of them only managed to get a small pile of somewhat dry logs piled together. But when they sat down to try to make a fire, the kindling wouldn’t catch - no matter who tried.

Zuko sat by the fireside, growing increasingly frustrated as he smashed the flint against the steel, the resulting sparks dying away each time. The others stood in a circle around the campfire pit, frowning. Zuko knew they were disappointed with the state of things more than they were with him, but he still felt like a failure.

One of the camp members sighed, hands on his hips. It was the same scraggly-bearded man who had told him off the day before. “We’ve been trying for ages, Lee. Give it up. Let’s get back out there and find more wood.”

Zuko let out a frustrated noise. “What we have is *fine* . If we could just get a big enough flame started…”

But they were all too defeated to wait. A litany of sighs sounded as the group turned their backs on him, heading once again towards the trees. Zuko burned with shame; they had already spent hours in the damp cold gathering wood. They all deserved the chance to rest in the warmth of the campfire.

He looked around. No one else around the camp was watching him, engrossed in whatever chores they had taken on. Only his uncle caught his eye, waving from across the camp. After a few last, paranoid looks, Zuko leaned in close to the wood, and held out one hand.

He bended a flame about the size of his palm, and with some coaxing, it managed to stay alive, gnawing away at the wood. Zuko smiled joyfully, and looked up, ready to shout for everyone to come back and see.

The man with the scraggly beard was standing there, staring at him. He must have turned back again to make sure Zuko was following.

All at once, Zuko felt his stomach drop. Had he been caught firebending? The man didn’t say anything, but he looked at the fire, and at Zuko, and at the fire again. He crouched down on the opposite side of the fire.

Then he chuckled. “I never thought I’d say this, but that’s a pretty handy power. You may’ve just saved us from freezing our asses off tonight.” Then, before Zuko could say anything, the man turned around and shouted, with a hand cupped up to his mouth: “Hey guys! You can relax and sit down! Lee got the fire going!”

The others were pleased. People came from all over the camp to huddle around the fire. Zuko received a few grateful claps on the shoulder. Iroh was there, too, and while he was happy to see his nephew shining under so much praise, Zuko caught him looking at the scraggly-bearded man with a troubled expression.

When they were ready to settle down for the night, Zuko and his uncle headed into the privacy of their shared tent. It was then that Iroh seized the chance to talk to him alone.

“That was quite a feat with the campfire today, Zuko. How did you finally get it to light?”

His tone was conversational, but he was clearly fishing for something. Zuko became nervous. They had to work hard to hide their identities, or they might lose their place in the camp. At worst, they would be turned over to the authorities - but at best, they might be left behind by the group. Both possibilities frightened Zuko to his core, so he could guess how angry his uncle might be to learn he’d threatened that tentative peace.

So he said in a nonchalant voice, “I just struck the flint really hard.”

“Really?” said Iroh. “I saw quite a few people try that, and it didn’t seem to be working.”

Zuko shrugged, giving nothing away. “I don’t know. I think the wood might’ve dried out a bit more, sitting around in the wind all that time.”

Iroh’s smile disappeared. Unsure how to read his expression, Zuko was frightened that he’d upset his uncle, and dreaded what would come next.

“Nephew, I saw you bending the fire,” Iroh confessed.

Zuko fumbled. “That’s impossible - I didn’t…”

“It looked like Ahn-ro might have seen you, too.”

“No he didn’t, because I wasn’t bending,” Zuko snapped, defensively. “Would you get off my back?”

The air in the tent seemed to sour. Zuko could barely bring himself to look at his uncle's face, he was so ashamed of himself for losing his temper. But he couldn’t risk being caught. If he got caught, his uncle might get angry. And if his uncle got angry…

“You don’t have to lie to me, Zuko.”

It would have been easy to say those words with contempt or impatience. But Iroh did neither. He said them plaintively. He said them gently. When Zuko finally braved a look into his eyes, they weren’t bitter at all. They were wounded.

When Zuko wouldn't respond, Iroh said it again. “You don’t have to lie to protect yourself, Zuko. I know you didn’t mean for that man to see you. But for our safety, you must communicate with me, or I cannot protect you.”

Finally, Zuko relented. “...He did see me. But he was really nice about it. I don’t think he means us harm.” Zuko scrubbed at his eyes for an excuse to look away. “Please don’t be mad at me, Uncle.”

“I will never be angry at you for making a mistake,” Iroh said, drawing close. “You don’t have to dread punishment from me. I’m a pushover - ask Azula.” Zuko allowed himself the smallest of laughs. Iroh responded with an encouraging smile, and added, “This is what I mean, when I say we should work on communicating more. I want us to be a proper family. I want us to talk without fear of retaliation.”

Now Zuko had a real reason to scrub at his eyes. “As if *Azula* won’t get angry at me.”

Iroh laughed softly, and put his arms around his nephew. “You’re right. I can’t promise *she’ll* never be angry with you. But I can promise neither of us are here to hurt you, Zuko. I want you to be able to be honest with us without being afraid.”

A lifetime of experience had told him that what Iroh was describing could never work. Yet thousands of miles from the Fire Nation capital, wrapped in the safety of his uncle’s embrace, Zuko was starting to believe they could make it work.

---

No matter what he does, the structure won’t stay upright. Zuko glares at the salvaged wood as if his frustration alone can assemble it, but alas. He eventually drops the large branch he’s holding to the ground, and it crinkles the tarp spread out on the ground as it rolls to a stop. With a sigh, Zuko leans up against the nearest tree.

These last few days, it feels like everything Zuko does takes gargantuan effort. He gets winded just packing up their things. Granted, he *has* been traveling for hours every day, often on foot. He should forgive his humanity, as Iroh has been saying.

At least his uncle isn’t here - Zuko loves Iroh, but he makes every chore at least ten times harder to complete, over-helping in a way that gets nothing done. Zuko glances across the bustle of the camp, past where the others are setting up their tents, and sees his uncle still hasn’t returned from foraging. Hopefully this time he won’t stuff anything in his mouth before showing it to the others here. He nearly poisoned himself last week mistaking white jade for white dragon. Thankfully there’s an herbalist traveling with the group, or Iroh might have died. (And Zuko reflects flippantly on it all now, but for an ugly moment, he’d had to reflect on a world where he had lost everything, *including* Iroh. It was the most distraught he’d been since arriving in the Earth Kingdom.)

While keeping an eye out for his uncle, Zuko tries to surreptitiously spy on the others as they erect their shelters, to see if he’s even close to correct. But he might as well be trying to read a foreign language. He rubs his temples, agitated.

“Do you need help, kid?”

Jolting in surprise, Zuko turns to see a little old woman looking at him expectantly. She has long silver hair tied up in an artfully messy bun atop her head. She’s the refugee camp’s resident herbalist, the one who saved Iroh. As grateful as Zuko is to her, he doesn’t remember her name.

Zuko grimaces. He doesn’t want to be a burden on a frail old woman, of all people. “No, you don’t have to worry about me. I’ll figure it out.”

“Will you?” She points a bony finger at the sad lump of branches and tarp. “For one, it’s never a great idea to build this close to the trees. It can be dangerous in high winds - the falling branches might flatten your tent.”

Zuko looks at his failure of a tent, then up into the canopy of trees. They all seem so ancient here in the Earth Kingdom, as tall as they are. He supposes it could be bad if something fell on him from that high. “I didn’t realize…”

The herbalist crouches down to heave one of the heavier branches up. It’s as tall as Zuko, and he’s got a head at least on this old woman. He dashes to her side. “I’ve got it!”

She gives a light-hearted chuckle. “You can grab that end there, but I’m not letting this baby go for anything.”

They manage to get the branch upright, and hold it standing between them. The herbalist pauses before they continue, flashing him a sympathetic look. “Y’know, there’s no harm in asking for help.”

“I know, but - I don’t want to bother anyone. And I don’t want to seem…” Like someone raised in a palace, with no survival knowledge. “...Stupid.”

“Yeah, but it’ll be worse if this structure collapses in the middle of the night,” the herbalist says. “Better to ask questions and look a little dumb than to get hurt, right?”

Working together, they manage to get the tent situated, so Zuko and his uncle will have a shelter for the next few days while all the refugees wait out the oncoming bad weather. When they’re finished, Zuko stands up and surveys their work with a smile. It’s no palatial estate, but he helped make it. He feels proud.

The herbalist brushes the dirt off her hands onto her skirt. “Nice work, kid. What’s your name again?”

Zuko bows and gives his pseudonym. “Lee.”

“Eun-sook,” the herbalist supplies, giving more of a low nod than a proper bow in return. “You should ask for help more often, Lee. You really shouldn’t be doing any labor alone in your condition.”

*Neither should you,* Zuko thinks. “This is an old injury. I can’t see so well out of this eye, but I figure I can still work…”

“That’s not what I mean.” Eun-sook fixes him with a curious look. “Do you really not know?”

Zuko shakes his head. Eun-sook takes a step back to analyze him, as if double-checking something. Then she reaches out towards him. “May I…?”

Out of shock alone, Zuko lets her place two warm palms against his stomach. “What are you…?”

“Don’t you feel that kicking?” she asks. “I’d put you at… four, five months?”

Zuko works his jaw for a moment before he can summon a single word. “But it… Someone said there was blood. And a doctor told me…”

“Bleeding can be bad,” Eun-sook admits. “But it’s not always the end.” She can tell he doesn’t quite believe her. She gives him a soft smile, and a hearty cheek-pinch that nearly cancels it out. “I’m not a hundred percent certain, but here’s the thing, Lee. You’re living in a refugee camp, and you’ve still managed to maintain quite a healthy weight. Why do you think that is?”

The exchange shakes Zuko to the core, and he feels like he’s outside his body for the rest of the afternoon, performing chores mechanically, without focus. On the one hand, he doesn’t want to get his hopes up. On the other… that feeling that pools in his chest, like warm honey. That feeling *is* hope, isn’t it?

It’s a relief when Iroh finally returns with the rest of the foraging group, his basket full of mushrooms, grinning from ear to ear. “Nephew, look! The frills on this one are simply exquisite.” He holds a dark brown mushroom with a wide cap aloft, but his nephew isn’t as eager to admire it. “Never mind that, Uncle! Something happened today.”

Zuko tells his uncle what the herbalist said to him, but Iroh doesn’t react right away. Instead he asks, “What do you think, nephew? Would it be a good thing, if she is right?”

Without even pausing to consider, Zuko nods. “Yes. After all that’s happened… I think I’d be relieved.”

Iroh breaks out into a gentle smile. “Then I hope she is right.”

The more Zuko thinks about it, the more he is assured of that hopeful feeling. It would be incredibly difficult in these circumstances. He doesn’t even have a home to offer this child yet. But at the very least he is free to give all his love without having to worry about protecting this child from their other parent.

“It’s just such a shock,” Zuko says. “I guess the doctor who examined me wasn’t very good at his job.”

Iroh strokes his beard thoughtfully. “Perhaps. Something has occurred to me, though, Nephew… Wasn’t your father’s original intent to take your child and then banish you, rather than keeping you locked up?”

“Yes - but I don’t see how that’s relevant.”

Iroh is inspecting the mushroom again, turning it over in his hand. Yet even as his wrist rotates around and around, Zuko gets the sense he isn’t really looking at it.

“This is all speculation, of course. But if Ozai thought there was any possibility you were still pregnant, he might follow you to the ends of the earth just to take it from you.” Iroh meets Zuko’s eyes. “In contrast. If he’s completely unaware that there *is* an heir out there, then you two could plausibly live out your lives in peace, apart from him.”

“What are you saying, Uncle?”

“I’m saying it’s possible that doctor was trying to ensure you wouldn’t be separated from your child.”

Stunned, Zuko can only stare at his uncle. “But why would the doctor lie like that for me? He doesn’t even know me!”

Iroh pats his nephew on the shoulder. “When it comes to the capacity for cruelty, mankind is boundless. But I promise you with that comes kindness in equal measure.”

Zuko doesn’t say anything to that. Sensing he needs a minute, Iroh gives one last squeeze of his shoulder, then joins some of the other refugees who are preparing food by the fire. When he has gone, Zuko’s eyes slide shut, and he flattens both of his hands over his stomach.

*Please,* he thinks. *Please,* ***please*** *stay with me.*

Strangely, he thinks of Ama. How absolutely sure he was that his first pregnancy would take. That his child would be born healthy, and lead a magnificent life. And while that prophecy may not have panned out for Ama, Zuko turns his face towards the warmth of the western wind sweeping through the camp, and feels that he knows.

---

The walls of Ba Sing Se are unlike anything Zuko has ever seen. He is used to cities, to palaces, to ramparts, but the sheer might of this fortress is unbelievable until you find yourself standing just below it, neck craning to see the sheer breadth of it. The enormous walls that surround the city are seemingly miles tall and completely smooth, making them impossible to scale.

When they were further back in line, Zuko could see the entire east side of Ba Sing Se’s wall from his vantage point on top of the hill. There may have been miniscule scratches one could see up close, but as a whole, the wall was unbroken except for one small, heavily guarded entrance in each cardinal direction. It’s hard to believe that just a few years before, Iroh had led an onslaught against this behemoth. There’s not a single mark to commemorate his efforts.

Zuko turns to his uncle, expecting wistfulness, and instead sees him gazing at the city with reverent eyes. “Who would have thought that all these years later, I’d finally get to cross these walls?” Iroh chuckles into his chest. “It just goes to show how much further you can get with fists lowered.”

Once they’ve all passed the checkpoint and made it inside the wall, Zuko and his uncle part ways with the other refugees. Zuko and Iroh are headed for a specific destination, while the rest of the group will be looking for the best place to settle down. Their goodbyes are stoic and mostly tearless, as they vow to see Lee and his uncle Mushi again soon.

“Knowing how these things go, all the refugees will probably be piled up in the slums,” Ahn-ro says, gruffly. “So if you ever want to find us, just head to the worst part of town.”

Eun-sook elbows him viciously in the side. “Don’t go muddying our nice goodbyes with your pessimism.” Then she turns to Iroh, handing him Zuko’s bedroll. “Here - can you carry them both?”

“You don’t need to-” Zuko starts, but his uncle and the herbalist both fix him with stubborn glares.

“I told you no heavy lifting,” Eun-sook says, wagging a finger in his face. “Not this far along!”

All the rest bid their goodbyes, their waving hands swallowed by the enormous city crowds. Beside him, Zuko hears his uncle give a loud, gooey sniff.

They head up a narrow, crowded street paved on an embankment. When they’ve crossed the peak, they can look down into the valley, where the residential district lies. They pause to survey it while Zuko catches his breath, one hand tucked under his growing stomach. He can feel kicking regularly now. He has finally gotten past the bizarreness of the sensation, instead feeling a curious rush of delight every time it happens. Surely it will get old, eventually. But for now, he feels just as hopeful looking at the beauty of the city before him as he does about the life growing inside of him.

“Uncle, where are we headed, again?” Zuko asks.

Iroh beams. “To see some old friends of mine.”

Zuko smiles wryly. “You still managed to make friends while *invading* this place?”

“No, no. These are friends I met afterwards.” Iroh had set his bag aside while they rested, and grunts now as he heaves it back onto his shoulders. “In any case, I believe they can offer us a place to stay for the night. Finally, we’re going to sleep under a sturdy roof - we may even get our own cots!” He grins, both hands squeezed into fists.

Zuko could laugh at how eager Iroh sounds. Once they were so accustomed to luxury, and now even the most meager accommodations are a privilege they can’t afford to waste. Surprisingly, Zuko isn’t nearly as bothered by sleeping on the ground as he thought he’d be. He used to spend so many nights wide awake in silken sheets, his mind spiraling with anxiety. Yet lately, in the midst of the wilderness, in outright *destitution* , he’s been sleeping like the dead. Maybe there’s something magic woven into his bedroll.

Iroh leads them, perhaps predictably, to a teahouse. Maybe it’s the pregnancy hormones, and maybe it’s the fact they were in line to get into the city for four hours this morning, but Zuko releases a ferocious huff. “ *Uncle* . Can we please keep the diversions to a minimum?”

“This isn’t a diversion,” Iroh insists, pushing the door open. “This is our destination!”

The teahouse is located downtown in a shabby building made from unpainted wood. Once inside, they walk past every table, heading straight for a door at the back of the room. There’s a man standing in front of it, and Iroh makes sure to catch his eye before spiriting an object out of his pocket. It’s hidden away again in the blink of an eye, but the man sees it, nods, and opens the door to allow Iroh and Zuko into the back room.

It hasn’t been easy for Zuko, but over the course of their shared journey, he has gradually let his uncle in on the unhappy secrets of his marriage. Zuko remembers one night in particular, hunched in the darkness of their shared tent, his tears darkening the dirt while he told his uncle how Zhao had kept him scared and isolated at the palace, how he’d preyed on Zuko’s insecurities to convince him Iroh couldn’t be trusted. He had unearthed an enormous portion of his soul, from the origin of his black eye, to the fight in the Lesser Hall, to the terrible isolation within the walls of the Kirachu estate. Zuko had even been honest with his uncle about the great anguish of Yan’s loss - because through it all, he had been one of Zuko’s only friends in Kirachu.

But there are still some things Zuko hasn’t been able to bear revealing to Iroh yet. For one, the violence of his marital bed. Never mind how uncomfortable it is to discuss sex with a family member, Zuko is still struggling to parse that part of his relationship himself. For another, his time with the Avatar and the White Lotus. Even with Iroh’s insistence that Azula has changed, their determined pursuit of the Avatar has Zuko leary to reveal what he knows.

The man guarding the back door isn’t the only person to see the object Iroh flashes from his pocket. In glimpsing the familiar emblem carved in stone, Zuko feels his shock transform his face. “Uncle - is that what I think it is?”

Iroh looks up at him with one eyebrow cocked in question, one hand still in his pocket. The door has been shut behind them, leaving them standing in a short, narrow hall by themselves.

Zuko holds out his hand. Iroh seems to hesitate, as if wondering whether he should deny having anything at all. But then he reaches out and drops the object into Zuko’s hand.

A White Lotus tile. Zuko’s breath hitches.

“You know more about the White Lotus than Zhao led all of us to believe,” Iroh says, rather than asks.

Zuko nods, lifting the tile so he can inspect it. The emblem doesn’t shimmer or disappear in the dim light. “I thought everyone was wiped out. I didn’t think the organization survived.”

Iroh’s eyes go soft as he beckons to his nephew, drawing him closer to the door at the end of the hall. “We may have suffered losses, Zuko. But so long as there are people out there who are willing to work towards the betterment of our world, hope will never be truly lost.”

He reaches out to twist the handle, and as the door opens, they’re met with a cacophony of voices from the room beyond. Stunned, Zuko steps inside. There are tables full of people with their heads bent towards one another, chattering away. A few glance their way, smiling simply because they are here, and must be welcome. There are so many of them, still, and seeing them, Zuko feels hope and relief flood his chest.

He has so much to ask his uncle, but he doesn’t know where to start. He stands, counting the many heads, trailing off somewhere around forty. Iroh comes up beside his nephew and lays a hand on his shoulder.

Zuko shakes his head. “You were with them all along. If only I’d known, I…”

Iroh squeezes his shoulder. “If I’d only been honest with you months ago, we could have saved you from a lot of heartbreak. We have much to catch up on - you’ll need to tell me about your work with the White Lotus in Kirachu, and I can tell you what your sister and I have been working on.”

Overcome, Zuko nods. He’s still looking around with disbelief, a part of him overjoyed to see these men, another part of him saddened by the lack of familiar faces. He finds himself searching for the unkempt beard, the tigermonkey emblem on the end of a cane. He even looks for Piandao’s close-cropped hair and silken clothes.

He doesn’t find them, of course. Those two will be lost to him forever. What he does see is a wide array of clothing and hairstyles, and the scent clinging in this closed space tells him there are people of all presentations here. The Earth Kingdom comes with its own aesthetics, and Zuko finds himself tracing the many boxy, emerald clothes with his gaze, wondering what the vibrant fashions of Ba Sing Se indicate about each person’s identity.

From a far table, there’s a cry of joy that sounds strangely familiar. Frowning, Zuko starts to walk towards the source of it. There’s a group of people huddled around a table, but between their bodies, he thinks he sees… a glimpse of blue.

When the crowd of excited White Lotus members parts, Zuko sees Sokka seated at a low table, utterly dominating a wizened-looking old man at a game of Pai Sho. After taking a moment to think, followed by a scratch of his lightly beard chin, Sokka slams down his final piece, and the onlookers go absolutely wild. The Water Tribe man sits back, preening while the others celebrate his victory, his wizened opponent scowling deeply enough to leave permanent marks in his face.

“Sokka?” Zuko calls out, without thinking, and when the other young man turns to look at him, there is an utterly dreadful moment where there is absolutely no recognition in his face. All at once, Zuko remembers how different his appearance is now, and feels his face flushing with shame.

Sokka breaks out into a huge smile that cannot seem to decide whether or not it wants to stay on his face. “Zuko!” he cries out, leaping to his feet. He starts to approach his old friend, arms out as if to embrace him, but then he looks down. Even through the boxy cut of his Earth Kingdom clothes, Sokka must see the bulge of Zuko’s stomach, because his eyes visibly widen.

There is no salvaging this moment. Sokka tries his damnedest, anyway. “What - what are you doing in the Earth Kingdom? Are you okay?” His eyes flicker downwards again.

Zuko crosses his arms over his stomach. “A lot has happened since we last saw each other,” he mutters, gaze cast on the floor.

Thankfully, he’s saved from having to elaborate when Iroh comes up beside him, momentarily distracting Sokka, who all but points at him in accusation. “Hey - it’s you! Azula’s cool uncle! Why are you here with Zuko?”

“Azula and Zuko are siblings, so that would make me his ‘cool’ uncle, too,” Iroh says, smiling patiently.

“Right. Duh. Of course I knew that…” Sokka trails off then, head pivoting as he looks around the room. Iroh seems to know the source of his anxiety.

“Azula is not here with us,” Iroh reassures him. Sokka is visibly relieved, and seems about to say so when Iroh clasps his hands together in apology and says, “Although she will join us, soon. I promise you she has changed and no longer wishes your friends any harm!”

Sokka seems to age a thousand years in an instant. He slumps forward witheringly as he says, “Great. Just great. Katara’s *really* going to love this one. It took her forever to warm up to Zuko, and he was nothing but nice from the beginning. Never mind that Aang will be thrilled, *she’s* going to be a nightmare…”

While he’s muttering to himself, pinching the bridge of his nose with one hand, Zuko takes the opportunity to turn to Iroh.

“*Cool* *uncle?*” he repeats, eyebrow cocked in disbelief.

“Hey!” Iroh raises his arms in mock-defense. “I helped them escape your sister’s wrath! That’s pretty cool, I think.”

Zuko shakes his head. “The fact I’m only just finding out you’re friends with the Avatar…”

“The same could be said of you,” Iroh counters, giving him a nudge. “You *do* know this young man is a friend of the Avatar, don’t you?”

Zuko nods. “I know.”

“Did you meet them when you helped them escape the palace?”

“I met them when they came to Kirachu.”

That visibly surprises Iroh. “The Avatar was in Kirachu?”

“Well, the Avatar’s gotta’ learn all four elements, and where better to learn fire than the fire-themed country?” Finally Sokka has stopped muttering to himself, and turns to them both now, his smile easier than before. “Zuko helped protect us while we were there. He kept our secret, even though his husband was looking for us. He taught Aang how to firebend. One time he even caused a distraction in the village when the guards were hunting for us, and later, when we were finally forced to leave Kirachu, he pretty much held off a whole *army* by himself…”

“It wasn’t that impressive,” Zuko mumbles, rubbing his arm. “You weren’t even there.”

“The way Yan made it sound, that’s how it went,” Sokka insists. “How is he, anyway?”

Zuko can’t bring himself to respond, gaze fixed on an errant crack in the floor. Iroh clears his throat. “Unfortunately, Yan did not make it out of the encounter alive. Zhao killed him.”

Sokka’s eyes all but bulge out of his skull. “His own *brother?* That’s positively evil!”

“Yes. But Zhao himself won’t be a problem anymore, either,” Zuko says stiffly, picking his gaze up from the floor.

He somewhat expects Sokka to cheer at that. Instead he cocks his head, looking at Zuko intensely. His gaze is complicated, like he wants to ask again if Zuko is alright.

Then a small smile tugs at the corner of Sokka’s mouth. “Hey; he won’t be back for a few hours, but you should stick around and talk to Aang.”

At that, Zuko’s grip on himself tightens. There is nothing he wants more in this world than the chance to see Aang again. But he is not the same person Aang fell in love with. That hair he so praised has all been shorn away. His face is permanently changed. And worst of all - he now can’t hide the pregnancy he lied about for all that time in Kirachu. If Aang sees him like this, pity alone may spur him into taking responsibility for Zuko, and Zuko simply couldn’t bear that.

In all his turmoil, Zuko fails to catch his uncle looking at him pensively. Iroh turns to Sokka.

“Suppose we wanted to find him right now - do you happen to know where he is?”

Zuko blushes angrily at his uncle. “It’s alright, Sokka - I don’t want to bother Aang when he’s busy,” Zuko insists, but Sokka waves him off.

“Nah, it’s no problem. You can find Aang in the lower ring. He’s had to spend a lot of time trying to recruit stuffy old nobles, lately, so he wanted to get back to helping some regular people. We don’t have to hide here, so if you ask around for the Avatar, you should be able to find him. I bet he’d be excited to see you!”

Zuko feels his face flush even darker. “Yeah, right. He probably won’t even recognize me.”

“You might not recognize *him!* ” Sokka counters. “He’s bald again!” And as if to demonstrate, he rubs his own decidedly not bald head.

But Zuko’s doubts cannot be so easily deterred. He touches the outer edge of his scar, feeling how warped the skin has become. He sees Sokka’s smile fade.

“Zuko, what happened after we escaped Kirachu? Is that…?”

Sokka trails off, but Zuko knows he’s asking about the burn. He doesn’t want to talk about it. He doesn’t want to talk about *any* of what happened. But Sokka deserves to know about his master. Zuko starts to open his mouth, to say the impossible words, but then there’s a gentle hand on his arm.

“Let me take care of catching Sokka up on what happened,” Iroh soothes. “You go see the Avatar.”

As always when someone tries to help him, the instinct is to fight it. But Zuko makes himself nod, before heading out onto the streets of Ba Sing Se.

Zuko finds his way to the lower ring through the kindness of strangers. It’s getting easier to ask for help, and with the exception of one man who was probably in a rush, everyone he asks stops to show him the way. By the time he has made it to his destination, the sky is a burnt gold, and the shadows that fall from the surrounding buildings are stark.

Eventually, he stops having to ask. He hears the same word on the lips of every passerby, sees it in the smiles of the people who run down the street. Counterintuitively, Zuko finds himself slowing down as he walks. The more people who stream past him, the more he seems to linger in alcoves and look over his shoulder at the path behind him, as if pondering how long it would take him to retrace his steps.

By the time the shadows have grown so long that they bisect the roads like prison bars, Zuko finds himself in a square with a big fountain, surrounded on all sides by unlit lamps. There’s a large group of people gathered here, and the words on everyone’s lips have grown to a deafening whisper: *The Avatar is here, the Avatar has come* . Zuko comes to a complete stop hundreds of feet away, watching them all from a safe distance.

Everyone is crowded around one man, who is seated on the lip of the fountain. He inclines his head, blue arrow bared to the crowd, listening thoughtfully to a girl who looks to be only seven or eight years old. When she has finished, the man nods, then stands. The whole crowd seems to shift in response to his movement. Even the crowd’s breath is in sync as he goes to light one of the lamps on the outer edges of the square.

Zuko’s heart trembles in his chest. He watches from a distance, not wanting to make himself known, somewhat ducking behind the others in the crowd. He has shaded himself from Aang’s view as he moves to each lantern and lights it with bending alone, illuminating the awed smiles of the people who have gathered to meet the Avatar. Again, Zuko is stunned to see so many people grateful to witness firebending.

As Aang draws close, Zuko can’t resist the fear that draws him further backwards, behind the other members of the crowd. He cannot bear to see Aang’s eyes slide unknowingly over him, so - so he’ll make it less painful by giving him no choice. If he isn’t even in the front row of people, Aang won’t be able to help not spotting him. It won’t hurt as terribly.

Aang steps up to light a lamp mere feet away from Zuko, and Zuko steps backwards into the empty space behind him. Then steps back further. And further. Zuko can feel the call to run, and steels himself to disappear into the farthest reaches of the shadows, where the light of the lamps won’t touch.

The lamp isn’t even illuminated yet when Aang’s hand seems to pause in mid-air. He looks up, staring into the crowd, his slightest movement forward drawing everyone but Zuko towards him for one desperate moment. But he raises a hand, murmurs, “Excuse me,” and the crowd obediently parts, and suddenly there is no one in between them, and Aang is looking right at Zuko.

For an instant, Zuko could mistake the look he sees in Aang’s eyes for something far less charitable. But then Aang is rushing towards him, the long orange sleeves of his robes flapping in the wind as he says, “It’s really *you* , isn’t it? I felt your chi, and I thought it couldn’t possibly - but it *is* you!”

And really, how is Zuko supposed to refuse the Avatar himself, when he all but flies into his arms? Zuko cannot believe how he had forgotten this, the way Aang’s head slots over his when they embrace, how it feels to bury his face against the other young man’s chest and smell, ever so faintly, the barest, most private hint of pheromones. He doesn’t know how to describe it, except to say that Aang smells as clean as the sea air, as calming as the trees after a heavy rain.

They pull away enough to gaze into one another’s faces without breaking their embrace. Aang’s hand comes up to trace Zuko’s scar, his expression wrought.

“I should have stayed,” he says. “I should have protected you.”

Zuko shakes his head gently enough to avoid dislodging Aang’s hand. “The price of this was protecting *you* . I’d pay it a thousand times over again.”

The look in Aang’s eyes is terribly sad. “I wouldn’t ever ask that of you. If you ever suffer like that on my behalf again, it’ll kill me.” His hand moves to cradle the back of Zuko’s head instead. “Are you really here with me? Can we be together for good, this time?”

And Zuko has to blink back tears. “If you’ll have me. I-I know the scar is awful, and you aren’t obligated to look past it.”

Aang shakes his head, and it’s puzzling, how his gaze can be so hard and so full of love at the same time. “I don’t care. I want you.”

“But Aang…”

While he can certainly feel it pressed against him, Zuko wrests one of Aang’s hands in his and presses it against his stomach, just in time to feel the kick inside.

“I’m sorry I didn’t tell you sooner,” Zuko whispers, eyes lowered in shame. “I was just - I was so afraid of what you’d say. You’re well within your rights to reject me. You didn’t sign up for this. After all, it’s-”

“It’s mine,” Aang interrupts, pressing his forehead to Zuko’s. Their hands intertwine just below Zuko’s ribcage. “If *you’ll* have *me* , then I say it’s mine, it’s ours. I want a life with you, Zuko.”

And while every traumatized nerve in Zuko’s body begs him to fight this - to deny that Aang should love him, to push him away, to stop this love before it can start in earnest, before its end can really threaten to destroy him - he is also incredibly tired of running away from the things he really wants. It feels good in Aang’s arms, so Zuko stays there, and tilts his head up.

Aang captures his lips in a kiss before Zuko can even close the space. Their teeth click before their lips slot into place, the copper taste of a happy ending thrumming on both of their tongues. And when they part, and Zuko looks to the sea of faces around them, not a single person avoids his gaze. Instead they crowd to see the person who made the Avatar so happy.

---

Several months later, Azula finally arrives in Ba Sing Se under the cover of night. Overjoyed, her uncle sets about brewing her a pot of his finest tea. But before she even gets a chance to enjoy it, her brother is sitting across from her, grilling her on all that has happened since they last saw one another.

“What’s happened to Wei?” Zuko asks. “How has Kirachu recovered? And Ama - have you heard anything about him?”

Azula lances him with an exhausted look. “No ‘how are you, Azula?’ You don’t want to know how *I’ve* been doing, having to return to our father’s house?”

That reminder quiets him somewhat, so the only sound in the room is a gentle cooing, and the sound of Azula finally getting to sip her tea.

Zuko supposes he came in a little too eager. Since he came to Ba Sing Se, he has been thoroughly cut off from most news concerning the Fire Nation. Even news relevant to the war has been hard to come by, what with the withering vestiges of the Dai Li’s propaganda machine so used to blocking all outside information. Internal Fire Nation politics were altogether impossible to gather.

That being said. “It must’ve been hard to pretend things were the same with Father. He doesn’t have the same power over you.” This point is emphasized by a pitiful whine that emits from Zuko’s arms.

“In some ways,” Azula sighs. “In other ways, he’s just as capable as ever of wounding me. Half the time, the only thing that keeps me going is the reminder of the end we have planned.” She sets her cup down, empty but for a few damp remnants of leaves. “Anyway - aren’t you going to introduce me?”

“Oh, right. I guess you haven’t seen her yet.” Zuko leans forward so his sister can get a better look at the baby wriggling in his arms. “This is Izumi. Izumi, this is your aunt, Azula.”

Izumi stops fighting her bindings long enough to fix Azula with what can only be described as a bewildered look. Azula gives a breathy laugh in return. “She’s huge. What was *that* labor like?”

Zuko shoots her an irritated look, then pulls Izumi close to his chest again, as if to hide her from view. “She isn’t huge. She’s a normal-sized baby.”

“She looks like a butcher’s block.”

“What does that even *mean?* ”

“It’s a compliment! She’ll be strong!”

Over by the hearth, Iroh clears his throat. “Perhaps I can take my grand-niece to bed, while the two of you catch up?”

They acquiesce. Zuko’s moody pout turns to a soft smile when he pulls Izumi into a quick good-bye, before handing her over to Iroh. She fusses a little, tiny fists swinging in the air, but it’s hard to resist Uncle Iroh’s soothing humming. By the time he has made his way out of the kitchen, the tiny cries have all but disappeared.

“To answer your first question,” Azula starts, somehow wrenching her brother’s devoted gaze from the doorway, “our father wasn't terribly happy with how he handled things with Zhao, so Wei is locked away beneath Caldera. I’ve tried to get my contact in the dungeons to talk to him, but no dice.”

“Maybe if we got the White Lotus’s help to break him out,” Zuko muses.

Azula’s expression is positively withering. “The White Lotus wants absolutely nothing to do with Wei. He got a major sect annihilated.”

“But he *saved* me.”

Azula scoffs. “He didn’t save Piandao, though. At best, the White Lotus is willing to look the other way if Wei happens to escape, but we’re not getting their help on this. Besides; half the problem is that he doesn’t *want* to leave.”

Zuko frowns. “I thought you said you couldn’t get in contact?”

“No, I said it was fruitless. No matter how hard we try to engage, Wei ignores us. He only responded once, and that was to say, ‘Let me be.’” Her deep-voiced, toneless impression of Wei has the perfect touch of wistfulness. Zuko would laugh if he wasn’t so disappointed by what she said.

Zuko gazes at the kitchen window. In the dark, he can see the twinkling lights of Ba Sing Se’s lower district. “Why would he want to stay imprisoned?”

Azula shrugs, her expression flat, lacking sympathy. “A good dog doesn’t protest its punishment. He’s probably just lying down and accepting whatever fate our father hands him.”

That doesn’t entirely make sense. Why, then, would Wei help Zuko escape execution? Zuko searches his mind for answers, and the only one that fits is that Wei is, in fact, accepting the punishment. But perhaps not out of any slavish devotion to their father. Zuko remembers Wei’s anguish at losing Yan, and wonders to what extent Wei blames himself for everything that happened to him.

“Fine. I’ll drop it for now, at least. Maybe we’ll get through to him when it’s all over and done with. How’s the rest of Kirachu?”

The damage from the fire Zuko had started was overblown by Zhao in a bid to get more funding for the island. While the fire had taken out a few miles of forest, no one had been hurt, and only one building on the edge of the village had been destroyed. Many of the trees had already begun to flourish again, filling in the charred dead space. It was all thanks to the recovery efforts of their new governor - a pencil-pusher whose name Zuko didn’t even recognize.
